docs.title: Build modular economics.
docs.text: A declarative, modular and machine verifiable language system for dynamic economics.

docs.title: About us
docs.text: Project Bellman is an Econ-ARK project for making economic models easier to express, inspect and reuse.

docs.title: 1 The project
docs.text:
Our aim is to keep an economic model understandable as it grows. In Bellman-SYM, a stage is one self-contained decision problem. Stages can be connected to form a model, while parameter values and numerical methods are specified separately.

We develop the language, its mathematical foundations and worked examples together. The model's equations and structure remain available for people and software to inspect.

Read the overview, explore a worked model, or follow the mathematical foundations.

docs.title: 2 People and support
docs.text:
The project's authors are Christopher Carroll, Alan Lujan and Akshay Shanker.

Project Bellman is part of Econ-ARK and is supported by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Meet the wider Econ-ARK team.

docs.title: 3 Take part
docs.text:
Questions, corrections and contributions to the code, documentation and examples are welcome on GitHub. To report a problem or suggest an improvement, open an issue. For a model example, include the equations and the behaviour you expect.

The software is available under the Apache License 2.0.

docs.title: Bellman-SYM
docs.text:
Summary

Write a household's consumption problem in .bl, inspect its equations, then separate consumption, discounting, and investment into reusable stages. YAML supplies their connections, numerical choices, and parameter values. This guide covers authoring, assembly, inspection, and the Python interfaces; Bellman calculus develops the mathematical foundations.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Overview: the stage, its perches and fields, and the joining of stages into periods and a trellis, in prose. Used by — Stages: the complete income-and-consumption tutorial. Formal account — Bellman calculus: staged Bellman problems and their mathematical interpretation.

docs.title: 1 Reading order
docs.text:
Begin with the buffer-stock consumption tutorial. The household observes income, consumes from its available resources, and saves without borrowing. A stage is a module of that decision problem with three information sets, its perches: arrival, decision and continuation. The later examples reuse consumption as a separate stage and join it to discounting and investment.

Step Read What to establish Write a stage Stages The household's information, admissible choices, resource transitions, and value equations. Inspect its meaning From syntax to a mathematical problem, then the API The same equations with explicit state arguments and their required assumptions. Reuse and compose Field equations, Periods, and Trellises Separate consumption, discounting, and investment; choose the period boundary and terminal inputs. Choose methods and parameters Methodization and The Bellman factory Numerical choices and economic parameter values for each use of a stage. Keep numerical results Solutions at the perches Where a solver keeps what it computes: one plain dictionary for each stage occurrence, keyed by perch and by field, filled by the stage's compiled kernels. Examine a numerical application the lesson tutorials/models/cons-port/03-solving-the-two-orders.ipynb of the repository The portfolio–consumption model solved in both orders of its stages and the consumption rules and risky shares compared.

The lesson solves with the model's own numerical tool; parsing or constructing a stage solves nothing. A stage occurrence is one use of a stage file at one position of a period. Each stage occurrence can have its own parameter values and numerical settings. Construction and specification prepare stage occurrences; solving additionally requires numerical routines and continuation or terminal data.

For discrete alternatives, read Branching, which uses the separate work-or-retire example. Choosing a continuous portfolio share is not a discrete branch.

For data indexed by a parameter-defined number of cities or shock outcomes, see Indexed data. For an integer state whose values mean, for example, newborn or old, see Category codes; Periods explains how connections preserve those meanings.

docs.title: 2 Files and authoring reference
docs.text:
File Contents Guide .bl Stage declarations, functions, shock laws, and equations. Stages and Field equations. Period and trellis YAML Stage occurrences and compatible field connections. Periods and Trellises. Methods file (.bl), with the settings and calibration YAML The methods, grids and handlers typed at the places of a stage, the settings they read and the economic parameter values. Methodization. Specification-recipe YAML Which sources supply methods, settings and calibration, their precedence, and period-dependent assignments. The Bellman factory.

For individual spellings, use Equation parsing rules, Perch tagging rules, Constraints for bounds and the complementary-slackness clause, Expression forms, Shock distributions, Method types, and Symbol conventions. Operations lists the kinds of operation of which a builder, the operator a block of a stage file defines, is composed, and Refusals the rules under which a stage file, an entry of a methods file or a model's files are refused. The model directory layout describes the files of a model and where each is kept.

docs.title: 3 Inspection and Python interfaces
docs.text:
Inspection is part of using Bellman-SYM. The API lists every function in three tables, one for each of bellman.stage, bellman.period and bellman.trellis, and every path of the stage object in a fourth, and its pages take the object one level at a time, from the stage to the binding verbs: the mathematical structure a constructed stage retains, its equations, its typed quantities and its numerical attachments. The factories load and specify those stages:

Page Responsibility The factory API The fourteen functions of the Bellman factory and the page that states each. Stage functions Load a stage file into a record, elaborate it, and bind one stage. Recipe functions Read a registry through its recipe: the merge, the slots and the fills. Period functions Append a period, derive the order of its stages from their fields, and make the drawing of the period. The trellis factory Read a trellis file, elaborate and bind every period, and make the drawing of the trellis.

For a new stage occurrence, loading and elaboration come first, then calibration, methodization and configuration, the order the factory uses. Each of the three bindings adds its binding to the stage occurrence it is called on and returns that stage; methodization must precede configuration, since the methods name the settings (Methodization §5). Inspecting the equations and attachments is separate from obtaining numerical policies.

docs.title: 4 Mathematical reference
docs.text:
The Bellman calculus guide explains the mathematical foundations. Within this language guide, Appendix C gives rules R1–R12 for interpreting equations, including the assumptions for representing fields as functions of states. Appendix D explains computation boundaries, collection selection, and implicit policy relations.

Folded abstract-grammar boxes use ASDL, a notation describing syntax-tree structure. Their constructor listings do not prove the economic assumptions needed for an equation's interpretation. The concept wiki defines recurring terms.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
Summary

Write a household's consumption problem in a .bl file. Declare what the household knows, what it chooses, and which equations determine resources, savings, and value. The example includes income risk and a borrowing constraint. Further examples declare indexed city data and integer states with recorded category meanings.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the stage, its perches and its fields in prose, on a buffer-stock model like this page's. Used by — Field equations: consumption as a separate stage file and its first-order equations; Periods: joining stages. Formal account — Appendix C: conditions for interpreting fields as functions of states.

docs.title: 1 Stages and perches
docs.text:
A household begins with nonnegative assets b, earns the gross return R, and observes positive income y. It chooses consumption c from resources w = R*b + y and retains savings a = w-c. Consumption must be strictly positive and savings nonnegative, so the feasible choices satisfy \(0<c\leq w\).

A stage is a module of a Bellman problem with three information sets, called perches. In this example they distinguish income arriving, consumption being chosen, and savings being available for continuation:

Perch What the household knows State used in this example Arrival Beginning assets, before the current income draw. b, beginning assets. Decision Beginning assets and realized income; consumption is chosen here. w, resources available to consume or save. Continuation The consumption choice and the resulting savings. a, savings available for the future.

A state summarizes the information needed for the remaining problem. We assume resources suffice for the consumption decision and savings suffice for continuation value. The household may remember more than these scalar states record; the perch describes its information, whereas the state supplies the arguments of its value function. These sufficiency assumptions are part of the economic model, not consequences of the notation.

docs.title: 2 Declarations and types
docs.text:
A declaration is a name, a colon and a type. The type says what the name may denote: a set of admissible values, called its declared set, a role in the decision problem, an information set, or a combination of these. The complete file in §4 declares a parameter, a shock, a control and a value this way:

β : (0,1)
y : ℝ₊₊
c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl
V : ℝ @ !vlu

A type is a list of components, written with @ between them. A component is either a set, written in mathematical notation, or a word with the prefix !. The components are unordered, so c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl and c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊ declare the same type. A type names at most one role and one perch: two different role words are refused under one-name-one-meaning, two different perch words under field-perch, and a word written twice is read once. A perch word is written only in a block's header: a top-level declaration, which stands on a line of its own outside the blocks, is refused under field-perch when it carries one. Several sets in one type declare their intersection: the declared name lies in each of them, as in β : (0,1) @ (0, R^(ρ-1)) (Symbols and conventions §9.2). Several sets are read on a top-level declaration of one name, and at most one of them may be other than an interval written out with its endpoints, such as (0,1) or [1, inf); a set named by a definition counts as not an interval. The one set that is not an interval is a set of numbers, so x : ℝ × ℝ @ (0,1) is refused under syntax. Two equal sets are read as one, and two intervals with no number in common, such as (0,1) @ (2,3), are refused under syntax. A name listed in a block's header carries one set, and several sets there are refused under readable-form. The sign @ stands between descriptions of one quantity; it never multiplies sets. A quantity valued in a product is declared with × inside its set, as x : ℝ × ℝ. The prefix is what marks a vocabulary word, so a bare word is always a name and no word is reserved.

Word What it says !arvl, !dcsn, !cntn The name belongs to the arrival, the decision or the continuation perch. !ctrl The name is a control, chosen at decision. !vlu The name is a value. !shck The name is a shock; a restatement where the name has a law, since the law makes the name a shock. !state The name is a state; a restatement, since a name with a set and a perch and no role word is a state. !node Written in a statement's annotation, not after a colon: the statement is a separately inspectable computation (Appendix D).

Parameters carry a set and neither a role nor a perch, as R : ℝ₊₊. States are declared with a set alone; their role is derived. A value carries its role word !vlu, and the control carries !ctrl. A marginal value is no field and has no role word: the derivative of a value is read where a line needs it, by the term D_{a}V[>], the derivative of the continuation value in the continuation coordinate a (Field equations §2).

A field name is local to the stage occurrence that declares it. Another stage may use the same spelling for a different field, and a matching name does not by itself connect the stages. All branches of one stage share its declarations, so separate branch states need separate names. A parameter has different scope: a name declared by two stages in one period denotes one period parameter, with one compatible declaration and one value; the same name in another period denotes another parameter. Fields and Parameters give these distinctions.

The colon binds to the smallest complete object on its left. In (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) the type belongs to c alone, and w is a reference to an earlier declaration. Parentheses make several names one object: (w, c) : S declares two names when S is a product with one factor per name, written out or defined by name, and each name lies in its own factor, so that (w, c) : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊₊ places w in ℝ₊ and c in ℝ₊₊. A set that is not such a product is refused under readable-form, and a feasibility constraint that couples a control with other names is written on the binder of the maximization (Constraints §1). Tuples nest inside a tuple, in a declaration and on a side of a block signature, as in ((k, h) : K, y) : !arvl with K a product of two factors, and an argument of a function is a single name. In a top-level declaration, a name inside a nested tuple is a parameter when no block's header lists it, like a name of a flat tuple. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). A tuple of two names and one name valued in a product are different declarations: (w, c) : ℝ × ℝ declares two names, each in ℝ, whereas x : ℝ × ℝ declares one name whose components are selected as x[1] and x[2] (Equation parsing rules).

A law is not a type. A shock's distribution is an object, like the number 0.96, and two shocks with the same distribution are not interchangeable, so the distribution is assigned on its own line with ~, before or after the line that declares the shock's set:

y : ℝ₊₊
y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y)

The fused form y : ℝ₊₊ ~ LogNormal(…) is not admitted. The distribution declaration makes y a shock; !shck may restate that role on the line of its set, y : ℝ₊₊ @ !shck. A joint distribution takes a tuple subject, (Ψ, θ) ~ N(…). Separate declarations imply conditional independence given the source coordinates unless one names the other as an argument. The stage records this factorization as an assumption. Shock distributions lists the families a shock's distribution may take, LogNormal among them.

Block signatures are typed the same way. In [id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊, y) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn], the word after each parenthesized side names the perch of every coordinate listed on that side, with two exceptions: a shock listed on a side is an argument of the block's equations and belongs to no perch, and a control is at decision wherever it is listed. A backward block's header lists the value fields it reads and writes and the controls at which its lines are read, and no state: a state of the perch at which the block's output stands is a coordinate of that output, which a line reads without listing it, and a listed state is refused under header-coordinate. It lists no marginal value either: a line reads the derivative of a value the header lists by the term D_{a}V[>], and a line of a value builder's block may state the derivative of the value the block writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), with nothing listed for it (Field equations §2). A value field the header lists and no line of the block reads is admitted. Where a line of the block reads another listed value, the unread one is left out of the block's builder, and the elaboration records it as a diagnostic, the header lists V[>], which no line of the block reads, in place of a refusal. A block whose lines read none of its listed values keeps them all as the inputs of its builder and records no diagnostic.

A state or a value is placed at a perch by each of its listings: by the perch word of the side, by a perch word in its own type, or by its mark [<] or [>]. Where a listing carries two of these they agree, and a disagreement is refused under field-perch. The same name listed at another perch is another field with its own set, as a at arrival and a[>] at continuation in the portfolio application's disc.bl. Where one name stands at both the arrival and the continuation perch, a line of a backward block names either state with its mark, a[<] or a[>]; the bare name there is refused under name-in-scope. A field's set may be written at any of its occurrences, in a top-level declaration or on a side, and several occurrences that write a set declare their intersection (Appendix C §2.4). With w : ℝ₊₊ on the side that writes w and w : ℝ₊ on a side that reads it, w lies in ℝ₊₊. The other direction, ℝ₊ written and ℝ₊₊ read, is refused under set-mismatch, because the set written where a block writes a field must lie in the set written where another block reads it. The package does not yet check this where it cannot compare the two sets, as with an endpoint that names a parameter (Appendix C §5.3). Every field, a shock included, has a declared set. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). The sets written for a field at several occurrences have a value in common. The package does not yet check this, except between a block that writes the field and a block that reads it (Appendix C §5.3). A side may omit its perch word only when every coordinate on it is a shock, a control, or carries its own perch word or the mark [<] or [>], as the output side of the portfolio application's policy signature (V[>]) : !cntn -> ς does. On a side without a perch word, a field that an earlier side placed must still carry its own perch word or its mark [<] or [>], so a perch is never guessed. Perch tagging rules gives the information-set reading of these rules.

Definitions and binders use the same colon. A named set is defined with :=, as Xa := ℝ₊ or Xa := [0, ā]. A function is defined with typed arguments, 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ), whose c is local to the definition and is not the stage's control. A definition without arguments whose right side is arithmetic in the parameters, h := 1/(1 - Γ/R), or is written by cases (Equation parsing rules §2), defines a derived parameter: calibration computes its value from the definition and refuses a value supplied for it (Parameters). The definition may declare the set its value lies in, as h : ℝ₊₊ := 1/(1 - Γ/R), and calibration then refuses values of the parameters at which the computed value lies outside that set. The set is written on the line of the definition: h : ℝ₊₊ on a line of its own beside h := 1/(1 - Γ/R) is refused under one-name-one-meaning. Similarly, the binder of a maximization ranges over a feasible set written after a colon, argmax_{c : Γ(w)}(…), with the bare binder argmax_{c} when the control's declared set is its feasible set (Constraints).

A parameter's set may be a union or a difference of sets of numbers. The union is written A \/ B and the difference A \ B. ρ : (0,1) \/ (1, inf) declares a risk aversion that is positive and is not one: a value lies in a union when it lies in at least one of its members. ρ : ℝ₊₊ \ {1} declares the same set as a difference: a value lies in a difference when it lies in the left set and outside the right. The signs ∪ and ∖ are second spellings of the two. A union or a difference is read in the declared set of a parameter, of a derived parameter and of a setting, which a methods file declares with its set (Methodization §4). It is refused in the set of a field, of a shock and of a function's argument, and it is not read after :=, in the definition of a named set or of a function. Types lists the role words, the perch words, the reserved sets, the forms a set may take and the limits on them.

These sets describe admissible economic values. A numerical grid used to approximate a continuous domain is written separately, in the methods file (Methodization §3.2).

The complete file uses the following spellings:

Spelling What the modeller states R : ℝ₊₊ The gross return is a strictly positive parameter. c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl Consumption is a strictly positive decision control. V : ℝ @ !vlu V is a real-valued value field. 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ) Utility is a function of positive consumption. a = w - c Savings equal resources less consumption. y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y) The separately declared income shock has the specified law. :: [id=savings] The equation has the address savings within its block.

Thus : declares a type, @ stands between its components, := defines, = states an equation, ~ supplies a shock distribution, and -> separates the two sides of a block signature. @ appears in one other place, at the start of a metadata line @key: value. The line @stage: buffer_stock names the stage, and a line with another key, such as @author: someone, is kept in stage.metadata (The stage §2). Each key is written once.

The file declares the discount factor β between zero and one and risk aversion ρ greater than one. For example, ρ = 2 gives utility \(u(c)=-1/c\), finite on positive consumption. This example excludes unit risk aversion, where the displayed formula would divide by zero. The income convention is explicit: conditional on arrival information, log income is normal with mean μ_y and standard deviation σ_y. This conditional distribution is constant given that information, so current income is independent of earlier observations. Positive income ensures positive resources even at zero beginning assets. A zero standard deviation gives deterministic positive income.

docs.title: 2.1 Indexed data
docs.text:
For a household choosing among J cities, the number of cities can remain a parameter when the stage is written. Declare the city set and the data indexed by it:

J : ℤ @ [1, inf)
L_J := {1, …, J}
δ : L_J → ℝ
dist : L_J × L_J → ℝ₊

The collection δ supplies one payoff per city, and dist supplies one distance per ordered pair of cities. If the current city is declared as a state i : L_J and the destination as a control j : L_J @ !ctrl, an equation reads their entries as δ[j] and dist[j][i]. Their use as indices does not determine their economic roles: i records the current location, j is chosen, and J determines the size of the common domain.

Every destination leads to the same successor stage, so the choice is one block and not a branching stage: [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (i_d, j : !ctrl @ L_J) : !dcsn -> (i_n : L_J) : !cntn] { i_n = j } retains the chosen city as the integer continuation state, and the number of cities stays the parameter J.

A numerical key must be integer-valued, including when a parameter determines it. A listed set such as S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ is also admitted, with an integer-valued parameter θ; its keys need not be consecutive. By contrast, entries such as payoffs, distances and wages may be real-valued. In q[s] with s : S_θ, the value of s identifies a key; it is not a position in the list supplied at calibration. Positions counted from one select components of a fixed tuple, as in x[1] and x[2] for x : ℝ × ℝ.

Calibration supplies the values of J, δ and dist, checking the integer bounds and the number and domains of their entries. A different J uses the same stage declaration with correspondingly sized data. Symbol conventions §9.2.1 gives the admitted index sets, data order and a calibration example. Each index's declared domain must fit the corresponding table domain: a state ranging over cities and an outside option cannot directly select from a table defined only on cities (Appendix D §5.2).

docs.title: 2.2 Category codes
docs.text:
A household's status can be an integer state whose codes have recorded meanings. Define the set and give each member a category name:

HouseholdStatus := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=1]
n : HouseholdStatus

The expression between braces is a comprehension: it contains the integers satisfying every condition after |, with i local to that definition. The annotation assigns the name newborn to 0 and old to 1. A state declared on HouseholdStatus therefore takes integer values, while the stage retains the correspondence between those values and their meanings. Recording categories does not create a branching stage; the blocks still specify the state transitions and any choices.

Equations use the codes. For example, a transition to old age is written n_next = 1, with n_next also declared on HouseholdStatus; writing n_next = old is refused because the annotation does not declare old as a name usable in equations. Ordinary arithmetic remains available, so 100 - 120*n equals 100 for a newborn household and −20 for an old one. With three or more categories, using an affine formula in the code imposes equal steps in that formula; assigning codes alone supplies no distance between categories.

The marked set must have a nonempty integer range bounded by literal inequalities, with exactly one name per code and one code per name. Use the shared identifier household_status when these meanings are used across stage files; Periods §2 explains how connections check them. The complete annotation rules and the distinction from collection index sets are in Symbol conventions §9.2.2.

docs.title: 3 Builder blocks
docs.text:
A field is a quantity interpreted in its declared information set. A block groups equations between declared inputs and outputs. These two blocks, taken from the complete file in §4, express the household's budget:

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊, y) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    w = R*b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = w - c                    :: [id=savings]
}

Read the first signature from left to right: beginning assets and the income shock determine decision resources. Here ℝ₊ means nonnegative real numbers and ℝ₊₊ means strictly positive real numbers. Income and the return parameter are declared elsewhere in the same file. The second signature declares c as a control, a quantity the household chooses at decision, and a as nonnegative continuation savings. Its equation and domains jointly impose the borrowing constraint; the maximization in §4 ranges over these feasible choices.

The words !arvl, !dcsn, and !cntn identify the three information sets, the perches. A shock listed on a signature side is an argument of the transition: listing y on the arrival side does not say that income has already been observed. Similarly, a control retains its decision role when a later block lists it with continuation inputs. Perch tagging rules explains both exceptions.

The identifiers arvl_to_dcsn, resources, and savings supply addresses for inspection and supported numerical methods. Their names do not supply mathematical equations. Renaming resources consistently changes its address but preserves w = R*b + y.

docs.title: 4 A complete stage file
docs.text:
Save this source as buffer_stock.bl. The final three blocks add current utility to continuation value, average over income before it is observed, and choose a feasible consumption maximizer:

@stage: buffer_stock

β : (0,1)
ρ : (1, inf)
R : ℝ₊₊
μ_y : ℝ
σ_y : ℝ₊
y : ℝ₊₊
y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y)

𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊, y) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    w = R*b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = w - c                    :: [id=savings]
}
[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]            :: [id=value]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = E_{y}(V)              :: [id=value]
}
[id=policy, (V[>]) : !cntn -> (c) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>]) :: [id=choice]
}

Here V[>] is the continuation-value input, V is decision value, and V[<] is arrival value. [<] and [>] select the stage's information sets; they do not mean the preceding and following calendar periods. A bare field or [~] uses the decision interpretation when its declaration and equation context establish it, as for V here. An ordinary collection selection such as q[a] has a different meaning from evaluating a function at q(a); see Equation parsing rules.

The continuation input is a function \(W:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) of savings, supplied by the next period or a terminal boundary. For a given feasible consumption choice, the value equation represents

\[ Q(w,c)=u(c)+\beta W(w-c). \]

The policy block chooses \(\pi(w)\in\arg\max_{0<c\leq w}Q(w,c)\), and decision value is \(v(w)=Q(w,\pi(w))\). Before income is observed, arrival value is \(B(b)=\int v(Rb+y)\,\nu_y(dy)\), where \(\nu_y\) is the specified income distribution. The expectation therefore uses the policy selected after income is observed. Setting \(W=B\) would be an additional stationary-model condition; the stage does not impose it.

Assume \(W\) is finite and continuous on every compact savings interval and select a measurable maximizer. The maximum is attained because utility tends to minus infinity at zero consumption while continuation value is bounded on the feasible savings interval. Concavity of \(W\) makes the consumption maximizer unique. The arrival equation additionally requires \(\int|v(Rb+y)|\,\nu_y(dy)<\infty\); bounded continuous \(W\) is a sufficient case under this lognormal distribution. Appendix C R5–R8 gives the state-representation, integration, and policy conditions.

This documentation example modifies the repository's applications/consumption-savings-iid/declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.bl: it uses wholly positive income, restricts the discount factor to (0,1), and states the choice by the maximization alone, as that application's stage file also does, over its declared feasible set Γ(w) = (0, w]; the application writes the candidate lines of the endogenous grid method and the derivative lines of its values in its methods file, methods.bl beside the stage file (Methodization). The displayed source is the example taught here; it does not certify the different application source.

docs.title: 5 Files and next steps
docs.text:
The stage file states the model equations. To solve a finite-horizon problem, supply continuation and terminal values, methods, settings, and calibration. The methods file is written in the same language, beside the stage file; the settings and calibration files are YAML. Field equations separates consumption from income and discounting so that these stage files can be joined in a period.

A block is the authored typed group of equations between declared inputs and outputs, and a builder is the operator that block defines: a transition, a value calculation, or a policy relation. The builder keeps the block's id as its name, and a reader reaches it in the elaborated stage by the pair of perches its block joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] for the block cntn_to_dcsn, the policy builder by its own key, stage.builder["policy"], or from a perch, which reaches the builders of the edge that leaves it, the step from that perch to the next: stage.dcsn.builder.bwd is the same builder, which constructs the value at the decision perch, stage.arvl.builder.bwd the builder of dcsn_to_arvl, and stage.dcsn.builder.policy that of policy. The backward builders used in solution form the graph stage.builder.bwd, and the forward ones used in simulation the graph stage.builder.fwd (The builders graphs §§1 to 3). To make one equation separately inspectable, add !node to its annotation; Field equations demonstrates this with savings. Neither a block's name nor a numerical-method choice supplies a missing equation.

For loading, use the factory API, and for inspection the API. The stage retains interpreted equations and definitions in a graph of mathematical operations and their typed connections. With the required assumptions, its field equations can also be inspected as functions of states. Their mathematical relationship is described in Appendix C.

Technical details

.bl inherits its syntax from dynspec, an expression language. Parsing constructs a temporary abstract syntax tree, a structured representation of the written file. Checked interpretation constructs the stage's semgraph, the semantic graph of its equations, and discards that tree and its source spans.

Abstract grammar: FILE

This is a projection of the dynspec host grammar in ASDL, the notation for syntax-tree constructors. * means an ordered list and ? means optional. The omitted declaration alternative and the definitions of the referenced sorts belong to the full grammar; this projection does not redefine them.

file = FILE(item* items)
item = Metadata(identifier key, scalar value)
     | Statement(stmt core, annotation? annot)
     | Block(annotation tag, item* body)

Keys. items preserves source order; key and value give metadata; core is a statement with optional annot; tag is a block header and body its contents. These are ASDL fields, not YAML keys to write in a .bl file. scalar, stmt, and annotation are host sorts.

Head. Stage metadata identifies the stage file; the syntax-tree root remains FILE.

Denotes. Interpretation constructs the declared stage equations and their typed connections, subject to Appendix C.

Status. The three item constructors shown retain their argument order and multiplicity. Scope, type agreement, and complete output definitions are construction checks, not consequences of this grammar box.

docs.title: Field equations
docs.text:
Summary

Separate consumption from income and investment so that the same consumption module can be reused. Its equations state the borrowing constraint and the optimal choice. A later variant derives interior candidates from the derivative of the continuation value and explains the additional conditions needed by the endogenous grid method.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: consumption after income is observed, declarations, and information sets. Used by — Methodization: numerical methods for authored computations; Periods: joining consumption, discounting, and investment. Formal account — Appendix C: field and functional interpretation; Appendix D: computation boundaries and indexing.

docs.title: 1 Consumption and savings
docs.text:
The household now enters the consumption stage with observed positive resources m. Resources do not change before its consumption decision, so the decision state is m_d = m. Consumption c leaves savings a = m_d-c, subject to \(0<c\leq m_d\). A field is a quantity interpreted in its declared information set; the signatures place resources at arrival and decision, the control at decision, and savings at continuation.

Save the following complete source as cons.bl:

@stage: cons
ρ : (1, inf)
𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)
[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (m : ℝ₊₊) : !arvl -> (m_d : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    m_d = m
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m_d, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = m_d - c
}
[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + V[>]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V
}
[id=policy, (V[>]) : !cntn -> (c) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + V[>])
}

V[>] denotes the continuation-value field, which a supplied function \(H:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) of savings represents. Holding consumption fixed, the backward block denotes the choice value, the objective before a policy is substituted:

\[ Q(m_d,c)=u(c)+H(m_d-c). \]

The policy block selects \(\pi(m_d)\in\arg\max_{0<c\leq m_d}Q(m_d,c)\), giving optimized value \(v(m_d)=Q(m_d,\pi(m_d))\). Because arrival resources already contain the information needed for this decision, arrival value equals \(v(m)\).

Assume \(H\) is finite and continuous on every compact savings interval and select a measurable maximizer. As in Stages, utility's limit at zero consumption gives attainment; concavity of \(H\) makes the maximizer unique. This value-only source includes zero savings and requires no positive continuation derivative. A constant terminal continuation is admissible and leads to consuming all resources.

There is no discount factor in this module. When it is joined to the separate discount stage, \(H\) already includes that stage's discounting. Periods supplies the discount and investment sources and explains their order. The earlier buffer_stock.bl combines income, consumption, and discounting in one stage; adding its discount factor again here would count it twice.

This source is a documentation variant of applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl: it excludes zero consumption and unit risk aversion and uses the constrained maximization as its operative line, the line the block computes with (Constraints §3), in place of the application's candidate line with its complementary-slackness clause, which §3 reads. A numerical solution also requires method choices, settings, and calibration, together with continuation and terminal inputs. The source does not choose those inputs.

docs.title: 2 Equations, definitions, and dependence
docs.text:
The := line defines utility as a function of its explicit argument. By contrast, a = m_d - c relates stage fields. When continuation value is represented as \(H(a)\), substituting the transition gives \(H(m_d-c)\), with consumption still free until the policy block selects it. This substitution uses the state-sufficiency assumptions in Appendix C R5–R7.

An alias is an explicit intermediate definition that can be substituted at its uses. Substitution preserves every declared output, the domains, and every free or bound dependency. The savings equation must continue to determine the output a even if its right side is substituted into a value calculation. The two-output example in Appendix D shows the same rule when a block promises two outputs: substituting one into the other does not delete either output.

The utility definition binds its argument c, a name local to the definition; argmax_{c} binds the control in its objective. A substitution must distinguish these scopes rather than identify variables solely by spelling. An implicit equation supplies a relation between unknowns and cannot be substituted as though it were an explicit alias.

A block identifier supplies an address, not a formula. The labels in §1 are descriptive conventions: typed signatures, economic roles, and equations identify what each block defines. Naming a block policy does not make an arbitrary equation an optimality condition.

A marginal value is the derivative of a value in a state coordinate of its perch. It is no field: a header lists value fields and controls alone, and a line reads the derivative where it needs it by the derivative term D_{a}V[>], the operator D applied to the value field written with its perch mark, the subscript naming a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark; D_{a}D_{a}V[>] is the second derivative. The term has this one spelling. It denotes a function of the value and no second object, so a block that reads it declares nothing about how the derivative is evaluated: that is a property of the value, fixed by the methods file of the stage that writes it (Methodization §5). A derivative line is a line of a value builder's block whose left side is a derivative term of the value the builder writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) in §3. It states the author's assertion that the derivative equals the right side, which holds under the envelope conditions, and it defines no new field. Such a line stands in the stage file, as in §3, or in the methods file beside it, in a block that names the value builder's block by its id (Methodization §1). The package never computes a derivative: it differentiates no value function, and a derivative that no line states and no representation evaluates is not part of the stage.

docs.title: 3 An implicit policy relation
docs.text:
The endogenous grid method calculates candidate consumption at given savings and then recovers the associated resources. To derive its interior equation from §1, assume \(H\) is differentiable at positive savings with finite strictly positive derivative. Differentiating the choice value with respect to consumption gives \(u'(c)-H'(m_d-c)\), so an interior optimum satisfies

\[ u'(c)=H'(m_d-c),\qquad f(a)=H'(a)^{-1/\rho},\qquad h(a)=a+f(a). \]

Here \(f(a)\) is candidate consumption and \(h(a)\) its resource coordinate. The source below includes zero savings, so also assume a finite strictly positive right derivative \(H'_+(0)\) and use it in \(f(0)\).

For this separate interior example, copy §1's source to cons_interior.bl and change its metadata to @stage: cons_interior. Keep the utility definition and both forward-transition blocks. Replace the three blocks cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, and policy by the following function definitions and blocks; the argmax policy from §1 is removed, not retained as a second policy:

𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ)             :: [id=marg_util]
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/ρ)        :: [id=inv_marg_util]

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V        = 𝑢(c) + V[>]          :: [id=value]
    D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                :: [id=marginal]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
}
[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])      :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]
}

The term D_{a}V[>] reads the derivative of the same continuation function \(H\) supplied through V[>]; how that derivative is evaluated was fixed where \(H\) was built, and this block declares nothing about it. The derivative line D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) states the derivative of the optimized value in cash on hand. Interpreting it so requires an optimal policy and the envelope conditions in Appendix C, R8, applied to consumption in §4.2 of that appendix; the stage lists the reading under marginal-reading and checks it against nothing. The arrival block writes no derivative line: its law between the perches is the identity, so the derivative of V passes through it to V[<]. If discounting is applied in another stage, both continuation value and its derivative must include it once.

At ρ = 2, marginal utility is \(1/c^2\) and its inverse on positive arguments is \(1/\sqrt{x}\). Their composition returns \(c\) for every positive \(c\). A constant continuation has derivative zero and is therefore outside this inverse-marginal example, although it is valid in §1.

The candidate fields c[>] and m_d[>] are represented by \(f(a)\) and \(h(a)\). Through the budget equation, the final line c = c[>] states the feasible relation

\[ \{(m_d,c):c=f(m_d-c),\ 0<c\leq m_d\}. \]

A relation is a set of state–control pairs. This relation defines a policy only where it determines one admissible control per resource state, or a suitable measurable selection is supplied. The equation neither instructs the program to copy an array nor establishes that an arbitrary root is optimal.

Elaboration keeps this division. The two explicit lines form one operation of the policy builder, an Aggregation keyed endoggrid:Aggregation, whose kernel, the map it applies at each saving, is \(G(w, a) = (w^{-1/\rho},\ a + w^{-1/\rho})\), with \(w\) the derivative of the continuation value at \(a\), which the term D_{a}V[>] reads. stage.dcsn.builder.policy['policy.endoggrid:Aggregation'].kernel() answers that map, and compile_kernel() compiles it, since 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is defined in closed form: the derivative term is one of the function's arguments (Expression forms §3). The policy builder is realized by a handler (Methodization §3.3). The last line forms the identification, a Pullback: the policy composed with the resource coordinate and equated to the candidate, \(\pi(h(a)) = f(a)\), which the policy builder's card prints as 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a), 𝑐 being the card's italic name for the policy. Its output is its own unknown, so it states a relation, which no query solves, and compile_kernel() refuses it. In applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, the methods file beside cons.bl, the first line of the block policy is the inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) with the clause ⟂ a >= 0; it forms an operation of its own, InvEuler:Aggregation, whose rule is the relation with its clause and whose kernel is its bound \(w^{-1/\rho}\), and the values the clause admits at zero saving give the policy's corner (Constraints §4.3). Neither form differentiates \(H\) or inverts marginal utility: the derivative is read by the term D_{a}V[>] and evaluated as the stage that built \(H\) fixed it, and the inverse is the definition 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣.

For a global optimality interpretation, assume concavity of \(H\) as well as the attainment conditions in §1. At the borrowing boundary \(a=0\), assume the finite right derivative \(H'_+(0)\) exists. Consuming all resources is optimal when

\[ u'(m_d)\geq H'_+(0). \]

The sign follows by differentiating with respect to savings: the derivative is \(-u'(m_d-a)+H'(a)\) and must be nonpositive at the left endpoint. Interior equality alone omits the cases with strict inequality. Thus cons_interior.bl states a candidate relation. A declaration of the full constrained policy writes the Kuhn–Tucker condition in one of its three spellings: the clause ⟂ m_d - c >= 0 on the decision-perch first-order condition, using the forward law a = m_d - c, a multiplier declared in the policy block, or the clause ⟂ a >= 0 on the continuation-marked candidate line written as the inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]), as applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, the methods file beside cons.bl, writes it (Constraints §4). The loading software reads that clause as the corner: at zero saving the candidate takes every value up to the interior value \(f(0)\), and the final line then gives consumption equal to cash on hand at every cash on hand up to \(f(0)\). A declaration may instead restrict the equality to its interior domain and separately state the borrowing-boundary branch, or retain the constrained maximization in §1. If a numerical method adds a boundary segment to the interior candidates, it must report that segment as an extension outside the authored equality. Attaching !egm does not declare the missing branch or establish global optimality; see Appendix C §4.5. The resulting policy must also cover the requested resource domain.

More generally, candidate controls \(U:S\to C\) and coordinates \(K:S\to X\) define pairs \((K(s),U(s))\), where \(S\) is the set that indexes the candidates, \(C\) the control domain, and \(X\) the state domain. They define one control on \(K(S)\) exactly when candidates with equal coordinates have equal controls. Measurability and coverage of the desired state domain are additional conditions. Appendix C R10 and R12 and Appendix D state these conditions without assuming every implicit relation is a function.

Interpolation may approximate candidate pairs on a numerical grid, with its interpolation and extrapolation assumptions stated. It does not add an equation to the model. An authored evaluate(knots, values, x) is a separate optional operation with declared arguments; choosing an endogenous-grid method creates neither that statement nor an automatic upper-envelope computation, which would compare competing candidates.

docs.title: 4 Statements and computation boundaries
docs.text:
In §1's dcsn_to_cntn block, replace the savings equation by:

a = m_d - c    :: [id=savings, !node]

The !node requests a computation boundary, a statement to inspect or realize as a unit. It preserves the budget equation and its output a. The marked statement's result is a function of its own in the constructed stage, one that the statements after it consume and that a numerical method can represent, by interpolation for instance; an unmarked intermediate quantity is substituted into the statements that use it and has no separate existence to which a method could attach. The block itself is authored, while subtraction or maximization inside an equation is a mathematical operation; nesting alone does not make it another authored !node place. Methodization describes which operations and boundaries support numerical methods.

A statement marked !doc contributes documentation and no defining equation. Removing an equation this way can change the model or leave an output undefined. Use the two marks separately: their combined meaning is not specified. An id without either mark supplies an address and changes neither the equation nor its mathematical status.

docs.title: 5 Expectations
docs.text:
The separate consumption module has no shock because resources are already observed. In the income-and-consumption stage, the backward equation V[<] = E_{y}(V) instead integrates decision value over income, conditional on arrival information. The income law is explicitly conditional and constant given earlier information; the expected value must be integrable. Income affects value through resources, so that dependence remains after the transition is substituted.

The scope of the expectation matters. E_{y}(V + y) integrates both terms; E_{y}(V) + y leaves the final shock outside the expectation. When income is unobserved at arrival, the latter cannot define arrival value. Equation parsing rules gives the function, law, and operator spellings; Perch tagging rules gives the information checks.

docs.title: Methodization
docs.text:
Summary

Methodization attaches numerical methods to the operators of a stage. The methods are written in the stage's methods file, a .bl file beside the stage file, whose blocks name the stage's blocks by their ids and add to them. Its entries give an operator a method and a grid, policy.method : !egm, and name the handler, the routine that carries the method out; the settings a method reads are declared in the same file with their sets and valued in a settings file. Typing a method adds no equation to the model: where a solution method brings lines of its own, the stage computes with them in place of the stage file's maximization and keeps the maximization as its statement of the choice.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and Field equations: the blocks, their ids and the derivative term that the entries and lines of a methods file refer to. Formal account — Methods: the method and the grid as components of an operator's signature, the grid as a discretized domain, the two erasures and the two levels; Appendix C R10 and §4.6: the reading of a solution method's lines. Used by — Trellises and The Bellman factory: the methods files a recipe names for each use of a stage; Methods and places and Parameters and settings: what the stage object answers about its methods and its settings. See also — Method types: every method word with the keyword arguments the package reads; the wiki entries methods, grid, addition, settings and handler.

Key terminology Term Meaning Operator One computation of a stage: a builder, the operator a block denotes; an operation inside it, such as an expectation or a maximization; or the Evaluation that stores a builder's result. Place and path A place is an operator that a methods file can name; its path is the name the file writes for it, such as policy, dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ or policy.evaluate (§2). Typing entry A line <path>.method : …, <path>.grid : … or <path>.handler : … that gives the operator at a path its method, its grid or its handler (§3). Method The numerical procedure chosen for one operator, named by a word and, where it takes options, the named options in parentheses, its keyword arguments: !egm, !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes) (wiki). Grid The finite set of points at which a function is computed and stored, written by one of three constructors: !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), one factor per coordinate; !Points(nodes=P), a finite set of declared points; or !Fibred(base=…, fibre=…), the feasible controls at each state of a base grid (§3.2; wiki). Handler The routine outside the language that carries a method out, named by a quoted string, "cons-port:egm" (wiki). Representation A method that stores a function from the data its place supplies and gives the function's values between those data: !Linear, piecewise linear interpolation; !pchip, piecewise cubic interpolation that keeps the monotonicity of the stored values; or !closed_form, the function's authored expression (§3.4). Data source The data a representation is built from, decided by its place: an authored table, the policy pairs that the endogenous grid method computes, a complete authored expression, or the values of the function at the points of the representation's own grid (§3.4). Solution method A method typed at a builder that says how the builder's output is computed: !egm, the endogenous grid method, brings the lines by which the policy is computed; !vfi, value function iteration, brings none; and !explicit reads the lines of its block, which define each output by an expression (§3.5). Setting A value a method reads, such as a grid's bounds and count or a node count, declared in the methods file with its set and valued in the settings file (wiki). Addition A methods file, so called because the package forms the union of its items with the stage file's items and removes nothing (wiki). Declared level, operative level The builders as the stage file states them, which stage.declared holds, and the builders the stage computes with, which stage.builder holds and in which a solution method's lines stand in place of the stage file's lines (§5). Derivative term, derivative line D_{a}V[>], the derivative of a value in a state coordinate of its perch, read where a line needs it; and a line whose left side is such a term, which states that derivative (Field equations §2).

docs.title: 1 A methods file beside its stage file
docs.text:
The buffer-stock stage, applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl, states the model and nothing about its computation. The household arrives with assets k. The permanent and transitory income shocks ψ and ξ then give its resources, m = R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ, from which it chooses consumption c and saves a = m - c; Γ is the growth factor of permanent income, and Γ_c(m) the set of feasible consumption levels. Its two value blocks and its policy block are:

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]               :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}((Γ*ψ)^(1-ρ) * V)     :: [id=value]
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{cp : Γ_c(m)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>])     :: [id=optimality]
}

Each block opens with a bracket that holds its id and its signature: the fields the block reads, an arrow and the fields it writes, each side followed by its perch, with @ !vlu marking a value and @ !ctrl a control (Stages §3). The mark after a field names its perch: V[>] is the value at the continuation perch, after the choice; V the value at the decision perch; and V[<] the value at the arrival perch, before the shocks are drawn. The policy block states the choice as a maximization over Γ_c(m), and the stage file writes no derivative, no grid and no method.

The methods file, methods.bl in the same folder, chooses how the stage is computed: the endogenous grid method for the policy, on a grid of savings; linear interpolation of the consumption function and of the arrival value; Gauss–Hermite quadrature for the expectation over the two shocks; and the two derivative lines that the endogenous grid method reads. With its comment lines left out, each a line that begins with #, the file is:

@methods: buffer_stock

n_a : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]
a_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the savings grid"]
a_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the savings grid"]
n_k : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the asset grid"]
k_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the asset grid"]
k_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the asset grid"]
n_ψ_nodes : ℕ        :: ["quadrature nodes of the permanent shock"]
n_ξ_nodes : ℕ        :: ["quadrature nodes of the transitory shock"]

[id=policy, policy.method : !egm | policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
    | evaluate.method : !Linear] {
    c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>])       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m[>] = a + c[>]                 :: [id=g_cntn_to_dcsn]
    c[~] = c[>]                     :: [id=cons_choice]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn] {
    D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                                  :: [id=marginal]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl
    | E_ψ_ξ.method : !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes)
    | evaluate.method : !Linear
    | evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k))] {
    D_{k}V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}(R * (Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) * D_{m}V)    :: [id=marginal]
}

The file is read as follows.

  • @methods: buffer_stock names the stage the file adds to, by the name the stage file declares after @stage:; a file that names another stage is refused (metadata-mismatch).
  • The eight declarations are the settings the file reads, each with its set and a description, in the form in which a stage file declares a parameter (§4). A count is a natural number, n_a : ℕ, and a bound of a grid is a point of the set the stage declares for the coordinate, a_min : Xa.
  • The block [id=policy, …] names the stage's policy block by its id and adds to it. Its bracket holds the id and three typing entries: the first follows the id after a comma, and each of the other two stands in a group of its own, opened by |. policy.method : !egm gives the policy builder the endogenous grid method, and policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) the grid of savings on which the method computes, one factor keyed by the coordinate a, with its bounds and its count written as the names of settings. evaluate.method : !Linear, whose path is read relative to the block, types piecewise linear interpolation at the Evaluation that stores the consumption function; it interpolates the pairs of resources and consumption that the method computes, and so the block writes no grid for it (§3.4). The three lines of the block are the lines of the method: the consumption chosen at each saving, from the inverted Euler equation, c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>]); the resources at which that consumption is chosen, m[>] = a + c[>], which is the law of motion a = m - c solved for m; and the identification c[~] = c[>], which states that the policy at those resources is the candidate. c[~] is the field c with its decision mark written out, the same term as c, and the consumption stage of §2 writes the same line as c = c[>]. The stage computes with these three lines in place of the maximization, and it keeps the maximization as the policy builder it declares (§5).
  • The block [id=cntn_to_dcsn] adds one line to the decision value block, the envelope condition D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c): the derivative of the decision value in resources, which the arrival block of the same stage reads inside its expectation.
  • The block [id=dcsn_to_arvl …] writes its first entry in a group of its own, opened by | after the id, which is read as an entry after a comma is, and it adds three entries and one line to the arrival value block: Gauss–Hermite quadrature at the expectation E_ψ_ξ, with one node count for each shock; linear interpolation at the Evaluation that stores the arrival value and its derivative, on the grid of assets k; and the derivative line of the arrival value, whose factor R*(Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) inside the expectation comes from the law of motion m = R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ and from the normalization (Γ*ψ)^(1-ρ) of the value. The policy builder of the period before reads this derivative as D_{a}V[>], through the trellis's connection of its savings a to the assets k (Trellises §2.1).
  • The file types nothing at the decision builder's Evaluation, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate. An Evaluation without an entry holds no method, and the package refuses nothing there; the envelope condition gives the derivative of the decision value at any resources through the consumption function, which policy.evaluate represents.

The package reads a methods file only when it is given the file's path. load_stage(stage_path, [methods_path]) reads the stage file with the methods files its list names, methodize(methods_path) gives a stage already elaborated its methods file, or a list of them, as its whole selection, replacing any earlier one, by elaborating the stage anew from the stage file and the files together (§7; The binding verbs), and in a trellis the recipe names each stage's methods files (§6). stage.methods then lists each place at which a component is typed, with what is typed there, and the signature of a builder prints its method and its grid beside the functions it reads and writes:

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl",
                                   ["applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/methods.bl"]))
print(stage.methods)
print()
print(stage.builder.policy.signature())

dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ      !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes)
dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate   !Linear   !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k))
policy                  !egm   !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
policy.evaluate         !Linear

in         𝑉≻ : Xa → ℝ
out        𝑐(m) : 𝒫({c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊) | c(m) ∈ Γ_c(m)})
method     !egm
grid       !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))

The out line writes the policy builder's output as a set of feasible consumption functions, 𝒫(…), the set of the maximizing policies, since a maximization may have several (A builder §2). Configuration assigns the values of the settings file, applications/buffer-stock/declaration/settings/buffer_stock.yml, to the declared settings, and stage.settings then prints each setting with its set, its value, the place that reads it, the method there and, for a bound or a count of a grid, the grid's kind:

stage.configure("applications/buffer-stock/declaration/settings/buffer_stock.yml")
print(stage.settings)

name       set  value  read at                by              grid
n_a        ℕ    960    policy                 !egm            !Cartesian
a_min      Xa   0.001  policy                 !egm            !Cartesian
a_max      Xa   20.0   policy                 !egm            !Cartesian
n_k        ℕ    960    dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate  !Linear         !Cartesian
k_min      Xa   0.001  dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate  !Linear         !Cartesian
k_max      Xa   20.0   dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate  !Linear         !Cartesian
n_ψ_nodes  ℕ    7      dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ     !gauss_hermite
n_ξ_nodes  ℕ    7      dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ     !gauss_hermite

The package solves nothing. It records the methods, and a handler, a routine outside the language, carries each out (§3.3); the buffer-stock file names no handler, so the program that solves the model reads the words from stage.methods and supplies a routine for each. The buffer-stock example quotes the file with its comments and shows the same calls.

docs.title: 2 The places an entry names
docs.text:
Every entry of a methods file names an operator of the stage by its path, written before the component: <path>.method, <path>.grid or <path>.handler. stage.places() lists the places of a stage, each by its path in the column address, with its kind, and the kind decides which method words the package admits there (Methods and places §1):

Path Place Kind a block id, policy or cntn_to_dcsn the builder the block denotes builder a block id and evaluate, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate the Evaluation that stores the builder's result, where a representation is typed: one entry for everything the Evaluation stores, or one entry for each stored object, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate[V[<]] for the value and dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate[D_{k}V[<]] for the derivative a derivative line states; the policy builder's object is its policy, policy.evaluate[c] operator evaluate a block id and the name of an operator, dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ every occurrence of that operator in the block operator E a block id, a line id and the name of an operator, dcsn_to_arvl.value.E_ψ_ξ one occurrence, in one line operator E the name of an operator alone, at file level, E_ψ_ξ every occurrence of the operator in the stage operator E a block id and a line id, cntn_to_dcsn.value a line with an id; a line marked !node is a computation whose result is stored as a function of its own, at its Evaluation, as cntn_to_dcsn.risk_ce.evaluate stores the certainty equivalent of the smooth-ambiguity stage statement, or node for a line marked !node the name of a function the stage file or a methods file defines, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 a declared function, where a representation or the closed-form inverse is typed, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣.method : !analytic_inverse at file level definition

An expectation is named by E_ followed by the shocks it integrates, joined by underscores in the order the stage file writes them, so that E_{ψ,ξ} is named E_ψ_ξ. Every other operator is named by its head: argmax for the maximization, solve for the implicit solution, upper_env for the upper envelope and evaluate for an Evaluation. Expression forms gives the forms of E, argmax and solve, and Operations the Evaluation. The derivative operator D is listed with its occurrences and admits no method: a derivative is read from a derivative line the author writes or, where no line states it, from the representation of the value (§5).

Inside a block's bracket a path is read relative to the block: method : !egm and policy.method : !egm both type the block's own builder, and evaluate.method : !Linear the Evaluation inside it. At file level a path is written in full, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.method : !Linear, and the package attaches the entry to the block its first segment names; an entry whose first segment names no block, the name of an operator alone or a function, stays at file level. A block of a methods file holds entries in its bracket and lines in its body, and a block with an empty body is refused, so the entries of a block to which the file adds no line are written at file level, each with its full path. The consumption stage of the portfolio application writes both forms in one file, applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl:

[id=policy, method : !egm | grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) | handler : "cons-port:egm"] {
    c[>]   <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0    :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                        :: [id=grid]
    c      = c[>]                            :: [id=identification]
}

cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.method : !Linear
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m))
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.handler : "cons-port:_make_interp"
arvl_to_dcsn.method : !deterministic
dcsn_to_cntn.handler : "cons-port:transition_fwd"

The candidate line of its block policy carries the borrowing constraint: consumption is at most the Euler candidate, the savings a are nonnegative, and the clause ⟂ states that one of the two inequalities holds with equality (Constraints §4.3). The five entries at file level type the decision builder's Evaluation, the forward builder from arrival to decision, and the handler of the forward builder from decision to continuation.

What a method does depends on the kind of its place.

  • At a builder, a solution method says how the builder's output is computed. !egm brings the lines by which the policy is computed, as the block policy above shows, and !vfi, value function iteration, brings none and leaves the maximization of the stage file to its handler. !explicit reads the lines of its block, as !egm does, each of which defines an output by an expression, in place of the maximization (§3.5). A forward builder carries the distribution of households over the states of one perch to the next perch and takes a method that represents that distribution, !deterministic or !histogram. The kind builder does not tell a forward builder from a backward one, so the package admits every word of a builder at both, and the author chooses the word that suits the builder.
  • At an Evaluation, a line or a declared function, a representation, !Linear, !pchip or !closed_form, stores the function there from the data the place supplies (§3.4).
  • At an operator inside a line, a method says how that one operation is computed: a quadrature rule or a discretization of the shock's law at an expectation, a search at a maximization, a root finder at solve, an upper-envelope scan at upper_env.

The package refuses the following entries, and each refusal names the line of the methods file and its rule (Refusals):

  • a method word that no row of Method types holds (syntax);
  • a path that names no place of the stage (name-in-scope);
  • a word at a place of a kind its row does not admit, such as cntn_to_dcsn.method : !Linear (method-admission);
  • a typing of the derivative operator, D.method (no-method-for-derivative);
  • one component written twice with different content, in one file or in two (declared-twice), and one component typed at one place by two paths, such as the whole of an Evaluation and one of its objects, or the name of an operator and one of its occurrences, or a representation typed both at a !node line and at its Evaluation, which store one function (component-typed-twice).

docs.title: 3 The three entries
docs.text: The method and the grid are components of the operator's signature, which the signature prints beside the functions the operator reads and writes, and the handler is a binding beside them. The three are written in the same way, <path>.<component> : <value>.

docs.title: 3.1 The method
docs.text: A method is a word, with keyword arguments where it takes them: !egm, !Linear, !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes), !vfi(tol=tol_v, n_c=n_c). Method types lists every word with the kinds of place it admits and the keyword arguments the package reads, each with the set its value lies in and whether the word requires it: the quadrature takes one node count for each shock the expectation integrates, written n_<shock>, and value function iteration takes a tolerance and a number of candidate levels. A keyword argument the row does not list is admitted and kept for the handler, which reads it or refuses it. The value of a keyword argument is the name of a setting a methods file declares, a quoted string, a tuple of such values, or a word, with keyword arguments of its own where it takes them. A method's entry writes no number: every number that a method reads is a setting, declared in the methods file and written in the entry by its name, as every argument of the buffer-stock file is, so that the number stands in the settings file and stage.settings lists it. Methodization refuses an entry that writes a number among the arguments of its method, as !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=7, n_ξ=7) does, at any depth of a tuple or of a word's own arguments (method-setting-declared), as it refuses a number among the factors of a grid (§3.2). A quoted string written in the entry is the value of the argument and is no setting. Methodization refuses a keyword argument whose value is or holds a name that no methods file declares as a setting, a parameter or a derived parameter of the stage among them, whatever the settings file holds (name-in-scope). Configuration requires a value for every setting a keyword argument names (setting-unvalued) and refuses a value outside the set the row names (method-option-value). A word the catalogue writes with a hyphen, gauss-hermite, is written in a methods file with an underscore, !gauss_hermite, and the package reads the two as one word.

docs.title: 3.2 The grid
docs.text:
The grid is the finite set of points at which the function at a place is computed and stored; between the points, the representation's interpolation supplies the values. It is written by its own entry at the place, <path>.grid : …, and where an Evaluation's stored objects are represented apart, by one entry for each, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate[D_{k}V[<]].grid : !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k)). The entry holds one grid constructor, the word that says how the points are built:

Constructor Meaning !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) the product of one set of points for each coordinate, each factor keyed by the coordinate's name as the stage file declares it; at least one factor is written !Points(nodes=P) the finite set of the declared points P, each point written in the domain's declared coordinate order; !Points alone is the empty grid !Fibred(base=!Points(nodes=B), fibre=!Cartesian(c=(Γ_c, n_c))) each state of the base grid paired with n_c points of the control's feasible set Γ_c at that state: a grid of feasible pairs of states and controls

A factor of !Cartesian takes one of four shapes, the first with an optional spacing word:

Factor Meaning a=(a_min, a_max, n_a) n_a evenly spaced points from a_min to a_max, the three names declared settings a=(a_min, a_max, n_a, !expmult) n_a points from a_min to a_max, spaced as the fourth element names: a spacing word, with keyword arguments where the spacing has a parameter, !expmult(nest=grid_phi), each numerical argument written as the name of a declared setting; the handler that builds the grid reads the word m=M_nodes the points of a node set: a setting the methods file declares on a product of one set for each point, M_nodes : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊, which the settings file values by the list of its points, at least two in strictly increasing order, M_nodes: [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]; or a set the stage defines by its integer members, M_nodes := {1, 2} ν=E_ν the quadrature nodes of the expectation E_ν, for a coordinate represented on a shock c=(Γ_c, n_c) n_c points of the feasible set Γ_c of a control, for a method that searches over the control

!Cartesian and !Points stand at every place whose method reads a grid: a representation, a solution method whose grid lies on the states of its output perch, such as !vfi, the endogenous grid method on the continuation states, and a place with no method word, whose handler reads the grid. The points of !Points are a set the stage defines by its finite members, B := {1, 2}, or a setting the methods file declares on a fixed finite product of points, P : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊, which the settings file values by the list of its points, P: [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]; on a domain of two coordinates each point is a pair, declared through a product set, X2 := ℝ × ℝ and P : X2 × X2 × X2. A setting declared on a set that is no fixed finite product of points, such as P : ℝ₊, or on a product whose points have another number of coordinates than the domain has, is refused where the grid is typed (grid-coordinate). A list with another number of points than the product has factors lies outside the declared set, and configuration refuses it (setting-outside-set; §4). Repeated points collapse in the set, and an interpolation procedure may still require at least two points. !Fibred stands where the domain of the problem is the base's states followed by the fibre's controls: at a solution method that chooses over the controls on the states of its output perch, such as !vfi, and at a representation or a place with no method word only for a function of those states and those controls. It is refused at the continuation grid of !egm, which holds no control, and at a representation of a function of the states alone. Its base is !Points or a !Cartesian term without feasible factors, and its fibre a !Cartesian term of feasible factors. A feasible factor written in !Cartesian without !Fibred, as in cntn_to_dcsn.grid : !Cartesian(c=(Γ, n_c)), is admitted and states a family of grids of the control, one at each state, and no one grid of pairs.

Each constructor may end with require= and one predicate word, or a tuple of them, which the resulting grid must satisfy: !Empty, the grid holds no point; !Cartesian, the grid is nonempty and holds every combination of its projected coordinate values; !NonCartesian, the grid is nonempty and misses some combination of them; and !UniformCartesian, the grid is Cartesian on at least one real coordinate, with at least two distinct, equally spaced values in every coordinate. A requirement is a property of the grid and no further component, and the predicate !Cartesian is distinct from the constructor of the same name. An outer requirement of !Fibred concerns the joint grid of pairs, and one written inside its fibre, fibre=!Cartesian(c=(Γ_c, n_c), require=!UniformCartesian), concerns the grid of the control at each state. An unknown word, and two words that contradict each other, are refused where they are written (grid-requirement). In !Cartesian, require= is read as a requirement only where its value is a predicate word or a tuple of them, so that a coordinate named require keeps its factor.

A bound, a count and a numerical argument of a spacing word are each written as the name of a setting a methods file declares. A factor that writes in such a place a number, or a name that no methods file declares as a setting, a parameter or a derived parameter of the stage among them, is refused where the grid is typed (grid-setting-declared), and so are declared points of !Points that are neither a declared setting nor a set the stage defines. So is a factor keyed by a name that is no coordinate of the function at the place, unless it is a feasible factor for a control or a quadrature factor for a shock, a constructor at a place it may not stand at, and a grid written at a place whose method reads no grid, such as a quadrature rule (grid-coordinate). Methodization does not check the declared set of a node set, so a setting declared on a set that is no product, such as M_nodes : ℝ₊, is admitted where the grid is typed. Configuration then refuses a list of points for it, which lies outside the declared set (setting-outside-set). It also refuses a single number, which is no node set (grid-bounds). A place without a grid entry, and a coordinate that no factor names, take the default: a grid of the kind !Cartesian over the state coordinates of the function the place holds, in declared order, with no number supplied and none required of the settings file, so that the handler supplies the numbers. For an Evaluation these are the states of the perch at which the stored function stands; for the endogenous grid method they are the states of the continuation perch, on which its grid of savings lies. The buffer-stock file writes no grid at policy.evaluate, and none is admitted there: !Linear at the closing Evaluation of an !egm builder reads the pairs of resources m[>] and consumption that the method computes at the savings on its grid, and a grid entry there is refused (grid-coordinate; §3.4).
