β = 0.95: bound 6, copied 1
β = 0.96: bound 6, copied 1
the trellis read back by the standard pickle equals it: True

Across nodes, the processes of a job that uses MPI, the message-passing standard of cluster computing, are started separately, one per core, and none is a copy of another. One rank, as such a process is called, builds the trellis and sends it to the others, with mpi4py model = comm.bcast(model if comm.rank == 0 else None, root=0), which writes and reads it with Python's standard pickle, as the last lines of the listing do (The stage §5). The durables trellis pickles to 10.7 MB, written in about 0.17 s and read by each rank in about 0.45 s, against about 12 s to build it. A trellis read in this way keeps none of the answers its stage occurrences had computed, so each rank asks it once for them, as the parent does on one node, and calls gc.freeze() once it holds the trellis.

docs.title: 7 The order of a period from its fields
docs.text:
Field dependencies determine the economic order of the stages within a period; the order of the template's list does not. When a trellis is elaborated, or a period of elaborated stages is accreted, the selected connections determine its joins. Each field belongs to its stage occurrence. An authored connector selects eligible continuation and arrival state fields before automatic matching; where either bare endpoint names several eligible fields, its stage key qualifies it. An unclaimed equal-name pair is selected only where its declared sets are compatible and it is the unique globally consistent choice. A continuation field that no join within the period reads is an output of that period and may be paired with the next period's arrival through the indexed inter-period connector. A complete route also needs the ordered state coordinates, joint forward law and backward value components to agree (Periods §2). The computation order follows from selected joins, and stages that depend on none of each other are computable together.

The connection report shows authored and inferred pairs, candidates left unresolved, compatibility diagnostics and routes whose complete state and value interfaces are established. It names an authored endpoint that names no eligible use or several, and a pair whose compatibility is not established. A malformed connector entry, a continuation use claimed twice by authored entries or a selected cycle is refused. The report and the period drawing read the same selection; neither invents a second joining rule. A selected pair alone does not certify an economically complete route.

The forward order, the backward order and the stages computable together are functions over the joins, and no graph of the period is stored. bellman.period.diagram_period(trellis, h) makes the drawing of periods[h] on request, in the format of a graph's diagram(): one box per stage, labeled by its key, standing in the forward order from left to right; one arrow per selected join, labeled by its field pair; and one unlabeled arrow to a plain label for each continuation field that no stage of the period takes. bellman.trellis.diagram_trellis(trellis, periods=None) shows the periods of an elaborated trellis, all of them or those whose indices periods lists, each as diagram_period shows it inside a frame labeled with h and, where the trellis's registry holds last_age, with the age; the terminal period stands at the right, so that economic time runs from left to right and the backward computation from right to left, as the drawing's title states; and every inter-period connector between two of those periods is shown as wires from the continuation fields that leave periods[h + 1] to the arrival fields of periods[h], each labeled with the connector's index and its field pair. Both calls return a drawing that a notebook displays, built from the dictionary and stored nowhere. The drawing of the three latest periods of the two-stage durables trellis, made by diagram_trellis(model, periods=[0, 1, 2]):

Each frame holds a box for the keeper and a box for the adjuster with their continuation fields shown as outputs of the period, in the terminal frame the six arrows run instead into the bequest's box, labeled a_nxt_kp → a_bq, h_nxt_kp → h_bq, z_nxt_kp → z_bq and likewise for the adjuster, and no wire joins one frame to another, since this trellis file writes no inter-period connector. A trellis of one stage over three periods, whose trellis file writes the connector {a: k} once to stand for every adjacent pair, shows the inter-period connectors:

Each wire runs from the continuation field a of the earlier period to the arrival field k of the later one and is labeled with its index, inter_connectors[1] between periods[2] and periods[1] and inter_connectors[0] between periods[1] and periods[0].

docs.title: From syntax to a mathematical problem
docs.text:
Summary

Read the income-and-consumption stage as a problem with explicit state arguments. The budget equation determines where continuation value is evaluated; the policy chooses consumption after income is observed; the arrival equation averages over income. The same reading applies when consumption is separated from discounting and investment.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: the complete buffer_stock.bl; Field equations: the reusable consumption source. Formal account — Appendix C: rules R1–R12; Appendix D: computation boundaries and indexing; Bellman calculus: mathematical foundations. Used by — Semantics and Methodization: the constructed stage read in words, and the selection of numerical methods for its equations.

docs.title: 1 State the consumption context
docs.text:
Use the complete buffer_stock.bl in Stages. Its fields are quantities interpreted in declared information sets, called perches. We use the following state and control notation:

Quantity Information and domain \(b\) Beginning assets, observed at arrival, in \([0,\infty)\). \(y\) Current income, drawn after arrival and observed before consumption, in \((0,\infty)\). \(w=Rb+y\) Decision resources in \((0,\infty)\), with gross return \(R>0\). \(c\) Consumption chosen at decision, with \(0<c\leq w\). \(a=w-c\) Savings available for continuation, in \([0,\infty)\). \(W\) Supplied continuation-value function on \([0,\infty)\).

Utility is \(u(c)=c^{1-\rho}/(1-\rho)\) for \(\rho>1\) and \(c>0\), and \(0<\beta<1\) is the discount factor. Under the example's explicit law, log income has mean \(\mu_y\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_y\geq0\), with a conditional distribution constant given arrival information. Write \(\nu_y\) for this positive income law.

Assume resources contain the information needed for the consumption problem and savings contain the information needed for continuation value. This does not say the household forgets its earlier observations. A representative is a function of the declared state describing a field; the state must suffice for that representation and for the required conditional laws. Choose representatives on every feasible state where the equations or alternative controls evaluate them. Agreement almost surely under one state distribution does not fix their values at all those states (Appendix C R5–R6).

docs.title: 2 Make the state arguments explicit
docs.text:
The following backward block is an excerpt from the complete buffer_stock.bl, with its budget transition and utility definition retained:

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]            :: [id=value]
}

V[>] denotes the continuation-value field, which the function \(W\) represents; holding a feasible consumption choice fixed, the field's value is \(W(a)\). Substitution of the savings transition gives the choice value, the objective with the control still an argument:

\[ Q(w,c)=u(c)+\beta W(w-c),\qquad w>0,\quad 0<c\leq w. \]

This is the reading of the value equation before a policy is evaluated. The control remains a decision choice even when the signature lists it alongside continuation inputs. The stage's information marks are not calendar-time subscripts.

Substitution must retain every declared output and every free or bound dependency. In particular, savings must still be determined by a = w-c even when w-c is also substituted into \(W\). The local utility argument and the control bound by argmax_{c} have distinct scopes. Appendix D gives a generic two-output example of this preservation rule. Marking the savings equation !node records a computation boundary without changing its budget relation; !doc instead removes its defining equation.

docs.title: 3 Choose consumption and average over income
docs.text:
The policy equation in buffer_stock.bl is c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>]). Its feasible set comes from positive consumption, nonnegative savings, and the budget equation. A policy is a measurable choice of consumption for each resource state. An optimal selection \(\pi\) and its decision-value function \(v\) satisfy

\[ \pi(w)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0<c\leq w}Q(w,c),\qquad v(w)=Q(w,\pi(w)). \]

For attainment, assume \(W\) is finite and continuous on every compact savings interval. It is then bounded on \([0,w]\), while utility tends to minus infinity as consumption tends to zero. The maximization excludes a sufficiently small interval near zero and attains its maximum on the remaining compact interval. Select a measurable maximizer; if \(W\) is concave, strict concavity of utility makes the maximizer unique. These are mathematical conditions, not conclusions of parsing argmax.

The arrival equation V[<] = E_{y}(V) averages the decision value after that policy has been selected. Substituting the resource transition gives

\[ B(b)=\int v(Rb+y)\,\nu_y(dy),\qquad b\geq0, \]

where \(B\) is arrival value. Require \(\int|v(Rb+y)|\,\nu_y(dy)<\infty\). Bounded continuous \(W\) is one sufficient case under the stated lognormal law, which has the required negative income moment. Appendix C R7–R8 gives the integration and policy conditions.

The order matters: consumption responds to realized income inside the expectation. Maximizing before income were observed would describe a different decision problem. The supplied \(W\) comes from an adjoining period or terminal boundary; the equation does not silently set \(W=B\). Stationary closure would be an additional model assumption.

docs.title: 4 Reuse the consumption module
docs.text:
The separate cons.bl in Field equations begins with observed resources \(m>0\), sets decision resources \(m_d=m\), and uses the same savings equation. Let \(H:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be its supplied continuation function. Because its value equation contains no beta, the choice value is

\[ Q_H(m_d,c)=u(c)+H(m_d-c),\qquad 0<c\leq m_d. \]

Apply the continuity, attainment, and measurable-selection conditions above to \(H\). Arrival resources are already observed, so the module evaluates its policy without taking another income expectation. When the adjoining discount and investment stages supply \(H=\beta P_v\), where \(P_v\) is investment value given next-period resource value \(v\), discounting appears exactly once. Periods derives the composed problem and states the additional conditions on \(P_v\).

The separate cons_interior.bl uses the endogenous grid method's candidate relation, described in Field equations. Its equation c = c[>] becomes a relation through savings, not an assignment or a guarantee of global optimality. Its inverse-marginal formula requires a finite strictly positive continuation derivative agreeing with the supplied value function. The first-order boundary criterion uses the finite right derivative at zero. To declare the full constrained policy, write the Kuhn–Tucker condition in one of its three spellings, the clause ⟂ m_d - c >= 0 on the decision-perch first-order condition using the forward law a = m_d - c, a multiplier declared in the policy block, or the clause ⟂ a >= 0 on the continuation-marked candidate line written as an inequality, which the loading software reads as the corner (Constraints §4); or restrict the equality to the interior and declare the boundary branch separately, or retain constrained maximization. A numerical boundary extension is not a solution of the unrestricted interior equality. Candidate coordinates must determine a measurable policy on the required domain. Those additional conditions do not belong to the value-only constrained source used above.

docs.title: 5 Inspect equations and then solve
docs.text:
A stage is inspected through the queries of the constructed object: its fields, its definitions table, its graphs, whose boxes open from whole builders down to their single operations, the conditions its construction states, and the card that denote() prints for any piece or definition (API). A builder's card prints each of its operations with its rule written at a point, the state arguments explicit (A builder §1), so the functions of §§2 and 3 are read from the constructed stage itself. On buffer_stock.bl:

Card Rule printed Function of §§2 and 3 The decision builder, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.denote() 𝑉(w) = 𝑢(𝑐(w)) + β · 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(w, 𝑐(w))) \(v(w)=Q(w,\pi(w))\) The policy builder, stage.dcsn.builder.policy.denote() 𝑐(w) ∈ argmax_{c ∈ ℝ₊₊} [𝑢(c) + β · 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(w, c))] the maximization of §3 The arrival builder, stage.arvl.builder.bwd.denote() 𝑉≺(b) = E_{y}[𝑉(𝑔≺(b, y))] \(B(b)\)

Here 𝑉≻ is the continuation value \(W\). The two laws of motion are 𝑔≻(w, c), the savings \(w-c\), and 𝑔≺(b, y), the resources \(Rb+y\). The decision builder's card writes the law at the policy out where a rule reads it, 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(w, 𝑐(w))), the continuation value at the savings the policy leaves. The analytic conditions the construction assumes, such as the integrability of the arrival expectation, are what stage.obligations() returns (The stage §5); the factory API states the calls that construct a stage.

Construction retains interpreted equations and definitions after discarding the temporary syntax tree. Inspection therefore needs neither a second source-string model nor an inferred policy formula based on block names.

Selecting methods, settings, and parameters prepares numerical calculation. Solving also requires the adjoining stages and terminal data; neither inspecting equations nor recognizing a place for a numerical method supplies those results. The lesson tutorials/models/cons-port/03-solving-the-two-orders.ipynb of the repository solves the portfolio–consumption model numerically, separately from the source-to-function derivation here.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Summary

A constraint on a choice is written in one of three places, according to what it is. A fixed bound is part of the control's declared set. A bound that depends on the state is a feasibility correspondence, a set-valued function defined at the top of the file and named in the maximization statement of the policy block. A constraint that binds at some states and not at others is written with the Kuhn–Tucker condition in one of three spellings, which denote one relation between the state and the choice under the hypotheses of §2: the complementary-slackness clause ⟂ after the first-order condition, a multiplier declared in the policy block, or the clause after the candidate line of the endogenous grid method. The candidate line written without a clause states the policy only at the states its candidates reach and nothing at the states where the constraint binds.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Field equations §3: the consumption stage and its inverse Euler line, the running example of this page. Formal account — Appendix C R10, §4.5 and §4.6: the reading of the clause and of the declared multiplier, and the theorem that the three spellings denote one relation and, under concavity, one policy. Used by — Methodization §8: how the lines of a method such as the endogenous grid method carry a constraint's clause. See also — A builder §§1 and 2: the policy builder, its operations and its printed card; Refusals: the rules under which the loading software refuses a writing.

docs.title: 1 Three kinds of constraint and where each is written
docs.text:
An economic model constrains a choice in three ways, and the language, Bellman-SYM, gives each its own place.

A fixed bound does not depend on the state. A portfolio share lies in \([0,1]\); investment is nonnegative; a labor supply lies in \([0,1]\). Such a bound is the control's declared set, written in the signature of the block where the control is introduced, for example ς : [0,1] @ !ctrl or i : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl. Nothing further is written, because the set is the constraint. Declarations, roles such as !ctrl and annotations :: [id=…] are read as in Stages §2, Symbol conventions and Equation parsing rules §1; [>] marks a field at the continuation perch, the information set at which the quantities after the decision are known (Stages §1).

A state-dependent bound is a feasibility correspondence, a function from states to sets, which the notation of the Bellman calculus writes \(\Gamma\). It is defined at the top of the file by a function definition whose body is a set rather than a formula, and it is named in the binder of the maximization statement of the policy block, the block of a stage that states how the control is chosen; the maximization statement names the control as a maximizer of its objective over its feasible set, and §4 states, for each spelling, whether it forms an operation. A statement marked !doc is a declaration: it forms no operation. A methods file attaches no method to it. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). A correspondence is not written as the type of a control: controls keep plain declared sets, and the loading software reads the feasible set from the maximization statement. It compares the feasible set with the control's declared set. Where it cannot show that the first lies within the second, it refuses nothing and records the condition range-compatibility, that the policy takes its values in the declared set. It leaves that condition undecided, also after calibration. For the correspondence Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := [0, x] and a control declared on ℝ₊₊, the card of the policy builder (§4) prints the condition under the heading Conditions as 𝑐(m_d) ∈ ℝ₊₊. The loading software records the same condition where no point of the feasible set lies in the declared set. The author therefore writes a feasible set that lies within the control's declared set.

In the maximization statement the binder introduces a bound variable, local to the statement, that ranges over the feasible set: argmax_{cp : Γ(w, h)} binds cp to \(\Gamma(w,h)\), the feasible set at the state \((w, h)\) of §5.2, with the same colon that types a declaration. When the bound is fixed the bare binder suffices, argmax_{i}(…), because the control's declared set is its feasible set.

A feasible set for a pair of jointly chosen quantities may be a product:

Γ(z : ℝ₊) := [0, z] × ℝ₊

The first component lies between zero and z, while the second is nonnegative. To couple components by a budget identity, write a set comprehension, which gives a domain and conditions on its members:

Γ(z : ℝ₊) := {q : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ | q[1] + q[2] = z}

Here q is one nonnegative triple, and its first two components must sum to z; its third component remains nonnegative. For z = 3, (1, 2, 0) is feasible, whereas (1, 1, 0) violates the equality and (1, 2, -1) violates nonnegativity. Comma-separated conditions must all hold, so an equality may be combined with inequalities. The policy's maximization statement retains this complete feasible set for the joint choice; Appendix C R7 states the separate requirements for a maximizer and its numerical selection.

An occasionally binding constraint holds with equality at some states and with slack at others: the borrowing limit that binds at low wealth, the irreversibility of investment that binds when capital is abundant, the collateral limit that binds when house prices fall. Its first-order condition is the Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2, which the language writes in one of three spellings (§4).

A fixed bound on a parameter is part of its declared set. A bound is an endpoint of the set, a number as in β : (0,1) or a formula of other parameters as in Γ : (0, R). A further bound is a second set written after @, and the declared name then lies in both: β : (0,1) @ (0, R^(ρ-1)) declares a discount factor below one and below R^(ρ-1). Calibration refuses a parameter's value that lies outside any of its sets, and names the bound it breaks. A bound that holds an expectation, or that calls a function other than log, exp, min and max, is not decided, and the membership is left required (Symbols and conventions §9.2). At most one of the sets is written otherwise than as an interval with its brackets. A named set such as Xa, or a reserved set such as ℝ₊₊, counts as such a set, so ρ : ℝ₊₊ @ (1, inf) is read and ρ : Xa @ ℝ₊₊ is refused under syntax. Several sets are read only on the declaration of one name on its own line at the top level of the file. A field listed in a block header carries one set, and a second set there is refused under readable-form (Symbols and conventions §9.2).

Abstract grammar: CorrDef 

stmt  += CorrDef(identifier name, coordinate* params, setexpr body)
params has at least one entry, each a typed argument; body is a closed or half-open interval, a finite set, a product of sets or a set comprehension, in the arguments. An open interval written alone as the body, (0, x), is read after := as a pair of values, so Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := (0, x) defines a function, not a correspondence. An open feasible set is written by comprehension, Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := {c : ℝ₊₊ | c < x}. As a factor of a product, (0, x) × ℝ₊, the same brackets are read as an open interval. A finite set is a set of labels, {work, retire}, an integer range, {0, …, J}, or a list of integers, {0, 1}. The package does not yet read an integer range or a list of integers written alone as the body (Appendix C §5.3). It refuses such a line under not-constructed. It reads either one as a factor of a product, {0, …, J} × ℝ. A comprehension may restrict its member by equalities and inequalities. A set comprehension is admitted in one other place, after := in the definition of a named set, which has no arguments, as in H := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} (Symbol conventions §9.2); marked !categories, such a set is bounded by inequalities alone, and an equality condition is refused under category-codes.

Keys. name is the correspondence's name, applied in a binder (§1); params are its typed arguments; body is the set it assigns to each argument value (§1).

Head. A function-definition line, name(arg : set, …) := body, whose body is a set rather than a formula.

Denotes. The feasibility correspondence \(\Gamma\) of Stages and perches §1, a function from decision states to sets of admissible controls.

Status. The loading software parses the definition and reads the feasible set from the binder of the maximization statement into the declared set of functions for the policy, which the policy card prints beside the policy's type as 𝑐(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d) (§4).

Abstract grammar: In 

subscript = Var(identifier name)
          | In(identifier var, expr set)
var is the bound variable; set is a named set or an applied correspondence. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). A reserved set such as ℝ₊₊ is refused in the binder under syntax.

Keys. var is the name bound by the operator (§1); set is the set it ranges over (§1).

Head. Inside the operator's subscript braces, argmax_{var : set}; the bare form argmax_{var} is Var.

Denotes. The maximization of Appendix C R7 over the set the binder names, with the variable local to the statement.

Status. The loading software parses both forms and records the binder with the operator occurrence. A maximization statement marked !doc is printed on the policy card under the heading Declared with the policy substituted for the control, 𝑐(m_d) ∈ argmax_{cp ∈ Γ(m_d)} [𝑢(cp) + 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, cp))], and forms no operation; written without the mark, it forms the Argmax operation that outputs the policy, and the card prints the same statement as that operation's rule (§4.1). For a binder over a named set, such as argmax_{cp : Xm}, the card prints 𝑐(m_d) ∈ Xm beside the policy's type, and it prints the statement with UNRESOLVED[Xm; free mathematical reference] in place of the set. The package does not yet print a named set there (Appendix C §5.3).

docs.title: 2 The Kuhn–Tucker condition
docs.text:
The running example is the consumption stage of Field equations §3. At cash on hand \(m_d > 0\) the household chooses consumption \(c > 0\) and saves \(a = m_d - c\), subject to the borrowing limit \(a \ge 0\), to maximize \(u(c) + V_\succ(a)\), where \(u\) is utility and \(V_\succ\) is the continuation value, the function the field V[>] denotes; the period's other stage, disc, applies the discount factor, so \(V_\succ\) is already discounted and no \(\beta\) appears (Appendix C §4.2). The page writes \(u'\) for marginal utility, 𝑑𝑢 in the file, \((u')^{-1}\) for its inverse, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣, and \(V_\succ'\) for the marginal value of saving, the derivative of the continuation value, which the derivative term D_{a}V[>] denotes and a card prints as D_{a}𝑉≻. Throughout, \(u'\) is a strictly decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\), and \(V_\succ\) is differentiable on \(X_a = \mathbb R_+\), from the right at zero, with derivative \(V_\succ'\) valued in \(\mathbb R_{++}\).

With a multiplier \(\mu\) on the borrowing limit, the Kuhn–Tucker condition of Karush (1939) and Kuhn and Tucker (1951) for this problem is

\[ u'(c) - V_\succ'(m_d - c) = \mu, \qquad \mu \ge 0, \qquad m_d - c \ge 0, \qquad \mu\,(m_d - c) = 0 . \]

The last three parts are complementary slackness: the multiplier and the slack \(m_d - c\) of the bound are nonnegative and their product is zero, so the Euler equation holds with equality where the household saves, and marginal utility may exceed the marginal value of saving where it saves nothing. The states at which the bound binds form the constrained region. The residual \(r = u'(c) - V_\succ'(m_d - c)\), the left side of the Euler equation less its right side, equals the multiplier, so the condition is

\[ r \ge 0, \qquad m_d - c \ge 0, \qquad r\,(m_d - c) = 0 , \]

written \(0 \le r \perp m_d - c \ge 0\) in the complementarity-problem literature (§6). This is the form the language writes. Under the concavity hypotheses of Appendix C §4.5 the condition has one solution at each \(m_d\), and that solution is the maximizer.

For an upper bound \(z \le b\) the slack is \(b - z\), and the residual is nonpositive, zero wherever the bound is slack. For two bounds on one quantity, \(lb \le z \le ub\) with \(lb < ub\), each bound has a multiplier, \(\mu_{lo}\) and \(\mu_{hi}\), at most one of them positive, and the residual is \(\mu_{lo} - \mu_{hi}\): nonnegative where the lower bound binds, zero where neither binds, and nonpositive where the upper bound binds.

docs.title: 3 The complementary-slackness clause
docs.text:
A statement of a block may have a clause after its equality or inequality:

    lhs = rhs ⟂ bound >= 0

The clause pairs the residual, the left side less the right side, with the slack of the bound, as in §2: on a lower bound >= the residual is nonnegative, the bound holds and their product is zero, so the equation holds wherever the bound is slack; on an upper bound <= the residual is nonpositive instead. The author orients the equation so that its residual has the sign its bound requires, as the examples of §5 do. After an inequality statement the residual takes the sign of that inequality, and the clause adds the bound and the zero product (§4.3). The sign is read from the relation as written, so a clause with one bound writes the bounded quantity first: a >= 0 on a continuation-marked candidate line, or m_d - c >= 0 on a decision-perch condition whose forward law is a = m_d - c. The reversed one-bound spelling ⟂ 0 <= a is refused under readable-form. The glyph is ⟂ (U+27C2); ⊥ (U+22A5) is not admitted. The rules under which the loading software refuses a writing are listed in Refusals.

A clause names one bounded quantity. On a statement it may have two bounds, written as an ascending chain of weak inequalities, from the lower bound through the bounded quantity to the upper bound:

    lhs = rhs ⟂ lb <= x <= ub

The two-bound clause states the condition of §2 for two bounds. The worker's saving stage of the pension application writes one on the pension deposit \(c_p\), which lies between zero and earnings \(w_d\), in the block policy of its methods file, applications/pension-retirement/declaration/stages/worker_saving/methods.bl, whose two lines are the first-order conditions of the stage's maximization, brought to the policy builder under time iteration (Methodization §5):

    𝑑𝑢(c) = β*(1 + 𝑑𝜒(c_p))*D_{y_p}V[>] ⟂ 0 <= c_p <= w_d

Its residual is the stationarity condition in the deposit less that in consumption. In a system of several conditions each clause is written so that its residual is the multiplier of its own bound, the other multipliers being eliminated by combining the first-order conditions; the loading software holds the statements as written and checks no such arrangement (Appendix C R10).

The clause is written on the first-order condition (§4.1), on the declaration of a multiplier (§4.2), or on the candidate line of the endogenous grid method (§4.3). Where the maximization statement is marked !doc and the control enters the first-order condition only through the law of motion, as in §5.1 and §5.3, the condition names no output of the block, and a block that states the control by that condition alone is refused under the rule output-defined; attached as the property of the maximization statement written without !doc, the first spelling of §4.1, the same condition is accepted.

Technical details

Where the left side of a statement is an expression rather than a name, as it is in the examples of §5.1 and §5.2, its unknowns are the outputs of the policy block that its two sides mention and that no other operative statement of the block defines by name, an operative statement being one the block computes with, so any line that is neither marked !doc nor attached to another line as its property by a dotted id (§4.1; Appendix C R10). Where the maximization statement is marked !doc it is not operative, so the control it names on its left side stays an unknown of the operative statements below it; in the first spelling (§4.1) it is written without !doc and is itself the operation that outputs the control. Several such statements of one block that share an unknown state one system, whose unknowns are taken in the order of the block's header.

Abstract grammar: Slack 

stmt  += Slack(stmt core, cond bound)
cond   = Rel(expr left, relop op, expr right)
relop  = Lt | Le | Eq | Ge | Gt
The statement core is an equality or an inequality; on an inequality the residual takes the sign of its relation. The relation bound is written with >= for a lower bound or <= for an upper bound (≥ and ≤ are the same spellings); left is the bounded quantity and right the bound, an expression in the stage's declared quantities, and a left that is a number or inf alone is refused. A clause with two bounds is the Between of the next box.

Keys. core is the equality or inequality whose residual the clause constrains (§3); bound is the relation the constrained quantity satisfies throughout (§3).

Head. The glyph ⟂ between the statement and its bound, on one statement line, before any annotation.

Denotes. The Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2 for the residual of core and the slack of bound, with the residual's sign taken from the relation of core; stated with its concavity hypotheses in Appendix C §4.5.

Status. The loading software parses the clause and keeps it with its statement. It reads the clause by the product of the residual and the slack: where the slack is positive the residual is zero, and where the slack is zero the residual has the sign the clause states; a chain has three such cases, one at each bound and one between them. This reading admits at each state exactly the values the condition of §2 admits, and nothing is solved. The card prints the clause in the rule of the operation its statement forms, read at the point, the state at which the rule holds: on a first-order condition, each function at the coordinates of its own perch and each continuation state replaced by the law of motion at the decision state and the policy, under the Argmax operation when the condition is its property and under an Aggregation of its own when the condition is an operative line (§4.1); on the candidate line, at the saving (§4.3). The statements of one system share one rule, their conjunction.

Abstract grammar: Between 

cond  += Between(expr lower, relop lo, expr middle, relop hi, expr upper)
lo and hi are both <= (or ≤), so the chain ascends from the lower bound through the bounded quantity to the upper bound. A descending, strict or mixed chain, a chain after an inequality statement and a chain on the declaration of a multiplier are refused.

Keys. lower and upper are the two bounds (§3); middle is the bounded quantity (§3); lo and hi are the two relation signs as written (§3).

Head. Two relation signs after the glyph ⟂, ⟂ lb <= x <= ub, on one statement line, before any annotation.

Denotes. With \(r\) the residual of the statement, the bounds \(lb \le x \le ub\) together with \(r\,(x - lb) \le 0\) and \(r\,(ub - x) \ge 0\): the residual is nonnegative where the lower bound binds, zero where neither binds and nonpositive where the upper bound binds, and with \(lb < ub\) it is the difference of the two bounds' multipliers (§2).

Status. The loading software parses the chain, keeps both relation signs, and prints the chain read at the point. On the card of the pension application's worker stage the chain on the deposit is printed after the clause of the first condition, whose bound prints as y_f ≥ 0: y_f is the name that the card's Where line gives to the financial saving in the law of motion. The refusals above are made under readable-form, and on a declaration under multiplier-declaration.

docs.title: 4 Three spellings of one condition
docs.text:
The endogenous grid method (Carroll 2006, §2.2) inverts the interior Euler equation on a grid of the continuation state, the state after the decision is taken (Stages and perches §1). In the running example the continuation state is the saving \(a\), with declared set Xa, and the law of motion \(g_\succ\), the map from the decision state and the control to the continuation state, is \(a = m_d - c\). Inverting the interior Euler equation \(u'(c) = V_\succ'(a)\) at each saving gives the candidate at each saving, which the field c[>] denotes, \(c_\succ(a) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\) (Carroll's equation 17), and the budget gives the cash on hand at each saving, which m_d[>] denotes, \(m_{d\succ}(a) = a + c_\succ(a)\) (his equation 18), written in the file by the grid line m_d[>] = a + c[>]; a card prints them 𝑐≻ and 𝑚_d≻. Where the candidate line has no clause, both are functions of the saving alone (Appendix C R8); with the clause of §4.3 they are correspondences of the saving alone, 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊ and 𝑚_d≻ : Xa ⇉ Xm, the double arrow marking a correspondence, each taking several values at zero saving; with the multiplier of §4.2 they are functions of the saving and the multiplier. Write \(\bar m = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(0))\) for the interior value at zero saving. The image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\) is the set of cash on hand that some saving reaches; under the hypotheses of Appendix C §4.5 it is \([\bar m, \infty)\).

The policy block's lines are read into the policy builder, the operator the block denotes, whose printed card lists its operations under the heading Operations, one entry each: the entry's number and its key: the id of the line it realizes followed by its kind, as in InvEuler:Aggregation, or the kind alone, as in Pullback and Evaluation, for an operation that no line of the block forms; the functions it reads after in: and those it writes after out:; and its rule after rule:, with a note at the right margin, on …, naming the set on which the rule holds. Under the heading Source the card gives the lines of the file its operations come from (A piece §1). An operation of a policy builder is of one of five kinds, each a row of Operations: a Pullback composes a function with a map, such as a continuation function with the law of motion; an Aggregation applies a pointwise map, or holds the relation its line writes, with the unknown on both sides where the line puts it there; an Expectation integrates over a shock; an Argmax maximizes an objective over the feasible set; and the Evaluation is the identity into the declared set of functions for the policy, the place at which a numerical method stores its representation of the policy. The three spellings share the header of the policy block and its maximization statement, which the second and the third mark !doc, as below, a declaration of what their operations are meant to reach that the operations neither confirm nor check, and which the first writes without the mark, as the operation itself (§4.1):

[id=policy, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c      = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])   :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    …
}

A stage file may instead write the maximization alone and leave the candidate lines to its methods file, whose block policy brings them to the policy builder under a solution method (Methodization §5). Such a block writes the second or the third spelling. It holds no maximization line, since the stage file's maximization stays the policy block's declared line, so the first spelling, a property of that line, has no line to attach to there; the first spelling belongs to a stage file that writes the maximization as an operation and attaches to it the first-order condition, which reads the derivative term D_{a}V[>]. The methods file of the portfolio–consumption demonstration, applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, writes the third spelling, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0.

docs.title: 4.1 The clause on the first-order condition
docs.text:
c      = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])   :: [id=optimality]
    𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m_d - c >= 0          :: [id=optimality.euler]

The first line is the maximization statement without the mark !doc: it is the operation that outputs the policy, and a method is attached to it. The second line is attached to the first as its property by the dotted id optimality.euler: it forms no operation, and the loading software neither checks it against the objective nor derives anything from it. Its bound writes the decision-perch expression \(m_d-c\) supplied by the law of motion \(a = g_\succ(m_d, c) = m_d - c\), so the property states the Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2 at every cash on hand \(m_d\). No candidate and no cash on hand at each saving is written, so a method attached to the Argmax operation solves the condition at each \(m_d\), by a root finder in \(c\) or by the endogenous grid method, which inverts the property for the candidate, as the lines of §4.3 do in the file, and forms the cash on hand by the law of motion. The operations are those of the maximization: a Pullback of the continuation value along the law of motion, an Aggregation that forms the objective, the Argmax over the feasible set with the policy as its output, and the Evaluation. The property prints under the Argmax entry, labeled by its id and read at the point, and no Declared section is printed, since no line is marked !doc. A block may instead keep the maximization statement marked !doc and write the first-order condition with its clause as an operative line of its own, 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m_d - c >= 0 :: [id=euler], as the pension application's worker stage writes its two conditions using its own forward laws. The condition then forms a Pullback of the derivative D_{a}𝑉≻ along the law of motion and an Aggregation whose rule is the relation with the policy on both sides, 𝑑𝑢(𝑐(m_d)) = D_{a}𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) ⟂ 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)) ≥ 0 on Xm, and a root finder is attached to that line.

docs.title: 4.2 The declared multiplier
docs.text:
μ[>]   : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0             :: [id=slackness]
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>] + μ[>]) :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]

The first line declares a multiplier: a field μ at the continuation perch with the declared set \(\mathbb R_+\), joined by its clause to the bound a >= 0. It is a declaration inside the block's body and defines no equation. The second line is the inverse Euler equation with the multiplier added, \(c = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a) + \mu)\). For the functions the block defines at the continuation perch, the candidate and the cash on hand, the declaration adds the coordinate \(\mu\) beside \(a\) and restricts the pair to the admitted pairs, those at which complementary slackness holds:

\[ A_{\succ,\mathrm{policy}} = \{(a, \mu) \in X_a \times \mathbb R_+ \mid a \ge 0,\ \mu\, a = 0\} , \]

where \(X_a\) is the declared set Xa of the saving; the half-line \(a = 0\) is thus declared by the file, not inferred. On this set the candidate and the cash on hand are functions of the saving and the multiplier, \(c_\succ(a, \mu) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a) + \mu)\) and \(m_{d\succ}(a, \mu) = a + c_\succ(a, \mu)\), while \(V_\succ\) and its derivative \(V_\succ'\) remain functions of \(a\) alone and the multiplier is an input or output of no block. The identification equates the policy at the cash on hand of each admitted pair with the candidate there, \(c(m_{d\succ}(a, \mu)) = c_\succ(a, \mu)\) on the image \(m_{d\succ}(A_{\succ,\mathrm{policy}})\). On the half-line \(\mu = 0\) that image is the image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\) of §4. On the half-line \(a = 0\) the candidate \((u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(0) + \mu)\) decreases from \(\bar m\) toward zero as \(\mu\) grows, because \(u'\) is a strictly decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\) (§2), so the image there is \((0, \bar m]\), the constrained region. Technical details

The card states the set of admitted pairs once, under the heading Where, as A≻,policy; its coordinates have no perch marks, because on a card μ≻ names the measure of the continuation state.

The bound is held as written, even where the declared set of the continuation state already implies it: the loading software compares no bound of a clause with a declared set, and on a state declared on \(\mathbb R\) the bound is the only place the constraint enters the set of admitted pairs; §5.2 writes such a bound. Because a bound may not name a control, a constraint on a control, such as the cap on the pension deposit in §3, is written with the clause on the first-order condition.

Abstract grammar: Complementary 

typer += Complementary(typer d, cond bound)
d declares one coordinate with the continuation mark [>] and one set; bound is one relation, a Rel written with the bounded quantity first, and a Between is refused here. The item is Declare(Complementary(d, bound), annot), so Declare keeps its two ASDL fields. The bound may name continuation states, other multipliers of the block, parameters, numbers and inf. A multiplier with a mark other than [>], a bound naming a control, a decision or arrival state or a candidate such as c[>], a second declaration of one name, a block header that lists the multiplier's name, and a declaration without its clause are refused.

Keys. d is the declaration of the multiplier, its name, its perch and its set (§4.2); bound is the constraint whose multiplier it is (§4.2).

Head. A declaration in the body of a policy block followed by the glyph ⟂ and one relation, μ[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0, before any annotation.

Denotes. For the functions its block defines at the continuation perch, the coordinate \(\mu\) beside the continuation states, the pair restricted to the admitted pairs \(\{(a, \mu) \mid \text{bound},\ \mu\, s = 0\}\), where \(s\) is the slack of the bound, \(x - b\) for x >= b and \(b - x\) for x <= b. The declaration forms no operation and no wire, a wire being an input or output of an operation on the card. That this spelling and the clause of §3 denote one relation is a theorem of Appendix C §4.5.

Status. The loading software parses the declaration, gives its name the role of a multiplier at the continuation perch, adds it to the coordinates of the functions its block defines there, forms the set of admitted pairs from the bound as written, with one bound and one product for each declaration where a block declares several (§4.5), and the identification, a Pullback, states the grid relation on the image of that set. The grid line is checked against the law of motion as in §4.3. The refusals above are made under multiplier-declaration, and that of a declaration without its clause under syntax.

docs.title: 4.3 The clause on the candidate line
docs.text:
c[>]   <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]

The first line, the candidate line, is the inverse Euler statement of Field equations §3 with <= in place of = and the clause of §3 after it. An inequality statement defines its left side as a correspondence, and the clause takes the sign of its residual from the inequality (§3). A value \(x\) is admitted at the saving \(a\) when

\[ x - (u')^{-1}\bigl(V_\succ'(a)\bigr) \le 0, \qquad a \ge 0, \qquad \bigl(x - (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\bigr)\, a = 0 . \]

A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is zero. Where the bound is slack, \(a > 0\), the residual is therefore zero and one value is admitted, \((u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\); where it binds, \(a = 0\), every \(x\) with \(0 < x \le \bar m\) is admitted, the lower end open because consumption is declared positive. The card writes the set admitted at \(a\) as 𝑐≻(a), so that 𝑐≻(0) is the segment \((0, \bar m]\). The second line gives each admitted value its cash on hand, \(a + x\). The third line, the identification, is a Pullback, the pullback of the policy along the cash on hand at each saving equated to the candidate; its rule is the grid relation 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa), the candidate and the cash on hand taking their values together, so that it states \(c(a + x) = x\) at every saving \(a\) and every value \(x\) admitted there:

\[ c(m_d) = m_d \quad \text{for } 0 < m_d \le \bar m, \qquad c\bigl(a + (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\bigr) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a)) \quad \text{for } a \ge 0 . \]

The first part is the corner, the pairs at which the household consumes all its cash on hand, and the second is the interior policy on the image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\); the two share the pair \((\bar m, \bar m)\). The corner is Carroll's segment from the origin to the first grid point (2006, §4.2.2, equation 29). Conditions
  grid:Aggregation  𝑚_d≻(a) ∈ Xm
  policy            egm-eligibility: the construction satisfies the declared
                      line where the continuation value 𝑉≻ is concave and
                      continuously differentiable on (0, ∞) with a finite
                      positive right derivative at 0   [required]

Method
  !egm   !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))   "cons-port:egm"            policy
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source  cons.bl
  30  c      = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])  :: [id=optimality]

Source  methods.bl
  29  c[>]   <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0          :: [id=InvEuler]
  30  m_d[>] = a + c[>]                            :: [id=grid]
  31  c      = c[>]                                :: [id=identification]

Definitions referenced
  Xm     cons:set:Xm
  Xa     cons:set:Xa
  𝑢      cons:function:𝑢
  Γ      cons:correspondence:Γ
  𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣  cons:function:𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣  methods.bl:19
  𝑔≻     cons:g:dcsn_to_cntn
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The card writes each rule at the saving; three answers beside it show the correspondences. The card of the first entry, cons.dcsn.builder.policy["InvEuler:Aggregation"].denote(), gives its output as 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊, and the card of the second gives 𝑚_d≻ : Xa ⇉ Xm. The query signature(), which answers an operation's inputs and outputs with their sets, gives as the output of the identification the set of policies \(f\) with \(f(a + x) = x\) for every saving \(a\) and every value \(x\) admitted there, the relation over the pairs each saving admits. The loading software checks the second line, the grid line, against the law of motion: it solves \(a = m_d - c\) for the decision coordinate, \(m_d = a + c\), puts the candidate in place of the control, and compares the result with the line. A line that does not agree, such as m_d[>] = a + 2*c[>], is refused under the rule grid-line-consistency, and the refusal names the line as written and the law solved for the coordinate.

Without the clause the candidate line is read as the equality selection, \(c_\succ(a) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\) at every saving, the part of the relation of §2 with \(\mu = 0\), and is no spelling of the Kuhn–Tucker condition. The identification then states the policy on the image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\); below it, where the constraint binds, it states nothing.

Abstract grammar: Inequality 

stmt  += Inequality(expr lhs, relop op, expr rhs)
The relation op is <= or >= for a bound (< and > are also admitted); lhs names the quantity defined and rhs is the bound the definition admits.

Keys. lhs is the quantity the statement defines as a correspondence (§4.3); op and rhs state the relation its values satisfy (§4.3).

Head. The relation sign between two expressions on a statement line, where an equation would have =.

Denotes. The set-valued relation \(\{\,\text{lhs} : \text{lhs} \le \text{rhs}\,\}\) at each state, a correspondence. Written as the inverse Euler line without a clause, it is read as the equality selection, the interior candidate \((u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\) at every saving, and is no spelling of the Kuhn–Tucker condition (§4.3). With a clause of one bound after it, the residual takes the sign of the relation and the clause adds the bound and the zero product: the Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2, one value at each saving where the bound is slack and, where it binds, the segment of values up to the interior value at zero saving, \(\bar m\) (§4.3).

Status. The loading software parses the statement, keeps the relation, and forms from it one Aggregation of the policy builder, whose output is the candidate at each saving and whose rule is the relation as written, read at the saving, 𝑐≻(a) ≤ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)). With a clause of one bound the rule holds the clause as well, 𝑐≻(a) ≤ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)) ⟂ a ≥ 0, the operation's record holds the values the clause admits at each saving, and the card of that operation prints its output as the correspondence 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊; a clause with two bounds after the inequality is refused under readable-form. The identification, a Pullback, states the grid relation 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa): with the clause it holds at every value admitted at each saving, the corner among them; without it the candidate is the interior value at every saving, and the relation states nothing below the image of the grid. No inverse of the cash on hand at each saving is formed.

docs.title: 4.4 One relation
docs.text: Under the hypotheses of §2 and the law of motion \(a = m_d - c\), the three spellings denote one relation between cash on hand and consumption: the pairs that satisfy the clause on the first-order condition, the pairs the declared multiplier reaches on its two half-lines, and the pairs of the grid relation of §4.3, corner included, are one set. The identity of the first spelling with the second uses only that 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is the inverse of \(u'\); that of the third with them also uses the monotonicity of \(u'\), through which \(x \le \bar m\) holds exactly when \(u'(x) \ge V_\succ'(0)\). For the first spelling, whose operation is the maximization and whose first-order condition is its property (§4.1), the pairs are those of the property; that the maximizer is among them, and is the only one, holds under the concavity hypotheses of Appendix C §4.5 and not otherwise. Appendix C §4.5 proves the identity and, under concavity hypotheses stated there, that the relation is the graph of one policy and that this policy maximizes the objective over the feasible set; the loading software checks none of these hypotheses. The spellings differ in what a method reads: the first states the condition at every decision state, for a method attached to the Argmax operation to solve; the second and the third state the candidate and the cash on hand at every saving, which the endogenous grid method, attached at the Evaluation, evaluates at the savings of its grid, joins with the pairs of the corner and interpolates as one function of cash on hand, without forming the inverse of the cash on hand at each saving (Appendix C §4.6).

docs.title: 4.5 A bound on both sides
docs.text:
Take a saving bounded on both sides, \(0 \le a \le \bar a\), with ā : ℝ₊₊ a declared parameter. In the first spelling the chain is written on the first-order condition, 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ 0 <= m_d - c <= ā, using the forward law \(a=m_d-c\). In the second each bound has its own multiplier, since a declaration's clause has one bound, and the two enter the inverse Euler line with the signs of §2:

    μ_lo[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0                    :: [id=slack_lo]
    μ_hi[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a <= ā                    :: [id=slack_hi]
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>] + μ_lo[>] - μ_hi[>])  :: [id=InvEuler]

In the third the correct writing is the equation with the chain and the interior value on the left, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) = c[>] ⟂ 0 <= a <= ā, whose residual is nonnegative at zero saving and nonpositive at the cap. The loading software refuses it under signature-complete, since a field is defined only by a line with its name on the left, so a bound on both sides is written in the first or the second spelling. A chain after the inequality, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ 0 <= a <= ā, is refused under readable-form, because a chain has a sign rule after an equation alone.

Warning

The line c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ 0 <= a <= ā is accepted but states the wrong constraint. Its residual, the candidate less the interior value, has the opposite sign to the Euler residual (Appendix C §4.5), so the chain places consumption above the interior value at zero saving and below it at the cap. The loading software checks no sign.

docs.title: 5 Examples
docs.text: Each example shows the transition block and the policy block; the declarations of parameters and shocks and the backward blocks of a complete stage file are omitted.

docs.title: 5.1 Irreversible investment
docs.text:
A firm with capital \(k\) and depreciation rate \(\delta\) chooses investment \(i \ge 0\), and its capital next period is \(k' = (1-\delta)k + i\). Investment cannot be undone, so the constraint binds when the firm would rather disinvest. The Kuhn–Tucker condition is

\[ 1 - \beta\, W'(k') \ge 0, \qquad i \ge 0, \qquad \bigl(1 - \beta\, W'(k')\bigr)\, i = 0 , \]

where \(W\) is the continuation value of capital and \(\beta\) the discount factor: the firm invests until the discounted marginal value of capital equals its unit cost, unless that value is below the cost, in which case it invests nothing. The bound is fixed, so the control's declared set is the nonnegative reals, and the clause is written on the first-order condition with the unit cost on the left, which makes the residual nonnegative at the bound.

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (k_d : ℝ₊₊, i : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (k_n : ℝ₊₊) : !cntn] {
    k_n = (1 - δ)*k_d + i
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (i : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    i = argmax_{i}(-i + β*V[>])     :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    1 = β*D_{k_n}V[>] ⟂ i >= 0      :: [id=investment]
}

In the fragment k_d is \(k\), k_n is \(k'\), V[>] is \(W\) and the derivative term D_{k_n}V[>] is \(W'\). The first statement, marked !doc, declares the control to be a maximizer over its declared set and forms no operation. Investment enters the first-order condition only through the transition, so the condition names no output of the block, and the loading software refuses the block under output-defined (§3). In the first spelling of §4.1 the maximization statement is written without !doc and the condition is attached to it as its property, :: [id=optimality.investment]; the block is then accepted, the maximization forming the Argmax operation that outputs investment and the condition printing under it.

docs.title: 5.2 A collateral constraint
docs.text:
A household with a house of size \(h\) and price \(p\) consumes \(c\) out of cash on hand \(w\) and may borrow against the house: end-of-period net assets \(a = w - c\) may be negative down to a fraction \(\theta\) of the house's value. The feasible set of consumption depends on the state, so it is a correspondence,

\[ \Gamma(w, h) = \bigl(0,\; w + \theta p h\bigr] , \]

and the Euler equation has the collateral limit as its bound. The house is held fixed within this stage, \(h' = h\).

Γ(x : ℝ₊₊, h : ℝ₊) := (0, x + θ*p*h]        :: [id=feasible]

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w : ℝ₊₊, h : ℝ₊, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ, h_n : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a   = w - c
    h_n = h
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{cp : Γ(w, h)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>])   :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    𝑑𝑢(c) = β*D_{a}V[>] ⟂ w - c >= -θ*p*h       :: [id=euler]
}

In the fragment h_n is \(h'\), and 𝑢 and 𝑑𝑢 are utility and marginal utility, defined as in Field equations §3. The Euler clause writes w - c for a and h for h_n, as the forward block defines them. At states where the limit has slack the Euler equation holds with equality. Where it binds, the household borrows the full \(\theta p h\), consumption is \(w + \theta p h\), and marginal utility exceeds the discounted marginal value of assets by the multiplier on the collateral constraint. The bound is an expression in declared quantities; a constant limit w - c >= 0 is the special case \(\theta = 0\).

docs.title: 5.3 A portfolio share with two bounds
docs.text:
A household allocates a share \(\varsigma \in [0,1]\) of its savings \(s\) to a risky asset with gross return \(\Psi\), the rest earning the safe gross return \(R\), and receives income \(\eta\); next period's resources are \(m' = s\,(\varsigma\Psi + (1-\varsigma)R) + \eta\). Both bounds are fixed, so the control's declared set states them, and with \(W\) the continuation value of resources the first-order condition, divided by the positive savings \(s\), holds with equality only in the interior:

\[ \mathbb{E}\bigl[W'(m')\,(\Psi - R)\bigr] \begin{cases} \le 0 & \text{if } \varsigma = 0, \\ = 0 & \text{if } 0 < \varsigma < 1, \\ \ge 0 & \text{if } \varsigma = 1 . \end{cases} \]

The two-bound clause of §3 states this condition exactly. Written with zero on the left and the expectation on the right,

    0 = E_{Ψ,η}(D_{m}V[>]*(Ψ - R)) ⟂ 0 <= ς <= 1

the statement has the residual \(-\mathbb E\bigl[W'(m')\,(\Psi - R)\bigr]\), which is nonnegative where the share is zero, zero in the interior and nonpositive where the share is one, as the display requires; written the other way round, it would have the opposite sign at each bound. The share enters the condition only through the transition, so a block that states the share by this line alone is refused under output-defined (§3). The block therefore writes the interior first-order condition with solve_{ς}, which names its unknown, and the declared set [0,1] states the two bounds; the maximization statement, marked !doc, declares the share to be a maximizer over that set and forms no operation:

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (s : ℝ₊₊, ς : [0,1] @ !ctrl, Ψ, η) : !dcsn -> (m : ℝ₊₊) : !cntn] {
    m = s*(ς*Ψ + (1-ς)*R) + η
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (ς : [0,1] @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    ς = argmax_{ς}(E_{Ψ,η}(V[>]))              :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    ς = solve_{ς}(E_{Ψ,η}(D_{m}V[>]*(Ψ - R)))   :: [id=foc]
}

In the fragment s is the savings allocated, m is \(m'\), the derivative term D_{m}V[>] is \(W'\), and E_{Ψ,η} is the expectation \(\mathbb{E}\) over the declared distribution of the shocks, under which \(W'(m')\,(\Psi - R)\) is assumed integrable. The solve_{ς} statement determines the share as a root of the residual in its argument (Appendix C R8) and states nothing at a corner. A method that solves the first-order condition must check both corners before accepting an interior root; the declared set is what tells it where the corners are. In the first spelling of §4.1 the two-bound line above is instead attached as its property to the maximization statement written without !doc, :: [id=optimality.foc], and the block is accepted, the condition with both corners printing under the Argmax operation.

docs.title: 6 Notation in the literature
docs.text:
The Kuhn–Tucker conditions with complementary slackness are stated in the standard texts on constrained optimization: Nocedal and Wright (2006, Theorem 12.1), whose condition (12.34e) is named the complementarity condition, and Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004, §5.5.2–5.5.3). The perpendicular sign for a pair of inequalities with a zero product is the notation of the complementarity-problem literature: Ferris and Pang (1997, §2.1) write the problem as \(0 \le x \perp F(x) \ge 0\) and explain the sign as adding the equation \(x^{\mathsf T} F(x) = 0\) to the stated inequalities; Cottle, Pang and Stone (1992) treat the linear problem in the form of the three conditions, and Facchinei and Pang (2003) the general theory. In economics, Brumm and Grill (2014, §2.1) write the borrowing constraint of their equilibrium conditions as \(0 \le b - \underline{b} \perp \mu \ge 0\) with the sign denoting orthogonality.

The notation entered computational economics through the complementarity formulation of equilibrium (Mathiesen 1985), the GAMS and PATH software (Rutherford 1995; Dirkse and Ferris 1995), and the toolkits for models with occasionally binding constraints. Dynare up to version 6 attaches the bound to an equation with the mcp tag; from version 7 it writes the bound after the equation separated by ⟂ (U+27C2, or _|_), with the residual positive at a lower bound, zero between the bounds, and negative at an upper bound, the convention of §3 (Dynare Team 2026, §4.12). Dolo writes an arbitrage equation as rhs-lhs ⟂ lb <= x <= ub and states the same sign at a binding lower bound (EconForge 2024).

In dynamic programming the same condition is usually written without the sign. Ljungqvist and Sargent (2018, §17.5 and §18.5.2) write the Euler equation of a household with a borrowing constraint as an inequality that holds with equality when savings are positive; Christiano and Fisher (2000) and Guerrieri and Iacoviello (2015) state the Kuhn–Tucker conditions of the investment constraint in equilibrium models, and Swarbrick (2021, §2) reviews the solution methods; Maliar, Maliar and Winant (2021, §4.1) rewrite the Kuhn–Tucker conditions of the constrained consumption problem as a single equation for solution by a neural network. Carroll (2006, §2.2) inverts the first-order condition on an exogenous grid of end-of-period assets, his equations 17 and 18 being the candidate and the cash on hand at each saving of §4, and handles the borrowing constraint by the segment from the origin to the first grid point (§4.2.2, equations 28 and 29); Hintermaier and Koeniger (2010) extend the method to occasionally binding constraints among endogenous variables. Dobrescu and Shanker (2024) define the inverse Euler problem on the observables, the post-decision states joined with the Kuhn–Tucker multipliers (§2.1, Definition 1; an observable is not a quantity the agent observes), pair the first-order condition with complementary slackness (§3, conditions (3) and (4)), index the pieces of the exogenous grid by the set of binding constraints (§4.1, equation (5)), give the invertibility results in §4.2 (Claim 4.1, Theorem 4.1 and Claim 4.2), and lay a piece out in any variables in one-to-one correspondence with its observables (§4.3); the one-dimensional case is the declared multiplier of §4.2. Their later paper (Dobrescu and Shanker 2026, p. 10) appends the constrained region, written as consumption values, to the endogenous grid, which is the corner of §4.3.
