The view is a sheet, the printed form every view of the package takes. Its first line is the sheet's address, BELLMAN-SYM / STAGE cons, with the version at the right margin; the second says what the object is, one stage occurrence of the file it was elaborated from; a heavy line closes the title. Each section opens with its label in capitals and a hairline to column 78, and no line of the sheet is wider. The printed record of a piece below the stage, its card, has the same width and a title over a heavy line, and opens each of its sections with a heading at the left margin instead (A piece §1).

Section What it prints PERCHES the fields of each perch with their roles, the marks ≺ ∼ ≻ standing for arrival, decision and continuation FIELDS the same fields by role, the states, the controls, the values and the shocks each on one line BLOCKS the blocks in file order, each with the arrow of its direction, its inputs, the coordinate it is read at and its outputs; a control a block names among its inputs is that coordinate and no wire, so it stands after at (The initial diagrams §3) DEFINITIONS the records by kind, with the count of each kind and the records in file order, the laws of motion and the value aggregators by their rules, so that the table says what the model is (The definitions table) GRAPHS the two initial diagrams as present or refused, and each builders graph's mapping, its inputs to its outputs, so that the sheet says what each graph maps and where each is asked for (The builders graphs) BINDINGS the three bindings, the section's hairline drawn in dashes while one is missing, each missing binding naming the verb that supplies it (The binding verbs) DIRECTIONS one line for each chain of blocks, the wires of each block grouped by perch on either side of the direction's arrow, the policy block on its own line; the card of each initial diagram prints the lines of its own direction under Source

stage.denote() answers the stage's two operators, the backward builders graph on value functions and the forward builders graph on measures, under the words backward and forward: the same two records that stage.builder.bwd.denote() and stage.builder.fwd.denote() answer on The builders graphs §3. The stage answers no signature(), since it is two operators and not one, and its sheet holds no card. Its record prints the two graphs' inputs and outputs and their builders in order, the line the policy is declared by, the conditions, the lines of the file, and at its foot the file, the perch marks the file writes and the appendix whose rules read it:

docs.title: 5 The stage's questions about itself
docs.text:
stage.fields() answers every field of the stage by its identity, with its perch, its role and its declared set.

print(stage.fields())

cons:arvl:m     ≺ arvl  state  in Xm
cons:arvl:l     ≺ arvl  state  in ℝ₊
cons:dcsn:m_d   ∼ dcsn  state  in Xm
cons:dcsn:c     ∼ dcsn  control  in ℝ₊₊
cons:cntn:a     ≻ cntn  state  in Xa
cons:cntn:V     ≻ cntn  value  in [-inf, inf)

stage.obligations() answers every condition the construction states, each under its name, with its formula or, where it has none, its sentence, and its status: [established] marks a condition that the declarations or the calibration settle, and a condition without the mark remains to be checked. A condition is required where no declaration settles it, which does not make it hold; assumed where the construction states it without deciding it; and established where the declarations or the calibration settle it, the declaration or the values it was decided on being its evidence. A status other than required is printed in brackets, and a part the package cannot derive is marked unresolved and never silently replaced. stage.diagnostics() answers nine questions about the completeness of the stage, in this order: complete_signature, whether every declared output is constructed; missing_builders, the blocks with no builder; exposed_inputs, the fields no block supplies; unused_outputs, the outputs nothing reads; forward_map, the lines that read a field of a later perch through a transition the stage does not write; builder_choice, the pairs of perches that several builders could serve; external_calls, the functions the lines call that no definition of the stage declares; unread_inputs, the value fields a backward block's header lists and no line of the block reads, each recorded as a diagnostic that names the block and the field and left out of the block's builder; and ready_for_interpretation, whether the stage is ready to be interpreted.

print(stage.obligations())
print()
print(stage.diagnostics())

Calibration establishes a condition at the bound values of the parameters (The binding verbs §2), and a condition that the symbols alone do not decide is recorded for calibration to settle. The weights of a mixture written as parameter names are one such condition: a mixture of distributions is a probability measure only if its weights lie between zero and one and sum to one. The consumption stage declares no shock, so this listing reads the consumption–savings stage applications/consumption-savings-iid/declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.bl, whose income is a mixture of a point mass at zero with weight p_zero and a lognormal draw with weight 1 - p_zero:

savings = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/consumption-savings-iid/declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.bl"))
for obligation in savings.obligations():
    if obligation.condition == "distribution-weights-are-a-probability-vector":
        print(obligation.condition)
        print(obligation.entries)
        print(obligation.explanation)

distribution-weights-are-a-probability-vector
('cons_savings_iid:distribution:y',)
the weights (p_zero, 1 - p_zero) of the Mixture declaration cons_savings_iid:distribution:y of y each lie in [0, 1] and sum to one

stage.encoding() answers a JSON-compatible mapping of this version, its definitions, its graphs, its bindings, its provenance, its conditions and its diagnostics, for a program that does not import the package; json.dumps(stage.encoding()) accepts it unchanged, and the package provides no decoder: a stage is constructed from its file, not rebuilt from the encoding.

print(sorted(stage.encoding()))

['bindings', 'builders', 'definitions', 'derived', 'diagnostics', 'initial_diagrams', 'metadata', 'name', 'obligations', 'package_version', 'provenance', 'schema', 'version']

The package holds one schema, bellman/display/stage-encoding-2.6.schema.json, whose identifier ends in /stage-encoding/2.6; it describes the whole document, and every document the package's tests store for a stage file is written under it. Under derived stand the answers the denotations give, each node with a kind spelled <namespace>.<Kind>, such as records.Wire or terms.Sym, in one of the five namespaces the schema lists, terms, semantic, records, predicates and methods. A namespace is a name of the schema and names no module of the package, so the modules may be rearranged without changing a stored document. The methods stand within the pieces where they are bound, with the values of the settings they name on a configured version, and the source text is not encoded. Each application stage that elaborates has its document <stage>.bl.stage.json in packages/bellman/tests/snapshot/corpus/<application>/, written on one line, and the specified consumption stage also has cons.bl.specified.stage.json. One record of the definitions table, the law of motion of dcsn_to_cntn, as the encoding writes it:

import json

held = stage.encoding()["definitions"]
[entry] = [item for item in held if item["identity"] == "cons:g:dcsn_to_cntn"]
print(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1, sort_keys=True)[:700])

    "__class__": "Named",
    "name": "Xm"
   }
  ],

    "__class__": "Named",
    "name": "ℝ₊₊"
   }
  ]

}

The entry of a set marked !categories (Symbol conventions §9.2) holds one key more, categories, with the identifier written after the marker, or null, and the pairs of a code and its category's name in increasing code order, {"identifier": "household_status", "codes": [ [0, "newborn"], [1, "old"] ]}; no other entry holds the key, which the schema admits as optional. Under derived the set's category map is the second denoted object of the set's card, a node of kind records.CategoryCodes with the same two fields.

A value an author writes, in a binding, in a method's settings or in the provenance, is encoded with one reserved key, so that json.dumps(stage.encoding(), allow_nan=False) also accepts the answer. A floating-point positive infinity is written {"$bellman": ["float", "inf"]}, and negative infinity and NaN "-inf" and "nan" in the same form, while the strings "inf", "-inf" and "nan" stay strings. An authored mapping that holds the key $bellman is written {"$bellman": ["mapping", …]}, with the list of its entries in their order, each a pair of the key and its encoded value, so that it is never read as a float. The rule applies to such values alone: the fixed fields of the graphs, the definitions and the methods are written as they are, and no admissible number is added or removed.

Within Python a version, and so a trellis of versions, is written and read back by the standard pickle, the form in which multiprocessing and mpi4py send an object from one process to another: what is read back equals what was written, and computes its answers again when they are asked for. Importing the module bellman.native.hypergraphs, which nearly every public name of the package imports (load_stage, load_trellis, the error classes and a bare import bellman do not) and which reading such a pickle imports, registers with the standard module copyreg a rule for types.MappingProxyType that holds in the whole Python process: pickle and copy.deepcopy, which otherwise refuse a read-only mapping, then accept any read-only mapping in that process and write it as a new read-only mapping over a copy of its entries.

From a shell, python -m bellman applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl prints the printed view of §3; --encoding prints the encoding, --dossier the printed answers of the stage with its source, and --refusals the catalogue of refusals. A command that succeeds exits with status zero; a refused stage exits with status one and its explanation.

docs.title: 6 What each check establishes
docs.text:
Check What it establishes Where it is reported Parsing The file is written in the grammar of the language. A ConstructionError under the rule syntax, with the line and a mark under the column. Construction The declarations, the block headers and the equations satisfy the rules by which a stage is constructed. A ConstructionError that names the rule and the item of the file. The analytic conditions That the declared sets contain the values and that each expectation is finite; the stage states no condition on whether a maximum is attained. stage.obligations(), each condition required or established; construction establishes none that the declarations do not settle. The numerical checks That a chosen routine approximates the solution adequately. Outside the package, with the routine.

Success at one level establishes none of the levels below it: a stage that is constructed has solved no household problem.

docs.title: The initial diagrams
docs.text:
Summary

stage.initial holds the two initial diagrams of a stage, backward and forward: the blocks of each direction on the fields they read and write. A block is read by its id as a key of the diagram that holds it, and a line of a block by a second key. This page states what each of them answers, with every listing printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below. Used by — The builders graphs: the same blocks as the operators they denote. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

The stage holds four graphs, and two words name any one of them: its level, the field level of the initial diagrams on this page or the operator level of the builders graphs, and its direction, backward or forward, which the paths of the builders write bwd and fwd (The builders graphs §1). stage.initial.forward is the graph at the field level in the forward direction, and stage.builder.bwd the graph at the operator level in the backward direction.

An initial diagram is a graph of the stage whose boxes are the blocks of the stage file and whose wires, the typed connections along which the boxes read and write, carry fields, one graph for each direction. The backward initial diagram holds the blocks whose outputs are values or the policy's control; the forward initial diagram holds the blocks whose outputs are states of a later perch. The two are separate graphs and no path puts them in one picture. They hold no operator: the operators stand in the builders graphs.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The two diagrams
docs.text:
stage.initial answers the two diagrams, stage.initial.backward and stage.initial.forward. Its list() names the blocks of both directions, and its methods the methods bound within them, empty before methodization.

print(repr(stage.initial))
print(stage.initial.list())

dcsn_to_arvl   block, backward
policy         block, backward
arvl_to_dcsn   block, forward
dcsn_to_cntn   block, forward

docs.title: 2 One diagram
docs.text:
stage.initial.backward answers one diagram. list() names its blocks with the fields each writes; signature() names the fields supplied to the diagram and the fields it produces; denote() answers the diagram's printed record, one entry per block and the lines of the file the blocks hold; diagram() answers its drawing, a Drawing that displays in a notebook and writes SVG by svg(); graph answers the hypergraph itself, an object of DisCoPy, the diagram library the package keeps its graphs in.

print(repr(stage.initial.backward))
print(stage.initial.backward.list())
print(stage.initial.backward.signature())

docs.title: The builders graphs
docs.text:
Summary

stage.builder reaches each builder of a stage by the ordered pair of perches it joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"], and each perch reaches the builders of the edge that leaves it, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd, a path defined as one such pair. The builders stand in two builders graphs: stage.builder.bwd, the backward builders on value functions that a solution applies, and stage.builder.fwd, the forward builders on measures that a simulation applies. Each graph answers the verbs of §3 and opens to a finer grain by an attribute. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; The initial diagrams: the blocks these graphs read as operators. Used by — A builder and A piece: what a builder and an operator inside it answer. Formal account — Operators and builders: the operators these graphs denote. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

A builders graph holds the blocks of one direction as the operators they denote, one box per block. That box is the block's builder: in the backward graph an operator on value functions, in the forward graph an operator on finite measures over the states. The block and its builder share the block's id and are two objects, so that a request about the block, stage.initial.backward["cntn_to_dcsn"], and one about the builder, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"], are different requests. Reaching a builder neither solves nor simulates anything; it answers what the operator is.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The builders by their two ends
docs.text:
A builder joins two perches in order: it reads the objects of the first perch and writes those of the second, as the header of its block declares them. The block cntn_to_dcsn reads the value at the continuation perch, !cntn, and writes the value at the decision perch, !dcsn, so its builder joins cntn to dcsn. That ordered pair is the builder's identity, and stage.builder is the mapping from each pair to the builder that joins it: stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] is the backward builder from continuation to decision, whatever id its block has. The words of a pair are the three perch words "arvl", "dcsn" and "cntn", which bellman.stage exports, so that after from bellman.stage import cntn, dcsn the same builder is stage.builder[cntn, dcsn].

print(repr(stage.builder))
print(stage.builder.view())

Builders('cons', 5 by their perches)
arvl_to_dcsn   arvl → dcsn, fwd
dcsn_to_cntn   dcsn → cntn, fwd
cntn_to_dcsn   cntn → dcsn, bwd
dcsn_to_arvl   dcsn → arvl, bwd
policy         policy, bwd

The short form counts the builders. view() prints one line for each builder, the forward builders first: the id of the block; the pair, written source → target, or for the policy builder its key, policy; and the word of the builder's direction, fwd for a forward builder and bwd for a backward one. list() answers that listing itself, a mapping from the id of each block to the pair and the direction word, which stage.list() shows under builder (The stage §4); methods answers the methods bound within the builders of both graphs (Methods and places §3). The policy block joins the same two perches as the block cntn_to_dcsn, reading at the continuation perch and writing the controls at the decision perch, so the policy builder is read by a key of its own, the word "policy": stage.builder["policy"] and the attribute stage.builder.policy answer the same builder, and the pair ("cntn", "dcsn") reads the decision builder alone.

In the notation of the calculus, the five builders of the consumption stage are these; \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) is the decision operator at a policy \(\pi\) (A builder §1).

Read as Block The builder In the calculus stage.builder["arvl", "dcsn"] arvl_to_dcsn carries the measure at arrival to the measure at decision \(\mathbb M_\prec\) stage.builder["dcsn", "cntn"] dcsn_to_cntn carries the measure at decision to the measure at continuation, at a policy \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] cntn_to_dcsn constructs the value functions at decision from those at continuation, at a policy \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) stage.builder["dcsn", "arvl"] dcsn_to_arvl constructs the value functions at arrival from those at decision \(\mathbb T_\prec\) stage.builder.policy policy constructs the policy, the controls as functions of the decision state the policy builder

The title of a builder's card prints its pair and after it, in brackets, the id of its block; the policy builder's title prints its key alone, POLICY BUILDER policy:

decision = stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"]
print(repr(decision))
print(str(decision.denote()).splitlines()[0])

Builder('cons', 'cntn_to_dcsn')
STAGE cons / BACKWARD BUILDER cntn → dcsn (cntn_to_dcsn)

The short form of a builder names the id of its block; A builder §1 prints the whole card. A pair that no builder joins is refused with a KeyError that names every builder of the stage by its pair, and the policy builder by its key, policy:

try:
    stage.builder["cntn", "arvl"]
except KeyError as refusal:
    print(refusal.args[0])

stage 'cons': no builder joins cntn → arvl; the builders are arvl → dcsn, dcsn → cntn, cntn → dcsn, dcsn → arvl, policy

A pair that two builders join, as two forward blocks from arrival to decision may, is refused in the same way, and the refusal names the two builders, each with the key of its graph that reads it by the id of its block (§3). Where the construction refused the graph of one direction, a pair of that direction raises the construction's refusal, NotConstructed (Refusals), while the pairs of the other direction still answer.

The declared builders, the operators the blocks of the stage file denote as elaboration builds them, are read by the same pairs through stage.declared: stage.declared["cntn", "dcsn"], stage.declared.policy and stage.declared.bwd answer as stage.builder does. The two differ as soon as a methods file adds a line: a derivative line the file adds stands at the Evaluation of the operative builder and not at the declared one's, and the lines of a solution method stand in the operative builder in place of the stage file's, stage.declared keeping each builder as the stage file states it (Methodization §5; Binding verbs; A builder §2). The card of a declared builder prints no binding, nor do the cards of the blocks and the lines of the initial diagrams, so that no binding changes them; their methods answers the methods the stage binds within them, which the cards of stage.builder print.

docs.title: 2 The perch paths
docs.text:
Each perch of the stage is an object of its own, stage.arvl, stage.dcsn and stage.cntn, and its builder reaches the builders of the edge that leaves it, the step from that perch to the next: fwd is the forward builder of the edge, which carries the measure at the perch to the measure at the next perch, and bwd its backward builder, which constructs the value functions at the perch from those at the next perch. At the decision perch, policy also reaches the policy builder. Each path is defined as one key of stage.builder and nothing else, so a path and its pair never disagree.

Path The key it reads The builder stage.arvl.builder.fwd stage.builder["arvl", "dcsn"] \(\mathbb M_\prec\) stage.arvl.builder.bwd stage.builder["dcsn", "arvl"] \(\mathbb T_\prec\) stage.dcsn.builder.fwd stage.builder["dcsn", "cntn"] \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) stage.dcsn.builder.bwd stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) stage.dcsn.builder.policy stage.builder["policy"], which stage.builder.policy also reads the policy builder stage.cntn.builder.fwd none refused: the forward pass leaves the stage at continuation, and the connector identifies the measure at continuation with the next stage's arrival measure stage.cntn.builder.bwd none refused: no value is built at continuation, and the connector identifies the continuation value with the next stage's arrival value

list() names the paths of one perch, each with the key it reads, in a listing keyed by the path, and prints none at continuation, which no edge of the stage leaves:

perches = {"arrival": stage.arvl, "decision": stage.dcsn, "continuation": stage.cntn}
for name, perch in perches.items():
    print(name)
    print(perch.builder.list())
print(stage.dcsn.builder.bwd == stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"])

arrival
stage.arvl.builder.fwd   arvl → dcsn
stage.arvl.builder.bwd   dcsn → arvl
decision
stage.dcsn.builder.fwd      dcsn → cntn
stage.dcsn.builder.bwd      cntn → dcsn
stage.dcsn.builder.policy   policy
continuation
none
True

The two paths at continuation are refused with the reasons of the table:

for word in ("fwd", "bwd"):
    try:
        getattr(stage.cntn.builder, word)
    except AttributeError as refusal:
        print(refusal)

stage 'cons': the forward pass leaves the stage at continuation, so `stage.cntn.builder.fwd` names no builder; the connector identifies the measure at continuation with the next stage's arrival measure
stage 'cons': no value is built at continuation, so `stage.cntn.builder.bwd` names no builder; the connector identifies the continuation value with the next stage's arrival value

The arrival perch refuses policy in the same way, since the policy builder stands at decision. A terminal stage writes no forward block from decision to continuation, so it refuses stage.dcsn.builder.fwd; the bequest stage of the durables application is one:

bequest = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/durables/declaration/stages/bequest/bequest.bl"))
try:
    bequest.dcsn.builder.fwd
except AttributeError as refusal:
    print(refusal)

stage 'bequest': no builder joins dcsn → cntn; like a terminal stage, the stage writes no forward block from decision to continuation, so `stage.dcsn.builder.fwd` names no builder

On a branching stage the decision edge still has one forward builder, which writes one measure for each branch: stage.dcsn.builder.fwd of the retirement choice applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/ret_choice/ret_choice.bl writes the measures μ_work≻ and μ_retire≻ (Branching).

docs.title: 3 The two graphs
docs.text:
stage.builder.bwd is the backward builders graph, the builders a solution applies, on value functions, and stage.builder.fwd the forward builders graph, the builders a simulation applies, on measures; the policy builder stands in the backward graph. A builder is also a key of its graph by the id of its block, stage.builder.bwd["cntn_to_dcsn"], which reaches each of two builders that join one pair.

print(repr(stage.builder.bwd))
print(repr(stage.builder.fwd))

The policy stands on no wire into the decision builder: the decision builder is the operator at a policy, and the policy's type is printed once, on the output of the policy builder, 𝑐(m_d) above.

Read as one operator, the backward graph takes the value functions supplied at the continuation perch to those of the arrival perch, the stage's contribution to the Bellman operator. Its wires carry value functions, or sets of functions where an operation admits several: an operation of the kind Argmax, whose output is the set of maximizing policies, and an operation whose output is among the unknowns of its own rule, such as identification:Pullback, the identification of the policy builder once the methods file has brought the lines of the endogenous grid method, which equates the policy at the cash on hand of each saving with the candidate consumption there (A builder §2; Operations §§1 and 4). An exact evaluation keeps such a set as it is, selecting no member. The policy builder states the policy, and which policy stands at the decision builder in a computation is stated at methodization. The policy is read where the control appears: in the law of motion, the aggregator and a conditional distribution of a decision builder, and in the push-forward of a forward decision builder, each of which the builder is stated at. An evaluation reads, selects and inserts no policy: it returns the field's function, and a set of feasible policies as that same set. The backward graph's printed record:

docs.title: 4 The grains
docs.text:
The grain of a graph is how far its boxes are opened. The stored graphs are at the builder grain, one box per block. primitives answers the same graph with every builder opened into its primitive operators, the finest boxes the construction makes, and sub_builders the graph with each line marked !node kept as a box of its own, a sub-builder. Each answers the same verbs as the graph, and a box at a finer grain is read by its whole name as a key of the graph at that grain.

print(repr(stage.builder.bwd.primitives))
print(stage.builder.bwd.primitives.list())
print(repr(stage.builder.bwd.primitives["cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation"]))

BuildersGraph('cons', 'backward', primitives)
1  cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback          primitive
2  cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation       primitive  → 𝑉
3  cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation        primitive  → 𝑉
1  dcsn_to_arvl:Pullback          primitive
2  dcsn_to_arvl:Aggregation       primitive  → 𝑉
3  dcsn_to_arvl:Evaluation        primitive  → 𝑉≺
1  policy:Pullback                primitive
2  policy.optimality:Aggregation  primitive
3  policy.optimality:Argmax       primitive  → 𝑐
4  policy:Evaluation              primitive  → 𝑐
Operator('cons', 'cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation')

A primitive operator's name is its builder and its kind, cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback, with a number where one builder holds several of one kind; an operator that realizes one line of the file carries that line's address in place of the bare builder, policy.optimality:Aggregation. Operations lists the kinds an operator can be. A box that acts on every value function its block reads on one base carries no field in its name, whether that is one function or several: cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback and dcsn_to_arvl:Pullback each act on the one value their block reads. Where two boxes of one kind and one law of motion remain in one builder, because they act on functions of different states, each keeps in its name the field it acts on; no stage under applications/ has two such boxes. The address of a line is the stable name: adding a statement to a file can merge two boxes of one kind into one box, whose name is then the builder's and no longer the line's, while the line's address is unchanged, which is why methods attach to lines.

The consumption stage writes no line marked !node, so its two finer grains hold the same boxes. The smooth-ambiguity savings stage applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl marks two, the risk and the ambiguity certainty equivalents that A builder §4 reads, and its backward graph counts a different number of boxes at each grain:

sa = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl"))
backward = sa.builder.bwd
for grain, graph in (("builder", backward), ("sub-builder", backward.sub_builders),
                     ("primitive", backward.primitives)):
    print(f"{grain:<12} {len(graph.graph.boxes)} boxes")

builder      2 boxes
sub-builder  12 boxes
primitive    19 boxes

A box that a grain merges exists only at that grain, so it is not reached from the stored graph's boxes but from the graph or the builder opened at that grain. A derivative line adds no box: in the buffer-stock stage applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl, whose value line and derivative line at the arrival perch each take an expectation, the expectation of the value is the one expectation box of the arrival builder, and the derivative line is recorded at that builder's evaluation. The consumption stage declares no shock, so none of its boxes is merged.

Reaching a piece resolves its pair, its perch path or its name against the stored graphs and stores nothing, so the box returned is the box the stored graph holds. Opening a finer grain builds fresh boxes, equal to the stored ones but not the same objects:

stored  = stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"].box
again   = stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"]["pullback"].box
derived = stage.builder.bwd.primitives["cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback"].box
print("the same box twice:     ", again is stored)
print("a box of a finer grain: ", derived is stored, "but equal:", derived == stored)

the same box twice:      True
a box of a finer grain:  False but equal: True

docs.title: 5 The hypergraph
docs.text:
graph answers the graph itself, a discopy.frobenius.Hypergraph in the package's frozen subclass.

Technical details

A box of the hypergraph records only its own ends, which DisCoPy, the diagram library the package keeps its graphs in, calls ports. Each port sits on the input side or the output side of its box and carries one Sort, the type of its wire: an identity, a kind (field, function or measure), a perch, a role, a domain and, for a function, the coordinates it is written in. No box records a connection to any other box.

The graph is the table that joins the ports. It numbers the wires, gives each number one Sort, and places every port, its own and every box's, on a wire. That is the whole of a hypergraph: dom and cod, its inputs and outputs, its boxes, spider_types, the sort of each wire number, and the three tables dom_wires, box_wires and cod_wires.

A connection is a shared wire number and nothing else. Where one wire carries an output port of one box and an input port of another, the output of the first builder is an input of the second. Where one wire carries several input ports, one function is read by several builders, a wire DisCoPy calls a spider. A graph has no arrows: the direction is read from the side of the box each port sits on, which is why one wire can be read by many boxes at once.

The tables of the backward graph, each box with the wires it has an input port on and the wires it has an output port on:

graph = stage.builder.bwd.graph
for wire, sort in enumerate(graph.spider_types):
    print(f"wire {wire}: {sort.inside[0].name}")
print("dom_wires ", graph.dom_wires)
for box, (inputs, outputs) in zip(graph.boxes, graph.box_wires):
    print(f"  {box.name:<14} in {inputs}  out {outputs}")
print("cod_wires ", graph.cod_wires)

wire 0: cons:function:cntn:V
wire 1: cons:function:dcsn:V
wire 2: cons:function:arvl:V
wire 3: policy:Evaluation:c:result
dom_wires  (0,)
  cntn_to_dcsn   in (0,)  out (1,)
  dcsn_to_arvl   in (1,)  out (2,)
  policy         in (0,)  out (3,)
cod_wires  (2, 3)

docs.title: A builder
docs.text:
Summary

A builder is the operator one block denotes, reached from the perch its edge leaves, the edge being the step from that perch to the next (The builders graphs §2): stage.dcsn.builder.bwd, a path that reads the pair of perches the builder joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"]. It answers the operations inside it, its inputs and outputs, its printed record, its drawing and its kernels, and opens to a finer grain by an attribute; an operation inside it is read by its name as a key. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, and §4 from applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl; §5 binds the calibration and the settings of the portfolio application to the methodized consumption stage.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The builders graphs: the pairs and the perch paths that reach the builders, and the graphs that hold them. Used by — A piece: what an operation inside a builder answers. Formal account — Operators and builders: the operator a builder denotes. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

A builder is one box of a builders graph at the builder grain. Inside it stand the operations it applies in order, each a primitive operator such as a pullback, an aggregation or an evaluation; Operations lists the kinds. Where a line of the block is tagged !node, marking a named computation of its own, the builder also holds a sub-builder, a box that keeps that computation closed.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 What a builder answers
docs.text:
list() names the operations inside the builder in order of application, each under the key that reaches it, with its kind and the function it writes. signature() answers the functions the builder reads and writes, each with its type: the value functions alone, each on its own wire, while a derivative the file states for a value stands at the builder's evaluation and on no wire; for the decision builder it is the signature of the operator at a policy, and it names no policy.

decision = stage.dcsn.builder.bwd
print(repr(decision))
print(decision.list())
print(decision.signature())

Builder('cons', 'cntn_to_dcsn')
1  Pullback     primitive
2  Aggregation  primitive  → 𝑉
3  Evaluation   primitive  → 𝑉
in         𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞)
out        𝑉 : Xm → [−∞, ∞)

A builder at a policy is a backward builder or a push-forward stated at the policy function: wherever its lines are written in the control, the policy stands in place of that coordinate. There is one such operator for each policy, all with the same inputs and outputs, which is why the calculus writes the policy as a subscript on the decision operator, and why policy iteration, which holds the policy fixed while it computes the value under that policy, can be stated at all. Its signature() therefore says nothing about the policy, whose type is printed on the policy's own wire, the output of the policy builder (§2), and on no line of the builder at a policy. The name the builder uses for the policy is a free name, declared by no header of the builder: the elaboration resolves it to the line of the policy block that defines it, and the function that stands in its place in a computation is supplied later, by the method or by the realization, the later step in which a numerical routine is supplied for each operator, as calibration supplies the value of a parameter. The policy is not a parameter of the model, one of the declared constants that stage.par lists (Parameters and settings).

denote() answers the builder's printed record, its card: the functions it reads and writes, the policy it is stated at, the law of motion it reads, the operations within it with their rules, the conditions the construction has not established, and the lines of the file it realizes. print(decision) prints the same card.

  Γ     cons:correspondence:Γ
  𝑔≻    cons:g:dcsn_to_cntn
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The card's title names the stage, the builder's direction and the builder by the pair of perches it joins, cntn → dcsn, with the id of its block in brackets, while the policy builder's card is titled by its key, POLICY BUILDER policy (The builders graphs §1). The card's Operations section lists the operations within the builder, one entry each, with a blank line between two entries. An entry opens with its number and its name; the next line gives its inputs after in: and its outputs after out:, out: standing at column 40, or on the next line where the inputs or the outputs leave it no room there; a short line follows, and every short line of a card ends at the same column; then the rule the operation applies stands after rule:, with the set on which it holds, on …, at the right margin or under the rule; on an evaluation, a derivative the file states for the value stands after derivative:, with the line that states it and its condition marginal-reading. The lines state the wiring: the name after out: in one entry is the name after in: in the entry that reads it, and an output the file does not name is written, in the entry that reads it, as the number of the entry that produced it, (1), as a paper cites an equation by its number. Where the operations form a chain, each one's outputs being the next one's inputs, the same wires in the same order, the entries stand in the order they are applied; otherwise each stands after every entry that writes a wire it reads. On a builders graph's card each builder is an entry with no number, and its operations stand beneath it, numbered and set further in (The builders graphs §3).

diagram() answers the drawing of the builder's interior, a Drawing; obligations() the conditions of its operations and of the lines it realizes; methods the methods bound at it or inside it, empty before methodization; and box the DisCoPy box itself, an object of the diagram library the package keeps its graphs in (The initial diagrams §2). In the drawing an aggregation is labeled Value aggregation 𝐺 where it produces value functions at a perch, as in the two backward builders, and Apply 𝐺 otherwise, as in the policy builder; where one builder holds several aggregations, as the policy builder does once the methods file has brought the lines of the endogenous grid method, the label names the statement each aggregates, Apply 𝐺 of the statement InvEuler, so that the two aggregations are told apart. The names of the operations carry the same distinction (§2). A pullback is labeled by the function it pulls back and the map it pulls back along: Pullback of 𝑉≻ along 𝑔 at 𝑐 in the decision builder, and Pullback of 𝑐 along 𝑚_d≻ for the identification of the methodized policy builder, which pulls the policy back along the map from each saving to its cash on hand and not along the law of motion (§2). A stage's two builders graphs, of which each builder is a box, are also read interactively in Google's Model Explorer, where each builder opens to its operations and a selected operation shows the rows of its card; the drawing remains the figure of this page (The view in Model Explorer).

docs.title: 2 The policy builder
docs.text:
stage.dcsn.builder.policy is the policy builder, the builder whose outputs are the controls. Its signature() carries the policy's type, the set of feasible policies where the file declares a feasibility correspondence, Γ here, beside the value functions it reads. The clause c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d) is the feasibility condition: the consumption the policy chooses lies in the feasible set that the correspondence Γ(x) := (0, x] of the file gives. On the symbolic stage the builder holds the maximization of the stage file's line optimality as three operations, the pullback of the continuation value along the law of motion, the aggregation of the objective and the maximization itself, and then its Evaluation:

print(repr(stage.dcsn.builder.policy))
print(stage.dcsn.builder.policy.signature())
print(stage.dcsn.builder.policy.list())

Builder('cons', 'policy')
in         𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞)
out        𝑐(m_d) : 𝒫({c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊) | c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d)})
1  Pullback                primitive
2  optimality:Aggregation  primitive
3  optimality:Argmax       primitive  → 𝑐
4  Evaluation              primitive  → 𝑐

The methods file beside the stage file, methods.bl, types the endogenous grid method on this builder, with its grid of savings and its handler, and brings the three lines by which the method computes the policy (Methodization §1). After methodization the operative policy builder holds those lines as its operations, each named by the id of its line, while the maximization stays its declared line, which stage.declared.policy holds and the card prints under Declared (Methods and places §3); the signature gains the method, the grid and the handler. The listing reads a second elaboration of the file with its methods file, so that stage stays symbolic for the rest of the page:

methodized = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl",
                                        ["applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl"]))
policy = methodized.dcsn.builder.policy
print(policy.signature())
for name in policy.list():
    print(name)

in         𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞)
out        𝑐(m_d) : 𝒫({c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊) | c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d)})
method     !egm
grid       !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
handler    "cons-port:egm"
InvEuler:Aggregation
grid:Aggregation
identification:Pullback
Evaluation

The four operations state the policy as the lines of the methods file's block policy write it, and Operations §4 states how each such line is read. InvEuler:Aggregation is formed by the candidate line c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0, which states the candidate consumption at each saving from the derivative term D_{a}V[>], the derivative of the continuation value in savings. Its clause ⟂ a >= 0, the complementary-slackness condition of the borrowing constraint, admits the interior value 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)) alone at a positive saving and every positive value up to it at zero saving, so the operation's output is typed as a correspondence, a map to sets, Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊ (Constraints §4.3). grid:Aggregation is formed by the grid line m_d[>] = a + c[>], the cash on hand at each saving and each value admitted there. identification:Pullback is formed by the identification c = c[>]: it reads the policy at that cash on hand and equates it with the candidate, a relation that must hold at every saving and every value admitted there, and its signature() answers the set of the feasible policies that satisfy it, which may be empty or hold several. Evaluation places that set in its declared carrier and selects no member; the handler of the method, cons-port:egm, stores its numerical representation of the function and asserts nothing about the set (Methods and places §2; Methodization §5).

print(policy["InvEuler:Aggregation"].signature())
print(policy["identification:Pullback"].signature())

in         𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞)
out        𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊
in         𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊
in         𝑚_d≻ : Xa ⇉ Xm
out        {f ∈ {c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊
           ) | c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d)} | ∀ a ∈ Xa, x ∈ 𝑐≻(a): (f(a + x) = x)} :
           𝒫({c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊) | c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d)})

A line marked !doc forms no operation, as the maximization objective of the portfolio stage applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/port/port.bl is marked. An argmax line that is not marked !doc forms an operation of the kind Argmax, whose output is the set of maximizing policies, as optimality:Argmax does above and choice:Argmax does in the policy builder of applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/ret_choice/ret_choice.bl.

docs.title: 3 A forward builder at a policy
docs.text:
stage.dcsn.builder.fwd carries the measure at decision forward through the law of motion at the policy. It answers the same verbs, and state_choice_measure() besides: the joint measure of the decision state and the control under the policy the builder is stated at, the measure against which a simulated moment of a control is an integral.

print(stage.dcsn.builder.fwd.list())
print(stage.dcsn.builder.fwd.state_choice_measure())

1  Pushforward  primitive  → μ≻
mu
  ↦ measure on {m_d, c ∈ Xm × ℝ₊₊ | c ∈ Γ(m_d)} given by
    B ↦ mu({m_d ∈ Xm | (m_d ↦ (m_d, c(m_d)))(m_d) ∈ B})

docs.title: 4 Grains and keys
docs.text:
primitives answers the builder with every sub-builder opened and sub_builders the builder with each !node line kept as a box; each answers the same verbs. An operation is read by its name after the builder's own, the kind compared without regard to case, decision["pullback"], or by the whole name. A tuple of keys reads one level further down per element: the first names a sub-builder, the next an operation inside it. The consumption stage writes no !node line, so this section reads the smooth-ambiguity savings stage, whose decision builder computes a risk certainty equivalent risk_ce and an ambiguity certainty equivalent ambiguity_ce, each marked !node.

sa = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl"))
print(sa.dcsn.builder.bwd.list())
print(repr(sa.dcsn.builder.bwd["risk_ce"]))
print(repr(sa.dcsn.builder.bwd["risk_ce", "expectation:1"]))
print(repr(sa.dcsn.builder.bwd.primitives))

A sub-builder is one named intermediate result: the construction keeps the operations of a line marked !node inside a box of their own, named <block id>.<line id>, and the two sub-builders are the first two boxes inside the decision builder. docs.title: 5 The kernels of a builder
docs.text:
kernels() answers one record of the builder's kernels, from which a numerical operator is built with no stage in hand: each operation in the order it is applied, with its printed kernel and the wires it reads and writes, and, where its kernel is an explicit function, its function with the names of its arguments and outputs, a derivative term the row reads standing among the arguments, G_policy_InvEuler(V≻, a, D_{a}(V≻); ρ) → c≻ for the candidate line InvEuler, or, for a row that states a relation its output satisfies with no explicit side, such as the identification of a policy block, whose compile_kernel() is refused under kernel-target (A piece §2), its printed relation; then the parameters with their values and the declared sets its operations are read on. The record refers to no stage, so cloudpickle saves it and another process reads it. The endogenous-grid step of the portfolio–consumption application is built from two such records of a specified version by one call of asva, the numerical toolkit installed beside the package, asva.egm(specified.dcsn.builder.policy.kernels(), specified.dcsn.builder.bwd.kernels(), savings, evaluation), the caller reading the savings grid and the evaluation grid from the settings. A piece §2 gives one operation's kernel as a function, and the lesson tutorials/topics/kernels.ipynb of the repository composes one step of the decision builder from its two kernels, compiles them with Numba and passes the values of a second calibration without compiling again; Solutions at the perches describes the dictionaries in which a solver keeps what the kernels compute.

kernels().grids holds the realized grid of each place within the builder that types a grid, by the address of the place: the grid's points at the bound settings and calibration, a RealizedGrid with the word of its outer constructor, its coordinates in their declared order and its finite points in the order they are constructed, a repeated point held once (Methodization §3.2 gives the grid entry). For a sub-builder it holds the places of the sub-builder's own node, and a grid typed at a declared function, outside every builder, stands in the record of no builder. On a version with no bound settings grids is None, since the counts and the bounds of a grid are settings. Where the construction cannot establish a grid's points and every property the grid requires, the place holds instead the Refusal that says why, under the rule grid-requirement and at the position of the entry, and the record prints it after not constructed:. Among the reasons are a coordinate of the place that no factor names; a factor of a feasible control written in !Cartesian without !Fibred, which is a family of grids, one at each state, and no one grid; and a fibre of two controls, whose joint sampling is unsupported. The construction supplies no default in any of these cases. The listing reads the version methodized of §2, calibrated and configured here:

print(methodized.dcsn.builder.bwd.kernels().grids)
methodized.calibrate("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml")
methodized.configure("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml")
for builder in (methodized.dcsn.builder.policy, methodized.dcsn.builder.bwd):
    for address, grid in builder.kernels().grids.items():
        print(f"{address:<22} {grid}")

None
policy                 !Cartesian on (a), 800 points: (1e-06,), (0.12515744430538173,), (0.2503138886107635,), …, (100,)
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate  !Cartesian on (m_d), 100 points: (0.01,), (0.11090909090909092,), (0.21181818181818182,), …, (10,)

The grid of savings of the endogenous grid method, !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), is the 800 equally spaced points from a_min to a_max that the settings give, and the grid of resources at the decision builder's Evaluation, !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m)), is the 100 equally spaced points from m_min to m_max; a coordinate prints as an integer where its value is one.

docs.title: A piece
docs.text:
Summary

A piece with no interior is either an operation inside a builder, one primitive operator, or an authored line inside a block. Each is read by its name from the piece that holds it and answers its printed record, its inputs and outputs, its conditions and its methods; an operation also answers the kernel it applies and that kernel as a Python function. §5 states the conventions by which every card is read, and §6 the types a wire and an operation answer. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — A builder: the builder whose operations are read here; The initial diagrams: the blocks whose lines are read here. Formal account — Operators and builders: the operators a kind of operation realizes. See also — Operations: the kinds an operation can be; API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 An operation
docs.text:
An operation is read from its builder by its name after the builder's own, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"], or from a graph at the primitive grain by its whole name, stage.builder.bwd.primitives["cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback"]. Its denote() answers its card: the functions it reads and writes with their types, the law of motion at the policy where the operation reads one, the rule it applies, the conditions the construction has not established, the line of the file it realizes and the records of the definitions table the card names. print(pullback) prints the same card.

pullback = stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"]
print(repr(pullback))
print(pullback.denote())

A card has its title over a heavy line; then its sections, each opening with its heading at the left margin, its content two columns in and a blank line between two sections; then a light line, the sections Source and Definitions referenced, and a heavy line that closes it. No line passes column 78, and a section with nothing to print is not printed. An operation's card has, in this order: Signature, its input wires under in and its output wires under out, each with its type, and a short line between the two; Where, the local names its rules use, each stated once: the law of motion at the policy where the operation reads one, with its type and its rule at a point, the law of motion read at one label of a branching block, the outputs of a law named by their fields, and the set of admitted pairs of a block that declares a multiplier (Constraints §4.2); Rule, the rule the operation applies; Conditions, the memberships the rule needs that the construction has not established; on a methodized version, Method, the method bound within the piece with its handler and, at the right margin, the place it is bound at, and Options, the method's options with the values of the settings they name, both left out on the card of a block, of a line and of a piece read through stage.declared, whose methods answers them; Source, which names the file once and gives each line the operation realizes, as the author wrote it, after its line number, with a section for each file where the lines stand in the stage file and its methods file; and Definitions referenced, the key of each declared name the card writes, followed by the file and the line where the methods file defines the name. A line of the file stands once on a card, under Source, and what it denotes stands in the sections above; the identity of a wire is on the record and in no column of the card.

Read along the wires of the decision builder: the continuation value 𝑉≻ is a function of savings a; the pullback composes it with the law of motion, so that 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ is a function of (m_d, c); the aggregation applies 𝐺; the policy indexes the pullback, the aggregation or the conditional distribution in which it occurs; and the evaluation returns 𝑉 under its field name as a function of m_d alone, with the derivative that the line cntn_to_dcsn.marginal states, D_{m_d}𝑉(m_d) = 𝑑𝑢(𝑐(m_d)), recorded beside it.

denote() is the one verb below the stage that answers a piece's record: an operation, a builder, a sub-builder, a builders graph at any grain, an initial diagram, a block and a line each answer it, and the definitions table answers it for one of its records, stage.definitions.denote(identity) (The definitions table §3). The record holds the mathematical structure of what the piece denotes: the typed wires, the image, the kernel with the statements it denotes and the objects they denote, the hypotheses, the conditions and, on a methodized version, the method bound within the piece, except on a block, a line and a piece read through stage.declared, whose records hold no binding; an aggregation's record also states, under affine, in which of its value inputs the map is affine, V in V≻ on the decision builder. It displays itself, so print(piece) and print(piece.denote()) write the same card, and the card is that record printed, never made by taking a printed line apart.

signature() answers the operation's inputs and outputs, the same wires with their types that the card's Signature section names; the identity of each wire stands on the record it answers, under .inputs and .outputs, and in no printed column. list() answers an empty listing, since an operation has no interior, and box answers the DisCoPy box, an object of the diagram library the package keeps its graphs in (The initial diagrams §2).

print(pullback.signature())
print(pullback.list())

in         𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞)
out        𝑉≻∘𝑔(·, 𝑐) : Xm → [−∞, ∞)
none

Two kinds of operation are the two actions of one law of motion 𝑔. A pullback composes a function with 𝑔, \(V \mapsto V \circ g\); a push-forward carries a measure through the same 𝑔, \(\mu \mapsto g_\# \mu\), the measure that gives a set \(B\) the value \(\mu(g^{-1}(B))\). With the pairing \(\langle \mu, V \rangle = \int V \, \mathrm d\mu\) the two satisfy \(\langle g_\# \mu, V \rangle = \langle \mu, V \circ g \rangle\): the average of 𝑉 under the measure the law of motion produces is the average, under the original measure, of 𝑉 at the law of motion's output. That change-of-variables identity holds for bounded measurable 𝑉 and wherever the two integrals are absolutely finite (Operators and builders §3), and it is why one word is used backward and the other forward. It is the deterministic statement: where a block reads a shock, the integral over that shock is a separate box on each side, an expectation in the backward graph and a box that extends the measure by the declared distribution in the forward graph. The consumption stage declares no shock, so neither box appears in its graphs. The push-forward's card:

docs.title: 2 The kernel
docs.text:
kernel() answers the kernel an operation applies, the pointwise function it reads from the definitions table and from which the card's Where and Rule sections are written: the law of motion 𝑔 for a pullback or a push-forward, the aggregator 𝐺 for an aggregation. Its attribute origins holds the records of the definitions table it is read from.

aggregation = stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["aggregation"]
print(aggregation.kernel())
print([record.identity for record in aggregation.kernel().origins])

𝐺 of cntn_to_dcsn: 𝐺(V≻, m_d, c) = 𝑢(c) + V≻
output V; unused m_d
['cons:G:cntn_to_dcsn']

The first argument of 𝐺, V≻, is its value input: the scalar continuation value the aggregator receives once the continuation value function has been composed with the law of motion, the continuation value at the saving a = m_d - c. The line outputs (V); unused m_d; V reads V≻, c records that m_d does not enter the output and then names the arguments the output reads: 𝑉 reads the value input and consumption. An aggregator with several outputs answers this way whenever they read different arguments, so that what one component depends on is read and not inferred from the list of unused arguments.

In a branching block, a pullback of one branch applies the complete law of motion, so its kernel() prints the components of every branch, with the coordinate whose value selects the branch, the label coordinate, among the unused arguments. The record's attribute section holds the kernel of that law read at the branch's label, the map the card's Where section defines, 𝑔_keep≻ for the branch keep of the durables model's tenure.bl: the same title, the law's arguments without the label coordinate, and the components of the fields the branch writes with their outputs and what each reads, printed by the same rules. section holds no Python text, since compile_kernel() compiles the complete law, and it is None on every other operation.

On a symbolic version as on a calibrated one, compile_kernel() answers the kernel as a Python function, whose arguments are those of the printed kernel in the same order, followed by the parameters the kernel reads. It evaluates the kernel at points; it neither integrates, nor chooses, nor solves.

import inspect

calibrated = stage.calibrate({"ρ": 2.0})
aggregator = calibrated.dcsn.builder.bwd["aggregation"].compile_kernel()
print(inspect.signature(aggregator))

(V_cntn, m_d, c, ρ)

The record kernel() answers holds under python the source text of one plain Python function, and compile_kernel() executes that text in a namespace holding NumPy alone and answers the function, which is attached to no stage. Its arguments are the kernel's own, in the printed order, followed by each parameter the kernel reads, in the order of the declarations, whose names parameters holds; a derived parameter is no argument, since the function assigns it from its definition, and the declared parameters that definition reads are arguments in its place; parameter_values holds the values the version's calibration binds to them, None on a symbolic version, where the caller supplies them. The values are passed at each call, so that a new calibration needs no new function. Given numbers the function answers a number, or a tuple of numbers where the kernel has several outputs, and given NumPy arrays it answers arrays:

aggregation = calibrated.dcsn.builder.bwd["aggregation"]
g = calibrated.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"].compile_kernel()
G = aggregation.compile_kernel()
print(g(2.0, 0.5))
print(G(4.0, 2.0, 0.5, *aggregation.kernel().parameter_values))
print(aggregation.kernel().python)

1.5
2.0
# bellman kernel of cons, cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation; cons.bl sha256 e60110b0b964ce482812c558922bc7aa6eaaf14421e2e162b9f87cc7b120a667; bellman 0.1.7
# 𝐺 of cntn_to_dcsn: 𝐺(V≻, m_d, c) = 𝑢(c) + V≻
# output V; unused m_d
# parameters: ρ ∈ [1, inf)
# names: V_cntn is V≻; u is 𝑢
import numpy as np

def G_cntn_to_dcsn(V_cntn, m_d, c, ρ):
    def u(c):
        return c**(1 - ρ)/(1 - ρ)
    V = u(c) + V_cntn
    return V

g(2.0, 0.5) evaluates the law of motion at m_d = 2 and c = 0.5 and returns the saving; G(4.0, 2.0, 0.5, 2.0) evaluates the aggregator at the continuation value 4, m_d = 2 and c = 0.5, with ρ = 2 passed last, and returns 𝑉, the one output that the line outputs (V) of the printed kernel names. The comment lines of the text name the stage, the operation, the stage file with the digest of its text, the package's version, the printed rule, the Python name given to each name of the file and the declared set of each parameter; they hold no date and no value, so the text of an unchanged model does not change. The function 𝑢 that the rule calls is written inside the function, so numba.njit(G) compiles it in one call, inspect.getsource(G) prints its definition and cloudpickle saves it. The standard pickle and Numba's cache refuse a function made in memory; for them, write the text to a file of your choosing and import the function from that file. A builder answers the kernels of all its operations as one record, kernels() (A builder §5).

compile_kernel() is refused with a ConstructionError under the rule kernel-target on an operation that applies no explicit function, an evaluation among them, whose kernel() states the identity it applies, and on a row that states a relation with no explicit side, the identification c = c[>]; an authored line refuses both verbs (§4). It is refused under the rule kernel-form on an operation whose kernel calls a function the stage file defines by a derivative or an inverse, 𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢) or 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 := Inv(𝑑𝑢), and the refusal names the call. A row that reads a derivative term compiles, the term among the function's arguments: the candidate line InvEuler of the policy builder reads D_{a}V[>], its kernel() prints the map with the term, (D_{a}𝑉≻, a) ↦ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻), and its compile_kernel() answers the function G_policy_InvEuler(V_cntn, a, argument, ρ), whose third argument takes the value of the term, since 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is defined in closed form (Expression forms §3).

docs.title: 3 Conditions and methods
docs.text:
obligations() answers every condition the operation owns, each with its status; a condition that the declarations or the calibration settle is marked [established], as the one below is. methods answers the method bound at the operation, empty before methodization.

pushforward = stage.dcsn.builder.fwd["pushforward"]
print(repr(pushforward))
print(pushforward.obligations())
print(pushforward.methods)

Operator('cons', 'dcsn_to_cntn:Pushforward')
range-compatibility   m_d − c(m_d) ∈ Xa   [established]
none

The one condition here is established: the declared sets decide that the law of motion at the policy takes its values in Xa, and the declaration is its evidence.

docs.title: 4 An authored line
docs.text:
A line of a block is read from its block by its id, stage.initial.backward["cntn_to_dcsn", "value"], and answers denote(), signature(), obligations() and methods; The initial diagrams §3 prints one. A line states a relation and applies no rule, so it refuses kernel() and compile_kernel(): the operation that realizes it is the piece that applies a rule. A line marked !doc has no box and answers denote() and methods alone; the consumption stage marks none, and its maximization optimality is a line with a box, whose card prints the line as the file writes it.

optimality = stage.initial.backward["policy", "optimality"]
print(repr(optimality))
print(optimality.denote())

docs.title: 5 Reading a card
docs.text:
These conventions are read across every card and every printed signature, and written on none of them.

  • x ↦ e binds the point, and an operator acting pointwise writes its image as x ↦ ….
  • ↦ maps a point to its image in a Defines line and in a rule; the file's := and its ids stand only in the lines of Source, as the author wrote them.
  • The policy is a free name: there is one operator for each policy, and that policy indexes the pullback, the aggregation or the conditional distribution in which it occurs. A decision builder's card names it under At, never as a parameter or as an input wire.
  • An evaluation is the identity on a function, or on a set of feasible policies, into its declared carrier.
  • Under Operations the pieces stand in the order of application, each after every piece that writes a wire it reads, and ∘ applies its right factor first.
  • A card's Conditions section carries no status word: the words required, assumed and established, and the evidence of a condition the declarations settle, stand on obligations() (§3).
  • A set written {f ∈ … | ∀ a ∈ Xa, x ∈ 𝑐≻(a): …}, as the identification's signature() prints it (A builder §2), is the set of the functions that satisfy the rule at every admitted pair, possibly empty, with no selection made.
  • A push-forward's rule gives the image measure at a set B, μ≻(B) = μ({m_d ∈ Xm | 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)) ∈ B}), the measure of the points the law of motion at the policy sends into B; and λ⊗P is the extension of a measure λ by the declared distribution P of a shock, whose rule integrates P against λ.
  • A mark at the right margin of a line is the region note on … of a rule, the set on which the rule holds, or the address at which a method is bound; undeclared in a type is a set the file does not declare; and ⇉ marks a correspondence.
  • Method names the numerical method bound within the piece, which is part of what the piece denotes on the version asked; a block, a line and a piece read through stage.declared print none, and their methods answers the methods bound within them.

docs.title: 6 Types and defining expressions
docs.text:
A wire's type is derived from the declarations when it is asked for and stored nowhere. The continuation input of the decision builder goes through seven steps from the file to the printed type:

  1. The file declares V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu.
  2. The declaration introduces a field, a named quantity at the continuation perch with the declared value set [-inf, inf).
  3. The builders graph has a wire for that input, whose Sort keeps the wire's identity and its field classification.
  4. The wire's mathematical type is derived from the declared sets of its ordered coordinates and its declared value set; where a control is among the coordinates, its feasibility correspondence also restricts the domain of the arguments. Here the type is the set of measurable functions from the savings set Xa, declared ℝ₊, to [-inf, inf).
  5. The query answers a structured carrier expression, which denotes that set of functions.
  6. The set itself is the carrier, and no object of the package is that set.
  7. The printed type, Xa → [−∞, ∞), is the printed form of the carrier expression.

The wire stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.signature().inputs[0] answers the derived type through .mathematical_type, a WireType with two attributes: .sort, the representation, the field classification where there is one, the ordered identities of the coordinates, the domain of the arguments and the result set; and .carrier, the structured carrier expression. The wire's .identity names the continuation input; neither the type nor the carrier identifies that particular input. A wire of an initial diagram is typed by the field it carries, printed {V≻}, and a wire of the forward graph by the finite measures on the states of its perch.

An operation's record answers its typed defining expression, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["Pullback"].denote().expression, the composition with the stage's law of motion, whose .bindings and .body are expression objects and not fragments of the printed card; denote().kernel.denoted[0] answers the .mathematical_type and the .expression of the law of motion itself. The definitions of a utility or an aggregator answer the same queries where their data determine them, and a component the package cannot resolve names the mathematical data it lacks rather than being assumed real-valued. Denoted.type and Denoted.rule are the printed forms of the carrier and of the defining expression, each computed from the object beside it, mathematical_type and expression, so that the card, the structured answer and the encoding present one object and never two readings of it. A set marked !categories (Symbol conventions §9.3) denotes a second object, its category map, and its card, stage.definitions.denote(identity), holds a second Denoted, whose expression is the set's CategoryCodes record, Definition.categories (The definitions table §2), and whose rule is the map as bellman.typing.category_codes.describe writes it, 0 ↦ newborn, 1 ↦ old (categories household_status), or (categories local to HouseholdStatus) where the marker names no identifier. Every answer of denote() whose definitions include the set holds both objects. A declaration of one real shock by N, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal or TypeIExtremeValue likewise denotes a second object, its measure at the written arguments under the symbol P_y (Shock distributions §1); the answers of denote() of the other records that read the declaration list it by its law alone, the measure standing on the declaration's own card, and the cards of the expectations and distribution extensions that read it print the law as written alone; the forward builder's card also names the measure P_y that its extension rule reads, as before.

A printed carrier, a function belonging to the set it denotes and a numerical representation of that function are three different objects. Methodization leaves the carriers unchanged, and a declared carrier says where an object must lie: it proves no measurability, finiteness or feasibility, and no numerical method's correctness. The restricted domains of the defining expressions state those requirements.

A wire that is the output of a joint choice answers two more attributes. Wire.controls names the declared controls of the policy, in the order the block writes them, and is empty on every other wire. Wire.component(name) answers the set-valued type of one of them, the set of functions of the decision state that agree, coordinate by coordinate, with some member of the joint set; it creates no wire, selects no policy, and raises KeyError for a name that is no control of the wire. A wire holds the carrier its query derived and no reference to its stage, which is how a card or an encoding is written away from the version it came from.

On a branching stage the continuation state space is the disjoint union of the branches' state spaces, \(\mathsf X_\succ = \bigsqcup_j \mathsf X_{\succ,j}\), one set for each label, named by the fields its branch writes. A function on it is the tuple \((Q_j)_j\) of functions, one on each branch's set, and a finite measure on it the tuple of measures, \(\operatorname{Meas}(\bigsqcup_j \mathsf X_{\succ,j}) \cong \prod_j \operatorname{Meas}(\mathsf X_{\succ,j})\), writing \(\operatorname{Meas}(\mathsf X)\) for the finite measures on \(\mathsf X\). Each branch value is therefore typed on its own branch's set, V_w[>] of the retirement choice on the set of a_w, and the forward builder writes one measure for each branch.

docs.title: Parameters and settings
docs.text:
Summary

stage.par answers a table of the parameters of a stage, the derived parameters the stage defines from them standing after the declared ones, and stage.settings a table of its settings; each entry is read by the name the file declares, stage.par["ρ"] and stage.settings["n_a"], and neither table can be edited. A parameter is part of the economic problem and is declared in the stage file; a setting is a numerical choice of a method, declared with its set in the methods file and valued by configuration. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, calibrated by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml, configured by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml, and methodized by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, the methods file beside the stage file, whose declarations fill the settings table's set column and whose entries fill its last three columns: the place at which each setting is read, the method there and, where the setting is a bound or a count of that place's grid, the grid's kind. The listings of §1.1 read instead the perfect-foresight stage file, applications/consumption-perfect-foresight-crra/declaration/stages/perfect_foresight/perfect_foresight.bl, which defines three derived parameters, calibrated by applications/consumption-perfect-foresight-crra/declaration/calibration/perfect_foresight.yml.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; The binding verbs: calibrate and configure, which bind the values these tables read. Used by — Methods and places: the methods that read the settings. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table; Methodization §4: the declaration of a setting and the settings file.

Parameters are the declared constants of the model, such as the risk aversion ρ, each declared in the stage file on a set and given a value by calibration; change one and the economic problem changes. Settings are the numerical choices of the methods, such as the bounds and the count of a grid, each declared in the methods file on a set and given a value by configuration; none of them is an assertion of the model. The two tables are queries: each reads the one place the stage holds what it answers, and neither keeps a copy.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The parameters
docs.text:
stage.par answers one row per declared parameter, with the set it is declared on, its value or, before calibration, the word unbound, and the description the file gives, and then one row per derived parameter (§1.1). stage.par["ρ"] answers the record of one parameter, keyed by its name as the file declares it, which prints on one line; its value is the number the calibration binds. list() answers the rows, a record that prints as the table, and view() the table as text. Since calibrate binds the stage it is called on, calibrated below is stage itself, now with its parameter's value:

print(stage.par)
calibrated = stage.calibrate("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml")
print(calibrated.par)
print(calibrated.par["ρ"])
print(calibrated.par["ρ"].value, calibrated is stage)

name  set       value    describes
ρ     [1, inf)  unbound
name  set       value  describes
ρ     [1, inf)  6.0
ρ = 6.0 : [1, inf)
6.0 True

The record is read from the parameter's declaration in the stage file and from the value calibration binds. The key is the name the file declares, and no other spelling is a key:

try:
    stage.par["rho"]
except KeyError as refusal:
    print(refusal)

"stage 'cons': 'rho' is no parameter of the stage; a parameter is read by the name the file declares, and the parameters are ρ"

docs.title: 1.1 Derived parameters
docs.text:
A derived parameter is a constant of the stage that a definition without arguments writes from the stage's parameters, such as human wealth h := 1/(1 - Γ/R); Equation parsing rules §2 gives the form, what its definition may read and the order in which the definitions are evaluated. stage.par lists the derived parameters after the declared ones, in file order, each with its definition in the column set and the description the file gives; where the definition declares the set in which its value lies, as that of q below declares (0,1), the set stands before := and the definition after it. Before calibration the value of a derived parameter is unbound. After calibration its value is its definition evaluated at the calibration values, computed each time the table is asked for and stored nowhere. The record of one derived parameter prints its definition after :=. The consumption stage file defines no derived parameter, so the listings of this section read the perfect-foresight stage file, which defines three from its four parameters: the return patience factor q, human wealth h and the natural borrowing limit L. A methods file may define a derived parameter as well, as the methods file beside that stage file defines the marginal propensity to consume κ := 1 - q (The definitions table §3). A definition in an addition, a methods file read with the stage file (The binding verbs §3), is read as the stage file's own, and it leaves the table when the addition is removed.

    "applications/consumption-perfect-foresight-crra/declaration/stages/perfect_foresight/perfect_foresight.bl"))
print(derived.par)
derived.calibrate(

print(derived.par)
print(derived.par["h"])

The calibration supplies no value for a derived parameter, since its definition gives the value. A calibration source that names a derived parameter is refused under derived-parameter, at the definition, and the refused binding leaves the stage as it was; the calibration the stage keeps holds the declared parameters alone. A definition that has no value at the calibration values, such as one that divides by zero there, is refused under the same rule, at that definition (Refusals):

from bellman.refusals import ConstructionError

try:
    derived.calibrate({"calibration": {"β": 0.9615384615384616, "ρ": 2.0, "R": 1.04, "Γ": 1.02, "h": 50.0}})
except ConstructionError as refusal:
    print(refusal)
print(derived.par["h"])
