docs.title: 2 The settings
docs.text:
stage.settings answers one row per setting, with the setting's name, the set the methods file declares it on, its configured value or the word unbound, the place at which it is read, the method typed there and, where the setting is a bound or a count of a factor of that place's grid, the grid's kind. The settings the methods file declares come first, in declaration order; a key of the settings file that no declaration names follows, with its value and the other columns empty, since it binds nothing (the last listing of this section). A method reads a setting by its name: here the grid of the representation at the decision builder's Evaluation, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m)), reads n_m, m_min and m_max as the count and the bounds of its grid of resources, and the grid of the endogenous grid method on the policy builder, grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), reads n_a, a_min and a_max as its grid of savings (Methodization §3.2). stage.settings["n_m"] answers the record of one setting, and its value is the configured value.

specified = (calibrated.methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl")
             .configure("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml"))
print(specified.settings)
print(specified.settings["n_m"])
print(specified.settings["n_m"].value)

print(len(bare.settings))

docs.title: Methods and places
docs.text:
Summary

stage.places() answers the places of a stage, the operators at which a methods file may type a method, a grid or a handler, each with its kind. methods, asked of the stage, a graph, a builder or an operation, answers the components typed within it, each read by its place's path as the methods file writes it, stage.methods["policy"]. Typing a method changes no equation of the model and runs no computation; where the method brings lines, the operative builders hold them and the declared builders keep the stage file's. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl and its methods file methods.bl, the addition beside it.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; The binding verbs: methodize, which reads the methods file with the stage file. Used by — Parameters and settings: the settings the typed methods read. See also — Method types: every method word, the kinds of place it admits and the keyword arguments the package reads; Methodization: the methods file; API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

A method names a numerical procedure for one operator of a stage, such as the endogenous grid method for the policy builder, a grid the points at which the function at the operator is stored, and a handler the routine that carries the method out. The methods file types each at a place, an operator it can name, written by its path: a block, the Evaluation that stores the block's result, an operator inside a line, a line, or a definition. The method and the grid are components of the operator's signature and the handler a binding beside them; the signature of a builder prints the three beside the functions it reads and writes, and nothing in the package executes them.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))
specified = (stage.calibrate("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml")
             .methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl")
             .configure("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml"))

docs.title: 1 The places
docs.text:
stage.places() answers one row per place, its path as a methods file writes it in the first column, address, and its kind in the second: a builder, by the id of its block; a line, by its address <block>.<line>, of the kind node where the line is marked !node and statement otherwise; an operator of one line, <block>.<line>.<operator>, of every line of a block, <block>.<operator>, or of every line of the stage, by the operator's head alone; and a definition, by its name. After the lines of the policy builder and of each backward value builder stand the places of the Evaluation that closes it, of the kind operator evaluate, where a representation of what the builder stores is typed: policy.evaluate and its one object, the policy, policy.evaluate[c], for the policy builder, and for a backward value builder the Evaluation as a whole, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate, and each object it stores, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[V] for the value function and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[D_{m_d}V] for the derivative of it that the stage's derivative line states, so that the value and its derivative may be represented together or each on a grid of its own (Methodization §2). A representation is typed at these places and at no builder. The consumption stage writes no line marked !node. The kinds are read from the objects of the stage, whatever is typed at them; the derivative operator D is listed and admits no method. The listing reads stage after the verbs above have bound it, so the three lines of the methods file's block policy stand among the places beside the stage file's maximization.

print(stage.places())

A path that names no place is refused when the methods file is read, as is an unknown method word and a known word at a place of a kind its row does not admit: a quadrature rule, for instance, belongs to an expectation and not to the policy builder. Method types states the kinds of place each word admits, and admitted_methods(stage, address) of bellman.stage answers the words admitted at one place. Typing a method runs nothing; where the method's row names a condition, such as egm-eligibility of the endogenous grid method, the stage records it among the builder's conditions, and the package does not check it (§3).

docs.title: 2 The methods typed at a stage
docs.text:
specified.methods answers every place at which a component is typed, one line each: the place, the method word with its keyword arguments, the grid where the place has one, and the handler, a quoted string, where one is named. The Evaluation of an !explicit builder at which no entry names a representation is listed with the closed form generated from the builder's entry, printed with that entry, generated from policy.method for the policy builder. Before methodization it is empty and prints none, as the stage elaborated from cons.bl alone shows; the binding verbs bind the stage they are called on, so stage and specified above name one stage.

print(elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl")).methods)
print(specified.methods)

none
arvl_to_dcsn            !deterministic
dcsn_to_cntn            "cons-port:transition_fwd"
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate   !Linear   !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m))   "cons-port:_make_interp"
policy                  !egm   !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))   "cons-port:egm"

The methods file types four places:

from pathlib import Path

print(Path("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")

@methods: cons
# The methods of the consumption stage, written as an addition to cons.bl
# beside this file: the endogenous grid method on the policy builder, with its
# grid of savings and the function egm of cons-port as its handler, and the
# three lines of the method, the inverted Euler equation with its Kuhn-Tucker
# clause, the inverted law of motion and the identification c = c[>], which
# stand in place of the declared maximization at the operative level while
# the declared level keeps the maximization of cons.bl; one linear
# representation of the decision value and of its stated derivative on the
# grid of resources; the deterministic arrival builder; and the handler of the
# forward decision builder, which takes no method word. The block `policy`
# carries no signature, since it adds no coordinate. The entries that add no
# line are file-level lines, each routed to its place by its path, since an
# empty body is refused. Each grid is its own typing entry at its place, one
# factor per coordinate keyed by the coordinate's name, and every setting a
# grid reads is declared above the blocks and lines with its set, a bound as
# a point of the set its coordinate is declared on, a count in ℕ.

[id=policy, method : !egm | grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) | handler : "cons-port:egm"] {
    c[>]   <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0    :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                        :: [id=grid]
    c      = c[>]                            :: [id=identification]
}

cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m))

dcsn_to_cntn.handler : "cons-port:transition_fwd"

The block policy of the methods file names the stage's policy block by its id. Its bracket types the policy builder's method, method : !egm, its grid of savings, grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), and its handler, handler : "cons-port:egm", by paths relative to the block, and its three lines are the lines of the endogenous grid method, which the operative builder holds in place of the maximization (§3). The five entries after it stand at file level, each with the full path of its place: the representation of the decision value and of its stated derivative at the decision builder's Evaluation, one entry for both, with its grid of resources and its handler; the method of the forward builder from arrival to decision; and the handler of the forward builder from decision to continuation, which has no method word. The settings the two grids name are declared above the block with their sets (Parameters and settings §2).

One place is read by its path as the methods file writes it: specified.methods["policy"] answers the components typed at the policy builder and specified.methods["cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate"] those at the decision builder's Evaluation. The answer is the place's record, which prints the word with its arguments, the grid as written and the handler, and holds each under word, grid and handler, with source, the data a representation reads, table, pairs, expression or own nodes (Methods §5), and generated_from, the entry a generated method comes from; a place at which no component is typed is refused with a KeyError that names the typed places.

print(repr(specified.methods["policy"]))
print(repr(specified.methods["cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate"]))
print(specified.methods["policy"].handler, specified.methods["dcsn_to_cntn"].word == "")
try:
    specified.methods["cntn_to_dcsn"]
except KeyError as refusal:
    print(refusal)

Every piece answers methods, the components typed at it or inside it, read from the typing entries of the stage; no piece keeps a copy. A builders graph, the backward graph stage.builder.bwd or the forward graph stage.builder.fwd, answers the components typed within it, and stage.builder those typed within both; a builder answers those typed at it or inside it, among them the representation at its Evaluation, which the builder holds under the key "evaluation"; and an operation or a line answers the components typed at it.

docs.title: The definitions table
docs.text:
Summary

stage.definitions is the read-only table of everything a stage file declares, each name once, and of every line its blocks write, in file order. A record is read by its identity as a key, list() answers the table grouped by kind and denote(identity) the card of one record. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, except the last, which is printed from the perfect-foresight stage file applications/consumption-perfect-foresight-crra/declaration/stages/perfect_foresight/perfect_foresight.bl with its methods file methods.bl, which defines a derived parameter, and its calibration file.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; Stage tutorial: the declarations as the file writes them. Used by — A piece: the kernels an operation reads from this table. Formal account — Fields, functions and types: the sets and functions a record denotes. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

The graphs of a stage refer to its definitions by identity, a key of the form <stage>:<kind>:<name>, cons:parameter:ρ, whose middle segment names the kind of the record; a line's record is keyed by the line's address instead, cntn_to_dcsn.value. Two kinds are made by the construction from the blocks: a record of kind g is a law of motion, the map a forward block applies to the state, and a record of kind G is a value aggregator, the pointwise function a backward block applies to the continuation value.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The table

stage.definitions is a read-only mapping from each identity to its record, in file order. list() answers the records grouped by kind, each with the set, the map or the relation it denotes, so that the table says what the model is.

print(stage.definitions.list())

docs.title: 2 One record
docs.text:
A record is read by its identity as a key and has eight attributes, which are attributes and not fields, a field being an economic quantity of the model: identity; kind, one of set, parameter, derived_parameter, distribution, function, function_alias, correspondence, g, G, line and multiplier; coordinates, the record's named coordinates, each with its declared set where the file declares one; equations, which for a law of motion or an aggregator holds the addresses of the block's lines and no copy of their algebra, and for a derived parameter the term of its definition; tags, the entries of a line's annotation; address, where the file writes the record, the block for a law of motion or an aggregator; ordinal, the position of a line among the items of its block's body, counted from 1 with the branches of a branching block counted in turn, which outside a branch is the n of an unnamed line's address <block>.<n> and is the number a refusal names a line by, and None on a record of any other kind; and categories, on a set marked !categories (Symbol conventions §9.2), its category map as one frozen CategoryCodes record of the identifier written after the marker, or None, and the pairs of a code and its category's name in increasing code order, CategoryCodes(identifier='household_status', codes=((0, 'newborn'), (1, 'old'))) for the set HouseholdStatus of that section, and None on every other record.

record = stage.definitions["cons:G:cntn_to_dcsn"]
for attribute in ("identity", "kind", "equations", "tags", "address", "ordinal"):
    print(f"{attribute:<12} {getattr(record, attribute)!r}")
print(f"{'coordinates':<12} {[name for name, _ in record.coordinates]!r}")

docs.title: 3 The card of a record
docs.text:
stage.definitions.denote(identity) answers the card of one record: the function or set it defines, the conditions on its values, the lines of the file it comes from and the records of the declared names it refers to. The card is asked of the table, since a record does not hold the stage it belongs to. The card of a set marked !categories prints the set's category map, the second object the set denotes (A piece §6), on the row under the set, 0 ↦ newborn, 1 ↦ old (categories household_status), and list() prints the same row. The card of a distribution declared by N, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal or TypeIExtremeValue prints in the same way the second object the declaration denotes, its measure at the written arguments (Shock distributions §1), on the row under the law: y ~ N(0, 1) is followed by P_y = measure on ℝ given by B ↦ …, and list() prints the same row. The row stands on the declaration's own card alone: the card of another record that reads the declaration lists it by its law.

docs.title: The binding verbs
docs.text:
Summary

stage.calibrate(source), stage.methodize(source) and stage.configure(source) each add one binding to the stage they are called on and return that stage: the values of the parameters, the methods of its pieces, or the settings those methods read. Nothing is copied, a later binding replaces the earlier one of its kind, and no verb solves anything. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, calibrated by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml, configured by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml, and methodized by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, the addition beside the stage file; the listing of §2 is calibrated instead at the mapping {"ρ": 2.0}.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the symbolic stage the verbs bind. Used by — Parameters and settings and Methods and places: the tables that read the bindings. See also — The trellis factory: the same three verbs applied to every stage of a trellis; API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

calibrate and configure each take one source, the path of a YAML file or a mapping of the same content, and methodize the path of a .bl addition or a list of them. calibrate binds a value to every declared parameter; methodize reads the additions with the stage file and holds the methods their entries type at their places; configure binds the settings those methods read. The recommended order is calibration, methodization and configuration: the parameter values complete the economic problem before the numerical choices are made, and the settings are read against the methods that name them.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The three verbs in order
docs.text:
The short form of a version names what it binds: symbolic, calibrated, methodized and specified are the four stopping points of the recommended order.

print(repr(stage))
backward = stage.initial.backward.graph
calibrated = stage.calibrate("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml")
print(repr(stage))
methodized = stage.methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl")
print(repr(stage))
specified = stage.configure("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml")
print(repr(stage))

ElaboratedStage('cons', symbolic)
ElaboratedStage('cons', calibrated)
ElaboratedStage('cons', methodized)
ElaboratedStage('cons', specified)

Each verb adds its binding to the stage it is called on and returns that stage, so calibrated, methodized and specified are three names of stage, and nothing is copied. A later binding replaces the earlier one of its kind: a second calibration replaces the values of the parameters, a second methodization replaces the whole selection of methods files, and a setting given again replaces its value. A binding that is refused leaves the stage as it was. The initial diagrams and the declared builders, stage.declared, are those the stage file states before and after every binding: calibrate and configure keep the objects, and methodize, which elaborates the stage anew from the union of the stage file with its addition, makes them again, equal to the ones before; the addition's entries and lines change the operative builders stage.builder and the definitions table stage.definitions, and nothing else (Methods and places):

print(specified is stage)
print(stage.initial.backward.graph == backward)

True
True

A record may hold the three sources itself, the calibration and the settings as mappings and the methods as the texts of its additions, and then one call binds them: elaborate_stage(record) reads the additions with the stage text and binds the calibration and the settings on the stage it constructs, copies that stage once, at the end, and a record whose sources are empty, such as the one load_stage(path) returns, gives the symbolic stage (The stage §1). The verbs remain the route for a version already made, such as stage here, and for a binding made after elaboration. An addition is read into the record by load_stage, given its path beside the stage file's:

from bellman.stage.sources import load_calibration, load_settings

record = load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl",
                    ["applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl"])
record["calibration"] = load_calibration("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml")
record["settings"] = load_settings("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml")
in_one_call = elaborate_stage(record)
print(repr(in_one_call), in_one_call.bindings == specified.bindings)

ElaboratedStage('cons', specified) True

docs.title: 2 Calibration
docs.text:
calibrate requires a value for every declared parameter, in the set the file declares it on; a name the stage does not declare is not bound, except the name of a derived parameter, h := 1/(1 - Γ/R), whose value is refused, since calibration computes it from the definition at the bound values before it decides the conditions below. Calibration judges the values in three steps. First it judges each declared value against its declared set, reading each parameter that the set names at its value, and refuses a value outside its set. Second it computes the value of each derived parameter from its definition at the declared values, and refuses a definition that has no value there, such as one that divides by zero. Third, at the declared and the derived values together, it judges the value of each derived parameter against the set its definition declares, as q : (0,1) := (β*R)^(1/ρ)/R declares (0,1), and every membership the first step left undecided, such as that of a parameter declared on (0, h). A derived value outside its set is refused with a sentence that names the derived parameter, its definition, the set and the values of the parameters read. A bound of a declared set whose arithmetic has no value at the calibration, such as 1/(R - 2) at R = 2, refuses the calibration. Where the three steps do not decide a membership, as for a parameter declared on a set whose bound holds an expectation over a shock y, (0, E_{y}(y)), the package binds the value given, and stage.obligations() lists the membership as the condition calibration-domain-membership, which stays required. The value must still lie in the set. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3).

A parameter declared on the functions from a finite integer or label set, δ : L_J → ℝ, takes a sequence with one entry per member in the members' order, nested for a product of index sets, or a mapping keyed by those integers or labels. The entries may be real-valued; the integer keys identify the entries and are not their values. The version holds the sequence, and a wrong count, a key the set does not hold or an entry outside the entries' set is refused naming the declaration and the key.

Calibration then decides every condition of the stage that involves parameters and numbers alone: a condition that holds becomes established, with the values as its evidence, and a condition that fails refuses the calibration. So stage.calibrate({"ρ": 1.0}) is refused, since the utility c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ) divides by 1 - ρ, while at ρ = 2.0 that condition is established, as the listing below shows; a condition that involves a field, a control, a function the file does not declare or an expression calibration cannot evaluate stays as the construction left it, and is never turned into a claim of proof. A source may be a mapping as well as a file:

at_rho_2 = stage.calibrate({"ρ": 2.0})
print(repr(at_rho_2), at_rho_2.par["ρ"])
print(at_rho_2.obligations())

ElaboratedStage('cons', specified) ρ = 2.0 : [1, inf)
arithmetic-definedness               ¬(1 − ρ = 0)   [established]
finite-real-arithmetic               The operands of Add at policy.optimality must be finite real numbers.
aggregation-admissibility            V(m_d) ∈ [−∞, ∞)
marginal-reading                     the right side of each derivative line equals the derivative, in the named coordinate, of the value the builder writes, under the envelope conditions: concavity of the continuation value, interiority of the maximizer or the multiplier's term at a binding constraint, differentiability of the reward in the control, a measurable selection of the policy, and differentiability of the value at the point read; listed and not checked
aggregation-admissibility            V≺(m, l) ∈ ℝ
finite-real-arithmetic               The operands of Add at policy must be finite real numbers.
finite-real-arithmetic               The operands of Add at policy.grid must be finite real numbers.
aggregation-admissibility            m_d≻(a) ∈ Xm
range-compatibility                  m_d − c(m_d) ∈ Xa   [established]
function-argument-domain-inclusion   The argument for x of cons:function:𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 at policy.InvEuler, from ℝ, must belong to ℝ₊₊.
egm-eligibility                      the construction satisfies the declared line where the continuation value 𝑉≻ is concave and continuously differentiable on (0, ∞) with a finite positive right derivative at 0

docs.title: 3 Methodization and configuration
docs.text:
methodize holds each entry of an addition at the place its path names: a method must admit the kind of place it is typed at, and an unknown method word, a path that names no place and a method at a place it does not admit are each refused. configure requires a value for every setting the methods files declare and for every name a bound method writes, and judges each value against its declared set, reading each parameter that the set names at its calibrated value, and each derived parameter at the value its definition takes at the calibration. A value outside its declared set is refused under setting-outside-set, and a declared setting with no value under setting-unvalued. configure then judges the values where the methods read them, so that a value inside its declared set can still be refused. A keyword's value outside the domain the method's row names is refused under method-option-value, as tol_v : ℝ valued at -1.0 is for !vfi(tol=tol_v). A grid whose bounds are out of order or outside the coordinate's declared set, whose count is below two or whose node set is not strictly increasing is refused under grid-bounds. A requirement written after require= that the grid built at the bound values does not meet is refused under grid-requirement. A grid beside an authored table is refused under representation-source where its points and the table's knots are both known exactly at configuration and differ (Settings §2; Refusals).

On a stage with no methods bound configure refuses nothing, and it binds the file's values as names no declaration holds, which stage.settings lists with no set; a later methodize judges them against the settings its additions declare. Where no calibration is bound, configure does not judge a value against a declared set that names a parameter, such as tol_s : (0, ρ), and binds the value. A setting bound before a calibration must lie in its declared set at the values that calibration binds. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). calibrate judges no setting bound before it. A later configure or methodize judges each bound setting at the calibration. Methodization may also precede calibration:

other_order = (stage.methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl")
               .configure("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml")
               .calibrate("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml"))
print(repr(other_order), str(other_order.methods) == str(specified.methods))

ElaboratedStage('cons', specified) True

No binding changes the initial diagrams or the declared builders, and the lines of a solution method change the operative builders alone (§1); nothing in the package executes a method: a method records how a piece is to be computed, and the routine that computes it is supplied outside the package. Methods and places reads the bound methods, and Parameters and settings the bound values.

docs.title: The view in Model Explorer
docs.text:
Summary

explore(stage) opens the four graphs of a stage version in Model Explorer, Google's viewer of large graphs, which runs in the browser: its two initial diagrams, the fields of the stage file in the boxes of their perches, related by its blocks, and its two builders graphs. In a builders graph each builder is a box that opens to its sub-builders and its primitive operators, each operator a box that names its kind above its symbol, every wire is an edge whose two ends hold its perch and its type, and a selected operation shows the rows of its card, its kernel and the method bound to it, each on its own line. The package writes the view as two files and serves the graph file to the viewer; a trellis is viewed in the same way, with a box for each period and for each stage occurrence inside it, a stage occurrence being one use of a stage file in a period (The Bellman factory §1), and the fill of a box names its level, from a period to a sub-builder. The view writes no mathematics of its own: an operator's symbol is the one the drawing prints, with each law of motion named as the operator's card names it and without the arguments of a law or an aggregator written out at a policy, (·, 𝑐) and (·, ·, 𝑐); every port's label is one the drawing prints; and the drawing that diagram() answers remains the figure of a page or a lesson. The examples are from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl where no other file is named.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The builders graphs: the two graphs and their grains, which the view draws as boxes inside boxes; A builder: the operations of a builder and their cards, which the side panel shows row by row. See also — Methods and places: the methods whose tags the boxes of §4.2 carry; The trellis factory: the trellises that §5 views.

Key terminology Term What it names Model Explorer Google's viewer of large graphs, the Python package ai-edge-model-explorer: a server on the reader's machine and a page in the browser. Layer A box of the view that is drawn closed and opens with a click to show what it holds: a builder or a sub-builder, and in a trellis a period or a stage occurrence. Node A box of the view that opens to nothing: a primitive operator, or one of the two nodes that hold a graph's own inputs and outputs. Port One input or one output of a node, the end of one wire. Side panel The pane at the right of the page, which lists the attributes of the node or the layer selected and the ports of a node. Overlay A set of lines in one color that the reader turns on and off: each line joins the two nodes of an edge of the graph (§4.1).

docs.title: 1 What a user writes
docs.text:
The view is written by two functions that stand in bellman.stage and in bellman.trellis, explore and write_model_explorer, defined in the module bellman.factory.model_explorer of the Bellman factory, and by no verb of the stage:

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, explore, load_stage, write_model_explorer

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))
paths, address = explore(stage)

explore(stage) writes the two files of §2 into the folder model-explorer/ beside the stage file, starts the viewer's server unless a server already answers at port 8080, and opens the page in the default browser with the layers of the builders open; port 8080 is a network port of the machine, not a port of a node. It prints the address and a reminder of the one setting of §6, and answers the paths of the two files and the address. The call that starts the server, the first explore of a notebook's kernel or of a script where no other process serves the port, also prints the viewer's own start-up lines, among them a second address and "Press Ctrl+C to stop.", which the reader may ignore. folder= names another folder for the files and port= another port; open_browser=False writes the files alone and answers the address None. explore(trellis) does the same for a trellis, the dictionary that elaborate_trellis returns, opens the layers of its periods and locates the page on the first period after the terminal one (§5).

write_model_explorer(stage, folder) writes the two files alone and answers their paths, the graph file first. serve, which answers the address of a page on the viewer's server that shows a graph file and opens no browser, is imported from the module:

from bellman.factory.model_explorer import serve

graph, overlays = write_model_explorer(stage, "model-explorer")
address = serve(graph, port=8080, layers=("cntn_to_dcsn", "policy"))

The page opens on the graph that graph_id= names, one of the four of §3.1, or, where none is named, on the backward builders graph backward, and on the file's first graph where it holds none, with the layers that layers names open, and fitted to the whole graph unless located= names a layer, located="periods[1]", which the page then selects and fits to its window. serve starts a server only where none answers on the port. A server that another Python process started, the kernel of another notebook for instance, serves the page as well, since the address names the graph file by its path on the machine; a port at which something other than the viewer answers is refused in one sentence. The server runs in a background thread of the process that started it and stops when that process ends. One server serves any number of pages at once, and each page stays independent of the others.

to_model_explorer and perch_overlays, functions of bellman.factory.model_explorer, answer for a stage or a trellis the same graphs and overlays as the viewer's own Python objects, without writing a file.

The viewer is installed with the package's extra explore, from the root of the repository:

pip install -e "packages/bellman[explore]"

Without it, a function of the module that needs the viewer raises an ImportError whose one sentence names the extra and the commands that install it.

docs.title: 2 The two files
docs.text:
The two files are named by the view's label: the stage's name, followed by a word for each binding the version holds, calibrated, methodized and configured, with a hyphen in place of each space; a trellis is labeled trellis. The symbolic version of cons writes two files:

  • cons.graph.json, the four graphs of §3.1, backward initial diagram, forward initial diagram, backward and forward, which the viewer opens as a model file;
  • cons.edge-overlays.json, the three perch overlays of §4.1, each holding every edge of the four graphs whose wire stands at its perch, which a reader loads through the viewer's panel of edge overlays.

cons methodized alone writes cons-methodized.graph.json and cons-methodized.edge-overlays.json, and the specified version, calibrated, methodized and configured, writes cons-calibrated-methodized-configured.graph.json and the file of overlays beside it. The viewer shows the label with its spaces, cons methodized, at the top of the page. The files are JSON in ASCII alone: every other character is written as its JSON escape, so that 𝑉≻ stands in a file as \ud835\udc49\u227b, which the viewer reads back as 𝑉≻. The viewer's server reads a file in the system's default encoding, which on some machines is not UTF-8, and a file in ASCII is read alike under any code page.

docs.title: 3.1 The graphs and their layers
docs.text:
The viewer shows one graph at a time, chosen at the top of the page, where four are listed: backward initial diagram and forward initial diagram, the two initial diagrams, the fields of the stage file at their perches, related by the blocks that read and write them; then backward, the builders a solution applies, on value functions, the policy builder among them, and forward, the builders a simulation applies, on measures (The builders graphs §3). explore(stage) opens the page on backward. The viewer lays out each graph itself, a builders graph from top to bottom and an initial diagram from left to right.

In an initial diagram the fields are the nodes and the blocks relate them, as the field diagram of the calculus is drawn (Fields, functions and types §2). Each perch that holds a field of the diagram is a layer named by the perch's word, arvl, dcsn or cntn, and the layers stand in the order the direction reads the perches, so that the forward diagram reads arrival, decision, continuation from left to right and the backward one continuation, decision, arrival. Each field is a node inside the layer of its perch, named by the field's identity, cons:dcsn:m_d, labeled as the drawing labels the field, V≻, m_d, a≻, and filled white; the fields of one perch stand one under another. A shock, which belongs to no perch, stands outside the layers. Each block is a node outside the layers, named and labeled by its id and filled white, with an edge from each field it reads and an edge into each field it writes, so that it stands between the perches it joins; the diagram opens no further layer, since a block's lines stand in its attributes (§3.3). The diagram has no nodes Inputs and Outputs: a field no block writes is one the diagram takes, and a field no block reads one it gives. The backward initial diagram of cons holds V≻ in the layer cntn, V and c in dcsn and V≺ in arvl, related by the three blocks cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl and policy, and the forward one m≺, m_d and a≻, one in each layer, related by arvl_to_dcsn and dcsn_to_cntn.

Each builder is a layer named by the id of its block: cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl and policy in the backward graph of cons. A builder's layer opens to its sub-builders, each a layer named by its builder and its key, such as cntn_to_dcsn/risk_ce in the savings stage applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl, and to its primitive operators, the finest boxes the construction makes (The builders graphs §4). These are the three grains a reader reaches from the stage, and the view shows no other. An operator formed by a line that is no sub-builder, such as the aggregation of the policy builder's candidate line, stands directly in its builder's layer.

Each primitive operator is a node. Its id is its whole name, cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, the key that reads it at the primitive grain, and its label is two lines. The first is the kind of its operator, as the attribute kind writes it (§3.3), followed, where the operator is stated at a policy (Operations §3), by at and the policies it is stated at, separated by commas: Pullback at 𝑐 in cons, and Pullback at 𝑐, ℎ_choice in the durables model's adjuster stage applications/durables/declaration/stages/adjuster_cons/adjuster_cons.bl, whose policy chooses consumption and housing together. The second is the symbol the drawing shows for the operator, without the arguments of a law or an aggregator written out at a policy, the (·, 𝑐) of the drawing's 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔(·, 𝑐) and the (·, ·, 𝑐) of its 𝐺(·, ·, 𝑐), which the operator's rules state in full (§3.3). The pullback of the decision builder is labeled Pullback at 𝑐 over 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ and its aggregation Aggregation at 𝑐 over 𝐺; the objective and the maximization of the policy builder, formed by the line optimality, are labeled Aggregation over 𝐺 · optimality and Argmax over argmax · optimality, and on a version methodized by the stage's methods file the candidate line and the identification that stand in their place are labeled Aggregation over 𝐺 · InvEuler and Pullback over 𝑐 ∘ 𝑚_d≻ (§4.2); and an evaluation names the outputs it produces, as the drawing does, so that the evaluation of the decision builder is labeled Evaluation over 𝑉(m_d). An evaluation with three or more outputs names the first two and counts the others, ending its label with and 1 more where it has three, and its rule rows and its output ports name them all (§3.2 and §3.3). A law of motion is named as the operator's card names it, so that the operators that read one law name it alike: the pullback of cntn_to_dcsn and the push-forward of dcsn_to_cntn both name 𝑔≻, the law from the decision perch to the continuation perch, 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ and 𝑔≻∗μ, and the pullback of dcsn_to_arvl and the push-forward of arvl_to_dcsn both name 𝑔≺, the law from the arrival perch to the decision perch, 𝑉 ∘ 𝑔≺ and 𝑔≺∗μ, where the drawing that diagram() answers writes the letter 𝑔 for both laws. Where a method is bound within the operator, the second line ends with its tag (§4.2). Inputs, Outputs and the fields and blocks of an initial diagram, which apply no operator, have labels of one line.

The view takes its colors from the project's site, and they tell apart the levels a reader opens and what each builder gives: navy for borders and labels, white and three pale blues for the fills, ultramarine for a builder's outputs, and orange for a refusal (§3.5). A node is white with a navy border and a navy label, and its border turns ultramarine under the pointer. The node of an operator that writes a wire read outside its builder's layer, by another builder, by Outputs or, in a trellis, by a join (§5), has an ultramarine border instead, which turns navy under the pointer, so that what each builder gives is seen at a glance: in the view of cons, the three evaluations of the backward graph and the two push-forwards of the forward graph. Each layer has a navy border and a navy label, and its fill names its level, one shade darker at each level a reader opens: in a trellis a period is white and a stage occurrence stands on the lightest of the three blues (§5), a builder stands on the second and a sub-builder on the third, the darkest. The perch layers of an initial diagram stand on the lightest blue, the shade of the stage they divide. The viewer draws no dashed border, by which the drawing marks an evaluation and a policy insertion; the first line of a label names the kind of every operator, and a kind has no color. The drawing that diagram() answers keeps its own colors.

Two further nodes, Inputs and Outputs, white with a navy border, stand in no layer and hold the graph's own inputs and outputs. The backward graph of cons takes the continuation value, 𝑉≻(a), from Inputs, and gives the arrival value and the policy, 𝑉≺(m) and 𝑐(m_d), to Outputs.

docs.title: 3.2 Wires and ports
docs.text:
Every wire of a builders graph is an edge from the node that writes it to each node that reads it; in an initial diagram a field is a node (§3.1), and an edge joins it to each block that writes or reads it. The ports of a node stand in the order of the wires its operator reads and writes, and the id of a port is the identity of its wire, such as cons:function:cntn:V, the same at both ends of an edge. The two ends of a wire hold the same attributes, and an attribute that would hold nothing is not written:

  • label, the wire's label as the drawing prints it, such as 𝑉≻(a) or μ≺;
  • perch, the perch the wire stands at, arvl, dcsn or cntn; a wire at no perch, such as the result of an aggregation, has none;
  • role, the role of the object the wire carries, such as value, control, state or measure;
  • type, the wire's type as a builder's signature() prints it, such as Xm → [−∞, ∞) or finite measure on Xm; on a field wire of an initial diagram, set instead, the field's declared set as the fields table prints it, [-inf, inf), where the header declares one.

The side panel lists the ports of a selected node, each with these attributes, and under an input also namespace, which the viewer adds. An input is headed by the wire's label followed, in parentheses, by the label of the node that writes the wire, whose two lines the panel prints on one: on cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, 𝑉≻(𝑔(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) (Pullback at 𝑐 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻). An output is headed by the label of the node that reads it, printed in the same way, or by output where several nodes read it, and its attribute label names the wire: the one output of Inputs is read by Pullback at 𝑐 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ of the decision builder and by Pullback 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ of the policy builder, so it is headed output and lists label 𝑉≻(a).

A parameter and the policy a builder is stated at are no wires: they stand in the rows of an operation's card, as the stage holds them, and each parameter stands with its declared set in the attributes of the layer of every builder whose operations read it (§3.3).

The edges that cross the border of a layer are the wires its operators read and write. A wire of a builder's signature that none of its operators reads is therefore no edge of its layer, and the whole signature stands in the attributes of the layer (§3.3).

docs.title: 3.3 The side panel
docs.text:
Selecting a primitive operator lists its attributes in the side panel, each on one line and in this order: the kind of the operator, the rules of the Rule section of its card, one attribute to a rule and numbered only where there are several, the lines of its kernel, the method bound within it where one is (§4.2), and the numbers of the lines of the stage file it realizes (A builder §1). A value wider than the panel is cut with an ellipsis, and a control at the end of its row expands it to the whole value. A rule that the card breaks over several lines stands on one line, and the region a rule holds on, which the card sets at the right margin or on a line of its own, follows the rule after two spaces, as one attribute: 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa) on policy.identification:Pullback of the methodized cons. On cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation of cons:

Attribute What it holds On cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation kind the kind of the operator (Operations) Aggregation rule, or rule 1, rule 2, … the rules of the card's Rule section rule: 𝑉(m_d) = 𝑢(𝑐(m_d)) + 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) kernel, or kernel 1, kernel 2, … the lines its kernel() prints (A piece §2) kernel 1: 𝐺 of cntn_to_dcsn: 𝐺(V≻, m_d, c) = 𝑢(c) + V≻kernel 2: outputs (V); unused m_d; V reads V≻, c lines the stage file and the numbers of the lines the card's Source section quotes, a run of consecutive lines by its first and its last, house_choice.bl 18–19, 22; the address the operator is born at is the first segment of its id, and the text of the lines is not repeated, since the rules state it cons.bl 22

An evaluation, whose kernel is the identity, lists under rule only the rows that type its outputs, 𝑉 : Xm → [−∞, ∞) on cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation, and none of the rules of the operation before it, which that operation lists. The stated derivative of the value, D_{m_d}𝑉(m_d) = 𝑑𝑢(𝑐(m_d)), stands at cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation with its source line cntn_to_dcsn.marginal and the obligation marginal-reading, beside the method bound there, and adds no edge. An operation that quotes no line of the stage file, such as the evaluation of dcsn_to_arvl, has no lines. The rows of the card's Where section, the local abbreviations its rules write, stand on the layer of the operation's builder, and those of its Conditions are not shown. Where a method is bound within the operator, the panel also lists method, handler, option and setting, the last two numbered in the same way (§4.2).

Selecting a layer lists inputs and outputs, the two sides of its builder's signature as signature() prints them, each on one line. On policy they are 𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞) and 𝑐(m_d) : 𝒫({c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊) | c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d)}). The layer of a builder, and not of a sub-builder, also lists what the builder's operations share, each on one line and numbered only where there are several. On the layer policy of cons:

Attribute What it holds On policy where, or where 1, where 2, … the rows of the Where section of the builder's card, the local abbreviations the rules of its operations write, each once, such as the law of motion at a branch in applications/housing-frictions/declaration/stages/house_choice/house_choice.bl, 𝑔_keep≻ : ℝ₊₊ × ℝ₊₊ → ℝ₊₊ × ℝ₊₊, 𝑔_keep≻(m_f, m_h) = 𝑔≻(m_f, m_h, keep) none feasible set, or feasible set 1, … on the layer of the policy builder, the definition of each feasible set its policy names, as the stage's definitions hold it Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := (0, x] parameter, or parameter 1, … each parameter the builder's operations read, directly or through a function such as 𝑢, in the order the file declares them, as stage.par prints it: its declared set, and on a calibrated version its value (Parameters and settings §1) ρ : [1, inf), unbound; on the calibrated cons, ρ = 6.0 : [1, inf) setting, or setting 1, … every setting the version binds, as stage.settings prints it, whether or not a method names it (Parameters and settings §2) none; on the configured cons, six, from n_a = 800 : ℕ, read at policy by !egm for its grid !Cartesian to m_max = 10.0 : Xm, read at cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate by !Linear for its grid !Cartesian

The settings are the version's, so every builder's layer of a configured version lists all of them. A sub-builder's layer lists its signature alone. Selecting Inputs or Outputs of a builders graph lists the graph's own signature as signature() prints it, under inputs or outputs, the wires as one object, which on the Inputs of the backward graph of cons is the one wire 𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞); their ports give the wires one by one. An initial diagram has neither node and lists its signature on no layer: the fields it takes and gives are the nodes no block writes and no block reads (§3.1), and the signature's line for a field, V≻ : {V≻}, restates the field's label.

Selecting a block of an initial diagram lists kind, which is block; header, the block's header as the file writes it after the id; statement, or statement 1, statement 2, …, each line of the block as the card's Source section quotes it, with its line number; and lines, the file and the numbers of the header's line and the quoted lines. On cntn_to_dcsn of cons the header is (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn, the statements 21 V = 𝑢(c) + V[>] :: [id=value] and 22 D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) :: [id=marginal], and the lines cons.bl 20–22. A block carries no method; the method bound within a line stands on the operator the line forms, in the builders graph.

Selecting a field of an initial diagram lists kind, which is field; perch, the perch the field belongs to, or, for a shock, which belongs to none, edge, the pair of perches of the transition that draws it as the fields table prints it, ∼→≻; role, where the field has one; set, its declared set as the fields table prints it, where a header declares one; and lines, the file and the line of the header that first lists the field, the order in which the fields table lists them (The stage §5). On V≻ of cons the rows are field, cntn, value, [-inf, inf) and cons.bl 20, the line of the header of cntn_to_dcsn; on c, which the header of the forward block dcsn_to_cntn lists at line 16, among the inputs the block is read at, before the header of policy writes it at line 29, lines is cons.bl 16. The ports of a field's node carry its label, perch, role and set, as every port does (§3.2).

docs.title: 3.4 The search box
docs.text: The search box at the top left of the page takes a regular expression and finds every node and layer whose label, or one of whose attributes, matches it; an attribute is read as key=value, and the id of a node counts among its attributes. kind=Aggregation finds the aggregations, and method=!egm every operator and every layer that lists !egm as its method. Expressions separated by spaces must all match.

docs.title: 3.5 A refused graph
docs.text: Where the construction refused a direction, its graph is one node with an orange border, forward:refused or backward:refused, labeled with the direction and the rule the refusal names, with the refusal's whole text in its attribute refusal; the other graph is drawn as usual, and an initial diagram the construction refused is one node in the same way, backward initial diagram:refused. The forward graph of the retiree stage applications/cagetti-denardi-2006/declaration/stages/retiree_death/retiree_death.bl is the one node forward builders graph refused (not-constructed), since the distribution of its shock y_n is written with a family whose set of results is not declared.

docs.title: 4.1 The perches
docs.text: The three perch overlays, arrival, decision and continuation, stand in the second file of §2, cons.edge-overlays.json, and the view opens without them. The viewer draws an overlay edge as a straight line from the border of one node to the border of the other, not along the edge of the graph, and neither an overlay nor its edges has a setting that makes it follow that edge; the perch of every wire stands on its ports (§3.2). A reader who wants the overlays opens the panel of edge overlays from the toolbar above the graph and loads the file with its button Upload. Each overlay is drawn in the color the project's site gives its perch, navy for arrival, a dark orange for decision and ultramarine for continuation, while a node it touches is selected, and paints every edge whose wire stands at its perch, with no label. The viewer also outlines the nodes a selected node reads from in green and those it writes to in orange, with the edges between them in the same colors; these colors are the viewer's own, which the two files do not set, and an edge they draw carries no label. Bellman Workbench, the editor that draws the same graph beside the stage file, marks the selected box and the wires that enter or leave it in a bright blue and outlines no other box, and its legend lists the color of each perch while its overlays are on (Bellman Workbench §2).

docs.title: 4.2 The methods
docs.text:
A method typed at a primitive operator is shown on the operator's node by one mark: the second line of its label ends with · and the method's word, written with its ! as the methods file writes it. On cons methodized by its methods file, applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation is labeled Evaluation over 𝑉(m_d) · !Linear, and no other node carries a word: the endogenous grid method is typed at the policy builder, a layer, and not at the Evaluation that closes it, which stays labeled 𝑐(m_d) (§3.3). The ! tells a word apart from the id of a statement, which a symbol may write after the same ·, 𝐺 · InvEuler. No color stands for a method: the method is named by its word, by which the search box finds it, method=!egm (§3.4), and the operation it realizes is stated in Method types. A version within which no method is typed, such as the symbolic cons, shows no mark.

The side panel of such a node lists the components typed at it: method, the word with its keyword arguments; grid, the grid as the methods file writes it; handler, the routine the methods file names (handler); and, on a configured version, setting, each setting the grid and the method name, as the version's settings print it (Parameters and settings §2), numbered where there are several, setting 1, setting 2. On the specified cons, calibrated by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/calibration/portfolio.yml, methodized as above and configured by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/settings/cons.yml, cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation lists, among its attributes, method !Linear, grid !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m)), handler cons-port:_make_interp and setting 1 m_min = 0.01 : Xm, read at cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate by !Linear for its grid !Cartesian. A method typed at a builder, and at none of its operators, stands in the attributes of the builder's layer, and no label carries its word: in the backward graph of the methodized cons, the layer policy lists method !egm, grid !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) and handler cons-port:egm, and in the forward graph the layer arvl_to_dcsn lists method !deterministic and the layer dcsn_to_cntn handler cons-port:transition_fwd. The builder's layer lists every setting of a configured version (§3.3). The legend of Bellman Workbench lists each method typed in the graph it shows with its place, an operator's id or a layer's name, !egm policy and !Linear cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation in the backward graph and !deterministic arvl_to_dcsn in the forward graph (Bellman Workbench §2).

docs.title: 5 A trellis
docs.text:
explore(trellis) and write_model_explorer(trellis, folder) take the dictionary that elaborate_trellis returns, or a version the trellis verbs bound (The trellis factory §§3 and 4), and write one collection of two graphs, the backward and the forward trellis and no initial diagram, labeled trellis: the files are trellis.graph.json and trellis.edge-overlays.json, which explore(trellis) writes into model-explorer/ in the working directory unless folder= names another. Where the construction refused one direction of a stage occurrence, the trellis's graph of that direction is one node labeled as in §3.5, whose attribute refusal opens with the occurrence's address. explore(trellis) opens the backward graph with its periods open and located on periods[1], the first period after the terminal one: the page selects that period's layer, lists its attributes, and fits the window to it, and the other periods stand beside it, a scroll away. A trellis of one period is fitted to the window whole.

Each period is a layer periods[h], white with a navy border, h being its index in the dictionary and periods[0] the terminal period; its attribute age shows the age where the trellis's registry gives last_age, as the drawing of diagram_trellis writes it, and the index stands in the layer's name and in no attribute. Each stage occurrence is a layer inside its period, named by its key, periods[0]/cons, whose attribute stage shows the stage's name and bindings; it holds that occurrence's builders exactly as the view of the stage does. Every node id and port id is the id in the stage's own view, prefixed by its occurrence, periods[0]/cons/cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, so that two occurrences of one stage are told apart. The viewer lays out the periods side by side and the stages of a period next to one another, each graph in the direction its wires pass, and the builders of an occurrence from top to bottom. In the forward graph economic time runs from left to right, with the terminal period at the right and the stages of a period in their forward order, as in the drawing of diagram_trellis; the backward graph, laid out in the direction its value functions pass, from the terminal period back, stands the other way round.

A join, which connects a continuation field of one stage occurrence to an arrival field of another (The Bellman factory §7), is drawn at the grain of the wires, from the node that writes a wire of one occurrence to each node that reads the joined wire of the other: forward, from the continuation measure of one occurrence to the arrival measure of the next; backward, from the arrival value of the later occurrence to the continuation value of the earlier one. The reading port holds the attribute join, the text the drawing writes on the wire: a for a field joined by its name, m_next → m where a connector renames it, and inter_connectors[0] a → k for a join between periods; in the backward graph it also holds paired by, the rule that paired the wire with the one that supplies it, one wire per role or equal name, the two rules below in their order, so that a pairing by equal names, the view's own convention, is never silent. A joined wire that no operator of its occurrence reads is a port of a node Inputs inside the occurrence's layer, so that its join is drawn. The policy of each occurrence, which no join reads, ends at a node Outputs inside the occurrence's layer, periods[0]/cons/GraphOutputs, so that no edge of a policy crosses the periods.

A trellis has no Inputs and no Outputs of its own. A wire that no join supplies enters the graph at a boundary node, and a wire that no join reads leaves it at one: a node at the graph's root, outside every layer, that holds the wire's one port and is joined by the wire's edge to the operator that reads or writes it. Its attribute kind names its role, start where the wire enters and end where it leaves, and its label, which its attribute label repeats, is a word for that role followed by the wire's own label: in the forward graph, starting data where the arrival measure of the first occurrence in time enters and terminal where the measure of the last one leaves; in the backward graph, terminal condition where the terminal value enters and result where the value of the first stage in time leaves. Its id is its kind followed by the id of the wire's port. In the trellis applications/cons-port/declaration/trellis.port-cons.yml, six periods of three stages, the forward graph begins at starting data μ≺, the node start:periods[5]/port/port:measure:arvl, and ends at terminal μ≻; the backward graph takes the continuation value of periods[0]/disc, the last stage of the terminal period, at terminal condition 𝑉≻(a), and gives the arrival value of periods[5]/port, the first stage in time, at result 𝑉≺(k).

Each edge of a join carries, under its attribute route, the record of the route that establishes it: the connection from one branch of the source occurrence into the destination occurrence, as connection_report answers it (The trellis factory §9). The record holds branch, the label of the source's branch, or null for a stage without branches; source and destination, the addresses of the two occurrences, periods[5]/port; source_fields and destination_fields, the continuation fields of the source and the arrival fields of the destination, in the route's order; pairs, one entry for each field joined, in the route's order, with source_field, destination_field, origin, authored for a pair a connector writes and inferred for one joined by equal names, and address, the entry that writes an authored pair, periods[5].connectors[0], or the period of an inferred one; status, certified or uncertified; and law, the joint measure the source's branch writes, port:measure:cntn. Every value is read from the route and none is computed by the view, so that the edge and the report agree; an edge that no route establishes, inside an occurrence or at a boundary node, has no attributes. Unlike the attributes of a node, those of an edge are not shown by the viewer's page, which reads no attribute of an edge; Bellman Workbench reads them.

The backward graph pairs the value wires a join carries by what the stage files state and nothing else. Where one value wire stands on each side of a join, the two are paired whatever their names; where several stand on either side, the wires of the same name are paired. Where a wire is then left with no counterpart, or with two, the backward graph is refused: it is one node whose attribute refusal counts the joins that leave a wire unpaired and states these two rules, and whose attributes join 1, join 2, … name each such join on a row of its own. The forward graph is drawn. The backward graphs of the pension, durables and housing models are not refused on this ground, since their joins carry value wires alone, which these two rules pair. A reader loads these three trellises through their registries and recipes, load_recipe("applications/pension-retirement/declaration", "spec.yml"), load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml") and load_recipe("applications/housing-frictions/declaration", "spec.yml") (Recipe functions §2), and gives explore the dictionary that elaborate_trellis returns for each. load_trellis refuses their files trellis.yml under the rule trellis-file-shape, since the periods of those files name each stage by its key alone and the recipe supplies its source and mappings (The trellis factory §1).

Building the view of a trellis takes a few seconds for the eighteen stage occurrences of trellis.port-cons.yml and tens of seconds for a hundred occurrences, since the graphs of each occurrence are built when first asked for.

A view of part of a trellis is asked for by the periods and the stage keys it holds, to_model_explorer(trellis, periods=range(0, 2), stages=["cons"]), the periods selected as diagram_trellis selects them: the view holds the occurrences of those periods whose keys are given, every period or every key where one of the two is not given, and the joins between them as above. A join that leaves the occurrences held is no edge between them: the wire it carries enters or leaves the graph at a boundary node of kind outside, one for each occurrence outside the view that such joins reach, labeled with that occurrence's address, which its attribute target repeats, periods[1]/disc, and named by its kind, the id of the wire's port and that address, outside:periods[1]/cons/cons:measure:cntn:periods[1]/disc; the wire's port names the join in join and those occurrences in outside, so that nothing is lost without a mark. An index the trellis does not hold, a key no period selected holds and a selection of no occurrence are refused under trellis-file-shape, each in one sentence.

unpaired_joins(trellis) answers the rows join 1, join 2, … of the refusing backward node as records, one UnpairedJoin for each join that leaves a wire unpaired, in the order of the rows: its label, the addresses of the two occurrences, the address in the trellis of the connector that makes it, inter_connectors[0] or periods[0].connectors[0], empty for a join by equal names, and each wire it leaves unpaired as an UnpairedWire, with its occurrence, its name as the stage file writes it, the stage file and the line of the header that first lists it. It takes periods and stages as to_model_explorer does, and answers no join where the graph is drawn.

docs.title: 6 The viewer's settings
docs.text:
The viewer's default text renderer cannot draw the mathematical letters of the labels on the canvas, and draws other characters in their place. The setting "Use SVG text renderer", among the advanced settings behind the gear icon at the top right of the page, draws every label exactly. The side panel draws every attribute exactly with either renderer. The browser keeps the setting in its local storage for the page's host and port, which is why every view is served from one port, 8080 unless port= names another: the setting is turned on once for that port, and a view served from another port needs it turned on again.

The view is an interactive reading of the stage and changes nothing in it. The drawing that diagram() answers (A builder §1) remains the recorded figure of a page and of a lesson, since a view opens only while a Python process serves it.

docs.title: Equation parsing rules
docs.text:
Summary

A .bl file contains declarations, function definitions, shock laws, and typed equation blocks. This reference explains their written forms and distinguishes parsing from the checks needed to construct a mathematical stage. Timing and information restrictions belong to Perch tagging rules.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: complete contexts for introductory fragments; Field equations: a consumption stage. Formal account — Appendix C: the interpretation of equations; Appendix D: nodes and collection selection. See also — Symbol conventions: notation; Operations: the kinds of the operations a builder holds, Argmax among them.

docs.title: 1 Statements and blocks
docs.text:
Equations are written directly inside braces, as in this complete transition fragment:

@stage: arithmetic

[id=transform, (a : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (y : ℝ, q : ℝ) : !cntn] {
    y = 2 + a    :: [id=shift]
    q = 4*y      :: [id=scale]
}

Each equation has a left and right expression separated by =. The optional :: [...] annotation gives an identifier, a documentation string, or a supported mark. A block's header supplies its identifier and the typed sides of its inputs and outputs. Newlines separate statements; parentheses group subexpressions. Use the braced block itself, without YAML quotes or a YAML | indicator.

Abstract grammar: Equation and annotation

This projection uses ASDL constructor notation. It shows the equation alternative and the annotation structure; other statement alternatives are omitted rather than redefined.

stmt = Equation(expr lhs, expr rhs)
annotation = Annotation(entry* entries)
entry = Tag(string tag)
      | KeyValue(identifier key, scalar value)
      | Typer(typer t)

Keys. lhs and rhs are expressions; entries preserves annotation order; tag is text; key and value record a named scalar; t is type material. expr, scalar, and typer are defined by the full grammar. * permits a list; it does not establish uniqueness or scope.

Head. = separates equation expressions; :: introduces the statement annotation.

Denotes. An equation imposes equality in its declared context. Its explicit or implicit reading depends on its dependencies and unknowns, as Field equations explains.

Status. Construction checks declarations, operator scope, domain agreement, and output definitions. A parsed equation is not evidence that those checks or its mathematical assumptions hold.

For example, substituting an undeclared name missing for a still has the grammatical shape of an equation. Construction must reject the unresolved reference and identify the statement and source span, the part of the source file where the error occurs. An empty body does not define an identity transition; write the identity equation explicitly.

docs.title: 2 Types and definitions
docs.text:
The colon : introduces type information, whose components are written with @ between them. := supplies a definition. The following top-level fragment can precede the consumption blocks in Field equations, replacing their corresponding declarations and utility functions:

Xm := ℝ₊₊
Xa := ℝ₊
ρ : (1, inf)
𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)
𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢)
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 := Inv(𝑑𝑢)

D_{c} differentiates the function with respect to its argument c. Applied to a value field with its perch mark, D_{a} forms the derivative term D_{a}V[>], which may also be written D_{a}(V[>]) with the same meaning: the derivative of the value in the state coordinate a of the perch at which the value is read, the coordinate written without its mark. A subscript that names no state coordinate of that perch, or names a discrete coordinate, is refused. Inv denotes an inverse function on an appropriate domain. Here marginal utility is strictly decreasing from positive consumption onto the positive reals, because ρ > 1; its inverse exists on positive arguments. A chosen name such as 𝑑𝑢 has no derivative meaning by itself. Similarly, a derivative term names the derivative of a value but differentiates nothing automatically.

Typed function arguments are local names with domains; do not give them field roles or perch marks. The name a comprehension binds is local in the same way: H := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} defines the named set of the integers i that satisfy both conditions and declares no field i (Symbol conventions §9.2). Define functions at the top level. A function definition written inside a block, such as 𝑞(x : ℝ) := x^2, is refused under the rule not-constructed, whether its body is a formula or a set. The refusal asks for the definition at the top level of the file. An equation inside a block whose left side is a call, such as 𝑞(a) = a^2, defines no function 𝑞. In a block that states a transition, such as transform in §3, the package reads this line as an equation that defines a from itself, and it refuses the block's law of motion under definition-order.

A function definition whose body is a set defines a feasibility correspondence. A product body keeps its factor order, Γ(z : ℝ₊) := [0, z] × ℝ₊. A comprehension binds its member locally and may use equality as well as inequalities:

Γ(z : ℝ₊) := {q : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ | q[1] + q[2] = z, q[3] <= z}

Both conditions hold together on the whole triple; q[1] selects its first component and z is the correspondence's argument. Equality is written in a comprehension only. Several sets in one type, written with @ between them as in β : (0,1) @ (0, R^(ρ-1)), declare their intersection, and at most one of them is written otherwise than as an interval with brackets. Several sets are read on a top-level declaration of one name only; on a field's listing in a block header they are refused under readable-form (Symbol conventions §9.2). Parenthesized expression tuples remain distinct from product sets, so a body (a, b) still defines a numerical pair. Constraints §1 explains how a maximization statement uses the feasible set.

A definition without arguments whose right side is arithmetic defines a derived parameter, a constant of the stage computed from its parameters. Human wealth relative to permanent income, h, and the interest factor normalized by growth, R_n, for example, are computed from the gross interest factor R and the growth factor Γ:

R : ℝ₊₊
Γ : ℝ₊₊
h := 1/(1 - Γ/R)
R_n := R/Γ

The outermost form of the right side decides that a definition is a derived parameter: a number, a sign, a sum, a difference, a product, a quotient, a power, a call of log, exp, min or max, a conditional if … then … else …, or a name the stage defines as neither a set nor a function. Any other right side keeps its own reading. A set expression, such as ℝ₊₊ or Xm × Xa, defines a named set, and D_{c}(𝑢), Inv(𝑑𝑢) or the name of a function defines a function of the stage. No other right side is read as a definition. Elaboration refuses under the rule not-constructed a right side that is a call other than those of log, exp, min, max, D and Inv, such as sqrt(R), 𝑢(R) or the grid constructor linspace(0, 1, 10); a tuple, such as (R, Γ); an expectation, such as E_{y}(y); or the bare name of a set the file defines, such as Xm. The definition of a derived parameter reads declared parameters, finite numbers and other derived parameters. It is formed by signs, sums, differences, products, quotients, powers, the calls log and exp, each of one argument, and the calls min and max, each of one argument or more, as in min(R, Γ), or it is written by cases, as this section states below. Elaboration refuses, under the rule derived-parameter and at the definition, a derived parameter whose definition reads any other name, such as a setting, a shock, a field, a set or a function; writes inf elsewhere than as a whole branch of a definition by cases; calls any other function, such as sqrt in h := 1/sqrt(1 - Γ/R); calls log, exp, min or max where the stage defines a function of that name, since in a derived parameter's definition the four are the functions of the language; writes any other form, such as an expectation; or writes a number that is not finite. A cycle among the definitions is refused under the rule definition-order.

Calibration supplies no value for a derived parameter, and a calibration source that names one is refused under derived-parameter. The value of a derived parameter is its definition evaluated at the calibration values, after the derived parameters it reads, by the rules of real arithmetic. A divisor is not zero. The argument of log is positive. A power with an integer exponent is defined at every base except zero, where the exponent must be positive, and a power with a noninteger exponent requires a positive base. min and max are the least and the greatest of their arguments, and every argument is evaluated and must have a value. Every operation and every call gives a finite real number, and a number that floating-point arithmetic rounds to zero from a nonzero result does not count as positive. A calibration at which a definition has no value is refused under derived-parameter, at that definition, with the operation that fails and the numbers it reads.

A derived parameter may be defined by cases. The right side of its definition is then a conditional, if test then a else b, written on one line, with or without a declared set before :=. The test compares two formulas by one of the relations <, <=, =, >= and >, of which ≤ and ≥ are second spellings of <= and >=, and its formulas read what the definition of any derived parameter reads. The two branches a and b are both written, and each is a formula, a further conditional, inf or -inf. Human wealth h, which is infinite where income grows at least as fast as it is discounted, and the lowest income ξ_min of a consumer who is unemployed with probability p_zero, with the income ξ_u in unemployment and an income of at least θ_min in employment, are written so:

R : ℝ₊₊
Γ : ℝ₊₊
p_zero : [0, 1)
θ_min : (0, 1]
ξ_u : ℝ₊
h : ℝ_{+∞} := if Γ < R then 1/(1 - Γ/R) else inf
ξ_min := if p_zero = 0 then θ_min else min(ξ_u, θ_min)

The value is the branch the test chooses, and the other branch is not evaluated, so that the division in the definition of h is not made at Γ = R. An equality compares the two computed numbers exactly, with no tolerance. A side of a test that floating-point arithmetic rounds to zero from a nonzero result decides no comparison, and the definition then has no value. Three cases are written by a conditional in the second branch, if Γ < R then 1 else if Γ = R then 0 else -1.

A branch written inf or -inf gives that infinity, the one value of a derived parameter that is no finite real number. Such a branch is admitted only where the definition declares a set that holds that infinity, such as a set of extended reals that holds that infinity, ℝ_{+∞} for inf, ℝ_{-∞} for -inf and ℝ̄ for both (Symbol conventions §9.2), or an interval closed at that infinite endpoint, (0, inf]. The declared set of a definition that writes none is ℝ (Kinds and sorts §4), so h := if Γ < R then 1/(1 - Γ/R) else inf is refused under derived-parameter when the file is read, and so is a definition whose declared set, by its form, cannot hold the infinity, such as ℝ₊₊ or (0, inf); the refusal gives a set to write. Where the closed endpoint of the declared set is the name of a parameter or of a derived parameter, as in (0, T], the file is read and calibration judges. At a calibration the value, finite or infinite, is judged against the declared set as the value of any derived parameter is, which the last paragraph of this section describes.

A declared set reads an infinite value where one of its endpoints, or a side of one of the conditions after the bar of a comprehension, as x < h in {x : ℝ | x < h}, is the bare name of the derived parameter, the name with no arithmetic. With debt : ℝ₊ @ [0, h), the set of debt is [0, ∞) where h is inf, and calibration decides the membership of the value of debt there as it does where h is finite; a lower endpoint valued at inf, as in (h, inf), leaves no number in the set. An endpoint that names a declared parameter valued at an infinity is read in the same way: with T : ℝ̄ calibrated at inf, debt : [0, T) declares debt on [0, ∞). No arithmetic of infinities is defined. A definition that evaluates a name valued at an infinity, in a formula, in a test, in a call or as the bare name, has no value, and the calibration is refused at that definition under derived-parameter. A bound of a declared set that computes with such a name, such as 2*h in [0, 2*h), or -h, has no value either, and the calibration is refused at that bound. A line of a block, or the body of a function, that computes with a derived parameter whose declared set may hold an infinity is read, and it owns the conditions that a parameter declared on that set gives it.
