After the substitution of R5, under which D_{a}V[>] denotes \(\mathrm{dv}_\succ(a)\), the derivative of \(\mathrm v_\succ\) at the saving \(a = w - c\), the residual is \(r(w, c) = \mathrm{du}(c) - \beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(w - c)\). The package does not yet record this residual (R10, §5.3). The clause denotes $$ r(w, c) \ge 0, \qquad w - c \ge 0, \qquad r(w, c)\,(w - c) = 0 . $$ Where saving is positive the Euler equation holds with equality; where the agent saves nothing, \(c = w\), marginal utility may exceed the discounted marginal value of saving. This is the Kuhn–Tucker system of \(\max_{0 < c \le w} \{\mathrm u(c) + \beta\,\mathrm v_\succ(w - c)\}\).

The solution under concavity. Suppose \(\mathrm u\) is strictly concave and continuously differentiable with \(\mathrm{du}\) a decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\), and \(\mathrm v_\succ\) is continuously differentiable with \(\mathrm{dv}_\succ\) positive, continuous, and nonincreasing. Then \(\mathrm f = \mathrm{du}^{-1} \circ (\beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ)\) is continuous and nondecreasing, \(\varphi = \mathrm{id} + \mathrm f\) is continuous and strictly increasing with range \([\mathrm f(0), \infty)\), the fiber condition holds on that range, and the system has exactly one solution at every \(w > 0\): $$ \pi^\ast(w) = \begin{cases} w, & 0 < w \le \mathrm f(0), \ \mathrm f(\varphi^{-1}(w)), & w > \mathrm f(0). \end{cases} $$ This \(\pi^\ast\) is the maximizer, because the objective is strictly concave in \(c\) and the Kuhn–Tucker conditions are then sufficient. Without the clause the statement 𝑑𝑢(c) = β*D_{a}V[>] denotes the interior relation only, which has no solution below \(\mathrm f(0)\); a method that returns \(c = w\) there is solving a problem the file has not declared, and the rules require it to report the extension rather than to return it silently.

Equality and complementarity are different. On the candidate relation, the equalities 𝑑𝑢(c) = β*D_{a}V[>], c = c[>], and w = w[>] have the same roots. They cannot all carry the same complementarity sign. Since \(\mathrm{du}\) is strictly decreasing, $$ \mathrm{du}(c)-\beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(a)\geq0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathrm f(a)-c\geq0. $$ The residual of c = c[>] is instead \(c-\mathrm f(a)\), with the opposite sign. The coordinate residual with the correct sign is \(\varphi(a)-w=\mathrm f(a)-c\) when \(a=w-c\). Thus converting an Euler complementarity condition into a candidate or coordinate condition requires orienting the residual correctly; equivalence of the underlying equalities is insufficient.

The declared multiplier. The same constraint can be written with its multiplier declared (R10). The policy block is then

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    μ[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0                 :: [id=slackness]
    c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>] + μ[>])   :: [id=candidate]
    w[>] = a + c[>]                    :: [id=coordinate]
    c    = c[>]                        :: [id=choice]
}

Its candidate and coordinate maps are defined on the observable set \(A_\succ = \{(a, \mu) \in \mathbb R_+ \times \mathbb R_+ : a \ge 0,\ \mu\, a = 0\}\): \(\mathrm U(a, \mu) = \mathrm{du}^{-1}(\beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(a) + \mu)\) and \(\mathrm H(a, \mu) = a + \mathrm U(a, \mu)\), and the block states \(\pi(\mathrm H(s)) = \mathrm U(s)\) for every \(s \in A_\succ\).

The clause on the candidate line. The same constraint can be written as a clause on the candidate line. The policy block is then

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0   :: [id=candidate]
    w[>] = a + c[>]                      :: [id=coordinate]
    c    = c[>]                          :: [id=choice]
}

After an inequality the residual takes the sign of that relation (R10), so the clause admits at each saving \(a\) the values \(x \in \mathbb R_{++}\) with \(x - \mathrm f(a) \le 0\), \(a \ge 0\) and \((x - \mathrm f(a))\,a = 0\): the one value \(\mathrm f(a)\) where \(a > 0\), and every \(x\) in \((0, \mathrm f(0)]\) where \(a = 0\). The coordinate line gives each admitted value its cash on hand \(a + x\), and the final line, rewritten at the continuation perch (R5), states \(\pi(a + x) = x\) for every saving \(a\) and every value \(x\) admitted there: \(\pi(\varphi(a)) = \mathrm f(a)\) where \(a > 0\), and \(\pi(x) = x\) for \(0 < x \le \mathrm f(0)\), the corner.

The three spellings denote one relation. Assume that 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is the inverse of 𝑑𝑢 on \(\mathbb R_{++}\), authored as in §4.2 or derived by Inv as here, and that the saving is \(a = w - c\). Then the clause of the first block and the declared multiplier of the second denote one relation between \(w\) and \(c\). For \((a, \mu) \in A_\succ\) put \(c = \mathrm U(a, \mu)\) and \(w = a + c\): then \(w - c = a \ge 0\), \(r(w, c) = \mu \ge 0\) and \(r(w, c)\,(w - c) = \mu\, a = 0\), which is the system of the clause. Conversely, a solution \((w, c)\) of that system gives \(a = w - c\) and \(\mu = r(w, c)\), a point of \(A_\succ\) with \(\mathrm H(a, \mu) = w\) and \(\mathrm U(a, \mu) = c\). If further \(\mathrm{du}\) is strictly decreasing, the clause on the candidate line of the third block denotes the same relation, and its pairs are those of the declared multiplier: the grid pair \((\varphi(a), \mathrm f(a))\) at a saving \(a > 0\) is the pair at \((a, 0)\), and the corner pair \((x, x)\) with \(0 < x \le \mathrm f(0)\) is the pair at \((0, \mu)\) with \(\mu = \mathrm{du}(x) - \beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(0)\), which is nonnegative exactly when \(x \le \mathrm f(0)\) because \(\mathrm{du}\) is strictly decreasing. Conversely the pair at \((0, \mu)\) is the corner pair at \(x = \mathrm U(0, \mu) \le \mathrm f(0)\). When \(\mathrm{du}\) is a decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\), the map \(x \mapsto \mathrm{du}(x) - \beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(0)\) carries \((0, \mathrm f(0)]\) onto \([0, \infty)\). The inequality statement written without the clause, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>]), its relation read as the equality on the grid, denotes the part of the relation with \(\mu = 0\) and is no spelling of the condition. The identity of the first block with the second uses no monotonicity and no concavity; that of the third uses the monotonicity of \(\mathrm{du}\) and no concavity.

One policy, the maximizer. Suppose further (H1) that \(\mathrm u\) is strictly concave and differentiable with \(\mathrm{du}\) a decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\), (H1′) that 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is its inverse, (H2) that \(\mathrm{dv}_\succ : \mathbb R_+ \to \mathbb R_{++}\) is continuous and nonincreasing, \(\mathrm{dv}_\succ(0)\) being the right derivative of \(\mathrm v_\succ\) at zero, and (H3) that the transition is \(\mathrm g_\succ(w, c) = w - c\). Let \(\bar w = \mathrm f(0) = \mathrm{du}^{-1}(\beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(0))\).

  1. The residual \(r(w, c) = \mathrm{du}(c) - \beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(w - c)\) is strictly decreasing in \(c\) on \((0, w]\) and tends to \(+\infty\) as \(c \to 0\), so the clause's system has one solution at every \(w > 0\): \(c = w\), with multiplier \(r(w, w) \ge 0\), when \(w \le \bar w\), and the unique interior root otherwise. The first block defines the policy \(\pi^\ast\) above.
  2. \(\mathrm H\) is a bijection of \(A_\succ\) onto \(\mathbb R_{++}\). On the half-line \(\mu = 0\) it is \(\varphi\), strictly increasing with range \([\bar w, \infty)\); on the half-line \(a = 0\) it is \(\mu \mapsto \mathrm{du}^{-1}(\beta\,\mathrm{dv}_\succ(0) + \mu)\), strictly decreasing with range \((0, \bar w]\); the two meet at \((0, 0) \mapsto \bar w\). The half-line \(a = 0\) reaches every \(w\) below \(\bar w\) because the declared set of \(\mu\), \(\mathbb R_+\), is unbounded.
  3. The policy of the second block, \(\mathrm U \circ \mathrm H^{-1}\), equals \(\pi^\ast\), by the identity of relations with items 1 and 2, and so does the policy the third block states, \(\mathrm f \circ \varphi^{-1}\) on \([\bar w, \infty)\) and the identity on \((0, \bar w]\).
  4. Both are the maximizer of \(\mathrm u(c) + \beta\,\mathrm v_\succ(w - c)\) over \((0, w]\) when \(\mathrm v_\succ\) is concave with derivative \(\mathrm{dv}_\succ\): for a concave objective and a linear constraint the Kuhn–Tucker conditions are sufficient (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004, §5.5.3), the conditions being those of Nocedal and Wright (2006, Theorem 12.1). Dobrescu and Shanker (2024, Proposition 3.1) state the corresponding result for the sequence problem, given a fixed and optimal sequence of future discrete choices; their Definition 1 names the property that roots coincide with solutions and proves nothing. Sufficiency is a property of the stage's problem: it holds or fails whichever method computes the policy. For the three blocks above, written in a stage file, it is stated here, on this page, and the stage records no condition for it. Where the endogenous grid method is typed on the policy builder, stage.obligations() lists the condition egm-eligibility (R8), that the continuation value is concave and continuously differentiable on \((0,\infty)\) with a finite positive right derivative at zero, and nothing checks it.
  5. The inequality statement without its clause agrees with \(\pi^\ast\) on \(\varphi(\mathbb R_+) = [\bar w, \infty)\), the image of its grid, and states nothing below \(\bar w\), where \(\pi^\ast(w) = w\) follows from item 1; with the clause it states \(\pi^\ast\) at every \(w > 0\), by item 3.

In general. Uniqueness and optimality of a root rest on concavity of the continuation value, equivalently \(\mathrm{dv}_\succ\) nonincreasing, with strict concavity of \(\mathrm u\); uniqueness of the multiplier given a root rests on the rank condition of Dobrescu and Shanker (2024, Assumption 3.3). Their Theorem 4.1 gives only local existence of the inverse near an interior solution in one constrained region, a piece of the observable set (their equation (5)); existence on a whole region needs the Poincaré–Miranda theorem (their §4.2 and online appendix, Corollary F.1) or, in one dimension, item 2. By their Claims 4.1 and 4.2 the grid a method inverts from has on each region the dimension of the state, one coordinate here: the saving on one half-line of \(A_\succ\) and the multiplier on the other. Condition (F), coverage and measurability are stated hypotheses (R10), injectivity being one stronger sufficient condition. Where the continuation value is not concave, the case their paper is written for, the three spellings still denote one relation but none defines a function: several roots stand at one state, and a method selects among them. For the third, two admitted pairs may then share one cash on hand with different candidates, and the stage states the relation and no selection among them. The rules check none of this.

docs.title: 4.6 The endogenous-grid policy with and without its final line
docs.text:
Take the policy block of §4.2 in its two forms.

With the final line. c = c[>] gives \(\{(w,c):c=\mathrm f(w-c),\ w-c\geq0\}\) on the declared control domain. By the budget identity this is the candidate relation below. Under condition (F), coverage of the chosen domain \(D\), and measurability, it defines a policy \(\pi\) on \(D\). In this savings example, injectivity of \(\varphi\) permits \(\pi=\mathrm f\circ\varphi^{-1}\).

Without the final line. The candidate and coordinate equations give the pairs \(P=\{(\varphi(a),\mathrm f(a)):a\in\mathbb R_+\}\), but no line states the policy, and the block is refused (R1). The final line is what states the relation on those pairs, rewritten at the continuation perch as \(\pi(\varphi(a)) = \mathrm f(a)\) (R10). The identities \(\varphi(a)-\mathrm f(a)=a\) and \(w=(w-c)+\mathrm f(w-c)\) for any explicit solution establish both directions of R10's consistency requirement, so the two readings of the final line give the same relation on the same domain. It is these equations and their declared types that justify the rewriting, not the conventional names of the aliases.

This relation does not by itself include every constrained corner. The boundary \(c=w\) below the threshold requires the correctly oriented condition of §4.5, the declared multiplier of §4.5, the clause on the candidate line of §4.5, or a separately declared boundary rule or branch. That condition need not be attached to one particular final-line spelling. In a more general model, the candidate and coordinate maps must specify the full required state dependence, satisfy the transition and feasibility conditions, and cover the solutions being claimed. Three perch/role labels alone do not establish those premises.

What the method adds. The endogenous grid method chooses an asset grid \(a_1 < \dots < a_N\), tabulates the pairs \((\varphi(a_i), \mathrm f(a_i))\), and takes as its approximate policy the function through those points, with a stated extrapolation beyond the last knot (the endogenous grid method of Carroll 2006). When the file writes the clause on the first-order condition, declares the multiplier, or writes the clause on the candidate line (§4.5), the segment \(c = w\) on \((0, \varphi(0)]\) is not something the method adds: it belongs to the exact relation the file states (§4.5, items 1 and 3), and the method computes it with the other points, by the segment to the origin, on the multiplier's half-line of the observable set, or at the values the clause on the candidate line admits at zero saving. Without any of the three, the segment lies outside the declared relation, and a method that returns it reports an extension (§4.5). If the method uses an interpolant, it agrees with its computed pairs at the knots. Those pairs equal the exact policy only when the supplied continuation values and candidate calculations are exact. Increasing knots are a diagnostic, not a proof of global injectivity or condition (F): behavior between sampled points is untested. The construction records none of these conditions: whether one holds, is established under the hypotheses of §4.5, is shown by a numerical diagnostic without such a proof, or is unverified is a statement about the problem and the method, made on no record of the stage.

An explicit evaluation. The author may instead write c = evaluate(w[>], c[>], w). With exact coordinate and candidate maps, and the functional interpretation of R10, this evaluates the same policy. With tabulated pairs the line evaluates the chosen interpolating representation, which generally approximates that policy. The package does not yet construct either reading: the rule of the line prints UNRESOLVED[evaluate; mathematical definition], also with !Linear typed at the line (R8, §5.3). Distinct knots alone neither choose an interpolant nor establish the exact policy between them (R7).

docs.title: 4.7 A discrete choice and the pension model
docs.text:
A discrete choice is written as a block whose one control is valued in a finite set of labels and whose output side is empty, with one nested block per label, in the order in which the set lists the labels; nested blocks in another order are refused under branch-labels. The backward block selects among the branch values by the control. Each continuation value stands at one position of the tuple, and that position decides the branch to which the value belongs; a value at two positions or at none is refused under branch-value-position. The policy block chooses the control by maximizing over the same tuple in the same order (R12):

@stage: ret_choice

δ : ℝ₊

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a : ℝ₊) : !arvl -> (a_d : ℝ₊) : !dcsn] {
    a_d = a
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}) : !dcsn -> ()] {
    [label=work,   () -> (a_w : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a_w = a_d }
    [label=retire, () -> (a_r : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a_r = a_d }
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V_w[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, V_r[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, d) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = (V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])[d]        :: [id=choice_value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V
}

[id=policy, (V_w[>], V_r[>]) -> (d)] {
    d = argmax_{d}(V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])  :: [id=choice]
}

R3. The continuation state is the disjoint union \(\mathsf X_\succ = \mathbb R_+ \sqcup \mathbb R_+\), one copy per label, each nested block defining the coordinates of its copy (Branching). The tuple (V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>]) is a family in label order, and [d] selects the entry the control names.

R5, R8, R12. With \(V_{w,\succ} = \mathrm v_w(a_w)\) and \(V_{r,\succ} = \mathrm v_r(a_r)\) and both branch transitions the identity, the choice value is \(Q(a, d) = (\mathrm v_w(a) - \delta,\ \mathrm v_r(a))[d]\), a selected policy \(\pi(a) \in \arg\max_d Q(a, d)\) with a tie-break the rules do not fix, and \(\mathrm v_\sim(a) = \max\{\mathrm v_w(a) - \delta, \mathrm v_r(a)\}\), the exact branch maximum. Forward, a state \(a\) is routed to the copy \(\pi(a)\) names (R9).

The pension model. The savings-and-retirement model of Druedahl and Jørgensen (2017), with a contribution cap, as solved by the inverse Euler method of Dobrescu and Shanker, combines the constructions above. Its worker stage has a decision state with three coordinates, liquid assets, pension assets and earnings, two controls, consumption and the pension deposit, and a continuation state with two coordinates, so both transitions are products (R3); its retirement choice is a branch of the form just shown; its earnings shock is realized between arrival and decision, so the expectation over it stands in the arrival block, V[<] = E_{w}(V) in dcsn_to_arvl, as in §4.4 (R7); and its first-order conditions, one per asset, form one system in two unknowns, which R10 reads as a solve over both, whose residuals are subject to the three constraints the model imposes, the liquidity constraint on the liquid asset, the no-withdrawal constraint on the pension, and the cap, with their appropriate inequality directions and multipliers in a coupled constrained system. R10's scalar lower-bound example is not a complete derivation of that system. Discrete retirement choice can create non-concavities and competing candidates; neither policy non-monotonicity nor non-injectivity of a particular coordinate map follows from the branch syntax alone. When candidates overlap and the required coverage and selection conditions hold, R12 describes selection by value; an upper-envelope method approximates that operation. The application's stage files stand under applications/pension-retirement/declaration/stages/: worker_saving.bl states the worker's maximization, the block policy of its methods file, applications/pension-retirement/declaration/stages/worker_saving/methods.bl, writes its two first-order conditions with the clauses ⟂ m_f - c - c_p >= 0 and ⟂ 0 <= c_p <= w_d of R10 under time iteration, and applications/pension-retirement/economics.md records their correspondence with the paper's equations.

docs.title: 5.1 The assumptions the rules record
docs.text:
Requirement Where it is used What must be established State sufficiency for the relevant fields and conditional laws R5 (A1), R7 the chosen arguments contain the information needed for the claimed representatives and kernels Measurable transitions and any required recovery maps R5 (A2–A3) compositions have the claimed domains and earlier quantities are available as functions of the chosen arguments Specified conditional shock laws R7, R9, §4.4 the integral uses the law for its actual conditioning context; a constant marginal law alone does not establish independence Integrability and permitted output values R7 expectations and subsequent arithmetic are defined in their stated domains Joint dependence for shocks used together R7, R9 a joint law or consistent conditional factorization is supplied; a product law needs conditional independence Attainment and measurable policy selection R7, R8 an optimizer can be chosen as a measurable function; the maximum value alone does not select it Root existence and measurable selection R8, R10 a policy can be obtained from the solution relation; uniqueness is sufficient for single-valuedness but does not replace all measurability conditions Sufficient optimality conditions R8, §4.5 a chosen root or constrained stationary point is a global optimizer Condition (F), domain coverage, and measurability R10, §4.6 the candidate relation defines the claimed policy; injectivity is one stronger sufficient condition for (F) Transition consistency and coverage of explicit solutions R2, R5, R10 the identification rewritten at the continuation perch agrees with the explicit policy equation; the construction checks the coordinate line against the transition A valid envelope theorem and derivative formula R8, §4.4 the stated derivative line is the derivative it claims, including constraints and transition derivatives Differentiation under the integral sign §4.4 the arrival derivative line, with the law's factor, is the derivative of the arrival value Domain and boundary restrictions R6, §4.2 formulas are defined at the parameter and state values being used

These are sufficient premises or explicit requirements for particular interpretations. Failure to verify one does not prove that the desired conclusion is false; it means that the stated justification is unavailable.

The rules record each assumption beside the operator that needs it. The stage records some of them as conditions, which stage.obligations() lists, and §5.3 lists the ones that a rule says the stage records and that the package does not yet record. Calibration decides a recorded restriction that reads parameters alone and refuses the values at which it fails, so that ρ = 1 is refused for the body of 𝑢 in §4.2. A recorded restriction that reads a state, a control or the argument of a function stays required and is not checked. A file that satisfies R6 and is read by the rules is a well-formed statement of a problem, not a proof that the problem has a solution.

docs.title: 5.2 What the rules do not decide
docs.text: The rules assign no numerical method. Quadrature for an expectation, interpolation for an evaluation, the grid on which a policy is tabulated, and the envelope step of a method attach afterwards (Methodization). The grid on which a problem is solved and the grid on which a population is simulated are two numerical choices with separate accuracy criteria, and neither is part of the declared sets or laws. Which quantities are recorded along a simulated path is a matter for the simulation and not for the stage.

docs.title: 5.3 Open points
docs.text:
• A functional-form spelling of a value statement, with the state arguments written, is intended to be admitted under the same context as the perch form (§1.4); which such spellings the grammar admits is a separate question from what they mean.
  • A tuple law can specify a joint distribution. Separate declarations on one edge are read as the product of §2.1, which the elaboration records as the condition joint-distribution-factorization. Any unsupported conditional-law spelling must be distinguished from the mathematical conditional kernel it intends.
  • A specialized form for a certainty equivalent under recursive preferences remains outside these rules; explicit transformations are read in their written order (R11).

The table below lists the rules that the language is meant to have and that the package does not yet check, or does not yet get right. Each row gives the sections of this appendix that the rule concerns and states the rule, then what the package does today, and the smallest text that shows it. The rows follow the order of those sections. A rule that another page states stands at the section of this appendix that it concerns, with a link to that page.

A text is the text of a stage file, with one line of the file on each line of the cell. A line @methods: t and the lines after it, up to a last line that begins with stage., are a methods file of the stage. A last line that begins with stage. is a call on the stage that the text gives, in which methods names that methods file. Where a cell holds two texts, an empty line stands between them. stage.fields() lists every field of a stage with its perch, its role and its declared set (The stage §5). A piece describes the kernel of an operation in its §2 and how a card is read in its §5.

Rule What the package does today Smallest text §1.1, §2.2. The mark [~] names a field at the decision perch, and a perch mark on a name agrees with the perch word of the side that lists the name. See also Symbol conventions §3 and Perch tagging rules §1. The package reads x[~] as the bare name x and checks nothing about the mark. A name marked [~] on an arrival side or on a continuation side is read as the field of that side: for the text, stage.fields() lists x as a state at the arrival perch. @stage: t[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (x[~] : ℝ) : !arvl -> (y : ℝ) : !dcsn] { y = x[~] } §1.1, R6. A backward line reads a decision state by its bare name, also where the stage places a state of the same name at another perch. The package refuses the line under name-in-scope, with the bare name and with the name marked [~]. The refusal tells the author to write w for the decision state, which is the spelling that it has just refused. @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊) : !dcsn -> (w[>] : ℝ) : !cntn] { w[>] = w - c }[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] { V = c + V[>] + 0*w } §1.2, R4. A value line defines a function of the state at its perch, so outside an expectation it reads no shock that this state does not determine. A shock that the header of a backward block lists, and that is drawn on an earlier edge or on no edge, is read as known on the lines of the block. The line is read, the rule that the card prints for the value function keeps the shock free, here 𝑉(m) = 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m)) + y, and no condition records the reading. @stage: ty : ℝy ~ N(0, 1)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ) : !cntn] { a = m }[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, y) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] { V = V[>] + y } §1.5, R10, §4.2, §4.4, §4.5. A derivative term on a line, D_{a}V[>] or D_{w}V, denotes the derivative of the value function that it names in the named coordinate, read at the point of the line: at the continuation coordinate on a candidate line, and at the image of the law of motion on a line of an earlier perch. The rule that the package records for such a line applies the derivative to a map whose body does not read the variable that the map binds. On a line of an earlier perch the body is the value composed with the law of motion, and the derivative is read at a point that the rule leaves free: the rule of the text applies the derivative to the map (a, unit) ↦ 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m, 𝑐(m))) at the point (a≻, ()). On a candidate line the body reads the line's own coordinate of the same name, so that the rule prints as the intended derivative. @stage: t𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m - c >= 0 } §2.1. The several sets in the type of one name have a number in common, also where one of them is a reserved set, a named set, a list of integers, a union or a difference, and where an endpoint of an interval is a formula. See also Symbol conventions §9.2, Stages §2 and Types §2.6. The package compares the intervals of the type alone, by those of their endpoints that are numbers or ratios of two integers. A set of another form and an endpoint that is a formula enter no comparison. The package reads both texts, and calibrate then refuses every value given for β. @stage: tβ : ℝ₊₊ @ (-2,-1)@stage: tβ : (0,1) @ (2*1, 3) §2.1. The value bound to a parameter lies in its declared set, also where that set is a set of extended reals, ℝ̄, ℝ_{-∞}, ℝ_{+∞} or ℝ_{±∞}. See also Symbol conventions §9.2 and The binding verbs §2. calibrate decides the membership of a number in a set of extended reals: a finite number lies in every such set, and an infinity in the sets that hold it, so that inf is refused for ℝ_{-∞}. A value that is no number, a string or the floating-point value NaN (not a number), is still bound there, and stage.obligations() lists its membership as the condition calibration-domain-membership, which stays required. In an interval whose bound is an expectation over a shock, such as (0, E_{y}(y)), it binds any number in the same way. @stage: tx : ℝ_{-∞}stage.calibrate({"x": float("nan")}) §2.1, §2.5, R7. In D_{c}(𝑢) the subscript names a formal argument of the function that is differentiated. See also Equation parsing rules §5. A subscript that names no formal argument of the function is read without a refusal: the text is read, although 𝑢 has the one argument c and the file declares no x. @stage: t𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^2𝑑𝑢 := D_{x}(𝑢) §2.1. The law of a shock gives probability only to values in the declared set of the shock, so a normal law of positive variance is not declared on a strictly positive set. See also Equation parsing rules §4. The package reads the stage and records the requirement as the condition law-support, which stage.obligations() lists as required. Calibration decides the condition for a truncated lognormal law, and leaves it required for a normal, a lognormal and a uniform law. @stage: ty : ℝ₊₊y ~ N(0, 1)[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : ℝ, y) : !arvl -> (m : ℝ) : !dcsn] { m = k + y } §2.1, §2.3. The words if, then and else are no names also as the id of a line's annotation, :: [id=if], as they are none as the id of a block. The package reads a line annotated :: [id=if] and gives the line the place arvl_to_dcsn.if. A methods file cannot address that place: the entry arvl_to_dcsn.if.method : … is refused under syntax, with the sentence that if is no name. The id of a block, [id=if, …], is refused under syntax. @stage: t[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : ℝ) : !arvl -> (m : ℝ) : !dcsn] {m = k :: [id=if]} §2.2, §2.4. Where one block writes a field and another reads it, the set written lies in the set read. See also Symbol conventions §9.3, Stages §2 and Perch tagging rules §2. The package refuses under set-mismatch only an inclusion that it decides to fail. Where it cannot decide the inclusion, as with an endpoint that names a parameter, it reads the stage, records no condition, leaves the field with no declared set, and binds a calibration at which the inclusion fails, as the first text shows at ā = 5. Where the block that writes a control also holds a line marked !doc with the control on its left side, it compares no sets for the control: the second text is read, and without its !doc line it is refused under set-mismatch. @stage: tā : ℝ₊₊[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (x : ℝ) : !arvl -> (y : [0, ā]) : !dcsn] { y = x }[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (y : [0, 1]) : !dcsn -> (w : ℝ) : !cntn] { w = y }stage.calibrate({"ā": 5.0})@stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {c = m/2 :: [id=half, !doc]c = argmax_{cp}(cp + V[>])} §2.3, R1, R10. A clause after ⟂ and the declaration of a multiplier are written in a policy block and in no other block. The package reads both in a block of any kind. A clause after a line of a value block or of a forward block is read and enters no rule and no condition of the builder. A multiplier declared there is recorded as a multiplier at the continuation perch, no observable set is formed, and a value line that reads it keeps it free in its rule: for the text the card prints 𝑉(m) = 𝑐(m) + 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m, 𝑐(m))) + ν≻. @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {ν[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0V = c + V[>] + ν[>] ⟂ m - c >= 0} §2.4. The declared set of a name is the intersection of the sets written for it. See also Symbol conventions §9.2 and Perch tagging rules §2. The package computes the intersection of sets that are written identically, of the sets ℝ, ℝ₊ and ℝ₊₊, and of intervals whose endpoints are numbers or infinity. For other sets, such as a named set beside the set that defines it, or an interval with an endpoint that names a parameter, it records the field with no set and refuses nothing, and the stage loses the condition range-compatibility of the line that writes the field. @stage: tXp := ℝ₊[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (x : ℝ) : !arvl -> (y : Xp) : !dcsn] { y = x }[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (y : ℝ₊) : !dcsn -> (w : ℝ) : !cntn] { w = y } §2.4. The sets written for one field at its several places have a value in common. See also Symbol conventions §9.3, Stages §2 and Perch tagging rules §2. The package compares only the set of a block that writes the field with the set of a block that reads it. A set declared on a line of its own beside the set of a header, and the sets of two blocks that read the field, are not compared: the stage is read, and the field is recorded with no set. @stage: tb : [-3, -1][id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ) : !dcsn] { w = b } §2.4, R1, R6. Every field, a shock included, has a declared set. See also Stages §2 and Perch tagging rules §2. A field that the block headers list with no set at any place is read: stage.fields() prints it with no set, the signature of its builder prints UNRESOLVED[k≺; argument set], and calibrate admits the stage. A shock with a law and no set is read as well. Only a name that the file declares nowhere is refused, under name-in-scope. @stage: t[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k) : !arvl -> (m) : !dcsn] { m = k } §2.4. In a declaration outside the blocks, a name inside a nested tuple is a parameter when no block header lists it, as a name of a flat tuple is. See also Stages §2. The package reads the declaration, and a line may read the nested names, but stage.par, the list of the parameters, omits them. calibrate requires no value for them and judges no value against their sets. @stage: t((p, q) : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊, r : ℝ)stage.calibrate({"r": 1.0, "p": -1.0}) R1. No statement of a block redefines an input of that block. The package compares the lines of a block with one another only. A line that writes an input, a state, a control or a value, is read, the lines that follow read what the line writes in place of the input, and calibrate admits the stage. For the text the kernel of the operation is 𝐺(V≻, m, c) = c + 0, in which the continuation value is unused. @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {V[>] = 0V = c + V[>]} R3, §4.7. Within an alternative of a branching block, a law of motion reads no continuation state of another alternative. See also Perch tagging rules §5. The package reads such a law and puts the law of motion of the other alternative for the state that the line names: for the text the law of motion is 𝑔(a_d, d) = (a_d + a_d, a_d). @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d : ℝ₊, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}) : !dcsn -> ()] {[label=work, () -> (a_w : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a_w = a_d + a_r }[label=retire, () -> (a_r : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a_r = a_d }}[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V_w[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, V_r[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, d) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] { V = (V_w[>], V_r[>])[d] }[id=policy, (V_w[>], V_r[>]) : !cntn -> (d : {work, retire} @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { d = argmax_{d}(V_w[>], V_r[>]) } R4, R10. The two sides of an implicit equation are one relation: a term on either side that reads a field of a later perch is composed with the law of motion and, across an edge that draws a shock, stands inside an expectation over that shock. The package checks the right side and the clause alone. A term on the left side that combines a field of a later perch, or its derivative, with other quantities, as 1*D_{a}V[>] does in the text, is read without the expectation, forms no Pullback, and stands in the rule uncomposed with the law of motion. With the sides exchanged, the line of the text is refused under shock-observed. @stage: tη : ℝ₊₊η ~ LogNormal(0, 1)𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊, η) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = (m - c)*η }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { 1*D_{a}V[>] = 𝑑𝑢(c) } R4. A refusal for a dependence on a shock that the construction has not shown to cancel reports that measurability has not been established, and does not assert that the value is unknown. The message of shock-observed says "so the value of V is not known at the arvl perch" wherever a forward block between the two perches lists a shock, also where its law of motion does not read the shock or the shock cancels in it, as in the text. @stage: ty : ℝy ~ N(0, 1)[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : ℝ, y) : !arvl -> (m : ℝ) : !dcsn] { m = k + y - y }[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] { V[<] = V } R5, R11. The rule of an output statement is its expression with the aliases of its block expanded, whether or not an intermediate line is marked !node. Where a block writes an alias before the output statement, the card of the builder prints the line of the alias as the rule of the output, while the function that the operation computes is the expanded expression. For the text the card prints 𝑉(m) = 𝑐(m), and the kernel of the operation is 𝐺(V≻, m, c) = c + V≻. @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {W = cV = W + V[>]} R5. Where a substituted alias depends on the output being determined, the statement gives the implicit relation of R10. A line whose left side is the bare control and whose right side reads a field of a later perch through an alias is refused under not-constructed. The same reading written in the line itself, c = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]), is read, and so is the alias inside solve_{c}(…). @stage: t𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {z = D_{a}V[>]c = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(z)} R5, §4.3. A statement across two perches states one relation, which is rewritten at the perch whose map contains no unknown. Read at the decision perch, the final line c = c[>] of a policy block is an implicit equation in the control, which needs no coordinate line. The package rewrites only the identification c = c[>] of a block that writes the coordinate line. A block that writes the candidate line and the final line without the coordinate line is read, as the text is: the card prints the type of 𝑐 in place of a rule for the operation of the final line, the record of that operation is UNRESOLVED[policy.2:Pullback; solution coordinate relation], and no refusal, condition or diagnostic reports it. With the coordinate line m[>] = a + c[>] and another right side on the final line, c = 1*c[>], the card prints 𝑐(m) = 1 · UNRESOLVED[c≻; free mathematical reference]. @stage: t𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])c = c[>]} R7. The differentiability that D_{c}(𝑢) assumes is recorded as a condition of the stage, as the bijection that Inv assumes is. stage.obligations() lists inverse-function-domain for Inv(𝑑𝑢). For D_{c}(𝑢) it lists only binding-domain, which requires that the bound variable have a declared domain, and no condition of differentiability. @stage: t𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-1)𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢)𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 := Inv(𝑑𝑢)[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : ℝ₊₊) : !arvl -> (m : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] { m = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(𝑑𝑢(k)) } R7. An order of expectations that needs a conditional law the file does not declare, a posterior among them, is refused under conditional-not-declared. In a backward block the package refuses such an order under that rule. In the objective of a policy block it refuses the order first under shock-observed, with a message that asks for an expectation that the line already writes, "Write the expectation over it, E_{ν}(…)". @stage: tν : ℝν ~ N(0, 1)Ψ : ℝ₊₊Ψ ~ LogNormal(ν, 1)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊, ν, Ψ) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = (m - c)*Ψ }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { c = argmax_{c}(c + E_{Ψ}(E_{ν}(V[>]))) } R7. The set of a binder, argmax_{var : set}, is a named set or a correspondence applied to its arguments. See also Constraints §1. The package reads set as an expression and checks only that its names are declared. A parameter, a state, a number, a pair such as (0, m) or the name of a correspondence without arguments is read, and the policy card prints the maximization over it, as in argmax_{cp ∈ ρ}. @stage: tρ : ℝ₊₊[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { c = argmax_{cp : ρ}(cp + V[>]) } R7. The body of a feasibility correspondence may be a finite set of integers, written as an integer range {0, …, J} or as a list {0, 1}. See also Constraints §1. Written alone as the body, either is refused under not-constructed. As a factor of a product, {0, …, 3} × ℝ, either is read. @stage: tΓ(x : ℝ₊₊) := {0, …, 3} R7. The policy card prints the set that a binder names in the statement of the maximization, also where the binder names a named set. See also Constraints §1. For a binder over a named set the card prints 𝑐(m) ∈ Xm beside the type of the policy, and UNRESOLVED[Xm; free mathematical reference] in place of the set in the statement. @stage: tXm := ℝ₊₊[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { c = argmax_{cp : Xm}(cp + V[>]) } R7. solve_{c}(r_1, …, r_k) denotes the relation of the feasible unknowns that satisfy every residual equation. For one unknown with two or more residuals the line is read without a refusal, the rule of its operation holds no residual, and the output of the operation is recorded as UNRESOLVED[policy.1:Aggregation; solve relation]. With the one residual c - 1/2 the card prints r₁ = c − 1/2 and c = solve_{c}(r₁). @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { c = solve_{c}(c - 1/2, c - 1/3) } R7. No method is attached to a statement marked !doc, which is a declaration and forms no operation. See also Constraints §1. The id of a !doc line is a place of the kind statement. methodize reads a representation such as !Linear typed there, holds the entry in stage.methods, and the policy card prints it under Method. @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {c = argmax_{c}(c + V[>]) :: [id=optimality, !doc]c = m/2}@methods: tpolicy.optimality.method : !Linearstage.methodize(methods) R8, §4.6. An authored c = evaluate(w[>], c[>], w) with exact candidate and coordinate maps denotes evaluation of the relation that the candidate line and the coordinate line determine. With tabulated pairs it evaluates the interpolating representation that the methods file types at the line. The package holds no definition of evaluate. The line is read, the rule of its operation prints UNRESOLVED[evaluate; mathematical definition], and stage.obligations() lists the condition external-callable-signature-and-provider for evaluate. The printed rule and the condition are the same where the methods file types a representation such as !Linear at policy.evaluate. @stage: t𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])m[>] = a + c[>]c = evaluate(m[>], c[>], m)} R8. Differentiability of a value at the point where a line reads its derivative is a condition that the stage records, the value being read as a locally Lipschitz function whose derivative is set-valued at a kink. The package defines the derivative as the limit of the difference quotients, a single number, and a line that reads D_{a}V[>] records no condition. stage.obligations() lists differentiability only under marginal-reading, for a derivative line, and under egm-eligibility, for a policy builder under !egm. @stage: t𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])m[>] = a + c[>]c = c[>]} R8. The lines of a solution method compute the policy of the declared maximization only under a condition, which the stage records under the method table's name for it. In the method table only !egm names such a condition, egm-eligibility. Under !time_iteration or !explicit the lines of the method stand in place of the maximization in stage.builder, and stage.obligations() lists no condition under which they compute its policy. @stage: t[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { c = argmax_{c}(c + V[>]) }@methods: t[id=policy, method : !explicit] { c = m/2 }stage.methodize(methods) R10. A system of candidate statements is reached by one solve occurrence at its first statement, so that a method addresses the system as one place. The package records the occurrence on some systems only. Where the first statement is 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m - c >= 0, as in the text, or 2*D_{a}V[>] = 𝑑𝑢(c) ⟂ m - c >= 0, the block has no place policy.solve, and an entry that types a root finder there is refused under name-in-scope. Where the first statement is 𝑑𝑢(c) - D_{a}V[>] = 0 ⟂ m - c >= 0, the block has the place. @stage: t𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m - c >= 0 }@methods: tpolicy.solve.method : !root_findstage.methodize(methods) R10. The bound of a clause is written with >= or <=. A clause with one bound and a strict sign is read as the clause with the weak sign: the card prints the sign as written, and the Kuhn–Tucker conditions that the package forms from the clause are those of the weak sign. A strict sign in a clause with two bounds is refused under readable-form. @stage: t𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m - c > 0 } R12. An authored upper_env denotes the upper envelope of R12: at each decision state, the control of a candidate that attains the greatest candidate value. The package holds no definition of upper_env and checks none of its arguments. The line is read with no value candidate among its arguments, as in the text, and with one argument or four, and a method such as !FUES is typed at policy.upper_env. The rule of the line prints UNRESOLVED[upper_env; mathematical definition], and stage.obligations() lists external-callable-signature-and-provider for upper_env. @stage: t𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/2)[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m : ℝ₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a = m - c }[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])m[>] = a + c[>]c = upper_env(m[>], c[>])} §5.2. A setting bound before a calibration lies in its declared set at the values that the calibration binds, a calibration that replaces an earlier one included. See also Methodization §7 and The binding verbs §3. configure admits a value whose set names a parameter while no calibration is bound, and calibrate judges no setting bound before it. The value stays bound outside its set until a later configure refuses it under setting-outside-set. In the order calibrate, methodize, configure, the call of configure refuses the same value. @stage: tR : ℝ₊₊[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : ℝ) : !arvl -> (m : ℝ) : !dcsn] { m = R*k }@methods: ttol_s : (0, R)arvl_to_dcsn.method : !deterministicstage.methodize(methods).configure({"tol_s": 5.0}).calibrate({"R": 1.04}) §5.2. A bound of a grid lies inside the declared set of its coordinate, read at the calibrated value of each parameter that the set names. See also Methodization §3.2 and Settings §2. configure decides the membership at the calibration that is bound, and refuses a bound outside the set there under grid-bounds. calibrate judges no bound of a grid again, so a calibration that replaces an earlier one leaves a bound outside the set of its coordinate, as in the text. Before a calibration is bound, configure refuses every bound on a coordinate whose set names a parameter, as not decidably inside the declared set. @stage: tXk := [k_lo, inf)k_lo : ℝ[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : Xk) : !arvl -> (m : ℝ) : !dcsn] { m = k }[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] { V[<] = V }@methods: tn_k : ℕk_min : ℝk_max : ℝdcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.method : !Lineardcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k))stage.calibrate({"k_lo": 0.0}).methodize(methods).configure({"n_k": 5, "k_min": 1.0, "k_max": 2.0}).calibrate({"k_lo": 1.5})

docs.text:
• Aliprantis, C. D., and Border, K. C. (2006). Infinite Dimensional Analysis: A Hitchhiker's Guide, 3rd ed. Springer. Theorem 18.19, the measurable maximum theorem.
  • Benveniste, L. M., and Scheinkman, J. A. (1979). On the differentiability of the value function in dynamic models of economics. Econometrica 47(3), 727–732.
  • Boyd, S., and Vandenberghe, L. (2004). Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press. §5.5.3, the Kuhn–Tucker conditions for convex problems.
  • Carroll, C. D. (2006). The method of endogenous gridpoints for solving dynamic stochastic optimization problems. Economics Letters 91(3), 312–320.
  • Clausen, A., and Strub, C. (2020). Reverse calculus and nested optimization. Journal of Economic Theory 187, 105019. The envelope conditions under which a stated derivative line holds.
  • Dobrescu, L. I., and Shanker, A. (2024). Using inverse Euler equations to solve multidimensional discrete-continuous dynamic models: a general method. Working paper, 7 December 2024. §2.1, Definition 1 and the inverse problem on observables; §3, Assumption 3.3, the rank condition, and Proposition 3.1, the sufficient first-order conditions; §4.1, equation (5), the constrained regions; §4.2, Claim 4.1, Theorem 4.1 and Claim 4.2, and the Poincaré–Miranda theorem for existence (online appendix, Corollary F.1).
  • Druedahl, J., and Jørgensen, T. H. (2017). A general endogenous grid method for multi-dimensional models with non-convexities and constraints. Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 74, 87–107.
  • Kallenberg, O. (1997). Foundations of Modern Probability. Springer. Lemma 1.13 (Doob–Dynkin), Theorem 5.4 (disintegration), and Theorem A1.7 (measurability of the inverse between Borel spaces).
  • Milgrom, P., and Segal, I. (2002). Envelope theorems for arbitrary choice sets. Econometrica 70(2), 583–601.
  • Nocedal, J., and Wright, S. J. (2006). Numerical Optimization, 2nd ed. Springer. Theorem 12.1, the first-order conditions.
  • Rincón-Zapatero, J. P., and Santos, M. S. (2009). Differentiability of the value function without interiority assumptions. Journal of Economic Theory 144(5), 1948–1964.
  • Rockafellar, R. T. (1970). Convex Analysis. Princeton University Press. Theorem 28.2, the existence of Kuhn–Tucker vectors, and Theorem 29.1, Kuhn–Tucker vectors as subgradients of the perturbation function.
  • Sargent, T. J., and Stachurski, J. Dynamic Programming, Vol. II: the aggregator and the policy operator.
  • Stokey, N. L., and Lucas, R. E., with Prescott, E. C. (1989). Recursive Methods in Economic Dynamics. Harvard University Press. Theorems 4.10 and 4.11, the differentiability of the value function; Chapter 7, conditional expectation.

docs.title: Appendix D — Nodes and field indexing
docs.text:
Summary

A statement's equations determine its mathematical meaning; !node marks a statement as an authored node, a computation that can be named and addressed separately. Perch marks identify fields in their information context, while other bracket selections require a declared collection or family. This appendix explains how these distinctions preserve composition in both the field diagram and the functional diagram that Appendix C reads.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Fields, functions and types: field and functional diagrams; Operators and builders: operations within a block. Builds on — Appendix C: the declared context, substitution, and the conditions for interpreting equations as functions or relations; Perch tagging rules: the information sets of fields. Used by — Methodization: numerical methods address the computations identified here.

docs.title: 1 What the marks describe
docs.text:
The rules concern a .bl stage file. A typing context collects the declared domains, roles, perches, the typed arguments of the declared functions, and shock laws. A perch is an information set, and a field is a random variable measurable at its declared perch. Representing that field by a function of the declared state requires the sufficiency assumptions of Appendix C §1.2 and R5.

Three pieces of syntax answer different questions:

  • A block's header, with its typed inputs and outputs, states which quantities it relates. Its equations determine the relation or operator.
  • An annotation such as :: [id=shift, !node] names a statement and marks it as an authored node: a computation to inspect or realize as a unit within the block.
  • A perch mark such as [>] identifies a field at continuation. It does not supply a state space, a representative function, or a numerical grid.

For example, this transition fragment has one real input and two real outputs. The intermediate result y is also a declared output:

[id=transform, (a : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (y : ℝ, q : ℝ) : !cntn] {
    y = 2 + a    :: [id=shift, !node]
    q = 4*y      :: [id=scale]
}

The header identifies a decision-to-continuation transition. Renaming transform or shift does not change that transition. The !node on the first line keeps that line as a unit of its own; the addition and multiplication are mathematical operations whether that mark is present or absent.

The statement mark is !node, written inside the annotation after ::. Methods remain in a separate methods file, and neither a block identifier nor a method name selects the block's mathematical formula.

docs.title: 2 What an equation determines
docs.text:
An explicit definition such as y = 2 + a gives a function when its arguments, domains, and dependencies are established. In §1, with \(a\in\mathbb R\), its representative is \(\mathrm g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(\mathrm g(a)=2+a\). The field equation and the function equation are related as Appendix C specifies; they are not the same kind of object.

An implicit equation instead states a relation. For example, suppose the stage declares \(a=w-c\) and the continuation candidate \(c_\succ=\mathrm f(a)\). The policy equation c = c[>] then gives $$ {(w,c):c=\mathrm f(w-c),\ (w,c)\text{ is feasible}}. $$ It defines a policy only where a unique solution, or a specified selection from its solutions, meets the required measurability conditions. Adding !node makes the relation separately addressable; it proves neither existence nor uniqueness and does not make a root an optimizer (Appendix C R8 and R10).

An alias is an explicit definition of an intermediate quantity that can be substituted at its uses. Substitution must preserve local binding, domains, shock dependence, and any retained control arguments. An implicit condition cannot be used as an assignment before its unknowns are determined. An equation defining a block output must continue to determine that output even if its expression is also substituted elsewhere.

A statement marked !doc is documentation and contributes no defining equation. Consequently, adding !doc can remove a condition from the mathematical problem; it is not equivalent to adding or removing !node. An identifier alone changes neither kind of statement.

docs.title: 3 Authored nodes and operator occurrences inside equations
docs.text:
There are three levels of detail within the diagrams of a stage:

  1. A block is represented as a unit with its declared inputs and outputs.
  2. A statement marked !node specifies a unit within that block.
  3. The mathematical operations inside each equation remain available at finer detail, including their arguments and local binding.

A computational statement is an authored node exactly when it carries !node. An operator occurrence is a particular use of an operation within an expression. An expectation, argmax, solve, upper_env, or an authored evaluate remains an operator occurrence even when its statement is unmarked. It does not thereby make that statement an authored node.

For example, this arrival-value fragment contains two expectations and no authored nodes:

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<]      = E_{y}(V)          :: [id=value]
    D_{b}V[<] = E_{y}(R*D_{w}V)   :: [id=marginal]
}

The surrounding stage supplies the transition w = R*b + y from the arrival state b to the decision state w, the law of y, the return parameter R, and the decision value field. The second line is a derivative line: it states the derivative of the arrival value in b, with the factor R that the transition contributes. Both integrations belong to the mathematical interpretation, subject to Appendix C R7. A numerical method can address them without adding !node to either line.

Arithmetic and the applications of declared functions also remain, within the equations that a block or a statement marked !node carries. Being mathematically represented does not make every operation a separate place: a place is an operator at which a methods file can type a method, which the stage lists with its path and its kind (Methodization §2; §6).

These three levels occur within both the field diagram and the functional diagram, and replace neither. Both sides of an implicit equation and the rule relating the two diagrams must remain available; a printed formula or a method attachment cannot replace those mathematical objects.

docs.title: 4 Composition and substitution
docs.text:
In §1, let \(\mathrm g(a)=2+a\) and \(\mathrm h(y)=4y\), both maps from \(\mathbb R\) to \(\mathbb R\). The second output is $$ \mathrm q(a)=\mathrm h(\mathrm g(a))=4(2+a). $$ The whole transition has type \(\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\) and is $$ \mathrm F(a)=\bigl(\mathrm g(a),\mathrm h(\mathrm g(a))\bigr). $$ Substituting 2 + a for y in the second equation preserves \(\mathrm F\). Deleting the first output would not: the block promises both y and q. Keeping shift as a node records the intermediate computation while the composite function remains \(\mathrm F\).

Composition requires matching types. For general maps \(\mathrm g:A\to B\) and \(\mathrm h:B\to C\), the composite \(\mathrm h\circ\mathrm g:A\to C\) is defined because the output of \(\mathrm g\) is an admissible input to \(\mathrm h\). If the second operation also needs a shock or another state argument, that argument must be retained; a node does not supply it.

A node also does not hide dependencies. If y depends on a shock, substitution must retain that dependence. An expectation integrates over that shock only when its stated binding and law require it; other free arguments remain free. The formal arguments of functions and operator-bound variables keep their own scope. A perch mark binds no variable; a statement identifier binds no mathematical argument (Appendix C R2, R4, R5, and R11).

Denotation means the mathematical object represented by an expression or diagram. For the same typed equations, adding or removing !node preserves their mathematical denotation while changing the recorded nodes: the marked statement's result becomes a function that later statements consume and a method may represent exactly or by an approximation. An operation occurring inside an unmarked statement also returns a function of the remaining arguments, but that function is not an authored object: it is obtained exactly through its definition and admits only the operation's own methods, never a representation (Appendix C R7, the result of an occurrence). #functional-semantics The diagrams therefore need not be identical. Likewise, equality of mathematical functions does not guarantee identical floating-point results after different numerical methods are attached.

Technical details

The substitution argument concerns equal denotations on the required domain, with local binding preserved. Almost-sure equality under one state law alone does not justify substituting representatives at states reached under a different policy or initial law. The distinction and the required representative choices are stated in Appendix C R5.

docs.title: 5 Field marks, collection selection, and function arguments
5.1 Perch marks
docs.text:
V[<], V, and V[>] identify the arrival, decision, and continuation value fields. V[~] is an explicit spelling of the decision field V. For other names, the complete declarations and headers establish the native perch. A non-native marked occurrence, such as c[>], needs a definition or supplied interpretation at that perch; it is not automatically equal to the decision control c.

The state at a perch can have several coordinates. A field marked [>] may therefore be represented by a function of a vector, not necessarily one scalar asset. Its arguments follow from the declared state and the equations, under the sufficiency assumptions of Appendix C. The mark alone establishes no factorization through a particular coordinate.

docs.title: 5.2 Collection and family selection
docs.text:
Brackets other than the perch marks require an appropriate collection or family. For a tuple, positions start at one: (y, q)[1] selects y. A named selector must resolve to a declared key or to a selector with a compatible domain. For example, the retirement choice uses

V = (V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])[d]    :: [id=choice_value]

Here the surrounding declaration gives d the ordered labels {work, retire}. work selects the first expression and retire the second. Each expression must have the required value type. The tuple of alternative values is distinct from the labeled union of successor state spaces (Appendix C R3 and §4.7).

An indexed collection may have a parameter-defined number of entries. With an integer parameter J, L_J := {1, …, J} and δ : L_J → ℝ, a name j : L_J selects the entry δ[j]; dist : L_J × L_J → ℝ₊ is selected as dist[j][i] when both names have suitable declared domains. The selector can be a state, a control or a parameter. Its declaration must establish membership in the index set; declaring it only on ℕ does not do so. Symbol conventions §9.2.1 states the admitted index sets and how calibration associates keys with entries.

For a product-valued field, q[>][1] first identifies the continuation field and then selects its first component. Put the perch mark before component selectors. An integer literal in brackets selects a component by position; it is not an inter-period time shift.

A name in brackets does not declare an information set

The spellings q[a] and q[y] do not by themselves declare that q is a function of the state a or the intermediate value y. They require an established indexed object and the appropriate selection rule. They neither bind the bracketed name in an equation's right side nor provide missing domains or measurability assumptions. A state can select an entry when its declared domain supplies suitable keys, as above. To apply a declared function to a state, use parentheses, 𝑞(a) (§5.3).

docs.title: 5.3 Explicit function arguments
docs.text:
Use a declared function when the intended mathematical map and its arguments should be explicit:

𝑔(a : ℝ) := 2 + a
𝑞(y : ℝ) := 4*y

The second declaration defines a function on \(\mathbb R\); its formal argument y is local to that function. In a field equation, 𝑞(y) applies the function to the field y, while 𝑞(𝑔(a)) writes the composition directly. Neither application changes the field's declared perch.

Suppose \(q_A:A\to Q\) is a function on a state space \(A\), with value set \(Q\), and \(g:A\to Y\) is an intermediate map. Representing \(q_A\) using only that intermediate value requires \(q_Y:g(A)\to Q\) with \(q_A=q_Y\circ g\). Such a function exists exactly when \(g(a_1)=g(a_2)\) implies \(q_A(a_1)=q_A(a_2)\). To construct it, set \(q_Y(g(a))=q_A(a)\); the condition makes the result independent of the chosen \(a\). Conversely, the composition forces equal \(g\) values to give equal \(q_A\) values. Measurability of \(q_Y\) remains a separate requirement. A bracket spelling cannot establish that equation. Appendix C R10 uses the same condition when candidate parameters represent a policy.

docs.title: 6 Addresses and numerical methods
docs.text:
An address identifies a declared block, statement, or operation for inspection or method attachment. The address says where to attach; the typed equations say what computation is being approximated. In the examples above:

  • transform addresses the whole transition, and transform.shift addresses the statement marked !node.
  • dcsn_to_arvl.value.E_y addresses the expectation in the named value equation. The statement's id=value identifies that occurrence; it does not make the statement a node.
  • A stage-wide E_y address applies to the occurrences of expectation over y covered by that methods interface. A statement-qualified address distinguishes the integration in the value line from the one in the derivative line when they need different attachments.

Use explicit statement identifiers for stable addresses. A line number is not a method address: inserting documentation must not redirect an attachment. Renaming identifiers consistently in the stage and its methods file preserves the equations and the intended attachments. Identifiers must be unambiguous in their enclosing scope.

An address used for inspection is not necessarily a place. An unmarked scalar alias can remain identifiable without defining a separate numerical task. An authored node, an operator occurrence and the Evaluation of a builder are places of different kinds, and typing a method requires a place of a kind the method admits and a method suitable for its mathematical operation (Method types).

The address <block-id>.<statement-id>.<operator> must identify the intended occurrence. If a statement contains two indistinguishable occurrences under that address, the attachment is ambiguous; it must not silently choose the first. A stage-wide attachment, where supported, is an explicit choice to govern the corresponding group.

Methods and their settings are written separately from the stage. A quadrature rule approximates an integral; a root finder approximates a solution of the stated relation. Neither supplies a missing shock law, constraint, or optimality condition. A numerical grid is part of a chosen representation, whereas the field's domain belongs to the model: the methods file writes the grid by its own entry at the place, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m)), one factor for each coordinate, and the method by its basis, such as !Linear (see Methodization §3.2).

The name evaluate. An authored evaluate(knots, values, x) denotes evaluation of a stated representation, with coordinates first and values second. The numerical interpolation and extrapolation must be specified as Appendix C R7 requires. It is an operation inside its line, with declared arguments, and a method attaches to it at its own address, <block-id>.<statement-id>.evaluate, where a representation needs no grid, since the first argument holds the knots; evaluate alone names the one authored occurrence of a stage and is refused where the stage authors none or several. A methods file also writes evaluate after a block id for the Evaluation that closes the builder, the place of a declared output representation, and may say which stored object it types: policy.evaluate for the policy function of the policy builder, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate for everything the Evaluation of a backward value builder stores, the value function and the derivative of it that a derivative line states, or cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[V] and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[D_{m_d}V] for each of them apart, with a grid of its own. That place names an operation every such builder closes with; it does not assert that an evaluate expression was written in the stage, and it creates none. A representation typed on the builder itself is refused under method-admission. See Methodization §2 for the written form.

docs.title: 7 Policy relations and numerical decomposition
docs.text:
The policy block of the consumption stage cons of Appendix C §4.2, written in the interior form with its candidate line an equation, provides an example in which an unmarked statement is a relation rather than an alias:

[id=policy, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])    :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]             :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                 :: [id=cons_choice]
}

The surrounding cons stage declares the transition \(a=m_d-c\) and the inverse marginal-utility function. Its continuation value, and so the derivative D_{a}V[>] that the candidate line reads, is already discounted; no discount factor should be inserted into this fragment. Appendix C §4.2 derives its functions and §4.5 states sufficient conditions and a constrained extension; the methods file applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, beside cons.bl, writes the candidate line as the inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0, whose clause states the borrowing constraint (Appendix C §4.5).

The first two lines define the candidate and its decision coordinate. The third identifies the decision control with the candidate. Read at the decision perch, it determines the control implicitly through the transition; rewritten at the continuation perch, through the coordinate map of the second line, it states the policy at the cash on hand of each saving, the relation the construction states (Appendix C R5 and §4.3). It remains a relation even though it has no !node mark and contains no written solve operator: the policy builder, the operator the policy block denotes, holds it as an operation whose output is its own unknown. A method may address it as a solution, and the methods interface records a solve place for it; that recognition does not turn it into an authored solve expression or erase either side of the equation.

The endogenous grid method approximates this relation by computing candidate pairs and representing the resulting policy, which the pairs determine under Appendix C R10's consistency, single-valuedness, coverage, and measurability conditions. When the final line is omitted, no line states the policy and the block is refused under the rule output-defined (Appendix C R1 and §4.6); an implementation does not invent a missing final equation or a place from the names of the lines.

Choosing a numerical method does not add evaluate, upper_env, or !node statements to the model. If a method internally interpolates or compares candidate values, those computations realize the stated problem. An authored upper_env is instead a mathematical operation in its own right, with the selection and attainment requirements of Appendix C R12. A method's internal steps may be displayed for inspection, but must remain distinguishable from the authored equations and their nodes.

docs.title: 8 Compositional meaning
docs.text:
The compositionality requirement is that the meaning of an expression is determined by the meanings of its parts. For a language with names, those meanings retain their declared context, free arguments, and local binding. An operator's interpretation can then combine them without guessing what a statement identifier was intended to mean. This is the denotational discipline described by Hutton (2023, §3), applied here to the field equations and typed operations of Appendix C.

It permits substitution of equal mathematical meanings within a valid context. It does not equate every diagram recording those meanings: an annotated diagram also records authored addresses and nodes. Removing a !node mark can preserve the represented mathematical function or relation while changing the diagram available for method attachment.

Technical details

A syntactic sort is a category of expressions. For an ordinary many-sorted signature, which lists constructors together with their input and output sorts, the freely generated terms form an initial algebra. Initial means that there is a unique map preserving those constructors into each specified algebra of the same signature (Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner, and Wright 1977, §2, Proposition 2.1). The target must already specify the mathematical sets and operations. The theorem does not choose missing interpretations, solve implicit equations, or prove their analytic assumptions. Binding and substitution require a representation that accounts for contexts; a many-sorted list of constructor arities alone is not a proof that those binding rules are respected (Lamiaux and Ahrens 2024, §1.1.1).

The formal implementation must preserve these distinctions when it constructs the two diagrams. This appendix specifies their mathematical meaning and authored nodes; it does not prescribe parser constructors, storage records, or an execution order for a numerical solver.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Goguen, J. A., Thatcher, J. W., Wagner, E. G., and Wright, J. B. (1977). Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras. Journal of the ACM 24(1), 68–95. §2, especially Proposition 2.1.
  • Hutton, G. (2023). Programming language semantics: It's easy as 1,2,3. Journal of Functional Programming 33, e9. §3, pp. 3–4.
  • Lamiaux, T., and Ahrens, B. (2024). An Introduction to Different Approaches to Initial Semantics. §1.1.1, on syntax with binding and substitution.

docs.title: Expression forms
docs.text:
Summary

An expression in a line of a stage file is built from names, numbers and arithmetic, and from nine named forms: the expectation E_{θ}(…), the maximization argmax_{c}(…), the implicit solution solve_{c}(…), the derivative D_{c}(𝑢) of a declared function and D_{a}V[>] of a value, the inverse Inv(𝑓), and the real functions exp, log, max and min. A shock's law is written on a line of its own, after ~. The table gives each form as a stage file writes it, what it computes, the object of the Bellman calculus it realizes where the calculus defines one, and the entry of the package that defines it. A methods file, the addition beside a stage file, writes its blocks in the same forms, and §4 says how its lines are read.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Field equations: the lines in which these forms stand; Constraints: the inequalities and the ⟂ clause a line may carry. Formal account — Operators: the operations the forms denote; Equation parsing rules §§4–5: the variable a form binds and the reading of a law. See also — Shock distributions: the families a law names; Symbol conventions: declarations, domains and type words.

docs.title: 1 Reading the table
docs.text:
Each row is one form. written gives the first occurrence of the form that the package finds in the stage files under applications/, printed back as normalized .bl text by to_source of syntax/source.py, so that E_{Ψ,θ} in port.bl shows as E_{Ψ, θ}, with the file, or says that no stage file writes it; the arithmetic row gives the six signs of the grammar, and the laws row the call of each family as the module docstring of distributions/families.py spells it. meaning gives, for an operator written with a subscript, the words the package attaches to it in OPERATOR_MEANINGS of typing/line_unknowns.py, followed for D by its defining expression; for a named function of the definitions table, its defining expression; and for the arithmetic, the names the grammar gives its six operations, add, sub, neg, mul, div and pow. denotes links to the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the object the form realizes, and shows a dash where E.3 defines no such object, as for a real function applied at each point, such as exp. The laws row also shows a dash: each family has its own row, with its own link to E.3, on the laws page. read from names the module under packages/bellman/bellman/, its table and the key: BOUND_OPERATORS for the four heads written with a subscript in braces, and PRIMITIVE_DEFINITIONS["definitions"] for the named functions, each of which it defines exactly.

A subscript in braces names the variable the form binds: the shock an expectation integrates, the control a maximization chooses, or the unknowns a solution solves for. The subscript of a derivative instead names an argument of a function the file has already defined, as in 𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢), or, where the operator is applied to a value field written with its perch mark, a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark: D_{a}V[>] is the derivative term, the derivative of the continuation value in the continuation coordinate a, and D_{a}D_{a}V[>] its second derivative. A stage file writes the term without parentheses, and the row of D shows the first spelling of D on the corpus as the package's printer writes it, D_{m_d}(V), the left side of the derivative line D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) of cons.bl. A subscript that names no state coordinate of that perch, or a discrete coordinate, is refused with the perch's coordinates named, and a derivative term of a value the block neither reads nor writes is refused as an undeclared name is (Refusals). A derivative term may stand on the right side of any line, where it reads a derivative, and on the left side of a line of a value builder's block, where it states the derivative of the value the builder writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) (Field equations §2). The term applies an operator to a function the graph already holds; the package reads it and differentiates nothing.
