* / ^ ** add, sub, neg, mul, div, pow — syntax/grammars/stage.lark, the rules sum, product, molecule and _POW laws N(μ, v) LogNormal(μ, σ) Uniform(a, b) TruncatedNormal(μ, σ, l, u) TruncatedLogNormal(μ, σ, l, u) TypeIExtremeValue(μ, s) DiscreteMarkov(Π, points) MarkovChain(Π, points) Mixture((f₁, J₁), …) Categorical((f₁, …)) Bernoulli(p) the law of a shock, written after ~ in its declaration; each family, its arguments and its meaning stand on the laws page — distributions/families.py, FAMILY_ARGUMENTS

A law names a shock, or a tuple of shocks, on the left of ~ and a family applied to its arguments on the right. Shock distributions lists the families and the meaning of their arguments; Equation parsing rules §4 states how separate laws and a joint law are read.

A braced form with any other head, such as max_{c}(…), is refused under the rule not-constructed of Refusals. A call of a name that neither the stage file nor the table defines, such as sqrt(x), has no definition and denotes nothing; define the function in the stage file instead, 𝑟(x : ℝ₊) := x^(1/2).

docs.title: 2 Arithmetic
docs.text:
Between the named forms stand numbers, the names of fields, parameters and functions, and the arithmetic of the grammar, syntax/grammars/stage.lark:

Written Reading a + b, a - b, -a Sum, difference and negation. A leading minus negates the product that follows it: -a*b is -(a*b). a*b, a/b Product and quotient. A product is always written with *. a^b, a**b Power. The exponent is a single term, a name, a number, a call or an expression in parentheses: c^(1-ρ). ∞, inf Infinity; both spellings are one constant. (a, b) A tuple, a finite family of values. x[1], (V_young[>], W_old[>])[s] Selection from a family, by position counted from one or by the label a coordinate takes. 𝑢(c) A function the stage file defines, applied to as many arguments as it declares.

A power binds more tightly than a product or a quotient, and these more tightly than a sum or a difference; parentheses group. A line relates two expressions by = or by one of the inequalities <=, >=, <, >, ≤ and ≥, and may carry a complementary-slackness clause after ⟂.

docs.title: 3 Forms that compile
docs.text:
A kernel is the function an operation of a stage applies: the law of motion 𝑔 that a pullback or a push-forward applies, and the value aggregator 𝐺 that an aggregation applies. compile_kernel() answers the kernel of such an operation as a plain Python function, made from the source text that kernel().python holds. It answers one where the row writes its output as a function of its inputs, or states a relation with an explicit side whose function it compiles: the candidate line c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0, which stands in methods.bl, the methods file beside cons.bl, compiles to the function 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]), whose arguments include the derivative term, while the relation with its clause remains the row's rule. A pullback or an aggregation whose row states a relation with no explicit side, such as the identification c = c[>], is refused under the rule kernel-target of Refusals. The function takes the kernel's arguments and then the parameters the kernel reads, and computes on numbers or on NumPy arrays. The values the calibration gives those parameters stand in kernel().parameter_values, None on a version not yet calibrated, and are passed at each call, so that a new calibration needs no new compilation. The text holds numbers and infinity, the kernel's arguments, the parameters, the arithmetic of §2, and the functions the stage file defines in closed form, such as 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ), written as functions inside the one function. An expectation over a label shock, a shock whose law gives each label of a finite set its probability, compiles to the sum of the values weighted by those probabilities.

The named functions exp, log and Inv, and a function the stage file defines by a derivative or an inverse, such as 𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢), have no compile rule: their definitions state what they denote, and a kernel that calls one is not compiled, under the rule kernel-form of Refusals. The same function written in closed form, 𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ), compiles. A call of max or min on a line of a block compiles where each of its arguments is one number: the kernel of the line L = max(L[>], b) writes the call as NumPy's np.maximum, and a call of min as np.minimum, by the rule that writes the two in the definition of a derived parameter. A call of max or min in the body of a function that the stage file defines, or with an argument that is a tuple or a collection, has no compile rule and is refused under kernel-form. The definition of a derived parameter is a further exception to the rule on the named functions: a kernel that reads the derived parameter writes the log, exp, min and max of its definition as NumPy's functions, and a definition by cases, if … then … else …, as a call of a function that evaluates the chosen branch alone where the test is one truth value and that, where the test is an array, takes at each entry the value of the branch that the test chooses there. The other operations, among them an expectation that stands as an operation of its own, whatever the law of its shock, and a maximization, have no compiled kernel: compile_kernel() refuses them under the rule kernel-target.

docs.title: 4 The blocks of a methods file
docs.text:
A methods file is the addition beside a stage file, methods.bl, a .bl file that opens with @methods: and the stage's name and that the package reads together with the stage file (Methodization). It is written in the forms of this page: it may define functions in closed form, 𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ), whose kernels compile as a stage file's do (§3); it may define a derived parameter, such as the marginal propensity to consume κ := 1 - q in the methods file of applications/consumption-perfect-foresight-crra/, which stage.par lists once the file is read with the stage file (Symbol conventions §8); and it declares the settings it reads in the form of a parameter's declaration, n_a : ℕ :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]. Its blocks name blocks of the stage file by their ids, [id=policy, …], and are written as a stage file's blocks are (Stages), with two differences: the bracket holds typing entries, method : !egm, grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), handler : "cons-port:egm" and, in groups opened by |, the entries of the operators inside the block, evaluate.method : !Linear; and a block that adds no coordinate to the stage's block carries no signature. The lines of such a block are appended to the stage block's lines:

Written Reading [id=policy, method : !egm \| grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))] { … } A block whose method is a solution method that brings lines: its lines are those by which the policy builder is computed, and they stand in place of the stage file's maximization at the operative level while the stage keeps the maximization as the declared line (Methodization §5). A line may read the derivative of a value by the term D_{a}V[>]. [id=cntn_to_dcsn] { D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) :: [id=marginal] } A block that adds derivative lines to a value builder's block, each stating a derivative of the value the builder writes as the author asserts it. The line is recorded at the builder's Evaluation as a stated derivative, beside the representation typed there; the builder gains no wire and no box, and its signature is unchanged.

An entry for a block to which the file adds no line is written at file level with the full path of its place, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.method : !Linear, since a block with an empty body is refused. A block whose id the stage file lacks is kept as a new block of the stage, written with its full signature. A line id written in both files and a component written twice with different content are refused under declared-twice, a coordinate typed differently in the two files under type-conflict, and a second definition of a field in a block whose method component holds no solution method under defined-once (Refusals). The demonstration's methods file is applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.bl, quoted on Methods and places §2.

docs.title: Shock distributions
docs.text:
Summary

A line such as y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y) declares the probability distribution of a shock, of a tuple of shocks jointly, or of each component of a collection of shocks, by one of eleven families. This page lists the families, with the arguments each takes and what they mean, links each to the object of the Bellman calculus a declaration denotes, and names the table of the package the row is read from. A declared distribution is what an expectation integrates against and what a forward builder extends a measure by.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Appendix E.3 Operators §4: the conditional distribution of a shock, a probability kernel, and the two operators that read it. Builds on — Stage tutorial §2: where a distribution is declared in a stage file. See also — Operations: the Expectation and DistributionExtension rows that read a declared distribution; Refusals: the smallest example of each rule a declaration can be refused under.

docs.title: 1 Reading a declaration
docs.text:
A declaration writes the shock on the left of ~ and a call of a family on the right. The shock's set is declared on its own line, y : ℝ₊₊, and the declaration gives the distribution of the shock over that set: the set says which values the shock can take, and the distribution how probability is spread over them.

A tuple subject declares one joint distribution of its shocks, (y, z) ~ N((μ_y, μ_z), ((σ_y^2, r), (r, σ_z^2))). An argument may name a parameter; a state or a control at the source perch of the shock's edge, where an edge is the step from one perch to the next that one forward builder makes; or another shock, called a parent of the declaration. The declaration is then the distribution of the shock conditional on those arguments, a probability kernel: a distribution for each value the arguments take. Ψ ~ LogNormal(ν, σ_Ψ) in sa_savings.bl is conditional on the shock ν, and y_n ~ MarkovChain(P_y, y_grid, y_wa) in worker_ageing.bl on last period's ability y_wa.

A shock is drawn on the edge of one forward builder: the builder whose block lists the shock among its inputs, or else the edge of a shock declared with it or of a shock whose declaration reads it. The declarations drawn on one edge form one joint distribution, the product of their conditional distributions, each given its parents and the states and controls it reads. Two declarations that do not name one another are therefore conditionally independent given those states and controls; stage.obligations() lists that product as the assumption joint-distribution-factorization. On the card a builder prints (Operations §1), the distribution of ψ prints as P_ψ: an expectation integrates against it, E_{ψ}[…], and a distribution extension extends a measure by it, μ≺⊗P_ψ.

A declaration of one real shock by N, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal or TypeIExtremeValue, the scalar families whose definition the package's table of definitions holds (the column definition of §2), denotes two objects: the law as written, the family applied to the written arguments, and the measure at those arguments, the family's definition with the written arguments in place of its variables. The card that stage.definitions.denote prints for the declaration gives the second on the row under the first, so that y ~ Uniform(a_y, b_y) has the row P_y = measure on ℝ given by B ↦ ∫_{x ∈ {x ∈ ℝ | x ∈ B ∧ a_y ≤ x ∧ x ≤ b_y}} [1/(b_y − a_y)] Lebesgue(dx): the probability of a set B is the length of the part of B in [a_y, b_y], divided by b_y − a_y. A Mixture, a declaration of a tuple subject and a declaration by any other family denote the law as written alone.

A shock may be declared on the functions from a finite index set to the reals, ε : I_J → ℝ with I_J := {0, …, J} (Symbols and conventions), so that ε has one real component ε[i] for each member i of I_J. A call of LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal or TypeIExtremeValue with real arguments is then the law of each component, and the declaration denotes the finite product of that law over the index set, printed ⊗_{i ∈ I_J} TypeIExtremeValue(0, 1) for ε ~ TypeIExtremeValue(0, 1); its measure, the second object, is the product of the scalar measures. The product of probability measures P_i on ℝ, one for each i in I_J, is the probability measure on the functions e from I_J to ℝ that gives the set of the functions with e(i) in B_i for every i the probability P_0(B_0) · P_1(B_1) · … · P_J(B_J). The components are therefore independent draws of one law, not copies of one draw, conditionally on the arguments the law reads, such as a parent shock η in ε ~ TypeIExtremeValue(η, 1), and the sentence of joint-distribution-factorization states it: the components of ε are independent, each with the law TypeIExtremeValue(0, 1), or conditionally independent given η for the law with the parent. N on such a shock is the joint normal law of its components, written ε ~ N(μ_ε, Σ_ε) with a mean μ_ε : I_J → ℝ and a covariance matrix Σ_ε : I_J × I_J → ℝ; it is not a product, and it denotes the law as written alone, as a Mixture on such a shock does.

The second argument

N(μ, v) takes the variance, not the standard deviation: sa_savings.bl writes ν ~ N(κ_1, σ_ν^2). LogNormal(μ, σ) takes the mean and the standard deviation of the logarithm of the draw, so μ is not the mean of the draw: buffer_stock.bl writes ψ ~ LogNormal(-(σ_ψ^2)/2, σ_ψ), whose mean is one. TruncatedNormal(μ, σ, l, u) takes the mean and the standard deviation of the normal law before the truncation to [l, u], so that σ is a standard deviation, not a variance as in N, and neither μ nor σ is the mean or the standard deviation of the draw. TruncatedLogNormal(μ, σ, l, u) takes the mean and the standard deviation of the logarithm, as LogNormal does, and its two endpoints in the draw's own units, so that TruncatedLogNormal(μ, σ, 0, inf) is LogNormal(μ, σ) and a bound stated as k standard deviations of the logarithm is written exp(μ + k·σ). TypeIExtremeValue(μ, s) takes a location and a scale, and the mean of the draw is μ + γs, γ ≈ 0.5772 being Euler's constant. A numerical routine written in another convention needs its arguments converted.

docs.title: 3 Conditions and refusals
docs.text:
A call of a family with a number of arguments the family does not take is refused under readable-form. An argument outside its family's domain is refused under distribution-domain: a negative variance, a negative standard deviation of the logarithm, weights outside the unit interval or not summing to one, a probability of Bernoulli outside [0, 1], and a mean or a covariance matrix that does not have the subject's dimension or a covariance matrix that is not symmetric positive semidefinite. A zero variance and a zero standard deviation of the logarithm lie in the domain: N(μ, 0) is a point mass at μ, and LogNormal(μ, 0) a point mass at exp(μ). A component of a Mixture written as a number is a point mass at that number, as the 0 of ξ ~ Mixture((p_zero, 0), (1 - p_zero, LogNormal(μ_ξ, σ_ξ))) in buffer_stock.bl.

The arguments of Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal and TypeIExtremeValue are real numbers, and the same rule refuses each of the following:

  • endpoints that are not in order, Uniform(1, 0), Uniform(1, 1) or TruncatedNormal(0, 1, 2, 2);
  • a standard deviation or a scale that is not positive, TruncatedNormal(0, 0, -1, 1), TruncatedLogNormal(0, 0, 0, inf) or TypeIExtremeValue(0, 0);
  • a negative lower endpoint of a truncated lognormal, TruncatedLogNormal(0, 1, -1, 1), since the draw is positive: TruncatedLogNormal(0, 1, 0, inf) is LogNormal(0, 1) itself, and TruncatedLogNormal(0, 1, 0.5, 2) the lognormal law conditional on [0.5, 2];
  • an infinite argument other than an endpoint of a truncation: Uniform(0, inf) is refused, whereas TruncatedNormal(0, 1, 0, inf) is the normal law truncated to the nonnegative half-line and TruncatedNormal(0, 1, -inf, inf) the normal law itself;
  • an argument whose names all have values and whose arithmetic has no number, 0/0, or is not a number, inf - inf;
  • a tuple written as an argument, Uniform((0, 1), 2), and an argument that reads a parameter declared on a collection, μ : I_J → ℝ, or on a product set, b : ℝ × ℝ;
  • a tuple subject, (y, z) ~ Uniform(0, 1), since each of the three is the law of one real subject or of each component of a collection.

Every component of a Mixture that is a call of N, LogNormal or one of the four families is checked as a declaration of that family would be, and a refusal names the component: Mixture((0.5, 0), (0.5, N(0, -1))) is refused for the negative variance of its N component. A refusal under distribution-domain names the declaration's line of the file.

Where an argument names a parameter, the condition is decided when the calibration gives the number, and a calibration whose values break it is refused under distribution-domain. In the meantime three conditions stand among stage.obligations(): the condition on weights as distribution-weights-are-a-probability-vector, the condition on the covariance matrix of a tuple subject as covariance-positive-semidefinite, and the condition on the parameters of Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal and TypeIExtremeValue, of a declaration or of a component of a mixture, as distribution-parameters-in-domain. The sentence of distribution-parameters-in-domain states the family's condition in the written terms, the parameters of the Uniform declaration two_nodes:distribution:y of y lie in the family's domain: a < b, with a = a_y and b = b_y, both finite. An argument that is a call, Uniform(exp(1), 3), or any other term outside the arithmetic of numbers and parameters the package evaluates, or that reads a state, a control or a parent shock, TypeIExtremeValue(0, z), keeps its condition as the obligation distribution-parameters-in-domain, which no calibration decides.

Every declaration also records the condition law-support: the distribution gives probability only to values in the shock's declared set. The package decides it at calibration where it knows the law's support and reads the bounds of the declared set: a truncated lognormal's support is [l, u], open at a lower endpoint 0 and at an upper endpoint inf, and calibrate establishes the condition when that interval lies within the declared set and refuses the calibration when it does not. For every other family the condition stays required and unchecked, so a normal distribution declared for a shock in ℝ₊₊ is not refused; a strictly positive shock takes a family whose draws are positive, such as LogNormal, or a mixture of such families with positive numbers. The numerical routine that provides a distribution to a solver is no condition of the stage: a solver reads one where a methods file names it and chooses its own otherwise.

The distribution of a shock whose labels select the branches of a block gives one probability to each label, written Categorical((p₁, …, pₙ)) in the order of the labels or Bernoulli(p) on two; any other is refused under branch-law. An expectation that needs a conditional distribution the declarations do not give, a posterior among them, is refused under conditional-not-declared.

A call of a family outside the table is not refused when the file is read: the declaration is kept as the file writes it, as the author's own distribution. The backward builders graph is constructed, but the forward builders graph is not: stage.builder.fwd holds a refusal under not-constructed, since a forward builder extends a measure only by the families of the table.

docs.title: Method types
docs.text:
Summary

A method type is a numerical method that a methods file can type at a place of a stage, such as !egm or !gauss_hermite, and a grid constructor is a word that writes the grid of a place, such as !Cartesian. This page holds one entry for each method type the package admits, registered representation families included, and one for each grid constructor: what it is, how a methods file declares it and where, its arguments, what it is compatible with, an example, whether a numerical implementation is identified, and its links. The entries are printed from the records the package's checks read, so that an entry and the checks cannot differ, and an entry that names a word absent from them is refused.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Methodization: how a methods file types a method, a grid and a handler at a place of a stage and declares its settings. Formal account — Methods: the method and the grid as components of an operator's signature; Operators: the operations the methods realize. See also — Expression forms: the forms a stage file writes, among them the operators E, argmax and solve at which a method may be typed; Refusals: the rules method-admission, method-setting-declared, component-typed-twice, grid-coordinate, grid-setting-declared, grid-bounds and method-option-value; the wiki entries methods and grid.

docs.title: 1 Reading an entry
docs.text:
Each entry has the same parts in the same order.

  • Declaration is the entry a methods file writes, <place>.method : !word or <place>.grid : !Word(…), with the places at which it may stand. The place is written as Methodization §2 writes it, in the bracket of the block that holds the operator or at file level with the full path. A word with a hyphen, !gauss-hermite, is written in a methods file with an underscore, !gauss_hermite, and the package reads the two as one word. The kinds of place are those stage.places() prints (Methods and places §1): a whole builder, named by the id of its block; a line marked !node or any other line with an id, named <block id>.<line id>; a defined function; and the occurrences of an operator, named by its head in one line, in a block or in the whole stage. The head evaluate names the Evaluation that closes a builder, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate, and each object it stores, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[V].
  • Type parameters index the type, such as the domain X of a grid; the place supplies each one, and none is a keyword a methods file writes.
  • Arguments are the keyword arguments the package reads, each with the kind of value it takes, what leaving it out means, its restrictions and its meaning. A number that a keyword takes is written as the name of a declared setting, so that the number stands in the settings file, and an entry that writes the number itself is refused (Methodization §3.1). A keyword the entry does not list is admitted and kept for the handler that carries the method out, which reads it or refuses it.
  • Compatibility names the grid or the data the method reads, the conditions configuration checks once the settings have values, and the obligations listed before numerical use; stage.obligations() lists a method's condition, and the package does not check it.
  • Example is a small declaration with its meaning.
  • Availability states the language's admission and, separately, whether a numerical implementation is identified. Admission alone establishes no numerical support.
  • Links give the formal definition, the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the object the method realizes where its places name an operator, the related entries, and the location of the definition in the package with its public link, or the statement that no exported revision holds it yet.

An entry that names a word absent from the records is refused (syntax), and so is a word typed at a place of a kind its entry does not admit (method-admission), one component written twice with different content (declared-twice) or typed at one place by two paths (component-typed-twice), and a typing of the derivative operator D (no-method-for-derivative). Configuration checks the values: a keyword's value outside the set its entry names is refused under method-option-value, and a grid's bounds out of order, outside the declared set or with a count below two under grid-bounds (Refusals). A method's entry that writes a number among its arguments is refused under method-setting-declared. A factor that writes a number, or names a setting no methods file declares, is refused under grid-setting-declared, and a factor keyed by a name that is no coordinate of the function at the place, or a grid written at a place whose method reads none, under grid-coordinate. A place without a grid entry, and a coordinate that no factor names, take the default, the product over the states of the perch the method's entry names, with no number supplied.

Grids and the model's sets

A grid is a numerical object, the finite set of points at which a function is computed and between which it is interpolated. Changing it changes the approximation and leaves the model as it was. A finite set of alternatives the household chooses from is part of the model and is declared in the stage file, and the scalars that define it are parameters.

docs.title: 2.1 !egm
docs.text:
In the endogenous grid method, the lines of the method's block invert the first-order condition on a grid of end-of-period savings to give the policy pairs, each a choice and the decision state at which it is chosen.

Declaration. <place>.method : !egm, at a whole builder and an occurrence of the operator argmax.

Type parameters. X is inferred from the attachment site. It is the set of states on which the method's grid lies; the place and the method's row determine it. A type parameter is no source keyword.

Arguments. No registered arguments; unlisted keywords are retained for the numerical handler.

Compatibility. Its grid lies on the states of the continuation perch; the grid constructors its place admits are !Cartesian and !Points. The obligation egm-eligibility states that the construction satisfies the declared line where the continuation value 𝑉≻ is concave and continuously differentiable on (0, ∞) with a finite positive right derivative at 0. Its grid lies on the continuation states, written by the builder's grid entry or taken as the default product over those states. Its block's lines stand in place of the declared lines at the operative level. A representation at the builder's closing Evaluation reads the pairs it selects and takes no grid there. A block of explicit formulas that reads no value input is refused, naming !explicit. The condition egm-eligibility is listed among the obligations and checked by nothing.

Example.

policy.method : !egm
policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))

The policy builder is solved by the endogenous grid method on n_a evenly spaced savings from a_min to a_max.

Availability. Admission: a row of the method table, admitted at a whole builder and an occurrence of the operator argmax. Numerical implementation: Application handlers realize it, such as cons-port:egm of the consumption-portfolio application and asva:make_egm_1d of the asva package; the package itself solves nothing.

docs.title: 2.4 !explicit
docs.text:
In the explicit solution of a policy or backward value builder, the lines of the method's block define every output by an authored expression of the states of the output perch, the parameters and earlier local names.

Declaration. <place>.method : !explicit, at a whole builder.

Type parameters. None.

Arguments. No registered arguments; unlisted keywords are retained for the numerical handler.

Compatibility. It reads no grid. The method admits the policy builder and backward value builders and refuses a forward builder and a grid. Each line defines one name by name = expression, reads no value input or its derivative, states no relation, applies no argmax, solve or upper_env, and defines or reads no field at another perch; every output has such a line and a compiled kernel. The declared optimization problem stays at the declared level. The builder's Evaluation takes the closed form generated from this entry unless an entry names another representation there.

Example.

[id=policy, policy.method : !explicit] {
    c = (1 - (R*β)^(1/ρ)/R)*(m - 1 + 1/(1 - Γ/R))    :: [id=consumption]
}

Consumption is the authored expression of resources and the parameters, which stands in place of the declared maximization when the stage is solved.

Availability. Admission: a row of the method table, admitted at a whole builder. Numerical implementation: The compiled kernels of the block's lines evaluate the solution; compiling establishes an evaluator and no optimality.

docs.title: 2.5 !Linear
docs.text:
The family represents a function on one real coordinate by continuous piecewise linear interpolation through strictly increasing nodes and the values aligned with them.

Declaration. <place>.method : !Linear, at a line marked !node, a line with an id, a defined function and an occurrence of the operator evaluate.

Type parameters. X is inferred from the attachment site. It is the domain of the represented function, whose coordinates are those of the place in their declared order. Y is inferred from the attachment site. It is the set of the represented function's values. A type parameter is no source keyword.

Arguments. No registered arguments; unlisted keywords are retained for the numerical handler.

Compatibility. Its grid lies on the states of the perch at which the function the place holds stands; the grid constructors its place admits are !Cartesian, !Points and !Fibred. The derivatives it evaluates are the first derivative, piecewise constant between its nodes and so a step function, which an inverse Euler step that reads it turns into a step candidate; the second derivative is zero and is not offered. The family reads an authored table evaluate(knots, values, x), the policy pairs !egm selects at the closing Evaluation of its builder, where a grid is refused, or its own nodes on the grid of its place, the default product over the function's coordinates where no grid is written. An optional grid beside a table discretizes the coordinates at which the table is evaluated, written as a name or as a tuple of names in the order of the grid's coordinates, and has exactly the table's finite support, compared at configuration where both are given exactly and otherwise before numerical preparation. Numerical use needs at least two finite strictly increasing nodes with aligned finite values, and an identified extension outside the node interval.

Stored data. The values at the nodes, aligned with the nodes in increasing order.

Example.

cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.method : !Linear
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m=(m_min, m_max, n_m))

The decision value is represented by linear interpolation between its values at n_m evenly spaced points of cash on hand from m_min to m_max.

Availability. Admission: a registered representation family; registration alone establishes no numerical support, admitted at a line marked !node, a line with an id, a defined function and an occurrence of the operator evaluate. Numerical implementation: The scalar evaluator consumption-perfect-foresight-crra:Linear, the class Linear of the perfect-foresight application's module code/closed_form_check.py, evaluates it and its first derivative and refuses a point outside the node interval; the package itself supplies no evaluator.

docs.title: 2.6 !pchip
docs.text:
The family represents a function on one real coordinate by piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation, with the shape-preserving slopes of PCHIP, through strictly increasing nodes and the values aligned with them.

docs.title: 2.7 !closed-form
docs.text:
The family represents a function by its complete authored expression, evaluated through the compiled kernel of that expression at the calibration.

docs.title: 3 The grid
docs.text:
A method that reads a grid takes it from the grid entry of its place, <place>.grid : !Cartesian(…), a typing beside the method's. The language admits these grid constructors:

constructor declaration !Cartesian <place>.grid : !Cartesian(<coordinate>=<factor form>, …) !Points <place>.grid : !Points(nodes=<declared points>)<place>.grid : !Points !Fibred <place>.grid : !Fibred(base=<!Points or !Cartesian term>, fibre=!Cartesian(<control>=(<feasible set>, <count>), …))

Each constructor may end with require=, one predicate word or a tuple of them, a condition on the resulting grid:

predicate meaning !Empty The grid holds no point. !Cartesian The grid is nonempty and holds every combination of its projected coordinate values. !NonCartesian The grid is nonempty and misses some combination of its projected coordinate values. !UniformCartesian The grid is Cartesian on at least one real coordinate, with at least two distinct, equally spaced values in every coordinate.

docs.title: 3.1 !Cartesian
docs.text:
The product of one finite node set per coordinate of the place, holding every combination of the coordinates' nodes.

Declaration. <place>.grid : !Cartesian(<coordinate>=<factor form>, …); at the grid of !egm, !vfi, !time-iteration, !Linear, !pchip, !histogram and !root-find, and at a place whose entries name no method word, for its handler. Each factor names a coordinate of the place, a control of the stage for a feasible-control factor or a shock for an expectation factor. The predicate words of require are written last.

Type parameters. X is inferred from the attachment site. It is the domain of the grid, whose coordinates are those of the function the place holds, in their declared order, or the continuation states for !egm. A type parameter is no source keyword.

Arguments.

argument type when left out restrictions meaning <coordinate> factor Optional: when it is left out, no value is supplied and the core records none. names a coordinate of the place, a control of the stage for a feasible-control factor or a shock for an expectation factor; written in one of the four factor forms; at least one factor is written, and a coordinate no factor names keeps its obligation At most one factor per coordinate, keyed by the coordinate's name. require predicate words Optional: when it is left out, no value is supplied and the core records none. one of !Empty, !Cartesian, !NonCartesian and !UniformCartesian, or a tuple of them, of which no two contradict each other The properties the resulting grid satisfies, decided at configuration where the bound values decide them and established before numerical use; inside the fibre of !Fibred they concern each fibre.

Factor forms. Each factor takes one of these forms:

form meaning parts a=(a_min, a_max, n_a) Equally spaced nodes from the lower bound to the upper bound, both included; with a spacing word written as a fourth item, a=(a_min, a_max, n_a, !expmult), the nodes that word's handler places between the bounds. lower: setting, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused.upper: setting, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused.count: setting, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused.spacing: spacing word, Optional: when it is left out, no value is supplied and the core records none. m=M_nodes The listed nodes, in their order. nodes: node set, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused. ν=E_ν The quadrature nodes of the expectation operator that integrates the shock coordinate. nodes: expectation operator, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused. c=(Γ_c, n_c) A grid of the control's feasible set at each state, a family of grids indexed by the states; !Fibred pairs it with the states of a base to make one joint grid. set: feasible set, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused.count: setting, Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused.

Compatibility. Stands at the grid of a representation, of a solution method on the states of its output perch, of !egm on the continuation states, and of a place with no method word for its handler. Bounds, counts and listed nodes are settings; configuration checks the bounds in order and inside the coordinate's declared set, each count at least two, listed nodes strictly increasing, and the requirements the bound values decide. A coordinate no factor names keeps its obligation, which numerical construction reports before the grid is used.

Example.

policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a), require=!UniformCartesian)

The grid of savings of !egm: n_a equally spaced points from a_min to a_max, both included, required to be uniform, which the construction establishes.

Availability. Admission: a grid constructor of the language, admitted by the lowering and the grid checks. Numerical implementation: The core constructs equally spaced and listed nodes at the configured settings, which a builder's kernels().grids holds. A spacing word is retained for its handler, of which the cons-port application implements the argument-free !expmult, and quadrature nodes come from the expectation's handler.

Links. formal definition; related entries !Points and !Fibred; source stage/grids.py, _DEFINED, line 353; public link unavailable until an exported revision holds the definition; read from stage/grids.py, GRID_CONSTRUCTORS, "Cartesian".

docs.title: 3.2 !Points
docs.text:
The finite support of declared points of the place's domain, each point given in the domain's declared coordinate order; !Points alone is the empty grid.

Declaration. <place>.grid : !Points(nodes=<declared points>)<place>.grid : !Points; at the grid of !egm, !vfi, !time-iteration, !Linear, !pchip, !histogram and !root-find, and at a place whose entries name no method word, for its handler. The points lie in the domain of the place, in its declared coordinate order. The predicate words of require are written last.

Type parameters. X is inferred from the attachment site. It is the domain of the grid, whose coordinates are those of the function the place holds, in their declared order, or the continuation states for !egm. A type parameter is no source keyword.

Arguments.

argument type when left out restrictions meaning nodes declared points Optional: when it is left out, no value is supplied and the core records none. a set the stage defines by its finite members, or a setting declared on a fixed finite product of points of the place's domain; each point has one coordinate for each coordinate of the domain, in its declared order, each a finite real inside the coordinate's declared set The name of the declared points; when it is left out, the grid is empty. require predicate words Optional: when it is left out, no value is supplied and the core records none. one of !Empty, !Cartesian, !NonCartesian and !UniformCartesian, or a tuple of them, of which no two contradict each other The properties the resulting grid satisfies, decided at configuration where the bound values decide them and established before numerical use; inside the fibre of !Fibred they concern each fibre.

Compatibility. Stands where !Cartesian stands. The points are a set the stage defines by its finite members, or a setting declared on a fixed finite product of points, X2 := ℝ × ℝ and P : X2 × X2 × X2; configuration checks each point's shape, its finite real coordinates, its membership of the coordinates' declared sets where that is decided, and the requirements. Repeated points collapse in the support, and an interpolation procedure may still require at least two nodes.

Example.

policy.grid : !Points(nodes=A_points)

The grid of savings of !egm is the set of the configured points of the setting A_points, declared A_points : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊: three points of the one coordinate a.

Availability. Admission: a grid constructor of the language, admitted by the lowering and the grid checks. Numerical implementation: The core constructs the support at the configured settings, which a builder's kernels().grids holds.

Links. formal definition; related entries !Cartesian and !Fibred; source stage/grids.py, _DEFINED, line 409; public link unavailable until an exported revision holds the definition; read from stage/grids.py, GRID_CONSTRUCTORS, "Points".

docs.title: 3.3 !Fibred
docs.text:
Each state of a finite base paired with the finite feasible grid of the control at that state: a grid of feasible pairs of states and controls.

Declaration. <place>.grid : !Fibred(base=<!Points or !Cartesian term>, fibre=!Cartesian(<control>=(<feasible set>, <count>), …)); at the grid of !vfi, !time-iteration, !Linear, !pchip, !histogram and !root-find, and at a place whose entries name no method word, for its handler. The domain of the occurrence is the product of the base's states and the fibre's controls; a place of any other coordinate domain refuses. The predicate words of require are written last.

Type parameters. X is inferred from the attachment site. It is the set of states of the occurrence, on which the base lies. C is inferred from the attachment site. It is the declared set of the fibre's control; the grid lies in the graph of the control's feasible set, a subset of X × C. A type parameter is no source keyword.

Arguments.

argument type when left out restrictions meaning base grid word Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused. !Points or a !Cartesian term without feasible-control factors, on the states of the occurrence; complete before numerical construction; a state no factor names keeps its obligation The grid of the states at which the control's feasible set is sampled. fibre grid word Required: an entry that leaves it out is refused. a !Cartesian term whose factors are feasible-control factors, c=(Γ_c, n_c); one control in the numerical construction; several controls or a coupled restriction report unsupported joint sampling The grid of the control at each base state, sampled from its feasible set. require predicate words Optional: when it is left out, no value is supplied and the core records none. one of !Empty, !Cartesian, !NonCartesian and !UniformCartesian, or a tuple of them, of which no two contradict each other The properties the resulting grid satisfies, decided at configuration where the bound values decide them and established before numerical use; inside the fibre of !Fibred they concern each fibre.

Compatibility. Stands at a solution method whose grid lies on the states of its output perch; such a method chooses or solves over the place's states and the stage's controls. Fibred stands at a representation or at a place with no method word only for a function whose coordinates are the base's states followed by the fibre's controls, and a representation of a function of states alone refuses it. The base is !Points or a !Cartesian term without feasible-control factors and must be complete before numerical construction; the fibre is a !Cartesian term of feasible-control factors. An outer requirement concerns the joint grid, and a requirement inside the fibre concerns each fibre.

Example.

cntn_to_dcsn.grid : !Fibred(base=!Points(nodes=B), fibre=!Cartesian(c=(Γ_c, n_c)))

With B = {1, 2}, Γ_c(m) = [0, m] and n_c = 2, the grid of value function iteration is the four pairs (1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0) and (2, 2).

Availability. Admission: a grid constructor of the language, admitted by the lowering and the grid checks. Numerical implementation: The core constructs the case of one control: at each base state it evaluates the control's feasible interval at the arguments the stage applies it to and places the declared count of equally spaced points, both closed finite endpoints included. An open or unbounded interval reports an unresolved numerical requirement, and several controls or a coupled restriction report unsupported joint sampling.

Links. formal definition; related entries !Points and !Cartesian; source stage/grids.py, _DEFINED, line 459; public link unavailable until an exported revision holds the definition; read from stage/grids.py, GRID_CONSTRUCTORS, "Fibred".

docs.title: Model directory layout
docs.text:
Summary

Each model of the repository has a folder of its own under applications/, and every such folder keeps the files the language reads in one subfolder, declaration/: the recipe, the trellis and period files, the calibration and settings files, and one folder for each stage, holding the stage file, its methods file and its note. Beside declaration/ stand the folder's first page, README.md, its economics.md, and its code, tests, a note on the papers it keeps for reference, and results. This page states the layout, the rules it follows and the variants of a model it admits. The package's functions that read these files require no layout, since they read the paths a recipe or a trellis file writes; the layout is the convention of the repository's model folders, which Bellman Workbench reads and a test of the repository checks.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Trellises §§1, 5: the trellis file, the period file and the recipe, and the paths a recipe writes; Methodization: the methods, settings and calibration files. Used by — The Bellman factory §3 and Recipe functions: the registry a recipe is read from; Bellman Workbench: the folder it opens and the folder its form new trellis writes.

Key terminology Term Meaning Model folder The folder of one model under applications/, laid out as this page states. Stage key The name under which a period lists a stage, chosen by the author. A model's recipe normally uses the name of the stage's folder, which the stage file and the note share; an equation variant or a second use of a stage lists the folder under another key (§§2.3, 3). Registry The folder a recipe stands in, from which every path the recipe writes is read; in a model folder, its declaration/ (wiki). Recipe The file spec.yml that names the trellis file, each stage's file and, for each stage, the ordered files from which its parameter values, its settings and its methods are read (wiki). Source A file of one kind a recipe names: a calibration or settings file of assignments, by its path without the extension, as calibration/durables, or a methods file, the .bl addition beside a stage file, by its path with it, as stages/tenure/methods.bl (wiki). Variant A second version of a model, written beside the first in the same folder (§3).

docs.title: 1 The layout
docs.text:
The durables model of Dobrescu and Shanker (2026), in which a household keeps or adjusts its housing stock over fifty-one ages, shows the layout:

applications/durables/
├── README.md                   the first page: the model in one sentence, a drawing where the folder holds one and the command that opens it
├── economics.md                the economics in full
├── declaration/                every file the language reads
│   ├── spec.yml                the recipe: trellis: trellis.yml and, for each stage, its stage file and its sources
│   ├── spec.two-stages.yml     a second recipe: trellis: trellis.two-stages.yml, with the same stage files
│   ├── trellis.yml             the periods, counted backward from the terminal one
│   ├── trellis.two-stages.yml
│   ├── period.yml              the template of one period, which the trellis file repeats
│   ├── period.two-stages.yml
│   ├── stages/
│   │   ├── tenure/             tenure.bl  methods.bl  tenure.md
│   │   ├── keeper_cons/        keeper_cons.bl  methods.bl  keeper_cons.md
│   │   ├── adjuster_cons/      adjuster_cons.bl  methods.bl  methods.adjuster_method.bl  adjuster_cons.md
│   │   └── bequest/            bequest.bl  methods.bl
│   ├── calibration/            durables.yml  wage_schedule.yml
│   └── settings/               durables.yml
├── code/                       wage_schedule.py, which writes each period's income into the trellis
├── results/                    what the code writes; git ignores it
└── tests/                      test_durables_ast.py

declaration/ holds every file the language reads: the recipe, the trellis and period files, the folders calibration/ and settings/, under stages/ one folder for each stage, holding its stage file, written in .bl, its methods file methods.bl, an addition to the stage file written in the same language, and its note; a second selection of a stage's methods is another addition in the same folder, methods.<variant>.bl. Beside declaration/ stand README.md, economics.md, code/ for the folder's programs, tests/ for its tests, results/ for what its programs write, paper/ for the descriptions of its stages that Bellman Workbench's button paper writes for a paper's model section (§4), and reference/ for a note, such as applications/benhabib-2019/reference/README.md, that cites the papers the folder keeps for reference and says where their PDF files are held; the PDF files themselves are not kept in the repository, and the durables folder keeps no such note. A folder holds only the parts its model has: applications/portfolio-choice/, whose stage files the portfolio–consumption application assembles, holds its stage folders, a README.md and its tests, and no recipe.

The portfolio–consumption application, applications/cons-port/, holds its stages under declaration/stages/, each stage's methods files beside its stage file, methods.bl and the replacing selections methods.<variant>.bl its trellis files name, and two recipes, one for each order of its period, each with its trellis file. Beside them stand its trellis files of records, declaration/trellis.<name>.yml, each of which writes every stage of a period as a record naming the stage file and the calibration, settings and methods files the stage is bound from, all of the folder's own declaration/, and is read with no recipe (Trellises §3). Beside declaration/ it keeps code/ for its numerical tool, tests/, notebooks/ for its notebook and its earlier reference notebook, and reference/legacy/ for its fixed numerical reference, with the reference's recorded sources in the earlier YAML form.

The form new trellis of Bellman Workbench writes a new model folder in this layout (Bellman Workbench §6), with two more files at the folder's top, beside its README.md: the record of the form's answers, answers.yml, and a .gitignore. The repository's test packages/bellman/tests/test_layout.py fails on a folder under applications/ that git tracks and that departs from the layout, so it fails on a tracked folder that holds those two files at its top.

docs.title: 2.1 What you write where
docs.text:
Every file the language reads stands under declaration/, and the only other files there are the notes of the stages, each in its stage's folder. A stage file holds the mathematics of one stage, its declarations, its typed blocks and its equations; its methods file, beside it, holds the numerical methods of its operators and the settings they read, declared with their sets (Methodization); the YAML files hold the rest: the periods and the trellis that compose the stages, the values of the settings, the parameter values, and the recipe that names them all. What the folder holds for its readers and for its programs, the README, the economics, the code, the tests and the note on its papers, stands beside declaration/.

The division between the stage file and the other files follows the economics. A finite set of choices belongs in the stage's domain definitions, and the grid sizes and tolerances that approximate a continuous domain belong in the settings. Keeping the files apart does not settle which is which, so decide for each number whether it changes the household's problem or only the numerical calculation.

declaration/ is the model's registry, the folder a recipe stands in and from which every path the recipe writes is read. load_recipe of bellman.trellis is therefore given declaration/ and the name of the recipe; run from the repository root, it reads the durables model:

from bellman.trellis import load_recipe

syntactic = load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml")
print(len(syntactic["periods"]), "periods, from", syntactic["provenance"]["trellis"]["path"])
tenure = syntactic["periods"][0]["stages"]["tenure"]
print(f"{'stage':12}{tenure['stage']['origin']}")
for kind in ("calibration", "settings", "methods"):
    for source in tenure["provenance"]["source_lists"][kind]:
        if "path" in source:
            print(f"{kind:12}{source['path']}")

51 periods, from applications/durables/declaration/trellis.yml
stage       applications/durables/declaration/stages/tenure/tenure.bl
calibration applications/durables/declaration/calibration/durables.yml
settings    applications/durables/declaration/settings/durables.yml
methods     applications/durables/declaration/stages/tenure/methods.bl

The call returns the syntactic trellis, the model as written, with one record for each stage and period. The record of the tenure stage in the terminal period, periods[0], names the stage file and the three files the stage is bound from, each read at the path the recipe writes. Bellman Workbench reads the same folder: it opens on a model folder, binds the open stage file through the recipe declaration/spec.yml where the folder holds one, and shows the folder's files in its tree (Bellman Workbench §1).

docs.title: 2.2 What a recipe names
docs.text: A recipe writes the path of every file it reads, from its own folder, and the package finds no file by a name or a suffix (Trellises §5). In the durables recipe, trellis: trellis.yml names the trellis file, and the entry of the stage key tenure names its stage file, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl, and lists its sources, the calibration and settings files named by their paths without the extension, calibration/durables and settings/durables, and the stage's methods file, an addition, by its path with it, stages/tenure/methods.bl. A trellis file names the period file it repeats, template: period.yml, from its own folder in the same way. A recipe without trellis:, or an entry without stage:, is refused with a sentence that says what to write, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl for the entry tenure (Refusals). A recipe and a trellis file that disagree on the stage keys are refused under the rule recipe-template-agreement, so that a mismatched pair does not load. A suffix in a file's name, the two-stages of spec.two-stages.yml, is for the reader alone: the links between a recipe, its trellis file and its period file are the lines these files write.

docs.title: 2.3 One folder for each stage
docs.text: The files of a stage stand together in one folder, declaration/stages/<stage>/: the stage file <stage>.bl and the note <stage>.md, the page that explains the stage, which share the folder's name, and the methods file methods.bl, an addition to the stage file. A method belongs to the operators of one stage, so a stage reused in another model is copied with its methods as one folder. Calibration and settings sources may be reused by stages, so they stand in declaration/calibration/ and declaration/settings/. Sharing a source file does not identify all its names across the model: two stages in one period that declare one parameter name share that period parameter, while their field names remain local and the same parameter name in another period denotes another parameter. The recipe names the two files of a stage's folder that the language reads, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl and the methods file stages/tenure/methods.bl, and it normally lists the stage under the folder's name as its stage key, as the durables recipe lists tenure; an equation variant or a second use of the stage lists the folder under another key (§3). A stage's folder holds the files the stage has: the bequest of the durables model, which has no note, holds its stage file and its methods file; the adjuster's folder holds a second addition, methods.adjuster_method.bl, which a recipe may name after the first.

docs.title: 2.4 Variants side by side
docs.text: A variant of a model stands beside the files it varies, in the same declaration/, and not in a folder of its own, and every link between its files is written in them. §3 sets out the three kinds.

docs.title: 2.5 The first page of a folder
docs.text: README.md is the page a visitor reads first. It states the model in one sentence, shows a drawing of the model where the folder holds one, gives the command that opens the folder in Bellman Workbench, bellman-workbench applications/durables, and names the folder the code writes into. economics.md, where a folder has one, holds the economics in full: the model's equations, its calibration with its sources, and what the stage files cannot state. A folder without economics.md, such as applications/portfolio-choice/, explains its model in its README.md and in the notes of its stages.

docs.title: 2.6 Where generated files stand
docs.text: The recordings of a model's stage files, the parsed term (<stage>.bl.ast.json) and the encoding of the elaborated stage (<stage>.bl.stage.json) of each, stand with the package's tests, in packages/bellman/tests/snapshot/corpus/<model>/, and not in the model folder. The test packages/bellman/tests/sym/test_corpus.py parses and elaborates every stage file under applications/ and compares the results with these recordings, and PYTHONPATH=. python tests/snapshot/record.py --corpus, run from packages/bellman/, writes them again. The model's code writes into results/, which git ignores, as it ignores model-explorer/, where Bellman Workbench writes the views it exports. The generated files a folder tracks are records kept on purpose: the portfolio–consumption application keeps its fixed numerical reference, reference/legacy/port_cons_h5.npz with its manifest, and reference/legacy/preflight.json, the record that identifies the notebook and the helper from which the reference was computed; the record of the comparison with that reference that its acceptance test writes, code/tests/evidence/reference-comparison.json and .txt; and the figures its earlier reference notebook drew, the PNG files under notebooks/port-cons/figures/, beside which stage_lifecycle.svg is a drawing and not a generated file.

docs.title: 3 Variants
docs.text:
A variant is a second version of a model that shares most of its files with the first. It is written beside the first, in declaration/, in one of three ways, according to what it changes.

  • A variant of the route, which changes the stages a period holds or how the periods are joined, is a second set of the three files: a recipe spec.<name>.yml, which names its trellis file under trellis:; the trellis file trellis.<name>.yml, which names its period file under template:; and the period file period.<name>.yml, the name between the dots being the author's choice. The durables folder keeps its route without the tenure stage in this way: spec.two-stages.yml names trellis.two-stages.yml, which names period.two-stages.yml, and the recipe names the same stage files and sources as spec.yml, without those of the tenure stage, so that load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.two-stages.yml") reads the second route (Trellises §5; The Bellman factory §3.6). Since the suffix links nothing, a recipe may name a trellis file of another suffix where that is the intent.
  • A variant of the values, which changes the numbers a stage receives and not the route, needs no second set of files. It is a further source file, such as calibration/near_terminal.yml or settings/fine.yml, which a recipe lists after the common one in a stage's list of sources, or in the list of sources of a range of periods, so that its values stand over the common ones (The Bellman factory §§3.2, 3.4). A variant supplied when the recipe is read is a fill, a mapping given by keyword to a slot, a place written $name in a list of sources (The Bellman factory §3.3).
  • A variant of an equation is another stage folder beside the first, holding the changed stage file, which a second recipe names under the same stage key in place of the first, as tenure: {stage: stages/tenure_flat/tenure_flat.bl, …} names the stage file of a folder stages/tenure_flat/.

Distinct uses of one stage file need distinct stage keys, each with its own bindings, also when the two uses stand in one period.

docs.title: 4 What each file contains
docs.text:
File Contents declaration/stages/<stage>/<stage>.bl The stage file: the declarations, typed blocks and equations of one stage. declaration/stages/<stage>/methods.bl The stage's methods file, an addition to the stage file beside it, which the package reads with the stage file: a .bl file that opens with @methods: and the stage's name, whose blocks name blocks of the stage by their ids and add their typing entries and their lines to them, and whose file-level entries type a place by its path (Methodization). Each of the four stages of the retirement-choice application has one. A replacing selection stands beside it as methods.<variant>.bl, as methods.bellman_method.bl of the benhabib-2019 application does, and a recipe's methods list names the file it binds. No .bl file stands outside a stage's folder. declaration/stages/<stage>/<stage>.md The stage's note, which explains the stage file. declaration/calibration/<name>.yml Economic parameter values, under the top key calibration. declaration/settings/<name>.yml Numerical setting values, under the top key settings. declaration/period.yml The period file: the stage keys of one period and the connectors within it. declaration/trellis.yml The trellis file: the periods of the model, each written out or given by a period file repeated, and the inter-period connectors. declaration/spec.yml The recipe: the path of the trellis file and of each stage's file, from this folder; for each stage and each kind, the ordered sources and slots; the registry block. README.md The folder's first page (§2.5). economics.md The economics in full (§2.5). code/ The model's programs: code that writes values into the syntactic trellis, supplies boundary data or calls numerical routines. tests/ The model's tests, such as the structural test that parses each stage file and compares its terms with terms written by hand. reference/ README.md, a note that cites the papers the folder keeps for reference and says where their PDF files are held; the PDF files are not kept in the repository. results/ What the model's programs write (§2.6). paper/ For each stage, the two files Bellman Workbench's button paper writes once and never rewrites: <stage>.md, the printed card of each of the stage's builders (A builder), the link to the drawing and a footnote with the SHA-256 digest of the stage file and of each file the stage is bound from; and <stage>.svg, the drawing of the graph of the stage's backward builders. An author converts the Markdown to LaTeX with Pandoc.

A calibration or settings file is read whether it is spelled .yml or .yaml, and the two are told apart by their top keys, not by their names or their extensions; a methods file is a .bl file, told apart from a stage file by its first line, @methods:. A connector selects a continuation state field of one stage occurrence and an arrival state field of another without changing either local name; an inter-period connector does so between consecutive periods. A bare endpoint must identify one eligible field at its side of the connection; a stage key qualifies an ambiguous endpoint (Periods §2). The recipe chooses the sources of each binding; it contains no stage equation and determines the sequence of periods only through the trellis file it names.

docs.title: 5 Paths in a model's documents
docs.text: The documents of a model folder, its README.md, its economics.md, its stage notes and the docstrings of its code, write a path in one of two ways. A path that says where a file of the folder stands is written from the model folder, declaration/stages/tenure/tenure.bl or declaration/calibration/durables.yml, whichever document writes it. A path quoted as a recipe or a trellis file writes it is kept as that file writes it, from the file's own folder, and is introduced as that file's line: the recipe's stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl, or its methods source stages/tenure/methods.

docs.title: 6 Paths and the readers
docs.text:
The functions that read files interpret their path arguments differently:

Reader Path supplied bellman.stage.load_stage(path) A .bl file, read into a record. bellman.trellis.load_trellis(file) A trellis file of records; the stage files and the mapping files it names are read from its folder. bellman.trellis.load_recipe(directory, recipe) A registry, in a model folder its declaration/, and the name of its recipe, spec.yml or a variant's spec.<name>.yml; the trellis file and the stage files are the paths the recipe writes, read from that folder. bellman.trellis.assemble_trellis(directory, recipe) The same two arguments; the specified trellis in one call.

load_recipe returns the syntactic trellis, and assemble_trellis elaborates and binds it in one call. load_trellis reads a trellis file whose periods write their stages as records, each naming its stage file and its three mappings inline or as paths, and needs no recipe. An application can also build the trellis dictionary itself, one period at a time with bellman.trellis.accrete. The trellis factory states these calls.

A record that elaborate_trellis of bellman.trellis reads holds a stage mapping with text and origin, as load_stage writes it, and mapping-valued calibration, settings and methods; a path string in place of the mapping is refused. Precedence is settled in the syntactic trellis before elaboration; the elaborator and the verbs merge no file and no default. The factory API gives the complete record. Moving a file requires updating the recipe, the trellis file or the application code that names it.

docs.title: 7 Stage files in the earlier YAML form
docs.text: load_stage of bellman.stage reads a stage file written in .bl and refuses any other file under the rule readable-file of Refusals. A stage written in the earlier YAML format is therefore rewritten in .bl, since changing its extension translates none of its declarations, type words, equations or shock laws. YAML remains the format of the recipe, the trellis and period files, and the calibration and settings files; a methods file is written in .bl, as an addition to its stage file. The earlier YAML stages of the portfolio–consumption application are kept, as recorded sources of its fixed reference, under applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/.

docs.title: 8 Related references
docs.text:
• Trellises states the trellis file, the period file and the paths a recipe writes.
  • Methodization describes the methods file and the settings and calibration files beside it.
  • Stage functions specifies loading, elaborating and binding one stage.
  • Period functions specifies accretion and the order of a period.
  • Recipe functions specifies the recipe, its merge and its slots.
  • The trellis factory specifies the trellis file and the calls on a trellis.
  • Bellman Workbench opens a model folder and writes a new one in this layout.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Summary

A builder of a stage is composed of primitive operators, and its card lists them under its operations, one row each, with what the row reads, what it writes and its rule. Every row of a card is of one of eight kinds. This page says which lines of a stage file form a row of each kind and in which builder it stands, and lists the operations of the package's table of definitions, the eight kinds and the one relation that is no kind, each with its defining expression, the operator of the Bellman calculus it denotes and the entry of the table that defines it.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Appendix E.3 Operators §4: the operator each kind realizes, with its domain and codomain. Builds on — The builders graphs and A builder: the builders, their cards and the names of their rows, printed from the package. See also — Shock distributions: what an expectation integrates against and a distribution extension extends a measure by; Methodization §2: the places at which a method may be typed.

Key terminology Term What it names Builder The operator one block of a stage file denotes: backward on value functions, forward on finite measures of the states, such as their probability distribution. A builder is reached by the pair of perches it joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"], or from the perch its edge leaves, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd or stage.arvl.builder.fwd; the policy builder is stage.dcsn.builder.policy. Card What a builder, or one of the operators in it, prints: its inputs and outputs, its operations and the lines of the stage file they come from. print(stage.dcsn.builder.bwd) prints the card of the decision builder. Row One primitive operator of a builder, listed on the card under its operations with a number, a name, what it reads (in), what it writes (out) and its rule. Grain How far the boxes of a graph, the operators it holds, are opened: stage.builder.bwd holds one box per builder, and at the primitive grain, stage.builder.bwd.primitives, one box per primitive operator; see semgraph. Kind Which of the eight primitive operators a row is, named in the row's name after the builder or the line: Pullback in cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback. Rule The equation or relation a row states, printed under the row, read at a point of the row's domain. Edge The step from one perch to the next that one forward builder carries. Law of motion The map 𝑔 that a forward block's lines define, from the states of one perch, with the control and the shock where the block reads them, to the states of the next. Value aggregator 𝐺 The map a backward line applies pointwise to the functions it reads, its right side read as a function of them; see aggregation. Policy The function the policy builder writes, 𝑐 of the decision state. A builder stated at the policy reads it as a fixed function, which the builder's card names under At. Declared carrier The set of functions in which the stage declares an output to lie: from the states of its perch to the set its block's header declares for it, and for a policy only the functions whose values are feasible.

docs.title: 1 Reading a row
docs.text:
A card lists the rows of a builder in the order in which they apply, each after every row whose output it reads. A row has a number, a name, what it reads, what it writes and its rule. The name is the builder, or the address of the line the row realizes, followed by the kind: cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback, policy.InvEuler:Aggregation, policy:Evaluation; the builder's own card leaves out the builder, InvEuler:Aggregation, Evaluation. Where one builder or one line holds several rows of one kind, a number, a label or the shocks the row concerns tell them apart, value:Expectation:1, arvl_to_dcsn:DistributionExtension:ψ. An input written as a number in brackets, (1), is the output of the row with that number. The API page on a builder, linked in the box above, prints the cards of cons.bl, the consumption stage of the portfolio application, and says how each entry of a card's Operations is read.

Five kinds stand in the backward builders, which act on functions, and three in the forward builders, which act on finite measures. Each builder is named below by the pair of perches it joins, as the title of its card prints it, cntn → dcsn for the decision builder, which stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] reads (The builders graphs §1); the policy builder is named by its own key, policy. The lines of a stage file form the rows of each kind as follows.

  • Pullback: the lines of a backward block that read functions of the later perch at the states of an earlier perch form one row that composes those functions with the law of motion of the forward block on the same edge, a = m_d - c in cons.bl. Such a row stands in cntn → dcsn, along 𝑔≻ read at the policy, and in dcsn → arvl, along 𝑔≺; in policy one stands along 𝑔≻ where an objective or residuals that the builder constructs read such a function, as the solve_{…}(…) line of port.bl does, and the identification line of §4 forms another, along the coordinate map 𝑚_d≻. Where the forward block branches, as in ret_choice.bl, one such row stands for each branch, Pullback:work and Pullback:retire, along the law of motion read at that branch's label, 𝑔_work≻(a_d) = 𝑔≻(a_d, work). A policy line written at the continuation perch, its left side marked [>], such as c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0 in the methods file of cons.bl, reads the function at the continuation states and forms none.
  • Aggregation: the lines of a backward block that write its values together form one in the block's builder, dcsn → arvl or cntn → dcsn, each right side read as the value aggregator 𝐺 and printed as one equation of the row's rule, as V = 𝑢(c) + V[>] alone forms the Aggregation of cntn → dcsn in cons.bl. A derivative line of the same block, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), forms no part of it: it states the derivative of the value the builder writes and stands at the builder's Evaluation. In a policy block, or in the block of a methods file that brings the lines of a solution method to the policy builder (Methodization §5), adjacent explicit lines written at the continuation perch together form one, as c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>]) and m[>] = a + c[>] of the block policy of the buffer-stock methods file, applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/methods.bl, form g_cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, and a line stating a relation, a solve_{…}(…) line and the objective of an argmax_{…}(…) line not marked !doc each form one, in policy (§4). In both kinds of block, a line that takes the expectation of an expression other than one function it reads forms one more for that expression, value:Aggregation:1 of dcsn → arvl in the buffer-stock stage file and foc:Aggregation:1 of policy in port.bl. A derivative line forms none: the derivative line of cntn → dcsn in port.bl, which takes the expectation of such an expression, stands at the builder's Evaluation, and the builder's card lists Pullback, value:Expectation:1, Aggregation and Evaluation. A line marked !node forms its own in its sub-builder and joins no other.
  • Expectation: an occurrence E_{θ}(·) in a line of a backward block forms one, one row per occurrence on the builder's card, value:Expectation:1; at the primitive grain of the whole graph, stage.builder.bwd.primitives, the box keeps the name of its line, prefixed by the id of its block, cntn_to_dcsn.value:Expectation:1 in port.bl, which is the name the table below shows. In policy, the objective of an argmax_{…}(…) line forms one where it holds an expectation, as in ez_savings.bl.
  • Argmax: an argmax_{…}(…) line of a policy block that is not marked !doc forms one, in policy, as d = argmax_{d}(V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>]) in ret_choice.bl.
  • Evaluation: no line forms one. It is the closing row of every backward builder, the policy builder among them, and of every sub-builder, the operator a line marked !node denotes, and it places each output in its declared carrier. On the card of policy of cons.bl its rule is the declared carrier with its feasibility, 𝑐 : Xm → ℝ₊₊, 𝑐(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d), since the relation that defines the function it carries is printed at the row that forms it, cons_choice:Pullback; the row's own card, stage.dcsn.builder.policy["Evaluation"], prints that relation under Rule, 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa).
  • DistributionExtension: a ~ line declaring the distribution of a shock forms one, one row per declaration, in the forward builder whose block lists the shock among its inputs.
  • PolicyInsertion: no line forms one, and no card shows one (§3).
  • Pushforward: the lines of a forward block, which define its law of motion, a = m_d - c in cons.bl, form one. It is the closing row of every forward builder, arvl → dcsn and dcsn → cntn, the latter along the law of motion read at the policy (§3).

docs.title: 2 The kinds and the relation
docs.text:
The table has one row for each operation that the package's table of definitions, PRIMITIVE_DEFINITIONS, defines, in that table's order: the eight kinds, and the relation that the rows of §4 read, which is no kind. The column operation names it, and kind of a row says whether a row of a card can be of it. written gives the first row of it on the stage files under applications/, read with cons.bl and port.bl of the portfolio application first: the lines of the file that the row realizes, as the row's card quotes them under Source, each on one line and without its annotation, then the row's name, the file and the builder that holds it, written as the key of stage.builder that reads it; where no stage file forms such a row, the cell says so. A pullback's card quotes the law of motion it composes along; an expectation's, the declaration of its shock's law and the line the expectation stands in; a distribution extension's, that declaration alone; and an Evaluation's, the derivative lines its block states, which form no part of the aggregation (§1). reads and writes gives what that row reads and writes, its in and out lines as its card prints them. rule gives that row's rule as the row's own card prints it, stated for the row's own functions, and §§1, 3 and 4 quote those of cons.bl; definition gives the operation's defining expression in the table of definitions, as the package prints it. denotes links to the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the operator the operation realizes. read from names the module, the table and the key of the definition, which states the defining map and its conditions exactly; primitive_definition in the same module returns the definition by its key.
