docs.title: Symbol conventions
docs.text:
Summary

Bellman-SYM distinguishes a field, its domain, and a function representing that field in state coordinates. Perch marks identify arrival, decision, and continuation information within a stage. Names such as V and policy are conventions; their declarations and equations determine their roles, and the derivative of a value is read by the term D_{a}V[>], not named by a field. The last section lists the punctuation, the reserved sets and the type words with which a stage file declares its objects.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: a complete stage file; Perch tagging rules: typing and information. Used by — Field equations, Periods, and Trellises. Formal account — Appendix C for mathematical interpretation; Appendix D for nodes and indexing. See also — Expression forms: the operators and functions a line of a stage file writes.

docs.title: 1 Reading a stage equation
docs.text:
The discounting stage multiplies the continuation value by the discount factor. This is its complete source:

@stage: disc

Xa := ℝ₊
β : (0,1)

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a : Xa) : !arvl -> (a_d : Xa) : !dcsn] {
    a_d = a
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d) : !dcsn -> (a[>] : Xa) : !cntn] {
    a[>] = a_d
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = β*V[>]                      :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
}

Here a, a_d, and a[>] are assets at three information contexts. The transition equations state that their values agree in this stage. The stage writes no derivative line: its two backward lines are a scaling and an identity of the value, whose state passes unchanged, so the derivative of the value passes through them, and a stage before this one that reads D_{a}V[>] of its continuation receives the derivative of the discounted value. No letters of a name establish a derivative; the derivative of a value is read by the term D_{a}V[>], which applies the operator D to the declared value in the named coordinate (§4).

The block identifier cntn_to_dcsn provides an address. Renaming it changes references such as the path of a place in a methods file, but does not change multiplication by β. In a model with a separate discounting stage, do not insert a second discount factor into the beta-free consumption equations.

docs.title: 2 Fields, functions, and spaces
docs.text:
A field is a named quantity of a stage: a state, a control, a value or a multiplier (Constraints §4.2) at one perch, or a shock, which belongs to no perch (§9.3). Once shocks are declared, fields may be interpreted as random variables on the underlying probability space. A state function represents such a quantity using explicit state arguments. A domain describes the values an object may take; it is distinct from the space of functions on a state domain.

Mathematical notation Object \(\mathsf X_\prec\), \(\mathsf X\), \(\mathsf X_\succ\) Arrival, decision, and continuation state domains. \(\mathrm x_\prec\), \(\mathrm x\), \(\mathrm x_\succ\) State fields taking values in those domains. \(\mathrm V_\prec\), \(\mathrm V\), \(\mathrm V_\succ\) Value fields. \(v_\prec\), \(v\), \(v_\succ\) Functions of state coordinates representing the value fields under the stated assumptions. \(g_\prec\), \(g_\succ\) Laws of motion, from arrival to decision and from decision to continuation. \(\pi\) A policy, meaning a measurable choice as a function of decision information. \(\mu\) A probability distribution. \(\mathbb T_\pi\) The backward value operator at a fixed policy. \(\mathbb M_\pi\) The forward distribution operator at that policy.

Sans-serif capitals denote spaces, italic letters denote functions, and roman letters denote the fields those functions represent, the same letter for both. These typography conventions help the reader; they do not type a source identifier. The source V[>] is a value field because of its declaration. A name such as V_fn has no reserved function meaning.

For example, if the continuation state field is \(x_\succ\) and a value field is measurable with respect to that state, an appropriate measurable factorization gives \(\mathrm V_\succ=v_\succ(x_\succ)\). The factorization requires the measurable-space assumptions stated in Appendix C. It does not follow from choosing a font, and it need not specify a unique extension away from the states represented by \(x_\succ\).

The notation \(L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F)\) denotes square-integrable fields on a probability space with information \(\mathcal F\). Use it only when square integrability is assumed. A declaration allowing extended values does not automatically put a field in \(L^2\).

docs.title: 3 Perches and information
docs.text:
A perch is one of the three information contexts within a stage:

Context Mathematical subscript .bl reference Type word Arrival \(\prec\) V[<] !arvl Decision \(\sim\), usually omitted V or V[~] !dcsn Continuation \(\succ\) V[>] !cntn

In a block's header a mark agrees with the perch word of its side: the listing (a[>] : Xa) : !arvl is refused under field-perch. The package reads a[~] as the bare name a, so the listing (a[~] : Xa) : !arvl, which breaks the rule, is read as the arrival field a. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3).

When nested information is assumed, the information structure can be written \(\mathcal F_\prec\subseteq\mathcal F_\sim\subseteq\mathcal F_\succ\). Stage marks alone do not establish this assumption. These inclusions need not be strict: an identity transition can reveal no additional information. Nor must a list of current state coordinates alone generate all past information. State sufficiency is an assumption used when passing to functions of those coordinates.

Information marks distinguish field references within the stage. They are not dates, and a perch is not an operator endpoint. In particular, a shock listed as a transition argument need not be observed before that transition. A decision control written beside continuation values is still a decision control. The rules for the sides of a block's header respect these role exceptions.

The diagram below records information order and the usual directions of transition and value calculations; its circles denote information contexts:

arrival information  ── state transition ──>  decision information
        ^                                            |
        | arrival value calculation                  | state transition
        |                                            v
        +                                  continuation information
                        <── backward value calculation ──

A stage can use pre-decision shocks, post-decision shocks, both, or neither. In a deterministic stage the law can be degenerate, but determinism does not require the arrival transition to be the identity. The equations decide the transition.

docs.title: 4 Operators and derivatives
docs.text:
The policy is written as a subscript: \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\). Superscripts can then denote iteration, such as \(\mathbb T_\pi^n\). When a stage index is needed it comes first, for example \(\mathbb T_{k,\succ,\pi}\). Omit an index only when its referent is unambiguous.

In the usual two-transition stage, backward composition is \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\), while forward composition is \(\mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec\). These equations specify order on compatible domains; the backward operator additionally depends on the declared reward and discounting. It must not be identified with a probability transition merely because both use the same state transition.

Technical details

For a transition-only calculation, let \((X,\mathcal X)\) and \((Y,\mathcal Y)\) be measurable state spaces. A probability kernel \(P\) assigns a probability measure \(P(x,\cdot)\) on \(Y\) to each \(x\in X\), with \(x\mapsto P(x,A)\) measurable for every \(A\in\mathcal Y\). For bounded measurable \(f:Y\to\mathbb R\), define \((Kf)(x)=\int f(y)P(x,dy)\), a bounded measurable function on \(X\). For a probability measure \(\mu\) on \(X\), define the probability measure on \(Y\) by \((M\mu)(A)=\int P(x,A)\mu(dx)\) for \(A\in\mathcal Y\). Integration then gives \(\int f\,d(M\mu)=\int Kf\,d\mu\). This identity concerns transition and expectation. Adding a reward, discount, or maximization requires the corresponding additional operations; a rewarded Bellman operator need not satisfy this identity.

A derivative expression applies the operator D to a function the file holds: to a declared function, D_{c}(𝑢), where the subscript names one of its formal arguments, or to a value field written with its perch mark, D_{a}V[>], where the subscript names a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark. The second form is the derivative term; it denotes the derivative of the value in that coordinate, a function of the value and no second object, and it has this one spelling. A name such as 𝑑𝑢 can be defined by a derivative expression or by a closed form, and a stage file may define dV = D_{a}V[>] and read the name. The package differentiates nothing: a kernel that calls a function defined by D_{c}(𝑢) has no compiled form and is refused under kernel-form, a kernel that reads a derivative term compiles with the term among its arguments (Expression forms §3), and the derivative of a value is evaluated as the stage that built the value fixed it (Methodization §5). A line whose left side is a derivative term of the value its builder writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), is the author's assertion that the derivative equals the right side, which holds under the envelope conditions; the stage lists the reading and checks it against nothing.

Expectation and maximization subscripts bind their integration and choice variables. The derivative subscript selects a declared formal argument of the function, or a state coordinate of the perch at which a value is read; it does not create a new local stage variable. An ordinary underscore is part of a name. Thus E_{θ}(V[>]) specifies integration over a shock, while μ_θ is simply a chosen parameter name. The operation forms are listed in Expression forms.

docs.title: 5 Equations and nodes
docs.text:
A block is an authored typed header and body. Its identifier provides an address, and its header and statements declare the fields and equations. A builder is the operator a block denotes. Within a block, !node marks a line as an authored node, a computation kept as a unit of its own that a method can address; in a backward block it forms a sub-builder of the block's builder. An expectation nested inside an equation remains a mathematical operation whether or not its containing statement is marked.

Conventional labels such as value, marginal, InvEuler, and cons_choice can make a file readable. They do not select mathematical rules. Likewise, calling a block policy does not insert optimization. A methods file can type a method at a line with an id or at an operator occurrence without !node; Methodization §2 lists the places a methods file names.

An unmarked explicit intermediate equation may be substituted while preserving all outputs and dependencies. An implicit equation instead defines a relation. For candidate state coordinates \(H(s)\) and controls \(U(s)\) indexed by \(s\), the pairs \((H(s),U(s))\) define one control on the image of \(H\) exactly when equal coordinates imply equal controls. Measurability, coverage of the intended state domain, and optimality remain separate conditions. Appendix D applies this distinction to the endogenous grid method.

docs.title: 6 Branches and collections
docs.text:
For a finite nonempty set of alternatives, a branch can have its own state coordinates and continuation value. A branch state can be described as a pair \((j,x_j)\), where \(j\) labels an alternative and \(x_j\) belongs to its state domain. When the domains differ, retaining the label is necessary to interpret the coordinates. When every alternative shares a domain \(X\), these pairs belong to the product of the alternative set and \(X\).

A tuple of continuation values and selection by the declared choice can express this distinction in .bl. Ordinary selection such as q[d] selects a collection entry; it does not declare a function over d. The complete retirement example in Branching supplies the domains, values, selection equation, and finite maximization. Finite maximization attains a value when the feasible set is nonempty and each candidate value is defined; ties still need a choice rule.

Stochastic alternatives use a declared joint or conditional law and an expectation instead. A list of marginal laws does not specify independence. Neither the spelling of a branch label nor a method tag decides whether the model maximizes or averages.

docs.title: 7 Stage and period indices
docs.text:
A stage occurrence is one use of a stage file under a particular key in a period. Reusing the same .bl source requires distinct occurrence keys; it does not identify the resulting stages or their bindings.

Notation or key Meaning periods[h] The period h periods before terminal. periods[0] The terminal period. inter_connectors[h] Field renaming joining period h+1 to period h. syntactic["periods"][h]["stages"][stage_name] The record of that occurrence and period: its merged parameter, setting, and method mappings. [<], [~], [>] Information contexts within one stage, independently of h.

Terminal continuation values are separate boundary data for period zero. A connector renames corresponding fields between occurrences; matching names alone does not prove matching domains or information roles. The per-stage mathematical graph and the syntactic trellis, a dictionary of stage records, serve different purposes; the order of a period's stages is computed from the fields they join. Periods and Trellises give their composition rules.

docs.title: 8 Parameters, settings, and interpretation
docs.text:
A parameter defines the economic problem; a setting controls a numerical calculation. A finite menu of housing sizes is a mathematical domain, so changing its endpoints or number of available sizes changes the problem. A grid approximating a continuous housing domain is a numerical choice. A simulation grid need not equal the solution grid.

A derived parameter is a constant of the economic problem that a definition without arguments writes from the declared parameters, such as human wealth h := 1/(1 - Γ/R), so that it is a parameter and not a setting; its definition may be written by cases, h : ℝ_{+∞} := if Γ < R then 1/(1 - Γ/R) else inf, with the declared set that its infinite branch requires (Equation parsing rules §2; Parameters and settings §1.1). The line that defines a derived parameter may declare the set in which its value lies, q : (0,1) := (β*R)^(1/ρ)/R, and calibration then refuses values of the parameters at which the derived value lies outside that set (§9.2).

The meaning map \(\Upsilon\) interprets declarations and equations. The representation map Ρ denotes their numerical realization after the required choices and bindings. Lowercase \(\rho\) remains available for an economic parameter, such as risk aversion. These names do not assert that interpretation or approximation is invertible, or that different numerical choices commute.

Elaboration keeps the fields, with the interpreted equation bodies and definitions, in the two initial diagrams, and derives from them, under explicit assumptions, the two builders graphs, on functions and on measures. The temporary syntax tree and source spans are discarded; a second independently editable function model is not required. See From source to a formal problem.

docs.title: 9 Declarations, domains and type words
docs.text: The reference page Types lists the role words, the perch words, the reserved sets, the forms of a set expression and the limits on them.

docs.title: 9.1 Punctuation
docs.text:
The examples are lines of the stage files under applications/portfolio-choice/: disc.bl, whose source §1 shows, cons.bl and noport.bl; the derived parameter h and the definition of q that declares its set are lines of perfect_foresight.bl under applications/consumption-perfect-foresight-crra/. The examples of the union and the difference are written for this table.

Spelling Use Example : Declare a type: a declared set (§9.2) or a role, on a line of its own or on a side of a block's header, and an information context on a side of a block's header only. A declaration on a line of its own that carries a perch word is refused under field-perch. β : (0,1); (a : Xa) : !arvl @ Write the components of a type with @ between them; their order does not matter. Several sets in one type declare their intersection (§9.2). c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊ \/, also ∪ Form the union of two sets of numbers, in the declared set of a parameter, a derived parameter or a setting (§9.2). ρ : (0,1) \/ (1, inf) \, also ∖ Form the difference of two sets of numbers, the members of the first that lie outside the second, in the same places (§9.2). ρ : ℝ₊₊ \ {1} :=, also <- Define a named set, which may be written as a comprehension (§9.2), a function, or a derived parameter (§8), whose definition may declare its set, q : (0,1) := (β*R)^(1/ρ)/R. Xa := ℝ₊; Xa := [0, ā]; 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ); h := 1/(1 - Γ/R) = State an equation inside a block, explicit or implicit. V = β*V[>] ~ Give a shock its law, on a line of its own. θ ~ LogNormal(μ_θ, σ_θ) -> Separate the input side of a block's header from its output side. (a : Xa) : !arvl -> (a_d : Xa) : !dcsn :: [id=…] Give a line an id, by which a methods file and the stage object name it. :: [id=value] @stage: name Name the stage, once in the file. @stage: disc

The argument c of 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) is local to the definition and declares no control, and a name such as 𝑑𝑢 differentiates nothing: the body of its definition defines the function. An equation is not an assignment or a policy function by its form alone: c = c[>] in the block policy of methods.bl, the methods file beside cons.bl, is an implicit relation between the policy and the candidate c[>], which the line m_d[>] = a + c[>] places at the cash on hand of each saving (Appendix D §7).

docs.title: 9.2 Domains
docs.text:
A domain is the set of values a field or a parameter may take, also called its declared set. These set names are reserved by the grammar and need no definition line:

Spelling Set ℝ All real numbers. ℝ₊, also R+ or R_{+} Nonnegative real numbers, zero included. ℝ₊₊, also R++ or R_{++} Strictly positive real numbers. ℤ Integers. ℕ Natural numbers; state a sharper lower bound where it matters. ℝ_{-∞} Real numbers with negative infinity adjoined, written with the ASCII hyphen. ℝ_{+∞} Real numbers with positive infinity adjoined. ℝ_{±∞}, also ℝ̄ Real numbers with both infinities adjoined.

A bare R, N or Z is an ordinary name and not one of these sets; R may be the gross return on assets. Define any other named set before using it, Xa := ℝ₊. A named set may also be an interval, Xa := [0, ā], Xa := (0, ā] or Xa := [0, ā), whose endpoints may name parameters; a field typed a : Xa then has the same declared set as a : [0, ā]. The same holds where one block header lists the field on Xa and another on [0, ā]. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). The open-open form is the exception: after :=, (0, ā) is read as a pair of values, which is neither a set nor a derived parameter, so the line Xa := (0, ā) is refused under not-constructed, even where nothing reads Xa. An open interval is written after the typing colon where it is used, a : (0, ā). An interval writes its endpoints with the usual brackets, (a,b), (a,b], [a,b) and [a,b], and an endpoint may be infinite, ρ : [1, inf); an interval that holds no number, such as (2, 1), is refused when the file is read. A finite set lists its labels, R_type := {r1, r2, r3, r4, r5} or, inline, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}, and a product uses ×, x : ℝ × ℝ.

The union of two sets of numbers is written A \/ B, also A ∪ B, and their difference A \ B, also A ∖ B: ρ : (0,1) \/ (1, inf) declares a parameter in one of the two intervals, and ρ : ℝ₊₊ \ {1} a positive parameter other than one. A value lies in a union when it lies in at least one member, and in a difference when it lies in the left set and outside the right. The product × is read before the two signs and the arrow → after them, and the two signs are read from left to right. The package prints them as \/ and \. A union and a difference are read in the declared set of a parameter, of a derived parameter and of a setting. They are refused in the set of a field, of a shock and of a function's argument, and they are not read after :=. A difference whose left side lies within its right side, as in (0,1) \ ℝ₊, holds no number and is refused under readable-form when the file is read, where the package can decide the inclusion. A difference that is a member of a union is not judged.

A declaration may write several sets in one type, with @ between them, and the declared name then lies in each of them, so that the sets declare their intersection: β : (0,1) @ (0, R^(ρ-1)) declares a discount factor in both intervals, below one and below R^(ρ-1). A bound is written as an interval, whose endpoints may name parameters and derived parameters and whose unbounded side is -inf or inf: θ : ℤ @ [1, inf) declares an integer of at least one. A parameter's or a setting's set that names a field is refused, and an undeclared name there is refused under name-in-scope; a shock inside an expectation over that shock is still read where its law reads no field, as in the bound (0, E_{Ψ}(Ψ^(1-γ))). At most one of the sets is written otherwise than as an interval with brackets, and a named set counts as such a set; a second such set is refused under syntax. The sets may be written in any order, and two equal sets are read as one. Two intervals of numbers with no number in common, such as (0,1) @ (2,3), are refused under syntax. Several sets are read on the declaration of one name on a line of its own only; on a field's listing in a block header they are refused under readable-form.

When values are bound, calibrate refuses a value outside any of the sets and names the bound it breaks. A value bound to a name declared on an extended real, ℝ_{-∞}, ℝ_{+∞} or ℝ_{±∞}, must lie in that set. calibrate decides the membership of a number: a finite number lies in each of the three sets, and an infinity in those that hold it, so that inf is refused for a name declared on ℝ_{-∞}. A value that is no number, such as a string, lies in none of them. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). An endpoint that is the bare name of a parameter or of a derived parameter valued at an infinity is read as that infinity (Equation parsing rules §2). A bound that reads a derived parameter is judged once calibration has computed the derived value from the declared values. The value of a derived parameter whose definition declares a set is judged against that set in the same step, and calibration refuses a value outside it with a sentence that names the parameter, its definition, the set and the values read. A bound whose arithmetic has no value at the calibration, such as 1/(R-2) at R = 2, refuses the calibration, and so does a bound that computes with a name valued at an infinity. A bound that holds an expectation over a shock, or that calls a function other than log, exp, min and max, such as a function the file defines, is not decided: the stage binds, and stage.obligations() lists the membership as required.

Adjoining infinity lets a value reach an endpoint; it does not make every operation on such values defined. An expectation needs integrability or an extended-value convention, and infinity minus infinity is undefined. Appendix C states the assumptions used for value equations.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Finite indexed data
docs.text:
A finite set of integer keys lists them, {0, 1}, or names the set its members lie in when a member names a parameter, S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ, with θ integer-valued. An integer range whose bounds may name parameters, L_J := {1, …, J}, with … or ... between the commas, holds every integer from the first bound to the second, including both bounds. The bounds and the listed members must be integers; their conditions are retained until calibration if they depend on parameters. A value such as 3.0 is integer-valued and identifies the same key as 3, without rounding another integer to it. Separately listed keys must be distinct. A bare {a, b} continues to list two labels.

A collection is declared with one entry per key, δ : L_J → ℝ, or per ordered pair, dist : L_J × L_J → ℝ₊. The admitted index sets are integer ranges, listed integer keys, finite label sets, and products of these sets. Selection uses a name declared on the corresponding index set: δ[j] selects the entry at j : L_J, and dist[j][i] the entry at the pair of keys. An integer literal in brackets denotes a position, and a collection on an index set is not selected by a position: δ[1] is refused under family-selection, although 1 is a key of L_J. Select with a name declared on the index set, δ[j] with j : L_J. Numerical keys must be integer-valued; the entries they identify, such as wages, distances and shock outcomes, may be real-valued. Separate indices of a finite shock distribution may identify equal numerical outcomes.

Calibration supplies a sequence in index order or a mapping from keys to entries. Integer ranges are ordered from the lower bound to the upper bound; listed sets retain the order in which their members are written. For example, declare:

θ : ℤ @ [1, inf)
S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ
q : S_θ → ℝ₊

The calibration fragment below sets θ to 5 and supplies 10.25 at key 0 and 20.75 at key 5:

θ: 5
q: [10.25, 20.75]

Writing q: {5: 20.75, 0: 10.25} gives the same association. If s : S_θ takes the value 5, q[s] selects 20.75; 5 is the key, not the fifth position. Calibration checks the integer keys, their distinctness, the data shape and the entries' declared domains. A matrix uses this order on each axis. Copying a collection between stages also requires matching key order (Periods §2).

Technical details

Compiled numerical selection uses signed 64-bit integers, with arithmetic checks that require each operand and intermediate result to fit that range. Constant integer expressions are evaluated exactly before the function is written. A power in an index bound or listed member requires a nonnegative integer exponent, which may depend on parameters, and parameter-dependent division is compiled only when the denominator is 1. For another division, supply the integer result as a separately declared parameter; the mathematical set remains available for inspection when compile_kernel() refuses the expression under kernel-form. A compiled integer calculation that overflows is refused rather than identifying another key.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Category codes
docs.text:
A named set may also be a comprehension, H := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1}, which binds the name i to the set after the colon and holds the members that satisfy every condition after the bar. Mark such a set with !categories to assign meanings to its integer members, called category codes:

HouseholdStatus := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=1]
n : HouseholdStatus

A marked comprehension must range over ℤ or ℕ, and every condition must compare its bound name with an integer literal by a strict or weak inequality, with the name on either side. The conditions must give a nonempty range bounded below and above. Parameter bounds and equality conditions are refused on a marked set, although equality remains available in ordinary unmarked comprehensions. A marked range over ℕ must have a lower bound of at least 1, since the language does not decide whether 0 is a natural number. The annotation supplies exactly one category name for each member, with no repeated name or code (§9.3).

Here the code 0 stands for a newborn household and 1 for an old one. The category map records these associations between codes and categories. Arithmetic on the field has its usual numerical meaning: 100 - 120*n is 100 for a newborn household and −20 for an old one. With three or more categories, a formula affine in the code gives equal steps between the values at successive codes; that is an assumption of the formula the author writes. Assigning codes supplies no distance between categories or meaning to interpolation between them. The word category here denotes a value of a categorical variable, as in a statistical value label. Appendix C §2.1 gives the mathematical interpretation.

A category name is not a name usable in stage equations. The transition to old age is written with the code, n_next = 1; n_next = old is refused under name-in-scope. The category map remains part of the set's displayed definition, denotation and exported stage, so the meanings can be inspected alongside equations using the codes. Unmarked comprehensions keep their ordinary set meaning.

The identifier household_status asserts shared category meanings across stage files. Two sets using it identify a category by that identifier and the category's name; a different identifier denotes different categories. Without an identifier, categories are local to the named set in its stage text and shared by occurrences of that text. Periods §2 states when fields using these meanings can be connected.

Important

A comprehension marked !categories is admitted as a field domain, but is not an admitted index set for a collection. Thus n : HouseholdStatus is admitted, while payment : HouseholdStatus → ℝ is refused under readable-form. Use the index-set forms in §9.2.1 for indexed data.

Technical details

A stage constructed by make_stage from a syntax tree has no stage text. A marked set without an explicit category identifier therefore has no established category identity for connections in such a stage; supply the identifier when constructing it this way.

docs.title: 9.3 Type words and statement marks
docs.text:
A type word is a word after ! that gives a field its role or its information context; the ! sets it apart from a name the author chooses.

Word Meaning !state A state field. !ctrl A control, chosen with the information of the decision perch. !shck A shock, whose law and timing are declared separately. A shock belongs to no perch: it is drawn on the edge between two perches, and a perch word or a mark [<] or [>] written on a shock is refused under field-perch. !vlu A value field. !arvl, !dcsn, !cntn The arrival, decision and continuation perches of §3.

Removing a word can change the problem: without !ctrl, c is no longer chosen. A parameter needs no word: a name declared with a set on a line of its own, which no block header lists, is a parameter, as β : (0,1) is, and a line of a block that writes it is refused under parameter-or-field.

A name is declared on a line of its own at most once (declared-once), and a role restated in a block header must agree with the first statement (one-name-one-meaning). A set restated in a block header need not equal the first. The field lies in each of the sets written for it, so that they declare their intersection, as several sets in one type do (§9.2), and these sets must have a member in common. The package does not yet check this, except between a block that writes the field and a block that reads it (Appendix C §5.3). The set written by the block that writes a field must also lie in the set written by each block that reads it; where the package can compare the two sets, a field that breaks this is refused under set-mismatch. The package does not yet check this where it cannot compare the two sets, as with [0, ā] written and [0, 1] read, since the endpoint ā names a parameter (Appendix C §5.3).

A word written on a side of a block's header follows the rules for roles: a shock listed as an argument is not thereby observed on that side, and a control listed beside continuation values remains a decision control (Perch tagging rules §2).

Two marks go in a line's annotation, :: [id=value, !node], and a third in the annotation of a named set, :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=1]:

Mark Effect !node Keep the line as a computation of its own, an authored node that a method can address, without changing its equation. !doc Exclude the line from the equations that define the model; it documents them. !categories Give each member of a named integer comprehension a category name (§9.2.2). Write the marker, optionally followed by one shared identifier, and one name=code entry per member.

No mark is a role of a field, and !node and !doc together have no specified meaning. A failed check of the category marker, its entries or its set, the marker on any other item, and a field declared on a set with category codes at one site and on another set at another are refused under category-codes.

Technical details

A category name begins with a letter and continues with letters, digits and _. Its code is decimal digits with an optional sign, read as an integer, so 0, -0 and 00 are one code. An id= entry supplies the declaration's address, and a double-quoted description may accompany the category entries.

Inside the brackets a double-quoted entry keeps its quotes and is read as a description, so ["!categories"] marks nothing, while :: "!categories", written without brackets, is the marker without codes and is refused. Single quotes are characters of the entry, so 'old=1' is the key 'old with the value 1', which a marked annotation refuses, and a single-quoted marker, ['!categories'], marks nothing.

docs.title: 9.4 Brackets
docs.text:
Written Reading V[<], V or V[~], V[>] The field at the arrival, decision or continuation perch (§3). x[1], q[a] Selection from a family, by position counted from one, by a label or by a key declared on the collection's index set; a position is a whole number. L_J := {1, …, J} The integers from the first bound to the second, each bound integer-valued and allowed to depend on parameters. S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ A finite set of integer keys in authored order, with integer membership and distinctness checked at calibration when they depend on parameters. δ : L_J → ℝ One parameter whose value is a collection with one entry, in ℝ, per member of L_J. (x, y) An ordered tuple. (x, y) : S Two names declared together, read where S is a product with one factor for each name, written out or named, S := ℝ₊ × [0, 1]; each name then lies in its own factor, x in ℝ₊ and y in [0, 1]. Any other S, such as a set that couples the two names, is refused under readable-form; a constraint that couples two controls is written in the feasible set of the maximization statement (Constraints §1). x : ℝ × ℝ One field whose values lie in a product set. 𝑞(x) A declared function applied to an argument.

In a type, (a,b) is an open interval; in an expression it is a tuple. Brackets never declare a function's domain: a function is defined with typed arguments. Equation parsing rules §3 gives the rules for functions and families.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Summary

A type is what a stage file or a methods file writes after a colon, such as ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl in the declaration c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl. Its components are sets, a role word and a perch word, written with @ between them, and several sets in one type declare their intersection. This page lists the objects of a stage with the type that each declaration writes, the role words, the perch words and their marks, the reserved sets, the forms in which a set is written, and the limits of the language on a type. Every table is printed from the package's own tables, so the page states each type as the package reads it.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages §2: declarations and types, with a complete file; Symbol conventions §9: the punctuation of a declaration, the domains and the type words. Formal account — Appendix D of the Bellman calculus: the classification of a field by its perch, its role and its value domain. See also — Refusals: every refusal rule, with the smallest example that breaks it; Rules and their code: the rules of the language beside the functions that check them.

docs.title: 1 What a type is
docs.text:
A declaration is a name, a colon and a type. In c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl the name is c and the type is ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl. A type has up to three kinds of component, written in any order with @ between them.

  • A set states the values that the name may take. Several sets in one type declare their intersection: β : (0,1) @ (0, R^(ρ-1)) declares a discount factor that lies in both intervals.
  • A role word states what the name is in the decision problem: a state, a control, a value or a shock.
  • A perch word states the perch at which the name stands, one of the three information sets of a stage.

A type holds at most one role word and at most one perch word. The components that a declaration writes depend on the object that it declares: a parameter is declared with sets alone, while a field has a set, a role and a perch.

docs.title: 2 The tables
docs.text:
§2.1 lists the objects of a stage. For each object it gives a line that declares it, taken from an application of the repository, the type which that line writes, the class of the record in which the package holds the object once the file is read, and the expression that reads the object from the stage object.

§2.2 to §2.4 list the words of a type: the role words, the perch words with the mark that a name carries for each perch, and the sets that the grammar reserves.

§2.5 lists the forms in which a set is written. The constructor of a form is the name that the abstract grammar of the language gives it (ASDL). Each row gives a declaration that writes the form, the set that the form holds, and the objects in whose type the package reads it.

§2.6 lists the limits of the language on a type. A refusal is the package's answer to a file that it does not read, and it names the rule that the file breaks (Refusals §1). Each row gives a line that breaks the limit and the rule of its refusal.

docs.title: 2.1 Objects of a stage
docs.text:

The expression in the last column is written for the stage that the file states; where the line stands in a methods file, the stage has that methods file read.

The declared set is the set written there, or ℝ where none is written; a definition by cases that writes the branch inf or -inf declares a set that can hold that infinity, as its form decides, as in h : ℝ_{+∞} := if Γ < R then 1/(1 - Γ/R) else inf. native/records.py: Definition stage.par["h"] setting A value that a numerical method reads, such as the number of points of a grid; a methods file declares it, and configure binds its value. n_a : ℕin methods.egm.bl ℕ: a set. native/records.py: Definition stage.settings["n_a"] function A function that the file defines by an expression in its arguments. 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)in perfect_foresight.bl ℝ₊₊ for the argument c: one set for each argument. No set is written for the values of the function. native/records.py: Definition stage.definitions["perfect_foresight:function:𝑢"] operator The operator that a block denotes, called a builder: it takes the functions, or the measures, at one perch to those at another. The package makes one on the states of each side of such a block, here on Xa at arrival and on Xm at decision. native/records.py: Sort stage.builder["arvl", "dcsn"].signature() grid The finite set of points at which a numerical method computes and stores a function. docs.title: 2.2 Role words
docs.text:
A role word follows ! among the components of a type, as in c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl. A field that carries no role word is a state, and the subject of a line that states a law with ~ is a shock. A multiplier takes no role word: a line inside a block declares it together with its clause, as μ[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0 does (Constraints §4.2).

role word state !state control !ctrl value !vlu shock !shck multiplier —

docs.title: 2.3 Perch words and marks
docs.text:
A perch word follows ! after a side of a block header, as in (k : Xa) : !arvl. A mark is written directly after a name and states the perch of that one field. A name at the decision perch is written without a mark, and V[~] is read as V.

perch word mark on a name arrival !arvl V[<] decision !dcsn none: V continuation !cntn V[>]

docs.title: 2.4 Reserved sets
docs.text:
The grammar reserves these names, and a file writes one without defining it. Symbol conventions §9.2 says what each set holds.

set also written kind of number interval ℝ — real (-inf, inf) ℝ₊ R_{+}, R+ real [0, inf) ℝ₊₊ R_{++}, R++ real (0, inf) ℤ — integer — ℕ — integer — ℝ̄ — extended real — ℝ_{+∞} — extended real — ℝ_{-∞} — extended real — ℝ_{±∞} — extended real —

docs.title: 2.5 Forms of a set expression
docs.text:
The last column names the objects of §2.1 in whose type the package reads the form. A field is taken there as a block header lists it, and §2.6 states what a declaration on a line of its own reads.

constructor written what it holds read in the type of Named R : ℝ₊₊ The set of that name: a reserved set of the language, here the strictly positive real numbers, or a set that the file defines after :=, Xa := ℝ₊. every object that is declared with a set Interval ρ : (1, inf) The real numbers between two endpoints, where a round bracket leaves its endpoint out and a square bracket includes it; an endpoint may read parameters, and -inf or inf leaves a side unbounded; an endpoint that is the bare name of a parameter or of a derived parameter which the calibration values at an infinity is read as that infinity. every object that is declared with a set FiniteSet d : {work, retire} The labels listed, which carry no arithmetic. field, shock, parameter, setting and function Product x : ℝ × ℝ The ordered tuples that take one component from each factor. field, shock, parameter, setting and function Comprehension θ : ℤ @ [1, inf) The members of one set that satisfy every condition stated, here the integers of at least one; several sets in one type are kept in this form, and a named set writes it with braces after :=, H := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1}. shock, parameter, derived parameter and setting IntegerRange j : {1, …, 5} Every integer from the first bound to the second, both included; a bound may read parameters, and ... is a second spelling of …. every object that is declared with a set Points s : {0, 1} The integers listed, in the order written; a list in which a member reads a parameter names the set its members lie in, {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ. every object that is declared with a set Functions δ : {1, …, 5} → ℝ The collections that hold one entry of the second set for each member of the first, which is a finite index set. field, shock, parameter, setting and function SetUnion ρ : (0,1) \/ (1, inf) The numbers that lie in at least one of the sets; ∪ is a second spelling of \/. parameter, derived parameter and setting SetDifference ρ : ℝ₊₊ \ {1} The numbers of the first set that the second does not hold; ∖ is a second spelling of \. parameter, derived parameter and setting

docs.title: 2.6 Limits on a type
docs.text:
The package refuses each line below, in a stage file that holds no other declaration, under the rule beside it.

limit a line that breaks it refusal Several sets in one type are one set of numbers and the intervals that bound it, so at most one of them is written otherwise than as an interval; a named set counts as such a set. θ : ℤ @ ℝ₊₊ syntax The several sets of one type have a number in common, which the package decides from the endpoints that are numbers or ratios of two integers, 1/3. β : (0,1) @ (2,3) syntax Several sets in one type restrict one declared name, and no declaration of several names carries them. (w, c) : ℝ @ (0, 1) syntax Several sets are read on a declaration that stands on a line of its own; a field listed on a block header and an argument of a function carry one set each. 𝑓(x : ℝ₊ @ (0, 1)) := x^2 readable-form A union and a difference are formed among sets of numbers; a set of labels, a product and a set of functions are no members of one. β : {a, b} \/ (0, 1) syntax A union and a difference are read in the set of a parameter, of a derived parameter and of a setting; the set of a field, of a shock and of an argument of a function holds neither. c : ℝ₊₊ \ {1} @ !ctrl readable-form The value of a named set, written after :=, is no union and no difference. Xρ := (0,1) \/ (1, inf) syntax The value of a named set holds no union and no difference inside it either, such as the set of the entries of a collection. Xq := {1, …, 2} → ℝ \ {0} readable-form A definition that declares a set reads at least one name; a value that reads none is a number, which the calibration supplies. ρ : ℝ := 2 readable-form A conditional, if … then … else …, stands as the whole right side of a definition without arguments or as a branch of another conditional, and inside no formula, no function's body, no line of a block and no endpoint of a set. x : (0, if 1 < 2 then 1 else 2) syntax In a derived parameter's definition inf and -inf stand only as a whole branch of a definition by cases; a definition that reads a name valued at an infinity where it is evaluated, in a formula, a call or a test, as the branch that its test chooses or as its whole right side, has no value at that calibration, and neither has a bound of a declared set that computes with such a name; a bound that computes with the written inf, (0, 2*inf), has none at any calibration; a bound that calls a function other than log, exp, min and max is not decided, whatever it computes with. x := 2*inf derived-parameter The words if, then and else are words of the language and no names. if : ℝ₊₊ syntax A branch written inf or -inf stands in a definition whose declared set can hold that infinity, and the set ℝ of a definition that declares none holds neither. h := if 1 < 2 then 1 else inf derived-parameter

docs.title: Asva
docs.text:
Summary

Asva is the numerical toolkit beside bellman. It builds two numerical steps of backward builders from functions the reader writes: the endogenous grid step, which it also builds from the records of a stage's kernels, and the step that evaluates functions known on a grid of decision states at the points of an arrival grid, through the transition from arrival to decision. It also replaces missing and infinite entries of value and policy arrays, and its runner repeats a computation over the variants of a model, saves solutions, computes moments of simulated data and estimates parameters, in one process or in several. Its functions take arrays, functions, dictionaries and those records, and import nothing of bellman: the structure of a model, its stages, periods, trellis and inter-period connectors, is defined in bellman, and asva holds none of it.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The Bellman factory: the recipe and the specified trellis, the runner's tests holding the fills of a recipe's slots; A builder §5: the record of a builder's kernels, from which egm builds the endogenous grid step. Used by — Numerical steps, The runner, Parameter sweeps, Saving solutions, Estimation and The cross-entropy method: the reference pages of the package. See also — Handler: the routine a methods file names for a method.

Key terminology Term Meaning Perch One of the three information sets within a stage: arrival, when the stage begins; decision, when the choice is made; continuation, after the choice (wiki). Handler The routine a methods file names for a method, written package:function, such as asva:make_egm_1d (wiki). Record of a builder's kernels What a builder's kernels() answers: for each of the builder's operations, in the order they apply, its printed kernel and the wires it reads and writes, and, where its kernel is an explicit function, its compiled function with the names of its arguments and outputs, or, for a row that states a relation its output satisfies, such as the identification of a policy block, its printed relation; the parameters' names and values; the declared sets; and, once the settings are bound, the grid of each place within the builder that types one, constructed at their values; with no reference to the stage (A builder §5). Endogenous grid method The method that computes the optimal choice at each point of a grid of the continuation state by inverting the Euler equation, and then the decision state at which that choice is made (Carroll 2006). Upper envelope Where the continuation value is not concave, the Euler equation has several solutions at some decision states; the upper envelope keeps, at each such state, the solution with the highest value. Registry and recipe A registry is the folder that holds a model's stage files and the files of their calibration, settings and methods; a recipe, a file such as spec.yml, lists for each stage the files from which its calibration, settings and methods are read (wiki). Slot and fill A slot is a $name in a recipe's list of files; a fill is the dictionary bound to it by the keyword of the same name (wiki). Test One variant of a model in a run: the fills of a recipe's slots, with a label, held as a TestSpec (The runner). Simulated method of moments Estimation that chooses the parameter values whose simulated moments come closest to the moments of the data (Estimation). Cross-entropy method A minimization method that draws candidate parameter values from a distribution and refits the distribution to the best of them (The cross-entropy method). MPI The Message Passing Interface, the standard for running one program as several processes that exchange data; Python uses it through the package mpi4py.

docs.title: 1 Installing and importing
docs.text: From the root of the repository, pip install -e packages/asva installs the package into the active environment. Each module is imported by its name, for instance from asva.egm_1d import make_egm_1d or from asva.run.sweep import sweep. The functions of asva.run.mpi use the package mpi4py when it is installed and run in one process when it is not; pip install -e "packages/asva[mpi]" installs asva together with mpi4py.

docs.title: 2 The modules
docs.text: Module Holds Page asva.egm_1d make_egm_1d and make_egm, the endogenous grid step on a grid of one dimension and of K dimensions; egm, the one-dimensional step built from the records of a stage's kernels Numerical steps §2, §3, §6 asva.compose_interp make_compose_interp, the step that evaluates functions known on a grid of decision states at the points of an arrival grid Numerical steps §4 asva.numerics clamp_value, clamp_policy and clamp_scalar Numerical steps §5 asva.simulate the forward simulator §4 asva.run.types, asva.run.make_test TestSpec, SimSpec, RunSpec and make_test The runner asva.run.sweep, asva.run.metrics, asva.run.mpi param_grid, sweep and SweepResult; the tables; the functions of MPI Parameter sweeps asva.run.io save_solution and load_solution Saving solutions asva.run.moments, asva.run.estimate the moment functions; the criterion, estimate and diagnostics Estimation, The cross-entropy method

docs.title: 3 Asva and bellman
docs.text:
A methods file may name an asva function as the handler of a method. The retirement-choice application attaches the endogenous grid method to the consumption stages of its retiree and its worker by entries such as the worker's, written in the bracket of the block policy of its methods file applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/worker_cons/methods.bl, an addition to the stage file: the method !egm, its grid of savings, one factor keyed by the coordinate b with the bounds and the count as settings, and the handler, the asva function named as a quoted string (Methodization):

[id=policy, method : !egm | grid : !Cartesian(b=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) | handler : "asva:make_egm_1d"
    | upper_env.method : !FUES(m_bar=m_bar) | upper_env.handler : "dcsmm:EGM_UE"] {
    c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{b}V[>])                 :: [id=InvEuler]
    w[>] = b + c[>]                            :: [id=endoggrid]
    v[>] = 𝑢(c[>]) + β*V[>]                    :: [id=cand_value]
    c    = upper_env(w[>], c[>], v[>])          :: [id=envelope]
}

bellman keeps the method on the policy builder, policy, whose lines the block of the methods file writes (the method type !egm), and records the handler's name with it; it neither imports the function nor calls it. The reader's own code builds the step and applies it: from the specified stage it computes the arrays and the functions that make_egm_1d or another asva function takes, or it passes the records of the stage's kernels to egm (Numerical steps §6).

A test of the runner holds fills keyed by slot name, and these are the keyword arguments of load_recipe and assemble_trellis of bellman.trellis, so that one test selects one variant of the model that a registry's recipe describes (The runner §2).

docs.title: 4 Simulation
docs.text: This release of asva does not simulate. The module asva.simulate is installed with the package, and its two functions that simulate a population of agents, simulate over the periods and simulate_period over the stages of one period, raise an error when they are called. The simulated panels that an estimation needs are therefore computed by the reader's own code (Estimation §1).

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Carroll, C. D. (2006). "The method of endogenous gridpoints for solving dynamic stochastic optimization problems." Economics Letters 91(3), 312–320.

docs.title: Numerical steps
docs.text:
Summary

make_egm_1d builds the step of the endogenous grid method on a one-dimensional grid of the continuation state from four functions of numbers that the reader writes, and make_egm builds the same step on a grid of K dimensions. make_compose_interp builds the step that evaluates arrays known on a grid of decision states at the decision states \(g(x)\) of the points \(x\) of an arrival grid, with the transition \(g\) and the interpolation supplied by the reader. The three functions of asva.numerics replace missing and infinite entries of value and policy arrays. egm builds the one-dimensional step from the records of a stage's kernels, the two grids supplied by the caller, and passes the parameter values at each call. make_egm_1d, make_egm, make_compose_interp and egm each return a function, and none of the functions on this page reads a stage.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Operators and builders: the backward builders whose numerical steps these functions compute. Builds on — Perch: the arrival, decision and continuation perches that the names of the arguments refer to. See also — Constraints §4: the inverse Euler statement of a stage file, which the endogenous grid method reads.

docs.title: 1 The names of the arguments
docs.text: The suffix of an argument's name gives the perch at which its quantity stands: _arvl the arrival perch, _dcsn the decision perch and _cntn the continuation perch (perch). v is a value, dv a marginal value, ddv the second derivative of the value, c a control and x the state coordinate of a grid; the suffix _i marks the entry at one grid point. The suffix _hat marks a result of the endogenous grid step before an upper envelope: where the continuation value is not concave, the Euler equation has several solutions at some decision states, and the upper envelope keeps, at each such state, the solution with the highest value. fixed_state is a state held constant during the step, such as the housing stock of a household that keeps its house, and is 0.0 when there is none.

docs.title: 2 The one-dimensional step
docs.text:
The endogenous grid method (Carroll 2006) computes, at each point of a grid of the continuation state, the control from the marginal continuation value there, and then the decision state from which that control leads to the point. make_egm_1d builds this step from four functions:

make_egm_1d(fn_inv_euler, fn_bellman_rhs, fn_cntn_to_dcsn, fn_concavity)

The four arguments are functions of numbers compiled with numba.njit, the decorator of the Numba package that compiles a Python function to machine code. Each holds the model's parameters as constants: Numba reads their values when it compiles the function, at the step's first call, so a model with other parameter values needs its own four functions and its own step.

Argument Called at grid point i as Returns fn_inv_euler fn_inv_euler(dv_cntn_i, fixed_state) the control, from the marginal continuation value: the inverse Euler equation fn_bellman_rhs fn_bellman_rhs(c_i, v_cntn_i, fixed_state) the value at the decision perch fn_cntn_to_dcsn fn_cntn_to_dcsn(c_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state) the decision state from which the control leads to the continuation state x_cntn_i: the point of the endogenous grid fn_concavity fn_concavity(c_i, ddv_cntn_i, fixed_state) a number that an upper-envelope step reads, such as the derivative of the continuation state with respect to the decision state

The call returns the step, a function that Numba compiles at its first call:

egm_step(dv_cntn, ddv_cntn, v_cntn, x_cntn, fixed_state)

Its first four arguments are one-dimensional arrays of one length: the marginal continuation value, its derivative and the continuation value at the points of the continuation grid x_cntn, and the grid itself. At each point the step calls the four functions in the order of the table, and it returns four arrays of the same length: the controls c_hat, the values v_hat, the endogenous grid x_dcsn_hat and the results of fn_concavity, del_a. The grid is an argument of the step, so one step computes on grids of every length without being compiled again. A function that Numba has not compiled is refused at the step's first call, with Numba's TypingError.

The example is one step of a consumption–savings problem at the decision perch: cash on hand \(m\), consumption \(c\) and savings \(a = m - c\), the utility \(u(c) = c^{1-\rho}/(1-\rho)\) with \(\rho = 2\), and the continuation value \(V_\succ(a) = -1/(1+a)\) on a grid of savings. The first-order condition \(u'(c) = V_\succ'(a)\) gives \(c = V_\succ'(a)^{-1/\rho} = 1 + a\); the point of the endogenous grid is \(m = a + c = 1 + 2a\); the value is \(u(c) + V_\succ(a) = -2/(1 + a)\); and the derivative of savings with respect to cash on hand, \(u''(c)/(u''(c) + V_\succ''(a))\), is one half at every point. The listing passes \(V_\succ'\), \(V_\succ''\) and \(V_\succ\) at the savings grid as the step's arguments dv_cntn, ddv_cntn and v_cntn, and names the endogenous grid, which is in cash on hand, m_hat.

import numpy as np
from numba import njit
from asva.egm_1d import make_egm_1d

ρ = 2.0

@njit
def inv_euler(dv_cntn, fixed_state):
    return dv_cntn ** (-1.0 / ρ)

@njit
def bellman_rhs(c, v_cntn, fixed_state):
    return c ** (1.0 - ρ) / (1.0 - ρ) + v_cntn

@njit
def cntn_to_dcsn(c, a, fixed_state):
    return a + c

@njit
def savings_slope(c, ddv_cntn, fixed_state):
    ddu = -ρ * c ** (-ρ - 1.0)
    return ddu / (ddu + ddv_cntn)

egm_step = make_egm_1d(inv_euler, bellman_rhs, cntn_to_dcsn, savings_slope)

a = np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0])
c_hat, v_hat, m_hat, del_a = egm_step((1 + a) ** -2, -2 * (1 + a) ** -3, -1 / (1 + a), a, 0.0)
print(c_hat, m_hat, v_hat.round(4), del_a)

[1.  1.5 2.  3. ] [1. 2. 3. 5.] [-2.     -1.3333 -1.     -0.6667] [0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5]

docs.title: 3 The step on K dimensions
docs.text:
make_egm(fn_inv_euler, fn_bellman_rhs, fn_cntn_to_dcsn, fn_concavity, params, n_dims, n_controls)

make_egm builds the same step on a grid of K = n_dims dimensions with n_controls controls. params is an array of the model's parameters, held by the step and passed to each function at every point. The four functions, compiled with numba.njit, also receive the grid point, since a coordinate of the grid may enter the utility, and they return what the table states:

Argument Called at grid point i as Returns fn_inv_euler fn_inv_euler(dv_cntn_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the controls, an array of length n_controls fn_bellman_rhs fn_bellman_rhs(c_i, v_cntn_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the value at the decision perch, a number fn_cntn_to_dcsn fn_cntn_to_dcsn(c_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the point of the endogenous grid, an array of length K fn_concavity fn_concavity(c_i, ddv_cntn_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the numbers an upper-envelope step reads, an array of length K

dv_cntn_i is the gradient of the continuation value at the point and ddv_cntn_i the diagonal of its matrix of second derivatives. The step is called as the one-dimensional step is, egm_step(dv_cntn, ddv_cntn, v_cntn, x_cntn, fixed_state), with arrays of these shapes for N grid points:

Array Shape dv_cntn, ddv_cntn, x_cntn (N, K) v_cntn (N,) the returned controls c_hat (N, n_controls) the returned values v_hat (N,) the returned x_dcsn_hat and del_a (N, K)

A coordinate that the decision leaves unchanged, such as the housing stock of a household that keeps its house, is returned unchanged by fn_cntn_to_dcsn, and fn_concavity may return 0.0 for it. The step constructs no grid: where the decision acts on fewer states than the continuation state holds, the grid lies on a set of lower dimension within the continuation states, and the reader constructs it before the call.

docs.title: 4 Composing with the arrival transition
docs.text:
make_compose_interp(g_transition, interp_fn)

g_transition(x_arvl, params) returns the decision states \(g(x)\) of an array of arrival states \(x\), params being an array of the model's parameters. interp_fn(xp, y_1, …, y_k, x) interpolates k arrays given at the points xp at the points x, both sorted in increasing order, and returns the k results as a tuple. The call returns the function

compose(x_dcsn_src, y_1, ..., y_k, x_arvl, params)

which computes the targets g_transition(x_arvl, params) and returns interp_fn(x_dcsn_src, y_1, …, y_k, targets): the arrays y_1 to y_k, given at the decision states x_dcsn_src, evaluated at the decision states \(g(x)\) of the points \(x\) of the arrival grid. For a transition \(g\) without a shock this is the pullback of each decision-perch function \(f\) along the transition, the composition \(f \circ g\), which is what the backward builder from the decision perch to the arrival perch computes. The step computes no expectation: with a shock in the transition, the reader integrates over it. The first argument is the grid of decision states, the last two are the arrival grid and the parameter array, and every argument between them is an array to interpolate. compose is a Python function, and the two functions given to make_compose_interp, g_transition and interp_fn, may be Python functions or functions compiled by Numba. Asva supplies no interpolation function; linear interpolation by numpy.interp is one the reader may pass.

The example continues §2. The arrival state is the assets \(k\) held before an income \(y\), so that cash on hand is \(m = Rk + y\), here with \(R = 1\) and \(y = 1\):

from asva.compose_interp import make_compose_interp

def arrival_to_decision(k, params):
    R, y = params
    return R * k + y

def interp_two(xp, y1, y2, x):
    return np.interp(x, xp, y1), np.interp(x, xp, y2)

compose = make_compose_interp(arrival_to_decision, interp_two)
k = np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0])
c_arvl, v_arvl = compose(m_hat, c_hat, v_hat, k, np.array([1.0, 1.0]))
print(c_arvl, v_arvl.round(4))

[1.   1.25 1.5  2.  ] [-2.     -1.6667 -1.3333 -1.    ]

Consumption, \((m + 1)/2\), is linear in cash on hand, so its interpolated values are exact. The value, \(-4/(m + 1)\), is not, and linear interpolation gives −1.6667 at \(m = 1.5\), where the value is −1.6.

docs.title: 5 Clamping values and policies
docs.text:
Function Returns clamp_value(arr, nan_val=-1e10) a copy of arr with every entry that is NaN or infinite, of either sign, replaced by nan_val, so that a state whose value is missing is never chosen clamp_policy(arr, min_val, max_val) a copy of arr with NaN replaced by min_val, the entries below min_val by min_val, and the entries above max_val, infinity included, by max_val clamp_scalar(val, min_val, max_val, nan_replacement) one number: nan_replacement for NaN, max_val for infinity, min_val for minus infinity, and otherwise val clipped to the interval from min_val to max_val

The three are compiled with numba.njit, so compiled functions may call them; the first two take one-dimensional arrays of floating-point numbers and leave them unchanged.

from asva.numerics import clamp_value, clamp_policy

print(clamp_value(np.array([1.0, np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf])))
print(clamp_policy(np.array([np.nan, -1.0, 0.5, 2.0, np.inf]), 0.0, 1.0))

[ 1.e+00 -1.e+10 -1.e+10 -1.e+10]
[0.  0.  0.5 1.  1. ]

docs.title: 6 The step from the records of a stage's kernels
docs.text:
egm builds the one-dimensional step of §2 from the records that the package bellman answers for a consumption stage, with no stage in hand:

step = egm(policy, decision, savings, evaluation)

policy and decision are the records stage.dcsn.builder.policy.kernels() and stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.kernels() (A builder §5): for each piece of the builder, its compiled function with the names of its arguments and outputs, and the parameters' names and bound values. egm reads from policy the inverse Euler equation and the endogenous grid, and from decision the law of motion and the aggregation, and refuses any other record. savings is the grid of the continuation state and evaluation the grid of the decision state, both read by the caller from the stage's methods and settings: the exogenous grid of savings, which the grid entry of the policy builder states, policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), and the grid of the decision state, which the grid entry of the decision builder's Evaluation states, as cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m)) does in the consumption stage of the portfolio application. Each entry gives the grid's kind, !Cartesian, and for each coordinate its bounds and its number of points as names of settings, whose values the stage's settings file binds (Methodization §3.2). The step returned, step(value, marginal), takes the continuation value and its derivative as functions of the continuation state and returns the arrays of one endogenous grid step, EndogenousGridStep: the control, the continuation state, the value and the marginal value on the evaluation grid, and the endogenous grid with its control and value on the savings grid. The three functions the step applies are compiled once for their text, and the parameter values are passed at each call, so a new calibration needs no compilation. The lesson tutorials/topics/kernels.ipynb of the repository shows the records the step is built from.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Carroll, C. D. (2006). "The method of endogenous gridpoints for solving dynamic stochastic optimization problems." Economics Letters 91(3), 312–320.

docs.title: The runner
docs.text:
Summary

The runner, asva.run, is used from Python. The variants of a model in a run are its tests: a test is a TestSpec, which holds a bundle, the dictionary from the names of a recipe's slots to the fills bound to them, and a label; make_test turns a list of bundles into tests. The slots of a test are the keyword arguments of load_recipe and assemble_trellis of bellman.trellis, so a test selects one variant of the model a recipe describes. RunSpec records a run for the reader's script. The reader's own function turns a test into a result, and the other modules of the runner repeat that function over the tests, tabulate, save and estimate.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Recipe functions: slots, fills, load_recipe and assemble_trellis. Used by — Parameter sweeps: the tests as the points of a sweep. See also — Asva §2: the modules of the package.
