    Carroll, C. D. (1997). Buffer-stock saving and the life cycle/permanent income hypothesis. Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(1), 1–55. ↩

  2. Bellman, R. (1957). Dynamic Programming. Princeton University Press.

    Stokey, N. L. and Lucas, R. E., with E. C. Prescott (1989). Recursive Methods in Economic Dynamics. Harvard University Press, §4.2, Theorem 4.6, p. 79, and §9.2, Theorem 9.6, p. 263. ↩

  3. Stoy, J. E. (1977). Denotational Semantics: The Scott-Strachey Approach to Programming Language Theory. MIT Press, §1.1, pp. 5–7, on referential transparency and substitution. ↩

docs.title: Stages and perches
docs.text:
Summary

A stage specifies a decision episode with arrival, decision, and continuation information. We define its transitions, feasible actions, and value evaluation, then distinguish the backward recursion from the forward propagation of distributions. State sufficiency and the required conditional shock laws are assumptions of the representation.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Illustrative example gives the consumption–savings factorization. Used by — Fields, functions and types develops the fields and functions at each perch; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C states the representation and binding conditions for written equations; Stages and Field equations give the .bl syntax of the stage defined here.

The illustrative example separates the optimizing decision builder \(\mathbb T_\succ\) from the fixed-policy builder \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\). With arrival builder \(\mathbb T_\prec\), their stage compositions are \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\) and \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\). A builder is the operator of one edge of the stage, or one of the two operators that are the image of no edge, the policy builder and the optimizing decision builder (Kinds and sorts §6): a backward builder specifies how a value function at one perch determines a value function at an earlier perch, and a forward builder how a measure at one perch determines a measure at the next. Kinds and sorts §6 derives the builders \(\mathbb T_\prec\) and \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\), and the forward builders of §1.2 below, as the images of the transitions of a stage under its models, where a transition is a law of motion with its shock law.

Section 1 defines the stage's mathematical data and the inputs and outputs of its operators; §2 defines the operators, and §3 states their information requirements. Authored stage declarations and equations use the .bl stage syntax of Bellman-SYM. The mathematical tuple below describes their interpretation at one calibration at which the stage is well posed (Kinds and sorts §§4 and 6), not a second source file or a retained parsing object.

docs.title: 1.1 Basic setup of the symbolic stage
docs.text:
The setup below fixes the mathematical data used in this representation. A stage is a tuple

\[ \bigl(\; \mathsf{X}_\prec,\ \mathsf{X}_\sim,\ \mathsf{X}_\succ;\quad \mathsf{A},\ \Gamma;\quad (\mathsf{Z}_\zeta, \mu_\zeta),\ (\mathsf{Z}_\eta, \mu_\eta);\quad g_{\prec},\ g_{\succ};\quad G_{\prec},\ G_{\succ} \;\bigr), \]

of eleven primitive objects, counting each shock pair as one entry:

  • three state spaces \(\mathsf{X}_\prec, \mathsf{X}_\sim, \mathsf{X}_\succ\), one at each of three indices that we call perches (arrival, decision, continuation);
  • an action space \(\mathsf{A}\) with a feasibility correspondence \(\Gamma : \mathsf{X}_\sim \rightrightarrows \mathsf{A}\) that pins down which choices are admissible at each decision state;
  • two shock pairs \((\mathsf{Z}_\zeta, \mu_\zeta)\), \((\mathsf{Z}_\eta, \mu_\eta)\), each a measurable shock space with a declared probability law, pre-decision (\(\zeta\)) and post-decision (\(\eta\)), describing within-stage randomness;
  • two forward transition maps \(g_\prec : \mathsf{X}_\prec \times \mathsf{Z}_\zeta \to \mathsf{X}_\sim\) and \(g_\succ : \operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma) \times \mathsf{Z}_\eta \to \mathsf{X}_\succ\), the first determining the decision state and the second the continuation state. Each jointly measurable transition map, together with its shock law, induces a probability kernel, indexed by an arrival state on the first edge and a feasible state–action pair on the second;

  • two pointwise aggregators \(G_\prec, G_\succ\). Writing \(\mathsf{L}\) for the value line in which rewards and values take their values — the extended reals \(\bar{\mathbb{R}}\) by default, declarable as the reals \(\mathbb{R}\) (\(\S 1.2\)) — and \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma) := \{(x, a) \in \mathsf{X}_\sim \times \mathsf{A} : a \in \Gamma(x)\}\) for the graph of the feasibility correspondence, each is a point-level (jointly measurable) map acting on a value variable, not a value function,

    \[ G_\succ : \mathsf{L} \times \operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma) \times \mathsf{Z}_\eta \to \mathsf{L}, \qquad G_\prec : \mathsf{L} \times \mathsf{X}_\prec \times \mathsf{Z}_\zeta \to \mathsf{L}. \]

    \(G_\succ(w, x, a, \eta)\) aggregates a continuation-value scalar \(w\) with the decision pair \((x, a)\) and the realized post-decision shock \(\eta\) — in the expected-utility case it contains a specified reward and discount (note below) — and \(G_\prec(w, x_\prec, \zeta)\) does the same on the arrival edge, the identity in \(w\) when that edge has no reward. The backward operators these kernels generate — read on value fields and on value functions — are assembled in \(\S 2\).

We use standard Borel state, action, and shock spaces: measurable spaces equivalent to Borel subsets of complete separable metric spaces, including real domains and finite products. The displayed fixed laws describe shocks independent of information at their source perch. This is a specialization used below, not a requirement of the Bellman calculus. More generally, replace them by specified probability kernels \(\mu_\zeta(\mathrm dz\mid x_\prec)\) and \(\mu_\eta(\mathrm dz\mid x,a)\) on every required source state and feasible state–action pair, retaining their conditioning arguments in every integral. A marginal law alone does not assert independence.

The backward kernel and preferences

In expected utility, \(G_\succ(w,x,a,\eta)=r(x,a,\eta)+\beta w\), where \(r\) is the one-stage reward and \(0<\beta<1\) is the discount factor. State- or action-dependent discounting can instead be declared explicitly. These maps are affine in \(w\): they add a reward to a linear continuation term. Integrating them yields an affine policy-evaluation operator, not the undiscounted Markov expectation operator.

Nonlinear preferences are written with each map placed where it belongs relative to the shock integral. A statement may apply one pointwise map inside the integral and another outside it, and an Epstein–Zin certainty equivalent, whose normalization sits outside the integral, is the case with both maps nonlinear; §2.3a gives the general form. The aggregator entry of the tuple for an edge is read as that pair of maps, the outer map being the identity in the form of §2.2. #todo resolved 12 September 2026: the extension is §2.3a.

docs.title: 1.1.1 What the perches do
docs.text:
A stage constitutes one self-contained decision episode, and its perches can be viewed as the decision maker's vantage points, ordered by how much the agent knows:

  • arrival (\(\prec\)) — entry to the stage, before any within-stage shock or decision;
  • decision (\(\cdot\)) — the point of choice, after the pre-decision shock has been observed and the arrival-to-decision transition \(g_\prec\) has occurred
  • continuation (\(\succ\)) — exit from the stage, after the action, any post-decision shock and the decision-to-continuation transition \(g_\succ\) has occurred.

Operationally, the sequence of events in the stage runs as follows. Given an initial arrival state \(x_{\prec}\), the agent draws an observable shock \(z_{\zeta} \in \mathsf{Z}_{\zeta}\), and the state transitions to the decision state \(x_{\sim} = g_{\prec}(x_{\prec}, z_{\zeta})\). Given a value function \(v_\succ\), the agent then selects a feasible action \(a \in \Gamma(x_{\sim})\) by applying some criterion to the decision-perch value the backward kernel \(G_\succ\) returns — the continuation value carried back to the decision perch, with the post-decision shock integrated out (\(\S 2\)). Once the action is taken and the unobserved shock is realized, the state transitions to \(x_{\succ} = g_{\succ}(x_{\sim}, a, z_{\eta})\).

Which shocks are present pins down the stage's timing, and there are four possible cases:

Case pre-decision \(\zeta\) post-decision \(\eta\) reading pre-decision only present — observe the shock, then a deterministic choice-to-exit move (the buffer-stock case) post-decision only — present choose first, then the shock resolves both present present the general stage deterministic — — pure optimization, no risk

The buffer-stock stage, as a tuple

The following state spaces, action space, shock laws, transitions, and backward kernels specify the buffer-stock stage.

  • States. \(\mathsf{X}_\prec = \mathbb{R}_{+}\) (arrival assets \(k\)), \(\mathsf{X}_\sim = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) (market resources \(m\)), \(\mathsf{X}_\succ = \mathbb{R}_{+}\) (end-of-period assets \(a\)).
  • Action and feasibility. \(\mathsf{A} = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) (consumption \(c\)), with \(\Gamma(m) = \{\, c \in \mathsf{A} : c \le m \,\} = (0, m]\).
  • Shock pairs. The pre-decision pair has \(\mathsf{Z}_\zeta \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{++}\) and \(\mu_\zeta\) the law of the labor-income draw \(y\); the post-decision space \(\mathsf{Z}_\eta\) is a one-point space (no post-decision shock).
  • Transitions. \(g_\prec(k, y) = R\,k + y\); \(g_\succ(m, c) = m - c\), deterministic because its shock slot is trivial, so its derived kernel is a point mass.
  • Backward kernels. \(G_\succ(w, m, c) = u(c) + \beta\, w\) — the expected-utility (affine) kernel of the note above, with nothing integrated since the post-decision edge is deterministic — and \(G_\prec(w, k, y) = w\), the identity kernel whose operator integrates the income draw over \(\mu_\zeta\).

The sequence of events: arrive holding \(k\); observe \(y\); have decision state \(m = g_\prec(k, y) = R\,k + y\); choose \(c \in \Gamma(m)\); exit with the continuation state \(a = g_\succ(m, c) = m - c\), which the next stage receives as its arrival state. This is the pre-decision-only case of the table above.

Relationship to standard MDP

A standard Markov decision process describes the next-state distribution with a single kernel \(\mathrm{P}(\cdot \mid x, a)\), resolved after the choice, with value

\[ v(x) = \sup_{a \in \Gamma(x)}\bigl\{r(x, a) + \beta\, \mathbb{E}[v(x') \mid x, a]\bigr\} \]

A stage makes the timing within an episode explicit. Its decision state includes information observed before choice, and its continuation state follows the action and any post-decision shock. The buffer-stock example has no post-decision shock within the chosen stage, but the next arrival expectation appears in the continuation function. Under a fixed policy the two transition maps compose into one state-transition kernel. The optimizing recursion additionally retains the order in which information is observed and choices are made.

The fully observed Markov decision process interpretation requires the chosen state to determine the relevant payoffs and conditional transition laws. Declaring a decision state does not prove that sufficiency. An observed variable that changes a future shock law must be retained or represented by another sufficient statistic. A partially observed model may instead use a belief state, a conditional distribution over the hidden state, if that state is sufficient. Neither case implies that the current state reconstructs every historical observation (§3).

Two devices make this timing visible. The perch indices name arrival, decision and continuation as the nested filtration of \(\S 3\); and because the pre-decision shock is observed before the action, the choice falls on a state already carrying the within-period information, with the continuation perch the post-decision state of approximate dynamic programming when the post-decision shock is trivial (Powell 2011). #check-details

docs.title: 1.2 Wiring the stage
docs.text:
The Bellman calculus stage records compositions through the inputs and outputs of its operators. Kinds and sorts §6 collects them in the operator signature of the stage, whose sorts name the spaces of value functions and of measures defined below and the set of policies, and whose symbols are the builders. First, note that intuitively, to use the stage to solve, we read it as an operator: hand it a continuation value, and it returns an arrival value,

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\pi}\;\colon\; v_\succ \longmapsto v_\prec, \]

a continuation value in, arrival value out contract that does not refer to the stage's internals nor any of the details of the syntactic declarations. The stages represented here have this input–output form; what changes between applications is the state space at each perch, the form of the transitions and their shock distributions, the feasibility correspondence, and the methods used to realize the builders.

Backward spaces and wiring For each perch \(m \in \{\prec, \sim, \succ\}\) we now add one additional space: the value functions at perch \(m\), simply written \(\mathsf{V}_m\). We can think of these as the space of \(\mathsf{L}\)-valued functions on \(\mathsf{X}_m\), so that evaluating a value function at a state, \(v(x) \in \mathsf{L}\), is ordinary function application. The chosen function domains must make the declared operations well-defined and closed under their compositions. Boundedness, continuity, integrability, and equivalence-class conventions are additional mathematical choices, not consequences of the declared set of a value field. The backward builders are named operations between these spaces,

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\succ,\pi} \;\colon\; \mathsf{V}_\succ \to \mathsf{V}_\sim, \qquad \mathbb{T}_{\prec} \;\colon\; \mathsf{V}_\sim \to \mathsf{V}_\prec. \]

The subscript \(\pi\) means that the policy is fixed: \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) is one operator for each \(\pi \in \Pi_\Gamma\), and the family \(\pi \mapsto \mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) is a map \(\Pi_\Gamma \to [\mathsf V_\succ \to \mathsf V_\sim]\), which currying, the correspondence between a map of two arguments and a map of the first argument alone whose value is a map of the second, identifies with a map \(\Pi_\Gamma \times \mathsf V_\succ \to \mathsf V_\sim\) in the category of sets, the spaces \(\mathsf V_\succ\) and \(\mathsf V_\sim\) being sets of functions. The policy is therefore not an input in a space of value functions and not an argument of the operator at a policy: it names the member of the family, and the semantic graph records it so, the operator at a policy answering the inputs and outputs of that member and the policy typed where the stage text defines it, on the output of the policy builder (see Operators and builders §6). The optimizing builder has the same input and output spaces but is denoted \(\mathbb T_\succ\), without \(\pi\). Its stage composite is \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\). The undiscounted expectation operators \(P_\prec\), \(P_{\succ,\pi}\), and \(P_\pi\) are defined separately in §2; only these have the plain distribution pairing.

Forward spaces and wiring The forward direction gets the same treatment: adjoin at each perch one further space \(\mathsf{M}_m\), the finite measures over perch-\(m\) states. A finite measure is specified by its integrals: for \(f\) a measurable real-valued function integrable under \(\mu\) on \(\mathsf{X}_m\),

\[ \langle \mu,\, f \rangle_m \;=\; \int_{\mathsf{X}_m} f\; d\mu \;\in\; \bar{\mathbb{R}}, \]

Bounded measurable test functions suffice to identify a finite measure: taking indicators of measurable sets recovers its values on measurable sets. A probability distribution is a finite measure of total mass one. The integral is finite for bounded measurable functions. Nonnegative or one-sided-integrable functions may also be used with extended values, provided that no subsequent expression forms an undefined difference of infinities. Finite collections of simulated states and histograms define empirical or discrete finite measures; normalization makes them probability distributions. Their accuracy as approximations to another measure is a numerical question. #check-details

The forward builders are named operations between these spaces of measures,

\[ \mathbb{M}_\prec \;\colon\; \mathsf{M}_\prec \to \mathsf{M}_\sim, \qquad \mathbb{M}_{\succ,\pi} \;\colon\; \mathsf{M}_\sim \to \mathsf{M}_\succ, \]

the single family letter \(\mathbb{M}\) naming both forward edge push-forwards, with the perch subscript marking the edge. The subscript \(\pi\) on \(\mathbb{M}_{\succ,\pi}\) records a need the transition itself imposes: \(g_\succ(x, a, \eta)\) takes an action argument, and pushing a distribution through it requires a policy function \(\pi\). The arrival push-forward \(\mathbb{M}_\prec\) has no policy argument. As on the backward side, \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) is one push-forward for each \(\pi \in \Pi_\Gamma\), and the family \(\pi \mapsto \mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) is a map \(\Pi_\Gamma \to [\mathsf M_\sim \to \mathsf M_\succ]\); the policy is not an input in a space of measures and not an argument of the push-forward at a policy, and the semantic graph records the push-forward at a policy with the measure it reads and the measure it writes.

docs.title: 1.3 The stage as a graph
docs.text:
A stage has a graph of three perches joined by two edges. Each edge has a forward transition and forward builder, and a backward builder. Section 1.2 specifies the domains and codomains of these builders; §2 defines their operations. The nodes represent information sets rather than individual states, and the graph records which operators can be composed.

Mathematical assumptions determine whether their stated domains and compositions are valid; numerical methods must satisfy the assumptions required by those operators. A changed economic model can require different state spaces or methods. Appendix C gives the mathematical stage representation; methodization attaches the numerical schemes.

One stage: the three perches with forward transitions ($g_\prec$, $g_\succ$) above and backward builders ($\mathbb{T}_{\prec}$, $\mathbb{T}_{\succ,\pi}$) below.

Solid arrows run forward, in the direction agents move (the transitions \(g_\prec\) and \(g_\succ\)); dashed arrows run backward, in the direction value propagates (the builders \(\mathbb{T}_{\prec}\) and \(\mathbb{T}_{\succ,\pi}\)). The next section walks these arrows in turn: first backward, then forward.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical elaboration
docs.text: The input and output spaces in §1.2 distinguish continuation, decision, and arrival functions. We now define their action. A pointwise aggregator \(G\) combines a continuation value with current state, action, and shock arguments. Integrating that expression gives a choice value, and a policy selects an action at each state. The transition, conditional distribution and aggregator at that policy define the fixed-policy builder. A supremum over all feasible actions gives the optimizing decision operator.

docs.title: 2.1 Conditional choice values
docs.text:
A field is a random quantity that a stage declares (Kinds and sorts §5). A field other than a shock is a random variable measurable with respect to the information at its perch, and a shock belongs to no perch. On a probability space \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\), let \(\mathrm X=\mathrm X_\sim\) be a decision state and \(\mathrm A\) a feasible action measurable at decision information \(\mathcal F_\sim\). A continuation field \(V_\succ\) is measurable at continuation information \(\mathcal F_\succ\); this alone does not place it in \(L^2\), the space of square-integrable random variables. If the following local payoff is integrable, its conditional expectation is

\[ \mathrm Q=\mathbb E[G_\succ(\mathrm V_\succ,\mathrm X,\mathrm A,\eta)\mid\mathcal F_\sim]. \]

This defines \(\mathrm Q\) along the specified random state and action, up to almost-sure equality. It does not define payoffs under actions that this trajectory never chooses. The arrival field is defined analogously by \(\mathbb E[G_\prec(V_\sim,X_\prec,\zeta)\mid\mathcal F_\prec]\). These formulas use the argument order declared in §1.1.

docs.title: 2.2 Function representation
docs.text:
Suppose \(\mathrm X_\succ=g_\succ(\mathrm X,\mathrm A,\eta)\) and the continuation field has a specified measurable representative \(\mathrm V_\succ=v_\succ(\mathrm X_\succ)\) almost surely. This representation requires a version of the field measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_\succ)\): a random variable agreeing with the field almost surely. Measurability with respect to \(\mathcal F_\succ\) alone does not ensure such a version. Here \(\sigma(X_\succ)\) denotes the information generated by the state. The state must also determine the conditional shock law and the payoff arguments used below. Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §1.2 and rules R5–R7, states these requirements.

For policy comparisons, specify \(v_\succ\) and the transition and shock law pointwise on their stated domains. For each continuation function in the chosen domain, require the following absolute integral to be finite at every feasible pair. Define the induced choice-value aggregator on every \((x,a)\in\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) by

\[ B_\succ(x,a,v_\succ) :=\int_{\mathsf Z_\eta} G_\succ\bigl(v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr) \,\mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta). \]

Under the fixed conditional law assumed in §1.1 and the integrability conditions above, substituting \((X,A)\) gives

\[ Q=B_\succ(X,A,v_\succ)\quad\text{almost surely}. \]

The first display defines a function on all feasible pairs. The second relates its evaluation to a conditional expectation along one trajectory. An almost-sure field identity by itself fixes a representative only almost everywhere under that trajectory's law; it cannot supply action values at other states or under policies that assign positive probability to previously null sets. This is why the domain and representative choices remain explicit.

docs.title: 2.3 Reward and continuation
docs.text:
When the kernel is affine in the value, \(G_\succ(w, x, a, \eta) = r(x, a, \eta) + \beta\, w\) (expected utility), the induced aggregator splits into an integrated reward and an expectation,

\[ B_\succ(x, a, v_\succ) = \bar{r}(x, a) + \beta\,(P_\succ\,v_\succ)(x, a), \qquad (P_\succ\,v_\succ)(x, a) = \int v_\succ(g_\succ(x, a, \eta))\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm{d}\eta), \]

with \(\bar{r}(x, a) = \int r(x, a, \eta)\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm{d}\eta)\). Here \(P_\succ\) is the Markov expectation operator of the edge — linear, positive, and mass-preserving (\(P_\succ\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\)), the pointwise transition expectation for the pair \((x,a)\). The induced \(B_\succ\) is affine, not linear: the reward sits outside the expectation, and the discounted kernel \(\mathrm{K} = \beta\,P_\succ\) (Stachurski's linear-decision-process form \(B = r + \mathrm{K}\,v\)) is positive linear but mass-preserving only at \(\beta = 1\). Under a fixed measurable feasible policy \(\pi\), define \(P_{\succ,\pi}f(x)=(P_\succ f)(x,\pi(x))\) and \(\bar{r}_\pi(x)=\bar{r}(x,\pi(x))\). The policy-evaluation operator is

\[ \mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}f=\bar{r}_\pi+\beta P_{\succ,\pi}f. \]

It is affine and preserves pointwise order. A nonlinear \(G_\succ\) can give a nonlinear integral aggregator of the displayed form. A recursion whose normalization sits outside the integral is the general form of §2.3a.

docs.title: 2.3a Aggregation inside and outside the integral
docs.text:
A statement of a backward block may apply one pointwise map to the continuation value before the shock is integrated and another to the result afterwards. For one statement with one expectation the choice-value aggregator therefore has the general form of two maps around one integral, $$ B_\succ(x,a,v_\succ) =G^{\mathrm{out}}\succ\Bigl(\int}G^{\mathrm{in}\succ\bigl(v\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta),\,x,\,a\Bigr), $$ where \(G^{\mathrm{in}}_\succ:\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf L\) is the arithmetic written inside the expectation and \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ:\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\to\mathsf L\) the arithmetic written outside it. The display of §2.2 is the case \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(w,x,a)=w\). The expected-utility statement written as a reward plus a discounted expectation, \(u(c)+\beta\,\mathbb E_\eta[v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta))]\), is the case \(G^{\mathrm{in}}_\succ(w,x,a,\eta)=w\) with \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(w,x,a)=u(c)+\beta\,w\). An Epstein–Zin recursion has both maps nonlinear, \(G^{\mathrm{in}}_\succ(w,x,a,\eta)=w^{1-\gamma}\) and \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(w,x,a)=\bigl(u(c)^{1-\rho}+\beta\,w^{(1-\rho)/(1-\gamma)}\bigr)^{1/(1-\rho)}\), and its normalization outside the integral is where \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) sits. A statement with several expectations, or a block split by !node statements into sub-builders, composes further maps and integrals in the order written; the two-map form is what one expectation gives.

The two placements coincide exactly when \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) is affine in \(w\). Then \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) passes through the integral by linearity, under the finite absolute integral required in §2.2, and the two maps collapse to the one kernel of §2.2; §2.3 is this case with \(G^{\mathrm{in}}_\succ\) the identity. When \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) is nonlinear the placement is part of the specification, and the two forms denote different operators.

Integrability is required of the inner integrand, \(\int_{\mathsf Z_\eta}\bigl|G^{\mathrm{in}}_\succ(v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta)\bigr|\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta)<\infty\) on every feasible pair, and \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) must be defined at the resulting values. The induced aggregator preserves pointwise order in \(v_\succ\) when \(G^{\mathrm{in}}_\succ\) and \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) are each nondecreasing in their value argument, which is the monotonicity that a recursive decision process requires of its aggregator (Sargent and Stachurski, Dynamic Programming, volume 2, the definition of a recursive decision process). The arrival edge has the same two-map form with \(G_\prec\), \(x_\prec\) and \(\zeta\) in place of \(G_\succ\), \((x,a)\) and \(\eta\).

A nonlinear \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) can also be written as its own edge: the inner integral is then the arrival builder of an edge that draws the shock, and \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) is the aggregator of the preceding decision edge, whose law of motion is deterministic. This re-timing exposes the intermediate information set as a perch. It is a modeling choice, not a requirement.

docs.title: 2.4 The arrival kernel
docs.text:
The arrival aggregator defines the arrival builder by

\[ (\mathbb T_\prec v)(x_\prec) =B_\prec(x_\prec,v) =\int G_\prec\bigl(v(g_\prec(x_\prec,\zeta)),x_\prec,\zeta\bigr)\,\mu_\zeta(\mathrm d\zeta). \]

Define the undiscounted transition expectation by

\[ (P_\prec f)(x_\prec)=\int f(g_\prec(x_\prec,\zeta))\,\mu_\zeta(\mathrm d\zeta). \]

When \(G_\prec(w,x_\prec,\zeta)=w\), the builder equals \(P_\prec\). This is the buffer-stock case. An arrival reward or nonlinear arrival aggregator must remain in \(\mathbb T_\prec\) and does not belong to \(P_\prec\).

docs.title: 2.5 The policy
docs.text:
The selection is a separate layer, acting on the induced aggregator, not part of the backward kernel. Abstractly,

\[ (\mathbb T_\succ\,v_\succ)(x) \;=\; \sup_{a \in \Gamma(x)} B_\succ(x, a, v_\succ), \]

We write a supremum because attainment is an assumption. If it is attained and a measurable feasible selection \(\pi(x)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{a\in\Gamma(x)}B_\succ(x,a,v_\succ)\) exists, then

\[ (\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ)(x)=B_\succ(x,\pi(x),v_\succ) =(\mathbb T_\succ v_\succ)(x). \]

Rule R7 of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C gives sufficient measurable-selection conditions. For arbitrary continuation functions we additionally require that the resulting decision function belongs to the chosen value-function domain. First-order conditions or an endogenous-grid inversion select an optimum only under the relevant sufficiency, feasibility, and coverage conditions; a numerical method does not establish those conditions.

The selection is an assumption

A maximizer set need not be nonempty or admit a measurable selection without further hypotheses. Different selections from that set have the same current choice value but can induce different continuation distributions. A different nonoptimizing selection gives policy evaluation without the equality to the supremum. #check-details-aas

docs.title: 2.6 Intermediate expressions
docs.text:
A backward block can contain several intermediate expressions. The following is mathematical notation, not a stage-file fragment:

\[ \mathrm W=\beta\,\mathrm V_\succ,\qquad \mathrm Q=\mathbb E[u(\mathrm A)+\mathrm W\mid\mathcal F_\sim],\qquad \mathrm V_\sim=\mathrm Q. \]

Here \(\mathrm A\) is a specified feasible decision action, \(\mathrm W\) is the discounted continuation field, and the conditional expectation defines the decision value. The individual expressions have different roles: pointwise scaling, expectation, and assignment. The .bl declarations and named blocks that express such equations are described in Bellman-SYM's Field equations page. Their operator decomposition is developed in Operators and builders. #todo Kinds and sorts §6 and Methods §§1 and 4 state how a numerical method targets an intermediate operation: the operation is one operator of the stage, and an entry of a methods file writes the method on its name. An account of the expressions above in those terms remains open; current authoring rules are defined in the syntax documentation.

Remark — where the expectation sits (the two forms)

A pre-decision shock is observed before choice, while a post-decision shock is not. Moving a physical shock between those information sets changes the decision problem. The illustrative example instead changes the boundary of the recursion while preserving when income is observed: it forms the next arrival expectation as a continuation function before the current choice. Such factorization must retain the relevant state and conditional law. With nonlinear aggregation the order of evaluation also matters; expectation may not be moved through it without an argument. Semi-conjugacy discusses alternative recursions. The post-decision terminology depends on the timing convention.1

docs.title: 2.7 The forward builders
docs.text:
The forward builders map finite measures on one state space to finite measures on the next. Fix a measurable feasible policy \(\pi\), and write \(g_{\succ,\pi}(x,\eta)=g_\succ(x,\pi(x),\eta)\). Define

\[ P_\pi=P_\prec\circ P_{\succ,\pi}, \qquad \mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec. \]

For bounded measurable test functions \(f\), \(P_\prec f\), \(P_{\succ,\pi}f\), and \(P_\pi f\) are bounded measurable functions at arrival, decision, and arrival respectively. Their forward counterparts are defined by

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu_\prec,f\rangle_\sim =\langle\mu_\prec,P_\prec f\rangle_\prec, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle_\succ =\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle_\sim. \]

Under the fixed conditional laws of §1.1 these are the image measures

\[ \mathbb M_\prec\mu_\prec=(g_\prec)_\#(\mu_\prec\otimes\mu_\zeta), \qquad \mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu=(g_{\succ,\pi})_\#(\mu\otimes\mu_\eta), \]

where \(\otimes\) is the product of independent probability laws and \(g_\#\) denotes the distribution induced by applying \(g\). For state-dependent conditional shock laws the corresponding joint law is formed from the state measure and its conditional kernel, not a product of marginals. When a shock is deterministic, its measure is a point mass; the buffer-stock continuation law is the image under \(m\mapsto m-\pi(m)\).

The composition gives

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\pi\mu_\prec,f\rangle_\succ =\langle\mu_\prec,P_\pi f\rangle_\prec. \]

The identities follow by integrating the same transition first conditionally on the source state and then over its distribution. They extend to absolutely integrable evaluations. At an identity connection between stages, the continuation law of the first is the arrival law of the second. A connection expressed as a renaming uses the corresponding identification of state coordinates; see Stage composition.

Transition pairing and value recursion

The pairing is with undiscounted \(P\), even under a fixed policy. For expected utility and the identity arrival aggregator,

\[ \mathbb T_\pi f=P_\prec\bar{r}_\pi+\beta P_\pi f. \]

Thus the reward-bearing Bellman operator is not the transpose of \(\mathbb M_\pi\). Taking \(f=0\) gives zero in the transition pairing, while a nonzero reward can give a nonzero Bellman update. Optimization and nonlinear preference aggregation are further operations with their own assumptions. Numerical implementations must approximate the declared laws consistently; the mathematical identity does not guarantee agreement between arbitrary implementations.

docs.title: 2.8 Breaking down builders into primitive operators
docs.text:
The continuation-to-decision builder combines simpler operators: pullback along the law of motion, expectation, reward aggregation, and, for optimization, selection. Pullback along the law of motion evaluates a continuation function at the state the transition determines. With additive expected utility and constant discount, the induced choice value is the expected reward plus the discounted expected continuation value (§2). Selection chooses a policy; that policy indexes the pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution of the fixed-policy builder. Exact Evaluation remains an identity on its function or feasible-policy set and makes no selection. An attained supremum is obtained only if the policy is a maximizer.

A handler is a numerical routine attached to an operator. A maximizing search and a first-order inversion may implement the same selection when their mathematical assumptions hold; they are not interchangeable without those assumptions. Operators and builders develops the decomposition, and Fields, functions and types states the inputs and outputs of its operations. The mathematical stage signature is described in Appendix C.

docs.title: 3. An information view
docs.text:
A perch represents an information set, formalized as a \(\sigma\)-algebra. It records what the agent knows at that point, and therefore what a policy may condition on. As a stage proceeds the agent only ever learns more, so the three information sets are nested,

\[ \text{arrival information} \ \subseteq\ \text{decision information} \ \subseteq\ \text{continuation information}; \]

Thus the arrival/decision/continuation split is not three times on a clock nor do the perches represent operators, they are three states of knowledge.

The information-set reading, formally

On \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\) the perches form a filtration, a nested family \(\mathcal F_\prec\subseteq\mathcal F_\sim\subseteq\mathcal F_\succ\) of information sets. A state \(X_p\) measurable at perch \(p\) satisfies \(\sigma(X_p)\subseteq\mathcal F_p\). State sufficiency means that the relevant payoffs and conditional future laws can be expressed using that state. It does not imply equality of these information sets: the agent may remember an old shock that no longer affects any payoff or transition.

A real-valued field \(Z\) has a measurable representation \(Z=z(X_p)\) almost surely when it is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_p)\). Measurability with respect to the larger \(\mathcal F_p\) alone is insufficient. Its representative is determined only almost everywhere under the law of \(X_p\), unless a pointwise domain-defined function is supplied. The precise representation requirements are in Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §1.2 and rule R5.

In a history-based construction, observed pre-decision shocks enlarge arrival information, and post-decision shocks enlarge decision information. A deterministic measurable policy action adds no information to the decision state on which it depends. Randomized policies require their additional randomization and its timing to be specified. #check-details-aas

In the surface syntax a perch is written as a perch word after a side of a block header, !arvl, !dcsn or !cntn, or as a mark on a name, [<], [~] or [>], where the decision mark is usually omitted; with marks, an arrival variable is written m[<], a decision variable m, a continuation variable a[>]. The tags say what is known where: m[<] asserts "\(m\) is settled on arrival," a declared control c is chosen at decision information, a[>] asserts "\(a\) is determined by the time we continue."

Next → 04. Fields, functions and types

  1. When the post-decision shock is trivial, as in the buffer-stock example, the continuation perch is the post-decision state of approximate dynamic programming (Powell 2011) and the afterstate of Sutton and Barto (1998). Hull (2015) studied post-decision-state value functions as a solution method for economic models, and Carroll's Solving MicroDSOPs works with the same object as the end-of-period (Gothic) value function. For that example, in Powell's timing, the decision perch is his pre-decision state, and a stage's arrival perch is the previous stage's post-decision state carried across the boundary. Hull, I. (2015). Approximate dynamic programming with post-decision states as a solution method for dynamic economic models. Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 55, 57–70. ↩

docs.title: Fields, functions and types
docs.text:
Summary

Fields name random quantities at a stage’s information sets. Their representing functions state how those quantities depend on the chosen state and any retained controls. We explain the assumptions behind substitution, the distinction between explicit definitions and implicit relations, and how the same authored model determines value recursion and distribution propagation.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches defines state spaces, transition expectations, and backward builders. Used by — Stages declares the fields in .bl; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C gives the binding and state-representation rules, and its Appendix D specifies local arguments, substitution, and retained outputs; Methodization states the supported addresses and attachment forms.

docs.title: 1. Declaring quantities and equations
docs.text:
Stages and perches names the two backward builders of a stage,

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\succ,\pi} : \mathsf{V}_\succ \to \mathsf{V}_\sim, \qquad \mathbb{T}_{\prec} : \mathsf{V}_\sim \to \mathsf{V}_\prec, \]

and their composition is the policy-evaluation Bellman operator for the stage,

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\pi} = \mathbb{T}_{\prec}\circ\mathbb{T}_{\succ,\pi}. \]

These are the central objects of a recursive dynamic program — the objects to which numerical and methodological assumptions attach. They are not, however, what a modeler should have to write down by hand each time they build an application. The surface syntax should ask for something closer to the economics: the concrete quantities — assets, income, consumption — and the equations relating them.

For the buffer-stock stage, the transition equations are

\[ m=Rk+y,\qquad a=m-c, \]

with \(k\geq0\), income \(y>0\), \(R>0\), and feasible consumption \(0<c\leq m\). The stage declares these relationships, its utility function, discount factor \(0<\beta<1\), income law, and choice rule. The stage syntax of Bellman-SYM specifies their .bl authoring form.

The illustrative example places next period's income expectation in the continuation function on assets. For a supplied measurable function \(v_\succ\) on assets, the optimizing decision operator is

\[ (\mathbb T_\succ v_\succ)(m) =\sup_{0<c\leq m}\{u(c)+\beta v_\succ(m-c)\}. \]

For fixed \(m\), the right side is a value; as \(m\) varies, it defines a function. We require the displayed values to be well-defined and the output to belong to the chosen function domain. A fixed measurable feasible consumption policy \(\pi\) instead gives

\[ (\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ)(m) =u(\pi(m))+\beta v_\succ(m-\pi(m)). \]

These are different operators. A supremum need not be attained, and an attained optimum still requires a measurable policy selection when a policy is needed. The fields and their representing functions allow the pointwise and function-valued statements to be connected explicitly.

docs.title: 1.1 Binding and composition
docs.text:
A binder introduces a local variable in an expression. In a supremum over consumption, consumption is bound; in an income integral, income is bound. The integrand may also depend on a free continuation function and on other state arguments. A grammar and its abstract syntax tree can record the binder and its body. Interpreting their scope and substituting expressions without capturing another local variable require the contextual rules of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §2.5 and rule R4.

The composition of two operators applies the first and then the second when their domains match. Here \(\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) evaluates the decision value under \(\pi\) and then the arrival value. The source equations, types, and bound and free arguments determine these operations under their declared mathematical assumptions. Arithmetic is parsed, and local scopes remain relevant after parsing. The operator description supplements the economic equations; it does not require the modeler to author an independent second model.

docs.title: 1.2 Variables as fields
docs.text:
A field is a named random variable that a stage declares (Kinds and sorts §5). A field other than a shock is measurable at its perch, one of the arrival, decision, or continuation information sets. On the underlying probability space \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\), a field \(Z\) at perch \(p\) takes values in its declared set \(D\) and is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_p\). A realization \(Z(\omega)\) is a point of \(D\); the field itself is not that point.

The state vector \(X_p\) takes values in the state space \(\mathsf X_p\). A measurable function \(z:\mathsf X_p\to D\) represents the field when \(Z=z(X_p)\) almost surely. This requires a version of \(Z\) measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_p)\), the information generated by the state; a version agrees with \(Z\) almost surely. Measurability with respect to the larger \(\mathcal F_p\) alone is insufficient. Relevant conditional laws and payoff arguments must also be determined by the chosen state. A declared set such as \(\mathbb R\) establishes neither integrability nor square integrability of \(Z\).

Fields are classified by perch, role, and declared set (Kinds and sorts §5). Perch marks [<], the unmarked decision form (equivalently [~]), and [>] identify information contexts. The roles are state, control, value, shock and multiplier, the last being the multiplier of a constraint on a choice. A shock takes its role from its law, is supplied on a transition with its timing, and belongs to no perch. In .bl, a type is written after a colon, its components with @ between them, and the components are conditions that hold together (Kinds and sorts §3, D7); §2 of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C specifies those declarations.

For a continuation value field, \(\mathrm V_\succ=v_\succ(\mathrm X_\succ)\) almost surely. The value function \(v_\succ:\mathsf X_\succ\to\mathsf L\) maps states to \(\mathsf L\), the declared set of the value field; evaluation at a point \(x_\succ\) gives a scalar \(v_\succ(x_\succ)\), while evaluation at \(X_\succ\) gives the random field. The declared set may include extended values only when the expressions involving them remain defined. We do not introduce a separately authored V_fn source variable.

In the stage syntax the derivative of a value is read by a derivative term, D_{a}V[>], the operator applied to the declared value field in the coordinate of its subscript; it is no field and has no role. Three different objects must not be conflated in one identifier. D_{x} is an operator, the derivative with respect to the variable in its subscript applied to the function that follows it — D_{c}(𝑢) is the function c ↦ ∂𝑢/∂c, and D_{a}V[>] is the derivative of the continuation value in savings — and it is never glued into a name. A derivative line, D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), states what the derivative of the value its builder writes equals. A name such as 𝑑𝑢 is an ordinary function name the modeler chose, whose letters mean nothing to the language; it may be defined through the operator (𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢)) or in closed form (𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ)). In that example \(\rho>0\) is the coefficient of relative risk aversion, and the marginal-utility function has positive-real argument and result domains.

For the buffer-stock stage, the mathematical declarations are:

Field Perch or transition Role Declared set Meaning \(k\) arrival state \(\mathbb R_+\) assets on arrival \(y\) arrival to decision shock \(\mathsf Z_\zeta\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}\) income observed before choice \(m\) decision state \(\mathbb R_{++}\) resources \(c\) decision control \(\mathbb R_{++}\), with \(c\leq m\) consumption \(a\) continuation state \(\mathbb R_+\) assets after consumption \(\mathrm V_\succ\) continuation value \(\mathsf L\) continuation value field

The constraint \(c\leq m\) relates two quantities; it is additional to the declared set \(\mathbb R_{++}\). The derivative term D_{a}V[>] requires a differentiable representing function where it is read; neither the term nor a derivative line proves differentiability or positivity. Appendix D formalizes the classifications. The field, function, and operator catalogues collect the objects used here.

Declared functions keep their typed arguments and result domains when their bodies are substituted into another expression. An argument local to a utility function is distinct from a same-named stage control. An operator has a domain and a codomain too, the space it reads and the space it writes; they are the carriers of the source sort and the target sort that form its rank (Kinds and sorts §§3 and 6).

One authored model

In the buffer-stock stage the transition \(a=m-c\), together with utility, discounting, and the feasible set, determines the optimizing decision operator displayed in §1. The income transition and its specified law determine the arrival expectation. Under a fixed policy, those transitions also determine the induced distribution laws. The forward reading uses the transition and policy; the backward reading additionally uses the authored value evaluation and, if requested, optimization.

The field and explicit-function diagrams are two mathematical representations of these same equations under the stated assumptions. The intended construction derives them from one .bl source, with its arithmetic and binding interpreted; the source contract does not itself establish completed software support. The temporary parsed tree is not an independently retained second source.

docs.title: 2. Field equations
docs.text:
The field diagram records the typed fields and the equations that relate them. Declared state coordinates determine the state vector at each perch. If a decision state has coordinates \(m\in\mathbb R_{++}\) and \(h\in\mathbb R_+\) with no further joint restriction, its state space is \(\mathbb R_{++}\times\mathbb R_+\). The declarations constrain the fields' values; they do not turn random fields into deterministic scalars.

The forward maps \(g_\prec\) and \(g_\succ\) determine later state coordinates from the required state, control, and shock arguments. The backward equations specify value evaluation. An expectation is applied where it is authored and under its conditional-law assumptions, not inserted merely because an intermediate expression mentions a later shock.

A transition with several outputs must determine every declared output. An explicit definition names a function once its dependencies and domains are established. An implicit equation instead specifies a relation in its unknowns; it defines a function only where uniqueness or a specified selection, with the required measurability, supplies one. Attaching a numerical handler does not establish existence, uniqueness, or optimality of its solution.

Explicit definitions may be substituted in dependency order, preserving local binding, controls, shock arguments, and every declared output. A fresh left-hand name alone does not make an equation explicit if the right side depends on the unknown being determined. Bellman-SYM's Appendix D, §§2–5, gives these rules. Named computation boundaries do not conceal dependencies or convert an implicit relation into an assignment.

For the buffer-stock stage, the field diagram is small:

┌───────────────┐  g≺    ┌───────────────┐  g≻    ┌────────────────┐
│  arrival  ≺   │ ─────▶ │  decision  ·  │ ─────▶ │ continuation ≻ │
│   k : ℝ₊      │        │   m : ℝ₊₊     │        │   a : ℝ₊       │
└───────────────┘        └───────────────┘        └────────────────┘
   g≺ : m = R·k + y                         g≻ : a = m − c

The arrows are the declared transitions \(g_\prec\) and \(g_\succ\) of Stages and perches §1.2, now annotated with their field equations. The diagram shows only the forward state transitions. The states of the three perches as vertices and the two transitions as edges form the declaration graph of the stage (Kinds and sorts §6). The stage also needs its value equations and policy rule for backward evaluation; a transition alone does not determine preferences or optimal choice.

Larger stages change the names inside the boxes, not the discipline. A housing stage can carry decision state \((m,h)\), controls \((c,h')\), and continuation state \((a,h')\); the decision-to-continuation edge then has two output equations, not two separate topological arrows. A genuine disjoint union of continuation spaces is different: that is branching, and belongs to Branching, not to the product structure of an unbranched perch.

Field diagrams compose through selected boundary pairings. A field belongs to its stage occurrence: a continuation field named \(a\) in one stage and an arrival field named \(a\) in another remain distinct until a connection pairs their eligible uses. Equal names can suggest a pair, but they establish neither its compatibility nor its economic meaning. If the names differ, as with post-decision assets \(a\) closing one buffer-stock stage and beginning-of-period assets \(k\) opening the next, a connector records the pairing without renaming either field. The resulting coordinate map reads the destination's ordered state coordinates from the source's ordered continuation coordinates. A substantive law of motion, such as return accumulation or an income draw, remains a transition inside a stage, not a connector. This is the field-level content of stage composition in Stage composition and the trellis construction in Periods and the trellis.

At this point we have a diagram, but not yet \(\mathbb{T}_{\succ,\pi}\), \(\mathbb{T}_{\prec}\), \(\mathbb{M}_{\prec}\), or \(\mathbb{M}_{\succ,\pi}\). The diagram represents the authored field equations; interpreting its complete context gives the functional operators.

docs.title: 3. Interpreting equations
docs.text:
Write \(\Upsilon\) for the interpretation from a typed expression, with its context and free inputs, to its mathematical meaning. Schematically,

field equations with context  -- Υ -->  explicit functions and relations

A signature lists sorts and operation symbols, each symbol with its input and output sorts (Kinds and sorts §3, D1). A target algebra supplies a mathematical set for each sort and an operation for each symbol. For an ordinary many-sorted signature, its ground terms (expressions with no free inputs) form an initial algebra: there is a unique operation-preserving interpretation into each specified target algebra. With free inputs, the corresponding free algebra additionally requires an environment assigning those inputs their meanings.1 Binding and substitution require the context-sensitive interpretation discussed in §1.1; a list of symbol arities does not prove those rules.

This uniqueness is conditional on the supplied interpretation. It does not choose a missing shock law, a continuation-function representative, or a selection from an implicit relation. The full stage equations specify transition, value evaluation, and policy operations. Interpreting those equations yields the operators used to solve and simulate the model.

The functional representation retains the equations' inputs, outputs, and dependencies. Equal mathematical expressions may be substituted in a compatible context, but every declared output remains part of the resulting function. A boundary shared by adjacent stages identifies compatible fields rather than duplicating their authored definitions. Actual stage occurrences remain distinct objects. The retained interpreted equation diagrams and definitions are described in Bellman-SYM's Appendices C and D.

docs.title: 4. Functions and distributions
docs.text: The functional diagram represents the declared equations using explicit state arguments, functions, and relations. Value recursion and distribution propagation use the same transitions and laws. They use different mathematical objects and operations, so their relation must be stated rather than inferred from a similar drawing.

docs.title: 4.1 Value recursion
docs.text:
Let \(\mathsf V_p\) be a specified domain of value functions at perch \(p\) for which the relevant operations are defined. In the notation of Stages and perches, the complete decision block defines either fixed-policy evaluation or optimization. The latter has the rank \(\mathbb T_\succ:\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\sim\), while arrival evaluation has the rank \(\mathbb T_\prec:\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec\). Thus

\[ \mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ: \mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\prec. \]

These builders depend on the declared rewards, laws, feasible set, and policy operation in addition to the transition maps.

For buffer-stock, the decision edge \(a=m-c\), with the supremum over feasible consumption, is read into

\[ (\mathbb{T}_\succ\,v_\succ)(m) = \sup_{0<c\le m} \{u(c)+\beta\,v_\succ(m-c)\}, \]

while the arrival edge \(m=Rk+y\) is read into

\[ (\mathbb{T}_{\prec}\,v)(k)=\mathbb{E}_y[v(R\,k+y)]. \]

These displays are not additional declarations. They are the value-side reading of the field diagram. The backward model of Kinds and sorts §6 sends the arrival edge to \(\mathbb T_\prec\) and the decision edge at a policy \(\pi\) to \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\); the optimizing decision builder \(\mathbb T_\succ\) is formed from the builders at a policy and is the image of no edge. The notation in Appendix E.3 records their ranks.

docs.title: 4.2 Distribution propagation
docs.text:
Write \(\mathsf M_p\) for the finite measures on the state space \(\mathsf X_p\), of which the probability measures are those of mass one (Stages and perches §1.2). The transitions and their specified conditional laws induce

\[ \mathbb M_\prec:\mathsf M_\prec\to\mathsf M_\sim, \qquad \mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}:\mathsf M_\sim\to\mathsf M_\succ, \qquad \mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec. \]

Here \(\pi\) is a measurable feasible policy. It may be supplied for simulation or obtained by solving the backward problem under its optimality assumptions. A supremum alone supplies a value, not a chosen policy.

For a bounded measurable test function \(f\), define the undiscounted expectation operators by

\[ (P_\prec f)(x)=\int f(g_\prec(x,\zeta))\,\mu_\zeta(\mathrm d\zeta\mid x), $$ $$ (P_{\succ,\pi}f)(x)=\int f(g_\succ(x,\pi(x),\eta))\, \mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta\mid x,\pi(x)),\qquad P_\pi=P_\prec\circ P_{\succ,\pi}. \]

The first operator takes decision functions to arrival functions; the second takes continuation functions to decision functions. With \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,\mathrm d\mu\), their distribution pairing is

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\prec f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle. \]

The identities also hold whenever the displayed integrals are absolutely finite. They follow from integration against the induced transition laws; composition reverses the order of the paired operators. No bijection between value functions and probability measures is claimed. Reward-bearing \(\mathbb T\) is not the paired linear operator: for constant-discount expected utility, \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}f=\bar r_\pi+\beta P_{\succ,\pi}f\), where \(\bar r_\pi\) is expected reward under \(\pi\).

Changing the income process changes the model and may require different sufficient state coordinates. Both forward and backward interpretations must use that revised state and law. Merely changing numerical integration for the same law is a method choice.

docs.title: 5. Refinement and numerical methods
docs.text:
Nothing above is yet a numerical method. The map \(\Upsilon\) produces mathematical operators. Methodization assigns methods to those operators; a handler supplies the numerical computation. This order matters: methods label operators that already have ranks and meanings; they do not supply the model's semantics.

Refinement first expands coarse operator symbols into finer terms. The optimizing continuation-to-decision builder decomposes into an aggregator kernel, its induced aggregator, and policy selection followed by insertion:

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\succ} \;\longmapsto\; \iota^{*}\circ\langle B_\succ,\ \operatorname{argmax}\circ B_\succ\rangle, \qquad \max := \iota^{*}\circ\langle \mathrm{id}_{\mathsf Q_\Gamma},\ \operatorname{argmax}\rangle, \]

In this composition display, \(B_\succ\) denotes the map from a continuation function \(f\) to the function \((x,a)\mapsto B_\succ(x,a,f)\). Here \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) denotes the chosen functions on feasible state–action pairs, and argmax denotes a specified measurable maximizer selection on the domain where one exists. Policy insertion maps a choice-value function and a measurable feasible policy to the decision function \(\iota^{*}(Q,\pi)(x)=Q(x,\pi(x))\). It differs from exact Evaluation, which carries the retained function unchanged into the function space of its output and neither supplies nor applies a policy. The display assumes attainment, compatible domains, and finite integrals. For the fixed independent shock laws used in Stages and perches, \(B_\succ\) is the induced aggregator

\[ B_\succ(x, a, v_\succ) \;=\; \int_{\mathsf{Z}_\eta} G_\succ\bigl(v_\succ(g_\succ(x, a, \eta)),\,x,\,a,\,\eta\bigr)\, \mu_\eta(\mathrm{d}\eta), \]

and the arrival builder is the policy-free aggregator \(\mathbb{T}_{\prec}\longmapsto B_\prec\), with \(B_\prec(x_\prec, v)=\int_{\mathsf{Z}_\zeta}G_\prec(v(g_\prec(x_\prec, \zeta)),\,x_\prec,\,\zeta)\,\mu_\zeta(\mathrm{d}\zeta)\).

A statement that applies a map outside the expectation denotes the two-map form of Stages and perches §2.3a; the displays here are its case with the outer map the identity.

A derived signature morphism assigns each coarse operation symbol a typed expression in finer operations. When every assigned expression denotes exactly the original operation under the chosen target interpretation, substitution preserves the meaning of a composite term. Free inputs retain their fixed environment. This is the exact-refinement argument developed in Appendix B; it does not imply an approximation bound or convergence of numerical policies.

The diagram can retain a builder as a named computation with operations inside it. An equation marked !node requests an authored computation boundary; arithmetic, expectation, and other operator occurrences remain represented inside equations even without that mark. Adding or removing a boundary preserves the mathematical function a builder denotes while changing the diagram available to numerical methods: the marked equation's result is a function in the diagram, which later operations consume and a method may represent exactly, through its definition, or by an approximation such as an interpolant; an unmarked intermediate expression is part of the operation that uses it and offers no such point. Bellman-SYM's Appendix D, §§3–4, gives the distinction.

A method may address an entire builder or a supported operation within it. A named inversion represents the solution relation of its equation until uniqueness or a specified measurable selection makes it a function. Numerical interpolation, differentiation, or root finding supplies an algorithm, not the missing existence or optimality argument. The supported addresses and attachment forms belong to Bellman-SYM's rules for methodization.

A cut in an explanatory hierarchy chooses which composite operations are evaluated as units. Exact interpretation can agree at different levels when the substitution condition above holds. An approximate handler instead requires its own error bounds and stability assumptions before local errors can be related to the final solution. Initiality supplies neither numerical tolerances nor policy convergence. Methods distinguishes a numerical method from the operation it approximates; unfinished method details remain with their owning chapters.
