docs.title: Operators and builders
docs.text:
Summary

These unfinished notes distinguish transition expectation, reward aggregation, policy selection, and a builder at a policy. They record the inputs and outputs of the operators and the assumptions needed when an implicit equation is interpreted as a function. The outline and its placeholders remain incomplete.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches defines the stage operators and their information requirements. Builds on — Fields, functions and types states the field and function distinction. Used by — Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, whose rules R7–R10 distinguish evaluation, selection, and implicit relations, and its Appendix D, whose §7 distinguishes an implicit policy relation from a selection and which defines the source marks; Field equations and Methodization, the source forms and attachment forms of the operators defined here.

Not yet drafted — stub notes only

Structural outline and placeholders only; not yet a finished chapter.

An operator maps objects in a specified domain to objects in a specified codomain. A builder composes simpler operators into the operator of one edge of the stage, or into the policy builder or the optimizing decision builder, which are the image of no edge: a backward builder is a value-recursion step, and a forward builder maps a distribution at one perch to a distribution at the next. We use \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) for decision evaluation under a fixed policy, \(\mathbb T_\succ\) for optimization, and \(\mathbb T_\prec\) for arrival evaluation. The corresponding stage compositions are \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) and \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\). Kinds and sorts §6 derives the builders \(\mathbb T_\prec\) and \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\), and the forward builders of §9 below, as the images of the transitions of a stage under its models, where a transition is a law of motion with its shock law. A handler is a numerical routine attached to an operator.

Here \(\mathsf L\) is the value line (the declared set of a value field), \(\eta\) and \(\zeta\) are the post-decision and pre-decision shocks on spaces \(\mathsf Z_\eta\) and \(\mathsf Z_\zeta\), and \(\Upsilon\) interprets the declared equations as mathematical operations. At perch \(p\), \(\mathsf V_p\) is a chosen space of value functions on state space \(\mathsf X_p\). The feasible state–action pairs form \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\), and \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) is a chosen space of choice-value functions on those pairs. Policies in \(\Pi_\Gamma\) are measurable and feasible. These domains must make each displayed operation defined and closed under the required compositions. Every expectation below requires absolute integrability on its stated domain; fixed shock laws in the displays are conditional laws independent of the source information. State-dependent laws retain their conditioning arguments.

docs.title: 1. The forward reading
docs.text: Forward operators act on distributions over state vectors; measurable transitions with specified shock laws induce pushforwards, the resulting distributions. (Placeholder.) Defines the push-forward (transfer / Perron–Frobenius operator); states the running example forward (the buffer-stock population transition).

docs.title: 2. The backward reading
docs.text:
The field reading starts from a random continuation field \(\mathrm V_\succ\), a decision state \(\mathrm X\), and a feasible decision action \(\mathrm A\), with the latter two measurable at decision information \(\mathcal F_\sim\). For integrable local payoff,

\[ \mathrm Q=\mathbb E[G_\succ(\mathrm V_\succ,\mathrm X,\mathrm A,\eta)\mid\mathcal F_\sim]. \]

This is a field identity along the chosen trajectory. To compare every feasible action, specify a continuation representative \(v_\succ\), the transition, and the conditional shock law on all required states and actions. Then the pointwise choice value is

\[ B_\succ(x,a,v_\succ) =\int_{\mathsf Z_\eta}G_\succ\bigl(v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta). \]

This is the form with the aggregation inside the integral. A statement may also apply a map outside it, \(B_\succ=G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(\int\cdots)\), the two-map form of Stages and perches §2.3a.

The corresponding almost-sure representation requires \(\mathrm V_\succ=v_\succ(\mathrm X_\succ)\) and state-generated measurability, as in Stages and perches §2.2. The declared set of a value field alone supplies no square-integrability claim. Selection chooses a policy; the transition, conditional shock law and aggregator indexed by that policy define the builder at the policy.

Level Input Operation Field random continuation field and random state/action conditional expectation of the integrable local payoff Function a specified continuation function pullback along the law of motion, pointwise aggregation inside the integral, the authored shock integral, then any aggregation written outside it

Pullback along the law of motion evaluates a function at the transition's output. A pointwise aggregation can also be applied to a function already expressed in the required arguments; no universal rule requires an immediately preceding substitution node.

docs.title: 3. Transition pairing
docs.text:
Write \(\mathsf M_p\) for finite measures on \(\mathsf X_p\), and \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,\mathrm d\mu\). Probability measures form the mass-one subset of \(\mathsf M_p\). For bounded measurable functions, define the undiscounted transition expectations

\[ (P_\prec f)(x)=\int f(g_\prec(x,\zeta))\,\mu_\zeta(\mathrm d\zeta), \qquad (P_{\succ,\pi}f)(x)=\int f(g_\succ(x,\pi(x),\eta))\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta). \]

The forward operators \(\mathbb M_\prec:\mathsf M_\prec\to\mathsf M_\sim\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}:\mathsf M_\sim\to\mathsf M_\succ\) satisfy

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\prec f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle. \]

(Placeholder.) Develop the pairing from integration against the transition laws. The formulas extend to absolutely integrable evaluations. They do not pair probability propagation with reward-bearing Bellman evaluation: in constant-discount expected utility, \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}f=\bar r_\pi+\beta P_{\succ,\pi}f\), where \(\bar r_\pi\) is expected reward under \(\pi\). Optimization and nonlinear aggregation remain separate operations.

docs.title: 4. Why the field graph supports both
docs.text: The same authored .bl equations specify transitions, laws, and value evaluation. (Placeholder.) Explain how forward propagation uses the transitions and a supplied policy, while backward evaluation additionally uses the reward and policy rule. The field and function diagrams are representations of that model under their stated assumptions; a bare transition graph does not determine preferences.

docs.title: 5. Evaluating and selecting actions
docs.text:
How a builder becomes a term. A builder equation is not a single operation but a composition of operations, each with stated inputs and outputs, inserted by the meaning map. The continuation-to-decision builder \(\mathbb{T}_{\succ}\) factors through:

  1. the point backward kernel

    \[ G_\succ:\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf L, \]

    acting on a value variable, not a value function;

  2. the induced aggregator

    \[ B_\succ:\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf Q_\Gamma, \qquad (B_\succ v_\succ)(x,a) = \int_{\mathsf Z_\eta} G_\succ\bigl(v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(d\eta); \]

  3. the policy selection and indexed-builder layer, on the domain of objectives admitting the specified measurable maximizer selection

    \[ \operatorname{argmax}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\to\mathcal P(\Pi_\Gamma). \]

    Here \(\operatorname{argmax}Q\) is the possibly empty set of feasible measurable policies that maximize \(Q\) at every state. On the domain where a measurable maximizer is specified, write

    \[ s:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\rightharpoonup\Pi_\Gamma, \qquad s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q \]

    for the selection rule. Thus \(\operatorname{argmax}\) states the maximizing correspondence, while \(s\) supplies one policy. For each \(\pi\in\Pi_\Gamma\), define the builder at that policy by

    \[ (B_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ)(x) = \int_{\mathsf Z_\eta} G_{\succ,\pi}\bigl(v_\succ(g_{\succ,\pi}(x,\eta)),x,\eta\bigr)\, \mu_{\eta,\pi}(d\eta\mid x). \]

    Here the policy is part of the indexed law of motion, aggregator and conditional distribution. Exact Evaluation is an identity on a function or a set of feasible policies; it neither supplies nor applies \(\pi\). In the endogenous grid method (EGM) and non-concave refinements a numerical method may also apply \(\operatorname{upper\_env}\) to its candidate representation.

Thus

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\succ}v_\succ =B_{\succ,s(B_\succ v_\succ)}v_\succ, \qquad (\max Q)(x)=Q(x,s(Q)(x)). \]

The maximum is recovered on this attained-selection domain. Without attainment the optimizing value is a supremum and this selection formula need not be defined. For additive expected utility with constant discount, \(B_\succ\) can be decomposed internally into pullback along \(g_\succ\), Markov expectation over \(\eta\), and reward aggregation. In the nonlinear-kernel case, that separation is not generally valid: \(B_\succ\) is the displayed integral of the pointwise aggregator.

Numerical methods may approximate expectations by quadrature, simulation, or finite summation. A first-order inversion approximates the same optimum as direct maximization only under its feasibility, optimality, selection, and domain-coverage conditions. Interpolation and candidate-envelope comparisons may be internal steps of a numerical method; choosing that method does not add an authored envelope equation or change exact Evaluation. An authored envelope operation has its own mathematical meaning and assumptions. Supported attachment forms are specified by Bellman-SYM's rules for methodization.

The transition maps, shock laws, feasibility graph, and aggregator kernels are model data. They generate operators under \(\Upsilon\), but their mathematical content is fixed by the stage file and its calibration. A handler may fuse neighboring operators in the realized computation, but the model-side term remains the same. Which operators become separate code and which are lumped is a methodization choice — a cut through the operator hierarchy — not something the calculus fixes.

The decision-to-arrival builder \(\mathbb{T}_\prec\) is the policy-free induced aggregator

\[ \mathbb{T}_\prec=B_\prec:\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec, \qquad (B_\prec v)(x_\prec) = \int_{\mathsf Z_\zeta} G_\prec\bigl(v(g_\prec(x_\prec,\zeta)),x_\prec,\zeta\bigr)\,\mu_\zeta(d\zeta). \]

With the identity arrival aggregator, \(G_\prec(w,x_\prec,\zeta)=w\), so \(\mathbb{T}_\prec\) is the pure Markov expectation over the pre-decision shock. The difference between the two backward edges is not "max versus no max"; it is that the decision edge has a policy selection and an indexed-builder layer while the arrival edge does not.

There is a useful spectrum of how much of this composition to expose. A modeler may write a generated Bellman line such as \(v(x)=\sup_{a\in\Gamma(x)}B_\succ(x,a,v_\succ)\), or may expose the induced aggregator and policy separately: \(Q=B_\succ(v_\succ)\), \(\pi=s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax} Q\), and \(v_\sim=B_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ\). These denote the same exact Bellman operator when the selection is greedy and measurable. Named equations can provide attachment points for methods that use post-decision values or marginal relations. A numerical recipe may instead compute intermediate objects internally; they need not all be authored equations.

docs.title: 6. Backward builders
docs.text:
A backward builder is a named composition of operators that maps the value functions at one perch to those at the preceding perch. The continuation-to-decision builder is

\[ (\mathbb{T}_{\succ}v_\succ)(x) =\sup_{a\in\Gamma(x)}(B_\succ v_\succ)(x,a), \qquad \mathbb T_\succ:\mathsf V_\succ\rightharpoonup\mathsf V_\sim, \]

defined at each \(v_\succ\) at which this function lies in \(\mathsf V_\sim\). Where \(s(B_\succ v_\succ)\) is defined, \(\mathbb T_\succ v_\succ=B_{\succ,s(B_\succ v_\succ)}v_\succ\). The decision-to-arrival builder is

\[ \mathbb{T}_\prec=B_\prec:\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec. \]

The full optimizing stage operator is \(\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{T}_\prec\circ\mathbb{T}_{\succ}\). A fixed-policy builder is also available:

\[ \mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ=B_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ. \]

At the supplied continuation function, the fixed-policy builder equals the optimizing value whenever the policy selects a maximizer at every decision state. This need not be the particular selection supplied by \(s\), and does not identify the two operators on all continuation functions. The selection and indexed-builder layer of a controlled-field builder is the subject of §7.

The builder at a policy and the policy layer. The builder at a policy is \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi} \colon \mathsf V_\succ \to \mathsf V_\sim\), one operator for each \(\pi \in \Pi_\Gamma\); \(\mathbb T_\succ\) keeps its meaning above, the optimizing builder. The policy layer is a second operator, whose inputs and outputs depend on its route. On the selection route, \(s \circ B_\succ \colon \mathsf V_\succ \rightharpoonup \Pi_\Gamma\), where \(s(B_\succ v_\succ)\in\operatorname{argmax}(B_\succ v_\succ)\) under the measurable-maximizer condition of §7.3. On the relation route, the method supplies a selection into \(\Pi_\Gamma\) from the solution of an authored relation.

The semantic graph constructs the builder at a policy and the policy layer and does not compose them. In this construction, the decision builder is the operator at a policy, its signature the inputs and outputs of \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\). The policy is a free name used by its indexed pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution, typed on the output of the policy builder and carried on no input wire. The policy builder stands in the same graph as its own part, inputs and output. Where a policy block reads a value the backward builders produce, that wire joins the two parts; no wire runs from the policy builder into a backward builder.

A method states how the two parts are combined: the optimizing rule \(v_\succ\mapsto B_{\succ,s(B_\succ v_\succ)}v_\succ\) of value-function iteration, the alternation of policy evaluation and policy improvement of Howard, or a route through a first-order condition such as the endogenous grid. The abstract dynamic programs of Sargent and Stachurski have the same two-part form: a value poset with a family of policy operators \(\{T_\sigma\}_{\sigma \in \Sigma}\) and a selection made outside the family. Their Bellman operator is \(Tv = \bigvee_\sigma T_\sigma v\) whenever the supremum exists, and it equals the optimizing rule under the attainment and measurable-selection conditions of §7.3. In their recursive decision process \((\Gamma, V, B)\), the policy operator is \(T_\sigma v = B(\cdot, \sigma(\cdot), v)\) and a greedy selector satisfies \(\sigma(x) \in \arg\max_{a \in \Gamma(x)} B(x, a, v)\). Their operators are self-maps of one value space, so the counterpart of \(T_\sigma\) is the stage composite \(\mathbb T_\prec \circ \mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) under the period identification (Sargent and Stachurski 2025, Dynamic Programming, vol. 2, chapters "Abstract Decision Processes", sections "ADPs on Posets" and "The Bellman Equation", and "Recursive Decision Processes", sections "Definition" and "Existence of Greedy Policies"). A fixed-policy calculation uses the operator at a policy supplied from outside.

docs.title: 7. Policy selection and the builder at a policy
docs.text: A controlled backward step separates the induced aggregator \(Q=B_\succ(v_\succ)\in\mathsf Q_\Gamma\), the maximizing set \(\operatorname{argmax}Q\subseteq\Pi_\Gamma\), a selected policy \(\pi=s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q\), and the decision value \(v_\sim=B_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ\). The surface may expose these as separate blocks or lines, but each part of the semantic split has its own inputs and outputs: \(B_\succ\) constructs the objective, \(\operatorname{argmax}\) gives its maximizing policies, \(s\) selects one when the required selection exists, and \(B_{\succ,\pi}\) contains the policy in its indexed transition, aggregator and conditional distribution.

docs.title: 7.1 The choice-value function
docs.text:
The objective is the induced aggregator applied to the continuation value:

\[ Q(x,a)=(B_\succ v_\succ)(x,a) = \int_{\mathsf Z_\eta} G_\succ\bigl(v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(d\eta). \]

In expected-utility buffer-stock form this reduces to \(Q(m,c)=u(c)+\beta\,v_\succ(m-c)\) when the post-decision shock is trivial. A map written outside the expectation gives the two-map form of Stages and perches §2.3a. Value function iteration (VFI), EGM under its applicability conditions, and policy iteration can use this same objective.

docs.title: 7.2 Selection and the indexed builder
docs.text:
The policy layer selects a policy, and the indexed builder returns the corresponding decision value:

\[ \pi=s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax} Q, \qquad v_\sim=B_{\succ,\pi}v_\succ, \qquad v_\sim(x)=Q(x,\pi(x)). \]
  • VFI / direct search: calculate the maximizing set by maximizing \(Q(x,\cdot)\) over \(\Gamma(x)\) and apply the specified measurable selection \(s\).
  • EGM / first-order inversion: realize the same selection by solving the first-order or Euler relation, usually at an interior marginal node of \(B_\succ\); if the endogenous-grid candidate needs envelope correction, apply \(\operatorname{upper\_env}\) to the method's candidate representation before using the selected policy in the indexed builder.

The recipes are extensionally equivalent only under the usual optimality, monotonicity/concavity or envelope, and measurable-selection assumptions. The recipe specifies a numerical method for the stated mathematical operator.

The source can specify maximization or an implicit policy relation. After a continuation candidate has been defined, c = c[>] may identify the decision control implicitly through the saving transition. That equation remains a relation until a unique solution or a specified measurable selection determines a policy. The endogenous grid method approximates the relation by candidate pairs and interpolation; its numerical steps are not automatically authored operations. Bellman-SYM's Appendix D, §7, states the distinction.

docs.title: 7.3 Why split selection from the indexed builder
docs.text:
The traditional Bellman equation \(v(x)=\sup_a B_\succ(x,a,v_\succ)\) gives the optimal value. Policy selection and the indexed builder provide its displayed decomposition under the stated attainment assumptions. The split keeps their inputs and outputs distinct. Direct search and first-order inversion can approximate the same selection target under the conditions stated above; their policies then index the law of motion, aggregator and conditional distribution. The bundled max form is recovered as

\[ (\max Q)(x) =Q(x,s(Q)(x)), \qquad s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q. \]

docs.title: 8. The defined field function with a handler
docs.text:
An explicit equation defines a function once its inputs, dependencies, and domains are established. A fresh name on the left does not suffice if substitution reveals dependence on an undetermined output. A residual equation states a relation; uniqueness or a specified measurable selection is needed for a function, and optimality is a separate condition.

Examples retained for this outline:

  • A forward residual \(F(a',d,c)=0\) determines the unknown \(a'\) only where existence and a suitable selection are established. Newton iteration is a numerical method for that relation.
  • An interior first-order condition \(\partial_c Q=0\) does not by itself handle bounds or establish a maximum. A first-order or endogenous-grid method requires the appropriate sufficiency and boundary conditions.
  • A function represented at grid points needs an interpolation rule for evaluation between those points. The table alone does not determine those values.

Function, relation, selection, and evaluation have different domains and meanings. A handler computes or approximates the chosen interpretation; it does not supply its mathematical selection theorem.

docs.title: 9. Forward builders
docs.text:
A forward builder pushes a distribution from one perch to the next along the same declared transitions: \(\mathbb{M}_\prec\) from arrival to decision along \(g_\prec\), and \(\mathbb{M}_{\succ,\pi}\) from decision to continuation along \(g_{\succ,\pi}(x,\eta)=g_\succ(x,\pi(x),\eta)\). The policy \(\pi\) is supplied by the policy selection layer, or externally for a fixed-policy calculation. In the semantic graph the decision push-forward is the push-forward at a policy, \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi} \colon \mathsf M_\sim \to \mathsf M_\succ\), its signature the measure it reads and the measure it writes; the policy indexes the transition and any policy-dependent conditional distribution, is typed on the output of the policy builder, and is carried on no input wire (§6).

The transition pairing is the one stated in §3, with \(P_\prec\) and \(P_{\succ,\pi}\). An arrival reward, discounted continuation, or nonlinear aggregator is not part of those probability-transition expectations.

(Placeholder.) Describe the available forward methods for the declared discrete-time transition, such as simulation and histogram approximation. Continuous-time evolution equations require a different model and are not automatically handlers of the displayed discrete-time stage.

docs.title: 10. Intermediate post-decision values
docs.text:
When the decision-to-continuation transition \(g_\succ\) factors through an intermediate state, its induced aggregator \(B_\succ\) can contain a named intermediate operation. What the EGM literature calls the post-decision value or marginal value is one such inner node, exposed so a policy handler can attach to it.

Some decision-to-continuation transitions factor through an intermediate post-decision state — the savings level \(a = m - c\) in consumption-savings, the post-adjustment housing \(h'\) in housing models. The factorization matters because the post-decision value function \(v_{\mathrm{pd}}\) can be represented as an intermediate function on the endogenous grid.

docs.title: 10.1 The factorization
docs.text:
For the alternative consumption–savings timing whose continuation state is next-period resources, let \(g_1(m,c)=a=m-c\) and \(g_2(a,y')=Ra+y'\). This differs from the earlier stage boundary, where continuation is saving and the next arrival stage contains income integration:

\[ m \;\xrightarrow{\,g_1:\, a = m - c\,}\; a \;\xrightarrow{\,g_2:\, m' = R a + y'\,}\; m'. \]

(Placeholder.) The composite is \(g_\succ(m,c,y')=g_2(g_1(m,c),y')\). The income shock \(y'\) enters in \(g_2\), with \(R\) the fixed return — after the decision. This is one timing convention used for the endogenous grid method (EGM); not all stages factor this way, but applicability of an endogenous-grid method requires its own factorization and invertibility or selection conditions.

docs.title: 10.2 The post-decision value function
docs.text:
In the affine expected-utility case, pulling the continuation value back along \(g_2\) and integrating out the post-decision shock produces the post-decision expectation node

\[ v_{\mathrm{pd}}(a) = \int v_\succ(g_2(a,\eta))\,\mu_\eta(d\eta), \]

and the induced aggregator is then \(B_\succ(m,c,v_\succ)=u(c)+\beta\,v_{\mathrm{pd}}(m-c)\) when the reward is decision-measurable. Its marginal \(v_{\mathrm{pd}}'(a)\) is used in the EGM first-order inversion where that marginal exists.

For a nonlinear aggregator kernel, do not assume this separation: the induced aggregator is the integral of \(G_\succ(v_\succ(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta)\) as a whole. A map written outside the integral stays outside it (Stages and perches §2.3a).

docs.title: 10.3 The factored induced aggregator
docs.text:
Returning to generic state \(x\) and action \(a\) (rather than the savings variable of §10.1), the sub-transition factorization records where the post-decision shock enters:

\[ (B_\succ v_\succ)(x,a) = \int G_\succ\bigl(v_\succ(g_2(g_1(x,a),\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(d\eta). \]

In the affine case, this may be implemented as an interior Markov expectation node followed by reward aggregation. The policy selection still sits outside the indexed builder:

\[ \mathbb{T}_{\succ}v_\succ =B_{\succ,s(B_\succ v_\succ)}v_\succ. \]

This is the operator-level reading of EGM: the handler may expose the post-decision expectation or marginal node, solve for a candidate policy, optionally apply \(\operatorname{upper\_env}\) to the candidate representation, and then use that policy in the indexed builder.

docs.title: 11. Numerical decomposition
docs.text: An EGM recipe needs the relevant transition and marginal information. It may obtain these from a builder or from supported named intermediate places, and may perform interpolation, envelope comparisons, and evaluation internally. (Placeholder.) This is the case of partial decomposition: the builder may remain opaque except for the named intermediate nodes a handler needs. The explanation of supported intermediate places remains unfinished; Bellman-SYM's Appendix D defines current source marks and numerical attachment boundaries.

docs.title: 12. Correspondence with Sargent–Stachurski
docs.text:
This folder Recursive dynamic programming reading \(G_\succ(w,x,a,\eta)\) value aggregator, the aggregator kernel acting on a value variable \(B_\succ(x,a,v)\) induced recursive dynamic programming aggregator after pullback along the law of motion and shock integration \(B_\succ:\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) objective constructor \(v\mapsto[(x,a)\mapsto B(x,a,v)]\) \(\operatorname{argmax}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\to\mathcal P(\Pi_\Gamma)\) set of greedy measurable policies, possibly empty \(s:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\rightharpoonup\Pi_\Gamma\) with \(s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q\) specified measurable selector on its domain \(B_{\succ,\pi}:\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\sim\) builder whose transition, aggregator and conditional distribution are indexed by \(\pi\) \((\max Q)(x)=Q(x,s(Q)(x))\) derived Bellman max on the selected attained domain \(\mathbb{T}_{\succ}v=B_{\succ,s(B_\succ v)}v\) optimal continuation-to-decision builder on that domain \(\mathbb{T}_\prec=B_\prec\) policy-free arrival aggregator \(\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{T}_\prec\circ\mathbb{T}_{\succ}\) stage operator

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Summary

A numerical method is written into the signature of the operator it serves. Beside its field component, the functions or measures an operator reads and writes, the signature carries two further components, the operator's method and its grid, each written as a typing of the operator's name. Operators compose over their field components alone; the labels of a composite are kept as a list and never combined. The methods an operator admits are those of its operation kind, the grid is the finite set of points at which a function is stored, and the handler, the program that computes the method, stands outside the calculus. Two erasures recover the model: one forgets the labels, the other forgets the methods file. Nothing is differentiated by the language.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Operators and builders: the operations and builders whose signatures the components extend; The stage term: the many-sorted signature of a stage; Fields, functions and types §1.2: the derivative term; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C: the interpretation rules that fix the meaning of each operation. Formal account — Functional programming §§5, 7 and 8: the term category, the binding maps with the two erasures, and the numerical realization; Kinds and sorts §§3 to 5: the classifier, the settings with their admissible set, and the grids as a kind of their own. Used by — Methodization: what the economist writes in a methods file; Method types: the catalogue of method words with the keyword arguments each reads; the wiki entries methods, grid, addition and settings.

Key terminology Term Meaning on this page operator, occurrence One operation of a stage, such as an expectation or an evaluation, or a builder composed of such operations; it reads and writes functions or measures. An occurrence is one operator with its identity, one box of the stage's builders graph. operation kind The kind of an operation in the operator catalogue: Pullback, Aggregation, Expectation, Evaluation, Argmax and the rest. It is a value of a classifier of the operators, and not a kind of Kinds and sorts §3, which holds every object of one nature. field component The inputs and outputs of an operator, \(X \to Y\), which decide what composes with what. label, method component, grid component The label of an operator is the pair of its method label and its grid label: a method word with its arguments and a grid word with its arguments. The method component is the label's first part, written policy.method : !egm; the grid component its second, written policy.grid : !Cartesian(…). signature of an operator Its field component with its method component and its grid component. The signature of a stage in Kinds and sorts §6 is another object, in which a label changes no rank. identity label The label of an operator that no entry names: the list with no entries, which adds nothing when the labels of a composite are concatenated. Evaluation The operation that stores a builder's result and closes the builder; a representation stands on it. handler The program that computes a method, named by a binding beside the term, written policy.handler : "cons-port:egm". addition A methods file: a .bl file unioned with the stage file before elaboration, which adds entries and lines and removes nothing (addition). rows The lines a solution method supplies, by which a builder is computed. declared level, operative level The stage file's own lines, and the lines a solution method puts in their place for computation. perch marks [<], [~], [>] The mark after a field names its perch: V[<] the value at the arrival perch, c[~] the consumption at the decision perch, V[>] the value at the continuation perch (perch). erasure A map that forgets the labels, or forgets the addition, and returns the model.

docs.title: 1 A method and its place
docs.text:
A stage file states a model: its fields, their laws of motion, its values and its maximization (Stages and perches). Computing the model requires choices the model does not make: how an expectation over a shock is integrated, how a function is stored between the points at which it is computed, how a maximization is carried out. A method is one such choice, named by a word. The word !gauss_hermite integrates an expectation by Gauss–Hermite quadrature, !Linear stores a function by piecewise linear interpolation, and !egm computes the policy by the endogenous grid method. A method serves one operator of the stage, an operation such as an expectation or an evaluation, or a builder composed of such operations (Operators and builders §6), and it is written on that operator's name and on nothing else: not on a field, which is a quantity and not a computation, and not on a side of a block header, the inputs before the arrow or the outputs after it, whose perch word types the states and the values listed on it (Kinds and sorts §5).

The economist writes the method in a methods file, an addition to the stage file, as a typing of the operator's method component, policy.method : !egm, and the operator's grid beside it, policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)); the Bellman-SYM page on methodization gives the written forms. This page gives the mathematics of the two entries: the signature of an operator with its components (§2), how such operators compose (§3), what a method is (§4) and what a grid is (§5), where the settings and the handler stand (§§6, 7), how the model is recovered from the methodized stage (§8), what a solution method changes in a stage (§9), and what no method may do (§10).

A method is not an argument of its operator. Two methods at one operator read the same inputs and write the same outputs, and they differ in the numbers they produce. Piecewise linear interpolation of \(x^2\) on the grid \(\{0, \tfrac12, 1\}\) gives \(\tfrac18\) at \(x = \tfrac14\), where the function is \(\tfrac1{16}\); on the grid \(\{0, \tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac34, 1\}\) it gives \(\tfrac1{16}\), since \(\tfrac14\) is then a node, and a cubic interpolant on the first grid gives a third number. The stored function changes with the method and the grid, while its domain and codomain, \(\mathbb R \to \mathbb R\), do not.

docs.title: 2 The signature with its components
docs.text:
Every operator of a stage has a field component, written \(X \to Y\): \(X\) is the sort of what it reads and \(Y\) the sort of what it writes, each the name of a space of functions or of the finite measures on the state space of a perch (The stage term §1). For a builder it is the rank of the builder in the operator signature of the stage (Kinds and sorts §6); an operation inside a builder has its rank in the finer signature of The stage term §3. The expectation of the buffer-stock arrival builder reads a function of the decision state and the shocks and writes a function of the arrival state; the policy builder reads the continuation value and writes the policy. The field component decides what composes with what, and it is the only component of the signature that the model fixes.

The signature of a methodized operator \(\omega\) carries two further components,

\[ \omega : M,\ G,\ X \to Y, \]

the method component \(M\) and the grid component \(G\). Each is a classifier in the sense of Kinds and sorts §3, D6, as Kinds and sorts §6 applies it to the operators: a function from the operators of the stage to a set of labels, whose fibers are the operators that share a label. \(M\) names the numerical method, chosen among the methods admitted at an operator of \(\omega\)'s operation kind (§4), and \(G\) names the grid on the domain of the function the operator stores or evaluates (§5). Each is assigned by one typing entry of the operator's name, policy.method : !egm and policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)). An operator that no entry names carries the identity label in that component, with one exception: the Evaluation of an !explicit builder carries the closed form generated from the builder's entry (§5). The handler, the program that computes the method, is no component of the signature; it is a binding beside the term (§7).

Formally, let \(\Sigma\) be the free category on the stage's operators: the graph whose vertices are the sorts of the wires with their perches, products of sorts among them, and whose edges are the operation symbols, each from its input sort to its output sort (The stage term §1). A morphism of \(\Sigma\) is a finite path of operation symbols, composed by concatenation, and a functor out of \(\Sigma\) is fixed by its values on the vertices and the edges, since a path is a finite sequence of edges (Kinds and sorts §6). A path is a term in which each operation reads one wire and no wire is read twice. In general an operation may read several wires and a wire may be read twice, and the terms of a stage are then the arrows of the free category with finite products on the same sorts and symbols, tuples of terms composed by substitution (Functional programming §5). The construction that follows is stated for paths. The label of an operator is the pair of its method label and its grid label: a method word with its arguments and a grid word with its arguments. Let \(\mathcal M\) be the free monoid on the labels, the finite lists of labels with concatenation as the tensor, written \(\odot\), and the list with no entries as the unit, the identity label; read \(\mathcal M\) as a strict monoidal category whose only morphisms are identities, acting trivially on \(\Sigma\), \(M \bullet X = X\). The parametrized morphisms of Capucci, Gavranović, Hedges and Rischel (2022, Definition 2, p. 236) form the bicategory \(\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal M}(\Sigma)\):1 its objects are those of \(\Sigma\), and a 1-cell from \(X\) to \(Y\) with parameter \(M\) is an object \(M\) of \(\mathcal M\) together with a morphism \(M \bullet X \to Y\), which under the trivial action is a path \(X \to Y\) carrying the list \(M\). Its 2-cells are identities, \(\mathcal M\) having no others, so it is a category. The parameter of a parametrized morphism is here a list of labels, and it is no parameter of the stage (Kinds and sorts §4). The methodized signature is \(\Sigma_m = \mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal M}(\Sigma)\), and a labeled generator is an operation symbol \(\omega\) with the one-element list \([\ell]\), \(\ell\) a label admitted at \(\omega\) (§4), or with the identity label. A methodized operator is therefore its field component together with its label. In a term that is no path, each occurrence of an operation symbol carries its label in the same way, one label for each occurrence and none composed with another. The label is a factor of its own beside \(X\) and no classifier of \(X\): a method is written on the operator, never on the field it reads, and never on the output field, since a wire carries no label.

docs.title: 3 Composition over the field component
docs.text:
Two operators compose when the output sort of the first is the input sort of the second, \(\operatorname{cod}(\omega_1) = \operatorname{dom}(\omega_2)\), and the condition reads the field components alone. The field component of the composite is the composite of the two maps. Its method component is the list of the two methods, kept and not composed, and its grid component the list of the two grids. A builder composed of a pullback, an aggregation and an evaluation carries the three labels of those operations; the stage operator carries the labels of its builders. Nothing of the model is lost in a composite, because the erasure of §8 returns the composite of the field components.

The labels are not composed because two labels have no product that is again a method: the catalogue admits a method at a generator of one of the operation kinds of §4, and a composite formed in \(\Sigma_m\) is of none of those kinds. A builder that admits a solution method, such as the policy builder under !egm, is one generator at the operative level, whose lines the method supplies (§9).

Formally, the composite of \(X \to Y\) with parameter \(M_1\) and \(Y \to Z\) with parameter \(M_2\) is the morphism \(X \to Z\) with parameter \(M_2 \odot M_1\), the two base morphisms composed and the two parameters tensored (Capucci, Gavranović, Hedges and Rischel 2022, Definition 2, item 3, p. 236).1 With concatenation as the tensor, the parameter of a path of labeled generators is the list of their labels, the later generator's first, and the identity label of a generator without an entry adds nothing to it. The list is the ruling's collection: each label stands in it beside the others, and none is composed with another.

docs.title: 4 The method as a type over the kind of operator
docs.text:
Which methods an operator admits depends on its operation kind. A quadrature rule is admitted at an expectation, an interpolant at the Evaluation that stores a builder's result, a solution method such as the endogenous grid method at the policy builder, a root finder at a maximization written as a first-order condition, and a discretization of a law at the expectation that integrates against it. The derivative operator D admits no method, because the language differentiates nothing (§10).

Formally, \(\mathrm{Method}\) is a family of sets indexed by the operation kinds: \(\mathrm{Method}(\kappa)\) is the set of the methods admitted at an operator of operation kind \(\kappa\), and the method component of an operator \(\omega\) of operation kind \(\kappa\) is a member of \(\mathrm{Method}(\kappa)\) or the identity label. The set in which the label lies depends on the operator it labels, which is all that a dependent type means here: the type system of the calculus has no dependent function types and is no dependent type theory (Kinds and sorts §1). The family is indexed by the operators through their operation kinds: the labels a method assignment may place on a generator \(\omega\) of operation kind \(\kappa\) are those of \(\mathrm{Method}(\kappa)\) and the identity label, the fiber of the family over \(\omega\), in the sense in which a family of sets indexed by a set is displayed as a map onto the index set, each set standing over its index (Jacobs 1999, §1.1, pp. 20–21).2 A method is a member of the fiber, written by its word with keyword arguments: !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes) is a member of \(\mathrm{Method}(\mathrm{Expectation})\) at an expectation over two shocks, !Linear(extrapolate=extrap_policy) a member of \(\mathrm{Method}(\mathrm{Evaluation})\), and !egm a member of the set at the policy builder. The value after each equals sign in these words is the name of a setting that the methods file declares, as in extrap_policy : {0, 1}. In a methods file the method word is the type that the entry writes after its colon (Kinds and sorts §§2 and 6), and the entry asserts that the operator has that method. The catalogue of method words with the operation kinds each admits is the Bellman-SYM reference page on method types. Methods have no subtyping: no method stands for another.

Every argument of a method word is a keyword argument, written key=value, whose value is the name of a declared setting (§6), a quoted string, or a word with its own arguments. No number is written in a method's entry, as none is written in a grid's (§5): every number that a method reads is a declared setting, which the entry names and the settings file values. Two versions of a stage that differ only in such a number therefore have one method assignment and differ in their configuration. The catalogue row lists the keywords the package reads, each with the set in which its value lies; a further keyword is read by the handler that computes the method (§7), so that an argument a handler needs can be written without a change to the language. What a method does outside its grid, such as extrapolation or clamping at the bounds, is a keyword argument of the method word and no part of the grid.

A method does one of three things to the stage, according to the operator it stands on. A representation, such as !Linear, !pchip or !closed_form, stores a function from the data its family accepts, among them its values on the grid its grid component names (§5): at the Evaluation that closes a builder, one entry for everything the Evaluation stores or one entry per stored object, evaluate[V[<]].method and evaluate[D_{k}V[<]].method, each with its own grid; or at a line marked !node, a computation inside a block that the author names so that a method can stand on it; or at a declared function. A solution method, such as !egm, stands on a builder and supplies the lines by which the builder is computed (§9); !vfi is a solution method that supplies no lines. A method of an operator of a line fixes how that operation is computed: a quadrature or a discretization of a law at an expectation, !gauss_hermite or !tauchen, and a root finder or a search at a maximization.

docs.title: 5 The grid as the discretized domain
docs.text:
A grid is the finite set of points of a function's domain at which a method computes and stores the function; between the points the representation supplies the values. The grid is written as its own component of the operator's signature, the discretized domain, by the entry policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)): the grid word !Cartesian names a product of one node set per coordinate, keyed by the coordinate's name, and a factor is a triple of declared settings, the lower bound, the upper bound and the count, with an optional spacing word, or a declared node set, or the expectation operator whose quadrature nodes the coordinate takes, or, for a control, its feasible set with a count. The wiki entry grid lists the four shapes of a factor with their spellings. Two further grid words stand in the same entry. !Points(nodes=P) is the finite set of the declared points P, each written in the domain's declared coordinate order, and !Points alone is the empty grid. !Fibred(base=…, fibre=!Cartesian(c=(Γ_c, n_c))) pairs each state of a finite base grid with the finite grid of the control's feasible set at that state, so that its points lie in the graph of the feasible set, the feasible pairs of state and control. Each grid word may carry require= with one predicate word, or a tuple of them, among !Empty, !Cartesian, !NonCartesian and !UniformCartesian: properties the resulting grid must have, not further components. No number stands in the entry: the bounds, the counts and the points of !Points are settings declared in the methods file (§6), or the points are a finite set the stage defines.

A grid's coordinates follow the arguments of the function held at its place, in declared order, including shock coordinates where present. Omitting a grid entry supplies no numerical bounds, counts or nodes. A partial entry leaves omitted coordinates in the function's domain. The endogenous grid method uses continuation-state coordinates for its solution grid, the predetermined end-of-period assets from which policy pairs are generated (Carroll 2006, §2.2, p. 315).3 An interpolant built from those pairs uses their decision-state nodes, not another independent policy grid. An authored evaluate(knots, values, x) instead reads its supplied table. Each representation family records the data sources it accepts, and the stage selects one in this order: an authored table; the policy pairs of !egm at the closing Evaluation of its builder, for a family that accepts them, where a representation grid is refused; a complete authored expression, which !closed_form reads without a grid and which the Evaluation of an !explicit builder takes where no entry names another representation; and otherwise the values of the function sampled on the representation's own grid. stage.methods[place].source names the selected source.

A grid is a numerical object and no part of the model. A discrete set that belongs to the economics, such as the set of housing sizes a household chooses among, is the declared set of a field, written in the stage file, and the scalars that define it are parameters (Kinds and sorts §§4 and 5; the catalogue Parameters and settings); a grid approximates a continuous domain and names settings. When configure binds the settings, the package checks each bound pair ordered and inside the coordinate's declared set, each count at least two, each node set strictly increasing, each declared point's shape, finite coordinates and, where it is decided, membership of the declared sets, and each written requirement that the bound values decide. Numerical construction establishes the remaining requirements and the feasible grids of !Fibred before the grid is used and reports a requirement it cannot establish; a builder's kernels().grids holds the constructed grid of each place or that report. It checks nothing about accuracy or about the region of the domain the model's distribution visits; those are propositions about the method, which the package does not check.

Formally, a grid on a domain \(X\) is a finite subset \(G \subseteq X\) with its inclusion \(\iota : G \to X\). Fix admitted functions \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb R^X\) and nodal data \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^G\) such that restriction \(r(f)=f\circ\iota\) maps \(\mathcal F\) into \(\mathcal A\). An interpolating representation supplies \(s:\mathcal A\to\mathcal F\) reproducing those data,

\[ r \circ s = \mathrm{id}_{\mathcal A}, \]

so that \(s\) is a section and \(r\) a retraction in the sense of Adámek, Herrlich and Strecker (2004, Definitions 7.19 and 7.24, pp. 106–107).4 Thus \(\mathcal A\) is a retract of \(\mathcal F\). The composite \(e=s\circ r\) on \(\mathcal F\) is idempotent, \(e\circ e=s\circ(r\circ s)\circ r=e\), and its fixed points are exactly the functions in the image of \(s\).

On at least two strictly ordered real nodes, piecewise linear and shape-preserving cubic interpolation can give different sections when their common admitted functions, data and evaluation domain satisfy these conditions. Evaluation beyond the knot interval requires a specified extension. Other fitting criteria need not reproduce nodal data, so the section law and this idempotence argument do not apply to every representation. The inclusion \(\iota\) is a map of sets and establishes no subsort relation between the grid and the domain; by Kinds and sorts §5 the grids form a kind of their own.

docs.title: 6 Settings
docs.text: A setting is a name declared with a set in a methods file, whose value a method or a grid reads: a bound or a count of a grid, a tolerance, the number of quadrature nodes, a rule chosen among finitely many names (Kinds and sorts §4). The methods file declares each setting it reads at file level, in the form a stage file declares a parameter, with its set and a description, n_a : ℕ, a_min : Xa for a bound on the set Xa the stage declares for the savings coordinate, tol_v : ℝ₊₊. The values stand in the settings file, and configure binds them as calibrate binds a parameter's value, refusing a value outside the declared set and a name with no value. The values bound form a configuration, one point of the admissible set of the settings at the bound calibration (Kinds and sorts §4). The declared sets of the settings define that set together with the conditions that a method word (§4) and a grid word (§5) put on the settings they name. A setting is told from a parameter by the file that declares it: a parameter is declared by the stage file, a setting by the methods file. A derived parameter, which a methods file may also define, as in h := 1/(1 - Γ/R), is defined by := and is no setting (Kinds and sorts §4; the wiki entry parameters). No value of a setting is part of a signature, and no number is: the grid component and the method word name the settings, and the configured values stand in the bindings. The wiki entry settings gives the declarations, the scope of a name and the table stage.settings.

docs.title: 7 The handler and the realization
docs.text:
A handler is the program that computes a method, named by its package and its function and written as a binding beside the term, policy.handler : "cons-port:egm", at any operator that admits a method, with or without a method word. The handler is no classifier of the signature, because it names a program and gives the operator no label. The calculus says what an operator means and which method labels it; the handler realizes the labeled operator under Ρ, the passage from the mathematical operations to their numerical representations (Ρ), written \(\mathrm P\) in the formulas below.

Formally, the exact semantics \(\Upsilon : \Sigma \to \mathcal B\) assigns each operation symbol its operation in the target algebra \(\mathcal B\) of the calculus, fixed on the edges by the interpretation rules of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C and extended to every path by composition. A label denotes nothing under \(\Upsilon\): the meaning of a methodized term is \(\Upsilon \circ U_m\), the meaning of its erasure (§8), which is the precise form of the statement that the model does not depend on its labels. A label is read by the numerical semantics \(\mathrm P\), a functor from the methodized terms, the paths of labeled generators that \(M_m\) of §8 produces, into the category \(\mathcal D\) of representations, whose value on a labeled generator \((\omega, M, G)\) is a morphism \(\mathrm P(\omega, M, G) : \mathrm P X \to \mathrm P Y\) of \(\mathcal D\), the routine the handler computes; since a methodized term is a path of labeled generators, \(\mathrm P\) is fixed on every one by its values on them. This is the shape of a handler of an algebraic effect in Plotkin and Pretnar (2009): each handler "corresponds to a model of the theory", and handling a term is the homomorphism the model induces (abstract; §3.2 for operation symbols with parameters, in that paper the values of base types that an operation symbol takes).5 Their model satisfies the equations of the effect theory; \(\mathrm P\) satisfies the arities of the labeled generators and nothing more, so it is a model of the signature, the theory without its equations. Functional programming §8 writes the realization of a fully specified expression \(e\) as \(\mathrm P_{c,m,s}(e)\), which is \(\mathrm P\) applied to the term \(K_s\, M_m\, \mathcal C_c(e)\) with its calibration \(c\), its method assignment \(m\) and its configuration \(s\) bound, as they stand in the configured version of the stage (Kinds and sorts §6).

Exact Evaluation carries the stored function unchanged. For an interpolating representation satisfying §5's law on its admitted functions and data, restriction followed by reconstruction is the idempotent \(s\circ r\) on \(\mathcal F\), and \(r\circ s\) is the identity on \(\mathcal A\). These conclusions depend on nodal reproduction; they are not general properties of every representation or fitting algorithm.

Whether the realized operator is close to the exact one, a relation between \(\Upsilon\) and \(\mathrm P\) composed with the maps that decode a representation, is the semiconjugacy of Semi-conjugacy: a proposition to be proved for each method under its conditions, and no typing fact.

docs.title: 8 The two erasures
docs.text:
Two things can be forgotten. Forget the labels: every operator keeps its inputs, outputs and equations, and its method and grid components become empty, while the lines a methods file added, the derivative lines and the rows of a solution method, remain. Forget the methods file: everything it added is removed, and the stage file's own term returns. The first says that the meaning of the operations does not depend on the labels; the second returns the model itself, the stage file.

Formally, the erasure of the labels \(U_m : \Sigma_m \to \Sigma\) is the functor that is the identity on objects and forgets the parameter of every morphism. A method assignment \(m\), the entries of a methods file read after the union with the closed forms that !explicit entries generate (§5), defines the methodization \(M_m : \Sigma \to \Sigma_m\) on each operation symbol \(\omega\) as \(\omega\) with the parameter \([m(\omega)]\), and with the identity label on every generator without an entry, so that \(M_m\) is total; it extends to every path by composition, the labels concatenated as §3 states, and is a functor because \(\Sigma\) is free on its operation symbols. The section law

\[ U_m \circ M_m = \mathrm{id}_{\Sigma} \]

holds on every path, since forgetting the parameter of \(\omega\) with parameter \([m(\omega)]\) returns \(\omega\) and a path's parameter is the concatenation of its generators' parameters: \(M_m\) is a section and \(U_m\) a retraction (Adámek, Herrlich and Strecker 2004, Definitions 7.19 and 7.24, pp. 106–107).4 \(U_m\) is many-to-one, and no isomorphism between a method and anything else is claimed.

The erasure of the addition \(U_a\) acts on the term before elaboration. A methods file is an addition \(A\), and the union \(S \sqcup A\) of the stage file \(S\) with it keeps the provenance of every item, the file and position it was written at (addition). \(U_a\) removes the items whose provenance is \(A\), so that

\[ U_a(S \sqcup A) = S . \]

The union is associative with the empty addition as its unit, and \(S\) stands as its leftmost operand, so several additions apply in the order the recipe of the stage's trellis lists them (specification factory) and \(U_a\) removes them together. \(U_a\) removes what \(U_m\) keeps: the derivative lines, the rows of a solution method, the declared settings and any coordinate an addition appends to a signature. On the elaborated stage the result of \(U_a\) is the declared level of §9, which the stage stores.

docs.title: 9 The two levels of a stage
docs.text:
A solution method computes a builder by lines of its own. The endogenous grid method computes the policy by the Euler equation inverted by the inverse marginal utility, the line of the endogenous grid and the identification of the policy with its candidate,

[id=policy, policy.method : !egm | policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
    | evaluate.method : !Linear] {
    c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>])       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m[>] = a + c[>]                 :: [id=g_cntn_to_dcsn]
    c[~] = c[>]                     :: [id=cons_choice]
}

where 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is the inverse of the marginal utility 𝑑𝑢 the stage defines, in place of the maximization c = argmax_{cp : Γ_c(m)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>]) the stage file declares, with Γ_c(m) the feasible set of consumption at resources m. The stage holds both. The declared level is the stage file's own lines, read by stage.declared; the operative level is the stage as it is computed, in which the rows of an addition's block whose method component holds a solution method stand in place of the declared lines of that block. A derivative line, D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), stands at both levels: it states a property of the value the model defines, the envelope condition, true under the conditions of §10, and defines no new field; the author may write it in the stage file or in the methods file, where derivatives are read, and it adds no step of computation. A solution method that supplies no rows, !vfi, leaves the declared lines in place at both levels. Where a block's method component holds no solution method, an appended line is an authored line of the block, and a second definition of a field is refused. The declared level is stored and not reconstructed, so the erasure of §8 returns it exactly. The stage's graphs as elaborated from the stage file, its two initial diagrams and its declared builders (semgraph), are unchanged by any binding; what a method changes stands in the operative builders alone, the builders as computed.

The condition under which the method's lines compute the maximization, the first-order condition being necessary and sufficient and the envelope condition holding, is an obligation: the stage lists it, under egm-eligibility, and checks nothing. Under that condition the operative builder denotes the declared operation; without it the two levels denote different operators. Whether two methods compute the same policy is a separate proposition with its own conditions, and no component of a signature claims it.

docs.title: 10 Nothing is differentiated
docs.text:
The language differentiates no expression: no derivative rule is attached to any operation kind, the derivative operator D admits no method, and the only analytic statement of a derivative is a line the author writes. The derivative of a value is read by the derivative term, D_{a}V[>], the derivative operator applied to a value field in the coordinate of its subscript (Fields, functions and types §1.2), and it is stated by a derivative line, D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), the envelope condition of the decision value. A row of a method that reads a derivative term declares a reading and nothing more.

Two facts about stored numbers are not differentiation of an expression. At realization, a handler that meets a derivative term no line states evaluates it through the representation the methods file fixed for that value, reading the slope of the stored interpolant, which for piecewise linear interpolation is a step function. Where a value passes through a builder whose lines are identities, expectations or scalings of the value it reads, the realization applies the same linear map to the stored derivative values, so that the envelope line of the decision value serves the stage before it; for an expectation this asserts that the derivative of the expectation is the expectation of the derivative, which holds under a dominating bound. The condition under which a stated derivative line holds, that the value is differentiable and the envelope theorem applies, is an obligation the stage lists under marginal-reading and checks nothing; the exchange of the derivative and the expectation is a condition recorded under the name differentiation-under-the-integral for the arrival builder it concerns, and no stage lists it yet. Where the law of motion between two perches is not the identity in the differentiated coordinate, the author writes the derivative line with the law's factor, as the buffer-stock arrival builder writes D_{k}V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}(R * (Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) * D_{m}V), with Γ the growth factor of permanent income.

docs.title: Stage composition
docs.text:
Summary

These unfinished notes describe composition of stages through compatible boundary fields. A connector selects a continuation-to-arrival field pair without renaming either field; a transformation must be specified by an equation.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches defines the stage operators. See also — Periods and the trellis discusses joins across dates. Used by — Period Syntax defines the YAML outer composition whose joins this chapter describes.

Not yet drafted — stub notes only

Structural outline only; the within-period composition chapter is not yet written.

Consider a period whose stage dependencies form a chain, indexed in forward economic order by \(k=1,\ldots,K\). The continuation fields of stage \(\mathbb{S}_k\) and the arrival fields of \(\mathbb{S}_{k+1}\) have separate stage-local identities. Selected pairs relate their eligible uses; an authored connector states a pair explicitly. If the ordered state coordinates form a compatible complete route and the stage operators are well defined on the required function spaces, the backward period operator for this chain is the composite \(\mathbb{T}_{\text{period}} = \mathbb{T}_{\mathbb{S}_1} \circ \ldots \circ \mathbb{T}_{\mathbb{S}_K}\), where each \(\mathbb T_{\mathbb S_k}\) is that stage's backward value operator. This conditional display is not a general composition theorem for all period shapes.

docs.title: 1. Connectors
docs.text: A connector pairs an eligible continuation state field of one stage occurrence with an eligible arrival state field of another. It does not change either stage's field name or equations. (Placeholder.) A simple pairing is \(a'\mapsto a\) when the two fields have compatible declared sets and the author establishes their common economic meaning, units and boundary information. Declared sets are compatible when the continuation field's set is contained in the arrival field's. In the terms of Appendix D, the continuation declaration \(f\) lies in \(\mathrm{Dom}[D_g]\) for the arrival declaration \(g\), that is, \(D_f\subseteq D_g\) (D6), so that the pairing sends every value of the continuation field to a value the arrival field admits. Equality \(D_f=D_g\) is not required: a declared set contains a field's values and need not be exhausted by them. When a route pairs whole ordered state tuples, the induced coordinate map reads the destination coordinates from those of the source; a crossed pairing can therefore be a permutation without an inverse state transition. A nonidentity economic transformation must appear in an authored stage equation. Equal names or domains alone do not identify arbitrary fields.

docs.title: 2. Composing stages into periods
docs.text:
The input-to-output signature is also the rule for joining stages. A period is a collection of stage occurrences (uses of stage modules) with selected connections. In the chain considered here, joining compatible boundary fields pairs the continuation state coordinates of one stage with the arrival state coordinates of its successor. The successor's arrival value then supplies the predecessor's continuation value under that coordinate map, provided the required value components agree and the declared set of each continuation state field lies in that of the arrival state field paired with it. Separate marginal shock laws do not establish the joint forward law needed for a complete route.

Two stages composed into a period; the double line in the center identifies the shared boundary perch $\succ^{0} = \prec^{1}$.

The double line denotes the boundary identification in this example. Operators compose right to left in the backward calculation, provided their domains and codomains agree after that identification. The equations, feasible sets and conditional laws retain their stage-specific assumptions.

Changing the order of names in a period's YAML list does not change the economic dependencies. Reordering the economic stages or changing a successor can instead change information, feasibility or rewards, and requires the model to be checked again. A stage can be reused with a compatible continuation problem; the composition rule is not a general invariance theorem for arbitrary swaps. Branch-specific successors require their explicit routes, as in Branching.

docs.title: 3. Intra-period vs inter-period connectors
docs.text: This file covers intra-period wiring (stage-to-stage within one period). Inter-period wiring (period-to-period, with occurrence-specific boundary identifications) is covered in Periods and the trellis.

Next → 8. Periods and trellis

docs.title: Periods and the trellis
docs.text:
Summary

These unfinished notes extend stage composition across periods and distinguish finite-horizon recursion from a stationary fixed-point problem. Boundary identifications and terminal data must match the declared domains.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stage composition defines compatible within-period joins. See also — Stages and perches states the local operators and information assumptions. Used by — Period Syntax and Trellis Syntax specify the outer YAML structure; Stages describes the source's typed declarations.

Not yet drafted — stub notes only

Structural outline only; the multi-period and trellis chapter is not yet written.

A period contains stage occurrences (uses of stage modules) connected through their boundary fields. A trellis orders period occurrences and their inter-period connections. A recursive problem also supplies terminal or infinite-horizon conditions; a one-stage problem is included as a special case.

docs.title: 1. Period as a local namespace
docs.text: A period contains stage occurrences and their dependencies, but each stage keeps its own field names. A name declared as a parameter by two stages of one period denotes one period parameter; the same spelling in another period denotes another. In a chain, selected dependencies determine a forward economic order. (Placeholder.) The period operator \(\mathbb{T}_{\text{period}}\) has the conditional composition reading described in Stage composition where compatible complete routes and operators are supplied; the period's boundary fields are the arrival of its first stage and the continuation of its last.

docs.title: 2. Inter-period connectors
docs.text: Between-period connectors pair one period's boundary continuation fields with the next period's boundary arrival fields. (Placeholder.) These are the inter-period connectors in the project's vocabulary — occurrence-specific selections, not changes to a field's local name. A nonidentity transformation must be authored as a stage equation; the connector performs no calculation. They differ from intra-period connectors, which join stages within a single period.

docs.title: 3. The trellis
docs.text:
A trellis is a finite-horizon sequence of period instances wired by between-period connectors. (Placeholder.) The backward recursion runs:

\[ v_{T+1} \;=\; v_{\mathrm{terminal}}, \qquad v_t \;=\; \mathbb{T}_{t}\, v_{t+1}, \qquad t = T, T{-}1, \ldots, 0. \]

Here \(t\) is forward economic time, \(T\) the last decision date, \(v_{\mathrm{terminal}}\) the supplied terminal value, and \(\mathbb T_t\) the possibly date-dependent period operator. The display uses compatible boundary identifications. The application's period index may instead count backward from terminal; §1 of Bellman-SYM's Trellis Syntax page defines that separate convention.

In the specified construction, each stage occurrence has a fresh graph and bindings even when module text is parsed once. The .bl syntax tree is temporary; interpreted equations and definitions remain. Periods, trellises, connectors, methods, settings and calibration retain their YAML outer forms. A mathematical composition expression does not assert one stored whole-trellis semantic graph.

docs.title: 4. Infinite horizon and the fixed point
docs.text:
For a stationary period operator mapping a chosen value-function space to itself, a candidate infinite-horizon value satisfies:

\[ v^\star \;=\; \mathbb{T}_{\text{period}}\, v^\star. \]

(Placeholder.) State the model-specific conditions for existence, uniqueness and iteration convergence. A contraction on a nonempty complete metric space is one sufficient route; monotone or other fixed-point arguments need their own assumptions. A one-period composition alone establishes none of these results.

docs.title: 5. Information and composition
docs.text: A staged description records the economic order, information available for each choice, and compatible interfaces. Composition then defines the larger recursion where each operation is well defined. (Placeholder.) Develop this account without treating every recursive program as an instance of the present finite stage representation.

docs.title: 6. Composition as identification of fields
docs.text:
For a chain of stages \(S_1,S_2\), selected pairs relate the continuation state fields of \(S_1\) to compatible arrival state fields of \(S_2\). A connector declares a pair and leaves each field's local name intact. A complete route establishes a coordinate map only when all ordered state coordinates, the joint forward law and the backward value components agree. Mathematical transformations belong in the equations, as in Stage composition.

Fields and value domains. A field is a random quantity on the model's probability space. A declaration that its values lie in a domain \(D\) does not make it square-integrable or select a particular function space. Measurability, integrability and a representative function require their stated assumptions. Fields, functions and types distinguishes these objects; the source's typed declarations are described on Bellman-SYM's Stages page.

Identification and names. A common compatible value domain is needed for a direct pairing but is not sufficient: assets and age can both take nonnegative real values while denoting different quantities. A boundary join must pair the intended quantities with compatible units and information. Under a common probabilistic interpretation, the equality \(X_{S_2,\prec}=X_{S_1,\succ}\) holds almost surely at that boundary when the connection pairs those coordinates; equality of their written names alone does not assert it. A declared transformation \(X_{S_2,\prec}=\varkappa(X_{S_1,\succ})\) instead requires the typed measurable map \(\varkappa\) in the model equations.

Composition of meanings. Under the fixed interpretation and compatible interfaces, evaluating a composition means composing its stage operators. The associativity of function composition permits regrouping an unchanged sequence; it does not permit arbitrary reordering or supply convergence. Initial-algebra semantics states the corresponding exact term argument with free inputs fixed.

Related theory

Algebraic composition provides an account of how declared operations form a larger expression. Its applicability here requires compatible domains and the same target interpretation. The mathematical expression is distinct from the stage-dependency graph used to order computation and from the application's period dictionaries.

Next → 9. Branching

docs.title: Branching
docs.text:
Summary

These unfinished notes distinguish choices between labeled alternatives from exogenous branch selection. Branch values must be evaluated at the same decision state before comparison, with feasibility and selection conditions stated.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches supplies the decision-state and continuation-value conventions. Formal account — Operator algebra §5 states the finite-branch interpretation. Used by — Branching gives current source examples; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C reads their selection and evaluation forms.

Not yet drafted — stub notes only

Structural outline only; the branching and coproduct chapter is not yet written.

A branch label distinguishes alternative continuations, such as work or retirement. A finite disjoint union can represent those labeled state spaces. A product state, by contrast, records several coordinates of one state; these constructions serve different purposes.

docs.title: 1. The coproduct continuation
docs.text:
For a finite number \(N\) of alternatives, a labeled continuation state space may be represented as a disjoint union:

\[ \mathsf{X}_\succ \;=\; \mathsf{X}_{\succ,\,1} \,\sqcup\, \mathsf{X}_{\succ,\,2} \,\sqcup\, \ldots \,\sqcup\, \mathsf{X}_{\succ,\,N}, \]

one summand per branch \(j\). (Placeholder.) Each branch has its own law of motion, possibly its own dimensionality, and its own continuation value \(v_{\succ, j}\).

docs.title: 2. Labeled alternatives and state coordinates
docs.text: A disjoint union records a label even when two alternatives use the same underlying state space or differ only in parameters. Conversely, different transition formulas do not by themselves force a particular representation. Choose a representation that retains the information needed for future laws, rewards and feasible choices. (Placeholder.) The relation between labeled alternatives and a common state space with a label coordinate remains to be explained.

docs.title: 3.1 Work or retire
docs.text:
The agent at the decision perch chooses \(d \in \{\text{work}, \text{retire}\}\). (Placeholder.) Retirement is absorbing only when the declared retired route excludes return to work. Let \(Q_{\mathrm{work}}(m)\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{retire}}(m)\) be branch decision values at current resources \(m\), including branch-specific rewards, transitions and any conditional continuous optimization. When the relevant maxima exist,

\[ v(m) \;=\; \max\bigl\{\, Q_{\mathrm{work}}(m),\; Q_{\mathrm{retire}}(m)\,\bigr\}. \]

A numerical candidate-envelope method may compare the branch candidates when its feasibility, coverage and selection conditions hold.

docs.title: 3.2 Default or repay
docs.text: The sovereign chooses \(d \in \{\text{repay}, \text{default}\}\). (Placeholder.) The model specifies the default regime, market access and any return to borrowing. Its continuation can be represented by a labeled alternative; the representation alone does not determine its state dimension or economic rules.

docs.title: 3.3 Adjust or keep housing
docs.text: The household chooses \(d \in \{\text{adjust}, \text{keep}\}\). (Placeholder.) The declared housing transitions and feasible regions determine the difference between the alternatives.

docs.title: 4. Choice and exogenous selection
docs.text:
Let \(Q_j(x)\) be the branch decision values on a common current state \(x\). There are two distinct aggregations:

  • Agent choice: \(v(x)=\max_{j\in J(x)}Q_j(x)\) for the finite nonempty feasible label set \(J(x)\), with a specified measurable maximizing selection when a policy is needed.
  • Exogenous selection: \(v(x)=\sum_j p(j\mid x)Q_j(x)\) for declared conditional branch probabilities \(p(j\mid x)\).

(Placeholder.) Develop numerical methods for these declared operations. A persistent regime requires the state to retain its relevant information; the label need not be a separate coordinate if a sufficient state already encodes it.

Selection and numerical envelopes

Finite choice and continuous choice can both be written as optimization, while a finite mixture is an expectation. Their domains and economic interpretation remain distinct. An envelope operation compares a specified candidate family and selected outputs; numerical candidate comparisons may also be internal to a method. An upper_env name does not guarantee candidate completeness, optimality or convergence. Ties may have positive probability, including under atomless state laws.

docs.title: 4.1 Branch values and policies
docs.text:
The mathematical decomposition is

\[ \pi(x)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in J(x)}Q_j(x), \qquad v(x)=Q_{\pi(x)}(x), \]

where a measurable selection is required for \(\pi\) to be an admissible policy. Equal branch values need not select a unique branch. Differentiating the selected branch gives a value derivative only under the appropriate envelope and differentiability conditions; no such conclusion is automatic at a tie.

Stage and branch equations are authored in .bl. The modeler chooses block and control names, including the branch label. Current branch indexing and authored selection/evaluation forms are specified in Bellman-SYM's Branching page and in rules R8 and R12 and §4.7 of its Appendix C. These source rules do not infer missing rewards or maximization conditions.

docs.title: 5. Choice-conditional values
docs.text: A choice-conditional value is the value of a specified branch, evaluated at the current decision state after accounting for that branch's reward and continuation problem. The optimized value is the maximum over feasible branch values, as in §4. This must not be confused with a continuation function on a branch's next-state space. (Placeholder.) Complete the literature discussion and worked calculations for these examples.
