docs.title: Appendix F — Operator algebra
docs.text:
Summary

Operator composition combines transition, reward, selection and evaluation operations with compatible types. The transition operators have a distribution/function pairing; optimizing operations require additional assumptions. This appendix distinguishes exact algebraic identities from numerical convergence claims.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Operators and builders defines the stage operators. Formal account — Initial-algebra semantics proves exact refinement for specified interpretations. Used by — Methodization attaches the methods, settings and calibration whose obligations §6 states; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C and Appendix D state the reading of the authored equations and their boundaries. See also — The stage term distinguishes mathematical composition from concrete source and storage.

“Operator algebra” here concerns composition of the Bellman calculus's operations, not a functional-analytic algebra of bounded operators. We state which additional structures each interpretation uses.

docs.title: 1. Signatures and operator types
docs.text:
A stage has two mathematical many-sorted signatures, together with model data and an interpretation. The sorts of its state signature name state spaces, and those of its operator signature name spaces of value functions, spaces of measures and the set of policies. The operation symbols of a signature have ranks \(\omega:s_1\times\cdots\times s_n\to s\). In a categorical presentation, objects represent these sorts and a morphism is a typed operation between them. A signature alone does not supply categorical products or coproducts.

At perch \(p\), write \(\mathsf V_p\) for a chosen value-function space on state space \(\mathsf X_p\), and \(\mathsf M_p\) for the finite measures on that state space, of which the probability measures are those of mass one (Stages and perches §1.2). Let \(\mathsf L\) be the value line, the declared set of a value field, \(\Gamma(x)\) the feasible actions, \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\), and \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) a chosen space of measurable choice-value functions on those pairs. The spaces must satisfy the closure and integrability requirements of the displayed operations.

Operators have domain sorts and a codomain sort, which together form the operator's rank. A first-order signature can treat them solely as operation symbols, without declaring an additional carrier of operator-valued data. This is a choice of signature, not a claim that functions can never be elements of a function space. Kinds and sorts §3, D1, defines the signature and the rank, and §6 there gives the two signatures of a stage.

docs.title: 2. Composition and builders
docs.text:
A categorical presentation must declare its generators, their types, the allowed composition operations and equations. For deterministic functions, product domains support pairing and copying of common inputs. A disjoint union represents labeled alternatives; its injections put each alternative into that union. These descriptions do not prove that every Bellman graph supports all the stated operations and identities.

Composition \(g\circ f\) requires compatible intermediate types. In the deterministic interpretation, a tensor \(f\otimes g\) acts on paired inputs. In a stochastic interpretation a tensor typically specifies independent joint transitions; this is not automatically a categorical product. Builder symbols can be primitive in a coarse signature and derived compositions in a finer one.

For a continuation field \(V_\succ\) with decision-measurable state \(X\) and feasible action \(A\), the trajectory payoff field is

\[ Q=\mathbb E[\mathrm G_\succ(V_\succ,X,A,\eta)\mid\mathcal F_\sim]. \]

Here \(\mathcal F_\sim\) is decision information and \(\eta\) the post-decision shock. The integrability actually required is that of the displayed local payoff. To compare every feasible action, specify instead the pointwise objective

\[ (B_\succ\mathrm v_\succ)(x,a) =\int\mathrm G_\succ\bigl(\mathrm v_\succ(\mathrm g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(d\eta), \]

with absolute integrability on every required pair. The map \(\mathrm g_\succ\) is the decision-to-continuation transition, \(\mathrm G_\succ\) the scalar payoff aggregator, and \(\mu_\eta\) its conditional shock law, with state/action arguments suppressed only when unnecessary. State representation and conditional-law assumptions relate this function to the trajectory identity almost surely; that identity does not determine counterfactual action values. A map written outside the integral, \(B_\succ=\mathrm G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(\int\cdots)\), is the two-map form of Stages and perches §2.3a; the display is its case with the outer map the identity.

Let \(\Pi_\Gamma\) be feasible measurable policies. On a domain admitting a specified measurable maximizing selection,

\[ \operatorname{argmax}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\to\Pi_\Gamma, \qquad \operatorname{evaluate}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\times\Pi_\Gamma\to\mathsf V_\sim, \qquad \operatorname{evaluate}(Q,\pi)(x)=Q(x,\pi(x)). \]

Then optimizing evaluation and its derived maximum satisfy

\[ \mathbb T_\succ=\operatorname{evaluate}\circ\langle B_\succ,\operatorname{argmax}\circ B_\succ\rangle, \qquad \max=\operatorname{evaluate}\circ\langle\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf Q_\Gamma},\operatorname{argmax}\rangle. \]

Without attainment the supremum value need not have this selected-policy representation. Direct search and first-order inversion approximate the same optimum only under their feasibility, sufficiency, selection and domain-coverage assumptions; at ties they need not select the same policy. Fixed-policy evaluation is \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}v=\operatorname{evaluate}(B_\succ v,\pi)\).

For the arrival transition \(\mathrm g_\prec\), pre-decision shock \(\zeta\), law \(\mu_\zeta\), and local aggregator \(\mathrm G_\prec\), arrival evaluation is

\[ \mathbb T_\prec=B_\prec:\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec, \qquad (B_\prec v)(x_\prec)=\int\mathrm G_\prec\bigl(v(\mathrm g_\prec(x_\prec,\zeta)),x_\prec,\zeta\bigr)\,\mu_\zeta(d\zeta). \]

The optimizing stage operator is \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\), and its fixed-policy counterpart is \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\).

A joint implicit system may specify several outputs with a product codomain. It defines a selected function only where existence and a specified measurable selection are established; roots need separate optimality conditions. A nested builder may appear inside another mathematical expression. These facts do not supply either a generic solver theorem or a new source grammar.

docs.title: 3. Interpretation and copying
docs.text:
An algebra supplies carriers and operations of the declared ranks. For ground terms its interpretation extends uniquely to composite terms; free-input terms also require an environment. For a category presented by generators and equations, an interpretation must additionally respect those equations and whichever categorical structures are required. The many-sorted initial-algebra theorem alone does not establish those further properties. Initial-algebra semantics gives the precise term-level statement.

Interpretation Objects and operations Conditions Value recursion value functions, local aggregation and selection/evaluation pointwise domains, integrability and specified selection where required Probability propagation state distributions and transition kernels under a supplied policy measurable transitions and conditional laws

Copying is available in the Markov category of probability kernels: a state can be duplicated by the diagonal map. What fails for a general stochastic transition is preservation of that copying. Duplicating one random draw produces the same outcome twice, while two independent draws need not agree. Deterministic transitions preserve the diagonal. Fritz (2020), §10, Definition 10.1 and Remark 10.2, describes this distinction; it does not prove that every operation in a particular Bellman diagram preserves copying.

DisCoPy supplies typed graph representations and composition operations. Any claimed universal property or equation-preserving interpretation still needs its own mathematical argument. The field and functional graphs represent the same authored equations under the assumptions of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C; they are not independently authored model sources.

docs.title: 4. Transition pairing
docs.text:
Write \(P_\prec\) and \(P_{\succ,\pi}\) for undiscounted transition expectations and \(\mathbb M_\prec,\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) for their forward probability propagation. With \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,d\mu\),

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\prec f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle. \]

These identities hold for bounded measurable \(f\) and extend to absolutely integrable evaluations. They compose with reversed order. Constant-discount expected utility instead gives \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}f=\bar r_\pi+\beta P_{\succ,\pi}f\), where \(\bar r_\pi\) is expected reward and \(0<\beta<1\) is the constant discount factor. An arrival reward or nonlinear aggregator also remains outside the transition pairing. Neither optimization nor a generic reward-bearing backward graph is the transpose of probability propagation.

docs.title: 5. Branching
docs.text:
A disjoint union \(\mathsf X_\succ=\bigsqcup_{j\in J}\mathsf X_{\succ,j}\) can represent labeled continuation alternatives, with \(J\) a finite label set. Two economic mechanisms determine how the label is obtained.

  • Agent choice: the policy chooses an alternative, possibly together with continuous controls. Branch values may be compared by a maximum when an optimum and a measurable maximizing selection exist. For a deterministic branch choice \(\pi_J(x)\), routing uses \(\mathbf1\{j=\pi_J(x)\}\). The maximizing decision is nonlinear in branch values; propagation under the resulting fixed policy is linear in the source measure.
  • Exogenous selection: a conditional law \(p(j\mid x)\) assigns branch probabilities. The backward expectation is a weighted sum of branch continuation values; the forward distribution is split using the same law. Finite mixtures need no action-feasibility coproduct condition. A persistent label is retained in the state when it affects future laws or payoffs; independence and persistence are model assumptions, not numerical methods.

For exhaustive mutually exclusive alternatives, the component output measures satisfy mass conservation:

\[ \sum_{j\in J}\mu_{\succ,j}(\mathsf X_{\succ,j})=\mu_\sim(\mathsf X_\sim). \]

An optimizing policy must specify its choice on ties, or supply an admissible randomized rule. Ties can occupy a positive-measure region even when states have an atomless law. A fixed tie-breaking rule makes the selected policy definite but does not by itself guarantee convergence of approximate policies. Exogenous routing is supplied by the model's conditional law; fixed-policy simulation can use an externally supplied policy.

Nonempty feasible sets, attainment and measurable selection are separate assumptions. Empty feasible sets may be assigned value \(-\infty\) in an extended-real convention, but have no feasible policy; this is not automatically the interpretation of a categorical initial object. Branching develops the economic cases.

Scope. Stationary distributions and tail behavior of iterated random transitions require invariant-measure and asymptotic analysis. They do not follow from the finite branching representation alone. A stationary distribution is a fixed point of probability propagation; one may introduce an operator that returns such a fixed point under additional assumptions.

docs.title: 6. Model interpretation and numerical realization
docs.text:
We distinguish the authored equations, a calibrated mathematical operator, a reference numerical approximation, and the package routine that computes it. These are different assignments, not automatically a chain of categorical functors:

\[ \text{equations and model parameters} \longrightarrow\text{mathematical operator} \longrightarrow\text{reference approximation} \longrightarrow\text{package computation}. \]

Calibration fixes parameter values in the model, at one point of their admissible set (Kinds and sorts §4). Method assignment specifies a numerical procedure; settings choose its resolution or tolerances. A reference approximation is the numerical map defined by that procedure and its settings, independently of one implementation. A handler is the package routine intended to compute it. Equations and stages are authored in .bl, and so are the methods, in a methods file that declares the settings they read; the calibration and the values of the settings are YAML, as Bellman-SYM's rules for methodization describe.

docs.title: 6.1 Conditions on realization
docs.text:
• L1 — Types. A numerical representation must state its own input and output domains and any maps between grid and exact objects. Equal mathematical ranks do not make different numerical representations identical.
  • L2 — Exact agreement. A definitionally expanded operator preserves its interpretation under the assignments in Initial-algebra semantics. Changing a method is intended to approximate the same calibrated target; initiality does not prove that the method succeeds.
  • L3 — Approximation. An error or convergence statement must specify the spaces, observables, approximation family and hypotheses. Convergence of individual primitive approximations requires suitable stability or continuity to yield convergence of their compositions. Value convergence need not imply policy convergence at ties. An envelope comparison can discard inferior candidates where its method applies; it is not a universal remedy for discontinuity or missing candidates.
  • L4 — Iteration. On a nonempty complete metric space, a self-map with a contraction modulus strictly below one has a unique fixed point and convergent exact iterates. Nonexpansiveness alone is insufficient. Convergence of approximate fixed points or iterates needs approximation and stability conditions beyond this exact contraction statement. Distributional convergence requires its own assumptions on the transition kernels and invariant measures.

The mathematical obligations therefore have two parts: relate the reference approximation to the target, and relate the package computation to that reference. Floating-point and implementation error may prevent exact equality even when the reference scheme is well defined. Neither part is proved by attaching a method name.

docs.title: 6.2 Endogenous-grid methods and envelopes
docs.text: Nested endogenous-grid methods and candidate-envelope methods may use different decompositions. Some methods compare outer choices while solving an inner conditional problem; others compare several candidate controls or values at the same state. Their dimensionality, interpolation and selection rules depend on the declared model and the method. A numerical envelope step need not be an authored upper_env equation, and a method name alone does not establish a particular rank or convergence theorem. The supported authoring boundaries are specified in Bellman-SYM's Appendix D.

docs.title: 7. Types and identities
docs.text:
An operator's mathematical type is its rank, its domain and codomain. Its declared name identifies an occurrence or definition in the source; equal denotations need not collapse distinct authored names, and equal names in different contexts need not identify one operation. Locally bound functions retain typed arguments and results. A numerical method record additionally states the representation and settings used by its handler.

For a differentiable scalar function on a product domain, the gradient collects partial derivatives:

\[ \nabla f=\langle\partial_{x_i}f\rangle_i. \]

The result has one component per coordinate, on the common domain where those derivatives exist. A scalar partial derivative alone does not specify that gradient.

docs.title: 8. Model data and induced operations
docs.text:
The transitions \(\mathrm g_\prec,\mathrm g_\succ\), local aggregators \(\mathrm G_\prec,\mathrm G_\succ\), feasibility correspondence \(\Gamma\), and shock laws are model data. A coarse signature may use them only as the data that define its builders' interpretations. A finer signature may expose the functions as typed operations or values in chosen function spaces. The distinction depends on the chosen signature; it is not an absolute division between functions that may and may not be operators.

Transition expectations require measurable transitions and conditional laws. Value evaluation requires integrable local payoffs on its stated domain. Optimization additionally needs an appropriate objective, feasible actions, and selection conditions when a policy is required. A general recursive preference cannot be inferred from one pointwise integrand if it uses additional normalization or a different order of expectation and aggregation. The extension to such preferences remains unfinished. #todo

With identity payoff aggregation and one feasible action, the decision builder reduces to its transition expectation. When the transition kernel is the point mass at the current state, this expectation is the identity. A scalar-multiplication method is not implied by the absence of choice.

docs.title: 9. Method assignment boundaries
docs.text: For a finite hierarchical tree, a cut chooses operation boundaries so each path from the root to a leaf meets exactly one selected box and none is nested within another. Rank and coverage checks establish structural compatibility; exact operation agreement or a numerical error/convergence result requires a separate argument. Initial-algebra semantics §5 states the exact case and preserves the open shared-graph question.

docs.title: 10. The roles of model and method data
docs.text:
Assignment Specifies Obligation Equations and domains mathematical form and allowed arguments well-defined operations under stated assumptions Calibration model parameter values intended economic instance Numerical method approximation procedure applicability to the target problem Settings resolution, tolerances and numerical conventions stated accuracy or convergence conditions Package handler computation of the reference approximation agreement with the reference, including implementation error

Connectors identify compatible fields between stages or periods. A nonidentity transformation must be authored explicitly; a renaming alone does not define it. Stage composition and Periods and trellis discuss these connections. A global categorical presentation remains subject to its declared equations and verified interpretation, rather than following from the table.

docs.title: 11. Related documents
docs.text:
• The stage term and Kinds and sorts.
  • Operator catalogue and Branching.
  • Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), “Initial algebra semantics and continuous algebras,” §2, pp. 71–75, for term and free-algebra interpretations.
  • Fritz (2020), “A synthetic approach to Markov kernels, conditional independence and theorems on sufficient statistics,” §10, for stochastic copying and deterministic maps.

The full categorical presentation beyond these stated structures remains to be verified against its selected target category. #todo

docs.title: Appendix G — Functional programming
docs.text:
Summary

A stage declares typed objects and equations from which Bellman operations are constructed. Calibration assigns economic parameter values; methodization writes a method and a grid into the signature of each operator a methods file names; configuration supplies the values of the settings they read. This appendix defines those objects and maps, states the composition they preserve, and works through an income-and-consumption stage. Backus's functional programming supplies the distinction between functions, represented functions and forms for combining them.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches defines the economic data and information. Fields, functions and types distinguishes fields from their representing functions. Formal account — Initial-algebra semantics gives the term-interpretation result. Operator algebra gives the economic and numerical conditions. Used by — Stages and Methodization give the concrete source and attachment rules, Equation parsing rules the admitted expression forms, and Bellman-SYM's Appendix C the interpretation rules that §3 names. The notation below describes their mathematics, not an additional source format.

docs.title: 1 Primitive objects and expressions
docs.text:
The Bellman-Euler Domain-Specific Declarative Language (BE-DDSL) distinguishes data, representations of functions, and operations on functions. A representation is a finite expression with declared meaning; it is an object that can be inspected and transformed before the represented function is applied. A number, an expression denoting a number, and an expression denoting a function therefore have different roles.

Let \(\mathbb O_P\) denote the language's primitive objects, the literals and supplied symbols from which expressions are formed. Separate them as

\[ \mathbb O_P=\mathbb O_P^{\mathrm{lit}}\sqcup\mathbb O_P^{\mathrm{sym}}. \]

The symbol \(\sqcup\) means that the two classes are distinguished even if their printed spellings coincide. The following table classifies their uses; each supplied symbol still requires its own type and interpretation.

Class Examples and meaning Literal data An integer or decimal literal denotes a number; a truth literal denotes true or false; a quoted string supplies text. A displayed quotient such as 1/3 is an expression using division, not necessarily a separate rational literal. Domain and law symbols Real domains, interval and product constructions, and a distribution family such as LogNormal denote spaces or laws when their required inputs are supplied. A symbol denoting a space is distinct from an element of that space. Pointwise operations Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, powers and comparisons act on their declared numerical domains. Operations on functions Expectation, evaluation, differentiation and optimization act on functions or relations, subject to their mathematical domains. Numerical method symbols A quadrature, interpolation or optimization method identifies a procedure for a stated operation. Its settings and eventual arrays or callable implementation are different objects.

Declarations, local function definitions, application, typed composition and finite tuple or record formation supply expression-forming rules. Punctuation spells those rules in source; a colon is not thereby an extra numerical operation. Bellman-SYM's equation parsing rules determine the admitted source forms. The table is a mathematical classification, not a claim that every conceivable constructor or numerical method is implemented.

Write \(\mathbb O\) for the class of finite, well-formed represented objects obtained from the supplied vocabulary and declared names. Finite tuples and records belong to this constructed class; their components need not all be literals. The primitive vocabulary itself need not be closed under every construction. In particular, assembling a tuple of primitive values does not turn that tuple into an additional primitive symbol.

A function object is an expression denoting a function with specified arguments and result. Let \(\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb O\) be their class, and let \(\mathbb T\subseteq\mathbb F\) consist of those denoting higher-order functions, functions whose inputs or outputs include functions. A transition \(g:X\times Z\to Y\) and utility \(u:C\to\mathbb R\) are function objects when represented; an expectation \(\mathcal V(Y)\to\mathcal V(X)\) and a Bellman operator are higher-order examples. Here \(\mathcal V(X)\) is a chosen class of value functions on \(X\), which no declaration fixes, with the regularity required by the operation. Membership in these classes depends on the interpretation, not on the spelling of a name.

There are two different uses of “primitive.” A primitive language operation, such as multiplication, is supplied by the language. An economic primitive, such as a utility function or transition law, is supplied by the model and may itself be defined by an expression. Conversely, a supplied integration operation can be mathematically substantial. The operator catalogue identifies the operations used in the calculus.

docs.title: 2 Declarations and function objects
docs.text:
A declaration environment \(D\) records the names in scope, their types, roles, information requirements and defining expressions where supplied. It also includes shock-law declarations and stage-level domain restrictions, which need not occur inside a builder's equations. It distinguishes an economic parameter from a local function argument, a state field from its state space, and an input function from a function the stage constructs. A name introduced by the modeler extends \(D\); it does not become a new built-in primitive.

Write \(D\vdash e:A\) to mean that expression \(e\) has type \(A\) under these declarations. The type of an expression is here the set in which its value lies, a set of values or of functions; Kinds and sorts §3 gives the sort that a type written in a file names. Two basic formation rules are

\[ \frac{D\vdash f:A\to B\qquad D\vdash x:A}{D\vdash f(x):B}, \qquad \frac{D\vdash f:B\to C\qquad D\vdash g:A\to B} {D\vdash f\circ g:A\to C}. \]

Application produces a result at an argument; composition produces a function. A local definition binds its formal arguments within its body. In the consumption source of Bellman-SYM's Stages page, for example,

ρ : (1, inf)
𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)

The symbol ρ is an economic parameter. The c in this definition is a local argument, distinct from a control with the same spelling in another scope. The definition represents the parameterized family \(u_\rho:\mathbb R_{++}\to\mathbb R\), with \(u_\rho(c)=c^{1-\rho}/(1-\rho)\). Calibration at \(\rho=2\) selects \(u_2(c)=-1/c\). It supplies no particular consumption argument.

The earlier function-object account can also describe a declared constant through a nullary operation, one with no arguments. Formally, a symbol of rank \(()\to A\) is interpreted by an element of \(A\), or equivalently by a function \(1\to A\), where \(1\) is a singleton. A named space can be treated this way in an algebra whose relevant carrier consists of spaces. A parameter could be treated in the same way, as a named nullary symbol to which calibration gives its interpretation. This is a precise way to express the declaration idea; it does not identify a space with a scalar or require the program to store a separate function for each name. Kinds and sorts §4 does not treat a parameter so. There a parameter is no symbol of a signature: the parameters of a file form one parameter vector, and each parameter denotes one coordinate of it. The stage as declared is then a family indexed by the admissible set of such vectors, and calibration chooses the index (§6 below).

An unbound economic parameter and a free continuation function are declared inputs of different kinds (Kinds and sorts §3). In the construction above, a parameter's name, declared set and binding remain inspectable even after calibration. It is not replaced everywhere by an anonymous numeric literal. Local argument binding is likewise retained in interpreted definitions so that substitution respects scope.

Parameters are not separate semgraph wires. A semgraph, the semantic graph of the constructed stage, retains the full definitions using their named parameters, along with parameter declarations and calibration. For example, \(u_\rho\) still has the consumption argument \(c\); \(\rho\) determines which function it is. The graph can display that function without a separate parameter input wire. This applies to the two initial diagrams, forward and backward, as well as to the two builders graphs. Parameters must be accounted for in the constructed graph's definitions, rather than removed from the drawing afterward.

docs.title: 3 A stage as a declaration unit
docs.text:
A symbolic stage is a finite collection of related declarations and typed equation groups. One way to record its structure mathematically is

\[ s=\bigl(D;\ (b,I_b,O_b,e_b)_{b\in B}\bigr). \]

Here \(B\) is the finite collection of authored builder identifiers; \(I_b\) and \(O_b\) are the ordered declared inputs and outputs of builder \(b\); and \(e_b\) is its collection of equations, local definitions and conditions. A builder is the operator that an authored typed block defines, the block stating a transition, a value calculation or a policy relation. This record describes information already present in a stage, not a proposed software class. An individual implicit equation can denote a relation until conditions make it a function.

The stage is closed with respect to declarations: every name used is supplied by the language, declared in the stage or bound locally. That does not make it a closed numerical calculation. A declared continuation function remains an input to the backward problem, and declared parameters still need values. Nor does closure prove that every output is well defined: equations and their domains must determine the outputs as functions or specified relations under the interpretation rules of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C.

The ordinary economic stage has the data

\[ \bigl(X_\prec,X_\sim,X_\succ;\ A,\Gamma;\ (Z_\zeta,\mu_\zeta),(Z_\eta,\mu_\eta);\ g_\prec,g_\succ;\ G_\prec,G_\succ\bigr). \]

The three \(X_p\) are state spaces at arrival, decision and continuation. The action space is \(A\), and \(\Gamma(x)\subseteq A\) is the set of feasible actions at decision state \(x\). Each \(Z\) is a shock space with its law \(\mu\), conditional on the relevant state or state–action pair when required. The transitions \(g_\prec,g_\succ\) determine the next state; the pointwise aggregators \(G_\prec,G_\succ\) combine a scalar continuation value with current quantities. Stages and perches §1 gives their complete domains. The perches are information sets; state arguments summarize what is needed from that information.

These economic primitives determine operations on value functions and distributions. They are distinct from the stage's source expressions and from the language's supplied primitive symbols. A stage occurrence supplies the equations, declarations and bindings needed for its particular position in a model. Different occurrences of the same source can have different parameter values or methods. Compatible stages compose through declared identifications of outgoing and incoming fields; those identifications do not supply a missing transition equation.

docs.title: 3.1 Income and consumption
docs.text:
Use the stage of §4 of Bellman-SYM's Stages page. Beginning assets are \(b\geq0\), observed income is \(y>0\), resources are \(w>0\), consumption satisfies \(0<c\leq w\), and continuation savings are \(a\geq0\). Its economic parameter vector is

\[ \theta=(R,\beta,\rho,\mu_y,\sigma_y),\qquad R>0,\quad0<\beta<1,\quad\rho>1,\quad\mu_y\in\mathbb R,\quad\sigma_y\geq0. \]

The income law \(\nu_\theta\) is that of \(y=\exp(\mu_y+\sigma_y Z)\) with \(Z\) standard normal and independent of arrival information. This statement fixes the meaning of the two lognormal parameters. The stage's pointwise definitions are

\[ \begin{aligned} g_{\prec,\theta}(b,y)&=Rb+y,& g_\succ(w,c)&=w-c,\\ u_\rho(c)&=\frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},& G_{\succ,\theta}(v,w,c)&=u_\rho(c)+\beta v,\qquad G_\prec(v,b,y)=v. \end{aligned} \]

The continuation input is a function \(W:\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\). The function \(g_\succ\) first supplies its argument, then \(G_{\succ,\theta}\) combines the resulting scalar with current utility. Thus

\[ Q_\theta[W](w,c)=u_\rho(c)+\beta W(w-c),\qquad (\mathbb T_{\succ,\theta}W)(w)=\sup_{0<c\leq w}Q_\theta[W](w,c), \]

and arrival evaluation is

\[ (\mathbb T_{\prec,\theta}v)(b) =\int v(Rb+y)\,\nu_\theta(dy),\qquad \mathbb T_\theta=\mathbb T_{\prec,\theta}\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\theta}. \]

Take \(W\) continuous, so it is bounded on every compact savings interval. Because \(\rho>1\), utility tends to minus infinity as consumption tends to zero; for each \(w>0\) the supremum is attained. A policy output additionally requires a specified measurable maximizing selection. The arrival calculation requires absolute integrability of the resulting \(v(Rb+y)\); these are the hypotheses used in the example of Bellman-SYM's Stages page. Continuation value, choice value, selected policy and numerical arrays are different objects.

At the operation level, Pullback along the law of motion names composition with \(g\), and Value aggregation \(G\) names the subsequent pointwise aggregation. A sub-builder is named by the function its complete equation and ordered arguments define. Keeping these operations inside their whole builders preserves both the Bellman decomposition and the equations defining it. Arithmetic inside \(g\) or \(G\) remains part of those definitions; it is not a further builder/primitive semgraph grain, or level of displayed decomposition.

docs.title: 4 Forms and represented functions
docs.text:
Backus distinguishes objects, functions, application, functional forms and definitions in an FP system.1 A functional form combines functions, or functions and objects, to produce another function. His FFP systems additionally represent functions systematically by objects.5 The represented-function classes in §1 apply this distinction to a typed economic vocabulary.

Form Function it defines Composition \((f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))\). Construction \([f_1,\ldots,f_n](x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_n(x))\), for functions sharing the argument domain. Condition Apply \(f\) or \(g\) according to a predicate evaluated at \(x\). This is a specified conditional choice, distinct from maximizing over branch values. Constant Return a supplied object, with the adopted rule for undefined arguments. Apply-to-all, or map Apply a function to every element of a finite sequence. Insert Combine a nonempty sequence from the right with a binary function: \(/f\,(x_1,x_2,x_3)=f(x_1,f(x_2,x_3))\).

Backus's particular FP object set contains atoms, finite sequences and an undefined object \(\bot\). Its functions are strict, meaning \(f(\bot)=\bot\), and a sequence containing \(\bot\) collapses to \(\bot\). His constant form therefore takes an argument and returns \(\bot\) on an undefined argument; it is not a nullary operation. Map preserves the empty sequence; insert on an empty sequence needs a specified suitable right identity. Changing the grouping of insert needs associativity. His additional while and binary-to-unary forms respectively repeat a function under a predicate and fix one argument of a function on pairs.2 These choices do not assign undefinedness to every infeasible action or identify undefinedness with a zero terminal value.

A supplied primitive and a definition have different status. A definition assigns a fresh name to a defining form, possibly recursively. Its meaning is obtained from that form; recursion may fail to terminate. Backus fixes a system through its atoms, primitive functions, forms and a set of definitions with distinct left-hand names.3 A local definition in the economic language additionally has its declared arguments and scope.

For total functions \(g:X\to Y\) and \(f_i:Y\to Z_i\), construction satisfies

\[ [f_1,f_2]\circ g=[f_1\circ g,f_2\circ g], \]

because both sides return \((f_1(g(x)),f_2(g(x)))\) for each \(x\in X\).4 This is an equation between functions. It permits substitution while economic parameters and all other inputs are held fixed. Shared randomness must also be preserved: \((U,U)\) for a single binary draw always has equal entries, whereas two independent fair binary draws have equal entries with probability one half.

In FFP an atom can represent a function, and a headed sequence can represent a form. Backus's representation function \(\rho\) assigns the represented function; his meaning function \(\mu\) evaluates expressions containing applications to objects. Some represented functions return further application expressions, so these two roles are distinct. His metacomposition rule interprets a sequence by applying the function represented by its first element to the pair consisting of the whole sequence and the original argument.6 For example, the controlling function for \(\langle\mathrm{CONST},a\rangle\) selects \(a\) from \(\langle\langle\mathrm{CONST},a\rangle,y\rangle\) on defined inputs. The rule permits new represented forms; it does not itself supply the meanings of Bellman builders.

The project's mathematical interpretation Υ and numerical realization Ρ below are distinct from Backus's \(\rho\) and \(\mu\). Representation by objects also leaves the choice of parser open. The current .bl language parses arithmetic and binding into a temporary syntax tree and retains interpreted equations and operations in the semgraph.

docs.title: 5 Interpretation and composition
docs.text:
A signature \(\Sigma\) specifies sorts and operation symbols with ranks, their ordered input sorts and their output sort (Kinds and sorts §3, D1). A target algebra assigns a mathematical set to each sort and an operation of the corresponding rank to each symbol. A homomorphism preserves these operations. Given a target algebra and an environment assigning meanings to free inputs, interpretation of finite terms extends uniquely from their constituents.7 We write this interpretation as \(\Upsilon_\theta(e)\) when the economic parameter assignment is \(\theta\).

For example, the interpretation of the represented composition of stage operations obeys

\[ \Upsilon_\theta(t_\prec\circ t_\succ) =\Upsilon_\theta(t_\prec)\circ\Upsilon_\theta(t_\succ) =\mathbb T_{\prec,\theta}\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\theta}. \]

In these composition formulas, \(t_\prec,t_\succ\) denote represented operator arrows with a formal value-function input. An operator can instead be encoded by a closed term \(h_\succ\) of function type, denoting a function \(\mathcal V(X_\succ)\to\mathcal V(X_\sim)\). Its continuation argument is an input of the denoted function, not a free variable of \(h_\succ\). Evaluating this function term at the formal input \(W\) gives the corresponding operator arrow \(t_\succ\); evaluating the application \(h_\succ(W)\) at a particular continuation requires an assignment to \(W\). The initial-algebra account distinguishes ground terms, those without free variables, from free terms and treats exact expansion of builders into constituent operations.

A category consists of objects, arrows, identities and associative composition of compatible arrows. For sets and total functions, its objects are sets and its arrows are functions. A categorical object is therefore a whole domain, whereas the represented objects in §1 are particular data or expressions. A functor assigns objects and arrows to another category, preserving domains, codomains, identities and composition.

For the structural statements below, use the checked first-order operation signature of Initial-algebra semantics. “First-order” means that terms are formed by applying declared operation symbols to terms: a function space can interpret one of the sorts, with evaluation or selection supplied as a typed operation. It does not supply a rule for binding a function argument. Local definitions are elaborated with their binding checked before this operation presentation is used.

Let \(\mathsf{Term}(\Sigma)\) have finite products of the sorts as objects and finite tuples of these well-typed operation terms, in listed input variables, as arrows. Composition substitutes terms for those variables; identity is the tuple of input variables. Arrows are identified by the structural rules for composition and tuple formation; renaming bound variables in retained definitions does not change their meaning. This is the free category with finite products on the signature; where every symbol has one input, its arrows from one sort to another are the paths that Kinds and sorts §6 calls terms. The functor claims below concern this represented operation category, rather than every raw source expression containing a binder. Additional economic equations require separate verification in a target interpretation.

The categorical product \(A\times B\) has projections selecting its components; \([f,g]\) is the unique function whose projections are \(f\) and \(g\). This justifies typed construction, without importing every product identity into Backus's different strict-sequence convention.

This construction is the setting in which calibration and methodization can be called functorial; §7 states methodization for paths of operation symbols, in which no tuple is formed. Their formulas specify the object and arrow assignments. It is not a claim that every transformation of program records, or every interpretation of stochastic diagrams, preserves all categorical structure.

docs.title: 6 Calibration
docs.text:
Let \(P\) be the declared economic parameter names. A calibration \(\theta\) is a point of their admissible set \(\Theta\), the assignments of a value to every name in \(P\) at which every condition of the parameter lines and of the definitions holds, joint restrictions included (Kinds and sorts §4). For the stage in §3.1, \(P=\{R,\beta,\rho,\mu_y,\sigma_y\}\). Writing only \(P\to\mathbb O_P\) describes a name-to-value assignment; functoriality concerns its extension to the represented operations and their compositions.

Consider a category whose objects are families of domains \((X_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\) and whose arrows are families of total functions \((f_\theta:X_\theta\to Y_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\). These claims cover operations that are total on their declared carriers. An unsolved implicit relation can be retained as an element of a relation-valued type; this does not make it a total function from states to controls. Identity and composition are defined separately at each \(\theta\). For a fixed \(\bar\theta\in\Theta\), calibration is the evaluation functor

\[ \mathcal C_{\bar\theta}:(X_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\longmapsto X_{\bar\theta}, \qquad \mathcal C_{\bar\theta}:(f_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\longmapsto f_{\bar\theta}. \]

It preserves identity and composition because

\[ \mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(\mathrm{id}_X)=\mathrm{id}_{X_{\bar\theta}}, \qquad \mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(f\circ g) =f_{\bar\theta}\circ g_{\bar\theta} =\mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(f)\circ\mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(g). \]

This also accommodates a domain such as \([0,a_{\max}]\) depending on a parameter: calibration selects the domain as well as the function on it. Every operation being composed must also be defined at the calibration, under the conditions that Kinds and sorts §6 states. A declaration alone does not establish the analytical conditions needed for a family of integrals or optimizing operations to be well defined.

On a represented expression, the corresponding specialization assigns each parameter its value and acts through its defining forms. In particular,

\[ \mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(f(x)) =\mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(f)\bigl(\mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(x)\bigr), \qquad \mathcal C_{\bar\theta}([f,g]) =[\mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(f),\mathcal C_{\bar\theta}(g)]. \]

Locally bound variables are not parameter names to replace. The same specialization applies to parameter-dependent laws, feasible sets and complete stage definitions. It is an algebraic account of their meaning; the current stage construction records bindings alongside retained symbolic equations.

For example, with \(\bar\theta=(1.04,0.96,2,0,0.1)\), the calibrated stage has

\[ g_{\prec,\bar\theta}(b,y)=1.04b+y,\qquad Q_{\bar\theta}[W](w,c)=-\frac1c+0.96W(w-c),\qquad y=\exp(0.1Z). \]

The transition still takes beginning assets and income; the choice value still takes a continuation function, resources and consumption. Calibration selects the economic instance without supplying those arguments or solving the stage. When two stages share one economic parameter, compatible composition uses the same binding for it. Distinct stage-local parameters may instead have distinct calibrations.

docs.title: 7 The binding maps
docs.text:
The three binding verbs with a source held fixed are maps from stage versions to stage versions, each writing one binding: \(\mathcal C_c(S) = \mathrm{calibrate}(S, c)\), \(M_m(S) = \mathrm{methodize}(S, m)\) and \(K_s(S) = \mathrm{configure}(S, s)\). Here a source is the set of assignments that one verb binds, parameter values \(c\), a method assignment \(m\) or settings \(s\); a stage version is a stage as it stands after its construction or after one of its bindings (Kinds and sorts §6); and \(\mathcal C_c\) is the calibration of §6 with \(\bar\theta = c\). The bindings are made in the order calibrate, methodize, configure, so a specified stage is \(S^{\mathrm{spec}} = K_s\, M_m\, \mathcal C_c(S)\). \(\mathcal C\) commutes with \(M\) and with \(K\) in bindings and graphs; \(K\) is defined on methodized versions only, since settings are read against the methods that name them; \(M\) is applied once, a version holding one methods binding. Three laws hold, verified on cons.bl and port.bl: a verb binds once from a merged source and refuses one that values fewer names than the stage requires; for complete sources \(c_1, c_2\) the versions \(\mathcal C_{c_2}(\mathcal C_{c_1}(S))\) and \(\mathcal C_{c_2}(S)\) have equal bindings and graphs; a binding changes neither the initial diagrams nor the declared builders, and what a solution method changes stands in the operative builders alone (Methods §9).

A method assignment \(m\) is the set of entries of a methods file, read after its union with the stage file: for each operator occurrence it names, a method with its keyword arguments and a grid (Methods §§2, 5), together with the closed form an !explicit entry generates at its builder's Evaluation where no entry names a representation. Fix the occurrences and their identities, and write \(\omega_i\) for one such operation symbol. The methodized signature \(\Sigma_m\) is the category of parametrized morphisms \(\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal M}(\Sigma)\) of Methods §2, taken over the free category \(\Sigma\) on the stage's operation symbols with the free monoid \(\mathcal M\) on the labels, a label being a pair of a method and a grid, acting trivially: a methodized morphism is a path of operation symbols carrying the list of its labels, so that the mathematical inputs and outputs are unchanged and the settings a method reads are named by its label and valued at configuration. Distinct occurrences can be distinguished even when they denote the same mathematical operation.

Methodization acts on generators by

\[ M_m(\omega_i)=\omega_i^{m(i)}, \]

assigns the identity label, the list with no entries, to every generator the assignment does not name, so that \(M_m\) is total, and extends to composites by

\[ M_m(\mathrm{id}_A)=\mathrm{id}_A,\qquad M_m(f\circ g)=M_m(f)\circ M_m(g). \]

Thus \(M_m:\Sigma\to\Sigma_m\) is a functor, since \(\Sigma\) is free on its operation symbols: the parameter of a composite parametrized morphism is the concatenation of its parts' parameters, the list of the labels along the path (Methods §3). The notation describes a fixed, consistent assignment: if the same represented occurrence is shared, its method is shared; different occurrence-specific choices require distinct occurrences in the source of this map. The union of the stage file with its methods files resolves the operator each entry names before this mathematical assignment is considered (addition); Bellman-SYM's rules for methodization state the places.

For an expectation occurrence, for example,

\[ E_y\longmapsto E_y^{\mathrm{GH}(n)}. \]

Here \(\mathrm{GH}\) denotes the Gauss–Hermite quadrature family and \(n\) is its node-count setting. The tag writes the name \(n\) and never a number, since a method's entry holds no number (Methods §4). The tag retains expectation as its mathematical target. The node count does not become an additional economic input of that expectation, and numerical representation can still use a different carrier, such as sampled values on a grid. Where an operator stores a function, the grid it stores it on is the second component of its label, written by its own entry, and no setting of the method (Methods §5).

Two erasures are defined. The erasure of the labels \(U_m : \Sigma_m \to \Sigma\) forgets the method and grid components of every morphism, is the identity on sorts, and preserves the underlying operation, its equations and its economic inputs. Then

\[ U_m\circ M_m=\mathrm{id} \]

on every path of \(\Sigma\), the section law, which holds on every stage because \(M_m\) assigns the identity label wherever no entry stands. The identity states what methodization retains. It does not say the numerical quadrature sum equals the exact expectation. \(U_m\) keeps the lines an addition appends to a block, the derivative lines and the rows of a solution method. The erasure of the addition \(U_a\) acts on the term before elaboration: the union \(S \sqcup A\) of the stage file \(S\) with a methods file \(A\) keeps the file and position of every item, and \(U_a\) removes the items written in \(A\), so that \(U_a(S \sqcup A) = S\); on the elaborated stage its result is the declared level, stage.declared, which the stage stores (Methods §§8, 9). A solution method assigned to a whole builder supplies the lines by which the builder is computed at the operative level and leaves the declared lines at the declared level; it does not delete the builder's definitions.

After \(m\) is selected, let \(N_m\) be the names of the settings the methods file declares, each with its set, and let \(s\) be a configuration: a point of the admissible set of those settings at the bound calibration, which gives each name a value of its set (Kinds and sorts §4); a value outside the set is refused. Configuration, denoted \(K_s\), binds the values the methodized symbols' labels name and leaves the labels as written; for example, with \(s(n) = 3\),

\[ K_s\bigl(E_y^{\mathrm{GH}(n)}\bigr)=E_y^{\mathrm{GH}(n)}\quad\text{with the binding } n = 3, \]

the value standing in the bindings of the stage version and not in the signature (Methods §6). Its object assignment retains the declared economic types. Its action on expressions preserves identity and composition by the same constituent-wise definition as \(M_m\). Hence it is a functor between the corresponding categories of method-annotated terms. A numerical domain that belongs to the model, such as an explicitly discrete action set, remains economic data; a grid chosen only to approximate a continuous function is the grid component of the operator's signature, whose bounds and count are settings (Methods §5).

A specified stage retains the model's equations together with \(c\), \(m\) and \(s\). Mathematical specialization of disjoint fixed assignments can commute, for example \(\mathcal C_c M_m=M_m\mathcal C_c\) when the same method assignment remains applicable on both sides. This does not assert that the public interface accepts every ordering, or that choosing a method according to parameter values is independent of calibration.

docs.title: 8 Mathematical and numerical realization
docs.text:
Three mathematical objects are associated with a fully specified operation:

Object What determines it Exact target \(\Upsilon_\theta(e)\) The economic expression and parameter assignment. Reference approximation \(\widehat e_{c,m,s}\) A fully specified mathematical algorithm, including its numerical settings. Executable realization \(\mathrm P_{c,m,s}(e)\) The selected implementation of that algorithm, including its numerical representations.

Here \(\mathrm P\) is the project's capital Rho, Ρ, written this way to distinguish it from the utility parameter \(\rho\). A handler is the implementation assigned to the stated operation and method. Its correctness means agreement with the reference algorithm under the chosen numerical conventions; accuracy means agreement of that algorithm with the economic target to a stated precision or in a justified limit. If numerical and exact functions have different domains, the comparison must include the maps between those representations. Operator algebra §6 states these separate requirements.

docs.title: 8.1 The arrival expectation
docs.text:
In §3.1 the exact operation is

\[ (E_{\theta}v)(b) =\int_{\mathbb R}v\bigl(Rb+e^{\mu_y+\sigma_y z}\bigr)\,\phi(dz), \]

where \(\phi\) is the standard-normal probability law and the integrand is absolutely integrable. Selecting Gauss–Hermite quadrature and \(n\) nodes gives the reference operation

\[ (\widehat E_{\theta,n}v)(b) =\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j\, v\bigl(Rb+e^{\mu_y+\sigma_y z_j}\bigr). \]

The nodes \(z_j\) and weights \(w_j\) here are normalized for the standard-normal law: weights sum to one. If a library returns nodes \(x_j\) and weights \(a_j\) for the weight \(e^{-x^2}\), use \(z_j=\sqrt{2}x_j\) and \(w_j=a_j/\sqrt{\pi}\).8 The expectation target, the chosen quadrature rule and an implementation's convention are therefore distinct inspectable objects.

For a numerical check of this one operation, take \(b=0\), \(v(w)=w\), \(\mu_y=0\) and \(\sigma_y=0.1\). The exact value is \(e^{0.005}\). One-node standard-normal quadrature has \(z_1=0,w_1=1\) and gives \(1\). Thus methodization and configuration preserve the identified target but give an approximation that is already different in this elementary case. The numerical analysis must justify how increasing resolution improves agreement for the intended function class.

Applied to the stage composition, the assignments give

\[ M_m(t_\prec\circ t_\succ) =M_m(t_\prec)\circ M_m(t_\succ), \qquad \widehat{\mathbb T}_{c,m,s} =\widehat{\mathbb T}_{\prec,c,m,s} \circ\widehat{\mathbb T}_{\succ,c,m,s}, \]

provided the numerical output of the decision operation is a valid input to the arrival operation, including any stated representation conversion. The first equation is structural functoriality; the second defines the composed numerical calculation. Neither equation supplies a bound on its distance from \(\mathbb T_\theta\). Substituting a candidate policy for a maximizer, changing shock dependence, or omitting a feasibility condition changes the economic target unless a separate equivalence has been established.

Forward probability propagation uses the same declared transitions and a supplied policy, where required. Its pairing with backward transition expectation holds under the integrability conditions in Operators and builders §3. Reward aggregation and optimization require their own interpretation. Likewise, fixed-point existence and convergence of repeated Bellman application require the conditions in Periods and the trellis; they are not consequences of the functor laws above.

  1. J. Backus (1978), “Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style? A Functional Style and Its Algebra of Programs,” Communications of the ACM 21(8), 613–641, §§11.2–11.2.3, p. 620. ↩

  2. Backus (1978), §11.2.4, pp. 621–622. ↩

  3. Backus (1978), §§11.2.5–11.2.6, p. 622. ↩

  4. Backus (1978), §12, especially the construction–composition law discussed in §12.9, p. 631. ↩

  5. Backus (1978), §13.1, p. 631. ↩

  6. Backus (1978), §§13.2–13.3.2, p. 632. ↩

  7. J. A. Goguen, J. W. Thatcher, E. G. Wagner and J. B. Wright (1977), “Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras,” Journal of the ACM 24(1), 68–95, §2, especially Propositions 2.1, 2.3 and 2.6, pp. 71–75. The categorical term presentation here uses typed substitution and finite products; additional equations must be satisfied by its interpretation. ↩

  8. NumPy, numpy.polynomial.hermite.hermgauss, specifies the weight \(e^{-x^2}\). The displayed conversion follows by substituting \(z=\sqrt{2}x\) into the standard-normal density. ↩

docs.title: Ingredients
docs.text:
Summary

This reference card lists the principal symbols used in the calculus. It distinguishes fields from their representing functions, fixed-policy evaluation from optimization, and transition expectation from reward-bearing Bellman operators.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches defines the stage notation. See also — Catalogues gives the longer type and method inventories. Used by — Symbol conventions and Bellman-SYM's Appendix C §1.5 record the source notation for these symbols.

Stub

This reference remains incomplete. The table summarizes the settled symbols; it does not define an additional source grammar or certify numerical-handler support.

docs.title: 1. Reading guide
docs.text: Follow the linked chapter for the domain restrictions and assumptions. At a perch \(p\in\{\prec,\sim,\succ\}\), \(\mathsf X_p\) is a measurable state space, \(\mathsf V_p\) a chosen function space and \(\mathsf L\) the value domain. Let \(\mathsf A\) be the action space, \(\Gamma(x)\subseteq\mathsf A\) the feasible actions and \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\). The letters \(x,a\) denote a generic state and action; in the buffer-stock example \(m,c,a\) instead denote resources, consumption and assets after consumption.

docs.title: 2. Symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning and type Defining relation or qualification Reference \(\mathcal F_\prec,\mathcal F_\sim,\mathcal F_\succ\) available information at arrival, decision and continuation \(\mathcal F_\prec\subseteq\mathcal F_\sim\subseteq\mathcal F_\succ\); distinct from state sufficiency Stages §1 \(X_p,\mathsf X_p\) random state vector and its measurable state space \(X_p:\Omega\to\mathsf X_p\), where \(\Omega\) is the outcome space Fields and functions §1 \(V_p,\mathrm v_p\) value field and representing function \(V_p=\mathrm v_p(X_p)\) almost surely when state-generated measurability and representative-domain conditions hold; \(\mathrm v_p\in\mathsf V_p\) Fields and functions §§1–2 \(\mathrm g_\prec\) arrival transition \(\mathsf X_\prec\times\mathsf Z_\zeta\to\mathsf X_\sim\) Stages §1 \(\mathrm g_\succ\) controlled continuation transition \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf X_\succ\) Stages §1 \(g_1,g_2\) sub-transitions through an intermediate state \(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)=g_2(g_1(x,a),\eta)\) in the stated factorization Operators §10 \(\Gamma\) feasible-action correspondence \(\Gamma:\mathsf X_\sim\rightrightarrows\mathsf A\) Stages §1 \(\zeta,\eta\) pre-decision and post-decision shocks random elements in \(\mathsf Z_\zeta,\mathsf Z_\eta\) with declared conditional laws Stages §1 \(\mathrm u,\beta\) utility and discount in the consumption example \(\mathrm u:\mathbb R_{++}\to\mathbb R\), \(\beta\in(0,1)\) Example \(\mathrm G_\succ,\mathrm G_\prec\) pointwise reward/continuation aggregators scalar continuation value is first: \(G_\succ(v,x,a,\eta)\) and \(G_\prec(v,x_\prec,\zeta)\); a statement may supply an inner map inside the shock integral and an outer map outside it (Stages §2.3a) Functions §1 \(K_g\) pullback along a measurable map \(g\) \(K_gf=f\circ g\); functions on \(g\)'s codomain map to functions on its domain Operators §2 \(\mathbb E_z\) shock integration maps an integrable function of retained arguments and \(z\) to a function of retained arguments, using their conditional law for \(z\) Operators §5 \(B_\succ\) induced aggregator, \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) \((B_\succ f)(x,a)=\int G_\succ(f(g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta)K_\eta(x,a,d\eta)\), where \(K_\eta\) is the conditional shock law; a map written outside the integral gives \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(\int\cdots)\) (Stages §2.3a) Operators §5 \(Q_f\) choice-value function on \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) \(Q_f=B_\succ f\); \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) is the chosen class of such functions Operators §7 \(\pi\) or \(\sigma\) feasible measurable policy, \(\mathsf X_\sim\to\mathsf A\) \(\pi(x)\in\Gamma(x)\); optimality is additional Functions §1 \(\operatorname{argmax}\) specified measurable maximizing selection on its admissible domain maps suitable \(Q\) to \(\Pi_\Gamma\), the feasible measurable policies; requires attainment/selection Operators §7 \(\operatorname{evaluate}\) evaluate a choice value under a policy \(\operatorname{evaluate}(Q,\pi)(x)=Q(x,\pi(x))\); separate from ordinary function-at-state evaluation Operators §7 \(\operatorname{upper\_env}\) comparison of a specified candidate family selected outputs and completeness/optimality requirements depend on the declared problem and method Operators §7 \(\mathfrak w=Wf\) post-decision expectation function, distinct from the operator \(W\) \(W:\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_a\), \((Wf)(a)=\int f(g_2(a,\eta))K_\eta(a,d\eta)\) where this state/law factorization is valid; discounting is outside \(W\) in this convention Operators §10 \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) fixed-policy continuation-to-decision evaluation \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}f=\operatorname{evaluate}(B_\succ f,\pi)\) Operators §7 \(\mathbb T_\succ\) optimizing continuation-to-decision operator \((\mathbb T_\succ f)(x)=\sup_{a\in\Gamma(x)}(B_\succ f)(x,a)\); the selection/evaluation factorization requires attainment Operators §7 \(\mathbb T_\prec\) decision-to-arrival aggregation \(\mathbb T_\prec=B_\prec\) on specified function classes Operators §5 \(\mathbb T_\pi,\mathbb T\) fixed-policy and optimizing stage operators \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\); \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\) Stages §2 \(P_\prec,P_{\succ,\pi},P_\pi\) undiscounted transition expectations \(P_\pi=P_\prec\circ P_{\succ,\pi}\), distinct from reward-bearing Bellman evaluation Operators §3 \(\mathbb M_\pi\) probability propagation under a fixed feasible policy \(\langle\mathbb M_\pi\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\pi f\rangle\) for bounded measurable or absolutely integrable tests, with \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,d\mu\) Operators §3 \(\mathbb T_{\mathrm{period}}\) composition across a period's compatible boundaries maps end-boundary functions to start-boundary functions; a self-map only under the required identification Stage composition §2 \(v^\star\) stationary infinite-horizon fixed point when established \(\mathbb T_{\mathrm{period}}v^\star=v^\star\); existence/uniqueness/optimality require hypotheses Periods §4 \(Q_j(x)\) branch decision value at a common current state includes the branch's current reward and continuation calculation, distinct from a function on its continuation state space Branching §§4–5

The integral rows require joint measurability and pointwise integrability on their full declared domains. Independent shock laws are special cases of the conditional laws displayed here. A scalar field domain does not establish those analytic properties. The post-decision factorization is the alternative timing stated in its source section, not a redefinition of the running example's continuation boundary.
