1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text: HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kNrm Prestate (arrival perch) \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}\) pLvlPrev Prestate (arrival perch) \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) PermShk Shock (decision perch) \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) TranShk Shock (decision perch) \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) yNrm Decision perch variable \(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\) pLvl Decision perch variable \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) bNrm Decision perch variable \(b_t \in \mathbb{R}\) mNrm Decision perch variable \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}\) cNrm Control (decision perch) \(c_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) aNrm Continuation perch variable \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}\) Rfree State-dependent rate \(R_t \in \{R^{\text{save}}, R^{\text{boro}}\}\) boro Borrowing indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{k_t < 0}\) live Survival shock \(\ell_{t+1} \in \{0,1\}\)

docs.title: 2.1 Overview
docs.text:
The ConsKinkedR model describes an infinitely-lived agent facing idiosyncratic income risk who accumulates a risk-free asset to smooth consumption over time. The key friction is a kinked interest rate schedule: the agent faces interest factor \(R^{\text{save}}\) when saving (\(k_t \geq 0\)) but pays a higher interest factor \(R^{\text{boro}} > R^{\text{save}}\) when borrowing (\(k_t < 0\)). This asymmetry captures realistic credit market imperfections such as credit card interest rates exceeding savings account returns.

The agent receives labor income subject to both permanent shocks \(\psi_t\) (affecting the income level permanently) and transitory shocks \(\theta_t\) (affecting only current income). Permanent income follows a geometric random walk with trend growth \(\Gamma\). The agent optimizes consumption to maximize expected discounted lifetime utility, subject to this kinked budget constraint and the risk of mortality.

docs.title: 2.2 State Space
docs.text:
Arrival (Prestate) Variables: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}\): normalized capital holdings at the beginning of period \(t\), measured relative to permanent income \(p_{t-1}\) from the previous period - \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\): permanent income level from period \(t-1\)

The arrival state space is \(\mathcal{K} \times \mathcal{P} \coloneqq \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}_{++}\).

Decision (Post-Shock) Variables: After observing shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\), the agent computes: - \(G_t \coloneqq \Gamma \psi_t\): realized permanent income growth factor - \(p_t \coloneqq p_{t-1} G_t\): updated permanent income level - \(R_t \coloneqq R^{\text{save}} + (R^{\text{boro}} - R^{\text{save}}) \mathbb{1}_{k_t < 0}\): realized interest factor - \(b_t \coloneqq \frac{R_t k_t}{G_t}\): normalized bank balances (capital plus interest, re-normalized by new permanent income) - \(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\): normalized labor income - \(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t\): normalized market resources (total resources available for consumption)

Continuation (Post-Decision) Variables: - \(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t \in \mathbb{R}\): normalized end-of-period assets

docs.title: 2.3 Action Space
docs.text: The agent chooses normalized consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\), implicitly determining end-of-period assets \(a_t = m_t - c_t\).

docs.title: 2.4 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income Shocks: Joint distribution of permanent and transitory shocks: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}} \quad \text{with support on } \mathbb{R}_{++}^2\)$

Typically specified with \(\mathbb{E}[\psi_t] = 1\) (so \(\Gamma\) captures expected growth) and \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_t] = 1\) (so the transitory shock is mean-preserving).

Survival Shock: $\(\ell_{t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\Lambda)\)$ where \(\Lambda \in [0,1]\) is the survival probability (LivPrb).

Initial Distributions: - \(p_0 \sim F_{p,0}\): initial permanent income distribution - \(k_0 \sim F_{k,0}\): initial normalized capital distribution

docs.title: 2.5 State Transitions
docs.text:
The dynamics unfold in the following sequence:

  1. Arrival: Agent enters period with \((k_t, p_{t-1})\)
  2. Income realization: Draw \((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}}\)
  3. Income update: Compute \(G_t = \Gamma \psi_t\) and \(p_t = p_{t-1} G_t\)
  4. Interest rate determination: Set \(R_t = R^{\text{save}}\) if \(k_t \geq 0\), else \(R_t = R^{\text{boro}}\)
  5. Resource calculation: $\(b_t = \frac{R_t k_t}{G_t}, \quad y_t = \theta_t, \quad m_t = b_t + y_t\)$
  6. Consumption choice: Agent chooses \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) optimally
  7. Asset accumulation: \(a_t = m_t - c_t\)
  8. Survival: Draw \(\ell_{t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\Lambda)\)
  9. Twist (if alive): Set \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(p_t\) carries forward as \(p_t\)

The state transition for survivors is: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t = m_t - c_t = \frac{R_t k_t}{G_t} + \theta_t - c_t\)$

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The agent's optimization problem decomposes into three value functions corresponding to the ADC (Arrival-Decision-Continuation) framework.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, before observing current income shocks, the agent's expected value is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \theta_t}\left[V^{\text{dec}}(k_t, p_{t-1}; \psi_t, \theta_t)\right]\)$

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{arr}} = \{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function
docs.text:
At the decision perch, after observing shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\), the agent solves: $\(V^{\text{dec}}(k_t, p_{t-1}; \psi_t, \theta_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{u(c_t p_t) + \beta \Lambda V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)\right\}\)$

where: - \(G_t = \Gamma \psi_t\) - \(p_t = p_{t-1} G_t\) - \(R_t = R^{\text{save}} + (R^{\text{boro}} - R^{\text{save}}) \mathbb{1}_{k_t < 0}\) - \(b_t = R_t k_t / G_t\) - \(m_t = b_t + \theta_t\) - \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) - \(u(\cdot)\) is the period utility function (typically CRRA: \(u(C) = \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)) - \(\beta\) is the time discount factor - \(\Lambda\) is the survival probability

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{dec}} = \{k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \theta_t\} = \{m_t, p_t, R_t\}\)

Equivalently, working with normalized consumption \(c_t\) (consumption divided by \(p_t\)): $\(V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, p_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{p_t^{1-\rho} u(c_t) + \beta \Lambda V^{\text{cont}}(m_t - c_t, p_t)\right\}\)$

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value Function
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, after the consumption decision but before next period's arrival: $\(V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t) = V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, p_t)\)$

where the twist mapping gives \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(p_t\) becomes next period's \(p_{t-1}\).

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{cont}} = \{a_t, p_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.4 Recursive Formulation
docs.text:
Combining the perches, the full Bellman equation is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \theta_t}\left[\max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{p_t^{1-\rho} u(c_t) + \beta \Lambda V^{\text{arr}}(m_t - c_t, p_t)\right\}\right]\)$

subject to the state evolution equations specified above.

The kinked interest rate creates a non-convexity in the budget constraint: the effective return on savings differs depending on whether \(k_t \gtrless 0\). This kink propagates through the policy function, potentially creating a region of rapid adjustment near \(k_t = 0\).

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for consumption at the decision perch yields: $\(u'(c_t p_t) p_t = \beta \Lambda \frac{\partial V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t}\)$

By the envelope theorem at the continuation perch: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t} = \frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, p_t)}{\partial k_{t+1}} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}}{\partial m_{t+1}} \cdot \frac{\partial m_{t+1}}{\partial k_{t+1}}\right]\)$

Since \(m_{t+1} = \frac{R_{t+1} k_{t+1}}{G_{t+1}} + \theta_{t+1}\) where \(G_{t+1} = \Gamma \psi_{t+1}\) and \(R_{t+1}\) depends on the sign of \(k_{t+1} = a_t\): $\(\frac{\partial m_{t+1}}{\partial k_{t+1}} = \frac{R_{t+1}}{G_{t+1}} \quad \text{for } k_{t+1} \neq 0\)$

At \(k_{t+1} = 0\), there is a kink in the marginal return: - Right derivative: \(\frac{R^{\text{save}}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\) - Left derivative: \(\frac{R^{\text{boro}}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\)

The Euler equation becomes: $\(u'(c_t p_t) = \beta \Lambda \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[u'(c_{t+1} p_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{R_{t+1}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\right]\)$

where \(R_{t+1} = R^{\text{save}} \mathbb{1}_{a_t \geq 0} + R^{\text{boro}} \mathbb{1}_{a_t < 0}\).

docs.title: 4.2 Normalized Euler Equation
docs.text:
Working with normalized consumption \(c_t \coloneqq C_t / p_t\) and assuming CRRA utility \(u(C) = \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\): $\(c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \Lambda \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\left(\frac{R_{t+1}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\right) \psi_{t+1}^{-\rho} c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\right]\)$

Simplifying: $\(c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \Lambda R_{t+1} \Gamma^{-1} \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\psi_{t+1}^{-\rho} c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\right]\)$

docs.title: 4.3 Envelope Condition
docs.text:
The envelope theorem at the decision perch gives: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}}{\partial m_t} = u'(c_t p_t) p_t = p_t^{1-\rho} c_t^{-\rho}\)$

This marginal value of resources is used in the backward iteration of the solution algorithm.

docs.text:
The model is well-suited for the Endogenous Gridpoint Method (Carroll, 2006), which inverts the Euler equation:

docs.title: 2.1 Primitives
docs.text:
This is an infinite-horizon consumption-saving model with a representative household facing idiosyncratic income risk and preference shocks. The household's problem features a kinky interest rate structure: the risk-free rate differs between borrowing and saving positions.

State space at arrival perch: \(\mathcal{S}_{\text{arrival}} = \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_+\), where the state is \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) with: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}\): normalized capital holdings (can be negative if borrowing) - \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_+\): permanent income level from previous period

Action space: \(\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{R}_+\), where \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) is normalized consumption.

Shock structure: At each period \(t\), three independent shocks are realized:

  1. Income shocks \((\psi_t, \xi_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}}\) where:
  2. \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is a permanent income shock with \(\mathbb{E}[\psi_t] = 1\)

  3. \(\xi_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is a transitory income shock with \(\mathbb{E}[\xi_t] = 1\)

  4. Preference shock \(\eta_t \sim F_{\text{pref}}\) affecting marginal utility

  5. Mortality shock with survival probability \(\pi \in [0,1]\)

Parameters: - \(R_{\text{boro}} > 1\): gross interest rate when borrowing (\(k_t < 0\)) - \(R_{\text{save}} > 1\): gross interest rate when saving (\(k_t \geq 0\)) - \(\Gamma > 0\): expected permanent income growth factor - \(\pi \in [0,1]\): survival probability

Typically, \(R_{\text{boro}} > R_{\text{save}}\), creating a kink at zero assets.

docs.title: 2.2 Timing and Information Structure
docs.text:
The within-period timing follows the Arrival-Decision-Continuation (ADC) protocol:

Arrival perch (beginning of period \(t\), pre-shock): - Agent enters with state \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) - Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{arr}} = \sigma\{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

Decision perch (post-shock, pre-decision): - Shocks \((\psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t)\) realize - Permanent income updates: \(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t \eqqcolon p_{t-1} \cdot G_t\) - Normalized labor income: \(y_t = \xi_t\) - Interest factor realizes: \(R_t = \begin{cases} R_{\text{boro}} & \text{if } k_t < 0 \\ R_{\text{save}} & \text{if } k_t \geq 0 \end{cases}\) - Bank balances: \(b_t = \frac{R_t \cdot k_t}{G_t}\) - Market resources: \(m_t = b_t + y_t\) - Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{dec}} = \sigma\{k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t\}\) - Agent chooses consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\)

Continuation perch (post-decision, pre-survival): - End-of-period assets: \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) - Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{cont}} = \sigma\{k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t, c_t\}\) - Mortality shock realizes: agent survives with probability \(\pi\)

Twist mapping (connector to next period): - If the agent survives: \((k_{t+1}, p_t) = (a_t, p_t)\) - If the agent dies: new agent drawn from initial distribution \((k_{t+1}, p_t) \sim F_{\text{init}}\)

docs.title: 2.3 Preferences
docs.text:
The household has period utility over consumption with preference shocks: $\(u(c_t, \eta_t) = \eta_t \cdot u(c_t)\)$

where \(u(\cdot)\) is a standard CRRA utility function (typically) and \(\eta_t\) is a multiplicative shock to marginal utility. The preference shock creates time-varying impatience or urgency to consume.

The household maximizes expected discounted lifetime utility: $\(\mathbb{E}_0 \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t \pi^t \eta_t u(c_t) \right]\)$

where \(\beta \in (0,1)\) is the discount factor and \(\pi^t\) accounts for survival probabilities.

docs.title: 2.4 Budget Constraint
docs.text:
The sequential budget constraints are:

  1. Beginning of period: Capital \(k_t\) earns interest rate depending on sign: $\(b_t = \frac{R_t \cdot k_t}{G_t}\)$ where \(R_t = \mathbb{1}_{\{k_t \geq 0\}} R_{\text{save}} + \mathbb{1}_{\{k_t < 0\}} R_{\text{boro}}\)

  2. Market resources: $\(m_t = b_t + y_t = \frac{R_t \cdot k_t}{G_t} + \xi_t\)$

  3. End-of-period assets: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t\)$

  4. Next period capital (for survivors): $\(k_{t+1} = a_t\)$

The normalization by permanent income \(p_t\) converts all nominal quantities to growth-adjusted terms, making the problem stationary despite permanent income growth.

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The value function is decomposed according to the ADC perch structure.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent has not yet observed the current period shocks. The arrival value function is:

\[V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t} \left[ V^{\text{dec}}(k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t) \mid \mathcal{F}_t^{\text{arr}} \right]\]

This represents the expected value before observing income and preference shocks, integrating over the joint distribution \(F_{\text{inc}} \times F_{\text{pref}}\).

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function
docs.text:
At the decision perch, after observing shocks, the agent solves:

\[V^{\text{dec}}(k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ \eta_t u(c_t) + \beta \pi V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t) \right\}\]

where: - \(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\) - \(G_t = \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\) - \(R_t = \begin{cases} R_{\text{boro}} & \text{if } k_t < 0 \\ R_{\text{save}} & \text{if } k_t \geq 0 \end{cases}\) - \(b_t = \frac{R_t \cdot k_t}{G_t}\) - \(m_t = b_t + \xi_t\) - \(a_t = m_t - c_t\)

The information set \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{dec}}\) includes all realized shocks: \(\{k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t\}\).

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value Function
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, the agent has chosen consumption but not yet resolved mortality uncertainty:

\[V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t) = V^{\text{arr}}(a_t, p_t)\]

This assumes that upon death, a new agent is born from the initial distribution, and we evaluate the equilibrium value at birth (in a stationary equilibrium, this equals the expected value of the initial distribution).

docs.title: 3.4 Complete Bellman Recursion
docs.text:
Combining all perches, the complete Bellman equation is:

\[\begin{aligned} V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) &= \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t} \left[ \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ \eta_t u(c_t) + \beta \pi V^{\text{arr}}(m_t - c_t, p_{t-1} \Gamma \psi_t) \right\} \right] \end{aligned}\]

where \(m_t = \frac{R_t k_t}{\Gamma \psi_t} + \xi_t\) and the kinked interest rate \(R_t\) depends on the sign of \(k_t\).

docs.title: 3.5 Normalized Formulation
docs.text:
Since the problem is normalized by permanent income, we can work with normalized variables exclusively. Define the normalized value function:

\[v(k_t) \coloneqq \frac{V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1})}{u(p_{t-1})}\]

Under CRRA utility \(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\), the normalized Bellman equation becomes:

\[v(k_t) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t} \left[ \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ \eta_t \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \pi (\Gamma \psi_t)^{1-\rho} v(a_t) \right\} \right]\]

This formulation isolates the scale-invariant structure of the problem.

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for consumption at the decision perch is:

\[\eta_t u'(c_t) = \beta \pi \frac{\partial V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t}\]

By the envelope theorem applied at the continuation perch:

\[\frac{\partial V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t} = \frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, p_t)}{\partial k_{t+1}} \bigg|_{k_{t+1} = a_t}\]

At the arrival perch, integrating over next period's shocks:

\[\frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, p_t)}{\partial k_{t+1}} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}, \eta_{t+1}} \left[ \eta_{t+1} u'(c_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{R_{t+1}}{G_{t+1}} \mid k_{t+1}, p_t \right]\]

where: - \(R_{t+1} = \begin{cases} R_{\text{boro}} & \text{if } k_{t+1} < 0 \\ R_{\text{save}} & \text{if } k_{t+1} \geq 0 \end{cases}\) - \(G_{t+1} = \Gamma \psi_{t+1}\)

docs.title: 4.2 Complete Euler Equation
docs.text:
Combining these expressions, the complete Euler equation is:

\[\eta_t u'(c_t) = \beta \pi \mathbb{E}_{t+1} \left[ \eta_{t+1} u'(c_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{R_{t+1}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}} \right]\]

where the expectation \(\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\) is taken over shocks \((\psi_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}, \eta_{t+1})\) conditional on the end-of-period state \((a_t, p_t)\).

docs.title: 4.3 Envelope Condition
docs.text:
The marginal value of arriving wealth satisfies:

\[\frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1})}{\partial k_t} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \xi_t, \eta_t} \left[ \eta_t u'(c_t) \cdot \frac{R_t}{G_t} \right]\]

This reflects that an additional unit of capital \(k_t\) increases market resources \(m_t\) by \(\frac{R_t}{G_t}\), with the marginal value weighted by the preference shock.

docs.title: 4.4 Kink at Zero Assets
docs.text:
The interest rate function \(R_t\) is discontinuous at \(k_t = 0\):

\[\lim_{k \to 0^-} R(k) = R_{\text{boro}} > R_{\text{save}} = \lim_{k \to 0^+} R(k)\]

This creates a kink in the value function and policy function at zero assets. The consumption function \(c(m_t, \eta_t)\) will have a discontinuous derivative at the wealth level corresponding to \(k_{t+1} = 0\).

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Labor-Saving Model with Intensive Margin
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kNrm Prestate/Arrival perch state \(k_t\) pLvlPrev Prestate/Arrival perch state \(p_{t-1}\) PermShk Arrival shock \(\psi_t\) TranShk Arrival shock \(\theta_t\) pLvl Decision perch state \(p_t\) bNrm Decision perch state \(b_t\) cNrm Control/Action \(c_t\) Lbr Control/Action \(\ell_t\) aNrm Continuation perch state \(a_t\) mNrm Market resources (derived) \(m_t\) yNrm Labor income (derived) \(y_t\) live Survival shock \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}}\)

Information Set Hierarchy: - Arrival perch: Agent knows \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) but not yet \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\) - Decision perch: Agent observes \((b_t, p_t, \theta_t)\) after shocks realize - Continuation perch: Agent has chosen \((c_t, \ell_t)\) and arrives at \(a_t\)

docs.title: 2.1 State Spaces
docs.text:
The model features a two-dimensional continuous state space at the arrival perch:

  • Normalized capital holdings: \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) represents beginning-of-period assets normalized by last period's permanent income \(p_{t-1}\)
  • Permanent income level: \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) represents the agent's permanent income level entering period \(t\)

At the decision perch, the state expands to include the realized transitory shock: - Normalized bank balances: \(b_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Permanent income level: \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) - Transitory productivity: \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\)

docs.title: 2.2 Action Space
docs.text:
The agent chooses two control variables:

  • Normalized consumption: \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) where \(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t\) represents normalized market resources
  • Labor supply: \(\ell_t \in [0, 1]\) represents the fraction of time allocated to work (intensive margin)

The agent simultaneously determines consumption and labor supply to maximize expected discounted utility subject to the budget constraint.

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Joint income shock distribution: The pair \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\) of permanent and transitory productivity shocks follows the joint distribution \(F_{\text{Inc}}(\psi, \theta)\) specified by IncShkDstn. We write: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{Inc}}\)$

These shocks realize at the beginning of period \(t\), after the agent arrives with state \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) but before consumption and labor decisions.

Survival shock: At the end of the period, the agent survives with probability \(\pi \in [0,1]\) (parameter LivPrb): $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)$

Non-survivors exit the model and may be replaced by newborns.

docs.title: 2.4 Transition Dynamics
docs.text:
The permanent income evolution follows: $\(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\)$ where \(\Gamma\) (PermGroFac) is the deterministic growth factor and \(\psi_t\) is the permanent shock.

Normalized bank balances reflect returns on previous assets, scaled by income growth: $\(b_t = \frac{R \cdot k_t}{\Gamma \cdot \psi_t}\)$ where \(R\) (Rfree) is the gross risk-free interest rate.

Labor income is generated by combining transitory productivity with chosen labor supply: $\(y_t = W \cdot \theta_t \cdot \ell_t\)$ where \(W\) (WageRte) is the wage rate and \(\theta_t \cdot \ell_t\) represents effective labor supply.

Market resources combine bank balances and labor income: $\(m_t = b_t + y_t = b_t + W \cdot \theta_t \cdot \ell_t\)$

End-of-period assets satisfy the budget constraint: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t = b_t + W \cdot \theta_t \cdot \ell_t - c_t\)$

Next period's normalized capital for survivors: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t\)$ Note that \(k_{t+1}\) is already normalized by \(p_t\), which becomes next period's \(p_{t-1}\).

docs.title: 2.5 Initial Distribution
docs.text: At model birth (initialization), agents draw: - Initial permanent income: \(p_0 \sim F_{\text{pLvl}}\) (pLvlInitDstn) - Initial normalized capital: \(k_0 \sim F_{\text{kNrm}}\) (kNrmInitDstn)

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The agent's problem decomposes into three value functions corresponding to the ADC (Arrival-Decision-Continuation) perches.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent has not yet observed income shocks. The arrival value represents the expected value before shocks:

\[\mathcal{V}^A(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{Inc}}}\left[\mathcal{V}^D(b_t, p_t, \theta_t)\right]\]

where the decision perch state variables are determined by: $\(\begin{aligned} p_t &= p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t \\ b_t &= \frac{R \cdot k_t}{\Gamma \cdot \psi_t} \end{aligned}\)$

Information set at arrival: \(\mathcal{F}^A_t = \{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function
docs.text:
At the decision perch, shocks have realized and the agent chooses consumption and labor supply:

\[\mathcal{V}^D(b_t, p_t, \theta_t) = \max_{c_t, \ell_t} \left\{ u(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t) + \beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{V}^C(a_t, p_t) \right\}\]

subject to: $\(\begin{aligned} y_t &= W \cdot \theta_t \cdot \ell_t \\ m_t &= b_t + y_t \\ a_t &= m_t - c_t \\ c_t &\geq 0, \quad \ell_t \in [0, 1], \quad a_t \geq 0 \end{aligned}\)$

Here \(u(\cdot, \cdot)\) is the period utility function over consumption in levels (\(c_t \cdot p_t\)) and leisure (\(1 - \ell_t\)), and \(\beta\) is the time discount factor.

Information set at decision: \(\mathcal{F}^D_t = \{b_t, p_t, \theta_t\}\)

Note on survival: The factor \(\pi\) represents the continuation probability. Non-survivors receive no continuation value, implicitly setting their terminal value to zero.

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value Function
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, decisions have been made and assets \(a_t\) are carried forward:

\[\mathcal{V}^C(a_t, p_t) = \mathcal{V}^A(k_{t+1}, p_t)\]

where the twist mapping determines next period's arrival state: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t, \quad p_{t} \text{ becomes } p_{t}\)$

This value represents the ex-post value of having chosen to save \(a_t\), normalized by permanent income \(p_t\), before next period's shocks.

Information set at continuation: \(\mathcal{F}^C_t = \{a_t, p_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.4 Complete Recursive Structure
docs.text:
Combining the three perches yields the complete Bellman operator:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal{V}^A(k_t, p_{t-1}) &= \mathbb{E}_{(\psi_t, \theta_t)}\left[\mathcal{V}^D\left(\frac{R \cdot k_t}{\Gamma \cdot \psi_t}, p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t, \theta_t\right)\right] \\ \mathcal{V}^D(b_t, p_t, \theta_t) &= \max_{c_t, \ell_t} \left\{ u(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t) + \beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{V}^A(b_t + W \cdot \theta_t \cdot \ell_t - c_t, p_t) \right\} \\ \end{aligned}\]

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equations
docs.text:
The optimal choices of consumption and labor satisfy the first-order conditions with respect to each control.

Consumption FOC: Taking the derivative with respect to \(c_t\):

\[u_c(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t) \cdot p_t = \beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{V}^C_a(a_t, p_t)\]

where \(u_c\) denotes the marginal utility of consumption.

Labor supply FOC: Taking the derivative with respect to \(\ell_t\):

\[-u_\ell(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t) = W \cdot \theta_t \cdot \beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{V}^C_a(a_t, p_t)\]

where \(u_\ell\) denotes the marginal utility of leisure (negative of marginal disutility of labor).

Combining FOCs: The labor-consumption tradeoff satisfies:

\[\frac{u_\ell(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t)}{u_c(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t)} = W \cdot \theta_t \cdot p_t\]

This is the intratemporal condition: the marginal rate of substitution between leisure and consumption equals the real wage (wage rate times transitory productivity).

docs.title: 4.2 Envelope Condition
docs.text:
The marginal value of assets at the continuation perch satisfies:

\[\mathcal{V}^C_a(a_t, p_t) = \mathbb{E}_{(\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1})}\left[\mathcal{V}^D_b(b_{t+1}, p_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{R}{\Gamma \cdot \psi_{t+1}}\right]\]

This follows from differentiating the arrival value with respect to \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and applying the chain rule through \(b_{t+1} = R \cdot k_{t+1} / (\Gamma \cdot \psi_{t+1})\).

By the envelope theorem at the decision stage: $\(\mathcal{V}^D_b(b_{t+1}, p_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}) = u_c(c_{t+1} \cdot p_{t+1}, 1 - \ell_{t+1}) \cdot p_{t+1}\)$

docs.title: 4.3 Intertemporal Euler Equation
docs.text:
Combining the consumption FOC with the envelope condition:

\[u_c(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t) \cdot p_t = \beta \pi \cdot R \cdot \mathbb{E}_{(\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1})}\left[\frac{u_c(c_{t+1} \cdot p_{t+1}, 1 - \ell_{t+1}) \cdot p_{t+1}}{\Gamma \cdot \psi_{t+1}}\right]\]

Since \(p_{t+1} = p_t \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_{t+1}\), this simplifies to:

\[u_c(c_t \cdot p_t, 1 - \ell_t) = \beta \pi \cdot R \cdot \mathbb{E}_{(\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1})}\left[u_c(c_{t+1} \cdot p_{t+1}, 1 - \ell_{t+1})\right]\]

This is the standard Euler equation relating current marginal utility to expected future marginal utility, adjusted for interest, survival, and discounting.

docs.title: 4.4 Policy Functions
docs.text:
The solution to the Bellman equation yields policy functions:

\[\begin{aligned} c_t &= c^*(b_t, \theta_t) \quad \text{(`cFunc`)} \\ \ell_t &= \ell^*(b_t, \theta_t) \quad \text{(`LbrFunc`)} \end{aligned}\]

These functions map the decision perch state \((b_t, \theta_t)\) to optimal choices. Note that permanent income \(p_t\) does not appear due to homotheticity assumptions typical in consumption-saving models. The normalization by permanent income ensures policy functions depend only on normalized states.

docs.title: 4.5 Endogenous Grid Method (EGM) Representation
docs.text:
For consumption-saving models, the endogenous gridpoint method can efficiently solve for policy functions by:

  1. Constructing a grid over end-of-period assets \(\{a_i\}\)
  2. Computing continuation values and marginal values on this grid
  3. Using the Euler equation to find consumption: \(c_i = (u_c)^{-1}\left(\beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{V}^C_a(a_i, p_t) / p_t\right)\)
  4. Computing beginning-of-period resources: \(m_i = a_i + c_i\)
  5. Interpolating to obtain \(c^*(m, \theta)\)

With labor supply, the intratemporal condition couples \(c_t\) and \(\ell_t\), requiring joint solution of both FOCs at each gridpoint.

docs.title: 5. Forward Operator
docs.text: The distribution of agents over states evolves through the model dynamics. Let \(\Phi_t(k, p)\) denote the joint probability measure over normalized capital and permanent income at time \(t\).

docs.title: 5.1 Transition Law
docs.text:
For survivors, the evolution from period \(t\) to \(t+1\) follows:

\[\Phi_{t+1}(K, P) = \pi \int \int \mathbb{1}\{a_t(b, p, \theta) \in K, p \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi \in P\} \, dF_{\text{Inc}}(\psi, \theta) \, d\Phi_t(k, p/\Gamma)\]

where: - $b = R \cdot k

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Saving Model with Markov State Transitions
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kNrm Prestate (Arrival perch) \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) pLvlPrev Prestate (Arrival perch) \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) zPrev Prestate (Arrival perch) \(z_{t-1} \in \{1, \ldots, N_z\}\) Mrkv, z Poststate (Decision perch) \(z_t \in \{1, \ldots, N_z\}\) PermShk Shock realization \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) TranShk Shock realization \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) yNrm Income at decision perch \(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\) pLvl Permanent income at decision \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) bNrm Bank balances at decision \(b_t \in \mathbb{R}\) mNrm Market resources (decision state) \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) cNrm Control variable \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) aNrm Postdecision state (Continuation perch) \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) live Survival indicator \(\ell_{t+1} \in \{0, 1\}\) Rfree[z] State-dependent return factor \(R(z) \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) PermGroFac[z] State-dependent growth factor \(\Gamma(z) \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) LivPrb[z] State-dependent survival probability \(\pi(z) \in [0, 1]\) MrkvArray Markov transition matrix \(\mathbb{P}_{z' \mid z} \in [0,1]^{N_z \times N_z}\) IncShkDstn[z] State-dependent shock distribution \(F_z(\psi, \theta)\) cFuncX Policy function \(c^*(z, m)\)

Timing convention: Variables at the arrival perch are indexed by their continuation-perch origin. The twist operation maps continuation-perch variables from period \(t\) to arrival-perch variables for period \(t+1\).

docs.title: 2.1 State and Action Spaces
docs.text:
The model features a three-dimensional state space at the arrival perch: - Normalized capital: \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+ \coloneqq [0, \infty)\), representing assets brought into period \(t\), normalized by permanent income \(p_{t-1}\) from the previous period. - Previous permanent income level: \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++} \coloneqq (0, \infty)\), the level of permanent income from the end of period \(t-1\). - Previous Markov state: \(z_{t-1} \in \mathcal{Z} \coloneqq \{1, 2, \ldots, N_z\}\), a finite discrete state space.

The arrival state is thus \((k_t, p_{t-1}, z_{t-1}) \in \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{++} \times \mathcal{Z}\).

At the decision perch, after observing the current Markov state \(z_t\) and income shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\), the agent observes: - Current Markov state: \(z_t \in \mathcal{Z}\) - Permanent income level: \(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma(z_t) \cdot \psi_t\) - Market resources (normalized): \(m_t = b_t + y_t\) where: - \(b_t \coloneqq \frac{R(z_t) \cdot k_t}{\Gamma(z_t) \cdot \psi_t}\) (normalized bank balances) - \(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\) (normalized labor income)

The decision state is \((z_t, m_t, p_t) \in \mathcal{Z} \times \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{++}\).

The action space consists of normalized consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\), which determines normalized end-of-period assets \(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\).

The continuation perch state is \((a_t, p_t, z_t)\), from which the agent may die with probability \(1 - \pi(z_t)\) or survive to enter the next period.

docs.title: 2.2 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
The model features two sources of randomness:

Markov state transitions: Given the previous discrete state \(z_{t-1}\), the current state evolves according to $\(z_t \sim \mathbb{P}(\cdot \mid z_{t-1}), \quad \text{where } \mathbb{P}_{ij} \coloneqq \Pr(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i).\)$

Income shocks: Conditional on the realized Markov state \(z_t\), the agent draws permanent and transitory income shocks from a state-dependent joint distribution: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{z_t}(\psi, \theta).\)$ Here \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is a multiplicative permanent shock and \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is a transitory shock to normalized labor income.

Mortality: At the end of the period, conditional on discrete state \(z_t\), the agent survives to period \(t+1\) with probability \(\pi(z_t)\): $\(\ell_{t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi(z_t)).\)$ If the agent dies (\(\ell_{t+1} = 0\)), we assume the value is zero and the agent is replaced by a newborn agent drawn from the initial distribution.

docs.title: 2.3 State Transitions
docs.text:
The timing and information structure follow the ADC perch decomposition:

  1. Arrival perch → Decision perch: The agent enters period \(t\) with arrival state \((k_t, p_{t-1}, z_{t-1})\). The Markov state transitions: $\(z_t \sim \mathbb{P}(\cdot \mid z_{t-1}).\)$ Income shocks are then realized: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{z_t}(\psi, \theta).\)$ The permanent income level evolves: $\(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma(z_t) \cdot \psi_t,\)$ where \(\Gamma(z_t)\) is the state-dependent expected permanent income growth factor. Normalized bank balances and market resources are computed: $\(b_t = \frac{R(z_t) \cdot k_t}{\Gamma(z_t) \cdot \psi_t}, \quad m_t = b_t + \theta_t.\)$ The information set at the decision perch is \(\mathcal{F}_t^d = \{z_t, m_t, p_t\}\) (plus all history).

  2. Decision perch → Continuation perch: The agent chooses consumption \(c_t\), determining end-of-period assets: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t.\)$ The continuation state is \((a_t, p_t, z_t)\). The information set at the continuation perch is \(\mathcal{F}_t^c = \{a_t, p_t, z_t\}\).

  3. Continuation perch → Next arrival perch (twist): The agent's survival is realized: $\(\ell_{t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi(z_t)).\)$ If the agent survives (\(\ell_{t+1} = 1\)), the continuation state maps to the next period's arrival state via: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t, \quad p_t \to p_t, \quad z_t \to z_t.\)$ More precisely, the twist operation is: $\(\text{twist}: (a_t, p_t, z_t) \mapsto (k_{t+1}, p_{t}, z_{t}) \coloneqq (a_t, p_t, z_t).\)$ This prepares the state for the next period's arrival perch, where \(z_t\) becomes \(z_{t-1}\) in the next iteration and \(p_t\) becomes \(p_{t-1}\).

docs.title: 2.4 Preferences
docs.text:
The model implicitly assumes time-separable CRRA preferences. Although not explicitly stated in the YAML, the typical specification is: $\(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}, \quad \rho > 0,\)$ with time discount factor \(\beta \in (0, 1)\). The value function at the decision perch is: $\(v(z, m, p) = \max_{c \in [0, m]} \left\{ u(c) + \beta \pi(z) \mathbb{E}_{z', \psi', \theta' \mid z} w(a, p, z) \right\},\)$ where \(a = m - c\) and \(w\) denotes the continuation value.

For normalized problems, it is common to assume that the value function is homogeneous of degree \(1-\rho\) in \(p\), so we can write: $\(v(z, m, p) = p^{1-\rho} \tilde{v}(z, m),\)$ where \(\tilde{v}\) is the normalized value function depending only on the discrete state and normalized market resources.

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: We decompose the recursive problem into three perches following the ADC framework.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Perch: Pre-Shock Expectation
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent has state \((k_t, p_{t-1}, z_{t-1})\) and awaits the realization of the Markov state \(z_t\) and income shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\).

The arrival value function \(V^a(k, p_{-1}, z_{-1})\) represents the expected value before these shocks are realized: $\(V^a(k, p_{-1}, z_{-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{z, \psi, \theta \mid z_{-1}} \left[ V^d(z, m, p) \right],\)$ where the expectation is taken over: - \(z \sim \mathbb{P}(\cdot \mid z_{-1})\) (Markov transition), - \((\psi, \theta) \sim F_z(\psi, \theta)\) (state-dependent income shocks),

and the decision-perch state is constructed via: $\(p = p_{-1} \cdot \Gamma(z) \cdot \psi, \quad b = \frac{R(z) \cdot k}{\Gamma(z) \cdot \psi}, \quad m = b + \theta.\)$

Information set at arrival perch: \(\mathcal{F}^a = \{k, p_{-1}, z_{-1}\}\).

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Perch: Post-Shock Optimization
docs.text:
At the decision perch, the agent observes the realized state \((z, m, p)\) and chooses consumption \(c\) to maximize: $\(V^d(z, m, p) = \max_{c \in [0, m]} \left\{ u(c \cdot p) + \beta V^c(a, p, z) \right\},\)$ where \(a = m - c\) is normalized end-of-period assets.

For normalized models with CRRA utility, we typically exploit homogeneity. Defining the normalized value function \(\tilde{V}^d(z, m) = p^{\rho-1} V^d(z, m, p)\) and normalizing \(\tilde{c} = c\), the normalized Bellman equation becomes: $\(\tilde{V}^d(z, m) = \max_{c \in [0, m]} \left\{ u(c) + \beta \tilde{V}^c(a, z) \right\},\)$ where $\(\tilde{V}^c(a, z) = \pi(z) \mathbb{E}_{z', \psi', \theta' \mid z} \left[ (\Gamma(z') \psi')^{1-\rho} \tilde{V}^d(z', m') \right],\)$ and \(m' = \frac{R(z') a}{\Gamma(z') \psi'} + \theta'\).

Information set at decision perch: \(\mathcal{F}^d = \{z, m, p\}\) (or \(\{z, m\}\) in normalized form).

The optimal consumption policy is denoted \(c^*(z, m)\) (the function cFuncX in HARK).

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Perch: Post-Decision Value
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, after choosing \(c\) and thereby determining \(a = m - c\), the agent faces mortality risk. The continuation value function is: $\(V^c(a, p, z) = \pi(z) \mathbb{E}_{z', \psi', \theta' \mid z} \left[ V^d(z', m', p') \right] + (1 - \pi(z)) \cdot 0,\)$ where the second term reflects that the agent receives zero continuation value if they die.

Given survival, the next-period decision state evolves as: $\(p' = p \cdot \Gamma(z') \cdot \psi', \quad k' = a, \quad m' = \frac{R(z') k'}{\Gamma(z') \psi'} + \theta'.\)$

In normalized form: $\(\tilde{V}^c(a, z) = \pi(z) \mathbb{E}_{z', \psi', \theta' \mid z} \left[ (\Gamma(z') \psi')^{1-\rho} \tilde{V}^d(z', m') \right],\)$ where $\(m' = \frac{R(z') a}{\Gamma(z') \psi'} + \theta'.\)$

Information set at continuation perch: \(\mathcal{F}^c = \{a, p, z\}\) (or \(\{a, z\}\) in normalized form).

docs.text: The full recursive structure is: $$\begin{aligned} V^a(k, p_{-1}, z_{-1}) &= \mathbb{E}{z \sim \mathbb{P}(\cdot|z})} \mathbb{E{(\psi,\theta) \sim F_z} \left[ V^d(z, m, p) \right], \ V^d(z, m, p) &= \max \left{ u(c \cdot p) + \beta V^c(m-c, p, z) \right}, \ V^c(a, p, z) &= \pi(z) \mathbb{E

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Medical Shock Model
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text: HARK Variable DDSL Concept Mathematical Notation Perch kLvl Capital at arrival (pre-shock) \(k_t\) Arrival pLvlPrev Permanent income at arrival \(p_{t-1}\) Arrival PermShk Permanent income shock \(\Psi_t\) Decision TranShk Transitory income shock \(\theta_t\) Decision pLvl Permanent income post-shock \(p_t\) Decision yLvl Labor income \(y_t\) Decision bLvl Bank balances \(b_t\) Decision mLvl Market resources \(m_t\) Decision MedShk Medical need shock \(\xi_t\) Decision cLvl Consumption (control) \(c_t\) Decision MedLvl Medical expenditure (control) \(\mu_t\) Decision xLvl Total expenditure \(x_t\) Decision aLvl End-of-period assets \(a_t\) Continuation live Survival indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live}}\) Continuation Rfree Gross interest rate \(R\) Parameter LivPrb Survival probability \(\pi\) Parameter MedPrice Relative price of medical care \(p_M\) Parameter

docs.title: 2.1 Overview
docs.text: The consumption-medical shock model extends the standard incomplete-markets consumption-saving problem by introducing a second consumption good—medical care—with stochastic marginal utility. The agent faces three sources of uncertainty: permanent income shocks \(\Psi_t\), transitory income shocks \(\theta_t\), and medical need shocks \(\xi_t\) that modulate the marginal utility derived from medical expenditure.

docs.title: 2.2 State Space
docs.text:
The arrival state (beginning-of-period, pre-shock) consists of: - Capital holdings: \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Previous period's permanent income: \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

The decision state (post-shock, pre-decision) augments the arrival state with realized shocks: - Market resources: \(m_t = R k_t + y_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Current permanent income: \(p_t = \mathbb{E}[p_t | p_{t-1}] \cdot \Psi_t\) - Medical need shock: \(\xi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

docs.title: 2.3 Action Space
docs.text:
The agent chooses two control variables: - Consumption expenditure: \(c_t \in [0, m_t + p_M \mu_t]\) - Medical care: \(\mu_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\)

These must satisfy the budget constraint: $\(x_t \coloneqq c_t + p_M \mu_t \leq m_t\)$

Equivalently, end-of-period assets must be non-negative: $\(a_t \coloneqq m_t - x_t \geq 0\)$

docs.title: 2.4 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income shocks \((\Psi_t, \theta_t)\) follow a joint distribution: $\((\Psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{Inc}}\)$

with properties: - \(\mathbb{E}[\Psi_t] = 1\) (permanent shocks are mean-preserving) - \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_t] = 1\) (transitory shocks are mean-preserving) - \(\Psi_t, \theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

Medical need shocks \(\xi_t\) follow an independent distribution: $\(\xi_t \sim F_{\text{Med}}\)$

with \(\xi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) representing the multiplicative factor on marginal utility from medical care.

Survival shocks are Bernoulli: $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live}} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)$

where \(\pi \in (0,1]\) is the survival probability.

docs.title: 2.5 Permanent Income Dynamics
docs.text:
Permanent income follows a deterministic growth path with stochastic innovations: $\(\mathbb{E}[p_t | p_{t-1}] = G(p_{t-1})\)$

where \(G: \mathbb{R}_{++} \to \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is the expected permanent income function. The realized permanent income incorporates the multiplicative shock: $\(p_t = G(p_{t-1}) \cdot \Psi_t\)$

docs.title: 2.6 Labor Income
docs.text: Labor income is the product of permanent income and the transitory shock: $\(y_t = \theta_t \cdot p_t = \theta_t \cdot G(p_{t-1}) \cdot \Psi_t\)$

docs.title: 2.7 Capital Accumulation
docs.text:
Bank balances at the decision node equal the risk-free return on capital: $\(b_t = R \cdot k_t\)$

Market resources are bank balances plus labor income: $\(m_t = b_t + y_t = R k_t + \theta_t p_t\)$

End-of-period assets are market resources minus total expenditure: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t - p_M \mu_t\)$

docs.title: 2.8 State Transition
docs.text:
The continuation state \((a_t, p_t)\) maps to the next period's arrival state conditional on survival: $\(k_{t+1} = \begin{cases} a_t & \text{with probability } \pi \\ \text{terminal} & \text{with probability } 1-\pi \end{cases}\)$

\[p_t \to p_{t+1}^{\text{prev}} = p_t\]

The twist operator connects end-of-period to beginning-of-period variables: \((a_t, p_t) \mapsto (k_{t+1}, p_t)\).

docs.title: 2.9 Initial Distribution
docs.text:
At birth, the agent draws: - Normalized capital: \(k_0/p_{-1} \sim F_{k,\text{init}}\) - Initial permanent income: \(p_{-1} \sim F_{p,\text{init}}\)

with capital level \(k_0 = p_{-1} \cdot (k_0/p_{-1})\).

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The value function is decomposed across three perches following the Abel-Eberly-Panageas timing structure.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value (Pre-Shock)
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent holds capital \(k_t\) and permanent income level \(p_{t-1}\) from the previous period. The arrival value is the expectation over all shocks before observing their realizations:

\[V^A(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\Psi_t, \theta_t, \xi_t)} \left[ V^D(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) \mid k_t, p_{t-1} \right]\]

where the decision state variables are: \begin{align} p_t &= G(p_{t-1}) \cdot \Psi_t \ y_t &= \theta_t \cdot p_t \ m_t &= R k_t + y_t \end{align}

Information set: \(\mathcal{I}_t^A = \{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value (Post-Shock, Pre-Decision)
docs.text:
At the decision perch, all shocks have been realized. The agent observes \((m_t, p_t, \xi_t)\) and chooses consumption \(c_t\) and medical expenditure \(\mu_t\) to maximize:

\[V^D(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) = \max_{c_t, \mu_t} \left\{ u(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) + \beta \pi V^C(a_t, p_t) \right\}\]

subject to: \begin{align} a_t &= m_t - c_t - p_M \mu_t \ a_t &\geq 0 \ c_t &\geq 0, \quad \mu_t \geq 0 \end{align}

The utility function \(u(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t)\) depends on the medical need shock \(\xi_t\), which modulates the marginal utility of medical care. A natural specification would be: $\(u(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) = \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \xi_t \cdot \frac{\mu_t^{1-\rho_M}}{1-\rho_M}\)$

where \(\rho\) is the coefficient of relative risk aversion for consumption and \(\rho_M\) is the curvature parameter for medical care utility.

Information set: \(\mathcal{I}_t^D = \{m_t, p_t, \xi_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value (Post-Decision)
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, the agent has chosen \((c_t, \mu_t)\), determined end-of-period assets \(a_t\), and survival uncertainty remains. The continuation value is:

\[V^C(a_t, p_t) = V^A(a_t, p_t)\]

This reflects the twist: end-of-period assets \(a_t\) become next period's capital \(k_{t+1} = a_t\), and current permanent income \(p_t\) becomes next period's lagged permanent income \(p_{t+1}^{\text{prev}} = p_t\).

Information set: \(\mathcal{I}_t^C = \{a_t, p_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.4 Complete Recursion
docs.text:
Combining the three perches, the full Bellman equation is:

\[\begin{align} V^A(k_t, p_{t-1}) &= \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_t, \theta_t, \xi_t} \left[ V^D(R k_t + \theta_t G(p_{t-1}) \Psi_t, G(p_{t-1}) \Psi_t, \xi_t) \right] \\[0.5em] V^D(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) &= \max_{c_t, \mu_t \geq 0} \left\{ u(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) + \beta \pi V^A(m_t - c_t - p_M \mu_t, p_t) \right\} \\[0.5em] &\quad \text{s.t. } c_t + p_M \mu_t \leq m_t \end{align}\]

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equations
docs.text:
The first-order conditions for interior solutions with respect to consumption and medical expenditure are:

Consumption: $\(u_c(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) = \beta \pi \mathbb{E}_{t+1} \left[ R \cdot u_c(c_{t+1}, \mu_{t+1}; \xi_{t+1}) \right]\)$

Medical expenditure: $\(\xi_t \cdot u_{\mu}(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) = p_M \cdot u_c(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t)\)$

This second condition states that the marginal rate of substitution between medical care and consumption equals the relative price: $\(\frac{\xi_t \cdot u_{\mu}(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t)}{u_c(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t)} = p_M\)$

docs.title: 4.2 Envelope Conditions
docs.text:
The envelope theorem applied to the decision problem yields:

With respect to market resources: $\(V^D_m(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) = u_c(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t)\)$

With respect to permanent income: $\(V^D_p(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) = \beta \pi V^A_p(a_t, p_t)\)$

docs.title: 4.3 Combined Euler Equation
docs.text:
Substituting the envelope condition into the consumption Euler equation: $\(V^D_m(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) = \beta \pi R \mathbb{E}_{t+1} \left[ V^D_m(m_{t+1}, p_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}) \right]\)$

This is the fundamental intertemporal optimality condition.

docs.title: 4.4 Endogenous Grid Method (EGM) Representation
docs.text:
The EGM algorithm exploits the Euler equation structure. For a given end-of-period assets \(a_t\), the right-hand side of the Euler equation can be computed: $\(u_c(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) = \beta \pi R \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}} \left[ u_c(c_{t+1}, \mu_{t+1}; \xi_{t+1}) \right]\)$

Given the medical expenditure first-order condition: $\(\mu_t = \left( \frac{\xi_t}{p_M} \right)^{1/\rho_M} c_t^{\rho/\rho_M}\)$

(assuming power utility), we can invert to find \(c_t\) as a function of \(a_t\), then compute: $\(m_t = c_t + p_M \mu_t + a_t\)$

This generates the policy function on an endogenous grid of \(m_t\) values.

docs.title: 4.5 Corner Solutions
docs.text:
If the borrowing constraint binds (\(a_t = 0\)), then: $\(m_t = c_t + p_M \mu_t\)$

The consumption Euler equation becomes an inequality: $\(u_c(c_t, \mu_t; \xi_t) \geq \beta \pi R \mathbb{E}_{t+1} \left[ u_c(c_{t+1}, \mu_{t+1}; \xi_{t+1}) \right]\)$

docs.title: 5.1 Individual State Transition
docs.text:
Given the policy functions \(c^*(m, p, \xi)\) and \(\mu^*(m, p, \xi)\), an individual agent with state \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) transitions to next period's state \((k_{t+1}, p_t)\) according to:

\begin{align} p_t &= G(p_{t-1}) \cdot \Psi_t, \quad \Psi_t \sim F_{\text{Inc}}^{\Psi} \ y_t &= \theta_t \cdot p_t, \quad \theta_t \sim F_{\text{Inc}}^{\theta} \ m_t &= R k_t + y_t \ \xi_t &\sim F_{\text{Med}} \ c_t &= c^(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) \ \mu_t &= \mu^(m_t, p_t, \xi_t) \ a_t &= m_t - c_t - p_M \mu_t \ k_{t+1} &= a_t \cdot \mathbb{1}_{\

docs.title: Perfect Foresight Consumption-Saving Model with Mortality Risk
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kNrm Prestate / Arrival perch \(k_t\) (normalized capital) pLvlPrev Prestate / Arrival perch \(P_{t-1}\) (permanent income) yNrm Computed constant \(y = 1\) (normalized income) pLvl Decision perch state \(P_t = P_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma\) bNrm Decision perch state \(b_t = R k_t / \Gamma\) mNrm Decision perch state \(m_t = b_t + y\) cNrm Control / Decision perch \(c_t\) (normalized consumption) aNrm Continuation perch \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) live Mortality shock \(\xi_t \in \{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(\xi_t=1) = \pi\) Rfree Parameter \(R\) (gross interest rate) PermGroFac Parameter \(\Gamma\) (permanent income growth) LivPrb Parameter \(\pi\) (survival probability)

Perch Structure: - Arrival perch: Agent begins period with \((k_t, P_{t-1})\) - Decision perch: After income realization, state is \((m_t, P_t)\) - Continuation perch: After consumption choice, state is \((a_t, P_t)\), then mortality shock realizes

docs.title: 2.1 Primitives
docs.text: The agent lives in discrete time \(t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) and faces mortality risk each period. The agent has CRRA preferences over consumption sequences with discount factor \(\beta\) and relative risk aversion \(\rho\).

docs.title: 2.2 State Variables
docs.text: At the arrival perch (beginning of period \(t\)), the state is \((k_t, P_{t-1})\) where: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) denotes normalized capital holdings (assets carried forward from period \(t-1\), normalized by permanent income \(P_{t-1}\)) - \(P_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) denotes the permanent income level from the previous period

docs.title: 2.3 Within-Period Dynamics
docs.text:
The within-period state evolution follows this sequence:

Step 1: Permanent income growth. At the start of period \(t\), permanent income grows deterministically: $\(P_t \coloneqq P_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma\)$ where \(\Gamma > 0\) is the permanent income growth factor.

Step 2: Bank balances. The agent receives the return on capital, normalized by the new permanent income level: $\(b_t \coloneqq \frac{R \cdot k_t}{\Gamma}\)$ where \(R > 0\) is the gross risk-free interest rate.

Step 3: Labor income. The agent receives normalized labor income: $\(y_t \coloneqq 1\)$ This normalization implies that labor income grows at rate \(\Gamma\) in levels (i.e., level labor income is \(P_{t-1}\), which after growth becomes \(P_t\), and \(P_t / P_t = 1\)).

Step 4: Market resources. Total normalized resources available for consumption are: $\(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t = \frac{R \cdot k_t}{\Gamma} + 1\)$

docs.title: 2.4 Action Space
docs.text: At the decision perch, given market resources \(m_t\) and permanent income \(P_t\), the agent chooses normalized consumption: $\(c_t \in [0, m_t]\)$

docs.title: 2.5 End-of-Period Assets
docs.text: After the consumption decision, normalized end-of-period assets are: $\(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\)$

docs.title: 2.6 Mortality Shock
docs.text: At the continuation perch, the agent faces a mortality shock \(\xi_t \in \{0, 1\}\) where: $\(\xi_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)$ with \(\pi \in (0,1]\) denoting the survival probability. If \(\xi_t = 1\), the agent survives to period \(t+1\); if \(\xi_t = 0\), the agent dies and receives continuation value zero.

docs.title: 2.7 State Transition
docs.text: For surviving agents (\(\xi_t = 1\)), the state at the arrival perch of period \(t+1\) is: $\(k_{t+1} \coloneqq a_t, \quad P_t \mapsto P_t\)$ where the twist mapping sends continuation perch state \((a_t, P_t)\) to arrival perch state \((k_{t+1}, P_{t+1}^{\text{prev}}) = (a_t, P_t)\).

docs.title: 2.8 Initial Distribution
docs.text: At model initialization (\(t=0\)), the agent's state is drawn from: $\((k_0, P_{-1}) \sim \mu_0\)$ where \(\mu_0 = \text{pLvlInitDstn} \times \text{kNrmInitDstn}\) is the product of independent marginal distributions over initial permanent income and normalized capital.

docs.title: 3.1 Utility Function
docs.text: Let \(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\) denote the period utility function with relative risk aversion \(\rho > 0\) (for \(\rho = 1\), \(u(c) = \log c\)).

docs.title: Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent has state \((k_t, P_{t-1})\) and has not yet observed the deterministic income growth. The arrival value is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}_t(k_t, P_{t-1}) = V^{\text{dec}}_t(m_t, P_t)\)$ where the transition to the decision perch is deterministic: $\(P_t = P_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma, \quad m_t = \frac{R \cdot k_t}{\Gamma} + 1\)$

Since there are no shocks between arrival and decision perches in this perfect foresight model, the arrival value equals the decision value.

docs.title: Decision Value Function
docs.text: At the decision perch, the agent observes \((m_t, P_t)\) and chooses consumption \(c_t\): $\(V^{\text{dec}}_t(m_t, P_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ u(c_t \cdot P_t) + \beta \cdot V^{\text{cont}}_t(a_t, P_t) \right\}\)$ where \(a_t = m_t - c_t\). Note that utility is defined over consumption in levels, \(C_t = c_t \cdot P_t\), but the value function is expressed in normalized terms.

docs.title: Continuation Value Function
docs.text: At the continuation perch, the agent has state \((a_t, P_t)\) and faces the mortality shock: $\(V^{\text{cont}}_t(a_t, P_t) = \pi \cdot V^{\text{arr}}_{t+1}(a_t, P_t) + (1-\pi) \cdot 0\)$ where the agent survives with probability \(\pi\) and transitions to the next period's arrival perch with \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(P_t\) serving as \(P_{t}^{\text{prev}}\) for the next period.

docs.title: 3.3 Normalized Bellman Equation
docs.text:
Define the normalized value function \(v_t(m_t) \coloneqq V^{\text{dec}}_t(m_t, P_t) / P_t^{1-\rho}\). Then the Bellman equation in normalized form is: $\(v_t(m_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ u(c_t) + \beta \pi \left(\frac{P_{t+1}}{P_t}\right)^{1-\rho} v_{t+1}(m_{t+1}) \right\}\)$

Since \(P_{t+1} = P_t \cdot \Gamma\), this simplifies to: $\(v_t(m_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \pi \Gamma^{1-\rho} v_{t+1}\left(\frac{R(m_t - c_t)}{\Gamma} + 1\right) \right\}\)$

docs.title: 3.4 Infinite Horizon Problem
docs.text:
In the infinite horizon stationary setting, the value function satisfies: $\(v(m) = \max_{c \in [0, m]} \left\{ \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \pi \Gamma^{1-\rho} v\left(\frac{R(m - c)}{\Gamma} + 1\right) \right\}\)$

The effective discount factor is \(\tilde{\beta} \coloneqq \beta \pi \Gamma^{1-\rho}\), which incorporates both time preference, mortality risk, and the growth rate of permanent income.

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for optimal consumption at interior solutions is: $\(u'(c_t) = \beta \pi \left(\frac{P_{t+1}}{P_t}\right)^{-\rho} \frac{R}{\Gamma} u'(c_{t+1})\)$

With CRRA utility \(u'(c) = c^{-\rho}\), this becomes: $\(c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \pi \Gamma^{-\rho} R c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\)$

Rearranging: $\(\frac{c_{t+1}}{c_t} = \left(\beta \pi R \Gamma^{-\rho}\right)^{1/\rho} = (\beta \pi)^{1/\rho} \left(\frac{R}{\Gamma}\right)^{1/\rho}\)$

docs.title: 4.2 Perfect Foresight Solution
docs.text:
In the perfect foresight case, the consumption function is linear in market resources: $\(c_t = \kappa \cdot m_t\)$ where the marginal propensity to consume \(\kappa\) satisfies: $\(\kappa = \left(1 + \left(\frac{R}{\Gamma}\right)^{1/\rho} (\beta \pi)^{1/\rho - 1} \right)^{-1}\)$

This can be derived by imposing the no-Ponzi condition and the transversality condition, along with the Euler equation.

docs.title: 4.3 Envelope Condition
docs.text:
The envelope theorem gives: $\(\frac{\partial v_t(m_t)}{\partial m_t} = u'(c_t(m_t))\)$

This states that the marginal value of wealth equals the marginal utility of consumption at the optimal policy.

docs.title: 4.4 Return-Impatience Condition
docs.text:
For a well-defined solution, we require: $\(\tilde{\beta} R < \Gamma\)$ or equivalently: $\(\beta \pi R \Gamma^{-\rho} < 1\)$

This return-impatience condition ensures that the agent does not want to accumulate assets indefinitely. When \(\tilde{\beta} R = \Gamma\), the consumption function has a non-zero lower bound (the agent never runs out of resources).

docs.title: 4.5 Analytical Solution
docs.text:
When \(\tilde{\beta} R < \Gamma\), the consumption function takes the form: $\(c(m) = \kappa m\)$ where: $\(\kappa = 1 - \left(\frac{\tilde{\beta} R}{\Gamma}\right)^{1/\rho} = 1 - (\beta \pi R \Gamma^{-\rho})^{1/\rho}\)$

The value function is: $\(v(m) = \frac{(\kappa m)^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} \cdot \left(1 - \tilde{\beta} \left(\frac{R}{\Gamma}(1-\kappa)\right)^{1-\rho}\right)^{-1}\)$

docs.title: 5.1 Distribution Dynamics
docs.text:
Let \(\Phi_t(k, P)\) denote the joint distribution of agents over normalized capital \(k\) and permanent income level \(P\) at the arrival perch of period \(t\).

The forward operator \(\mathcal{T}\) maps \(\Phi_t\) to \(\Phi_{t+1}\) according to:

Step 1: Deterministic transformation. Given \((k_t, P_{t-1}) \sim \Phi_t\), compute: - \(P_t = P_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma\) - \(m_t = \frac{R k_t}{\Gamma} + 1\) - \(c_t = c(m_t)\) (apply optimal policy) - \(a_t = m_t - c_t\)

Step 2: Mortality selection. The agent survives with probability \(\pi\). For surviving agents: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t, \quad P_t^{\text{prev}} = P_t\)$

Step 3: Distribution update. The distribution at \(t+1\) is: $\(\Phi_{t+1}(dk', dP') = \pi \int \mathbb{1}\{a_t(k,P) \in dk', P\Gamma \in dP'\} \, \Phi_t(dk, dP)\)$

where \(a_t(k,P) = m_t(k,P) - c(m_t(k,P))\) with \(m_t(k,P) = \frac{Rk}{\Gamma} + 1\) and \(P' = P \cdot \Gamma\).

docs.title: 5.2 Ergodic Distribution
docs.text:
In the infinite horizon setting with constant parameters, if the system has a stationary distribution \(\Phi^*\), it satisfies: $\(\Phi^* = \mathcal{T}(\Phi^*)\)$

However, because permanent income grows deterministically at rate \(\Gamma\), the level distribution of \(P\) does not have a stationary distribution—it shifts rightward each period. The normalized distribution over \((k, P/\bar{P}_t)\) where \(\bar{P}_t\) is the mean permanent income may converge to a stationary distribution under appropriate conditions.

docs.title: 5.3 Cohort Interpretation
docs.text: Alternatively, we can interpret \(\Phi_t\) as the distribution of a single cohort over time. With mortality rate \(1-\pi\), the cohort size shrinks by factor \(\pi\) each period. The distribution of survivors evolves according to the forward operator above.

docs.title: 5.4 Cross-Sectional Distribution
docs.text: If we consider a steady-state economy with overlapping generations where new agents are born each period with distribution \(\mu_0\), the cross-sectional distribution is: $\(\Phi^{\text{cross}}(dk, dP) = \sum_{s=0}^{\infty} \pi^s \mu_0^{(s)}(dk, dP)\)$ where \(\mu_0^{(s)}\) denotes the distribution of the cohort born \(s\) periods ago, evolved forward \(s\) periods under the policy function.

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Perfect Foresight Consumption-Saving Model with Mortality Risk
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text: HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation Description kNrm Prestate (arrival perch) \(k_t\) Normalized capital at beginning of period pLvlPrev Prestate (arrival perch) \(p_{t-1}\) Permanent income level from previous period yNrm Intermediate \(y_t\) Normalized income (deterministic) pLvl Intermediate \(p_t\) Current permanent income level bNrm Intermediate \(b_t\) Normalized bank balances (post-return capital) mNrm Decision perch state \(m_t\) Normalized market resources cNrm Control (action) \(c_t\) Normalized consumption aNrm Continuation perch state \(a_t\) Normalized end-of-period assets live Shock \(\zeta_t\) Survival indicator cFunc Policy function \(c(\cdot)\) Consumption policy Rfree Parameter \(R\) Gross risk-free interest rate PermGroFac Parameter \(\Gamma\) Permanent income growth factor LivPrb Parameter \(\mathcal{L}\) Survival probability

docs.title: 2. Model
docs.text:
We consider an infinite-horizon consumption-saving problem with deterministic income growth and mortality risk. Time is discrete and indexed by \(t \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}\).

State Variables. The agent's state at the beginning of period \(t\) (arrival perch) consists of: - Normalized capital holdings \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\), representing assets carried forward from the previous period - Previous period's permanent income level \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

Action Space. At the decision perch, the agent observes normalized market resources \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) and chooses normalized consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\).

Permanent Income Dynamics. Permanent income evolves deterministically: $\(p_t \coloneqq p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma\)$ where \(\Gamma > 0\) is the permanent income growth factor.

Budget Constraint. The agent receives deterministic normalized labor income \(y_t = 1\) each period. After the risk-free return \(R\) is applied to beginning-of-period capital, normalized bank balances are: $\(b_t \coloneqq R \cdot \frac{k_t}{\Gamma}\)$

The normalization by \(\Gamma\) accounts for permanent income growth between periods. Normalized market resources are then: $\(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t = R \cdot \frac{k_t}{\Gamma} + 1\)$

After choosing consumption \(c_t\), normalized end-of-period assets are: $\(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\)$

Mortality Risk. At the end of each period, the agent survives with probability \(\mathcal{L} \in (0, 1]\) and dies with probability \(1 - \mathcal{L}\). We represent this via a survival indicator: $\(\zeta_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mathcal{L})\)$

State Transition. If the agent survives (\(\zeta_t = 1\)), next period's normalized capital is: $\(k_{t+1} \coloneqq a_t\)$

If the agent dies (\(\zeta_t = 0\)), the optimization problem terminates (or the agent is replaced by a newborn with initial distribution).

Information Structure. At the beginning of period \(t\), the agent observes \((k_t, p_{t-1})\). The permanent income update and budget constraint computations occur before the consumption choice, so at the decision perch the agent observes \((m_t, p_t)\). The mortality shock \(\zeta_t\) is realized after the consumption-saving decision.

Initial Distribution. The agent begins with initial draws: $\(k_0 \sim \mu_{k,0}, \quad p_{-1} \sim \mu_{p,0}\)$ where \(\mu_{k,0}\) and \(\mu_{p,0}\) are specified initial distributions.

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text:
The value function can be decomposed according to the ADC (Arrival-Decision-Continuation) perch structure.

Arrival Value Function. At the arrival perch, the agent has state \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) and has not yet computed market resources. The arrival value is: $\(V^A(k_t, p_{t-1}) = V^D(m_t, p_t)\)$ where the transition to the decision perch involves the deterministic transformations: $\(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma, \quad m_t = R \cdot \frac{k_t}{\Gamma} + 1\)$

Since these are deterministic, there is no expectation operator between arrival and decision perches.

Decision Value Function. At the decision perch, the agent observes \((m_t, p_t)\) and chooses consumption \(c_t\) to maximize: $\(V^D(m_t, p_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ u(c_t \cdot p_t) + \beta \mathbb{E}[\zeta_t \cdot V^C(a_t, p_t)] \right\}\)$ subject to \(a_t = m_t - c_t\), where: - \(u: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}\) is the period utility function (typically CRRA: \(u(C) = \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\) for \(\rho > 0, \rho \neq 1\)) - \(\beta \in (0,1)\) is the time discount factor - Consumption in levels is \(C_t = c_t \cdot p_t\) - The expectation is taken over the survival shock \(\zeta_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mathcal{L})\)

Continuation Value Function. At the continuation perch, the agent has chosen assets \(a_t\) and observes permanent income \(p_t\). Before the survival shock realizes: $\(V^C(a_t, p_t) = V^A(k_{t+1}, p_t)\)$ where \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) (the twist operation).

The survival shock expectation yields: $\(\mathbb{E}[\zeta_t \cdot V^C(a_t, p_t)] = \mathcal{L} \cdot V^A(a_t, p_t) + (1-\mathcal{L}) \cdot 0 = \mathcal{L} \cdot V^A(a_t, p_t)\)$

Normalized Bellman Equation. Combining the perches, the recursive problem can be written in normalized form. Define the normalized value function \(v(m_t) \coloneqq V^D(m_t, p_t) / p_t^{1-\rho}\) (under CRRA utility). Then: $\(v(m_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ u(c_t) + \beta \Gamma^{1-\rho} \mathcal{L} \cdot v(m_{t+1}) \right\}\)$ where \(m_{t+1} = R \cdot \frac{a_t}{\Gamma} + 1\) and the optimization is over normalized quantities.

Information Sets. - Arrival perch \(\mathcal{F}^A_t\): \(\{k_t, p_{t-1}, \text{history up to } t-1\}\) - Decision perch \(\mathcal{F}^D_t\): \(\mathcal{F}^A_t \cup \{p_t, m_t\}\) (deterministic updating) - Continuation perch \(\mathcal{F}^C_t\): \(\mathcal{F}^D_t \cup \{c_t, a_t\}\)

docs.title: 4. First-Order Conditions
docs.text:
Euler Equation. The first-order condition for consumption \(c_t\) is: $\(u'(c_t \cdot p_t) \cdot p_t = \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathbb{E}_t\left[\frac{\partial V^A(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t}\right]\)$

By the envelope theorem at the next period's arrival perch: $\(\frac{\partial V^A(k_{t+1}, p_t)}{\partial k_{t+1}} = \frac{\partial V^D(m_{t+1}, p_{t+1})}{\partial m_{t+1}} \cdot \frac{\partial m_{t+1}}{\partial k_{t+1}} = u'(c_{t+1} \cdot p_{t+1}) \cdot p_{t+1} \cdot \frac{R}{\Gamma}\)$

Substituting \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(p_{t+1} = p_t \cdot \Gamma\): $\(u'(c_t \cdot p_t) \cdot p_t = \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot R \cdot u'(c_{t+1} \cdot p_{t+1}) \cdot p_{t+1} / \Gamma\)$

Normalized Euler Equation. Dividing through by \(p_t\) and using \(p_{t+1} = p_t \cdot \Gamma\): $\(u'(c_t) = \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot R \cdot \Gamma^{-\rho} \cdot u'(c_{t+1})\)$

For CRRA utility \(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\), we have \(u'(c) = c^{-\rho}\), so: $\(c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot R \cdot \Gamma^{-\rho} \cdot c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\)$

or equivalently: $\(c_{t+1} = c_t \cdot (\beta \mathcal{L} \cdot R)^{1/\rho} \cdot \Gamma^{-1}\)$

Perfect Foresight Solution. In this perfect foresight model (no income shocks), the consumption function takes the form: $\(c_t = \chi(m_t)\)$ where \(\chi: \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+\) is the consumption policy function. Given the linear structure, this is typically: $\(c(m) = \kappa \cdot m\)$ for some marginal propensity to consume \(\kappa \in (0,1)\) determined by: $\(\kappa = \frac{1}{1 + \psi}\)$ where \(\psi\) satisfies: $\(\psi = \left(\frac{R \beta \mathcal{L}}{\Gamma^\rho}\right)^{1/\rho} (1 + \psi)\)$

This can be solved for \(\psi\) (and hence \(\kappa\)) given parameters.

Envelope Condition. The marginal value of market resources at the decision perch is: $\(\frac{\partial V^D(m_t, p_t)}{\partial m_t} = u'(c_t \cdot p_t) \cdot p_t = u'(c_t) \cdot p_t^{1-\rho} \cdot p_t^\rho = u'(c_t) \cdot p_t\)$

EGM Representation. The Endogenous Grid Method can be applied by computing: 1. For a grid of end-of-period assets \(\{a^i\}\), compute next period's resources: \(m_{t+1}^i = R \cdot a^i / \Gamma + 1\) 2. Evaluate next period's consumption: \(c_{t+1}^i = c(m_{t+1}^i)\) 3. Back out current consumption via the Euler equation: \(c_t^i = [(\beta \mathcal{L} R / \Gamma^\rho) \cdot (c_{t+1}^i)^{-\rho}]^{-1/\rho}\) 4. Compute current resources: \(m_t^i = a^i + c_t^i\) 5. Interpolate to obtain \(c(m)\)

docs.title: 5. Forward Operator
docs.text:
The forward operator describes how the distribution of agents evolves over time.

Cross-Sectional Distribution. Let \(\Phi_t(k, p)\) denote the joint distribution of normalized capital and permanent income at the beginning of period \(t\).

Transition Operator. Given policy function \(c(m)\), the distribution evolves as: $\(\Phi_{t+1}(k', p') = \int \mathbb{1}\{k' = a(k, p), p' = p \cdot \Gamma\} \cdot \mathcal{L} \, d\Phi_t(k, p)\)$ where: - \(m = R \cdot k / \Gamma + 1\) (market resources) - \(c = c(m)\) (consumption policy) - \(a = m - c\) (end-of-period assets)

Marginal Distributions. The permanent income distribution evolves deterministically: $\(\Phi_{t+1}^p(p') = \Phi_t^p(p' / \Gamma)\)$ since \(p_{t+1} = p_t \cdot \Gamma\) with certainty (ignoring mortality exits).

The normalized capital distribution evolves according to: $\(\Phi_{t+1}^k(k') = \mathcal{L} \int \mathbb{1}\{k' = m - c(m)\} \, d\Phi_t^{k,m}(k, m)\)$ where \(\Phi_t^{k,m}\) is the joint distribution of \(k\) and the induced \(m = R k / \Gamma + 1\).

Invariant Distribution. A stationary distribution \(\Phi^*(k, p)\) (if it exists) satisfies: $\(\Phi^*(k', p') = \int \mathbb{1}\{k' = a(k, p), p' = p \cdot \Gamma\} \cdot \mathcal{L} \, d\Phi^*(k, p)\)$

However, with deterministic permanent income growth (\(p_t = p_0 \cdot \Gamma^t\)), the permanent income level grows without bound, so there is no invariant distribution in levels. The model is typically analyzed in normalized units or along a balanced growth path.

Balanced Growth Path. On a balanced growth path, the distribution of normalized variables \(\Phi^*(k)\) (integrating out \(p\)) satisfies: $\(\Phi^*(k') = \mathcal{L} \int \mathbb{1}\{k' = a(k)\} \, d\Phi^*(k)\)$ where \(a(k) = m - c(m)\) with \(m = R k / \Gamma + 1\).

Mortality Replenishment. The factor \(\mathcal{L}\) represents survival. In steady state, the \((1-\mathcal{L})\) fraction who die are replaced by newborns drawn from the initial distribution \(\mu_{k,0}\): $$\Phi^*(k) = \mathcal{L} \cdot T\Phi^* + (1-\mathcal{L}) \cdot \mu_{k,

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Portfolio Choice with Risky Assets
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation Perch kNrm Beginning-of-period normalized wealth \(k_t\) Arrival (prestate) pLvlPrev Inbound permanent income level \(P_{t-1}\) Arrival (prestate) SharePrev Previous period risky share \(\varsigma_{t-1}\) Arrival (prestate) Risky Risky asset return realization \(R_t\) Shock Rport Portfolio return realization \(\mathcal{R}_t\) Post-shock Adjust Portfolio adjustment indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t}\) Shock yNrm Normalized labor income \(y_t\) Post-shock pLvl Current permanent income level \(P_t\) Post-shock bNrm Normalized bank balances \(b_t\) Post-shock mNrm Normalized market resources \(m_t\) Decision (poststate) cNrm Normalized consumption \(c_t\) Control (decision) Share Current risky share \(\varsigma_t\) Control (decision) aNrm Normalized end-of-period assets \(a_t\) Continuation live Survival indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1}\) End-of-period shock PermShk Permanent income shock \(\psi_t\) Shock TranShk Transitory income shock \(\theta_t\) Shock

Perch Structure: - Arrival Perch: \((k_t, P_{t-1}, \varsigma_{t-1})\) — agent enters period with these state variables - Decision Perch: \((m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1}, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t})\) — agent makes consumption and portfolio decisions - Continuation Perch: \((a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t)\) — agent ends period with these state variables

docs.title: 2.1 State Spaces
docs.text:
The arrival state consists of three variables: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized wealth at the beginning of period \(t\), representing assets carried forward from period \(t-1\), normalized by permanent income \(P_{t-1}\) - \(P_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — permanent income level from the previous period - \(\varsigma_{t-1} \in [0,1]\) — the share of wealth allocated to risky assets in the previous period

The decision state augments the arrival state with realizations of shocks: - \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized market resources available for consumption and saving - \(P_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — updated permanent income level - \(\varsigma_{t-1} \in [0,1]\) — previous risky share (still relevant if adjustment is not possible) - \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} \in \{0,1\}\) — indicator for whether portfolio rebalancing is feasible this period

The continuation state consists of: - \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized end-of-period assets - \(P_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — permanent income level - \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) — risky asset share chosen this period

docs.title: 2.2 Action Spaces
docs.text:
The agent chooses: - \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) — normalized consumption - \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) — share of end-of-period assets invested in risky assets (subject to adjustment constraints)

When \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} = 0\), the agent cannot adjust the portfolio share, so \(\varsigma_t = \varsigma_{t-1}\) is enforced.

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Within-period shocks are drawn from a joint distribution: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t, R_t) \sim F_{\text{shock}}\)$ where: - \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — permanent income shock with \(\mathbb{E}[\psi_t] = 1\) - \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — transitory income shock with \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_t] = 1\) - \(R_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — gross return on risky assets

The adjustment opportunity occurs with probability: $\(\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} = 1) = \lambda\)$ where \(\lambda \coloneqq \texttt{AdjustPrb}\).

End-of-period survival occurs with probability: $\(\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1} = 1) = \mathfrak{p}\)$ where \(\mathfrak{p} \coloneqq \texttt{LivPrb}\).

docs.title: 2.4 Parameters
docs.text:
• \(\mathsf{R} \coloneqq \texttt{Rfree} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — gross risk-free return factor
  • \(\Gamma \coloneqq \texttt{PermGroFac} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — expected permanent income growth factor
  • \(\mathfrak{p} \coloneqq \texttt{LivPrb} \in [0,1]\) — survival probability
  • \(\lambda \coloneqq \texttt{AdjustPrb} \in [0,1]\) — probability of being able to adjust portfolio share

docs.title: 2.5 Transition Dynamics
docs.text:
From arrival to decision perch:

Upon arrival with state \((k_t, P_{t-1}, \varsigma_{t-1})\), shocks are realized: 1. Draw \((\psi_t, \theta_t, R_t) \sim F_{\text{shock}}\) 2. Calculate permanent income growth: \(G_t \coloneqq \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\) 3. Update permanent income: \(P_t = P_{t-1} \cdot G_t\) 4. Calculate realized portfolio return: \(\mathcal{R}_t \coloneqq \mathsf{R} + (R_t - \mathsf{R}) \cdot \varsigma_{t-1}\) 5. Calculate normalized bank balances: \(b_t \coloneqq \mathcal{R}_t \cdot k_t / G_t\) 6. Calculate normalized labor income: \(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\) 7. Calculate normalized market resources: \(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t\) 8. Draw adjustment opportunity: \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\lambda)\)

From decision to continuation perch:

Given decisions \((c_t, \varsigma_t)\): 1. Calculate normalized end-of-period assets: \(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\) 2. The continuation state is \((a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t)\)

From continuation to next arrival perch (twist):

The mapping from continuation perch at time \(t\) to arrival perch at time \(t+1\) is: 1. Draw survival: \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mathfrak{p})\) 2. If \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1} = 1\): \((k_{t+1}, P_t, \varsigma_t) \leftarrow (a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t)\) 3. If \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1} = 0\): agent is replaced by a newborn with initial distribution

This twist operation reveals the recursive structure: end-of-period normalized assets \(a_t\) become next period's normalized wealth \(k_{t+1}\), permanent income \(P_t\) becomes \(P_t\) (carried forward as \(P_{t-1}\) notation in next period), and the chosen risky share \(\varsigma_t\) becomes \(\varsigma_{t-1}\) in the next period.

docs.title: 2.6 Preferences
docs.text:
The agent has time-separable CRRA preferences over consumption in levels: $\(u(C_t) = \frac{C_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

where \(C_t = c_t \cdot P_t\) is consumption in levels. The normalization by permanent income yields utility from normalized consumption: $\(\tilde{u}(c_t, P_t) = \frac{(c_t \cdot P_t)^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} = \frac{P_t^{1-\rho} \cdot c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

The agent maximizes expected discounted lifetime utility with discount factor \(\beta\).

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The recursive structure decomposes across three perches, reflecting the timing of information revelation and decisions.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent holds state \((k_t, P_{t-1}, \varsigma_{t-1})\) and faces uncertainty about shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t, R_t, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t})\). The arrival value is:

\[V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, P_{t-1}, \varsigma_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\psi, \theta, R, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj}})} \left[ V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1}, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t}) \right]\]

where the expectation is taken over the joint shock distribution, and the decision state variables are determined by: - \(G_t = \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\) - \(P_t = P_{t-1} \cdot G_t\) - \(\mathcal{R}_t = \mathsf{R} + (R_t - \mathsf{R}) \cdot \varsigma_{t-1}\) - \(b_t = \mathcal{R}_t \cdot k_t / G_t\) - \(y_t = \theta_t\) - \(m_t = b_t + y_t\)

Information set at arrival: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{arr}}_t = \{k_t, P_{t-1}, \varsigma_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function
docs.text:
At the decision perch, all within-period shocks have been realized. The agent observes \((m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1}, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t})\) and chooses \((c_t, \varsigma_t)\) to maximize:

\[V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1}, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t}) = \max_{c_t, \varsigma_t} \left\{ \tilde{u}(c_t, P_t) + \beta V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t) \right\}\]

subject to: - \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) - \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) - If \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} = 1\): \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) (free choice) - If \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} = 0\): \(\varsigma_t = \varsigma_{t-1}\) (constrained)

This can be written more explicitly as: $\(V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1}, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t}) = \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} \cdot V^{\text{adj}}(m_t, P_t) + (1 - \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t}) \cdot V^{\text{fxd}}(m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1})\)$

where:

Adjustment case (\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t} = 1\)): $\(V^{\text{adj}}(m_t, P_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0,m_t], \varsigma_t \in [0,1]} \left\{ \tilde{u}(c_t, P_t) + \beta V^{\text{cont}}(m_t - c_t, P_t, \varsigma_t) \right\}\)$
