Information set at decision: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{dec}}_t = \{m_t, P_t, \varsigma_{t-1}, \mathbb{1}_{\text{adj},t}, \psi_t, \theta_t, R_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value Function
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, the agent has made decisions \((c_t, \varsigma_t)\) and holds state \((a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t)\). The continuation value accounts for survival uncertainty:

\[V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t) = \mathfrak{p} \cdot V^{\text{arr}}(a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t) + (1 - \mathfrak{p}) \cdot V^{\text{death}}\]

where \(V^{\text{death}}\) is the value of death (typically normalized to zero), and we use the twist mapping: \((k_{t+1}, P_t, \varsigma_t) = (a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t)\) for the surviving agent.

Substituting \(V^{\text{death}} = 0\): $\(V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t) = \mathfrak{p} \cdot V^{\text{arr}}(a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t)\)$

Information set at continuation: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{cont}}_t = \{a_t, P_t, \varsigma_t, m_t, c_t\}\) (all within-period information)

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Saving Model with Preference Shocks
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
This table maps HARK variable names to DDSL/ADC concepts and establishes the formal mathematical notation used throughout this document.

HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation Description kNrm Prestate (arrival) \(k_t\) Normalized capital at period start pLvlPrev Prestate (arrival) \(P_{t-1}\) Permanent income from previous period yNrm Intermediate \(y_t\) Normalized labor income (transitory shock) pLvl Intermediate \(P_t\) Current permanent income level bNrm Intermediate \(b_t\) Normalized bank balances after returns mNrm Decision perch \(m_t\) Normalized market resources PrefShk Shock (decision) \(\xi_t\) Marginal utility multiplier cNrm Control (decision) \(c_t\) Normalized consumption choice aNrm Continuation perch \(a_t\) Normalized end-of-period assets live Survival indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live}}\) Binary survival outcome PermShk Shock (permanent) \(\psi_t\) Permanent income shock TranShk Shock (transitory) \(\theta_t\) Transitory income shock

Timing convention: Period \(t\) begins with prestate \((k_t, P_{t-1})\). Income shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\) realize, transforming the state to decision perch \(m_t\). The agent observes preference shock \(\xi_t\) and chooses \(c_t\), yielding continuation state \(a_t\). The twist mapping connects \(a_t \to k_{t+1}\) and \(P_t \to P_t\) (carried forward).

docs.title: 2.1 State Spaces
docs.text:
Prestate (Arrival Perch): The agent begins period \(t\) with: - Normalized capital holdings: \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Previous period's permanent income: \(P_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

Decision Perch: After income realization but before consumption choice: - Normalized market resources: \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Preference shock realization: \(\xi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

Continuation Perch: After consumption choice: - Normalized end-of-period assets: \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Updated permanent income: \(P_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

docs.title: 2.2 Action Space
docs.text:
The agent's control is normalized consumption: $\(\mathcal{C}(m_t, \xi_t) = \{c_t \in \mathbb{R}_+ : c_t \leq m_t\}\)$

The budget constraint requires consumption not to exceed available market resources.

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income Shocks: The joint distribution of permanent and transitory income shocks is: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{Inc}}\)$ where \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is the permanent shock and \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is the transitory shock (normalized labor income).

Preference Shocks: The marginal utility multiplier follows: $\(\xi_t \sim F_{\text{Pref}}\)$ where \(\xi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) scales the marginal utility of consumption.

Survival: At the end of each period: $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)$ where \(\pi \coloneqq \texttt{LivPrb}\) is the survival probability.

Initial Conditions: At model birth (\(t=0\)): $\(P_{-1} \sim F_{P,\text{init}}, \quad k_0 \sim F_{k,\text{init}}\)$

docs.title: 2.4 State Transitions
docs.text:
The state evolves through the following sequence within period \(t\):

Step 1 (Income Realization): Shocks realize and permanent income updates: $\(\begin{align} (\psi_t, \theta_t) &\sim F_{\text{Inc}} \\ G_t &\coloneqq \Gamma \cdot \psi_t \\ P_t &= P_{t-1} \cdot G_t \end{align}\)$ where \(\Gamma \coloneqq \texttt{PermGroFac}\) is the deterministic growth factor.

Step 2 (Market Resources): Capital earns returns and combines with labor income: $\(\begin{align} b_t &= \frac{R \cdot k_t}{G_t} \\ m_t &= b_t + \theta_t \end{align}\)$ where \(R \coloneqq \texttt{Rfree}\) is the gross risk-free rate. Note that \(b_t\) represents normalized bank balances after both capital returns and permanent income growth.

Step 3 (Preference Shock and Consumption): The preference shock realizes and consumption is chosen: $\(\begin{align} \xi_t &\sim F_{\text{Pref}} \\ c_t &= c^*(m_t, \xi_t) \end{align}\)$ where \(c^*(\cdot, \cdot)\) is the optimal consumption policy function.

Step 4 (Asset Accumulation): End-of-period assets are determined by the budget constraint: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t\)$

Step 5 (Survival and Twist): The survival outcome realizes, and for survivors: $\(\begin{align} \mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t+1} &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi) \\ k_{t+1} &= a_t \\ P_t &\to P_t \text{ (carried forward)} \end{align}\)$

Non-survivors exit the model with terminal utility zero.

docs.title: 2.5 Preferences
docs.text:
The agent has time-separable preferences with CRRA utility modified by multiplicative preference shocks. The period utility function is: $\(u(c_t, \xi_t) = \xi_t \cdot \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$ where \(\rho > 0\) is the coefficient of relative risk aversion (not explicitly in parameters but implicit in HARK's implementation). The preference shock \(\xi_t\) multiplicatively scales marginal utility, creating heterogeneity in consumption propensities.

The discount factor is \(\beta \in (0,1)\), and survival probability \(\pi\) compounds with time preference.

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The value function is decomposed across three perches following the ADC framework.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value (Prestate)
docs.text:
At the beginning of period \(t\), before income shocks realize, the agent's value is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, P_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}\left[V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, \xi_t, P_t) \,\Big|\, k_t, P_{t-1}\right]\)$

The expectation is taken over \((\psi_t, \theta_t, \xi_t)\), which determine \((m_t, P_t)\) through: $\(\begin{align} G_t &= \Gamma \psi_t \\ P_t &= P_{t-1} G_t \\ b_t &= \frac{R k_t}{G_t} \\ m_t &= b_t + \theta_t \end{align}\)$

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}^{\text{arr}}_t = \{k_t, P_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value (Post-Shock, Pre-Choice)
docs.text:
After observing market resources \(m_t\) and preference shock \(\xi_t\), the agent solves: $\(V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, \xi_t, P_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{\xi_t \cdot \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \pi \cdot V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, P_t)\right\}\)$

subject to the budget constraint: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t\)$

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}^{\text{dec}}_t = \{m_t, \xi_t, P_t\}\)

The term \(\beta \pi\) combines time preference and survival probability. Non-survivors receive zero continuation value.

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value (Post-Choice)
docs.text:
After choosing consumption, the continuation value is: $\(V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, P_t) = V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, P_t)\)$

where the twist mapping gives: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t\)$

Note that \(P_t\) carries forward unchanged: the permanent income state at the end of period \(t\) becomes the "previous" permanent income for period \(t+1\).

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}^{\text{cont}}_t = \{a_t, P_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.4 Recursive Formulation
docs.text:
Combining the three perches, the full Bellman equation is: $\(\begin{align} V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, P_{t-1}) &= \mathbb{E}_{(\psi_t,\theta_t,\xi_t)}\left[\max_{c_t \leq m_t} \left\{\xi_t \cdot \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \pi \cdot V^{\text{arr}}(m_t - c_t, P_{t-1}\Gamma\psi_t)\right\}\right] \\ \text{where} \quad m_t &= \frac{R k_t}{\Gamma \psi_t} + \theta_t \end{align}\)$

This formulation makes explicit that: 1. The expectation is taken before observing shocks 2. Market resources \(m_t\) depend on realized permanent shock \(\psi_t\) 3. Permanent income evolves as \(P_t = P_{t-1} \Gamma \psi_t\) 4. The continuation value depends on assets \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) and updated permanent income \(P_t\)

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for optimal consumption, when interior (\(c_t \in (0, m_t)\)), is: $\(\xi_t \cdot c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \pi \cdot \frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(a_t, P_t)}{\partial a_t}\)$

The left side is the marginal utility of consumption scaled by the preference shock. The right side is the expected marginal value of saving.

docs.title: 4.2 Envelope Condition
docs.text:
The marginal value of wealth at the arrival perch satisfies: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, P_{t-1})}{\partial k_t} = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, \xi_t, P_t)}{\partial m_t} \cdot \frac{\partial m_t}{\partial k_t} \,\Big|\, k_t, P_{t-1}\right]\)$

where: $\(\frac{\partial m_t}{\partial k_t} = \frac{R}{G_t} = \frac{R}{\Gamma \psi_t}\)$

At the decision perch, the envelope theorem gives: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, \xi_t, P_t)}{\partial m_t} = \xi_t \cdot c_t^{-\rho}\)$

Combining these: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, P_{t-1})}{\partial k_t} = \mathbb{E}\left[\xi_t \cdot c_t^{-\rho} \cdot \frac{R}{\Gamma \psi_t} \,\Big|\, k_t, P_{t-1}\right]\)$

docs.title: 4.3 Euler Equation in Expectation Form
docs.text:
Substituting the envelope condition into the Euler equation: $\(\xi_t \cdot c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \pi \cdot \mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\xi_{t+1} \cdot c_{t+1}^{-\rho} \cdot \frac{R}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\right]\)$

where \(\mathbb{E}_{t+1}\) denotes expectation conditional on information at the end of period \(t\) (i.e., conditional on \(a_t, P_t\)).

This can be rewritten in terms of normalized consumption growth: $\(\xi_t = \beta \pi R \cdot \mathbb{E}_{t+1}\left[\xi_{t+1} \cdot G_{t+1}^{\rho} \cdot \left(\frac{c_{t+1}}{c_t}\right)^{-\rho}\right]\)$

docs.title: 4.4 Endogenous Grid Method (EGM) Representation
docs.text:
HARK implements this model using the Endogenous Grid Method. The algorithm works backward from a grid of end-of-period assets \(\{a_j\}\):

Step 1: For each \((a_j, P_t)\) and each realization \((\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1})\), compute: $\(\begin{align} G_{t+1} &= \Gamma \psi_{t+1} \\ k_{t+1} &= a_j \\ m_{t+1} &= \frac{R k_{t+1}}{G_{t+1}} + \theta_{t+1} \\ c_{t+1} &= c^*(m_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1}) \end{align}\)$

Step 2: Compute the expected marginal value: $\(\mathcal{E}_j(P_t) = \mathbb{E}\left[\xi_{t+1} \cdot c_{t+1}^{-\rho} \cdot \frac{R}{G_{t+1}} \,\Big|\, a_j, P_t\right]\)$

Step 3: Use the Euler equation to find consumption on the endogenous grid: $\(c_j(\xi_t, P_t) = \left(\beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{E}_j(P_t) / \xi_t\right)^{-1/\rho}\)$

Step 4: Invert the budget constraint to find the endogenous grid of market resources: $\(m_j(\xi_t, P_t) = a_j + c_j(\xi_t, P_t)\)$

Step 5: Interpolate to construct \(c^*(m, \xi_t)\) for all \(m\).

The preference shock \(\xi_t\) creates multiple consumption functions—one for each realization of \(\xi_t\)—that must be integrated over when computing expectations at the arrival perch.

docs.title: 5. Forward Operator
docs.text: The forward operator describes how the cross-sectional distribution of agents evolves over time. Let \(\Phi_t(k, P)\) denote the joint density of normalized capital and permanent income at

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Saving with Risky Asset Allocation
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kNrm Prestate (arrival perch) \(k_t\) pLvlPrev Prestate (arrival perch) \(p_{t-1}\) PermShk Arrival shock \(\psi_t\) TranShk Arrival shock \(\theta_t\) yNrm Post-shock state \(y_t\) G Post-shock state \(G_t\) pLvl Post-shock state \(p_t\) bNrm Post-shock state \(b_t\) mNrm Decision perch state \(m_t\) cNrm Control (decision) \(c_t\) Share Control (decision) \(\varsigma_t\) wNrm Post-decision state \(w_t\) Risky Continuation shock \(R_t\) Rport Post-continuation state \(R_t^{\text{port}}\) aNrm Continuation perch state \(a_t\) qNrm Post-continuation state \(q_t\) live Survival shock \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t}\) dead Death indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{dead},t}\)

Timing convention: The model operates in normalized space where all monetary variables are divided by permanent income from the previous period. The twist mapping connects end-of-period normalized assets \(a_t\) to beginning-of-next-period normalized wealth \(k_{t+1}\), and current permanent income \(p_t\) to next period's incoming permanent income \(p_t\) (which becomes \(p_{t}\) at the start of period \(t+1\)).

docs.title: 2.1 State Spaces
docs.text:
Arrival (Prestate) Space: At the beginning of period \(t\), the agent arrives with: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized wealth (assets from previous period divided by \(p_{t-1}\)) - \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — permanent income level carried forward from previous period

Decision Space: After observing income shocks, the agent has: - \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized market resources (cash-on-hand) - \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — updated permanent income level

Continuation Space: After making consumption and portfolio decisions but before observing asset returns: - \(w_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized wealth after consumption - \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) — portfolio share in risky assets - \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — permanent income level

Terminal Space: After asset returns realize: - \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) — normalized end-of-period assets - \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) — permanent income level

docs.title: 2.2 Action Spaces
docs.text: The agent chooses: - \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) — normalized consumption - \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) — portfolio share allocated to risky assets

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income Shocks (Arrival): The joint distribution of permanent and transitory income shocks is given by $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{Inc}}\)$ where \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is the permanent income shock (typically mean-one) and \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is the transitory income shock (also typically mean-one).

Asset Return Shocks (Continuation): The risky asset return is drawn from $\(R_t \sim F_{\text{Risky}}\)$ where \(R_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is the gross return factor on the risky asset.

Survival Shocks: At the end of each period, the agent survives with probability \(\pi \in (0,1]\): $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)$

docs.title: 2.4 Transition Equations
docs.text:
The dynamics unfold in three stages within each period:

Stage 1 (Arrival to Decision): Given prestate \((k_t, p_{t-1})\) and income shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\):

The permanent income growth factor is $\(G_t \coloneqq \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\)$ where \(\Gamma > 0\) is the deterministic permanent income growth factor.

Permanent income evolves as $\(p_t \coloneqq p_{t-1} \cdot G_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\)$

Normalized bank balances account for permanent income growth: $\(b_t \coloneqq \frac{k_t}{G_t}\)$

Normalized labor income equals the transitory shock: $\(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\)$

Normalized market resources combine bank balances and labor income: $\(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t = \frac{k_t}{G_t} + \theta_t\)$

Stage 2 (Decision to Continuation): Given decision state \(m_t\) and choices \((c_t, \varsigma_t)\):

Normalized wealth after consumption is $\(w_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\)$

Stage 3 (Continuation to Terminal): Given continuation state \((w_t, \varsigma_t)\) and risky return \(R_t\):

The realized portfolio return is $\(R_t^{\text{port}} \coloneqq R_f + (R_t - R_f) \cdot \varsigma_t\)$ where \(R_f > 0\) is the risk-free return factor.

Normalized end-of-period assets are $\(a_t \coloneqq R_t^{\text{port}} \cdot w_t = [R_f + (R_t - R_f) \cdot \varsigma_t] \cdot w_t\)$

Risky asset holdings are $\(q_t \coloneqq a_t \cdot \varsigma_t\)$

Twist (Terminal to Next Arrival): The normalized assets and permanent income from period \(t\) become the arrival state for period \(t+1\): $\(k_{t+1} \coloneqq a_t, \quad p_t^{\text{incoming}} \coloneqq p_t\)$

where \(p_t^{\text{incoming}}\) serves as \(p_t\) in the next period's dynamics (i.e., what we called \(p_{t-1}\) when indexing from period \(t+1\)'s perspective).

docs.title: 2.5 Preferences
docs.text:
The agent has time-separable CRRA preferences over consumption with discount factor \(\beta \in (0,1)\) and relative risk aversion \(\rho > 0\): $\(u(C) \coloneqq \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

In normalized form, with consumption \(c_t\) measured relative to \(p_{t-1}\), actual consumption is \(C_t = c_t \cdot p_{t-1}\), giving: $\(u(c_t \cdot p_{t-1}) = \frac{(c_t \cdot p_{t-1})^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} = p_{t-1}^{1-\rho} \cdot \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

docs.title: 2.6 Initial Conditions
docs.text: At model birth (period 0), the agent draws: - \(p_{-1} \sim F_{p,\text{init}}\) — initial permanent income level - \(k_0 \sim F_{k,\text{init}}\) — initial normalized wealth

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The value function is decomposed across three perches, each corresponding to a different information set within the period.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function (Pre-Income Shock)
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, before income shocks are observed, the value function is: $\(\mathcal{V}_t^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \theta_t}\left[\mathcal{V}_t^{\text{dec}}(m_t, p_t) \,\big|\, k_t, p_{t-1}\right]\)$

where the expectation is over income shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{Inc}}\), and market resources are determined by: $\(m_t = \frac{k_t}{\Gamma \psi_t} + \theta_t, \quad p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\)$

Information set at arrival perch: \(\mathcal{I}_t^{\text{arr}} = \{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function (Post-Income, Pre-Decision)
docs.text:
At the decision perch, after observing income shocks, the agent solves: $\(\mathcal{V}_t^{\text{dec}}(m_t, p_t) \coloneqq \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t], \,\varsigma_t \in [0,1]} \left\{p_{t-1}^{1-\rho} \cdot u(c_t) + \beta \pi \cdot \mathcal{V}_t^{\text{cont}}(w_t, \varsigma_t, p_t)\right\}\)$

where \(w_t = m_t - c_t\) and \(p_{t-1}\) is the permanent income level used for normalization.

Note on normalization: Since \(p_t = p_{t-1} \cdot G_t\), we have \(p_{t-1}^{1-\rho} = (p_t / G_t)^{1-\rho}\). The normalized flow utility is: $\(p_{t-1}^{1-\rho} \cdot \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} = \left(\frac{p_t}{G_t}\right)^{1-\rho} \cdot \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

Information set at decision perch: \(\mathcal{I}_t^{\text{dec}} = \{m_t, p_t, p_{t-1}\} = \{m_t, G_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value Function (Post-Decision, Pre-Return)
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, after making consumption and portfolio choices but before observing asset returns: $\(\mathcal{V}_t^{\text{cont}}(w_t, \varsigma_t, p_t) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{R_t}\left[\mathcal{V}_{t+1}^{\text{arr}}(a_t, p_t) \,\big|\, w_t, \varsigma_t, p_t\right]\)$

where the expectation is over risky returns \(R_t \sim F_{\text{Risky}}\), and end-of-period assets are: $\(a_t = [R_f + (R_t - R_f) \cdot \varsigma_t] \cdot w_t\)$

By the twist mapping, \(a_t\) becomes \(k_{t+1}\) and \(p_t\) becomes \(p_t^{\text{incoming}}\) (the permanent income at arrival in period \(t+1\)).

Information set at continuation perch: \(\mathcal{I}_t^{\text{cont}} = \{w_t, \varsigma_t, p_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.4 Complete Recursive Formulation
docs.text:
Combining all three perches, the complete Bellman equation is:

\[\mathcal{V}_t^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \theta_t}\left[\max_{c_t, \varsigma_t} \left\{p_{t-1}^{1-\rho} \cdot u(c_t) + \beta \pi \cdot \mathbb{E}_{R_t}\left[\mathcal{V}_{t+1}^{\text{arr}}(a_t, p_t)\right]\right\}\right]\]

subject to: \begin{align} G_t &= \Gamma \cdot \psi_t\ p_t &= p_{t-1} \cdot G_t\ b_t &= k_t / G_t\ m_t &= b_t + \theta_t\ w_t &= m_t - c_t\ a_t &= [R_f + (R_t - R_f) \cdot \varsigma_t] \cdot w_t\ c_t &\in [0, m_t]\ \varsigma_t &\in [0,1] \end{align}

docs.title: 3.5 Stationary Formulation
docs.text:
For an infinite horizon problem with no explicit time dependence in primitives, we drop time subscripts and write:

\[\mathcal{V}^{\text{arr}}(k, p) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi, \theta}\left[\max_{c, \varsigma} \left\{p^{1-\rho} \cdot u(c) + \beta \pi \cdot \mathbb{E}_{R}\left[\mathcal{V}^{\text{arr}}(a, p')\right]\right\}\right]\]

where primes denote next-period values and: - \(m = k/(\Gamma \psi) + \theta\) - \(p' = p \cdot \Gamma \cdot \psi\) - \(w = m - c\) - \(a = [R_f + (R - R_f) \cdot \varsigma] \cdot w\)

docs.title: 4.1 Consumption Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition with respect to consumption \(c_t\) is:

\[p_{t-1}^{1-\rho} \cdot u'(c_t) = \beta \pi \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{V}_t^{\text{cont}}}{\partial w_t}(w_t, \varsigma_t, p_t)\]

By the envelope theorem on the continuation value: $\(\frac{\partial \mathcal{V}_t^{\text{cont}}}{\partial w_t} = \mathbb{E}_{R_t}\left[R_t^{\text{port}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{V}_{t+1}^{\text{arr}}}{\partial k_{t+1}}(a_t, p_t)\right]\)$

where \(R_t^{\text{port}} = R_f + (R_t - R_f) \cdot \varsigma_t\).

The envelope condition from the arrival value with respect to \(k_{t+1}\) involves: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{V}{t+1}^{\text{arr}}}{\partial k}} = \mathbb{E{\psi \cdot u'(c_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\frac{1}{G_{t+1}} \cdot p_t^{1-\rho

1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation Perch k Normalized capital (arrival) \(k_t\) Arrival/Prestate live Survival shock \(\ell_t \in \{0,1\}\) Arrival theta Transitory income shock \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) Arrival b Bank balances \(b_t \coloneqq k_t R_{t-1} / \Gamma\) Decision/Postshock m Market resources \(m_t \coloneqq b_t + \theta_t\) Decision c Consumption (control) \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) Decision a Assets after consumption \(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\) Continuation stigma Portfolio share (control) \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) Continuation risky_return Risky asset return shock \(R^e_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) Continuation R Realized portfolio return \(R_t \coloneqq R_f + (R^e_t - R_f)\varsigma_t\) Continuation u Flow utility \(u(c_t)\) Reward

Timing Convention: The model operates in normalized units where all level variables are divided by permanent income. The state variable \(k_t\) represents normalized capital at the beginning of period \(t\) (arrival perch), before shocks are realized.

docs.title: 2.1 Primitive Spaces
docs.text:
State Space: \(\mathcal{K} = \mathbb{R}_+ \cup \{0\}\) represents normalized capital holdings.

Action Spaces: - Consumption choice: \(\mathcal{C}(m) = [0, m]\) where \(m \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is market resources - Portfolio share: \(\mathcal{S} = [0, 1]\) represents the fraction invested in the risky asset

Shock Spaces: - Survival: \(\mathcal{L} = \{0, 1\}\) where \(\ell = 1\) indicates survival - Transitory income: \(\Theta = \mathbb{R}_+\) - Risky return: \(\mathcal{R}^e = \mathbb{R}_+\)

docs.title: 2.2 Preferences and Technology
docs.text:
The agent has CRRA preferences with risk aversion parameter \(\rho > 0\): $\(u(c) \coloneqq \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

The agent discounts future utility at rate \(\beta \in (0,1)\) and faces survival probability \(p \in (0,1]\) each period.

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Survival shock: \(\ell_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) where \(\mathbb{P}(\ell_t = 1) = p\).

Transitory income shock: \(\theta_t\) follows a mean-one lognormal distribution: $\(\log \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}\left(-\frac{\sigma_\theta^2}{2}, \sigma_\theta^2\right)\)$ such that \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_t] = 1\).

Risky asset return: \(R^e_t\) follows a lognormal distribution: $\(\log R^e_t \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\log(R_f + \pi) - \frac{\sigma_r^2}{2}, \sigma_r^2\right)\)$ where \(R_f\) is the risk-free gross return, \(\pi\) is the equity premium, and \(\mathbb{E}[R^e_t] = R_f + \pi\).

All shocks are mutually independent across time and within periods.

docs.title: 2.4 Dynamics and Timing
docs.text:
The model unfolds in two blocks corresponding to distinct decision stages:

Block 1: Consumption-Normalized (within period \(t\))

  1. Agent arrives with normalized capital \(k_t\)
  2. Survival shock \(\ell_t\) and income shock \(\theta_t\) are realized
  3. If \(\ell_t = 0\), the agent dies and receives terminal value zero
  4. If \(\ell_t = 1\), portfolio from previous period returns, generating bank balances: $\(b_t \coloneqq \frac{k_t R_{t-1}}{\Gamma}\)$ where \(\Gamma > 0\) is the permanent income growth factor and \(R_{t-1}\) was the realized return from period \(t-1\)
  5. Market resources combine balances and income: $\(m_t \coloneqq b_t + \theta_t\)$
  6. Agent chooses consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) observing \(m_t\)
  7. Assets after consumption: $\(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\)$

Block 2: Portfolio-Choice (continuation of period \(t\))

  1. Agent observes assets \(a_t\) after consumption
  2. Agent chooses portfolio share \(\varsigma_t \in [0,1]\) investing in risky asset
  3. Risky return shock \(R^e_t\) is realized
  4. Portfolio return is determined: $\(R_t \coloneqq R_f + (R^e_t - R_f)\varsigma_t = R_f(1-\varsigma_t) + R^e_t \varsigma_t\)$
  5. Capital evolves to next period: $\(k_{t+1} \coloneqq a_t\)$

The normalization by permanent income growth \(\Gamma\) ensures stationarity of the distribution of normalized variables.

docs.title: 2.5 Borrowing Constraints
docs.text: The specification includes BoroCnstArt: None, indicating no artificial borrowing constraint beyond the natural constraint that \(c_t \leq m_t\) and \(a_t \geq 0\).

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The value function decomposes across three perches following the Arrival-Decision-Continuation (ADC) framework:

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value (Prestate Perch)
docs.text:
At the beginning of period \(t\), before shocks are realized, the agent holds normalized capital \(k_t\). The arrival value is:

\[v^A(k_t; R_{t-1}) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{\ell_t, \theta_t}\left[\ell_t \cdot v^D(m_t) \mid k_t, R_{t-1}\right]\]

where the expectation is over survival and income shocks, and conditional on surviving (\(\ell_t = 1\)), market resources are: $\(m_t = \frac{k_t R_{t-1}}{\Gamma} + \theta_t\)$

Information set: \(\{k_t, R_{t-1}\}\) and knowledge of shock distributions.

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value (Postshock Perch)
docs.text:
After observing market resources \(m_t\) (having survived and received income), the agent chooses consumption:

\[v^D(m_t) \coloneqq \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{u(c_t) + \beta p \cdot v^C(a_t)\right\}\]

where: - \(u(c_t) = \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\) is flow utility - \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) are assets after consumption - \(\beta p\) is the effective discount factor accounting for survival probability - \(v^C(a_t)\) is the continuation value

Information set: \(\{m_t\}\) and all parameters.

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value (Post-Decision Perch)
docs.text:
After choosing consumption, the agent holds assets \(a_t\) and must choose portfolio allocation:

\[v^C(a_t) \coloneqq \max_{\varsigma_t \in [0,1]} \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[v^A(k_{t+1}; R_t) \mid a_t, \varsigma_t\right]\]

where: - \(R_t = R_f + (R^e_t - R_f)\varsigma_t\) is the portfolio return - \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) is capital entering next period - The expectation is over the risky return shock \(R^e_t\)

Information set: \(\{a_t\}\) and knowledge of the risky return distribution.

docs.title: 3.4 Complete Bellman Recursion
docs.text:
Combining all three perches, the complete recursion is:

\[v^A(k_t; R_{t-1}) = p \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\theta_t}\left[\max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{u(c_t) + \beta p \cdot \max_{\varsigma_t \in [0,1]} \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[v^A(a_t; R_t)\right]\right\}\right]\]

subject to: $\(\begin{align} m_t &= \frac{k_t R_{t-1}}{\Gamma} + \theta_t\\ a_t &= m_t - c_t\\ R_t &= R_f + (R^e_t - R_f)\varsigma_t\\ k_{t+1} &= a_t \end{align}\)$

docs.title: 4.1 Consumption Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for consumption \(c_t\) yields the standard Euler equation:

\[u'(c_t) = \beta p \cdot \frac{\partial v^C(a_t)}{\partial a_t}\]

By the envelope theorem applied to the continuation value:

\[\frac{\partial v^C(a_t)}{\partial a_t} = \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[\frac{\partial v^A(k_{t+1}; R_t)}{\partial k_{t+1}} \cdot \frac{\partial k_{t+1}}{\partial a_t}\right] = \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[\frac{\partial v^A(a_t; R_t)}{\partial k}\right]\]

where we use \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(\partial k_{t+1}/\partial a_t = 1\).

Applying the envelope theorem to the arrival value:

\[\frac{\partial v^A(k_t; R_{t-1})}{\partial k_t} = p \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\theta_t}\left[u'(c_t) \cdot \frac{R_{t-1}}{\Gamma}\right]\]

Combining these, the consumption Euler equation becomes:

\[u'(c_t) = \beta p^2 \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{t+1}}\left[u'(c_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{R_t}{\Gamma}\right]\right]\]

In CRRA form:

\[c_t^{-\rho} = \beta p^2 \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{t+1}}\left[c_{t+1}^{-\rho} \cdot \frac{R_t}{\Gamma}\right]\right]\]

docs.title: 4.2 Portfolio Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for portfolio share \(\varsigma_t\) is:

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial \varsigma_t} \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[v^A(a_t; R_t)\right] = 0\]

Computing the derivative:

\[\mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[\frac{\partial v^A(a_t; R_t)}{\partial R_t} \cdot (R^e_t - R_f)\right] = 0\]

Using the envelope condition:

\[\frac{\partial v^A(k_{t+1}; R_t)}{\partial R_t} = p \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\theta_{t+1}}\left[u'(c_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{k_{t+1}}{\Gamma}\right]\]

The portfolio Euler equation becomes:

\[\mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[(R^e_t - R_f) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\theta_{t+1}}\left[u'(c_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{a_t}{\Gamma}\right]\right] = 0\]

In CRRA form:

\[\mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[(R^e_t - R_f) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\theta_{t+1}}\left[c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\right]\right] = 0\]

docs.title: 4.3 Endogenous Grid Method (EGM) Representation
docs.text:
The consumption problem is well-suited for EGM. Given a grid of assets-after-consumption \(\{a^{(i)}\}\), we can compute:

  1. Marginal continuation value: $\(v^C_a(a^{(i)}) = \mathbb{E}_{R^e_t}\left[\frac{\partial v^A(a^{(i)}; R_t)}{\partial k}\right]\)$

  2. Consumption from Euler equation: $\(c^{(i)} = \left(\beta p \cdot v^C_a(a^{(i)})\right)^{-1/\rho}\)$

  3. Endogenous market resources: $\(m^{(i)} = a^{(i)} + c^{(i)}\)$

This generates policy function \(c(m)\) by interpolation on the \((m^{(i)}, c^{(i)})\) pairs.

The portfolio choice typically requires numerical optimization or root-finding for each asset level \(a_t\).

docs.title: 5. Forward Operator
docs.text: The distribution of agents evolves through the joint dynamics of consumption and portfolio choices.

docs.title: 5.1 Distribution Evolution
docs.text:
Let \(\Psi_t(k)\) denote the cumulative distribution function of normalized capital at the beginning of period \(t\) across surviving agents. The forward operator maps \(\Psi_t \mapsto \Psi_{t+1}\).

Step 1: Portfolio returns and consumption

Given \(k_t\) drawn from \(\Psi_t\) and previous period's return \(R_{t-1}\) (which may be deterministic in steady state or drawn from an ergodic distribution):

  1. Survival shock: agent survives with probability \(p\)
  2. Market resources: \(m_t = \frac{k_t R_{t-1}}{\Gamma} + \theta_t\) where \(\theta_t\) is drawn from the transitory income distribution
  3. Consumption: \(c_t = c^*(m_t)\) from the consumption policy function
  4. Assets: \(a_t = m_t - c_t\)

Step 2: Portfolio choice and capital evolution

  1. Portfolio share: \(\varsigma_t = \varsigma^*(a_t)\) from the portfolio policy function
  2. Return realization: \(R^e_t\) drawn from risky return distribution
  3. Portfolio return: \(R_t = R_f + (R^e_t - R_f)\varsigma_t\)
  4. Next period capital: \(k_{t+1} = a_t\)

docs.title: Buffer Stock Consumption Model (Normalized)
docs.text:
Source

Application folder: applications/buffer-stock/, which holds the model's stage file, declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl, beside it its methods file, methods.bl, an addition to the stage file, and its settings file, declaration/settings/buffer_stock.yml, in the layout of Model directory layout. A related single-stage model, whose income is drawn independently each period and has no permanent component, is the application applications/consumption-savings-iid/.

The canonical consumption-savings model with permanent and transitory income shocks, normalized by permanent income.

This example presents the buffer stock saving model (Carroll, 2024) in its normalized (ratio) form. Normalizing by permanent income reduces the state from two variables \((\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{P})\) to one \((m = \mathbf{m}/\mathbf{P})\), yielding a stationary single-stage problem suitable for EGM.

Source

Based on Carroll (2024), "Theoretical Foundations of Buffer Stock Saving," Problem \(\mathscr{P}_N\).

docs.title: Model Overview
docs.text: Feature Description Stages 1 (consumption-savings with expectation and maximization) Shocks Permanent (\(\psi\)) and transitory (\(\xi\)), IID Solution Endogenous Grid Method (EGM) State Normalized market resources \(m\) Horizon Infinite (stationary)

docs.title: Bellman Equation
docs.text:
\[ v(m) = \max_{0 < c < m} \left\{ \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\Gamma \psi')^{1-\rho}\, v\!\left(\frac{R\,(m - c)}{\Gamma \psi'} + \xi'\right)\right] \right\} \]

subject to:

\[ \begin{aligned} a &= m - c \\ m' &= \frac{R}{\Gamma \psi'}\, a + \xi' \end{aligned} \]

Variables (all normalized by permanent income \(P_t\)):

  • \(m\) = market resources
  • \(c\) = consumption
  • \(a\) = end-of-period assets
  • \(\psi\) = permanent income shock (\(\mathbb{E}[\psi] = 1\), \(\psi \in [\underline{\psi}, \bar{\psi}]\))
  • \(\xi\) = transitory income shock (\(\mathbb{E}[\xi] = 1\); equals zero with probability \(\wp > 0\))
  • \(R\) = gross interest rate
  • \(\Gamma\) = deterministic permanent income growth factor
  • \(\beta\) = discount factor
  • \(\rho\) = coefficient of relative risk aversion (\(\rho > 1\))

The weighting factor \((\Gamma \psi)^{1-\rho}\) arises from normalizing the value function: \(v(m) \;=\; \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{P})\,/\,\mathbf{P}^{1-\rho}\).

docs.title: First-Order Conditions
docs.text:
Euler equation:

\[ c^{-\rho} = R\,\beta\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\Gamma \psi')^{-\rho}\, c'(m')^{-\rho}\right] \]

Envelope condition:

\[ v'(m) = c(m)^{-\rho} \]

docs.title: State-Space Diagram
docs.text:
(k) ──shocks (ψ, ξ)──▶ (m) ──c──▶ (a)

A single stage per period: the arrival state \(k\), the assets carried from the previous period, is transformed by two shocks into market resources \(m\); consumption \(c\) determines the end-of-period assets \(a = m - c\).

docs.title: Stage File
docs.text:
The stage file, declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl, states the model: the sets of resources and assets, the parameters with their descriptions, the log-mean of the positive transitory draw as a derived parameter, the two shocks and their laws, utility and the set of feasible consumption, the two forward blocks, the two value blocks and the policy block, whose line is the maximization alone.

@stage: buffer_stock

Xm := ℝ₊₊
Xa := ℝ₊₊

β : (0,1)        :: ["discount factor"]
ρ : (1, inf)     :: ["coefficient of relative risk aversion, greater than one"]
R : ℝ₊₊          :: ["gross interest rate"]
Γ : ℝ₊₊          :: ["deterministic permanent income growth factor"]
σ_ψ : ℝ₊         :: ["standard deviation of the log permanent shock"]
σ_ξ : ℝ₊         :: ["standard deviation of the log transitory shock, conditional on a positive draw"]
p_zero : (0,1)   :: ["probability ℘ of a zero transitory draw"]
μ_ξ := -log(1 - p_zero) - σ_ξ^2/2   :: ["log-mean of the positive transitory draw, at which E[ξ] = 1"]

ψ : ℝ₊₊
ψ ~ LogNormal(-(σ_ψ^2)/2, σ_ψ)
ξ : ℝ₊
ξ ~ Mixture((p_zero, 0), (1 - p_zero, LogNormal(μ_ξ, σ_ξ)))

𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)         :: [id=util]
𝑑𝑢     := D_{c}(𝑢)                   :: [id=marg_util]
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 := Inv(𝑑𝑢)                    :: [id=inv_marg_util]

Γ_c(x : ℝ₊₊) := {c : ℝ₊₊ | c < x}   :: [id=feasible_consumption]

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (k : Xa, ψ, ξ) : !arvl -> (m : Xm) : !dcsn] {
    m = R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ               :: [id=market_resources]
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : Xa) : !cntn] {
    a = m - c                       :: [id=savings]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]               :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}((Γ*ψ)^(1-ρ) * V)     :: [id=value]
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{cp : Γ_c(m)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>])     :: [id=optimality]
}

docs.title: Arrival Transition
docs.text:
The arrival block arvl_to_dcsn writes \(m = R\,k/(\Gamma\psi) + \xi\), which combines two steps from the levels problem:

  1. Bank balances: \(b = R\,k/(\Gamma\psi)\), where the denominator \(\Gamma\psi\) is the realized permanent income growth factor.
  2. Market resources: \(m = b + \xi\), adding transitory income.

docs.title: Builders
docs.text:
• cntn_to_dcsn, the decision value builder: \(V = u(c) + \beta V^{>}\), at the consumption the policy chooses.
  • policy, the policy builder: the maximization of \(u(c') + \beta V^{>}\) over consumption \(c' < m\).
  • dcsn_to_arvl, the arrival value builder: \(V^{<} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi}[(\Gamma\psi)^{1-\rho}\, V]\), the decision value read at \(m = R\,k/(\Gamma\psi) + \xi\).

The stage file states no derivative and no numerical method: the methods file beside it states the derivatives and selects the methods, as the next section shows.

docs.title: Methods and Settings
docs.text:
The methods file, declaration/stages/buffer_stock/methods.bl, stands beside the stage file and is an addition to it: a .bl file read by the same grammar, whose blocks name the stage's blocks by their ids and add to them, and which the package reads together with the stage file before it elaborates the stage (Methodization). The addition names the endogenous grid method, !egm, as the policy builder's method, with the exogenous grid of savings, !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)), as its grid, and appends the method's three lines to the policy block: the inverted Euler equation, the grid line that gives the resources at each saving, and the identification of consumption with its candidate. When the stage is solved, the three lines stand in place of the maximization, which remains the stage's statement of the choice. The consumption function is read by linear interpolation at the policy builder's Evaluation, policy.evaluate, between the pairs the method computes; those pairs give its nodes, so the entry writes no grid there, and a grid written there is refused. Each value builder gains its derivative line: the envelope condition D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) of the decision value, and the derivative of the arrival value, whose weight \(R\,(\Gamma\psi)^{-\rho}\) inside the expectation comes from the factor \(R/(\Gamma\psi)\) of the law of motion and the normalization \((\Gamma\psi)^{1-\rho}\) of the value. At the arrival builder the expectation over the two shocks is taken by Gauss–Hermite quadrature, with one node count per shock, and the arrival value and its stated derivative are represented together, named once at that builder's Evaluation, by linear interpolation on the grid of assets, !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k)). The eight settings the entries read are declared at the top of the file with their sets, a count in ℕ and a bound a point of Xa; their values stand in the settings file.

@methods: buffer_stock
# The methods of the buffer-stock stage, an addition to buffer_stock.bl, the
# stage file beside this one. The endogenous grid method stands on the policy
# builder with its exogenous grid of savings a; its three lines, the inverted
# Euler equation, the inverted law of motion and the identification of the
# chosen consumption with the candidate, stand in place of the maximization
# when the stage is solved, and the maximization remains the stage's
# statement of the choice. The consumption function is read by linear
# interpolation at the policy builder's Evaluation, between the pairs the
# method computes, and that Evaluation takes no grid of its own, since the
# pairs give its nodes. Each value builder gains its derivative line: the
# envelope condition of the decision value, and the derivative of the
# arrival value, whose weight R*(Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) inside the
# expectation comes from the law m = R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ and the normalization
# (Γ*ψ)^(1-ρ) of the value. At the arrival builder the expectation over the
# two income shocks is taken by Gauss-Hermite quadrature with one node count
# per shock, the point mass of the transitory shock at zero exact, and the
# arrival value and its derivative are represented together, by linear
# interpolation on the grid of assets k, named once at that builder's
# Evaluation. The settings the entries read are declared first, with their
# sets: a count in ℕ and a bound a point of Xa, the set the stage declares for
# the savings and the assets. Their values are recorded in
# declaration/settings/buffer_stock.yml and are those of the HARK solution of
# this model in the QuantEcon community library
# (projects/HARK/buffer-stock/tutorial.ipynb, HARK 0.17.1): seven nodes per
# shock and 960 points from 0.001 to 20 for the savings and for the assets.
# HARK's seven values per shock are equiprobable conditional means and its
# grid is exponentially nested; here the rule is Gauss-Hermite and each grid
# is stated by its bounds and its count.

n_a : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]
a_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the savings grid"]
a_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the savings grid"]
n_k : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the asset grid"]
k_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the asset grid"]
k_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the asset grid"]
n_ψ_nodes : ℕ        :: ["quadrature nodes of the permanent shock"]
n_ξ_nodes : ℕ        :: ["quadrature nodes of the transitory shock"]

[id=policy, policy.method : !egm | policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
    | policy.evaluate.method : !Linear] {
    c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>])       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m[>] = a + c[>]                 :: [id=g_cntn_to_dcsn]
    c[~] = c[>]                     :: [id=cons_choice]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn] {
    D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                                  :: [id=marginal]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl
    | E_ψ_ξ.method : !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes)
    | evaluate.method : !Linear
    | evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k))] {
    D_{k}V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}(R * (Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) * D_{m}V)    :: [id=marginal]
}

The settings file, declaration/settings/buffer_stock.yml, gives the numbers of quadrature nodes of the two shocks, the exogenous grid of savings and the grid of assets:

# The buffer-stock stage's numerical settings: the quadrature nodes of the two
# income shocks at the arrival builder's expectation, the exogenous grid of
# savings a of the endogenous grid method, and the grid of assets k on which
# the arrival value and its derivative are represented. The values are those
# of the HARK solution of this model in the QuantEcon community library
# (projects/HARK/buffer-stock/tutorial.ipynb): seven points per shock, and 960
# asset points from 0.001 to 20, one grid in that solution for savings and for
# assets.
settings:
  n_ψ_nodes: 7
  n_ξ_nodes: 7
  n_a: 960
  a_min: 0.001
  a_max: 20.0
  n_k: 960
  k_min: 0.001
  k_max: 20.0

The folder holds no recipe, so load_stage is given the stage file and its addition together, and configure then binds the settings:

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage(
    "applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl",
    ["applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/methods.bl"],
))
configured = stage.configure("applications/buffer-stock/declaration/settings/buffer_stock.yml")
print(configured.settings)

name       set  value  read at                by              grid
n_a        ℕ    960    policy                 !egm            !Cartesian
a_min      Xa   0.001  policy                 !egm            !Cartesian
a_max      Xa   20.0   policy                 !egm            !Cartesian
n_k        ℕ    960    dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate  !Linear         !Cartesian
k_min      Xa   0.001  dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate  !Linear         !Cartesian
k_max      Xa   20.0   dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate  !Linear         !Cartesian
n_ψ_nodes  ℕ    7      dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ     !gauss_hermite
n_ξ_nodes  ℕ    7      dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ     !gauss_hermite

docs.title: Period and Trellis
docs.text: The model is stationary: every period holds the one stage with the same parameters, and the inter-period connector joins the end-of-period assets \(a\) of one period to the arrival state \(k\) of the next. The application holds no recipe and no trellis file; Trellises states how a trellis is written.

docs.title: Solution Method: EGM
docs.text:
The Endogenous Grid Method solves this model by inverting the Euler equation:

  1. Start with continuation marginal value \(dV^{>}(a)\) on an exogenous grid of end-of-period assets \(\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}\).
  2. Expectation (the derivative line of dcsn_to_arvl): \(dV^{<}(a_i) = R\,\mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi}[(\Gamma\psi)^{-\rho}\, dV(Ra_i/(\Gamma\psi) + \xi)]\).
  3. InvEuler: \(c_i = (\beta \cdot dV^{<}(a_i))^{-1/\rho}\).
  4. Endogenous grid (g_cntn_to_dcsn): \(m_i = a_i + c_i\).
  5. Envelope (the derivative line of cntn_to_dcsn): \(dV_i = c_i^{-\rho}\).
  6. Iterate until convergence.

The normalization weight \((\Gamma\psi)^{-\rho}\) in the marginal-value expectation (step 2) is the key difference from a model without permanent income growth.

docs.title: Calibration (Baseline)
docs.text:
The application holds no calibration file. A baseline calibration takes R = 1.03, β = 0.96, Γ = 1.03, ρ = 2, σ_ψ = 0.1, σ_ξ = 0.1 and p_zero = 0.005. The numerical settings are those of the settings file above.

The log-mean of the positive transitory draw, μ_ξ := -log(1 - p_zero) - σ_ξ^2/2, is a derived parameter: a constant that the stage file defines from its parameters with :=, which takes the value of that definition at each calibration. The calibration supplies no value for it, and a calibration that does is refused under derived-parameter. The definition makes the mean of the transitory draw one at every calibration, since the positive draw, LogNormal(μ_ξ, σ_ξ), has mean \(\exp(\mu_\xi + \sigma_\xi^2/2)\):

\[ \mathbb{E}[\xi] = \wp \cdot 0 + (1 - \wp)\, \exp\!\left(\mu_\xi + \tfrac{\sigma_\xi^2}{2}\right) = (1 - \wp)\, \exp\!\left(-\log(1 - \wp)\right) = 1 . \]

At \(\sigma_\xi = 0\) the positive draw is the point mass at \(\exp(\mu_\xi) = 1/(1 - \wp)\), and the declared set \((0, 1)\) of p_zero keeps that point finite. stage.par lists the derived parameter after the declared ones, with its definition and, once the stage is calibrated, its value:

calibrated = stage.calibrate({"R": 1.03, "β": 0.96, "Γ": 1.03, "ρ": 2.0, "σ_ψ": 0.1, "σ_ξ": 0.1, "p_zero": 0.005})
print(calibrated.par)

name    set                         value                   describes
β       (0, 1)                      0.96                    discount factor
ρ       (1, inf)                    2.0                     coefficient of relative risk aversion, greater than one
R       ℝ₊₊                         1.03                    gross interest rate
Γ       ℝ₊₊                         1.03                    deterministic permanent income growth factor
σ_ψ     ℝ₊                          0.1                     standard deviation of the log permanent shock
σ_ξ     ℝ₊                          0.1                     standard deviation of the log transitory shock, conditional on a positive draw
p_zero  (0, 1)                      0.005                   probability ℘ of a zero transitory draw
μ_ξ     -log(1 - p_zero) - σ_ξ^2/2  1.2541823544285312e-05  log-mean of the positive transitory draw, at which E[ξ] = 1

docs.title: Permanent Income Normalization
docs.text: Dividing by \(P_t\) (for quantities) and \(P_t^{1-\rho}\) (for the value function) eliminates the permanent income state. The cost is a growth-adjusted arrival transition and a normalization weight \((\Gamma\psi)^{1-\rho}\) inside the expectation operator.

docs.title: Natural Borrowing Constraint
docs.text: The transitory shock \(\xi\) has a point mass at zero (probability \(\wp > 0\)): the agent may receive zero income. This prevents the agent from choosing \(c = m\) (which would risk zero consumption next period), generating a natural borrowing constraint without an explicit lower bound on assets.

docs.title: Weighted Expectations in the Arrival Builder
docs.text: The arrival builder dcsn_to_arvl writes the value, and its derivative line in the methods file states its derivative, each as a \((\Gamma\psi)\)-weighted expectation. This weight is an artifact of the normalization, not an economic primitive: in the levels problem, the arrival builder would be a plain expectation \(V^{<} = \mathbb{E}[V]\).

docs.title: Consumption-Savings with IID Shocks
docs.text:
Source

Application folder: applications/consumption-savings-iid/, which holds the model's stage file, declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.bl, beside it its methods file, methods.bl, an addition to the stage file, and its settings file, declaration/settings/cons_savings_iid.yml, in the layout of Model directory layout. The YAML files shown on this page are the model's earlier dolo-plus form, which is no longer in the repository.

A single-stage lifecycle model solved via EGM.

This example demonstrates the simplest complete dolo-plus model: a single stage containing both expectation and maximization, designed for solution via the Endogenous Grid Method (EGM).

docs.title: Model Overview
docs.text: Feature Description Stages 1 (self-contained stage with both expectation and maximization) Shocks IID log-normal income shock Solution Endogenous Grid Method (EGM) State Wealth w (cash-on-hand)

docs.title: Economic Problem
docs.text:
The agent solves: $$ V(b) = \mathbb{E}_y \left[ \max_c \left{ u(c) + \beta V(a) \right} \right] $$

where: - b = beginning-of-period assets (prestate) - y = income shock (exogenous) - w = exp(y) + b*r = cash-on-hand (state after shock) - c = consumption (control) - a = w - c = end-of-period assets (poststate)

docs.title: ADC Stage Structure
docs.text:
[ARRIVAL] ───g_ad───▶ [DECISION] ───g_de───▶ [CONTINUATION]
    b          y           w        c            a
              shock       choice
  • Arrival → Decision: Income shock realized, w = exp(y) + b*r
  • Decision → Continuation: Consumption choice, a = w - c

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
The application folder holds the stage file, its note and its methods file in the stage's folder, the settings file under declaration/settings/, and the structural test:

File Purpose declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.bl The stage file: declarations, the values and the maximization declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.md The stage's note, which explains the stage file and the methods file declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/methods.bl The methods file, an addition to the stage file: the endogenous grid method on the policy builder with its grid of savings and the method's three lines, the inverse Euler line, the endogenous grid and the identification of the policy, the derivative lines of the two value builders, and, after the blocks, the linear reading of the consumption function, the closed-form inverse of the marginal utility, Gauss–Hermite quadrature at the two expectations over income, and the representations of the arrival value and of its derivative on the grid of the arrival assets declaration/settings/cons_savings_iid.yml The settings file: the values of the settings the methods file declares, the grid of savings, the grid of the arrival assets and the quadrature nodes tests/test_cons_savings_iid_ast.py The structural test, which parses the stage file and compares its terms with terms written by hand

The earlier dolo-plus form, from which the listings below are taken, kept the model in four YAML files:

File Purpose stage.yaml Stage syntax (symbols, equations) calibration.yaml Parameter values settings.yaml Grid sizes, bounds methodization.yml Solution scheme (EGM recipe)

docs.title: Stage YAML
docs.text:
name: consumption_savings_iid_egm_doloplus

symbols:
  spaces:
    Xb: "@def R+"     # prestate assets
    Xw: "@def R+"     # cash-on-hand
    Xa: "@def R+"     # end-of-period assets
    Y:  "@def R"      # income support

  prestate:
    b: "@in Xb"
  exogenous:
    y:
      - "@in Y"
      - "@dist Normal(μ_y, σ_y)"
  states:
    w: "@in Xw"
  poststates:
    a: "@in Xa"
  controls:
    c: "@in R+"

  values:
    V: "@in R"
  values_marginal:
    dV: "@in R+"

  parameters:
    β: "@in (0,1)"
    γ: "@in R+"
    r: "@in R++"
    μ_y: "@in R"
    σ_y: "@in R+"

equations:
  # Half-transition: shock realization
  arvl_to_dcsn_transition: |
    w = exp(y) + b*r

  # Budget constraint
  dcsn_to_cntn_transition: |
    a = w - c

  # Reverse state for EGM
  cntn_to_dcsn_transition: |
    w = a + c

  # Backward builder with EGM sub-equations
  cntn_to_dcsn_opr:
    Bellman: |
      V = max_{c}((c^(1-γ))/(1-γ) + β*V[>])
    InvEuler: |
      c[>] = (β*dV[>])^(-1/γ)
    MarginalBellman: |
      dV = (c)^(-γ)

  # Expectation operator
  dcsn_to_arvl_opr:
    Bellman: |
      V[<] = E_{y}(V)
    MarginalBellman: |
      dV[<] = r * E_{y}(dV)

docs.title: Single Stage with Both Operators
docs.text: Unlike the port-with-shocks model (which separates expectation and maximization), this model contains both in one stage: - dcsn_to_arvl_opr: Expectation over income shock - cntn_to_dcsn_opr: Maximization via EGM

docs.title: EGM Sub-Equations
docs.text: The cntn_to_dcsn_opr block contains: 1. InvEuler: Compute consumption from marginal value 2. MarginalBellman: Envelope condition for marginal value 3. cntn_to_dcsn_transition: Reverse mapping w = a + c

docs.title: Marginal Value Propagation
docs.text:
The MarginalBellman in dcsn_to_arvl_opr: 

dV[<] = r * E_{y}(dV)
propagates the expected marginal value, accounting for the return r.

docs.title: cons_stage
docs.text:
Deterministic consumption stage (EGM-compatible).

This stage models the consumption choice given cash-on-hand. It's designed to be compatible with the Endogenous Grid Method (EGM).

docs.title: Stage Structure
docs.text:
[ARRIVAL] ──g_ad──▶ [DECISION] ──g_de──▶ [CONTINUATION]
    m                   m_d       c           a
  • Arrival state: m (cash-on-hand from noport/port stage)
  • Decision state: m_d = m (trivial transition)
  • Control: c ∈ (0, m) (consumption)
  • Continuation state: a = m_d - c (post-consumption assets)

docs.title: YAML Specification
docs.text:
name: cons_stage

symbols:
  spaces:
    Xm: "@def R++"
    Xa: "@def R+"

  prestate:
    m: "@in Xm"

  states:
    m_d: "@in Xm"

  poststates:
    a: "@in Xa"

  controls:
    c: "@in R+"

  values:
    V[<]: "@in R"
    V: "@in R"
    V[>]: "@in R"

  values_marginal:
    dV[<]: "@in R+"
    dV: "@in R+"
    dV[>]: "@in R+"

  parameters:
    β: "@in (0,1)"
    ρ: "@in R+"

  settings:
    n_m: "@in Z+"
    m_min: "@in R+"
    m_max: "@in R+"

equations:
  # Trivial arrival-to-decision
  arvl_to_dcsn_transition: |
    m_d = m

  # Budget constraint
  dcsn_to_cntn_transition: |
    a = m_d - c

  # Backward builders (multiple sub-equations for EGM)
  cntn_to_dcsn_builder:
    Bellman: |
      u = (c^(1-ρ))/(1-ρ)
      V = max_{c}(u + β*V[>])
      c = argmax_{c}((c^(1-ρ))/(1-ρ) + β*V[>])
    InvEuler: |
      c[>] = (β*dV[>])^(-1/ρ)
    MarginalBellman: |
      dV = (c)^(-ρ)
    cntn_to_dcsn_transition: |
      m_d[>] = a + c[>]

  dcsn_to_arvl_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V[<] = V
    ShadowBellman: |
      dV[<] = dV

dolo_plus:
  dialect: adc-stage
  version: 0.1
  equation_symbols:
    arvl_to_dcsn_transition: g_ad
    dcsn_to_cntn_transition: g_de
    cntn_to_dcsn_builder: T_ed
    dcsn_to_arvl_builder: T_da
  builder_sub_equations:
    T_ed:
      Bellman: T_ed_Bellman
      InvEuler: T_ed_InvEuler
      MarginalBellman: T_ed_MarginalBellman
      cntn_to_dcsn_transition: g_ed
    T_da:
      Bellman: T_da_Bellman
      ShadowBellman: T_da_ShadowBellman
  slot_map:
    prestate: m
    poststate: a

docs.title: EGM Sub-Equations
docs.text:
The cntn_to_dcsn_builder contains multiple sub-equations for EGM:

Sub-equation Purpose Bellman Standard value function recursion InvEuler Inverse Euler equation: c = (β * dV)^(-1/ρ) MarginalBellman Envelope condition: dV = u'(c) cntn_to_dcsn_transition Reverse state: m = a + c

docs.title: Marginal Values
docs.text: The values_marginal group declares shadow values dV (with perch tags) used by EGM. These represent marginal utility of wealth at each perch.

docs.title: Slot Map
docs.text:
• Input: m (cash-on-hand)
  • Output: a (post-consumption assets)

docs.title: noport_stage
docs.text:
Shock realization stage with no decision.

This stage models the realization of an income shock without any choice by the agent. It's used as:

  • A "no-portfolio" period (noport → cons)
  • A bridge when converting from post-consumption assets a to cash-on-hand m

docs.title: Stage Structure
docs.text:
[ARRIVAL] ──g_ad──▶ [DECISION] ──g_de──▶ [CONTINUATION]
    k                   k_d        θ           m
  • Arrival state: k (investable assets from previous period)
  • Decision state: k_d = k (trivial, no choice)
  • Shock: θ ~ LogNormal(μ_θ, σ_θ) realized after decision
  • Continuation state: m = k_d * R + θ (cash-on-hand)

docs.title: YAML Specification
docs.text:
name: noport_stage

symbols:
  spaces:
    Xk: "@def R++"
    Xm: "@def R++"
    Θ:  "@def R++"

  prestate:
    k: "@in Xk"

  exogenous:
    θ:
      - "@in Θ"
      - "@dist LogNormal(μ_θ, σ_θ)"

  states:
    k_d: "@in Xk"

  poststates:
    m: "@in Xm"

  values:
    V[<]: "@in R"
    V: "@in R"
    V[>]: "@in R"

  parameters:
    R: "@in R++"
    μ_θ: "@in R"
    σ_θ: "@in R+"

  settings:
    n_m: "@in Z+"
    m_min: "@in R+"
    m_max: "@in R+"
    n_θ_nodes: "@in Z+"

equations:
  # Trivial transition (no shock between arrival and decision)
  arvl_to_dcsn_transition: |
    k_d = k

  # Shock realized after decision
  dcsn_to_cntn_transition: |
    m = k_d*R + θ

  # Backward builders
  cntn_to_dcsn_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V = E_{θ}(V[>])

  dcsn_to_arvl_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V[<] = V

dolo_plus:
  dialect: adc-stage
  version: 0.1
  equation_symbols:
    arvl_to_dcsn_transition: g_ad
    dcsn_to_cntn_transition: g_de
    cntn_to_dcsn_builder: T_ed
    dcsn_to_arvl_builder: T_da
  slot_map:
    prestate: k
    poststate: m

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
1. No decision: The cntn_to_dcsn_builder is pure expectation (no max or argmax)
  2. Shock timing: Income shock θ is realized after the trivial decision
  3. Slot map: Defines how this stage connects to others (k in, m out)

docs.title: Formal MDP: No-Portfolio Stage (noport_stage)
docs.text: Source: the stage file port-with-shocks/library/noport_stage.yaml of the earlier dolo-plus YAML design; the file is no longer in the repository.

docs.title: Rosetta Stone
docs.text: DDSL abstract This stage YAML Arrival state \(x_{\prec}\) \(k\) (investable assets) prestate: k Decision state \(x\) \(k_d\) (identity) states: k_d Continuation state \(x_{\succ}\) \(m\) (cash-on-hand) poststates: m Control \(a\) (none) — Pre-decision shock \(\zeta\) (none) — Post-decision shock \(\eta\) \(\theta \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_\theta, \sigma_\theta)\) exogenous: θ \(\mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim}\) identity: \(k_d = k\) arvl_to_dcsn_transition \(\mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}\) \(m = k_d R + \theta\) dcsn_to_cntn_transition \(\mathbb{B}\) (decision builder) \(v(k) = \mathbb{E}_\theta[v_{\succ}(kR + \theta)]\) cntn_to_dcsn_builder \(\mathbb{I}\) (arrival builder) \(v_{\prec} = v\) (identity) dcsn_to_arvl_builder

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
An agent enters the stage with investable assets \(k \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\). There is no decision; the stage serves purely as a shock-realization bridge that converts an asset position into cash-on-hand.

State space. \(\mathsf X_{\prec} = \mathsf X = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) (assets), \(\mathsf X_{\succ} = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) (cash-on-hand). The action set is a singleton (no control).

Shock process. A transitory income shock \(\theta\) is realized between decision and continuation (post-decision only configuration, \(\mathsf Z_{\prec} = \{\varnothing\}\)):

\[ \theta \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_\theta, \sigma_\theta). \]

Transitions.

\[ \mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim} \colon k \mapsto k_d = k \qquad\text{(identity)}, \qquad \mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ} \colon (k_d, \theta) \mapsto m = k_d R + \theta. \]

docs.title: Perches
docs.text: Perch Variable Space Description \(\prec\) (arrival) \(k\) \(\mathsf X_{\prec} = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) Investable assets \(\cdot\) (decision) \(k_d\) \(\mathsf X = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) Investable assets (identity, no choice) \(\succ\) (continuation) \(m\) \(\mathsf X_{\succ} = \mathbb{R}_{++}\) Cash-on-hand (after shock)

docs.title: Filtration
docs.text:
\[ \mathcal F_{\prec} = \mathcal F \subset \mathcal F_{\succ}. \]

The arrival and decision information sets coincide (no pre-decision shock). The continuation information set is strictly larger: the shock \(\theta\) is revealed.

docs.title: Builders
docs.text:
Decision builder \(\mathbb{B}\) (cntn → dcsn). Since there is no control, \(\mathbb{B}\) is a pure conditional expectation:

\[ (\mathbb{B}\, v_{\succ})(k) = \mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[v_{\succ}(kR + \theta)\bigr]. \]

Arrival builder \(\mathbb{I}\) (dcsn → arvl). The identity:

\[ v_{\prec}(k) = v(k). \]

Stage operator. \(\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{I} \circ \mathbb{B} = \mathbb{B}\), since \(\mathbb{I}\) is trivial:

\[ (\mathbb{T}\, v_{\succ})(k) = \mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[v_{\succ}(kR + \theta)\bigr]. \]

This is the operator \(\mathbf{E}\) in the noport–cons conjugation.

docs.title: Bellman Equation
docs.text:
Since there is no control, the stage Bellman equation reduces to:

\[ v_{\prec}(k) = \mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[v_{\succ}(kR + \theta)\bigr]. \]

There is no optimization and hence no policy function, no Euler equation, and no first-order conditions.

docs.title: Forward Operator
docs.text:
Given a distribution \(\mu_{\prec}\) over arrival states \(k\), the forward operator pushes \(\mu_{\prec}\) through the shock realization:

\[ \mu_{\succ}(A) = \int \Pr(kR + \theta \in A) \, \mathrm{d}\mu_{\prec}(k). \]

Since the arrival builder is identity, \(\mu = \mu_{\prec}\) and the full forward map is \(\mathrm{F} = \mathrm{F}_{\succ}\).

docs.title: YAML
docs.text:
name: noport_stage

symbols:
  spaces:
    Xk: "@def R++"
    Xm: "@def R++"
    Θ:  "@def R++"

  prestate:
    k: "@in Xk"

  exogenous:
    θ:
      - "@in Θ"
      - "@dist LogNormal(μ_θ, σ_θ)"

  states:
    k_d: "@in Xk"

  poststates:
    m: "@in Xm"

  values:
    V[<]: "@in R"
    V: "@in R"
    V[>]: "@in R"

  parameters:
    R: "@in R++"
    μ_θ: "@in R"
    σ_θ: "@in R+"

equations:
  arvl_to_dcsn_transition: |
    k_d = k

  dcsn_to_cntn_transition: |
    m = k_d*R + θ

  cntn_to_dcsn_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V = E_{θ}(V[>])

  dcsn_to_arvl_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V[<] = V

docs.title: port_stage
docs.text:
Portfolio allocation stage with post-decision correlated shocks.

This stage implements portfolio choice where the agent allocates wealth between risky and risk-free assets before shocks are realized.

docs.title: Stage Overview
docs.text: Feature Description Prestate k (investable assets) Control ς (risky share ∈ [0,1]) Shocks Joint post-decision (Ψ, θ) Poststate m (cash-on-hand)

docs.title: ADC Structure
docs.text:
[ARRIVAL] ───g_ad───▶ [DECISION] ───g_de───▶ [CONTINUATION]
    k                   k_d, ς       Ψ,θ           m
              identity          portfolio+shocks
  • Arrival → Decision: Identity transition k_d = k
  • Decision → Continuation: Portfolio return with shocks realized

docs.title: Economic Problem
docs.text:
The portfolio stage solves: $$ V(k) = \max_{\varsigma} \mathbb{E}_{\Psi,\theta} \left[ V^{e}(m) \right] $$

where cash-on-hand after portfolio choice and shock realization is: $$ m = k \cdot (\varsigma \Psi + (1-\varsigma) R) + \theta $$

  • ς = risky share (fraction in risky asset)
  • Ψ = risky return shock (log-normal)
  • θ = transitory income shock (log-normal)
  • R = risk-free gross return

docs.title: Stage YAML
docs.text:
name: port_stage

symbols:
  spaces:
    Xk: "@def R++"
    Xm: "@def R++"
    Π:  "@def [0,1]"
    Rp: "@def R++"
    Θ:  "@def R++"

  prestate:
    k: "@in Xk"

  states:
    k_d: "@in Xk"

  controls:
    ς: "@in Π"

  # Shocks realized after the portfolio decision (post-decision timing)
  exogenous:
    Ψ:
      - "@in Rp"
      - "@dist LogNormal(μ_Ψ, σ_Ψ)"
    θ:
      - "@in Θ"
      - "@dist LogNormal(μ_θ, σ_θ)"

  poststates:
    m: "@in Xm"

  values:
    V[<]: "@in R"
    V: "@in R"
    V[>]: "@in R"

  parameters:
    R: "@in R++"
    μ_Ψ: "@in R"
    σ_Ψ: "@in R+"
    μ_θ: "@in R"
    σ_θ: "@in R+"
    ρ_ζ: "@in [-1,1]"   # correlation parameter

equations:
  # No shocks between arrival and decision
  arvl_to_dcsn_transition: |
    k_d = k

  # Joint post-decision shocks realized in dcsn→cntn
  dcsn_to_cntn_transition: |
    m = k_d*(ς*Ψ + (1-ς)*R) + θ

  # Decision value: max-over-expectation (post-decision shocks)
  cntn_to_dcsn_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V = max_{ς}(E_{Ψ,θ}(V[>]))
      ς = argmax_{ς}(E_{Ψ,θ}(V[>]))

  # No expectation at arrival (deterministic arvl→dcsn)
  dcsn_to_arvl_builder:
    Bellman: |
      V[<] = V

docs.title: Post-Decision Shock Timing
docs.text:
Unlike the noport stage, the portfolio decision ς is made before shocks are realized. The shocks appear in the dcsn_to_cntn_transition, meaning:

  1. Agent observes k at arrival
  2. Agent chooses portfolio allocation ς
  3. Shocks (Ψ, θ) are then realized
  4. Cash-on-hand m is computed

docs.title: Max-over-Expectation Structure
docs.text:
The Bellman equation has the form: 

V = max_{ς}(E_{Ψ,θ}(V[>]))

This is a max-over-expectation (rather than expectation-over-max), which is characteristic of portfolio problems where the decision must be made before uncertainty resolves.

docs.title: Joint Correlated Shocks
docs.text: The shocks Ψ (risky return) and θ (income) can be correlated via the ρ_ζ parameter, allowing for realistic modeling of return-income correlations.

docs.title: Period Usage
docs.text:
This stage is used in:

  • port_cons_period: port → cons (portfolio choice, then consumption)
  • cons_port_period: cons → port (consumption first, then portfolio)

See Port-with-Shocks for composition details.

docs.title: Formal MDP: Portfolio Stage (port_stage)
docs.text: Source: the stage file port-with-shocks/library/port_stage.yaml of the earlier dolo-plus YAML design; the file is no longer in the repository.

docs.title: Rosetta Stone
docs.text: DDSL abstract This stage Stage name port_stage Arrival state \(x_{\prec}\) \(k\) Decision state \(x\) \(k\) Continuation state \(x_{\succ}\) \(m\) Control \(\varsigma\) Exogenous shocks \(\Psi, \theta\) (post-decision)

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A household enters the stage with investable assets \(k \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) and chooses a risky portfolio share \(\varsigma \in [0,1]\). After the portfolio decision, a joint shock vector \(\zeta \coloneqq (\Psi, \theta)\) is realized, determining the continuation state.

State and action spaces. The state space is \(X_k \coloneqq \mathbb{R}_{++}\) and the action space is \(\Pi \coloneqq [0,1]\). The feasibility correspondence is \(\Gamma(k) = [0,1]\) for all \(k\).

Shock process. The shocks are realized after the portfolio decision (post-decision timing):

\[ \Psi \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_\Psi, \sigma_\Psi), \qquad \theta \sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_\theta, \sigma_\theta). \]

A correlation parameter \(\rho_\zeta\) is declared but not yet wired.

Transitions. The arrival-to-decision transition is the identity \(k_d = k\). After the decision and shock realization, cash-on-hand is

\[ m = k \bigl(\varsigma \, \Psi + (1-\varsigma)\, R\bigr) + \theta, \]

where \(R > 0\) is the gross risk-free return.

docs.title: Bellman Equation
docs.text:
This stage has a "max-over-expectation" structure: the agent chooses \(\varsigma\) before the shocks are realized, so the expectation is inside the max. The arrival-to-decision transition is identity, so the Bellman equation is:

\[ v(k) = \max_{\varsigma \in [0,1]} \; \mathbb{E}_{\Psi,\theta} \Bigl[ v_{\succ}\!\bigl(k(\varsigma \Psi + (1-\varsigma)R) + \theta\bigr) \Bigr], \]

where \(v_{\succ} \colon \mathbb{R}_{++} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the continuation value function. The optimal risky share is

\[ \varsigma^*(k) \coloneqq \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\varsigma \in [0,1]} \; \mathbb{E}_{\Psi,\theta} \Bigl[ v_{\succ}\!\bigl(k(\varsigma \Psi + (1-\varsigma)R) + \theta\bigr) \Bigr]. \]

The arrival value function is the identity: \(v_{\prec}(k) = v(k)\).

docs.title: First-Order Conditions
docs.text:
At an interior solution \(\varsigma^* \in (0,1)\), the first-order condition is

\[ \mathbb{E}_{\Psi,\theta} \Bigl[ v'_{\succ}(m) \cdot k\,(\Psi - R) \Bigr] = 0, \]

where \(m = k(\varsigma^* \Psi + (1-\varsigma^*)R) + \theta\). This is a nonlinear equation in \(\varsigma\) that typically requires numerical root-finding for each \(k\).

docs.title: Forward Operator (Population Dynamics)
docs.text:
Given a distribution \(\mu\) over arrival states \(k\), the forward operator pushes \(\mu\) through the optimal policy and shock realization:

\[ m = k\bigl(\varsigma^*(k)\,\Psi + (1-\varsigma^*(k))\,R\bigr) + \theta, \qquad k \sim \mu, \quad (\Psi,\theta) \text{ drawn independently}. \]

The continuation-state distribution is

\[ \mu_{\succ}(A) = \int \Pr\!\bigl(k(\varsigma^*(k)\Psi + (1-\varsigma^*(k))R) + \theta \in A\bigr)\, \mathrm{d}\mu(k). \]

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Symbol Value Description \(R\) 1.02 gross risk-free return \(\mu_\Psi\) 0.04 log-mean of risky return \(\sigma_\Psi\) 0.15 log-std of risky return \(\mu_\theta\) 0.0 log-mean of transitory income \(\sigma_\theta\) 0.1 log-std of transitory income \(\rho_\zeta\) 0.0 shock correlation (placeholder)

docs.title: Port-with-Shocks Model
docs.text:
Source

The YAML stages of this page are the earlier form of the portfolio–consumption model, kept as recorded sources of its fixed reference under applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/. The model's current stage files are the .bl files under applications/cons-port/declaration/stages/, written with the maximization alone, and its recipes and trellis files stand beside them in applications/cons-port/declaration/ (Model directory layout). Earlier reference notebook: applications/cons-port/notebooks/port-cons/solve_port_cons_ffp.ipynb

A modular lifecycle model with portfolio choice and correlated shocks.

This example demonstrates how dolo-plus stages compose into different period configurations, showing the power of modular stage-based specification.

docs.title: Model Overview
docs.text: Feature Description Stages 3 reusable stages (noport, port, cons) Periods 3 configurations from same stage library Shocks Log-normal income and return shocks Solution EGM for consumption, grid search for portfolio

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
The port-with-shocks model separates three concerns:

  1. Shock realization (noport_stage): Transforms assets to cash-on-hand via income shock
  2. Portfolio allocation (port_stage): Allocates wealth before shocks resolve
  3. Consumption choice (cons_stage): Optimizes consumption given cash-on-hand

By combining these stages differently, we get distinct economic models from the same building blocks.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text: Stage Type Decision Prestate → Poststate noport_stage Shock realization None k → m via m = k*R + θ port_stage Portfolio ς (continuous) k → m via m = k*(ς*Ψ + (1-ς)*R) + θ cons_stage Consumption c (continuous) m → a via a = m - c

docs.title: noport_stage (Shock Realization)
docs.text:
No decision—just shock realization:

k ──[θ shock]──▶ m = k*R + θ
Symbol Role k Investable assets (prestate) θ Transitory income shock m Cash-on-hand (poststate)

docs.title: port_stage (Portfolio Choice)
docs.text:
Portfolio decision before joint shocks:

k ──[choose ς]──[Ψ,θ shocks]──▶ m = k*(ς*Ψ + (1-ς)*R) + θ
Symbol Role k Investable assets (prestate) ς Risky share (control) Ψ, θ Return and income shocks m Cash-on-hand (poststate)

docs.title: cons_stage (Consumption)
docs.text:
Deterministic consumption (EGM-compatible):

m ──[choose c]──▶ a = m - c
Symbol Role m Cash-on-hand (prestate) c Consumption (control) a End-of-period assets (poststate)

docs.title: Period Configurations
docs.text: The library defines three period YAML files, each composing stages in a different order.

docs.title: Period 1: cons_period (noport → cons)
docs.text:
File: cons_period.yaml

name: cons_period

stages:
  - noport_stage
  - cons_stage

Flow: k ──[θ shock]──▶ m ──[choose c]──▶ a

  • No portfolio decision; income shock is realized via noport_stage
  • noport_stage outputs m, cons_stage expects m — implicit identity connector (no connector needed)
  • Between-period link: k_{t+1} = a_t (rename at trellis/assembly level)

This is the simplest consumption-savings model with exogenous income risk.

docs.title: Period 2: port_cons_period (port → cons)
docs.text:
File: port_cons_period.yaml

name: port_cons_period

stages:
  - port_stage
  - cons_stage

Flow: k ──[choose ς, then Ψ,θ shocks]──▶ m ──[choose c]──▶ a

  • Portfolio allocation is made first, then joint return and income shocks are realized
  • port_stage outputs m, cons_stage expects m — implicit identity connector
  • Between-period link: k_{t+1} = a_t

This is the standard lifecycle portfolio-consumption model (e.g. Cocco, Gomes, Maenhout 2005).

docs.title: Period 3: cons_port_period (cons → port)
docs.text:
File: cons_port_period.yaml

name: cons_port_period

stages:
  - cons_stage
  - port_stage

connectors:
  - from: cons_stage
    to: port_stage
    rename: {a: k}

Flow: m ──[choose c]──▶ a = k ──[choose ς, then Ψ,θ shocks]──▶ m'

  • Consumption is chosen first, then remaining assets are allocated across portfolio
  • cons_stage outputs a but port_stage expects k — explicit rename connector {a: k} is required
  • Between-period link: m_{t+1} = m'_t (identity, since port outputs m and cons expects m)

This reversal illustrates the key composition feature: the same stages produce a different economic model simply by changing the order and adding a connector.

docs.title: Connectors and Inter-period Connectors
docs.text:
The three period files show how modular stage composition works in practice:

Period Stages Connector Between-period rename cons_period noport → cons identity (omitted) a → k port_cons_period port → cons identity (omitted) a → k cons_port_period cons → port {a: k} (explicit) m → m (identity)

Key observation: When stage output names match the next stage's input (m → m), the connector is identity and is omitted. When they differ (a → k), an explicit connector provides the rename. This is the inter-period connector condition from the DDSL foundations.

docs.title: Trellis Construction
docs.text:
A trellis composes periods across time with inter-period connectors. For example, an infinite-horizon cons_period trellis:

periods:
  - cons_period       # noport → cons, outputs a

inter_connectors:
  - rename: {a: k}    # between-period: a_t → k_{t+1}

For cons_port_period, the inter-period connector would be identity since the period already outputs m and expects m at arrival.

docs.title: Post-Decision Shock Timing
docs.text:
In port_stage, the portfolio decision ς is made before shocks (Ψ, θ) resolve. This is expressed by:

  1. Shocks in exogenous block (not in arvl_to_dcsn_transition)
  2. Bellman: V = max_{ς}(E_{Ψ,θ}(V[>]))

docs.title: EGM Compatibility
docs.text:
The cons_stage is designed for EGM solution:

  • Contains InvEuler equation: c[>] = (β*dV[>])^(-1/ρ)
  • Contains reverse transition: m_d[>] = a + c[>]
  • No shocks within the stage (expectation handled by preceding stage)

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
