The module's file name is fixed by the program: HANDLERS_FILE = "matsya_handler.py" in configuration.py, which check_files requires; the qualifier distinguishes these functions from the Rosetta-stone handler. The module has 2,210 lines: the thirteen Matsya handlers, one for each slot (a slot is a Matsya handler name with its ordered parameter names, as SLOTS in configuration.py fixes them), and the optional fourteenth, conversation_reply, the slot of OPTIONAL_SLOTS; two public functions besides, structure_of, which reads the structure a description states under its heading Structure, and target_question, the fixed question of a job whose target cannot hold that structure; 47 helper functions whose names begin with an underscore; one helper class _Calls; eighteen public constants, among them the two lists of concepts from which an initial search is built (LANGUAGE_TERMS and ECONOMIC_CONCEPTS), the conversation role's key, guides and named fields (CONVERSATION_ROLE, CONVERSATION_GUIDES and CONVERSATION_FIELDS) the fixed headings STRUCTURE_HEADING of the description and FILL_HEADING of a recipe's note, ROUND_TRIP_RULES, what the files of a target cannot state, and SOURCE_KIND_LABEL, the label under which the Model-prose-writer's message names the kind of the source material; twelve private compiled regular expressions, two of them the headings of a paper in Markdown and in LaTeX, the tuple _LATEX_LEVELS of LaTeX's sectioning commands by rank, the two tuples of patterns compiled from those lists and the sets _ANSWER_FIELDS and _SUBMIT_FIELDS of the fields of the conversation role's answer and of its submit_job. Its docstring states the rules it is written under: a Matsya handler receives the job frame and uses the bellman package, the comparator, the form check and the exception classes through it; a Matsya handler calls a language model only through the Matsya handler call; and the module imports only the standard library, plus, for normalize_source and select_pages, two of the four Matsya handlers whose parameter lists have no frame parameter, the package modules matsya_service.guide_pages and matsya_service.source. Nothing enforces the import rule: the loader only imports the module.

The program calls two Matsya handlers by name, normalize_source to turn the request's source into a Source record and cycle to run the job. The other eleven run only when cycle or another Matsya handler calls them. The turn runner calls conversation_reply by name for each turn (§7).

docs.title: 2 The thirteen Matsya handlers
docs.text:
Matsya handler and parameters What it does Role it calls cycle(frame, request) runs preparation and any distribution check, writes and elaborates the initial declaration once, then runs up to the cycle limit of iterations; each iteration writes prose from the preceding elaborated semantic object, reports the prose judge's findings, writes and elaborates one new declaration, and compares adjacent elaborated semantic objects; returns the record with status converged, not_converged or needs_input none directly prepare(frame, source, calls, limit, formulation, target) preparation, from the source material \(P\) to the description \(M\) (Bellman-SYM writer §1): binds the reading controller to the source preparer, makes the job's initial search from the concepts the source material names, the new concepts first for a job that continues an earlier job of its session, calls the source preparer, SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, with the job's target and the kind of the source material, paper or description, for up to limit ordinary answers and its requests within its request rounds, checks the JSON answer and, on a paper, its references, each a quotation that must stand in the section of the heading it names and that the record holds with the lines it stands on, runs the form check, which the source preparer's own text states with the heading Structure before the seven of the paper form, reads the structure under that heading (structure_of), returning a description whose structure it cannot read as a failure of its form, and has the judge compare the description with the source; returns ready with the description, needs_input with questions, or not_converged with a reason SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, BellmanStageProse_judge write(frame, description, calls, feedback, initial_refusal, references, formulation, target) writing, the map \(\Upsilon_0\) (Bellman-SYM writer): binds the reading controller to the Bellman-SYM writer, reusing preparation's passages for the initial declaration or searching from the prose of a later iteration; calls the writer with the target and structure for up to writer_rounds ordinary answers, parses and elaborates the files, and sends a refused file and the elaborator's refusal back for repair; returns the files, the elaborated semantic object or None, and the record of each round BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration verify_distribution(frame, description, variable, evidence, calls) asks whether the description specifies the law of a named random variable; returns specified, missing or unclear with quotations and one question, after checking that every quotation occurs in the description distribution_check prose_write(frame, outcome, calls) prose writing, the map \(\Upsilon_1\) (Prose writer): prints the dossier of the preceding elaborated stage or trellis, calls the prose writer with the stage-interface pages and the dossier, and retries a failed form check within prose_writer_rounds; returns the iteration's prose and its form findings even when the check still fails ElaboratedSemanticObject_to_BellmanStageProse judge(frame, source_text, description, form, calls, formulation, target) calls the judge with the two texts in both orders, making up to judge_rounds attempts for each order; during an iteration it compares the prepared prose with the new prose and applies the target's comparison rule; returns the two reports and whether they agree; the result is recorded but does not decide convergence BellmanStageProse_judge compare(frame, left, right) computes ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator: returns the comparator's profile of two elaborated stages or trellises by calling the job frame's compare; calls no language model none citations(files, description) reads each stage file block by block and returns, for every block, the sentences cited on # from: "..." lines and whether each occurs in the description once spacing is normalized none unresolved_note(files) true unless note.md says exactly none or none. in any letter case, the section ## Values left to $fill of a recipe's note set aside, so a missing note counts as unresolved none call(frame, role, parts, calls, instructions) puts the role's text, or instructions when a text is given in its place (every Matsya handler passes None), first under the label the instructions, passes the number of leading guide parts as the cached prefix, sends the message through the job frame's call, records a role_call_started event and then a completed, stopped, refused or failed event, appends the call's record to calls, and returns the answer text; a call the program refuses at a language-model token ceiling (What Matsya reads §4) raises CeilingReached and leaves no event after role_call_started the named role writer_references(frame, index, excluded) makes the initial search of an invocation through the reading controller, which it receives as index: the query the invocation was bound with, at most retrieval_passage_limit passages, which the controller restricts to the collections the job's principal may read, requiring no mark model_prompt, with the source clusters excluded; excluded may add clusters to that exclusion; returns an empty list without an index, with a limit of 0 or without a query none select_pages(guide, manifest_entry, selected) returns the chosen pages of one guide unaltered and in the guide's order; called by the module's helper _pages_of when a Matsya handler assembles a role's guide parts none normalize_source(source) turns the request's source into the frame's Source record none conversation_reply(frame, turn, calls), optional one turn of conversation mode (§7): searches once from the question, supplies the outputs of the job the conversation discusses, the session's selected job or else its latest current job, has the prose writer describe the dossier of a stage file the turn names, calls the conversation role through _requests within its request rounds, checks each answer's form, citations and decision list and sends a failed answer back within conversation_rounds; returns answered, needs_input or incomplete with its citations and decision list conversation_answer, ElaboratedSemanticObject_to_BellmanStageProse

Of the thirteen Matsya handlers, five, prepare, write, verify_distribution, prose_write and judge, call a role, each through the Matsya handler call, which sends the message; cycle calls the roles only through these five; and compare, citations, unresolved_note, writer_references, select_pages and normalize_source call none. The judge has two uses in a job: in preparation, to compare the prepared description with the source, and in each numbered iteration, to compare the prepared description \(M\) with that iteration's prose. The optional conversation_reply calls the conversation role through call and, for a stage file the turn names, the prose writer through prose_write.

docs.title: 3 The sequence inside cycle
docs.text:
cycle runs prepare first. It searches from the source material's concepts, writes the prepared model prose \(M\), and checks the prose against the source. A preparation with unresolved questions returns needs_input unless the request set force, in which case the source material is used as \(M\) and the questions and writer's assumptions are retained. The structure stated in \(M\) must fit the requested target; otherwise the job returns a question before writing files. When \(M\) names an income process only by a general distribution function, verify_distribution asks whether its law is specified. The initial write then writes \(D\) from \(M\) and elaborates \(D\) to \(E\). A supplied starting_declaration takes the place of this initial writer call; if the elaborator refuses it, the refusal is passed to write for repair. The initial writing is recorded separately, as initial_writing, at cycle 0.

For each numbered iteration, prose_write reads the dossier of the preceding elaborated semantic object and produces new prose. The judge compares that prose with the prepared \(M\) for a diagnostic report. write then writes one new declaration from the new prose and elaborates it. compare checks this elaborated semantic object against the preceding one. Thus iteration 1 is \(E \to M' \to D' \to E'\) and compares \(E\) with \(E'\). If they differ, iteration 2 is \(E' \to M'' \to D'' \to E''\) and compares \(E'\) with \(E''\). It does not repeat write(M) or produce an extra \(E'''\) in iteration 2. A successful comparison ends the job converged with the reason semantic_fixed_point; otherwise the next iteration begins from the latest \(E\), up to the cycle limit. citations checks the declaration's quotations against the prose from which that declaration was written, and unresolved_note checks its writer's note. Those results and both prose judges' reports remain available for review; none decides convergence.

A writing whose last answer requests material after its allowed request rounds ends not_converged with request_rounds_exhausted. If an iteration cannot produce an elaborated semantic object, it records no comparison for that iteration; the latest successful writing remains available. A call refused at a language-model token ceiling ends not_converged with token_ceiling_reached, retaining the calls and writings recorded so far. A cancellation stops before the next language-model call, after any call already sent finishes.

Inside prepare and write, every call to a role goes through _requests. Each message holds the cached prefix (the instruction text and the guide pages the settings name), then the reading controller's parts (the retrieved passages, the addresses the role may request with its remaining allowances, and the material its requests added with their outcomes, each item once), then the task's input, the formulation, the job's target and, for the writer, the structure the description states, and any correction feedback, which stand in every message of the invocation. _requests examines each answer for the request form before the role's own parsers; a request is answered by the controller, which consumes a request round and no ordinary round, and the role is called again with the result; the first ordinary answer goes to the role's parsers and consumes one of preparer_rounds or writer_rounds. When the role answers with a request and no request round, or no ordinary round, remains, the controller executes nothing and _requests returns None, which ends the invocation with request_rounds_exhausted.

The writer returns the files of the job's target and no other, which the job frame's elaborate_files(files, target) checks: for a stage, one stage file <key>.bl and the note note.md, elaborated as one text; for a period, the stage files and period.yml, elaborated as a trellis of that period repeated twice and then held, printed and compared as its one period; for a trellis, the stage files, a period file for each period template, period.yml or period.<name>.yml, and trellis.yml, elaborated as a trellis; and for a recipe, the files of a trellis, the recipe spec.yml, a methods file stages/<key>/methods.yml for each stage the description says how to solve, calibration/<model>.yml and settings/<model>.yml, written into a temporary folder in the model folder's layout and read by the Bellman factory's load_recipe with no fill, then elaborated and bound by specify_trellis with the kinds of binding the recipe holds, so that a calibration whose slot $fill stands unbound, or a stage without a methods file, is checked for what it holds. A recipe is held, printed and compared as the trellis of its elaborated stages, since its methods, calibration and settings are read from files and not written back into prose. A converged job's artifacts place each stage file under declaration/stages/<key>/ and every other file but the note under declaration/ at the path its name writes, which puts a recipe's methods files in their stages' folders.

The initial_writing record holds the first declaration's rounds, files, citations and digest. Each numbered cycle holds its prose writing, judging, one declaration writing, comparison, citation check and writer's-note check. The job runner reports preparation, writing, prose_writing and judging; initial writing uses cycle 0. Every language-model call is recorded with its role, message digest and length, answer digest, token counts and any provider failure. The job runner's progress callback raises JobCancelled before the next call when cancellation was requested, so a call already sent finishes and no further one starts. The processor records under reading the identities of the guide pages and index passages each call received, the searches it made and the outcome of requests; the record holds no message text.

The job store keeps this record whole, and GET /v1/model-iterations/{job_id} returns one of two views. The default products view holds the schema, target, structure, status, reason, prepared prose (description), questions, paper checks and cycles_run, the count of numbered iterations. available_writing holds the latest nonempty parsed files, their cycle number (0 for the initial declaration), and the prose from which they were written; last_cycle holds the final numbered iteration's files, judging and adjacent comparison, which may be absent if that iteration stopped early. last_completed_comparison identifies the latest pair actually compared by left and right cycle numbers, even when the final iteration stopped before comparison. reading is reduced to index and guide digests, and usage to calls and tokens charged. The full view, view=full, holds initial_writing and all numbered cycles for examination or training. products_view in processor.py derives the default view from that record.

For a period, trellis or recipe, the elaboration bridge reads Bellman's selected connections once from the stage occurrences already constructed. The dossier names the resolved stage and field at each selected connection, including connections between periods. Its digest records the ordered stage occurrences, those connections and the effective parameter values in each period. The deterministic comparison checks the connections and effective values under one matching of the stage occurrences and their names. A connection or route that Bellman cannot certify, including a backward value type that does not match, is returned as a refusal before the two declarations can compare equal. A complete recipe uses the trellis returned after its requested bindings have been applied. If $fill still leaves a parameter without a value in a period, the digest and dossier distinguish known source values from bound values and name the unresolved period. Matching partial recipes can compare equal as declarations; the missing value remains unbound.

docs.title: 4 The job frame a Matsya handler receives
docs.text:
The job frame is one record, the dataclass Frame of frame.py, built by the processor for each job; the word frame alone names the package. A Matsya handler uses the bellman package and the meaning-map-training package only through the job frame and imports neither.

Attribute What it is texts the seven instruction texts by role key, and the conversation role's when the configuration enables it guides, guide_manifest the three guides by short name (writer, reader, calculus) and their entries of the page manifest: the ordered pages and, for a manifest of the form matsya-guides/3, each saved page's sections, authored links and tag memberships settings the checked settings, with roles as RoleSettings records and ceilings, the language-model token ceilings, as a Ceilings record call(role, parts, prefix) the function that sends a message to the provider: the ordered parts of one message and the number of leading parts marked for the prompt cache; returns the answer with its token counts. It is the method call of the fixed caller ProviderCaller of roles.py, which counts the message's tokens first, refuses a message that would not fit the language model's context window with PromptTooLong and a call that would pass a token ceiling with CeilingReached, and charges every attempt to the job's token ledger record, progress the job's record, begun by the processor, and the job runner's progress callback index, source, references, earlier the reading controller ReadingController of retrieval/context.py, which the processor builds over the snapshot of the retrieval index the job holds and which is a Matsya handler's only access to the index and to the guides' records: bind binds it to the role of an invocation of prepare or write, search makes the invocation's initial search, reuse places passages an earlier invocation retrieved, request_of and resolve examine an answer for the request form and answer a request through the snapshot's related and read (The retrieval index §9) or the guides' records, parts gives the parts it writes into the next message, and called, ordinary and end record the calls, the ordinary answers and why the invocation stopped (What Matsya reads §5); the job's Source record; the passages of preparation's initial search; and earlier, the job of the same session that this job continues, with its identity, status, source digest, description, questions, formulation and concepts, or None join_parts, sha256 the joining of a message's parts under ===== <label> ===== lines, and the digest function elaborate_text, elaborate_trellis, period_joins, dossier_lines the four functions of the bellman package that the frame calls: the elaboration of one text and of a trellis, the joins of a period, and the dossier printer elaborate_files, dossier_of, parse_writer_files, digest_of, profile_equal, allowed_declaration_name, form_check (check_reader_form in the module), compare (compare_outcomes in the module) the functions of meaning.py: parse a Bellman-SYM writer's answer into files, elaborate them (elaborate_files, which computes the Bellman-SYM elaborator BellmanSYMDeclaration_to_ElaboratedSemanticObject), print the dossier with the stage names hidden, compare two elaborations with the comparator of packages/meaning-map-training (compare, which computes ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator), check a description's form targets the four targets of a job, stage, period, trellis and recipe, in the order in which each holds the one before it (TARGETS of meaning.py), which the Matsya handler cycle reads to decide whether the job's target holds the level of the structure the description states errors the exception classes a Matsya handler raises or catches: ModelAnswerError, MeaningRefusal, IncompleteResponse, PromptTooLong, ProviderError, ProviderRefusal, ProviderRejected, and the set STOP_REASONS

For a turn of conversation mode the turn runner fills the same record: index is the reading controller bound to the turn (§7), source is None, record holds the turn's identifiers, and call is the fixed caller's, wrapped so that the turn runner records each call and its events itself; the call list a Matsya handler receives for a turn is its own and no record reads it.

A Matsya handler raises ModelAnswerError when a language model's answer lacks the required structure or evidence, with one of the 27 validation codes the program fixes, such as json_decode, judge_quotes or writer_input_quote; the job runner records such an error as invalid_model_response.

docs.title: 5 How the program loads and checks the module
docs.text: configuration.load runs its checks in a fixed order and stops at the first failure: the files against manifest.json; the three guides against their page manifest, the page markers and, for a manifest of the form matsya-guides/3, each page's saved digest, its sections' spans and the targets of its available links; settings.json; the import of the Matsya handler module under the module name matsya_configuration_handlers; and the thirteen signatures, with conversation_reply when the settings name the conversation role, each name present and callable with exactly the slot's parameter names in the slot's order, read with inspect.signature. Type annotations, default values and return types are not compared, and no other function is checked, so helpers may be added, renamed or removed freely, and a configuration that does not name the conversation role may hold a function named conversation_reply, which is then not checked. Before the signatures the loader reads the conversation role's parts together, after the settings' types and before the readers of roles, ceilings and reading: the role's reading entry, its entry in ceilings.roles, ceilings.turn, conversation_rounds and conversation_pages, then the text texts/conversation-answer.md; a part missing with the role, or present without it, refuses the folder naming that part. A failed check raises ConfigurationRefused, whose detail names the file or the Matsya handler: when a check fails at the start of a job, the job fails with the code configuration_refused and no language model is called; when it fails before the server starts, matsya-serve refuses to start. The folder is checked on three occasions on a server: by matsya-serve before the server starts, by the application's start-up, and at the start of every job, so an edit to the folder takes effect at the next job. Two commands act on the folder: python -m matsya_service.configuration manifest <folder> --version <version> rewrites manifest.json from the files present, and python -m matsya_service.configuration check <folder> loads the folder as a job would and prints its version and digest, then a line that names the form of the guides' page manifest and says whether its relationship records were checked, or configuration_refused with the detail.

docs.title: 6 Changing a Matsya handler, adding a helper, adding a slot
docs.text:
To change what a Matsya handler does while keeping its name and parameter names, edit the module, rewrite the manifest with the manifest command, and run the check command. The package's tests do not load the configuration folder that the service uses: they copy a second configuration kept for the tests under packages/matsya/tests/fixtures/configuration/, whose Matsya handler module and eight texts, the conversation role's among them, are byte-identical with the service's folder on 9 October 2026, so a change to the service's module is tested only when the same change is made to the test copy. The test copy's guides are written by the guide builder from the small documentation tree of packages/matsya/tests/fixtures/documentation/, which holds a stand-in for each core page and the pages that test the links and tags, under that tree's own construction policy.

Adding a helper needs only that it be written in the module and called from one of the thirteen Matsya handlers, since the program neither calls nor checks it.

Adding a slot, renaming one, changing a slot’s parameter names, adding a role or adding a setting changes the program. Each requires coordinated changes to the program and configuration. An optional slot, such as conversation_reply, stands in OPTIONAL_SLOTS with the role that requires it in ROLE_SLOTS, an optional role in OPTIONAL_ROLES of roles.py and its settings in OPTIONAL_SETTINGS, and the loader checks them only in a configuration that names the role. A new slot needs its entry with ordered parameter names in SLOTS of configuration.py, a call to it from the program or from another Matsya handler, the function in every configuration's module including the test copy, rewritten manifests, and a corresponding row in the handler table in §2. A new role needs its key in ROLES of roles.py, a text texts/<role key with hyphens for underscores>.md, an entry in the roles object of settings.json, and a Matsya handler that calls call(frame, "<role key>", parts, calls, None). A new setting needs its key and type in SETTINGS of configuration.py, the key in settings.json, and a Matsya handler that reads frame.settings["<key>"], because the loader refuses a key present in only one of the two.

A trained candidate is a new configuration folder with its own manifest and version, and a candidate whose Matsya handler module differs from its parent's is recorded as a commit together with the run that accepted it.

docs.title: 7 One turn of conversation mode
docs.text:
A configuration that enables the conversation role, conversation_answer, answers a question asked in a session in a turn, which the route POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns appends to the session as an entry of the user and records as queued. The turn runner, TurnRunner of conversation.py, which the program holds and a training pass does not change, then loads the configuration, fixes the turn's snapshot of the index, builds the turn's language-model token ledger, binds the reading controller (What Matsya reads §8), reads again the passages the previous turn cited, elaborates a stage file the request names, and calls conversation_reply(frame, turn, calls). turn is the record Turn of conversation.py: the turn's identifier and session, the question and its entry number, the named fields, the elaborated stage file or its refusal, never the file's text, the session's entries up to the question, the previous turn's decision list, the retained passages and the snapshot's digest.

The starting conversation_reply places the guide pages conversation_pages names, which the controller reports as frame.index.pages, after the instruction text as the cached prefix; makes one search from the question through frame.index.search; has the controller supply, with frame.index.supply_job, the outputs of the job the conversation discusses, which the turn runner names: the session's selected job or else its latest job that holds a record and was current at its end, never a job that was not current unless the selection names it; the label of each output of a job that was not current states the version of the session's text the job was built from and the version the text is at now, the turn's result names the job under job, and the job's stage files are never supplied this way; and, for a stage file that elaborated, calls prose_write on the elaborated semantic object, so that the role receives the dossier and the prose writer's description of it. It then calls the role through _requests, as prepare and write call theirs, so that every answer is examined for the request form before any other parser and a request is resolved by the controller within the role's request rounds. An ordinary answer is read as one JSON object with _json_answer and checked: its status and fields, each citation with frame.index.check_citation, the check the turn runner makes again, and the form of each item of the decision list. A failed answer is sent back with your previous answer and the faults of your previous answer until conversation_rounds answers have been given. The Matsya handler returns answered with the answer, and with submit_job when the role starts a job at the user's request, checked against cycle_maximum, or needs_input with the role's questions, each with its citations and decision list, or incomplete with request_rounds_exhausted or conversation_rounds_exhausted, no citation and the previous decision list, and records why the invocation stopped with frame.index.end.

The turn runner checks the return: a return of another form ends the turn failed with processing_failed; a citation of material not supplied in the turn, or with a quote absent from it, ends the turn incomplete with unsupported_citation; an incomplete status must agree with the turn's record of allowances, ceilings and calls; and a call refused at a ceiling, or one the provider could not complete, ends the turn incomplete whatever conversation_reply returns or raises. It decides whether the turn is current, appends the answer, or the questions, as entries whose origin is the turn and which reply to the question, and stores the record. The turn's states, statuses, reasons, fixed sentences and record are the program's, so that a Matsya handler can change what the role reads and how its answers are repaired, but not the permissions, the snapshot, the limits or the acceptance of an answer.

docs.title: Updating Matsya configurations
docs.text:
Summary

This page describes how a Matsya configuration is prepared on a developer's computer, published to the service, selected for a job or a question, compared with another on the same source and made the default. The service keeps every published configuration unchanged under its ID, pins the ID to each job and turn when it accepts the request, and changes its default without a restart. A request without an ID uses the service's current default.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Matsya developer guide §1, which identifies the program and the contents of a configuration. See also — What Matsya reads, for the instruction texts, settings and saved guides; The command reference §9 and Reaching the service by HTTP §8, the commands and routes of publication and selection.

docs.title: 1 What is selected
docs.text:
A configuration is a checked folder containing the instruction texts, settings, Matsya handlers, saved guides and manifest.json described in the developer guide §1. Its version is the human-readable value in the manifest. Its configuration ID is the SHA-256 digest of that manifest: a value that identifies the exact list of files and their digests. A published configuration is retained without modification, so an ID continues to name the same contents; a changed file produces a different ID.

The default configuration is the published ID the service selects when a request names no ID. A configuration ID is a selector, not a credential. A Matsya token authorizes a person's access to the service; the client must supply one whether or not a request names a configuration ID. Publishing configurations and changing the default require a separate administrator permission: the service reads a service-owned JSON file, named by MATSYA_CONFIG_ADMIN_GRANTS_FILE, with exactly one principal_ids array of the principal IDs allowed to do both, and reads it again at every such request, so that the operator grants or revokes the permission by replacing the file. An absent or invalid file grants the permission to no one.

The service keeps the published folders under MATSYA_CONFIGURATIONS_ROOT, each under its ID, and the register of selectable IDs, the default and the publication and default-change events in its job database. At a start whose register holds no default, the service installs the folder MATSYA_CONFIGURATION names under its ID and makes it the first default; at every start it moves an unlisted folder under the root aside and refuses to start without a registered, checked default. The retrieval index is a separate service input. Publishing a configuration does not rebuild or transfer it, and changing documents in a repository does not update the index or the saved guides already inside a published configuration.

docs.title: 2 Prepare and publish a candidate
docs.text:
1. Start from a complete configuration folder. Change the chosen instruction texts, settings or Matsya handlers, assign a new version, regenerate its manifest and check every listed file. Keep a checked local copy named by the manifest's digest and a separate revision record naming its parent, added/changed/removed paths, reason and source-code commit. The register stays outside the checked folder: adding a record inside it would itself change the folder's ID. A candidate remains unchanged after publication.
  2. An administrator publishes that folder with bellman-matsya configuration publish <folder>, or publish_configuration(folder) of the Python module. The client sends the folder's files, by their paths relative to the folder, as a ZIP archive to POST /v1/configurations. The service refuses a request from a principal the grant file does not name before it reads the archive; checks the archive's entries, refusing an absolute name, a . or .. component, a backslash, a duplicate name, a file and a directory of one name, a link, any other non-regular entry, and a body or contents beyond 24 MiB; extracts the files into a staging folder under the root; checks every file against the manifest; imports matsya_handler.py and checks the whole configuration as a job would; checks the files again after the import; and then moves the folder under its ID and registers it with a publication event. A new ID answers 201 and an ID already published 200, each with the ID and the version. A refused archive installs nothing and leaves no selectable ID. Publishing the same contents again returns the same ID; it cannot replace the contents of an existing ID.
  3. Keep the returned ID with the local revision record. Publication makes the candidate available for selection but does not make it the default, alter another user's job or update the retrieval index.

The administrator permission matters because a configuration includes matsya_handler.py, Python code that the service executes. A normal Matsya token is not sufficient to publish it; any Matsya token may select a published ID.

docs.title: 3 Select a configuration for work
docs.text:
A job request accepts an optional configuration_id. The client exposes it as --configuration-id <id> on bellman-matsya job submit and bellman-matsya project submit, and as the argument configuration_id of submit_job, start_job and project.submit. The same option is available on bellman-matsya ask and the Python ask for a conversation turn. When the ID is absent, the service uses its default; a user does not need a configuration ID for ordinary work. A malformed ID is refused with 422 and an unpublished one with 404, without creating work.

At submission, the service resolves the selected or default ID and stores it with the job in the transaction that accepts the request, before the job is queued, so that a concurrent change of the default and a submission take one definite order; a job that later fails or is cancelled keeps the ID. The worker reads the stored ID and loads that exact retained folder, verifying its manifest, even if the default changes while the job waits; it never takes the folder from the request or the then-current default, and a damaged folder fails the job with configuration_refused rather than falling back. The request's cycle limit is checked against the selected folder's settings. Job status and results return the resolved ID, so a locally saved record identifies what ran; the record's versions.configuration.manifest_sha256 equals it. A conversation turn likewise selects a configuration, which must enable the conversation role, else the question is refused with 422 and nothing is appended; a job the turn starts inherits its ID. If a job asks for more input, the continued attempt begun by the user's reply inherits that job's ID. A repeated delivery_id with the same question and selector returns the first turn and its ID even after the default has changed; a repeated delivery_id with another question or selector is refused with 409. Search requests still use the retrieval index and need no configuration selector.

docs.title: 4 Save and compare results
docs.text:
Run each candidate on the same directly submitted source text, target and other fixed inputs. A queued job built from a session can read entries added after submission, so a session revision does not fix its source for a controlled comparison. Each job's status carries three digests beside its configuration ID: request_sha256, the digest of the accepted request without the configuration ID, fixed at acceptance; source_sha256, the digest of the source text the job reads, fixed at acceptance for a directly supplied source and when the job starts for a session's text, a description stripped of surrounding whitespace and a paper unchanged; and index_digest, the digest of the retrieval index the job selected when it began. Each is null until fixed. Hold access grants, the index, saved guides, package code, comparator and token ceilings fixed across candidates; changing any of those requires a new comparison of both candidates under the new common inputs. Record a changed provider model in a candidate's settings explicitly.

bellman-matsya job export <job> <folder> [--overwrite], or export_job(job, folder, overwrite=...), saves the full job response as job.json, including its configuration ID and any status or error when no model files were produced. It refuses to replace an existing file unless --overwrite is given; --json prints the full response while saving it. The existing bellman-matsya job files <job> <folder> --all-iterates command saves available model files and the iteration record when a result exists. For a controlled pair of jobs, submit the same source text directly (--no-session in the CLI), target and source-cluster exclusions to each configuration; a session may change before a queued job begins. Organize exported records by source case and configuration ID.

The paired check reads two exported job.json files, their local configuration snapshots and the source as it was submitted, and sends no request:

meaning-map-config-pair records/case-1/<id A>/trial-1/job.json records/case-1/<id B>/trial-1/job.json \
  snapshots/<id A> snapshots/<id B> \
  --source-file case-1.md --source-kind description --output records/case-1/pair.json

The Python function is meaning_map_training.configuration_pair.compare_exports(left_job, right_job, left_snapshot, right_snapshot, source_kind, submitted_text). The record it writes has the schema matsya-configuration-pair/1, the two jobs' identifiers, states, errors, configuration IDs, request, source and index digests, whether each holds a full result and each result's status, and its comparison_state: comparable when both full results exist, their request, source and index digests are present and agree, each result's configuration files match its snapshot, and the two results agree on the index, the guides, the grants, the package versions, the comparator, the model key and the source cluster, and the two snapshots' ceilings are equal; refused, with the fields named, on a present mismatch, a wrong snapshot or a missing required field, even when the other job has no full result; and otherwise status_only, when either full result is absent or a job's provenance is unverified, retaining both outcomes and making no semantic claim. The command exits 0, 1 or 2 for the three states and writes pair.json in every case. A changed provider model between the two snapshots is reported, not refused. comparable means that the inputs were suitable for assessment, not that one candidate is better. Agreement of two adjacent elaborated semantic objects within one job answers whether that iteration converged; it does not by itself show that one configuration is better than another.

Collecting job records through the client and checking a pair are possible with this code. The development, held-out and control measures require a separate training-specification revision; a single architect job does not supply every trial needed for acceptance.

docs.title: 5 Make an accepted candidate the default
docs.text: After the candidate meets the project's acceptance rule, an administrator selects its published ID as the new default with bellman-matsya configuration set-default <id>, or set_default_configuration(id), backed by PUT /v1/configurations/default, and records the choice with the installation. The service accepts only a published, checked ID, changes the default and writes its event, with the former and the new ID, in one database transaction, and answers with the former ID, the new ID and its version. The change is effective for the next request without a restart. This selection is separate from publication and from any individual job request. Jobs already submitted keep the ID resolved for them; subsequent requests without an ID use the new default, and GET /v1/index names the current default's ID and version.

docs.title: Matsya in three parts
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya turns an economist's description of a dynamic model, or a paper, into a declaration in Bellman-SYM, the project's language for staged Bellman problems, checks the declaration, and answers questions about models and about the language. It has three parts, and this page says what each does and what it does not do: matsya-client, the command you run on your own machine, a program with no language model in it; matsya-architect, the service's job side, which builds and checks a declaration in one run; and matsya-master, the service's conversation side, which answers one question at a time. It then defines the words that the parts share, session, job, turn, version, label and target, and shows how a piece of work moves between the parts.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Matsya, the entry page, which says what Matsya does and for whom and maps the pages of its documentation. Continued by — The roles and the work of a job, which names the language-model roles that do the work of a job and of a turn and says which command answers which request. For an assistant — For an assistant using Matsya, the page that an assistant running the client's commands for you reads first: the files the client keeps, the commands of a project folder in their order, and the form of every answer. Explained for developers in — the Matsya developer guide, which describes the program, the configuration, the retrieval index and the Matsya handlers. See also — the wiki pages Matsya collection, Matsya handler and Matsya instructions; Stages in the language guide, for the stage files a job writes.

Note

The service and the client are updated separately. Some installed services still stop on a prose-judge disagreement and do not retain unfinished writings. Those behaviors require a service update; installing this client alone does not change them. The job behavior described below applies after that service update.

docs.title: 1 The three parts
docs.text:
matsya-client is the command bellman-matsya and the Python module bellman_matsya, installed on your machine from the package bellman-matsya-client. It is a program: it holds no language model and makes no decision about economics. It sends your requests to the service with your Matsya token, the password-less identifier, msy_ followed by 32 hexadecimal characters, that the service's administrator gives you and that the service checks on every request; it waits for a job and prints its progress; it writes the files a job produced into a folder in the layout the project's applications use; and it composes the job's report from the job's record (§2). Everything it prints or writes is either the service's answer or a fixed sentence. The Matsya token is required for every request. Anthropic, the provider of the service's language models, charges each language-model call of a job or a question to the account that an Anthropic API key identifies. By default that key is the service key, the service's own Anthropic API key, which stays on the server. A registered holder of a Matsya token may also give the client a personal Anthropic key, an Anthropic API key of their own, so that the language-model calls of the jobs and questions they start are charged to their own Anthropic account; the personal key is an optional addition to the Matsya token, never a substitute for it, and is added only after the Matsya token has been configured (Working with Matsya from the command line §1.1).

matsya-architect is the job side of the service. One job begins with preparation, done once: from the source material, the text of a session or a file submitted on its own, the Model-prose-writer restates the model in prose; the prose-source-judge compares that prose with its source and records any disagreement for the user to assess. Prose-to-Bellman-Sym then writes the initial declaration, and the elaborator checks its stage files. Each subsequent iteration reads the latest elaborated semantic object back into prose, writes one new declaration from that prose, elaborates it, and compares it with the preceding elaborated semantic object. The job ends converged when those adjacent elaborated semantic objects are equivalent. The judges' reports, block quotations and writer's note remain available for the user to assess; none decides convergence. If the comparison differs, another iteration may run within the allowed limit. A job also ends earlier when its stage files cannot be repaired, or when a limit on reading or language-model text is reached. A question the job cannot settle ends it; your reply starts a new job. The question reaches the session only when the job has a session and you added no entry while it ran, including a question to matsya-master; otherwise it remains in the job's record, and you start the next attempt by submitting again. A job runs on the server for minutes and is charged by its language-model tokens, the pieces of text that the provider counts in every message and answer.

matsya-master is the conversation side of the service. It answers one question at a time, asked in a session, from four things: the passages of the retrieval index that your Matsya token may read, the project's documentation and the literature among them; the session's text; the outputs of the session's jobs; and, when the question names a stage file of your own, what the elaborator, the program that checks stage files, makes of it. Its answers quote their sources and cite them. It writes no stage file itself. When you ask it to build, it submits a job to matsya-architect from the session, and tells you so by the job's label.

Part Where it runs What it does What it does not do matsya-client your machine sends requests, waits, writes the folder, composes the report nothing with a language model matsya-architect the server builds and checks a declaration in one run of cycles talk to you while it runs matsya-master the server answers one question in a session; submits a job when asked write a stage file; cancel or select a job

You may type the commands of matsya-client yourself, or have an assistant, such as Claude Code, read these pages, run the commands on your machine and read what they print. The assistant's program runs locally; the language model it calls may run elsewhere. The assistant is not part of Matsya and sends the same requests through the same commands.

Both sides of the service read the retrieval index, the store of passages, short pieces of the indexed files, each with its place in its file, from which a search returns those that best match a query. The indexed files are this project's documentation and stage files, the source code and documentation of HARK, the paper Theoretical Foundations of Buffer Stock Saving, a literature on dynamic programming and journal articles; a request reads only the parts that the service's administrator has granted to the holder of its Matsya token (Collections and weights §§1–2). Each version of the index is named by its digest, a 64-character code computed from the index's contents, which changes whenever the index is rebuilt.

docs.title: 2 Sessions, jobs and turns
docs.text:
A session is the kept, numbered text of one model: the description you write, a paper you attach, the questions you ask matsya-master, the questions Matsya puts to you and your replies, and the answers of matsya-master, of which only those you accept belong to the text a job reads. Each of these is an entry of the session, numbered in the order the entries arrive, and the version of the text is the number of the last entry you wrote or accepted; an entry Matsya writes does not change the version. A session is neither a job nor a conversation: both sides use it. A session may hold nothing but questions and answers, or it may prepare and hold several jobs.

A job is one run of matsya-architect, from one version of the text, and it names its target, the level of the declaration it is to return: a stage, one decision problem, written as one stage file; a period, the stages of one model period and the connections between them, written as the stage files and the period file period.yml; a trellis, the model's periods in time up to the terminal period, written as the stage files, the period files and the trellis file trellis.yml; or a recipe, the files of a trellis with a methods file for each stage whose solution method the source states, the calibration and settings files and the recipe file spec.yml, which Bellman Workbench loads and solves. The model prose states the model's structure, its stages, its periods and how the periods repeat; a target that holds that structure is admitted, a wider one included, and a narrower one ends the job with one question before any stage file is written (The roles and the work of a job §1). The wiki pages stage, period, trellis and specification factory define the four objects in the language.

Within its session a job has a number, its rank among the session's jobs, and a label that names the model, the target, the version of the text the job read, its number and its state, for instance "Household with firms · trellis · version 2 · job 7 · running". A job that was still running when you wrote an entry, a question to matsya-master included, is marked text changed since while it runs and built from an earlier version once it has ended converged, not converged or with questions; its questions are not added to the session (§1), and matsya-master discusses it only when you select it (§3). Several jobs may belong to one session; each keeps its own record, and submitting again never overwrites an earlier job.

A turn is one question answered by matsya-master in a session: the question, the passages read, the answer with its citations, and the record of what was read. A turn makes a few calls of a language model, where a job makes several in preparation, initial writing and its iterations, so a turn usually takes less time and costs less than a job.

Once a job has run, the service keeps its record: the initial declaration, what each numbered iteration produced and found, and an account of every call it made; a job that failed, that a restart of the service interrupted, or that was cancelled before it started holds none. What the service returns by default is the available declaration files and the prose from which they were written, even when a later iteration produced no files or the job ended not_converged; the questions, when it stopped for input; the prose judges' findings; the latest completed comparison of adjacent elaborated semantic objects and whether a later iteration stopped before comparison; and the language-model tokens charged. Files from a not_converged job are proposals for review; the status and reason remain with them. The full record, including each iteration's prose and files, is returned when requested for examination or training.

docs.title: 3 How a piece of work moves between the parts
docs.text:
You write the model's description in a Markdown file and submit it. matsya-client creates a session named after the file, appends the text to it, and asks the server to start a job from that session. matsya-architect runs the job; matsya-client, asked to wait with bellman-matsya job wait, prints each step and cycle, and, asked with bellman-matsya job files once the job has ended, writes the stage files, the model prose and the report into a folder.

If the job ends with a question, the question is an entry of the session. You reply with a file, naming the question's entry; the first reply starts the next job, which reads the text with your reply in it. The question's entry names the job that asked it, and the command that adds the reply prints the job it started.

You ask about the result in the same session: what the declaration assumes, how a constraint is written, why a judge disagreed. matsya-master answers each question from the index, the session's text and the job's outputs, and names the job it read. The job it reads is the session's selected job, the job of the session that you chose with bellman-matsya session select; when none is selected, it reads the latest job of the session that holds a record, was not cancelled and ran while you added no entry to the session. If you say "submit this as a job", matsya-master starts one from the session's text as it then stands, your request included, and its answer gives the job's label; matsya-client can stay attached to that job until it ends and then write the folder.

Nothing passes between matsya-architect and matsya-master except through the session's written record and the jobs' stored results. Neither reads the other's working memory, and the client reads only what the server returns.

docs.title: For an assistant using Matsya
docs.text:
Summary

This page is for an assistant, such as Claude Code, that runs bellman-matsya on your machine for you (Matsya in three parts §1). The assistant's program runs locally; the language model it calls may run elsewhere. This is the first page the assistant reads. It names Matsya's three parts; lists the files the client keeps on your machine, with the sessions and jobs kept on the service; gives the commands of a project folder in order; and states the form of their answers and refusals. Each section names the page that explains its subject in full, and The command reference gives the exact form of every command.

Relationship with other documents

Continued by — Matsya in three parts and The roles and the work of a job, which define the words this page uses; then the pages of the four groups, in the order in which the entry page Matsya maps them. See also — The command reference, every command with its options, printed lines, exit statuses and JSON fields; Working on a project folder, the work of §4 followed through one project with what each command prints. Explained for developers in — the Matsya developer guide, which says what each role of the service is given and what it returns.

docs.title: 1 What Matsya is
docs.text: Matsya is a service of Project Bellman. From an economist's description of a dynamic model, written in prose and displayed equations, or from the text of a paper, it writes the model's declaration in Bellman-SYM, the project's language for staged Bellman problems, checks the declaration, and reports where the declaration and the source disagree; when the source leaves something necessary unsaid, it ends its work with a question for the user. It also answers questions about a model, about its declaration, about the language and about the literature on dynamic programming, and every answer quotes and cites the passages it rests on. The user owns the model and its description: Matsya proposes files, and the user decides whether to keep them.

docs.title: 2 The three parts
docs.text:
Matsya has three parts, which Matsya in three parts §1 defines:

  • matsya-client is the command bellman-matsya and its Python module, installed on the user's machine from the package bellman-matsya-client. It holds no language model; it sends the user's requests to the service with the user's Matsya token and prints or writes what the service answers. It is the part you run.
  • matsya-architect runs jobs on the server. A job is one attempt to write and check the files of a model at a target, from the text of a session or from a file; it takes minutes, it is charged by its language-model tokens, and it asks nothing while it runs. A question it cannot settle ends the job, and the user's reply to the question starts the next job.
  • matsya-master answers one question at a time in a session, the kept and numbered text of one model, in a turn that takes about a minute and costs far less than a job. It writes no stage file; when the user asks it to build, it starts a job from the session.

The words session, job, turn, version, label and target are defined in Matsya in three parts §2, and the roles that do the work of a job in The roles and the work of a job §1. That page's §3 says which command answers which kind of request, and the two rules an assistant follows: start a job only when the user asks for a build, and answer a job's questions in the session.

docs.title: 3 Where the client keeps its files
docs.text:
The client keeps three kinds of file on the user's machine.

  1. The configuration file ~/.config/bellman-matsya/config.toml, in the user's home folder, which bellman-matsya configure writes as a private file. It holds the user's Matsya token and may hold a custom service address. The client otherwise uses the built-in address http://45.55.225.169:8710. The environment variables BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN and BELLMAN_MATSYA_SERVER, when set, override the saved token and service address. bellman-matsya alone says whether a Matsya token is saved, and no command prints the Matsya token. When none is saved, the user runs bellman-matsya configure, which, run without an option, asks only for the Matsya token; Working with Matsya from the command line §1 describes the installation and the set-up. Beside that file the client may keep a second private file, ~/.config/bellman-matsya/anthropic-key, which only the user can read and which holds the user's personal Anthropic key, the user's own Anthropic API key, under which the language-model calls of the jobs and questions the user starts are charged to the user's Anthropic account in place of the service's account (Matsya in three parts §1). The key is optional and is added only after the Matsya token: bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key asks for the key without showing it and saves it, and on a machine where no Matsya token is configured it asks for nothing and saves nothing; bellman-matsya configure --clear-anthropic-key deletes the file, after which new jobs and questions use the service's key, unless BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY is set and not empty. A nonempty environment variable BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY supplies a key without saving it, and the client uses it in place of the saved key. bellman-matsya alone prints, after its line on the Matsya token, one line that says which key the next job, question or reply will use, the user's or the service's, and never prints the key itself. The key is the user's to enter, in the user's own terminal: an assistant never asks for the key, never receives it in chat and never types it, whether at the prompt of configure, in a command or in the environment variable.
  2. In a project folder (§4), the folder .bellman-matsya/, which bellman-matsya project init writes. .bellman-matsya/project.json holds the identifier of the folder's session, the service's address and the digest of economics.md as the session last received it, a code computed from the file's bytes by which bellman-matsya project submit tells whether the file has changed. .bellman-matsya/README.md is a short note for a model that opens the folder: that the folder is a Matsya project, its session's identifier and the service's address, the files the client keeps and writes there, and the commands used most. A later bellman-matsya project pull --replace can write an open writer's note to .bellman-matsya/writer-note.md. Beside .bellman-matsya/, bellman-matsya project init creates the folder's AGENTS.md, with a paragraph that names the note and bellman-matsya docs, when the folder has none; when the folder has one, the command prints the paragraph for the user to add.
  3. The outputs of jobs: the files bellman-matsya project pull writes into the project folder or into a sub-folder of it, and the model folders bellman-matsya job files writes into a folder the user names.

Everything else is kept on the server: the sessions with their entries, the jobs with their labels and records, the questions of the jobs and the user's replies, and the turns with their answers. The client keeps no copy of them and reads them from the server each time they are asked for, with bellman-matsya project status in a project folder or bellman-matsya session show <session> anywhere; in a project folder, bellman-matsya alone also prints the folder's session, the label of its latest job and any question awaiting a reply. The pages of this guide are installed with the client, in the folder that bellman-matsya docs --path prints.

docs.title: 4 The work of a project folder
docs.text:
A project folder is a folder that holds one model in the layout of the project's applications and remembers the identifier of the model's session: economics.md, the user's description of the model, which is the source of the folder's jobs and which the client never writes; declaration/, the model's stage files and its period, trellis, recipe, methods, calibration and settings files as they stand, possibly none; and .bellman-matsya/ (§3). The folder's target is read from declaration/: recipe when a methods, calibration, settings or recipe file is present, otherwise trellis when trellis.yml is present, otherwise period when a period file is present, and otherwise stage. A piece of work on the folder uses these commands, in this order, each run in the folder.

  1. bellman-matsya project init, once. It creates the folder's session, named after the folder; appends economics.md to the session as its first entry when the folder holds one with text; writes .bellman-matsya/project.json and .bellman-matsya/README.md; and creates AGENTS.md, or prints its paragraph, as §3 says. It refuses a folder that is already a project. bellman-matsya project init <folder> does the same for another folder, which it creates when it does not exist.
  2. bellman-matsya project submit, when the user asks for a build. When economics.md has changed since the session last received it, it appends the file to the session as a new entry. It sends, as the job's starting declaration, the files of declaration/ that a declaration holds: the stage files and the period, trellis, recipe, methods, calibration and settings files, which the job's first cycle checks in place of its first writing; the notes beside the stage files, and any other file, are left out, and the command names them. It then submits a job from the folder's session at the folder's target, and prints what it sent, the target, the job's label and the command bellman-matsya job wait <job>, which prints the job's steps until the job ends. --target names another target, and --max-cycles n limits the cycles of writing and checking.
  3. bellman-matsya project status, to see where the work stands. It prints the folder's session: its identifier, its entries, its jobs with their labels, the selected job, the questions awaiting a reply, and the two commands, written with the session's identifier, that answer a question and that ask one; and it says whether economics.md has changed since the session last received it.
  4. bellman-matsya project pull, to write the files of a job. It writes the products of the latest ended job of the folder's session that holds a record, or of the job that bellman-matsya project pull <job> names. Without an option, it writes the full model folder into the sub-folder bellman-matsya-output/job-<number>/, or into the sub-folder that --into <subfolder> names, which must be new or empty, and leaves the folder's declaration untouched. With --replace, it writes the job's declaration files to their corresponding paths under declaration/, report.md and any model prose as model-prose.md. It writes an open writer's note to .bellman-matsya/writer-note.md, apart from the author's stage page. It never writes economics.md and keeps declaration files the job did not produce. A job that has ended has not necessarily converged: show the user report.md, whose section Status gives the job's final state and its reason, and use --replace only when the user asks for the folder's files to be replaced.

Two plain commands complete the work, each with the session's identifier that bellman-matsya project status prints.

  • A question about the model, about a job's outputs or about the language: bellman-matsya ask <session> "<question>". It is one turn of matsya-master, whose answer names the job it read and cites its sources. It starts a job only when the question asks for one, such as "Submit this as a job."
  • A reply to a job's questions: write the user's answer to all the questions in one file and run the command that bellman-matsya project status prints under the question, bellman-matsya session add <session> <file> --replies-to <n>, with the file's path in place of <file>. The first reply to the questions of the session's latest job starts the next job at once, with the reply in its text; follow it with bellman-matsya job wait <job> and write its files with step 4. A job's questions are the user's to answer: show them to the user, and send the user's answer, not one of your own.

Working on a project folder follows these commands through one project, with what each prints.

docs.title: 5 The form of every answer
docs.text:
Every command but bellman-matsya alone, bellman-matsya configure and bellman-matsya docs takes the option --json, with which it prints its answer as JSON in place of the lines it prints for a person: a command of a project folder prints the answer the client composes from the folder and the service's answers, and every other command prints the service's answer as it arrived. Read that form. A command ends with one of four exit statuses:

  • 0 when it was carried out;
  • 1 when the service refused the request, when the request could not be sent, when a file could not be read or written, or when the client refused a personal Anthropic key (§3): the command prints one sentence after Error: on the standard error stream, the service's own sentence when the service refused. The client refuses the key, before any request, in four cases: bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key run on a machine where no Matsya token is configured; a key typed at that command's prompt that is empty or contains a space, a line break or another character that an HTTP header does not allow; a key selected from BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY or from the saved file that has the same fault; and a command that would send the key to a service address that is neither an HTTPS address nor an http address whose host is localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1. A command that sent the user's key also ends with status 1 when the service's answer shows that it accepted the job, the question or the reply under its own key: the command prints its usual lines, then a sentence that names the work;
  • 2 when the client refused the command without carrying it out: arguments the command does not accept, for which it prints its usage line and one sentence that names the fault and sends no request; or a command of a project folder that cannot be carried out where it is run, such as one run in a folder that is not a project, for which it prints one sentence after Error:;
  • 130 when the command was stopped with Ctrl-C: a job or a turn it was waiting for goes on running on the server, and the command prints the command that reads it.

The sentence of a refusal names what to change; read it before running the command again.

docs.title: 6 The command reference
docs.text: The command reference gives every command of the client with its syntax, each option and its default, each line the command prints and when, the exit status of each outcome and each field of its --json answer; read it before running a command whose form this page does not give. bellman-matsya docs lists the pages of this guide with their titles, bellman-matsya docs 05-the-command-reference prints that page, and bellman-matsya docs --all prints every page in order. With --online, a page is read from the public Matsya client repository as it stands today, which may describe a newer client than the one installed.

docs.title: The roles and the work of a job
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya's work is done by language-model roles, each with a fixed instruction text, a fixed input and a fixed output, called by the program in a fixed order; nothing else in Matsya decides anything about economics. This page names the roles of a job and the cycle in which they run, the role of a turn and the programs that check what the roles return, says what each receives and returns, and then says which command a user, or an assistant working for the user, runs for each kind of request: a question, a build, a reply to a question of matsya-architect, a reading of the result, a stop. The three parts of Matsya and the words session, job, turn, version, label and target are defined in Matsya in three parts.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Matsya in three parts, which defines the three parts and the words session, job, turn, version, label and target. Continued by — Working with Matsya from the command line, which follows one piece of work through the commands of §3. Explained for developers in — the Matsya developer guide: What Matsya reads for what each role is given, and The Matsya handlers for the program that calls the roles.

docs.title: 1 The roles of a job
docs.text:
A job of matsya-architect runs the Model-prose-writer and the prose-source-judge once, in preparation. It then writes and elaborates the initial declaration. Each iteration reads the latest elaborated semantic object, writes prose from it, writes and elaborates one new declaration from that prose, and compares the two adjacent elaborated semantic objects. Each language-model role has a fixed instruction text, input and output. The report lists the tokens charged to each role (Matsya in three parts §1).

Role Receives Returns What it is for Model-prose-writer the source material: the session's text or the submitted file, with the passages of the index that match it and the pages of the reference guides the model prose: the model restated as a paper's model section under fixed headings, first its structure, the model's stages, its periods with the connections between their stages, and how the periods repeat in time, then its states, controls, shocks and their timing, laws of motion, the recursion, the condition that determines the policy and the parameters; or questions when the source leaves a necessary thing unsaid to fix what model is meant before anything is written in the language prose-source-judge the model prose and the source material for each of ten economic items, from the state space and the timing of information to the terminal condition and the parameters, whether the prose omits, adds or contradicts something the source says, with the sentences quoted; it reads the two texts in both orders to report where the prepared model prose differs from the source, for the user to assess Prose-to-Bellman-Sym the prepared model prose for the initial declaration, or the prose written from the preceding elaborated semantic object for an iteration, with the language guide and retrieved passages the stage files of the declaration, in Bellman-SYM, each block quoting in a # from: line a sentence of the prose it reads, with a note of what the prose left open; with them the other files of the job's target, as Matsya in three parts §2 lists them to write and repair one declaration from the prose it receives the elaborator (a program, not a role) the stage files acceptance, or a refusal naming the rule, the line and what to write instead, which goes back to Prose-to-Bellman-Sym for repair to check that the files parse and satisfy the rules of the language the distribution check the model prose with an income or shock variable whose probability distribution the writer could not write, or an income the prose describes only by a general distribution function, and the reason whether the prose specifies that probability distribution, with the sentences quoted, and otherwise one question for the user to ask the user, before or during writing, for a probability distribution the prose leaves unspecified, instead of letting the writer supply one Semantics-to-Prose the dossier of the latest elaborated semantic object, the account the program prints of what it states, without the source or prepared model prose the model prose that semantic object states, under the same headings to read the semantic object back without seeing what was intended prose-roundtrip-judge the prepared model prose and the prose written from the latest elaborated semantic object for each of the same ten items, whether the two agree, with the sentences quoted to report prose differences for the user; this report does not decide convergence the comparison of elaborated semantic objects (a program, not a role) the elaborated semantic object before an iteration and the one constructed during it whether the two objects represent the same model, up to the names chosen, with the first difference when they do not to decide whether that iteration has reached the semantic fixed point

Preparation runs once. The Model-prose-writer writes the model prose, in up to three attempts when its answer or form needs correction. The prose-source-judge then reports any disagreement with the source. That report remains with the job; disagreement alone neither repeats preparation nor prevents a stage file from being written. A question about a necessary economic fact still goes to the user. The program also checks the structure described in the model prose. A target that holds that structure, or a wider one, is admitted; a narrower target ends the job needs_input with a question naming a suitable target.

The Model-prose-writer should identify the main Bellman problem even when it appears inside a general-equilibrium model, an estimation exercise or a computation using the sequence-space Jacobian method. Several sectors, equations, linked stages or decision branches can belong to one problem. When the source instead offers several distinct Bellman problems and the user has selected none, Matsya should ask “Select a Bellman problem:”, followed by the candidate problems and their sections in the source. For example, a paper with separate retirement, housing-adjustment and housing-with-renting applications requires a choice between those applications; the worker and retiree branches within the retirement application remain together.

A justified selection question is a valid architect response, recorded as needs_input. Writing waits for the user's choice, so no E–E′ comparison exists yet. The optional formulation identifies the chosen problem; target identifies the kind of declaration to return. A user who already supplies a formulation should not be asked to select it again. The reply procedure is in §3.

The prepared prose M produces the initial declaration D and its elaborated semantic object E. Iteration 1 reads E to produce M′, then writes D′ and elaborates it to E′; the program compares E with E′. If they differ, iteration 2 reads E′ to produce M′′, then writes D′′ and elaborates it to E′′; the program compares E′ with E′′. Iteration 2 does not write another declaration from M or produce E′′′. The job ends converged only when adjacent elaborated semantic objects are equivalent: one stage for a stage target, or the stages and their joins for a period, trellis or recipe target. The prose judges, the quotations and the writer's note remain in the record for the user to assess; none decides convergence. If the permitted iterations end with differing elaborated semantic objects, the job ends not_converged with the reason cycle_limit_reached. If a declaration cannot be elaborated, there is no comparison for that iteration. Agreement between adjacent elaborated semantic objects does not establish agreement with the source.

A job also ends not_converged before its cycles are spent when the elaborator still refuses the stage files after the writer's attempts (stage_file_refused), when a role has used up its requests for more pages or passages (request_rounds_exhausted), or when a call would pass a ceiling of language-model tokens (token_ceiling_reached); the report's section Status names the reason. A job that stopped at a question, the Model-prose-writer's, the question of a narrower target or the distribution check's, ends needs_input; the questions stand in the session for the user to answer when the job has a session and the user added no entry to it while the job ran, and otherwise in the job's record alone, where bellman-matsya job status <job> prints them.

For a model of several stages, the comparison reads the connections Bellman selected between their fields, including connections between periods. A connection that names no unique field, has incompatible fields, or cannot carry the required continuation values is returned for correction; it cannot count as an equivalent elaborated semantic object. For a recipe, the comparison also reads the parameter values that its periods supply. If a $fill slot leaves one period without a value, the dossier names that period and any values other periods state. The elaborated semantic objects of two recipes can compare equivalent while that value remains unbound.

docs.title: 2 The role of a turn
