A search first gathers candidates from each collection it reads: the 200 passages closest to the query in meaning, the 200 that best match the query's words and, when the query holds mathematical symbols, the 200 that hold the most of them. Each candidate receives the score

\[ \text{raw score} = 0.7\,\text{lexical} + 0.3\,\max(0, \text{dense}) + 0.3\,[\text{phrase}]. \]

Here lexical is the larger of two numbers: the score \(1/(1+r)\) of the full-text search, the search for the query's words in the passages' headings and texts, for the passage's rank \(r\), counted from 0, among the passages of its collection that best match those words, with common words such as "the", "of" and "model" left out; and the share of the query's mathematical symbols that the passage holds. Dense is the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the query and of the passage: the embeddings are the vectors of numbers that the embedding model assigns to texts so that texts of similar meaning receive similar vectors, and the cosine similarity of two vectors is the cosine of the angle between them, 1 when they point in the same direction and smaller the more their directions differ, down to −1. The last term, phrase, is 1 when the whole query, ignoring case, occurs in the passage's heading or text, and 0 otherwise. The raw score is multiplied by the collection's weight, and the search returns the passages with the highest weighted scores, up to limit, a tie going to the passage with the higher lexical score.

Every collection has the weight 1, except buffer_stock, whose weight is 0.01 in a search that reads more than one collection and names no source_ids; in such a search the passages of that one paper rank below those of the other collections unless the request raises its weight. A search of one collection, or a search restricted to named sources, gives every collection the weight 1. A factor in boosts multiplies this default. In a search of all permitted collections, which is the search a request without collections makes, "boosts": {"buffer_stock": 100} restores Buffer Stock Theory's weight to 1. In a search of buffer_stock alone its weight is already 1, and the same factor makes it 100, which changes no ranking, since every passage of that search is multiplied by the same weight.

A weight changes the order of the passages and nothing else: it makes no passage more reliable and changes no permission. A factor of 0 gives the passages of a collection the score 0 without removing them from the candidates; to leave a collection out, give an explicit collections list that omits it. The scores rank passages for one query; they are not probabilities that a passage answers the question.

docs.title: 5 What a passage holds
docs.text:
Each passage that a search returns, and the passage that GET /v1/passages/{passage_id} returns, holds these fields:

  • passage_id, its identifier, a 64-character code computed from its file, its location and its text;
  • source_id, the identifier of its source, which source_ids accepts; corpus, its collection; and access, the part of the collection it belongs to, public, private or article;
  • path, the file's path within its collection's folder, and title, the source's title where the list of indexed sources gives one, else null;
  • kind, the form of the file, markdown, text, pdf or notebook, and authority, the kind of source, such as canonical for a published page of this project, primary for an article or a paper itself and secondary for a reading of one;
  • version, the fixed commit of HARK or of Buffer Stock Theory; for the article PDFs, and for the transcriptions and secondary readings of some of the same articles, the label of the selected set of articles; and null for every other source;
  • location, where the passage stands in its file: its heading; its first and last lines, line_start and line_end; its first and last characters, char_start and char_end; in a PDF, page, the page's position in the file counted from 1, which can differ from the page number printed on it (page_basis is then pdf_ordinal); in a transcription with page markers, the page that the markers give, with page_basis markdown_marker and the printed_page_label; in a notebook, cell_number and cell_type; in a stage file, stage_name and block_id; and in a page whose headings the index records, section, the identifier of the innermost section;
  • text, the passage itself;
  • index_digest, the version of the index read; manifest_digest and corpus_revision, the versions of the list of sources and of the collection's files from which the index was built; and file_sha256 and passage_sha256, the digests of the file and of the passage's text;
  • source_cluster, the group of sources of §6 to which the source belongs, or null; source_root, the folder the file was read from; and model_prompt, a mark of the list of indexed sources that restricts no search.

A search adds five numbers to each passage:

Field What it is raw_score the score before the collection's weight (§4) retrieval_weight the collection's default weight multiplied by its factor in boosts score raw_score multiplied by retrieval_weight, by which the passages are ordered lexical_score the lexical part of the score, from the query's words or its mathematical symbols dense_score the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the query and of the passage

To cite a passage, keep its passage_id with the index_digest of the answer that returned it. GET /v1/passages/{passage_id}?index_digest=… returns the passage again while the service keeps that version of the index and your Matsya token may read its collection (Reaching the service by HTTP §4). Check a mathematical claim against the cited source before relying on it, above all in a passage of a PDF, whose extracted text can lose mathematics.

docs.title: 6 What Matsya reads when a job writes or a turn answers
docs.text:
The options of §3 belong to the two search routes alone. When a job writes or a turn answers, the program makes its own searches. None of them passes boosts, and each reads several collections, so the default weights of §4 apply: 0.01 for Buffer Stock Theory and 1 for every other collection.

In a job, the Model-prose-writer and Prose-to-Bellman-Sym, the roles described in The roles and the work of a job §1, receive the passages of an initial search whose query names the concepts the source material names, at most four passages at present, and each may request further searches and passages within allowances that the configuration sets. The initial Bellman-SYM writing reuses preparation's passages; each numbered iteration's writing searches from its own prose. These searches read the collections that the job's owner may read: the published parts for every Matsya token, and each private collection under its grant. They also leave out every source that carries a source cluster, the label with which the list of indexed sources groups the sources of one paper or one package, so that a job about a paper does not retrieve that paper's own text. When the job's request names model_key and source_cluster (Reaching the service by HTTP §5), the job leaves out the sources of those clusters alone; when it names neither, which is the case of every job that matsya-client or matsya-master starts, the job leaves out every source that carries a cluster. At present every source of HARK, of Buffer Stock Theory and of the articles carries a cluster, and no source of the repository or of the literature does, so that a job whose request names no cluster reads the repository and, under its grant, the literature. The full view of a job's record names, under reading, the passages each message of a role held.

In a turn, the conversation role of matsya-master reads in the same way, through an initial search whose query is the question and through requests of its own, from every collection that the person asking may read, and it leaves out no source, since a turn writes no declaration. The passages of the literature and of the articles therefore reach the conversation role for a Matsya token granted them, as they reach the answers of POST /v1/search and POST /v1/answer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Summary

The overview pages give an informal account of the written Bellman-SYM language and its semantics. We start by reviewing Project Bellman's core concepts and terminology, including the stage, perches and fields, and how stages join into a larger structure, the trellis. We then turn to how a stage file (a .bl file) is written, and to the project workflow. We also describe what elaboration builds from a stage file, how parameter values, methods and settings are attached to a stage, and which fields a stage returns as functions.

Relationship with other documents

Used by — Stages: the line-by-line reading of a stage file like the one used here; Periods and Trellises: several stages and several periods. See also — API: the constructed object in detail; Factory API: the loading and binding calls in full. Formal account — Bellman calculus: the mathematics the graphs represent; Appendix C: the rules that interpret equations as functions.

Page Contents Core concepts Introduces the necessary ideas and terminology to use Bellman-SYM. We cover how a model is written as stages, periods and a trellis, what the stage files mean, how a solver is built from that meaning through the Rosetta stone, and what follows for the workflow. The stage Using a running example, reviews the components of a stage: perches, fields and kernels. The Bellman-SYM language Shows how a stage is written in a stage file. We read the buffer-stock file and explain how its objects are typed and how its blocks are written. Periods and trellis Shows how connectors join stage files into periods, and periods into a trellis. We build a two-period trellis from the repository's portfolio application. Semantics Describes what elaboration builds from a stage file, on the buffer-stock stage: the table of definitions, the two initial diagrams and the two builders graphs, and how parameter values, methods and settings are then attached. Workflow Sets out the four steps of the workflow, and lists the files that make up a project and what each one states. Fields, evaluation and methods Explains which fields a stage returns as functions, what the evaluation of a field does, and where a numerical method may stand. Key terminology Term Meaning Stage One self-contained decision problem, written as one stage file, a .bl file (The stage). Perch One of the three information sets within a stage: arrival, decision and continuation (The stage §1.1). Field A typed economic quantity of a stage, such as a state, a control, a shock or a value, known at one perch (The stage §1.2). Block The unit that connects one perch to the next, forward or backward, with typed inputs, outputs and equations (The Bellman-SYM language §2.2). Semgraph (semantic graph) What elaboration builds from the stage files: a typed table of every declared object and graphs whose boxes are the model's operators (Core concepts §3). Elaboration The step that reads the stage files and constructs the semgraph (Workflow §1; The stage). Specifying a stage The three bindings, calibration, methodization and configuration, made in that order, which attach parameter values, methods and settings to a stage (Core concepts §3; The binding verbs). Initial diagram The blocks of one direction on the fields they read and write; one graph backward and one forward (The initial diagrams). Builders graph The same blocks as the operators they denote, on function wires backward and on measure wires forward (The builders graphs). Grain How far a graph's builders are opened: at the builder grain, one box per block; at the primitive grain, each block opened into its primitive operators (The builders graphs §4). Builder The operator a block denotes; one box at the builder grain (A builder). Connector A mapping that identifies a field of one stage with a differently named field of another (Periods and trellis). Period, trellis A period joins the stage occurrences of one horizon step; a trellis joins periods across time (Core concepts §2; Periods and trellis). Specified stage A stage that has been elaborated, calibrated, methodized and configured (Core concepts §3; The binding verbs).

docs.title: Install Bellman Workbench
docs.text:
Bellman Workbench lets you edit Bellman-SYM model files and inspect their diagrams. You can use it in a browser or in the desktop application, which opens the same interface in its own window.

Installing the desktop application does not install Python or Bellman. Both versions need the Python packages bellman and bellman-workbench, installed together as below. You do not need the desktop application to use the browser version.

No ready-made desktop installer is currently published on the download page. You can use the browser version now, or build the desktop application in §3.

docs.title: 1 Install the Python packages
docs.text:
Install Python 3.12 or later and Git, then open Terminal on macOS/Linux or PowerShell on Windows. Download the source:

git clone https://github.com/econ-ark/bellman.git
cd bellman

Create a virtual environment, a folder that keeps this installation's Python packages together, and install both packages. Keep this terminal in the bellman folder for the commands below.

On macOS or Linux:

python3 --version
python3 -m venv venv
venv/bin/python -m pip install --upgrade pip
venv/bin/python -m pip install -e "packages/bellman[explore]" -e packages/bellman-workbench

If python3 --version reports a version older than 3.12, use the newer Python executable in the next line, for example python3.13 -m venv venv.

On Windows:

py -3 --version
py -3 -m venv venv
.\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip
.\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e "packages/bellman[explore]" -e packages/bellman-workbench

If py -3 --version reports a version older than 3.12, select your installed newer version when creating the environment, for example py -3.13 -m venv venv.

The commands install Bellman, the Workbench interface and their Python dependencies. The -e option uses the code in your downloaded folder, so keep that folder and venv/ in place.

docs.title: 2 Open the browser version
docs.text:
On macOS or Linux:

venv/bin/bellman-workbench applications/cons-port

On Windows:

.\venv\Scripts\bellman-workbench.exe applications/cons-port

Your browser opens at localhost:8765. The command starts a server on your own computer; keep the terminal open while you work, and press Ctrl+C there to stop it. Replace applications/cons-port with your own model folder when ready.

Choose a .bl model file in the file tree to edit it and see its diagram. Save writes the edited text to disk. Follow the Workbench quickstart to inspect the portfolio stage in the supplied model.

docs.title: 3 Build and install the desktop application
docs.text:
Complete §1 first. Install Node.js 22 with npm, Rust and the Tauri prerequisites for your operating system. Tauri is the software used to build the desktop application. From the bellman folder:

cd packages/bellman-desktop
npm ci
npm run build

The application and installers are written under packages/bellman-desktop/src-tauri/target/release/bundle/, relative to the repository root. On macOS, copy Bellman Workbench.app from its macos/ subfolder into Applications and launch it. This local build is not a signed public release. Desktop installation has been checked on macOS; Windows and Linux installation checks remain outstanding.

On first launch:

  1. Choose Settings → Workbench command… and select the executable inside the environment created in §1: venv/bin/bellman-workbench on macOS/Linux, or venv\Scripts\bellman-workbench.exe on Windows. Select this file, not the Python executable.
  2. Choose File → Open Project… and select your model folder, for example applications/cons-port. The folder normally contains declaration/; see Model directory layout.
  3. Alternatively, use File → Open File… for a .bl file or a model recipe, spec.yml or spec.<name>.yml, which names the files used to assemble a model. Previously opened folders appear under Recent projects.

The application starts the Workbench server for you; no terminal command is needed for later launches. Closing a model window stops its server. The editor and diagrams work as described in §2.

docs.title: 4 Update an installation
docs.text:
Close the Workbench's model windows or stop its browser command. In the downloaded bellman folder, run:

git pull --ff-only

Then repeat the two pip install commands in §1 and reopen the Workbench. If Git reports conflicting local edits, keep those edits and resolve them before updating.

An installed desktop application uses updates from the Python environment selected in Settings → Workbench command… when a new model window opens. Changes to the desktop application itself, such as its menus or opening screen, require repeating §3 and replacing the installed application. There is no automatic updater.

docs.title: 5 If something does not open
docs.text:
What happens What to check The desktop application cannot start bellman-workbench Select the executable from §3 in Settings → Workbench command…, then open the project again. Python reports that bellman is missing Install both packages with the command in §1, using the same environment. The page says No stage file. Open a model folder containing .bl files, such as the supplied example in §2.

For paper exports and other static diagrams, also install Graphviz, or install Node.js and run npm ci in the repository root. This extra step is not needed for the interactive Workbench graph.

docs.title: How Bellman-SYM works
docs.text:
Summary

A model is written as stages, which are joined into periods and a trellis. Bellman-SYM elaborates the stage files into a semantic graph, a record of the model's operations and of their mathematical meaning that a person and a machine can read and that depends on no solver. The graph makes solver code verifiable, since every routine has a stated mathematical operation to compute, and a change of numerical method leaves the stage files unchanged.

Bellman-SYM is a highly expressive declarative functional programming system for dynamic recursive problems.

docs.title: 1 What Bellman-SYM does
docs.text:
Consider a household that arrives with assets, receives income, chooses consumption, and saves what remains. In Bellman-SYM, this decision problem is written as a modular stage in a stage file, a .bl file. Although an economist first describes the problem as relations between economic quantities such as consumption and income, its solution and simulation are higher-order operations, that is, operations on functions rather than on numbers. In the Bellman equation of such a problem, for instance, the expected continuation value function is combined with current utility and maximized over the feasible choices to obtain the decision value function. These operations define the stage's Bellman operator, but how they compose, and the numerical assumptions under which they are approximated, are usually left implicit or embedded in numerical procedures.

Bellman-SYM makes the structure of solution and simulation explicit through elaboration, which turns the stage files into a semantic graph that depends on no solver and that a person and a machine can both read. The semantic graph is a typed record of the meaning of the written model: it records the functional operations, the mathematical objects on which they act and which they produce, and how they compose3 (in the terms of universal algebra, a many-sorted algebra2). The map that takes the stage files to their elaborated meaning is what we call the meaning map, Υ (Upsilon, see Figure 1). The graph is then a single source from which the model can be implemented, in different numerical implementations and under different calibrations and settings, or its theoretical structure written out.

Drawn in the axonometric manner of the modularity figure. At the left, you, drawn as the Adam Smith avatar; you write the stage files, a pile of sheets. Elaboration, the meaning map Upsilon, turns them into the semantic graph, a platform carrying the stage's two operators as boxes on a wire between its three perches, inside a region marked as the meaning, the model stated in full. The graph's denotations give the formal mathematics, a sheet above the files with the Bellman equation and the law of motion on it, which you read back. Compiled by Rho, on whose arrow the AI sits, inside a band marked outside Bellman-SYM, it gives code, a fan of three tiles named HARK, Dolo and QuantEcon. You write V(m) = maxcu(c) + β E V′(m′)m′ = R(m − c) + y′ denotations read Formal math Stage files Υ elaborate the meaning ≅ the model, stated in full x≺ x x≻ Semantic graph outside Bellman-SYM AI Ρ compile HARK Dolo QuantEcon Compiled code Figure 1. The meaning map Υ: elaboration turns the stage files into the semantic graph, whose denotations are the formal mathematics; the representation map Ρ (Rho) compiles the graph into code, a step outside Bellman-SYM.

Expressive power

Bellman-SYM can express recursive decision processes in the sense of Sargent and Stachurski,4 a class of dynamic programs more general than Markov decision processes. It includes life-cycle and infinite-horizon models, models with discrete choices and branches, and the individual problems of heterogeneous-agent models together with the distributions they generate.

docs.title: 2 Modularity
docs.text:
A stage represents a single decision problem as a Bellman operator, that is, as one recursive program. In the household's consumption and saving problem, the stage states what the household knows before its income is drawn, what it learns when the income is realized, what it chooses, and how its continuation value is formed. The three points at which its information is fixed, arrival, decision and continuation, are the stage's perches.

The internal structure of a stage follows the information available within its decision problem, not the model around it: a stage is a self-contained program that refers neither to the rest of the model nor to its position in time. Modularity means that stages can be joined into a period, the stages that together make up one step of the horizon, such as one year of a life cycle, and periods can be joined in turn into a trellis, the sequence of periods across the horizon. Provided that their inputs and outputs agree in type, stages can be rearranged or replaced within a period and reused across models, so a richer model is built by adding stages to an existing one rather than by rewriting it.

Three axonometric drawings of the housing tenure model, left to right. Stochastic decision stages: six loose modules named on their front faces, tenure choice, owner housing, owner consumption, renter housing, renter consumption and portfolio choice, each with a green square socket at its arrival end and a cyan peg at its continuation end; the tenure choice carries two pegs, one for owning and one for renting, and the portfolio choice two sockets. Period: a plate on which the modules are assembled, the tenure choice first, then the owner's two stages in one lane and the renter's two in another, with a thin line over the top faces tracing the two routes and a peg seated in a socket at every seam; four modules are lowered into place one after another, and then, after a pause, the portfolio choice is lowered onto the period's end, where the two routes rejoin. Trellis: the life cycle, six of its twenty periods drawn, each a plate carrying a small copy of the period and each beginning on the last stage of the one before it, each level in its own shade of blue; the periods are lowered in one by one. The sequence plays once. tenurechoice ownerhousing ownerconsumption renterhousing renterconsumption portfoliochoice Stochastic decision stages Period Trellis Figure 2. The housing tenure model assembled from its stages, with a period drawn as a plate: the tenure choice stage forks into an owner's lane and a renter's lane, a portfolio stage from another model is added where the lanes rejoin, and six of the twenty periods of the life cycle are stacked into the trellis.

docs.title: 3 Layers of meaning and computational representation
3.1 Specifying a stage
docs.text:
The semantic graph denotes the mathematical operations required to solve and simulate the model, and a numerical implementation must approximate them. Bellman-SYM lets you declare the numerical assumptions explicitly as methods, such as linear interpolation, Monte Carlo simulation and the endogenous grid method.1 Because the theory of the stage is written first and the methods are declared separately, the same stage can be implemented in different toolkits and with different numerical approaches, and each implementation can be checked against the mathematical model that it approximates.

Each method is declared in a methods file and attached to a place in the stage: to a whole block, as the endogenous grid method is attached to the policy block; to an operation inside a block, as a quadrature rule is attached to an expectation; or to a named function that is to be stored, as linear interpolation is. The numerical options of a method, such as the size of a grid, are its settings, whose values are supplied separately.

Settings are distinct from the model's parameters, the exogenous economic quantities that enter its theoretical description rather than its numerical methods. Parameter values are also supplied separately from the symbolic model, so that the theoretical model, its calibration and its numerical approximation remain distinct. Even without parameter values, methods or settings, elaboration produces a symbolic stage, whose semantic graph represents the theory with the parameters left symbolic. The stage is then specified by supplying parameter values through calibration, attaching methods through methodization, and supplying their settings through configuration, in that order (Figure 3).

Three axonometric drawings: symbolic stage plus specifications gives the specified stage. Symbolic stage: the block of the modularity figure, with its green arrival socket, its cyan continuation peg and two square pads on top, its two operators. Specifications: three separate groups of scattered pieces, four short plugs marked beta, rho, R and sigma, labelled parameter values, in the stage's navy; four tapered blocks named on their faces EGM, VFI, linear and Gauss-Hermite, labelled methods, in a middle blue; three dials with a flange and a pointer, labelled settings, in a light blue. Specified stage: the block with the plugs in its front face, the Gauss-Hermite and EGM blocks on its two pads, and a dial on each; the plugs slide into the face, then the methods and then the dials are lowered into place, once. Symbolic stage β R ρ σ parameter values EGM linear VFI Gauss-Hermite methods settings Specifications Gauss-HermiteEGM Gauss-HermiteEGM Specified stage + Figure 3. Calibration, methodization and configuration produce successive versions of a stage, each leaving the preceding version unchanged; parameter values enter the stage itself because they determine the economic problem, whereas methods and settings can be changed without altering it.

docs.title: 3.2 From semantics to code
docs.text:
Once a stage has been specified, you can use its semantic graph to assemble code that solves and simulates the model. This step, realization, is the representation map Ρ (Rho) of Figure 1, and it lies outside Bellman-SYM. The graph identifies the mathematical operation that each routine must implement, the method chosen for it, and how its inputs and outputs connect to the rest of the calculation, so you can draw on the routines of an existing toolkit or write your own while keeping an explicit account of the model that they are intended to approximate.

The Rosetta stone supports this step by recording which operations and methods are realized by routines in toolkits such as HARK, Dolo and QuantEcon, together with the conventions under which each correspondence holds. Its cards are being rebuilt one at a time from routines that have been checked.

docs.title: 3.3 Matsya
docs.text: Project Bellman's AI assistant, matsya, which is to draft stage files from a prose description and to assemble solver code from the semantic graph and the Rosetta stone, is not part of this release; its page returns when it is written.

docs.title: 4 Workflow
docs.text:
The workflow separates the description of the economic problem from the choices made to compute its solution.

  1. Write the stages. Describe each decision problem in a stage file, stating its timing, information, choices and equations, and state how the stages join into periods and how the periods form the model's trellis.
  2. Elaborate and inspect the model. Bellman-SYM produces a semantic graph that makes the functional operations and their composition explicit. The resulting symbolic stage lets you check the mathematical problem before supplying parameter values, numerical methods or settings.
  3. Specify the stages. Supply parameter values through calibration, attach numerical methods through methodization, and supply their settings through configuration, in that order. Each step adds its binding to the stage; the specified stage, the stage after the three, records the choices needed for implementation but is not yet solver code.
  4. Realize and check the model. Implement the graph's operations with routines from the chosen toolkit or with your own code, and compose them to solve and simulate the model. Then check the numerical approximation against the mathematical description that the graph retains.

  1. Carroll, C. D. (2006). The method of endogenous gridpoints for solving dynamic stochastic optimization problems. Economics Letters, 91(3), 312–320. The end-of-period value function is equation (11), p. 314. ↩

  2. Goguen, J. A., Thatcher, J. W., Wagner, E. G. and Wright, J. B. (1977). Initial algebra semantics and continuous algebras. Journal of the ACM, 24(1), 68–95, §2, pp. 71–75. ↩

  3. Backus, J. (1978). Can programming be liberated from the von Neumann style? A functional style and its algebra of programs. Communications of the ACM, 21(8), 613–641, §12, pp. 625–630. ↩

  4. Sargent, T. J. and Stachurski, J. (2025). Dynamic Programming, Volume I: Finite States. Cambridge University Press, Chapter 8, "Recursive Decision Processes"; and Dynamic Programming, Volume II: General States, forthcoming, online draft edition at dp.quantecon.org, Chapter 7. ↩

docs.title: The stage
docs.text:
Summary

We use a simple buffer-stock model to introduce the structure of a stage, a self-contained decision problem with three perches corresponding to the information sets at arrival, decision and continuation. Its economic quantities are fields, classified by role, by declared set and, except for shocks, by perch, and related across perches by two laws of motion and a value aggregator. The stage file states this theoretical model alone, as a symbolic stage.

A stage is a self-contained decision problem whose description uses no information or notation from elsewhere in the model. It can be viewed as a description of a Bellman operator, expressed through objects typed according to the Bellman calculus, Project Bellman’s type system. These types are general enough to represent any Bellman operator of a recursive decision process.

docs.title: 1 Structure of a stage
docs.text:
To make this concrete, consider a consumption–saving problem with i.i.d. income and no borrowing, the simplest buffer-stock model. The normalized buffer-stock model adds permanent shocks and income growth; here, the sequence within the stage is:

  1. The household arrives with assets b.
  2. Income y is drawn from a lognormal distribution, giving the household market resources m = R*b + y, where R is the gross return.
  3. It chooses consumption c, subject to 0 < c ≤ m.
  4. It leaves with savings a = m - c, which it takes into the next stage.

Stage utility is 𝑢(c) = c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ), with constant relative risk aversion ρ > 1. Before introducing the value functions and Bellman equation, we place these economic quantities at their respective perches.

docs.title: 1.1 Perches
docs.text:
A perch identifies a point in the stage by the information available to the household there—its viewpoint, hence the name. The stage begins at the arrival perch, before any within-stage shock has been drawn or decision made. Once the observable shocks have been revealed, the household reaches the decision perch, where it makes its choice. The continuation perch follows that choice.

In our example, step 1 is the arrival perch, where b is known. Steps 2 and 3 place the household at the decision perch, where it knows its resources m and chooses c, while step 4 is the continuation perch, where savings a are known.

The perch indices are < (\(\prec\)) for arrival, > (\(\succ\)) for continuation and ~ (\(\sim\)) for decision, with the decision mark usually omitted.

docs.title: 1.2 Fields
docs.text:
The economic quantities of a stage—assets b, income y, resources m, consumption c, savings a and the value at each perch—are called fields. A field appears in stage equations much as a variable does in a paper, but the term makes its mathematical classification explicit. In conventional notation, a variable may be a number, a vector, a random variable, a realization or a function of the state, with the distinction left to context.1

For a stage file to determine a Bellman problem, each object must instead have a well-defined type. A field is classified by its role, which is state, control, shock, value or the multiplier of a constraint (Constraints §4.2), by its declared set, the set in which its values lie, and, unless it is a shock, by its perch. Its type states this classification. Together with the stage’s equations, which state the kernels (§1.3), the types of the fields determine the stage’s semantic graph.

In the buffer-stock model, the value field is written V[<] at arrival, V at decision and V[>] at continuation. Parameters such as β and R, by contrast, are not fields: they are declared with their sets and receive values at calibration.

The table summarizes the fields of the example.

Field Perch Role Declared set b, assets arrival state \(\mathbb R_+\) y, income drawn between arrival and decision shock (lognormal) \(\mathbb R_{++}\) m, resources decision state \(\mathbb R_{++}\) c, consumption decision control \(\mathbb R_{++}\) with c ≤ m a, savings continuation state \(\mathbb R_+\) V[<], V, V[>] arrival, decision, continuation value \(\mathbb R\)

docs.title: 1.3 Kernels
docs.text:
With the fields placed at their perches, we can write the stage’s Bellman equation in functional notation:

\[ V(m) = \max_{0 < c \le m} \bigl\{u(c) + \beta V_{\succ}(m-c)\bigr\}, \qquad V_{\prec}(b) = \mathbb E_y\bigl[V(Rb+y)\bigr], \]

where \(V_{\succ}\) is the continuation value function supplied to the stage. The conditions under which the maximum is attained and the expectation is finite are given in Stages §4.

These equations combine maximization with four relations between fields at adjacent perches. Three are given by kernels, the pointwise functions used by the stage’s operations: two laws of motion and a value aggregator.

  • The arrival law of motion, m = R*b + y, gives the decision state from arrival assets and realized income.
  • The decision law of motion, a = m - c, gives the continuation state from resources and the consumption choice.
  • The value aggregator, V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>], combines current utility with discounted continuation value.

The fourth relation, V[<] = E_{y}(V), takes the expectation over income to obtain the arrival value from the decision value; its aggregator is the identity. The Bellman calculus denotes the two laws of motion by \(g_{\prec}\) and \(g_{\succ}\), and the value aggregator by \(G\).

The elements of a stage

Together with the perches, fields and kernels described above, the buffer-stock stage declares its parameters, shock law and choice:

  • Its parameters are β (the discount factor), ρ (relative risk aversion), R (the gross return), and μ_y and σ_y (the mean and standard deviation of log income). Each is declared with its set and receives a value at calibration.
  • Its shock is income y, declared with its lognormal distribution.
  • Its choice is stated in the policy block as c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>]), with maximization over feasible consumption, 0 < c ≤ m.

The stage file brings these objects together and declares how the kernels combine with operations such as maximization and expectation. It states only the theoretical model, which elaborates as a symbolic stage. Parameter values, methods and settings are attached afterwards to produce a specified stage (Core concepts §3).

  1. Sussman, G. J. and Wisdom, J. (2014). Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, second edition, MIT Press, preface: “Symbols have ambiguous meanings that depend on context, and often even change within a given context.” ↩

docs.title: The Bellman-SYM language
docs.text:
Summary

A stage is written in a stage file (a .bl file), and we read the buffer-stock file part by part. Every object has a type, and a field's type says where the field is known and what values it takes. The file opens with a preamble that declares parameters, shocks and functions. Its five blocks follow: two state the laws of motion, two state how value is computed backward, and one states the choice. Annotations give blocks and equations addresses; a numerical method can attach at an address only when the constructed object there admits that method.

Now that we have the core concepts, let's turn to the Bellman-SYM language. We write the stage of the previous page as a stage file, and the next page joins stage files into periods and a trellis.

docs.title: 1 The stage syntax
docs.text:
We declare a stage in a stage file (a .bl file). A stage file declares the objects of a stage (The stage §1), together with their types. The types are the information, necessary and sufficient, that Bellman-SYM needs in order to turn the equations of the file, which are written as in a paper, into the operators that give the model its meaning.

It is useful to understand what the types do before writing a file.

docs.title: 1.1 Typing
docs.text:
Every object in a stage is typed with a colon :. A field's type gives its set of values and its perch: b : ℝ₊ @ !arvl declares b a field known on arrival with values in ℝ₊. A field known at decision need not be known on arrival; seen from the arrival perch it is random, and a law of motion, with its shock, determines it from the arrival fields. Each object is typed once in the stage file.

A type may have several components: a set, a role word such as !ctrl for the control, and a perch word such as !arvl, joined by @ in any order. A shock's distribution is not a type and is written on its own line with ~. Stages states the typing rules in full.

docs.title: 2.1 Preamble
docs.text:
The buffer-stock stage file first declares its parameters, its shocks and its functions, in what we call informally the 'preamble' of the stage. Each declaration is a name, a colon and a type: β : (0,1) says that the discount factor lies in the open unit interval. Here is the buffer-stock preamble. 

@stage: buffer_stock

# Declare parameters, shocks and functions
β : (0,1)
ρ : (1, inf)
R : ℝ₊₊
μ_y : ℝ
σ_y : ℝ₊
y : ℝ₊₊
y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y)
𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)

docs.title: 2.2 Blocks
docs.text:
A block connects one perch to the next, forward or backward. Its header, an annotation in square brackets, names the block and types its inputs and outputs; its body, in braces, holds the equations. Two blocks state the laws of motion, arvl_to_dcsn and dcsn_to_cntn; two state how value is computed backward, cntn_to_dcsn and dcsn_to_arvl; and the policy block states the choice. Let's look at the arvl_to_dcsn block:

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊ @ !arvl, y) -> (m : ℝ₊₊ @ !dcsn)] {
    m = R*b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}

Note that the body of a block begins with { and ends with }, and that within it each equation has a field on its left side and a formula on its right. A block is annotated in the square brackets before its body, and an equation after the :: symbol: the annotation :: [id=resources] gives the equation its address. An id has no mathematical meaning: it gives the line an address, by which a methods file names it. Methodization lists the constructed operators, evaluated fields and builders to which methods can attach.

A forward block's header lists every field its equations read that no earlier line of the block defines, including a control or a shock, and the state fields it writes. A backward block's header lists the value fields it reads and writes and the controls at which its equations are read, and no state. For example, the value equation V = 𝑢(c, H_d) + β*V[>] in a housing stage reads H_d, a decision state, without listing it: that state is a coordinate of the decision value. A state of the backward block's input perch must instead be reached through the law of motion. A state listed on a backward header is refused.

A field can also be defined within a block. Such a field is neither a state nor a control; it is just an intermediate quantity. For instance:

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊ @ !arvl, y) -> (m : ℝ₊₊ @ !dcsn)] {
    rtrns_b = R*b  
    m = rtrns_b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}

The underscore in rtrns_b is part of the name and indexes nothing.

Combining the other blocks, the whole stage file is:

@stage: buffer_stock

# Declare parameters, shocks and functions
β : (0,1)
ρ : (1, inf)
R : ℝ₊₊
μ_y : ℝ
σ_y : ℝ₊
y : ℝ₊₊
y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y)
𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)

# Blocks

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊ @ !arvl, y) -> (m : ℝ₊₊ @ !dcsn)] {
    m = R*b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = m - c                    :: [id=savings]
}
[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]            :: [id=value]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, V : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = E_{y}(V)              :: [id=value]
}
[id=policy, V[>] : !cntn -> c] {
    c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>]) :: [id=choice]
}

In the blocks above, V[>] is the continuation value the stage receives, V the decision value, and V[<] the arrival value; the marks [>] and [<] select perches, not calendar periods. Listing y among the inputs of the first block makes income an argument of its law of motion; it does not place y at the arrival perch, whose information is everything known before income is drawn. The operator E_{y} averages over the income law, and argmax_{c} gives the set of feasible maximizers: the policy block states that the policy lies in that set, and choosing one member of it is the task of a numerical method (Stages §4 says when a maximizer exists).

Note that the file has no line for the borrowing constraint: the equation a = m - c and the declared domains of c and a jointly impose 0 < c ≤ m, and the maximization ranges over these feasible choices.

docs.title: Periods and trellis
docs.text:
Summary

A period connects stage fields; a trellis connects periods. We introduce the consumption, discounting and investment stages, then inspect a runnable reference variant with investment and discounting in each of six periods.

A model with more than one decision is several stage files joined by connectors. The repository's portfolio application has three.

Stage file Contents cons.bl Chooses consumption from resources m and leaves assets a. disc.bl Discounts value and passes assets through. port.bl Chooses the risky share before the return and next income are drawn, and produces next resources m_next.

Within a period, field names belong to their own stage. Consumption's continuation assets a and discounting's arrival assets a are distinct fields, selected as one connection only if they are the unique compatible, globally consistent same-name pair. An authored connector selects fields whether their names agree or differ: {"disc.a": "k"} specifies discounting's continuation assets and investment's arrival capital. The stage-key prefix identifies the source when several stages have an outgoing a; it does not rename the field. Periods gives the complete rule.

Between periods, inter_connectors[h] joins the outgoing fields of period h+1 to the incoming fields of period h, where h counts backwards from the terminal period, h = 0.

The checked reference variant below contains a portfolio stage and a discount stage in each of six periods. It shows one connection within the terminal period and one from the period before it. Its trellis file carries each stage's source and bindings, so load_trellis reads the model as written and specify_trellis elaborates, calibrates, methodizes and configures every occurrence. connection_report reads the selected connections; periods=[0] keeps pairs touching the terminal period. Run this listing from the repository root:

from bellman.trellis import connection_report, load_trellis, specify_trellis

source = load_trellis("applications/cons-port/declaration/trellis.reference-port-only.yml")
model = specify_trellis(source)
report = connection_report(model, periods=[0])

print(len(model["periods"]), len(report.pairs), len(report.routes), len(report.diagnostics))
for pair in report.pairs:
    print(f"{pair.writing} -> {pair.reading} ({pair.origin}, {pair.compatibility})")

6 2 2 0
periods[0].port.w -> periods[0].disc.a (authored, compatible)
periods[1].disc.a -> periods[0].port.k (authored, compatible)

The first pair joins the portfolio stage to discounting inside the terminal period. The second joins the preceding period's discount stage to the terminal period's portfolio stage. The stage keys and period indices identify the fields; the pair changes neither stage's local name. The report also checks complete state and value routes, including the forward joint law, as Periods explains. The four numbers and two pair lines above were checked against the package in this checkout.

A trellis is also built one period at a time. bellman.trellis.accrete(trellis, period, inter_connector=None) appends a period, the one earlier in time, to a trellis that starts as {"periods": [], "inter_connectors": []}, the terminal period first. A hand-written trellis can use accrete once for the terminal period and again for each earlier period, passing that pair's inter-period connector with the later call. Periods and Trellises explain the period boundary and the terminal continuation value that the trellis needs.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
Summary

Elaboration reads a stage file and constructs one Python object, the stage object. We describe what it holds, in words and on the buffer-stock stage: the table of everything the file declares, two graphs of the blocks on the fields they read and write, and two graphs of the operators the blocks denote, backward on value functions and forward on finite measures. We then describe how parameter values, numerical methods and settings are attached, and what a stage with all three attached still does not contain.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: perches, fields and the Bellman equation of a stage; The Bellman-SYM language: the buffer-stock stage file this page reads. Used by — Workflow: elaboration and specification as steps of the workflow. See also — The stage and the pages after it in the API: every object of this page with the listing the package prints for it. Formal account — Bellman calculus: the mathematics the graphs represent; Appendix C: the rules by which equations are read as functions.

Key terminology Term What it names Block A group of equations of a stage file between declared inputs and outputs: forward when it writes the states of a later perch, backward when it writes values or the control (§2). Semgraph (semantic graph) What elaboration builds from a stage file: a table of every declared object and four graphs whose boxes are the blocks and the operators they denote (§1). Elaboration The step that reads a stage file and constructs the stage object (§1). Initial diagram The blocks of one direction on the fields they read and write; one graph backward and one forward (§3). Builders graph The same blocks as the operators they denote, on function wires backward and on measure wires forward (§4, §5). Builder The operator a block denotes; one box of a builders graph (§4). Grain How far a graph's boxes are opened: one box per block, or each block opened into its primitive operators (§4). Specifying a stage The three steps, calibration, methodization and configuration, that attach parameter values, methods and settings (§6). Specified stage A stage that has been elaborated, calibrated, methodized and configured (§6).

We read the repository's buffer-stock stage, applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl. It is the normalized buffer-stock model: the household arrives with assets k, a permanent income shock ψ and a transitory shock ξ give its market resources m, it chooses consumption c, and it saves a = m - c. Each perch carries a value, and the derivative of a value is read where it is needed by a derivative term, D_{a}V[>] for the derivative of the continuation value in savings. The policy block states the maximization alone, c = argmax_{cp : Γ_c(m)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>]). The three lines of the endogenous grid method stand in the methods file beside the stage file, applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/methods.bl, an addition to the stage file that is read together with it (Methodization §1), appended to the policy block: consumption from the inverted Euler equation at each level of savings, c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>]), the resources at which that consumption is chosen, m[>] = a + c[>], and the line c[~] = c[>], which states that the policy at those resources is that consumption. The derivatives of the decision value and of the arrival value stand in the same file, each appended to the block of the value builder that writes the value (§6).

docs.title: 1 What elaboration builds
docs.text:
Elaboration reads the stage file and constructs one object, the stage object. The object is a stage occurrence: the file elaborated at one position of a period, with its own parameter values, methods and settings. One file may be elaborated at several positions, and each elaboration is a separate object that shares nothing with the others. The file is parsed once, and the parsed syntax tree is discarded once the object is constructed: everything the rest of this page describes is read from the object, never from the text again.

The object holds the stage's declared name, the file's other @ lines, a table of definitions, four graphs, the bindings and the provenance, which records the file, its digest and where each binding was read from. The table and the four graphs together are the stage's semgraph, its semantic graph. A graph here is made of boxes joined by wires, each wire carrying one typed object, and the package stores each graph as a hypergraph of the diagram library DisCoPy, a graph whose wires may join several boxes. Nothing else is stored: whatever the table and the graphs determine is computed when it is asked for.

For a model of several stages, each stage file is held in a record, a dictionary with the file's text and the three mappings of methods, settings and calibration, and a trellis arranges the records into periods (Periods and trellis). Elaborating a trellis constructs one stage occurrence at each position and attaches nothing yet.

docs.title: 2 The definitions
docs.text:
Every name the file declares is kept once, as a record with a kind and an identity of the form <stage>:<kind>:<name>, and the graphs refer to the records by identity. A line of a block is a record too, named by its address, such as cntn_to_dcsn.value. The sets, the parameters, the distributions of the two shocks, the utility function, its marginal utility, the inverse of that marginal utility and the correspondence of feasible consumption each have one record.

A block is forward when it writes the states of a later perch and backward when it writes values or the control, and two kinds of record are made from the blocks. The law of motion 𝑔 of a forward block is the map from the fields it reads to the fields it defines: for the saving block, (m, c) ↦ m − c, whose declared sets state the borrowing constraint. The value aggregator 𝐺 of a backward block is the map that combines the continuation value with current quantities into the block's value: for the decision block, (V[>], m, c) ↦ 𝑢(c) + β V[>]. Each record prints its own card, the printed description the package gives of one piece of the stage: the function it denotes under Defines, any conditions on its values under Conditions, the statements of the file it comes from under Source, and the key of each declared name it writes, the parameters among them, under Definitions referenced.

The equations keep the names of the parameters; their values arrive later, with calibration (§6). Each argument of 𝐺 is a number, not a function, and is written in roman type; the functions the operators read are written in italic. A declared set imposes a condition that a reader or a routine must check: the construction states the condition and does not establish it.

docs.title: 3 The two initial diagrams
docs.text:
An initial diagram has one box per block of one direction, wired by the fields those blocks share, so that every wire is a field. The forward diagram is supplied with the arrival assets k[<] and the two shocks, and produces the continuation assets a[>]. The backward diagram is supplied with the continuation value V[>] and produces the arrival value V[<] and the policy c.

Consumption is written by the policy block, and no wire carries it to another block. The decision block and the saving block list c among their inputs, but a control that a block lists among its inputs is a coordinate, the variable its lines are written in, not a field that another block supplies. Neither block has an input wire for it, and the Signature section of each block's card, which lists the wires, does not list it.

The two diagrams are read separately. The forward one is not supplied with the continuation value, the backward one is not supplied with the arrival state, and neither computes what the other computes.

docs.title: 4 The backward builders
docs.text:
In the backward builders graph every wire carries a function and every box is an operator on functions. At the builder grain each block is one box, its builder, the operator the block denotes. The decision builder takes the continuation value function 𝑉[>] and returns the decision value 𝑉; the arrival builder takes 𝑉 and returns the arrival value 𝑉[<]; the policy builder takes 𝑉[>], the one function its maximization reads, and returns the policy 𝑐. The two derivative lines of methods.bl, each appended to the block of the value builder that writes the value, state the derivative of the decision value in resources, D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), and the derivative of the arrival value in assets, with the factor of the law of motion; methodization records each at the Evaluation of the builder that writes the value, and neither adds a box (§6).

The decision builder is a builder at a policy. Its equations are written in the control, and the policy 𝑐 stands in place of the control wherever it appears, in the law of motion and in the aggregator, so each policy gives one operator, all with the same inputs and outputs. The policy is no input wire of the decision builder: it is a name the builder's operations refer to, and its type is printed once, on the output of the policy builder.

A grain chooses which boxes are opened without changing what the graph represents. At the primitive grain each builder is opened into its primitive operators, the finest boxes the construction makes. A value statement becomes a chain of boxes of a few kinds. The pullback composes the continuation function with the block's law of motion, so that 𝑉[>] becomes 𝑉[>] ∘ 𝑔. The expectation integrates over the shocks the distribution declarations name. The aggregation applies the block's 𝐺 at each point. The evaluation returns the result unchanged, under the field's name and in the set the file declares for it. Arithmetic, parameters and named functions are not boxes: they are part of the rule of the box that applies them. In the policy block, the maximization becomes a pullback of the continuation value along the law of motion, an aggregation that forms the choice value, an argmax and the evaluation. Once the methods file's block policy brings the lines of the endogenous grid method (§6), the operative policy builder's operations are those lines instead: the inverted Euler equation and the line that gives resources become one aggregation on functions of savings, and the line c = c[>] becomes a pullback of the policy along the map from savings to resources, a relation that the policy must satisfy at the resources that map reaches.

Read the decision builder from the top. The pullback gives the continuation value at savings, a function of resources and consumption; the aggregation adds current utility to the discounted continuation value, which is the choice value

\[ Q(m,c)=u(c)+\beta\,W(m-c), \]

where \(W\) is the continuation function on the wire 𝑉[>]. With the policy in place of the control, c = 𝑐(m), this is the decision value 𝑉, which the evaluation returns under its name. On the arrival builder the pullback reads the decision value at R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ, an aggregation applies the map the value statement writes inside its expectation, and the expectation integrates over ψ and ξ; the derivative line of the arrival value in methods.bl, appended to the arrival builder's block, D_{k}V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}(R * (Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) * D_{m}V), keeps the factor R/(Γ*ψ) of the law m = R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ. From syntax to a mathematical problem writes the same equations with their state arguments explicit.

The Bellman equation needs analytic conditions that the construction does not establish: that each expectation is finite, that the maximum is attained and that a measurable maximizer exists. The stage lists the first among its obligations, the conditions it states, each under its name with its formula or sentence, and a mark where the declarations or the calibration settle one; it states nothing about the second or the third.

docs.title: 5 The forward builders
docs.text:
In the forward builders graph each wire carries a finite measure over the states of a perch, the distribution of the population, whose total mass need not be one; a shock's own distribution remains a probability measure. Each box carries a measure forward through the same equations. Only the two forward blocks appear. The distribution extension extends a measure over the states by the distribution of a shock, giving the joint measure of the states and the shock; this stage has two, one for ψ and one for ξ. The push-forward carries the joint measure through the law of motion m = R*k/(Γ*ψ) + ξ.

The second forward builder is one push-forward at the policy: it carries the decision measure through a = m − 𝑐(m) to the continuation measure μ[>], referring to the policy as the decision builder does, and no wire joins it to the policy builder. The forward graph can therefore be evaluated only once a policy has been chosen, by the backward graph or by the user. The two graphs are two readings of one set of equations, on functions and on measures, and Operators and builders states the duality that relates them.

docs.title: 6 Specifying the stage
docs.text:
Three steps specify a stage. Calibration supplies a value for every declared parameter. Methodization types a numerical method at a place of the stage, the written address of one of its operators: a block, a named statement, an operator occurrence such as the expectation E_ψ_ξ, a definition, or the Evaluation that closes a builder, such as policy.evaluate, where a representation is written. Configuration supplies the settings the attached methods read, such as the size of a grid. We make them in that order, and each adds its binding to the stage it is called on and returns that stage; nothing is copied, and a later binding replaces the earlier one of its kind (The binding verbs). The equations keep the names of the parameters, so a sweep over β binds each value in turn to the one stage, whose graphs no binding changes. The buffer-stock methods file, methods.bl beside the stage file, names the endogenous grid method on the policy builder and appends the method's three lines to the policy block under the method !egm, so that the operative builder's operations are the three lines of the method while the stage keeps the maximization as the builder it declares, and appends one derivative line to each of the decision and arrival builders' blocks, which is recorded at that builder's Evaluation as the stated derivative of the value. The stage lists the condition under which the method's lines give the policy the maximization defines, egm-eligibility, and the reading of each derivative line, marginal-reading, among its obligations, and checks neither.

For a trellis, the three trellis verbs bind every stage occurrence from the mappings its record holds (Workflow §1). A specified stage is the result: constructed, calibrated, methodized and configured. #specification

docs.title: 7 What a specified stage is not
docs.text: Nothing above has solved the household's problem, and a specified stage does not contain a solution. It contains no numerical routine: an entry of a methods file names a technique and a routine without running them. It contains no terminal data: the continuation value 𝑉[>] is an input the stage leaves open, supplied by the next period or by a terminal value function. And it has established none of the analytic conditions of §4. Solving requires the routines, the composed model and the continuation or terminal data. Methodization describes the routines, and Trellises the terminal data.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Summary

Project Bellman's workflow has four steps, from writing the stages to realizing them as code. We set out each step and the call that performs it, and then list the files that make up a project and what each one states. A numerical grid belongs to the settings, because it approximates a function on the domain that the stage file declares. The loaders read each file at the path written for it, and the repository's model folders keep their files in one layout.

docs.title: 1 The four steps
docs.text:
Step Description Implemented by Writing the stages Write a dynamic problem as stages, and join stages into periods and periods into a trellis (The stage, the language, periods and trellis). One stage file per stage, and either a Python dictionary that arranges the stages into periods and the periods into a trellis, built one period at a time with bellman.trellis.accrete, or a period template, a trellis file and a recipe in a registry (The Bellman factory). Elaboration Bellman-SYM reads the stage files and constructs a semantic graph for every stage the dictionary names (The stage). bellman.stage.load_stage and bellman.stage.elaborate_stage for one stage file; bellman.trellis.load_trellis or bellman.trellis.load_recipe, then bellman.trellis.elaborate_trellis, for a trellis Specifying the stages Parameter values, numerical methods for the operators and settings are attached, in that order (The binding verbs). stage.calibrate, stage.methodize and stage.configure for one stage; bellman.trellis.calibrate_trellis, bellman.trellis.methodize_trellis and bellman.trellis.configure_trellis for a trellis, each given the dictionary of records it binds with; or the single call bellman.trellis.assemble_trellis(directory, recipe) for a registry and its recipe Realization A numerical routine is supplied for each operator, and the routines together perform, for example, value iteration, policy iteration or simulation. Code that you write, or a toolkit recorded in the Rosetta stone.

Each attachment adds its binding to the stage it is called on and returns that stage; nothing is copied, and a later binding replaces the earlier one of its kind. Realization lies outside Bellman-SYM.

docs.title: 2 Structuring a project
docs.text:
File or source Contents Stage files (.bl) Declarations, functions, shock laws and equations. Period YAML Which stage occurrences a period contains and the connectors between them. Trellis YAML, or a trellis assembled in Python as in Periods and trellis Which periods the model has, each written out or a period template repeated, and which fields join adjacent periods. Methods file (methods.bl beside the stage file) The methods, grids and handlers typed at the places of the stage, the lines a solution method brings, and the settings they read, declared with their sets. Settings YAML Numerical options and approximation grids. Calibration YAML Economic parameter values. Recipe YAML (spec.yml) The path of the trellis file and of each stage's file, from the recipe's folder; for each stage and each of the three kinds, the ordered files and slots that supply it, and the periods a file or a stage applies to.

A finite grid approximates a function on its mathematical domain; it does not replace the domain declared in the stage file.

The files above, kept in a registry, which in a model folder is its subfolder declaration/, are read in one call: load_recipe(directory, recipe) of bellman.trellis reads the registry through its recipe and returns the syntactic trellis, the model as written, a dictionary of records in which every adjustment is made, a value that differs by period among them; elaborate_trellis and the three trellis verbs, which bellman.trellis also holds, then construct and bind it, and its assemble_trellis(directory, recipe) returns in one call the trellis those calls make. A fill, a dictionary bound by keyword to a slot of the recipe, changes parameter values or settings without editing a file, and only the stages whose mapping changed are bound again. The Bellman factory is the route through these calls on the durables model, and the factory API lists them. #spec_factory

The layout of a model folder

A model folder keeps every file the language reads in its subfolder declaration/, the registry from which its recipe's paths are read, and gives each stage a folder there that holds the stage file, its methods file and its note; Bellman Workbench reads the model from declaration/. The loaders themselves require no layout, since they read the paths a recipe or a trellis file writes, and placing the files in one folder does not choose a horizon, connect fields or solve a model. Model directory layout states the layout and its rules.

docs.title: Bellman Workbench
docs.text:
For task instructions, start with the Workbench guide.

Summary

Bellman Workbench is a browser editor for Bellman-SYM with a live semantic view. It opens on a model folder, shows the open stage file beside the graph the elaborator makes of it, and redraws that graph at every pause of the typing, so that a file and its meaning are read as one object. Nothing in the graph is drawn by hand: every box came from a line of the file, a click on a box of a stage's graph takes you to that line, and a line the language refuses is marked at its line and column, its sentence in the package's own words standing in the page's one list of refusals, while the last good graph stays, dimmed. A folder with a recipe or a trellis file opens on its trellis, each period a frame holding its stage occurrences, with the recipe in the panel under the editor while the recipe is open, whose entries take the folder's calibration, methods and settings files; a double click on an occurrence opens its stage file as the trellis binds it there, and a step back returns to the trellis. In the forward trellis graph, a connection dragged from one stage to another, a stage dropped on a period and a period added each type a line into a file, and the graph is then drawn from the file (§8). The Workbench solves nothing, keeps nothing you did not type apart from the records and saved copies of what you asked Matsya for (§5), and stores nothing outside the model folder but the views of the trellis's stages and the bound trellis, which it writes to the user's cache folder (§7), the service's session identifier for the folder, which it writes under the user's configuration folder (§5), and the sizes and folds of the window's regions and the choice high contrast, which the browser keeps (§1); git is the only history of the files.

Relationship with other documents

The content of the graph pane, element by element, is on The view in Model Explorer. The workflow the Workbench sits in is on Workflow, and the language it edits on The Bellman-SYM language. The card and the kernel Details prints for a box are those of A piece, the kernel of a box of one branch holding that branch's part of the law of motion alone, and a builder's signature that of A builder.

docs.title: 1 Starting it
docs.text:
Follow Install Bellman Workbench to install the Python packages and choose the browser or desktop version. In the desktop application, File → Open Project… opens a model folder. File → Open File… opens a stage or recipe. File → Welcome returns to the list of recent projects. Both versions use the same editor and diagrams.

With the Python environment active, start the browser version on a model folder from a terminal:

bellman-workbench applications/cons-port

A page opens in the browser at http://localhost:8765/, on the folder's trellis where the folder holds a recipe or a trellis file, and otherwise on its first stage file; in a model folder these files stand under declaration/, the subfolder that holds every file the language reads (Model directory layout). The page's graph files, fonts and interface files are installed with the Workbench and served from your machine, and a folder holding no stage file shows No stage file. The window has a main bar across its top and four columns under it. The main bar holds, at its left, the project's mark, a link to this page, the icon buttons Back and Forward (§7), and the toggles Files and Inspector, which close and open the regions of those names at the window's left and middle; in its middle, the path that names what the window shows and how you reached it, durables › spec.yml › periods[3] › tenure, its last two parts the selected occurrence where one is selected (§7), its hover the whole path, and the path cut at its left where the bar is too narrow for it; and, at its right, the icon Go to, which opens Goto Anything (§3), and the toggles Details and Matsya, which close and open the two columns at the window's right. The first column holds the folder's files under the head Files, each with git's letter for its state and the word unsaved for a file whose text in the page differs from the file on disk. The second holds the open file in a code editor, under the row of its tabs, over the Inspector, the panel that shows what the open file declares or binds: a stage file's fields with their sets and roles, and its parameters, settings and methods as the recipe gives them (§2), or the stage rows of the recipe the trellis is read under (§7). The third holds the graph the elaborator makes of the file, the Semantic graph, under the bar that names it, over the panel Details, which describes what you select in the graph (§3). The fourth holds the column of Matsya, the service that reads the project's documentation, theory and examples; the column asks it questions, searches its sources, asks it for jobs that write and check the model's files and adopts the files a job returns (§5). The Problems button at the right end of the graph's bar lists current errors and model checks (§3). The status line runs along the foot of the first three columns (§4). Opening another file in the tree adds a tab for it above the text and shows it, and shows its graph where the file is a stage file, a recipe or a trellis file; each tab keeps the unsaved text of its file until it is saved or reloaded, and the folder stays. Lesson 01 of the tutorials reads the same file of the portfolio model in a notebook. In the Files tree, use the arrow keys to move, expand or collapse a folder. Home and End go to the first and last visible rows. Enter opens a file.

Each column takes its width from a handle on its edge, which you drag: the handle at the right of the tree sets the folder's width, the one between the text and the graph the widths of both, and the one on Matsya's left edge Matsya's width; the handles on the top edges of the Inspector and of Details set their heights. A drag stops where a region would become narrower or shorter than its least size, the size at which it stays readable, and a double click on a handle returns its region to its default size. The four toggles of the main bar, each at the end of the bar on the side where its region opens, close and open the regions, each drawn as its region's icon with the region's name as its hover: a stack of sheets for Files, a window with a panel at its foot for Inspector, the semantic brackets ⟦·⟧ for Details and a speech bubble holding Υ for Matsya. The toggle of an open region is drawn in full ink with a blue line under it, and that of a closed region in a fainter ink. Files folds the folder to a narrow strip, which shows the folder's name and the open file's path reading upward; Inspector closes and opens the panel under the editor, and is drawn faint and does nothing while the open file gives it nothing to show, as a trellis file or a period file, its hover then naming the file, Nothing to inspect in trellis.yml; Details closes and opens Details, which also closes by the × at the right end of its head; and Matsya folds Matsya's column, which then takes no width, as the button at the top of that column also does. Details has a head: its name, what it shows, then an icon that shows the panel in a wide panel over the window, which × or Escape closes, and its ×. The Inspector has no head and no ×; its strip holds its tabs, the open file's name, whose hover is the file's path, and the same icon, whose second click, like Escape, returns the panel to its place under the editor. The browser keeps the sizes and the folds for the model folder, so that the folder opened again shows its regions as you left them; none of them is written in the model folder. When the window narrows, Matsya narrows first and then the graph, each to its least width, and then the folder folds to its strip, while the text keeps its width as long as the window allows; a fold made in this way is not kept. In a narrow window, choose Files, Source, Graph or Matsya to give that area the full width. Problems opens the graph's list of errors and checks. Following a source link shows the editor. Widen the window to see the columns together. After a drag or a double click changes the pane's size, a graph whose view has not changed since it opened opens again at the new size, and any other graph is fitted to its pane.

The Workbench as it stood on 8 October 2026, before the main bar replaced the breadcrumb and the occurrence line under the tree, the Inspector replaced the recipe under the tree and the panel of types, and the cards of stage occurrences, the cables and the view tabs `Stage` and `Trellis` were added and the controls took their present words.

docs.title: 2 The two panes
docs.text:
The editor holds the open file under a row of tabs, one for each file opened, in the order opened, the first row of its column under the main bar. A tab reads unsaved while its text differs from the file on disk, and its × closes it; while the text is unsaved, × does nothing and its hover reads Save the file first. At the right end of the row stand the toggles Types and Notes and the button Save. The text is colored by the language's grammar: perch and role tags, sets, numbers, the block's id in its header, and the annotation of a statement, :: [id=util], each in their own color. The stage's name on its @stage line is drawn large, and an annotation stands at the right end of its statement's line, or under the statement where the pane is too narrow for both. Lines wrap at column 78, where the language keeps them, and a wrapped line is indented by four characters. A narrow strip at the editor's right edge, the minimap, draws each line of the file as a short mark whose length follows the line's, the block headers brighter and the stage's name in blue; a click on a mark moves the editor to that line. The toggle Types, pressed while the editor shows the bracketed entries of headers and annotations, the types, draws every header and annotation as its name alone, [arvl_to_dcsn], when it is released, and in full again when it is pressed; the file is never changed by it. The quoted explanation in an annotation, a note such as :: ["discount factor"], :: [id=marginal_tax, "the marginal tax rate, …"] or a bare quoted annotation, :: "…", is drawn as a small note glyph in place of the quoted text, the annotation's other entries standing as written. Resting the pointer on the glyph for a moment, or reaching it from the text by Escape and then Tab, shows the explanation in a floating preview, formatted as Markdown, its mathematics between \( and \) or \[ and \] typeset; the preview stays while the pointer is over it and closes on Escape or when the pointer leaves both. Enter or a click on the glyph shows the line as written, for editing, until the cursor leaves the line, and a line that holds the cursor or a refusal is always drawn as written; the toggle Notes, which is not pressed when the page opens, draws every note as written while it is pressed. None of this changes the file or marks it unsaved; a # comment and an annotation's other entries are drawn as before. The button Save writes the buffer to disk, and besides it only the choice Save of a build and Replace model files in Matsya's column write a model file (§5); before every save the file on disk is compared with the one the page remembers, and a file that another tool or another tab changed meets the choice Compare, Overwrite or Reload, framed in orange while the list under the Problems button holds the file changed on disk (§3), and is overwritten by nothing on its own.

Under the text of a stage file the Inspector shows the stage's types. Its strip, its only head, holds its four tabs, Fields, Parameters, Settings and Methods, each with a hover that says what it lists, then at its right the open file's name, whose hover is the file's path, and the icon that shows the panel wide (§1); the panel keeps one height on every tab, a tab's rows scroll within it, and the tab chosen stays chosen when you open another stage file and return. Over the recipe the trellis is read under, the same panel shows the tab Recipe alone (§7), and over any other file it does not appear.
