The law of motion is \(g_\succ(\mathrm m_d, \mathrm c) = \mathrm m_d - \mathrm c\), utility is \(u\), and the continuation value function is \(V_\succ : \mathsf X_a \to [-\infty, \infty)\). A policy is a measurable function \(c : \mathsf X_m \to \mathbb R_{++}\) with \(c(\mathrm m_d) \in \Gamma(\mathrm m_d)\) for every \(\mathrm m_d\). Roman \(\mathrm c\) is a consumption value and italic \(c\) is a policy.

docs.title: 1 A value function at a policy
docs.text:
The block cntn_to_dcsn holds the line V = 𝑢(c) + V[>], an equation between fields. At a policy \(c\), consumption is \(c(\mathrm m_d)\) and saving is \(\mathrm m_d - c(\mathrm m_d)\), so the line defines the decision value function

\[V(\mathrm m_d) = u(c(\mathrm m_d)) + V_\succ(\mathrm m_d - c(\mathrm m_d)) \qquad (\mathrm m_d \in \mathsf X_m).\]

The function \(V\) has the single argument \(\mathrm m_d\), and the policy is no argument of it. The policy enters wherever the control appears, in the reward and in the law of motion alike, and we write the two at the policy as

\[G_{\succ, c}(\mathrm m_d, \mathrm w) = u(c(\mathrm m_d)) + \mathrm w, \qquad g_{\succ, c}(\mathrm m_d) = g_\succ(\mathrm m_d, c(\mathrm m_d)),\]

so that \(V(\mathrm m_d) = G_{\succ, c}\big(\mathrm m_d, (V_\succ \circ g_{\succ, c})(\mathrm m_d)\big)\). The convention follows Sargent and Stachurski, who set \(r_\sigma(x) = r(x, \sigma(x))\) and \(P_\sigma(x, x') = P(x, \sigma(x), x')\), and their policy operator is \((T_\sigma v)(x) = r(x, \sigma(x)) + \beta \sum_{x'} v(x') P(x, \sigma(x), x')\), a function of the state alone; Hernández-Lerma et al. abbreviate \(c(x, f(x))\) and \(F(x, f(x))\) to \(c(x, f)\) and \(F(x, f)\).

A function of the state and a consumption value together, \((\mathrm m_d, \mathrm c) \mapsto u(\mathrm c) + V_\succ(g_\succ(\mathrm m_d, \mathrm c))\), is needed in one place only: inside a maximization, where \(\mathrm c\) is the variable that the maximization ranges over. The line c = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>]) of the policy block is such a place. A policy found by inverting an Euler equation forms no such function.

docs.title: 2 Which fields are evaluated
docs.text:
The header of a block is its bracketed first line, which lists the block's inputs and outputs with their perches. A field is evaluated, meaning that the stage returns its function under the field's name, in two cases.

  1. The field is an output in a block's header. The header [id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>], c) : !cntn -> (V) : !dcsn], written here without its types, returns \(V\); a derivative line of the block, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), states the derivative of that value in the decision coordinate and returns no further field. The header of the policy block returns the control \(c\). The inputs of a header are evaluated elsewhere: \(V_\succ\) by the stage that follows, and the policy by the policy block.
  2. The field is the left side of a line marked !node. In applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl the line CE = E_{Ψ}(V[>]^(1-γ))^(1/(1-γ)) :: [id=risk_ce, !node] returns the certainty equivalent \(CE\).

Every other field is a part of a longer expression. For an unmarked line such as W = β*V[>], the expression of \(W\) is substituted wherever \(W\) is used, and the stage returns no function under that name. A block defines a symbol once.

docs.title: 3 Evaluation
docs.text: Evaluation takes the expression on the right side of an evaluated field's line, such as \(x \mapsto f(g(h(x, l(x))))\), and returns a function \(p\) with \(p(x)\) equal to the expression at every \(x\). In the exact mathematics \(p\) is the expression computed at each \(x\), and evaluation changes nothing. Numerically, \(p\) may be an approximation, such as an interpolant of the expression's values on a grid. The approximation is a different function, with mathematics of its own, which the stage does not describe: the stage records the method, its options and what it requires.

docs.title: 4 Where a method stands
docs.text:
A methods file, the .bl file beside the stage file that the package reads with it, types numerical methods at places of the stage (Methodization). The smooth-ambiguity savings stage's file, applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/methods.bl, writes among its entries, in the bracket of its block cntn_to_dcsn:

    | risk_ce.E_Ψ.method : !gauss_hermite(n_Ψ=n_Ψ_nodes)

    | risk_ce.evaluate.method : !Linear
    | risk_ce.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m), ν=E_ν)

A method that computes an operation stands on the operator. Gauss–Hermite quadrature is a rule for one integral against a normal or lognormal distribution, and risk_ce.E_Ψ names the expectation in the line risk_ce. A method that stores a function stands where a function has a name: !Linear holds \(CE\) by its values on a grid and reads it between them by linear interpolation, and risk_ce.evaluate names the Evaluation of the line that returns \(CE\). The grid is the place's own entry, !Cartesian, a product of one set of points per coordinate: the resources m_d from a lower bound to an upper bound with a count, the three names declared settings, and the ambiguity coordinate ν on the quadrature nodes of the expectation E_ν. A method of one kind is refused at a place of the other. Quadrature says how the expectation inside the line is computed and says nothing about how \(CE\) is held, so the package refuses it on the line itself. An entry risk_ce.method : !gauss_hermite(n_Ψ=n_Ψ_nodes) in that bracket is refused under the rule method-admission, and the refusal names the line of the methods file and says: “the entry cntn_to_dcsn.risk_ce.method : !gauss_hermite(n_Ψ=n_Ψ_nodes) types cntn_to_dcsn.risk_ce, a place of the kind node, with !gauss_hermite, whose row of the catalogue admits operator E; write the word at a place of a kind it admits, or a word that admits this place”.

A keyword argument a method requires is written beside its word, its value the name of a declared setting, and configure refuses a value outside the setting's declared set.

The places a stage admits are its own answer, stage.places(), with the kind of each. A method that stores a function admits the evaluated fields, a declared function and the stored form of a builder's output, at the Evaluation that closes the builder, which the methods file names by the builder's id: policy.evaluate for the policy function, and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate for a value function and the derivative of it that a derivative line states together, or cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[V] and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate[D_{m_d}V] for each apart. A method that computes an operation admits the operator. A function that the file does not name, such as \(V_\succ \circ g_\succ\), is no place at all: an author who wants it stored writes it on a line of its own and marks the line !node.

docs.title: Abstract dynamic program (ADP)
docs.text: An abstract dynamic program (ADP), in Sargent and Stachurski's terminology, was previously called an abstract decision process in this wiki. An ADP specifies a partially ordered value space and a family of policy evaluation maps; it does not require a particular state representation or source language.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a partially ordered set and \(\{T_\sigma:\sigma\in\Sigma\}\) a nonempty family of order-preserving self-maps on \(V\). The index \(\sigma\) names a policy. When each \(T_\sigma\) has a unique fixed point \(v_\sigma\), that point is its policy value. The optimal value is \(\sup_\sigma v_\sigma\) when this supremum exists in the specified value space.

The associated Bellman operator is

\[ Tv=\sup_{\sigma\in\Sigma}T_\sigma v, \]

where the supremum must exist in \(V\). An arbitrary partially ordered set does not ensure this. A policy is greedy for \(v\) when its update attains that supremum; existence of the supremum does not imply existence of a greedy policy.

Sargent and Stachurski's fixed-point-to-optimality result assumes well-posed policy maps, a fixed point \(\bar v\) of \(T\), a \(\bar v\)-greedy policy, and the implication \(T_\sigma v\leq v\Rightarrow v_\sigma\leq v\). These assumptions connect the operator equation to optimal policy values. They are not consequences of declaring an ADP.

docs.title: Relation to staged models
docs.text:
The recursive decision process (RDP) adds feasible actions and a choice-value aggregator that constructs the policy maps. A stationary composition of stages can define an ADP when it preserves a specified value space and order. An individual stage may instead map between the value spaces of different perches, and a finite-horizon problem requires terminal data rather than a stationary fixed point.

Value-function iteration applies \(T\) repeatedly. Policy iteration alternates policy evaluation and greedy policy selection. Their convergence requires additional assumptions; assigning a numerical method does not establish them. semiconjugacy (strong / order) describes specified relations between alternative operator forms.

Reference: Sargent and Stachurski, Dynamic Programming, Volume II: General States, 10 April 2026 edition, Definition 2.1.1, §2.1.1, and Theorem 2.1.7 and Corollary 2.1.8, pp. 66–67.

docs.title: Accretion modules
docs.text:
Accretion constructs a finite-horizon model backwards, adding one period at a time to the periods already specified. In Bellman-SYM the resulting sequence is a trellis: periods together with explicit connections between them. The reusable components are stage files, which state the equations, and period descriptions, which specify how the stage occurrences, the elaborations of a stage file at the positions of a period, are connected.

For example, we can first specify the final year of a household's life, then add the preceding retirement years, and finally the working years. Each addition supplies the equations and parameter values for that year and connects it to its successor. A longer model can reuse the same stage files while changing the income process, survival probabilities or available decisions across periods.

docs.title: Backward construction
docs.text:
We start with an empty sequence and construct the model in the following order.

  1. Specify the terminal period, including any continuation data required after its decisions, and add it to the sequence.
  2. Construct the preceding period from its stage files, with the parameter values and the numerical choices, its methods and settings, appropriate to that period.
  3. Declare the inter-period connector, which identifies compatible outgoing fields of the earlier period with incoming fields of its successor. Add the new period and its connection to the sequence.
  4. Repeat until the sequence includes every period to be modeled.

A period can contain several stages. Within-period connectors state which stage outputs supply which subsequent inputs; inter-period connectors do the same across dates. A connector identifies or renames compatible fields. Changes in resources, income or other quantities require equations in the stages, rather than an implicit transformation inside the connector.

The period records are ordinary dictionaries and lists, which can be assembled interactively or generated in a loop from a parameter schedule. A stage file need not receive the horizon or its position in the sequence: those belong to the model assembly. Each use of a file creates a separate stage occurrence with its own parameter values and numerical choices.

docs.title: Relation to backward induction
docs.text:
Accretion assembles a model; backward induction solves its successive decision problems using the solution already obtained for the next period. The two can be interleaved: after specifying and solving the terminal period, we can add and solve one earlier period at a time. Alternatively, we can assemble the finite sequence before solving it. Assembly alone produces no policy function.

Consider a final-period problem in which resources are nonnegative, any consumption between zero and available resources is feasible, utility is strictly increasing in consumption, and unspent resources have no terminal value. Its solution is to consume all resources. The preceding period's problem then uses that terminal rule to value saving. Carroll (2006, §2) describes the recursion from a final-period consumption rule to earlier rules. The choice of numerical method for each step is separate from the order of the recursion.

HARK provides a related computational arrangement: its one-period solver receives the next period's solution and the inputs for the current period. Its architecture guide documents this separation. The accretion convention of the Bellman factory uses the same backward dependence, while keeping model assembly distinct from numerical solution.

docs.title: Period indices
docs.text:
Let the nonnegative integer \(h\) count periods before the terminal period. A trellis stores its periods in accretion order: periods[0] is the terminal period, periods[1] is its predecessor, and so on. Chronological order is the reverse. If the sequence contains \(n \ge 1\) periods, its inter-period joins have indices \(0 \le h < n-1\): inter_connectors[h] joins the continuation fields of periods[h + 1] to the arrival fields of periods[h]. There is no inter-period join in a one-period model. Values used in backward induction are read in the opposite direction to the forward evolution of the state.

The terminal period can contain decisions of its own. Any continuation value supplied after those decisions is separate terminal data, rather than an additional period or an inter-period connector. The trellis guide states this convention.

Appending an earlier period does not change the indices of periods already present. If economic age is measured in one-period units and terminal age is \(T\), the age at index \(h\) is \(T-h\). Age-dependent wages or survival probabilities can therefore be supplied from a parameter schedule when each stage occurrence is constructed. Where age is itself a state of the economic model, the stage file declares it as a field.

An extensible sequence is still a finite-horizon model. An infinite-horizon problem needs its own formulation or a justified limit of finite-horizon problems; numerical solutions also require convergence and accuracy checks. A terminal decision problem and a terminal value supplied to initialize a recursion are distinct modeling choices; HARK's discussion of terminal solutions illustrates the distinction.

docs.title: Reusing model components
docs.text:
The Bellman factory organizes inputs for repeated construction. A registry stores named sources of parameter values, numerical settings and methods; a recipe selects and combines those sources for the required stage occurrences; load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) of bellman.trellis returns the syntactic trellis whose records hold the merged mappings, and assemble_trellis, also of bellman.trellis, elaborates and binds it in one call. A model-building loop can use the resolved inputs for an age profile without putting the entire life cycle into each stage file.

The registry and recipe are optional means of supplying these inputs. A modeler can instead construct the period records directly. The trellis guide describes those records, and the factory guide describes the factory's calls. Neither route makes a terminal condition, an equation or a numerical method unnecessary.

docs.title: Current implementation
docs.text:
Accretion is how accrete and elaborate_trellis of bellman.trellis work. A trellis is a dictionary, {"periods": [...], "inter_connectors": [...]}, each period {"stages": {key: record or stage}, "connectors": [...]}; an empty one is {"periods": [], "inter_connectors": []}. accrete(trellis, period, inter_connector) appends a period and the mapping that joins it to the period appended before it, and rewrites no existing record. elaborate_trellis(syntactic, previous=None) constructs the stage occurrences from the records, copies those that are already elaborated and, given a second argument, those whose record is unchanged, and derives each period's joins from the fields; the three trellis verbs calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis bind every stage occurrence from the mapping the syntactic trellis holds at its key.

The application supplies the sequence of periods and its connections; no function of the package appends a period of its own accord, runs backward induction or solves a life-cycle model. The trellis guide distinguishes the representation from the operations available on it.
