docs.title: elaborated stage
docs.text:
Summary

The elaborated stage is the object the elaborator constructs from a stage file: the complete typed statement of the problem the file states, with every field, shock, law, builder and kernel explicit. It is read as a Backus FFP system, with definitions as the named objects and functions, sorts on the wires, boxes as functional forms applied to kernels, and queries as functions on the object. It is the object that is inspected, compared and described; the file is not read as text once it elaborates.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Υ §1: the elaborator, the computed step of the meaning map, which constructs this object; The stage: how a stage is made and the seven attributes it holds. Used by — Prose writer: the description of this object in words from its printed form; Judge §4: the comparator, which compares two of these objects up to a renaming. See also — semgraph: the four graphs the object holds; Functional programming and FFP: the reading of §2.

The elaborated stage (ElaboratedStage) is the object elaborate_stage and elaborate_trellis produce from a .bl stage file. It is a stage occurrence, that file elaborated at one position of a period with its own three bindings; each binding adds to it in place and returns it, and a text derived from the file is elaborated as its own stage occurrence with its origin recorded. It has seven attributes and nothing else: name, metadata, definitions, initial, _builders, bindings and provenance (The stage §2). initial holds the two initial diagrams, stage.initial.backward and stage.initial.forward, the backward and the forward blocks on field wires, two separate graphs; _builders holds the two builders graphs under a private name, and a reader reaches them through stage.builder: stage.builder.bwd, the backward builders and the policy builder on function wires, and stage.builder.fwd, the forward builders on measure wires, with each builder read by the ordered pair of perches it joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"], the policy builder by its own key, policy, or from the perch its edge leaves, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd (The builders graphs §§1 and 2). The word for the seven is attributes, never fields, since a field is a named quantity of a stage, at a perch unless it is a shock. Everything the seven determine is a query, never a stored member.

docs.title: 1 The complete typed statement of the problem
docs.text:
The elaborated stage is the complete typed statement of the problem the stage file states, and the problem is of higher order, because its entities include functions on the sets of the perches and the operators between them: every field with its perch and its set, every shock with its timing, every law, every builder as a typed map between function spaces, and the kernel of every box. In the round trip of Matsya, the project's service that writes a model's declaration from source material, the object that the elaboration of a declaration constructs is written \(E\) and named ElaboratedSemanticObject: it is an elaborated stage when the declaration is one stage file, and an elaborated trellis, whose stages are elaborated stages, when the declaration states several. Neither the stage file nor a description of the model in prose is such a statement. The stage file declares a field's set and perch where it introduces the field and leaves the rest to be resolved: the sort of a wire, the domain of a function, the coordinates a function is written in, the perch at which a shock is available, and the operators a block's lines fold to are derived by the construction and written nowhere in the file. A prose description states them informally. The elaborator, the computed step of Υ, makes every such commitment explicit in the elaborated stage or refuses the file, so that two agents cannot agree falsely on an ambiguous text: an ambiguity in the file is a refusal, and an agreement on the elaborated stage is an agreement on the complete statement.

In the sense of formal ontology, the elaborated stage is the problem's ontology made explicit. Guizzardi and Guarino (2024, §2.1) define an ontology as "a specific theory about the kinds of entity and their ties that are assumed to exist by a given description of reality"; the kinds of entity here are the sets, the fields, the functions, the laws, the operators and the parameters, and their ties are the typed wires and the kernels that join them. The word elaboration is used in the sense of programming-language theory, the translation of a surface syntax into a fully explicit, typed core form, which fails where the source does not type-check (Pfenning 2021, §§1 and 4; Ferreira and Pientka 2014, abstract), as Υ §1 states.

The elaborated stage is therefore the object that is compared and described. Two stage files that differ in spelling or in the order of their blocks elaborate to one stage; a comparison of two declarations is made on their elaborated stages, up to a renaming of names (Judge §4), and a description of a declaration in words, by the prose writer, is written from the elaborated stage's printed form and from nothing else. Nothing reads a stage file as text once it can be elaborated.

docs.title: 2 The object read as an FFP system
docs.text:
Backus's FFP has three tiers: objects, functions on objects, and functional forms that make functions from functions (Functional programming and FFP, functional form). The elaborated stage is an implementation of that reading.

  • Definitions are the named objects and functions. definitions is an ordered mapping from an identity to a Definition record: a set, a shock probability distribution (record kind distribution), a parameter, a function, a function alias, a correspondence, a g, a G or a line, the record of one statement. A set or a parameter is an object; a named function, a law of motion g, a value aggregator G and a shock probability distribution are functions: the kernels, that is, in Backus's sense, the parameters of the operators' forms, which are no economic parameters. Each is held once and referred to by identity.
  • Wires carry objects, and each wire has a sort. A wire carries one object, a field in an initial diagram, a function in the backward builders graph, a measure in the forward builders graph, and its sort is one Sort record: identity, kind, perch, role, domain, and for a function wire its coordinates. A DisCoPy type is a tuple of sorts, one per wire.
  • Boxes are functional forms applied to kernels. A primitive operator is a Box whose data is a tuple of references to definitions: a pullback refers to a g record, an aggregation to a G record, an expectation to a distribution record. What the box denotes is the image of its kernel under a fixed functional form, precomposition for a pullback, postcomposition for an aggregation, integration for an expectation (operator); a builder is a Bubble composing them (builder).
  • Queries are functions on the object. denote(), view() on the stage, fields(), kernel(), compile_kernel(), par, settings and the rest read the graphs and the table and store nothing. Each piece answers for itself: stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"].denote() answers the record whose printed form is that box's card, and stage.definitions.denote("<identity>") answers it for that definition; stage.view() is the stage's own sheet. A query that takes a box as an argument is implementation and is bound as no method. The graphs themselves are stage.builder.bwd.graph and stage.initial.backward.graph, and stage.builder.bwd.primitives and stage.builder.bwd.sub_builders are the same graph at the two grains a reader is offered (API §1).

docs.title: 3 What an identity string is
docs.text: An identity has the form <stage>:<kind>:<name>: cons:set:Xm, cons:parameter:ρ, cons:g:dcsn_to_cntn, cons:correspondence:Γ. The middle segment is the kind of the record, the package's word for what the record defines: set says the record defines a set, g that it defines a law of motion. It is no sort: the package's Sort records stand on wires, and the record kinds are a different list from the kinds of Kinds and sorts §3. Sort.domain retains the set term or None, including named-set references, inline intervals and intersections; Sort.coordinates contains coordinate identities. A record's kind is not its domain. A field wire's identity is <stage>:<perch>:<field> (cons:arvl:m), with the word shck in the place of the perch for a shock, which belongs to no perch; a function wire's names the perch and the value it carries (cons:function:cntn:V), and a box's name is its block and operation kind, with the statement's address in place of the block for an operator belonging to one statement (cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback, policy.InvEuler:Aggregation).

docs.title: 4 How the queries read them
docs.text: stage.fields() walks the blocks of the two initial diagrams in file order and reads the sorts on their input and output wires; it keeps no table. stage.par reads the parameter records of definitions and joins each with the value the calibration bound, unbound where there is none, and then the derived_parameter records, each with its declared set where it declares one and its definition evaluated at the calibration (parameters); stage.par["ρ"] answers one parameter's record, whose value is the number. A box's kernel().origins resolves its data through definitions. A box's own denote() builds its record from three sources: the line records for the statements the kernel denotes, the g, G or distribution record for the object those statements denote, and the box's dom and cod for the typed wires; the card is that record printed and is not made by taking a printed line apart. Its compile_kernel() executes the kernel's Python text, kernel().python, and answers one plain function of the kernel's arguments and then the parameters it reads, on a symbolic version as well, kernel().parameter_values giving the calibration's values in that order; a row whose rule has no explicit side, such as the identification of a policy block, is refused under the rule kernel-target. Nothing a query returns is stored as a member of the object: an answer is kept on the stage it was asked of, and a binding discards the kept answers it changes.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: semgraph · builder · operator · field · Υ · prose writer · judge · Functional programming and FFP · Functional form

docs.title: Expression
docs.text: An expression combines names, literals and operations. In Bellman-SYM, expressions occur on both sides of equations and within the definitions of functions, shock probability distributions and sets. For example, m_d - c denotes savings in the context supplied by the complete consumption stage. Arithmetic is parsed and its interpreted structure is retained; it is not opaque formula text reserved for a solver.

docs.title: Names, application and binding
docs.text:
Declarations determine a field's domain, role and information context. Parentheses apply a function; ordinary brackets select a collection entry. Perch marks distinguish arrival, decision and continuation references. A function argument or an expectation or optimization binder governs local identities: the same printed name in another scope need not denote the same variable.

The derivative term on a value field, D_{a}V[>], a named marginal-utility function such as 𝑑𝑢 and differentiation of a declared function such as D_{c}(𝑢) are distinct forms. The term alone does not establish that a supplied representation evaluates the derivative; how a derivative is evaluated is fixed where the value is built. Likewise, an implicit policy equation remains a relation until its selection and other mathematical conditions are established.

A block is a complete authored typed group of equations, and the operator it denotes is its builder. An expression inside a block is not automatically another block, builder or authored node. Whole mathematical operations and !node boundaries can be inspected separately; addition and power remain inside their equation and function definitions. See semgraph and methodization.

docs.title: Functional expressions
docs.text:
At the mathematical level, an expression can also represent a composition of functions. Backus (1978), Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?, §13.1 p. 631, represents functional forms by object sequences. The representation and meaning functions are part of the system's description (§13.3.1 p. 632). This comparison does not prescribe Bellman-SYM's parser or eliminate its temporary parsed AST (abstract syntax tree).

Use Field equations and Equation parsing rules for current source forms.

docs.title: Functional programming and FFP
docs.text: Backus's FP systems distinguish objects, functions, application, functional forms, and definitions. A functional form combines functions, or functions and objects, to form a function. Composition and construction are examples. An algebra of such forms supports reasoning about complete functions rather than an instruction sequence.

docs.title: What FFP adds
docs.text:
In Backus's formal systems for functional programming (FFP), objects systematically represent functions, and object sequences can represent functional forms. The first element determines the form; the remaining elements supply its arguments. Backus distinguishes the meaning of an expression from the function represented by an object.

This is a source for the project's emphasis on explicit composition of meaningful operations. It does not require that a compiler avoid a parsed AST, that all expressions be opaque strings, or that a staged economic language contain no bound variables. Those are separate design questions. Backus's later abbreviation AST means applicative state transition, not abstract syntax tree.

docs.title: In the Bellman calculus
docs.text:
The useful connection to the Bellman calculus is composition of whole mathematical operations with known types and stated laws. The semgraph (semantic graph) retains builders and their named operations or authored computations. Internal scalar expressions still have representations, but scalar arithmetic is not an additional advertised level of that graph.

An algebraic identity applies only under its mathematical interpretation and domain assumptions. A numerical replacement also needs an accuracy or correctness argument; functional style alone provides no such guarantee.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Backus, John (1978). “Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style? A Functional Style and Its Algebra of Programs.” Communications of the ACM 21(8), 613–641. §§11.2–11.2.4, 12, 13.1–13.3.2; §14 for applicative state transition systems.

docs.title: Field
docs.text:
A field is a named quantity of a stage with a declared set: a state, a control, a value or the multiplier of a constraint, each at a perch, or a shock, which belongs to no perch. In the buffer-stock stage, beginning assets are a field at arrival; resources and consumption are fields at decision; savings and the continuation value are fields at continuation. Once a stage declares shocks, its fields may be interpreted as random variables on an underlying probability space. The field, a function representing it in state coordinates, and the value of that function at one state are distinct objects. Stages §2 explains declarations, Appendix C §2 gives their interpretation, and Kinds and sorts §5 classifies fields.

A field name is local to its stage occurrence. The same spelling in another stage denotes another field, even when both stages stand in one period. An equation uses its own stage's declarations; a connector selects eligible continuation and arrival fields for composition without changing their names. All branches of one stage share that stage's field names, so distinct branch states require distinct names. A parameter follows a different rule: two stages in one period that declare the same parameter name share one period parameter.

docs.title: 1 What the word replaces
docs.text:
The word "variable" does five jobs in a written economic model. It is a symbol in an equation; a coordinate of the state space; a random quantity whose value depends on the history of shocks; a realized number; and, once the model is solved, a function of the state such as \(v(x)\). An economist moves between these readings without noticing, and in a paper that costs nothing. A stage file cannot afford the ambiguity, because the checks the construction performs each ask a question that only one of the five readings can answer: is this quantity known at arrival or only at decision? is this the value or the value function? is the w on the output side of one block the same object as the w[>] on the input side of the next?

"Field" names the declared quantity, which stands at a perch unless it is a shock. Under a stochastic interpretation it is a random quantity, and its perch is an information set. The other readings keep their own words: a set for the values a coordinate may take, a realization for a number, and a representing function for a function of state coordinates. The symbol is the field's name.

docs.title: 2 Why the word is "field"
docs.text:
In physics a field is a quantity attached to every point of a region: the temperature at each point of a room, the electric field at each point of space. Three features of that usage carry over. The field has a value at each point, and the value at a point is what an observer there can measure. The field is not any one of its values. And the field is not the law that determines it; Maxwell's equations relate the values of the electromagnetic field at neighboring points, but the field is the thing the equations are about, not the equations.

In a stage the points are the perches, the three information contexts of arrival, decision and continuation. Under the stochastic interpretation, measurability with respect to a perch's sigma-algebra states that the field's value can be read from the information available there. The same written base name at two perches, w and w[>], identifies two fields, equal only when a statement says so (Appendix C §1). The equations inside a block relate fields at neighboring perches, \(X_\sim = \mathrm g_\prec(X_\prec,\zeta)\) almost surely under that interpretation.

The probabilist's usage supplies one interpretation rather than the definition. A random field is a family of random variables indexed by a set of points. After shocks and an underlying probability space have been specified, the fields of a stage can be read as such a family indexed by name and perch, a shock by its name alone.

Economists already work with this object under another name. Stokey and Lucas define a plan as "a value \(\pi_0 \in X\) and a sequence of measurable functions \(\pi_t : Z^t \to X\)" (Stokey and Lucas 1989, Recursive Methods in Economic Dynamics, chapter 9 §9.1): a choice that is a measurable function of the history of shocks observed so far. A field is that object, given a name and placed at an information set inside a period of the model's trellis rather than at a date.

docs.title: 3 Two senses the word does not have
docs.text: The word has no connection with the algebraic field, the structure that makes \(\mathbb R\) a field. Nor does it mean the field of a record in a data structure, a named position holding a value.

docs.title: 4 What the word buys
docs.text:
Four things become statable and checkable.

  1. Where a quantity is known. A field other than a shock has one declared or inferred perch. A shock belongs to no perch: it is drawn between two perches and is known at the perch after its draw, according to the stage timing; a control is at decision wherever it is listed; a perch is never guessed (Perch tagging rules).
  2. A field and its representing function are distinct objects. Under the stochastic interpretation, the continuation value V[>] is a random variable measurable at continuation. A representing function \(\mathrm v_\succ : \mathsf X_\succ \to \mathsf L\) satisfies \(V_\succ = \mathrm v_\succ(X_\succ)\) almost surely, and it exists only when a version of the field is measurable with respect to the information generated by the state. The initial diagrams are drawn on fields; the builders graph of the backward builders is drawn on functions.
  3. Sameness across perches is asserted, not assumed. w[>] = a + c[>] is a statement the modeler writes; without it the two fields are unrelated.
  4. A domain is not integrability. A field declared in \(\mathbb R\) is not thereby integrable or square-integrable, and its representative is not thereby continuous; those remain obligations the construction records rather than facts it assumes (Periods and trellis §6).

docs.title: 5 Classification
docs.text: A field is classified by its role, its declared set and, unless it is a shock, its perch, and its type names the sort that is the intersection of the sorts these name (Kinds and sorts §5). The roles are state, control, value, shock and multiplier. A parameter and a declared function are not fields. In one stage's semgraph, a field is a wire of an initial diagram with local identity <stage>:<perch>:<field>, the word shck standing in the place of the perch for a shock; in a trellis, its stage occurrence address distinguishes it from the same local wire of another occurrence. A statement is represented by a box between field wires, and a builder acts on the functions or the measures that represent fields.

docs.title: Forward builder
docs.text: A forward builder propagates a probability distribution through declared transitions and the conditional distributions of the shocks. It is the builder of a forward block of a stage file, reached from the perch its edge leaves: stage.arvl.builder.fwd from arrival and stage.dcsn.builder.fwd from decision, the paths that read the pairs stage.builder["arvl", "dcsn"] and stage.builder["dcsn", "cntn"] (The builders graphs §2). On the decision edge it also needs a supplied feasible measurable policy. It acts on measures, rather than returning a state-transition function alone: the package states its operators on finite measures, of which a probability measure is the case of mass one, as a Pushforward along a law of motion and a DistributionExtension by the distribution of a shock (operations §2).

docs.title: Decision-edge construction
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be the decision-state space, \(\Gamma(x)\) the feasible actions, \(D=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\), \(Z\) the shock space and \(Y\) the continuation-state space. Assume a measurable law of motion \(g:D\times Z\to Y\), a conditional probability kernel \(\kappa(d,dz)\) and a feasible measurable policy \(\pi\). Write \(j_\pi(x)=(x,\pi(x))\).

For a measurable map \(h\), its pushforward \(h_\#\) gives the distribution of \(h\) applied to a draw. Let \(L_\kappa\) extend a measure \(\nu\) on \(D\) to the joint distribution \(\nu(dd)\kappa(d,dz)\). Then

\[ M_\pi=g_\#\circ L_\kappa\circ(j_\pi)_\#: \mathsf M(X)\to\mathsf M(Y), \]

where \(\mathsf M(S)\) is the set of finite measures on a measurable space \(S\). The operator \(M_\pi\) preserves mass, so it sends probability measures to probability measures. The construction uses a conditional joint distribution. A product of state and shock marginals is justified only by the declared independence assumptions. Transition guards must hold under the joint distribution; dropping infeasible probability mass would change the model. If a policy is only an implicit relation, the construction needs a valid selected policy: the decision push-forward is the operator at that policy, one operator for each policy, and reads the policy on no wire.

docs.title: Transition pairing
docs.text:
The corresponding undiscounted transition expectation is

\[ (P_\pi f)(x)=\int f(g(x,\pi(x),z))\,\kappa((x,\pi(x)),dz). \]

For bounded measurable \(f\), or when the required integrals are absolutely finite,

\[ \int f\,d(M_\pi\mu)=\int P_\pi f\,d\mu. \]

This identity follows by evaluating the same transition conditionally on the source state and then integrating its distribution. It does not pair probability transport with the entire backward builder: rewards, discounting, nonlinear aggregation and optimization are separate operations.

The arrival builder has the corresponding law of motion and distribution extension and is stated at no policy, no choice being made there. At stage level, forward propagation composes arrival then decision transition, \(\mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec\). The paired expectations compose in reverse order. For a deterministic transition with no shock, the distribution extension is the identity.

docs.title: State sufficiency
docs.text:
A state representation must retain the information needed for the conditional distributions and the policy problem. Measurability of a trajectory at a perch does not prove that an arbitrarily chosen state suffices. Conditional-expectation projection of a history-dependent policy is not a general optimality-preserving construction.

See Stages and perches, Operator algebra and methodization. A numerical simulation or distribution approximation must support the declared transition and policy.

docs.title: Functional form
docs.text: A functional form, in Backus's terminology, combines existing functions, or functions and objects, to form a new function. It describes how functions are assembled, rather than one particular evaluation at an argument.

docs.title: Two examples
docs.text:
For functions \(f:Y\to Z\) and \(g:X\to Y\), composition forms \(f\circ g:X\to Z\), with \((f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))\).

For functions \(f_i:X\to Y_i\), construction forms the tuple-valued function

\[\langle f_1,\ldots,f_n\rangle:X\to\prod_iY_i, \qquad x\mapsto(f_1(x),\ldots,f_n(x)).\]

These are typed mathematical examples; Backus presents FP on a common object domain with its own convention for undefined values. The notation here does not identify every Bellman operation with one of his primitive forms.

docs.title: In staged problems
docs.text:
After compatible connectors identify their fields, the operators of the stages can be composed into the operator of a period. The law of motion and the value aggregator remain whole operations in this account. Numerical methods used to implement them belong to methodization.

Backus calls the functions or objects supplied to a form its parameters. In model documentation, reserve the bare word parameters for quantities defining the economy, and say arguments of the form when that distinction matters. ASDL fields are a different notion: named positions in a syntax constructor, not the economic fields of a stage.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Backus, John (1978). “Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style? A Functional Style and Its Algebra of Programs.” Communications of the ACM 21(8), 613–641, §11.2.4, pp. 621–622. See Functional programming and FFP for FP and FFP.

docs.title: Grid
docs.text:
Summary

A grid is the finite set of points of a function's domain at which a numerical method computes and stores the function; between the points the method's interpolant supplies the values. It is the discretized domain. The grid word that names it, with its arguments, is the grid label of the operator that holds the function, beside the operator's inputs and outputs (Methods §2), and is written at the operator's place as its own entry. The grid word is one of three constructors: !Cartesian, a product of one node set per coordinate, policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)); !Points, a finite set of declared points; and !Fibred, the feasible values of a control at each state of a base grid. A grid word takes settings or sets the stage defines among its arguments, and it takes no number.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Methods §5: the grid as a finite subset of the domain and a representation as a section over it. Builds on — Methods: the method component the grid stands beside; Settings: the declared names a factor reads. Used by — Methodization: the written form of a methods file; Method types: the method words that read a grid and the grid constructors.

docs.title: 1 What is written
docs.text:
A grid is written at the place of the operator whose function it discretizes, as the typing of the operator's grid component, and the entry holds one of three grid constructors, the words that say how the points are built. The constructor !Cartesian is a product of one node set per coordinate of the function, keyed by the coordinate's name as the stage file declares it; at least one factor is written:

policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k), p=(p_min, p_max, n_p))
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m=(m_min, m_max, n_m, !expmult(nest=grid_phi)))
risk_ce.evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(m_d=(m_min, m_max, n_m), ν=E_ν)
policy.grid : !Cartesian(c=(Γ_c, n_c))

A factor takes one of four shapes. A triple of declared settings gives the lower bound, the upper bound and the count of evenly spaced points, with an optional fourth element naming an uneven spacing by a word with its own keyword arguments: !expmult(nest=grid_phi), the multi-exponential spacing, denser near the lower bound, whose nesting factor is the setting grid_phi, or !geometric, the geometric spacing. A declared node set, m=M_nodes, lists the points. The expectation operator whose quadrature nodes the coordinate takes, ν=E_ν, stands for a coordinate represented on a shock, as the smooth-ambiguity application's risk_ce is represented on resources and on the ambiguity shock. A control's factor is its feasible set with a count, c=(Γ_c, n_c), where Γ_c is the set of feasible consumption the stage defines: the grid of a maximization lies in the states and the control it searches, so the feasible set at each state is discretized with that count. Written in !Cartesian without !Fibred, such a factor states a family of grids of the control indexed by the states, one at each state, and no one grid of pairs. The spelling follows the EconForge interpolation library, whose uniform Cartesian grid is a tuple of lower bound, upper bound and count, one per axis.

The constructor !Points(nodes=P) is the finite set of the declared points P, each point written in the domain's declared coordinate order, and !Points alone is the empty grid. The points are a set the stage defines by its finite members, B := {1, 2}, or a setting declared on a fixed finite product of points, P : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊, which the settings file values by the list of its points; on a domain of two coordinates each point is a pair, declared through a product set, X2 := ℝ × ℝ and P : X2 × X2 × X2. Repeated points collapse in the set, and an interpolation may still require at least two points.

The constructor !Fibred(base=!Points(nodes=B), fibre=!Cartesian(c=(Γ_c, n_c))) pairs each state of the base grid with n_c points of the control's feasible set Γ_c at that state, so that its points lie in the graph of the feasible set, the set of feasible pairs of states and controls. The base is !Points or a !Cartesian term without feasible factors, and the fibre a !Cartesian term of feasible factors. At each state the package places the count of evenly spaced points on the closed feasible interval, both endpoints included: with B := {1, 2}, Γ_c(m) := [0, m] and n_c = 2, the grid is the four pairs (1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0) and (2, 2). A feasible interval that is open or unbounded, and a fibre of several controls, whose joint sampling is not supported, are reported as unresolved and not sampled.

!Cartesian and !Points stand wherever a method reads a grid, and at a place with no method word whose handler reads it. !Fibred stands where the domain of the problem is the base's states followed by the fibre's controls: at a solution method that chooses over the controls on the states of its output perch, such as value function iteration, and at a representation only of a function of those states and those controls. It is refused at the continuation grid of the endogenous grid method, which holds no control, and at a representation of a function of the states alone.

Each constructor may end with require= and one predicate word, or a tuple of them, that the resulting grid must satisfy: !Empty, the grid holds no point; !Cartesian, the grid is nonempty and holds every combination of its projected coordinate values; !NonCartesian, the grid is nonempty and misses some combination of them; and !UniformCartesian, the grid is Cartesian on at least one real coordinate, with at least two distinct, equally spaced values in every coordinate. A requirement is a property of the grid and no further component, and the predicate !Cartesian is distinct from the constructor of the same name. Outside the fibre of !Fibred a requirement concerns the joint grid, and inside it the grid of the control at each state. The fibred grid above is !NonCartesian, since it misses the combination (1, 2) of its projected values, and the requirement !Cartesian there is refused at configuration. An unknown word, and two words that contradict each other, are refused where they are written.

Every name in a factor is a declared setting, a declared node set, the feasible set of a control or an expectation operator of the stage, and the points of !Points are a declared setting or a set the stage defines; a number is refused. The settings are declared in the methods file with their domains, n_a : ℕ, a_min : Xa, and the values stand in the settings file (settings). At configuration the package checks each bound pair ordered and inside the coordinate's declared set, each count at least two, each node set strictly increasing, each declared point's shape and finite coordinates, inside the coordinates' declared sets where that is decided, and each requirement that the bound values decide; it checks nothing about accuracy. A declared set that reads a parameter is read at the calibration that is bound.

Once the settings are bound, the package constructs each grid at their values, and a builder's kernels().grids holds, for each place within the builder that types a grid, the realized grid, with its coordinates in declared order and its finite points, or the reason the construction cannot establish them and every required property, such as a coordinate that no factor names; no default is supplied (A builder §5).

docs.title: 2 The default and what lies outside
docs.text:
An operator that writes no grid entry has a grid built by the constructor !Cartesian over every state coordinate of the domain of the function it holds, in declared order: for the Evaluation that stores a builder's result, the states of the perch at which the stored function stands; for a solution method, the states its rows name, which for the endogenous grid method are the states of the continuation perch, the input perch of the policy builder, since the method's grid is the predetermined grid of end-of-period assets from which the points of the policy are generated (Carroll 2006, §2.2, p. 315). The default fixes the constructor and the coordinates and supplies no number; where a method needs bounds and counts, the entry writes them. The representation of the policy at the closing Evaluation of an !egm builder writes no grid entry, and one written there is refused: it reads the pairs of resources and consumption that the endogenous grid method computes at the savings on its grid, which give its nodes.

What a method does outside its grid, extrapolation or clamping at the bounds, is a keyword argument of the method word, its value a declared setting, as the durables application writes !Linear(extrapolate=extrap_policy) with extrap_policy : {0, 1}, and no part of the grid, which states its bounds only.

docs.title: 3 What a grid is not
docs.text:
A grid is a numerical object and no part of the model. A discrete set that belongs to the economics, such as the set of housing sizes a household chooses among, is the declared set of a field in the stage file and no grid, and the scalars that define it are parameters. A grid approximates a continuous domain, and the grid word that names it takes settings among its arguments. The grid is the object a representation is built on, and the representation, !Linear or !pchip, is a method: two methods over one grid store different functions between the same points. A representation may also be built from data that need no grid of its own, an authored table, the pairs of the endogenous grid method or the authored expression that !closed_form reads (Methods §5).

Formally, a grid on a domain \(X\) is a finite subset \(G \subset X\) with its inclusion \(\iota : G \to X\); restriction \(r(f) = f \circ \iota\) takes a function to its values at the nodes, and a representation is an interpolant \(s\) with \(r \circ s = \mathrm{id}\), a section in the sense of Adámek, Herrlich and Strecker (2004, Definitions 7.19 and 7.24, pp. 106–107), so that the represented functions form a retract of the function space. Methods §5 states this with its consequences. The inclusion of \(G\) in \(X\) is a map of sets and establishes no subsort relation (sort).

docs.title: Handler
docs.text: A handler is the executable callable used to carry out a selected numerical operation. A method is the algorithmic choice; the handler is its particular implementation. Methodization associates a method with a supported operation of a stage, while settings supply numerical choices such as a grid size or tolerance.

docs.title: Implementation and mathematical meaning
docs.text:
A handler's inputs and outputs must match the operation's required objects. Where a toolkit uses a different representation, an adapter converts the inputs into that representation and converts the results back. The adapter and the callable are distinct parts of the calculation.

For example, a solver may represent a continuation value by an interpolated function and the probability distribution of a shock by finitely many weighted outcomes. Its recorded contract must state where it is exact and which approximations are introduced. Neither an import path nor a method name proves correctness or semiconjugacy (strong / order).

docs.title: Finding an implementation
docs.text:
A methods file, the addition to the stage file, names the handler as a binding of the operator's place, written as the method is and valued by a quoted string that gives a package and the name of a callable in it: the consumption stage of the portfolio application binds !egm with policy.handler : "cons-port:egm", and the retirement application's consumption stages bind it with policy.handler : "asva:make_egm_1d", the one-dimensional endogenous-grid step of asva, the numerical toolkit installed beside the package. A handler may be written with or without a method word, and it is no component of the signature: the method and the grid are (Methods §7). A handler builds its numerical operator from the records that a builder's kernels() answers, which refer to no stage, from the grid the operator's grid component names, and from the keyword arguments of the method word beyond those the package reads.

A handler is not the mathematical definition of the operation. Those definitions remain in the stage and the Bellman calculus.

docs.title: Initial algebra
docs.text: An initial algebra is an algebra from which there is exactly one structure-preserving homomorphism to every algebra in the specified category. For an ordinary many-sorted signature, the ground term algebra has this property. The target operations must already be supplied; initiality does not choose their meanings or prove their analytic assumptions.

docs.title: Ground terms and free inputs
docs.text:
A signature specifies sorts and typed operation symbols. Its ground terms contain no free inputs. Their interpretation in a target algebra \(A\) is the unique homomorphism \(T_\Sigma\to A\).

For terms with free input names \(X\), use the free algebra \(T_\Sigma(X)\). An environment assigns each input a value of its declared sort in \(A\). There is a unique homomorphism extending that environment. Different environments or target operations can give different interpretations; uniqueness is conditional on those choices.

Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), §2, Proposition 2.1, p. 71, establishes initiality of the many-sorted term algebra. Their Propositions 2.3 and 2.6, pp. 72 and 75, give the free-input extension. Their Proposition 1.1 states uniqueness of an initial algebra up to isomorphism within the specified category.

docs.title: F-algebras
docs.text:
For an endofunctor \(F:C\to C\), an F-algebra consists of an object \(A\) and a map \(\alpha:F(A)\to A\). A homomorphism \(h:(A,\alpha)\to(B,\gamma)\) satisfies \(h\circ\alpha=\gamma\circ F(h)\). An initial F-algebra, when it exists, has exactly one such homomorphism into every F-algebra.

For a one-sorted operation signature, the polynomial functor \(F_\Sigma(X)=\coprod_{\omega\in\Sigma}X^{n_\omega}\) records the argument count \(n_\omega\) of each symbol. Its initial algebra is the ordinary ground term algebra, with the appropriate convention for empty carriers. A many-sorted version instead acts on families of sets indexed by the sorts. This construction is a mathematical description, not an identification with a particular software graph.

docs.title: Application to the Bellman calculus
docs.text:
In the Bellman calculus, a coarse builder can be assigned a finer expression of the same type. Exact interpretation agrees with that expansion when the target uses those assigned operations and the same free inputs. If the theory imposes equations, the expansion must respect them. Numerical approximation needs a separate argument; see adequacy.

Source binding, implicit equations and graph storage have additional requirements. Bellman-SYM uses a transient parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) and a retained semgraph (semantic graph). Shared term evaluation preserves meaning under the required purity and input assumptions; it does not equate sharing one random draw with independent resampling. Initiality establishes neither runtime correctness nor an automatic functor from the initial diagrams, the graphs of a stage on its fields, to the builders graphs, on functions; initial there names the graph elaboration constructs first and not an initial algebra.

See Initial-algebra semantics, Bellman algebra and Lawvere theory.

docs.title: Judge
docs.text:
Summary

The judge is the map \(J : (M, M') \to\) a table of agreement, from two descriptions of a model in prose and displayed equations, each named BellmanStageProse, to a table that says, on ten items, whether the second states what the first states. A language model computes it in the role BellmanStageProse_judge, under that role's instruction text; the map is not that text. Its table is recorded and is never the quantity a training revision is chosen to raise. It is not the comparator ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator, \(\cong\), the program that compares the objects the elaboration of two declarations constructs, each named ElaboratedSemanticObject.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Prose writer: the map that writes the description \(M'\) that \(J\) compares; Bellman-SYM writer: the map that wrote the first description \(M\) as a declaration. See also — Elaborated stage: the object the comparator compares when a declaration is one stage file; Υ: the meaning map whose computed part, the Bellman-SYM elaborator, stands between the two writers.

docs.title: 1 The map
docs.text: \(J\) takes two descriptions: a write-up \(M\), the description from which the round trip started, prepared from the source material \(P\) (SourceMaterial, the paper or the user's text that states the problem); and a description \(M'\), written by the prose writer from \(E\), the object the elaboration of the declaration written from \(M\) constructs. It returns a table over ten items: the state space; timing and information; the shocks; the transitions; the payoff and the aggregator; the constraints; the recursion; the optimality condition; the terminal or boundary condition; the parameters. On each item it counts three things separately: the omissions, statements of \(M\) on the item that \(M'\) does not make; the additions, statements of \(M'\) that \(M\) does not make; and the contradictions, statements of \(M'\) that contradict \(M\). It quotes the passages behind every count. An item agrees when all three counts are zero. The table also says whether \(M'\) has the form of a paper's model section and is not a transcription of a file.

docs.title: 2 How it is computed
docs.text: A language model computes the map under the instruction text of BellmanStageProse_judge, one of the Matsya instructions, the file texts/BellmanStageProse-judge.md of the configuration folder Matsya runs under. The program sends the message twice, with the two texts in both orders, and an item agrees only when both answers say so, since a language model that compares two texts can favor one for its position (the Matsya handler judge of the configuration's module matsya_handler.py). In the measuring runs \(J\) is run on a language model of a third family, never on the prose writer's, by the rule of independence those runs follow. The map is not its instruction text.

docs.title: 3 What the table is for
docs.text: The table of \(J\) is an instrument of measurement, recorded beside the trial it concerns and read by a person. It is never the quantity a revision of an instruction text is chosen to raise: a training revision is accepted on the mechanical measures, whether the files elaborate, whether the round trip closes under the comparator, agreement with checked pairs of a description and a stage file, and numerical reproduction, and \(J\) checks the prose writer on a sample of trials. Within one job of the Matsya service the agreement of \(J\) is one of the two conditions under which the job stops, the other being that the comparator finds the two elaborations \(E\) and \(E'\) equal. When the service prepares the description \(M\) from the source material \(P\), a paper's page text or a typed description, it also applies the judge to \(P\) and the prepared \(M\).

docs.title: 4 Comparing texts and comparing elaborated semantic objects
docs.text:
The comparator, ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator, \(\cong : (E, E') \to\) a comparison profile, is a program and not a role: no language model computes it and it has no instruction text. It compares \(E\) and \(E'\), the elaborations of the declarations written from \(M\) and from \(M'\), up to a renaming of their names, on every item the dossier prints: the fields with their perches and sets, the parameters, the functions with their definitions, the laws with their conditioning, the blocks with their typed inputs and outputs, and the kernel of every box. It answers a profile that reports, for each kind of item, agreement, difference or an undecided residue, with the renaming it used and the first item on which the two differ, and it calls no language model (meaning_map_training/compare.py of the package packages/meaning-map-training/, which the Matsya handler compare reaches through the job frame, the record a Matsya handler receives). Two elaborations are equal only when every compared stage is equal and the connections between the stages agree; equality is no proof that either states the source material \(P\) faithfully. \(J\) compares two texts; the comparator compares two elaborated semantic objects. The round trip, \(E' \cong E\), is decided by the comparator, and the comparison of \(M'\) with \(M\) by \(J\) is a check on the prose writer. Two texts have no canonical form, which is why the second comparison needs a language model and the first does not.

For a trellis, this program matches stage occurrences and their field names jointly with the selected connections within and between periods. For a recipe it also matches the effective parameter values after the same name correspondence. A value stated for one period is retained even when another period has an unbound $fill slot. Matching partial recipes can compare equal as declarations; the missing value remains unbound. A connection or route Bellman cannot certify yields a refusal before the program can report equality.

docs.title: Lawvere theory
docs.text:
A single-sorted Lawvere theory is a small category with finite products whose objects are the finite powers of a distinguished object. A morphism from its n-fold power to that object represents an n-argument operation; equations are represented by equalities of morphisms. A model in sets is a functor that preserves these finite products.

A signature lists operation symbols and their input/output types. It can generate a free theory; imposing equations produces an equational theory. A theory therefore specifies more than an arbitrary list of typed operations. In the many-sorted version, objects are finite products of a specified family of basic sorts.

docs.title: Relation to Bellman operations
docs.text:
This provides one possible categorical account of an algebraic language. Applying it to a Bellman model requires specifying the sorts, the operators and the equations and checking that the proposed interpretation preserves them. In particular, stochastic tensor operations need not be categorical products, and copying a draw differs from independent resampling.

An interpretation homomorphism from a term algebra is not itself the same object as a model functor from a Lawvere theory. The general initial-algebra theorem does not establish a complete Lawvere-theory model of every retained Bellman graph. Operator algebra states the structures and qualifications used in the current calculus.

See signature, initial algebra and Bellman algebra.

docs.title: Matsya collection
docs.text:
Summary

A Matsya collection is one of the five groups into which the list of indexed sources divides the files of Matsya's retrieval index: this project's repository, the private literature, the journal articles gathered for the iteration of the meaning map Υ, HARK and Buffer Stock Theory. Matsya is the project's service that writes a model's description in prose, named BellmanStageProse, and its Bellman-SYM declaration from source material, and answers questions with passages retrieved from that index. A search names the collections it reads, each collection carries one ranking weight, and a user reads a private collection only under a grant.

Relationship with other documents

Used by — Prose-to-Bellman-Sym: the passages sent to Prose-to-Bellman-Sym, and to the Model-prose-writer, the role that prepares the description from the source material, come from searches and requests that read every collection the user may read (§4). See also — Prose writer and Judge: the two other maps of the Matsya service recorded in this wiki; Handler: the Rosetta-stone term, which names a solver and has nothing to do with a collection.

docs.title: 1 The five collections
docs.text:
Collection What it holds Access repository The public pages of this project's repository, and a private part of its development notes public, with a private part under grant literature The private literature collection: books and papers on dynamic programming, category theory and computation grant articles The journal articles gathered for the iteration of the meaning map Υ grant hark The files of HARK, Econ-ARK's Heterogeneous Agents Resources and toolKit, at one fixed version public buffer_stock The source of the Buffer Stock Theory paper at one fixed version public

The list of indexed sources, selected on 7 October 2026 and renewed on 9 October, holds 814 sources: 197 of the repository, 153 of the literature, 230 articles, 209 of HARK and 25 of Buffer Stock Theory. The service's list of indexed sources, and the index itself, record each source's collection under the name corpus. A collection is not the same as a checkout: the journal articles are drawn from the literature checkout, 220 of them, and from this repository, the other 10.

The index also records, within each collection, each admitted document with the sections its headings open, the links its authors wrote and the tags it carries. A link resolves only to an admitted document of its own collection read from the same checkout: a destination that names a document of another collection, as when an article text names a note of the literature collection kept in the same checkout, is recorded as unavailable for that reason, and a link is never followed to read the file it names. Two documents are associated through a shared tag only when the tag is on their collection's list of usable topic tags: nineteen tags that name objects of the language for the repository, twenty-two topic tags of its notes for the literature, and none for the articles, HARK and Buffer Stock Theory. The two operations that read these records, related and read, apply the permissions a search applies, by collection and access class, to every document they would name.

docs.title: 2 What a collection does in a search
docs.text:
A request names the collections to read; when the request omits that field, the service reads the repository and Buffer Stock Theory, and an empty list is refused. Every candidate passage is scored by one formula,

\[ \text{score} = 0.7\,\text{lexical} + 0.3\,\max(0, \text{dense}) + 0.3\,[\text{phrase}], \]

where lexical is the larger of two numbers, the passage's full-text rank score, \(1/(1 + r)\) for its rank \(r\) among the passages that best match the query's words, and the share of the query's mathematical symbols the passage contains; dense is the cosine similarity between the embeddings of the query and of the passage, the numerical vectors that the embedding model assigns to a text; and the last term is added when the whole query, ignoring case, occurs in the passage's heading or text. The score is then multiplied by the collection's weight. Every collection has weight 1 except Buffer Stock Theory, whose weight is 0.01 in a search that reads more than one collection without naming sources, so that the paper's own passages do not outrank the passages of the other collections; a search of one collection, or of named sources, gives every collection weight 1. A request may multiply the weight of a collection it reads by a factor from 0 to 1000.

docs.title: 3 Access by collection
docs.text: The public parts of the repository, HARK and Buffer Stock Theory are open to every authenticated user. The literature, the articles and the private part of the repository each require a grant, recorded against the user in the service's grant file, which may also give a default list of grants to every user it does not name, while a user it names holds exactly the grants named there. A request that names a collection the user holds no grant for is refused, and a passage is returned only when the user may read its collection and, within the repository, the public or private part it belongs to.

docs.title: 4 The searches made in a job
docs.text: A job is the run that one request to Matsya starts, in which language models write a description and a declaration and the round trip repeats until the two agree. In a job the Matsya handlers read the index through the reading controller, the part of Matsya's program that stands between them and the index and holds every search and request within fixed permissions. The Matsya handler writer_references makes the initial search of preparation, whose query names the concepts the source material names, for the passages sent to the source preparer, the role SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, which prepares the description from the source material, and to the Bellman-SYM writer, the role BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration; the reconstruction, in which the Bellman-SYM writer writes again from the prose writer's description, makes a search of its own from that description; and the two roles may request further passages within allowances set in the configuration folder Matsya runs under. Every search and every request reads the collections the user may read, the public collections for every user and each private collection only under a grant, whether or not a page is marked for use in a language model's message, with the sources of the paper under study left out, and an initial search returns at most the number of passages that configuration sets, four at present. The passages of the literature and the articles are therefore placed in the messages of a job only for a user granted those collections.

docs.title: Matsya handler
docs.text:
Summary

A Matsya handler is a Python function in a configuration's matsya_handler.py file. These functions coordinate the work of a job of architect mode (a request to POST /v1/model-iterations): they select input material, call language-model roles, process their answers and arrange the elaboration of the declarations and the comparison of the elaborated semantic objects (elaborated stage). A configuration that enables the optional conversation role holds a fourteenth Matsya handler, conversation_reply, which answers one question asked in a session, a turn of conversation mode (a request to POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns). Python executes the Matsya handler; a language model is called only where that function requests one.

Relationship with other documents

Uses: Matsya instructions specify what the language model should do, while Reference guides in Matsya supply documentation. See also: Handler describes the separate use of this word for an implementation of a numerical operation in a solver.

docs.title: 1 Where Matsya handlers belong
docs.text:
A configuration is the folder containing Matsya's instructions, guides, settings and coordinating functions. Its matsya_handler.py file contains thirteen required functions and, in a configuration that enables the conversation role, a fourteenth, conversation_reply, which only such a configuration must hold. These are executable code, stored separately from the instruction texts supplied to language models.

The frame is the Matsya package that loads the configuration, defines the required function names and parameters, and provides access to language-model calls, the Bellman-SYM elaborator, the comparator and job records. For each job it builds one record holding these facilities and the job's data, the job frame (the class Frame), which most Matsya handlers receive as their frame argument. Small functions such as select_pages and normalize_source receive their inputs directly.

A Matsya handler coordinates a task such as writing a declaration. A numerical handler implements a selected numerical operation, such as an endogenous-grid step. Keeping the qualifier “Matsya” identifies which meaning is intended.

docs.title: 2 The required functions
docs.text:
Function Work performed cycle Coordinate preparation, declaration writing, prose writing, judging and reconstruction; repeat or stop according to the job's results and limits. prepare Obtain the economic description of the model, BellmanStageProse, from the source preparer, the role SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, and check its form and, through the role BellmanStageProse_judge, its agreement with the source material. The source preparer may first request further documentation within its allowances. write Ask the Bellman-SYM writer, the role BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration, for declarations, pass them to the Bellman-SYM elaborator, and request corrections after a refusal within the configured limit. The Bellman-SYM writer may first request further documentation within its allowances. verify_distribution Ask the role distribution_check whether the description supplies a usable law for a named random variable. prose_write Ask the prose writer, the role ElaboratedSemanticObject_to_BellmanStageProse, for a description of the elaborated semantic object \(E\) and check the answer's required form. judge Ask the role BellmanStageProse_judge to compare descriptions and process its reports of agreement or disagreement. compare Call ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator, the program that compares two elaborated semantic objects. This comparison does not call a language model. citations Check whether quotations attached to declaration blocks occur in the supplied description. unresolved_note Treat the Bellman-SYM writer's note as unresolved unless it says none, with an optional final period and ignoring case. call Assemble the role's instructions and input material, invoke the configured language-model caller and record the call's outcome. writer_references Make the initial search of a preparation or a reconstruction through the reading controller: a query built from the concepts the source material or the description names, and at most the configured number of passages of the collections the user may read. select_pages Select named pages from a saved reference guide in guide order. normalize_source Convert the request's source material into the source record used by the job. conversation_reply Optional, for a configuration that enables the conversation role: answer one question asked in a session. It searches the index once from the question, assembles the role's message from the guide pages, the passages found, the session's entries before the question, the outputs of the job this conversation discusses, the session's selected job or else its latest current job, and, for a stage file the question names, its dossier with the prose writer's description of it; it calls the conversation role, has the reading controller answer the role's requests, checks each answer's citations against the material supplied in the turn and sends a failed answer back for repair within the configured rounds.

The functions have different responsibilities. In particular, write includes a language-model call, whereas compare invokes a deterministic comparison program. The thirteen required functions therefore do not represent thirteen language-model roles or thirteen calls per job.

The compare handler receives the resolved connections selected from the same elaborated stages as the dossier. A recipe's effective period parameter values are compared with the connections. An uncertified connection or route is returned to write for correction before the comparison can report equality.

docs.title: 3 A declaration-writing example
docs.text:
Suppose the supplied description states a household's consumption problem.

  1. The write Matsya handler selects the language-guide pages and combines them with the description, any permitted retrieved guidance and any correction feedback.
  2. It calls the call Matsya handler for the role BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration, the Bellman-SYM writer. That function puts the writer's instruction text before the selected material and requests an answer from the configured language model.
  3. The language model may answer with one request in place of the files, for instance to read the definition of a perch from a guide page that the stage page links to. The write Matsya handler recognizes the request before it parses any files, has the reading controller answer it, and calls the role again with the page placed after the stable beginning of the message. The requests count against an allowance of their own and not against the rounds of correction.
  4. The language model returns declaration text. The write Matsya handler parses the returned files and calls the Bellman-SYM elaborator through the job frame.
  5. If the elaborator refuses a declaration, the Matsya handler can return the refusal to the language model for correction within the configured round limit. Its result includes the files, the elaborated semantic object, where the elaboration succeeded, and the round records.

This separates three contributions: instructions tell the language model what to produce, reference pages explain the language, and Matsya handler code determines how the call and its answer are processed. The Matsya handler does not become the language model that writes the declaration.

docs.title: 4 How Matsya handlers are loaded and changed
docs.text:
At the start of a job, Matsya checks the configuration's files against its manifest, the record of their content hashes, and checks each reference guide against its page manifest, the record of the pages the guide holds. A page manifest of the form that the guide builder now writes, matsya-guides/3, also records each saved page's sections, links and tags, and Matsya checks those records against the saved guide. It then imports matsya_handler.py, requires each named Matsya handler to be callable and checks its parameter list, the ordered names of the arguments the function accepts, against the package's requirements. It requires conversation_reply only of a configuration that names the conversation role among its roles, which must then also hold the role's instruction text and settings; a configuration that holds some of these parts without the others is refused. These checks establish file identity and compatible parameter names; they do not prove that a Matsya handler implements the intended economic task correctly.

The processor builds the job frame from the loaded texts, guides, settings and program functions, then calls cycle with it to coordinate the job. The job frame's index is the reading controller, the part of the program through which the Matsya handlers read the retrieval index and the guides' records: a Matsya handler binds it to the role of each run of prepare or write, and it then answers that role's requests for further documentation, refuses an address the role was not shown, a guide the role may not read or a passage of a collection the user may not read, holds the role within the allowances of the settings, and keeps a record of each request's outcome, which the processor writes into the job's record. A Matsya handler may narrow its searches and cannot widen them. Matsya handlers use the job frame's functions for the elaboration and for the comparison of elaborated semantic objects. In the current configuration, language-model calls go through the call Matsya handler. These calls reach the language model's provider through the frame. The frame counts the language-model tokens of each message before sending it (a token is the unit of text, a word or part of a word, in which the provider counts and prices a message) and refuses a call that would carry the tokens charged to its role, or to the whole job, past a ceiling, a limit the settings place on those tokens over all of a job's calls. After such a refusal the processor ends the job not_converged with the reason token_ceiling_reached, whatever cycle returns or raises, so a Matsya handler that catches the refusal can neither continue the job nor report another outcome.

A turn of conversation mode is run by the program's turn runner, which builds a job frame for the turn as the processor builds one for a job and calls conversation_reply once. The turn runner binds the reading controller to the snapshot of the index the turn reads, to the collections the person asking may read, to the allowances of the conversation role and to three reference guides, so that the Matsya handler places in a message only passages of the collections the person may read, the rule a job's reading controller applies as well. It counts the turn's tokens against a ceiling of its own, and it checks the Matsya handler's answer: every citation must name material supplied to the role in the turn and quote it, and a call refused at a ceiling ends the turn incomplete with the reason token_ceiling_reached, whatever the Matsya handler returns. The Matsya handler chooses the reading and assembles the messages; the turn runner alone sets the permissions, the snapshot and the limits and accepts or refuses the answer.

A revised Matsya handler is a code change to the configuration and requires an updated manifest and evaluation of its behavior. Changing a required function's name or parameter list also requires a corresponding change to the package's interface. Rebuilding guides or the retrieval index does not rewrite matsya_handler.py, and replacing the language model used by a role does not itself rewrite its Matsya handler.

Important

Review this entry whenever the Matsya build changes. If the change affects the required Matsya handlers, their parameters, their responsibilities or their relation to the frame, update this entry in the same change.

docs.title: Matsya instructions
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya instructions (matsya_instructions; in prose, the instruction texts) are the saved texts that tell each language-model role what task to perform, which evidence it may use and what answer it must return. They are stored in the configuration's texts/ folder and supplied when the language model is called. Earlier project documents call them skills. Editing them changes the instructions supplied to a language model; it does not change the language model's learned numerical parameters.

Relationship with other documents

Used by: Matsya handlers assemble the language model's input and process its answer. See also: Reference guides in Matsya supply documentation alongside the instructions; Bellman-SYM writer describes one role governed by them.

docs.title: 1 What an instruction text specifies
docs.text:
A role is a task assigned to a language model, such as writing a Bellman-SYM declaration or comparing two descriptions. Its instruction text specifies the permitted evidence, the task's rules and the required answer format. For example, the Bellman-SYM writer's instructions require it to base a declaration on the supplied economic description of the model, BellmanStageProse, and identify the statements supporting its equations.

The instructions form one part of the prompt, the text supplied to a language model for a call. Other parts may include reference-guide pages, retrieved passages, the particular economic description and feedback on an earlier answer; the messages of the source preparer and the Bellman-SYM writer also list the addresses of further documentation they may request, with their remaining allowances, and the material their earlier requests added. The economic description states the model to represent; the instructions state what to do with that description.

A configuration is the folder containing these texts, the reference guides, settings and the Python functions that coordinate the roles. The settings select the language model for each role separately from its instruction text. A role, its instructions and the language model executing it are therefore three distinct objects. The settings also limit how many language-model tokens one call and a whole job may use; a token is the unit of text, a word or part of a word, in which the language model's provider counts and prices a message.

The Bellman-SYM writer's instructions allow joined fields to retain the same local name. They ask for a short mapping such as {a: b} whether the names agree or differ, and a stage-qualified endpoint only when the bare field name is ambiguous. A parameter's supplied value is shared across the stages of its period.

docs.title: 2 The seven instruction texts
docs.text:
The configuration contains one file for each role. A file's name is the role's key with each underscore written as a hyphen: for example, BellmanStageProse-to-BellmanSYMDeclaration.md supplies the role BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration, the Bellman-SYM writer.

File under texts/ Task specified SourceMaterial-to-BellmanStageProse.md Extract an economic description from the supplied source material, or identify the information needed to do so (the source preparer); it also explains the request by which the role may first read further documentation. BellmanStageProse-to-BellmanSYMDeclaration.md Write a Bellman-SYM declaration from an economic description (the Bellman-SYM writer); it also explains the request by which the role may first read further documentation. ElaboratedSemanticObject-to-BellmanStageProse.md Write an economic description from the dossier, the printed form of the elaborated semantic object (the prose writer). BellmanStageProse-judge.md Compare descriptions and report omissions, additions and contradictions in the economic model (the judge). distribution-check.md Check whether the selected description specifies a usable probability law for a named random variable. paraphrase.md Rewrite a description in different words while preserving its mathematical statements, notation and assumptions. typed-form-writer.md Express the printed stage object in a prescribed form listing states, controls, shocks, equations and conditions, with supporting line references. conversation-answer.md, optional Answer a question asked in a session from the material supplied for it, quoting the material each claim rests on, keeping apart what a source says, a comparison and the role's own deductions, and asking the user when a choice is open (the conversation role, conversation_answer); it explains the requests by which the role may read further documentation and the outputs of the session's jobs, and states that the role writes no declaration.

A job of architect mode (a request to POST /v1/model-iterations) uses the first five roles as needed. The program that measures a training pass (round_trip.py of packages/meaning-map-training) calls the role paraphrase to compare reconstructions under changed wording. The typed-form text is required in the configuration, but the current job and that program both write the description from the dossier with ElaboratedSemanticObject-to-BellmanStageProse.md. Seven required instruction files therefore do not imply seven roles running in every job. The eighth text, conversation-answer.md, belongs to the optional conversation role: a configuration holds it only when its settings name that role, and then a question asked in a session (a request to POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns) is answered by the role under it, with the prose writer called on the dossier of a stage file the question names.

docs.title: 3 How a call uses the instructions
docs.text:
1. At the start of a job, Matsya loads the configuration and checks its files against the manifest, a record of the configuration's version and content hashes identifying the saved files.
  2. The Matsya handler for the task selects the relevant material, such as an economic description, guide pages and feedback.
  3. The call Matsya handler places the role's instruction text first, followed by those material parts. It uses the saved role text unless an explicit instruction text is supplied for that call.
  4. Before the message is sent, Matsya asks the language model's provider to count its language-model tokens. It refuses a message that would not fit the language model's context window, the most text the model can hold in one call, its answer included, and a call that would carry the tokens used by the role, or by the whole job, past a limit of the settings; either refusal ends the job without that call's answer.
  5. The selected language model produces an answer. The Matsya handler then parses the answer and applies the checks required for that task. The source preparer and the Bellman-SYM writer may instead answer with one request, a JSON object of a fixed form that their instructions explain, asking to read a guide page or an index passage, or to list what is recorded as related to one; the Matsya handler recognizes a request before it parses the answer, the program answers it within the role's allowances, and the role is called again with the result. Documentation obtained in this way explains how the language states a model; it supplies no fact about the user's model.

For the Bellman-SYM writer, the instructions require declaration files, the guide pages explain how to write them, and the task material states the particular economic model. The Matsya handler sends this input and passes the returned files to the Bellman-SYM elaborator. The language model produces the files; the elaboration is performed by the program.

docs.title: 4 When instructions change
docs.text:
Instruction texts are authored or revised as part of a configuration. After a text changes, the configuration's manifest must be updated before that configuration is used. The job record identifies the configuration and its file hashes, so the instruction version used in a run can be recovered from the corresponding saved configuration.

The guide builder, the script matsya_guide_builder.py, copies documentation pages into the reference guides under its construction policy and records their sections, links and tags. It does not generate these instruction texts. Rebuilding the retrieval index likewise leaves them unchanged. Revising instructions, changing the coordinating Matsya handlers and training a language model's numerical parameters are separate changes that can be evaluated separately.

Important

Review this entry whenever the Matsya build changes. If the change affects the roles, instruction files, loading or use of instructions in a call, update this entry in the same change.

docs.title: Methodization
docs.text:
Methodization binds numerical methods to the operators of a stage. A method names a technique and is a label on the operator it serves, beside the operator's inputs and outputs, written as a typing of the operator's name; a handler identifies the routine that performs it; the settings are the declared names whose values the methods read. None supplies a missing model equation or proves that a computed policy is optimal.

The methods of a stage are written in its methods file, the addition to the stage file: a .bl file read by the stage grammar and unioned with the stage file before elaboration. The buffer-stock addition binds the endogenous grid method on the policy builder, with the method's grid of savings, and piecewise linear interpolation on the Evaluation that stores the policy:

@methods: buffer_stock

n_a : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]
a_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the savings grid"]
a_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the savings grid"]

[id=policy, policy.method : !egm | policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
    | evaluate.method : !Linear] {
    c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>])       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m[>] = a + c[>]                 :: [id=g_cntn_to_dcsn]
    c[~] = c[>]                     :: [id=cons_choice]
}

The method stands on the policy builder, policy: the block of the addition names the stage's block by its id, its entry policy.method : !egm types the builder's method component, its entry policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) types the builder's grid component, the group | evaluate.method : !Linear types the Evaluation inside the block, and its three lines are the rows by which the method computes the policy at the operative level, the stage keeping the declared maximization in stage.declared (addition §3). stage.methods["policy"] answers the method by the place it binds at. A handler is written as a binding in the same form, policy.handler : "cons-port:egm", with or without a method word. The settings the entries name are declared in the addition with their domains and valued in the settings file.

docs.title: Where a method stands
docs.text:
A method type states the kinds of place it admits and the keyword arguments it reads (method types).
