A place is what stage.places() lists: a whole builder; the Evaluation that closes a builder, where a representation of what it stores stands; a line marked !node or any other statement with an id; a function the stage file defines; or one occurrence of an operator inside a line. The path written before .method names it:

Path Place Block id, policy The builder the block denotes, where a solution method such as !egm or !vfi stands. Block id and evaluate, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate The Evaluation that closes the builder, where a representation stands: one entry for everything the Evaluation stores, or one entry per stored object, evaluate[V[<]] for the value and evaluate[D_{k}V[<]] for the derivative a derivative line states, each with its own grid. Block id and line id, cntn_to_dcsn.risk_ce One authored line, marked !node here, whose result a representation can store at its Evaluation. Block id and operator, dcsn_to_arvl.E_ψ_ξ Every occurrence of that operator in the block; the operator alone at file level, E_ψ_ξ, every occurrence in the stage. Block id, line id and operator, dcsn_to_arvl.value.E_ψ_ξ One occurrence. Function name, 𝑢 A declared function, where a representation can store it.

stage.places() lists the places of a stage with the kind of each. A term address can be inspectable without admitting a method; the derivative operator D admits none. Interpolation or an upper-envelope routine does not create an authored equation. The constrained part of the policy must be declared, as the clause on the candidate line of the consumption stage's methods file declares the corner, or an added numerical boundary segment identified as an extension outside the interior equality (Constraints §4.3).

docs.title: Specification contract
docs.text:
The stage verb stage.methodize reads its additions into the stage, which is elaborated anew from the union, so that the stage carries the method and grid components and the handlers the additions type. In a trellis, elaborate_trellis reads at every position the additions the recipe names for the stage occurrence, in order, with the stage text, and methodize_trellis binds nothing more. A component typed by two files with different content is refused, an unknown method word and an unresolved path are refused, and a method at a place of a kind it does not admit is refused naming the place.

The entry specified stage states the order of the bindings. The specification factory states how the recipe combines its sources, and it creates no mathematical object. Whether a handler can carry a method out requires checks of the implementation in addition to the declared contract. See Methodization and Stage functions.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Summary

A method is the numerical procedure chosen for one operator of a stage: a quadrature rule for an expectation, an interpolant for the function an Evaluation stores, a solution method such as the endogenous grid method for the policy builder. It is named by a word with keyword arguments, !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes), !Linear(extrapolate=extrap_policy), !egm, and written as the typing of the operator's method component, policy.method : !egm, so that the method is a label on the operator, beside its inputs and outputs and its grid. The model does not depend on it: forgetting every label leaves the model's operations unchanged, and forgetting the methods file returns the stage file.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Methods: the signature with its components, composition, the method as a type, the handler, the erasures and the two levels. Builds on — Grid: the discretized domain beside the method; Settings: the names a method's arguments read; Addition: the methods file that writes the entries. Used by — Methodization: the binding of methods to a stage and the places they bind at; Handler: the program that computes a method; Method types: the catalogue.

docs.title: 1 Where a method stands
docs.text:
A method types an operator and nothing else: not a field, which is a quantity and not a computation, and not a side of a block header, the inputs before the arrow or the outputs after it, whose perch word types the states and the values listed on it. The entry is written in the methods file, an addition to the stage file, inside the bracket of the block that holds the operator, [id=policy, policy.method : !egm | evaluate.method : !Linear] { … }, the block's own method in the first group and each inner operator's in a group opened by |; or at file level with the full path, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.method : !Linear. The places that admit a method are those stage.places() lists: a builder; the Evaluation that stores the builder's result, named by what it evaluates where the value and its stated derivative are represented apart, evaluate[V[<]].method and evaluate[D_{k}V[<]].method; an operator of a line, such as the expectation E_ψ_ξ or the maximization argmax; a line marked !node, a computation inside a block that the author names so that a method can stand on it; and a declared function. The derivative operator D admits no method.

Which methods an operator admits depends on its operation kind, the name under which the package lists the operation, such as Expectation or Evaluation. The methods admitted at one operation kind form one set (Methods §4), and the catalogue Method types lists each word with the kinds of place it admits and the keywords the package reads. A further keyword is read by the handler that computes the method. A method takes keyword arguments only, each valued by the name of a declared setting, a quoted string or a word with its own arguments. Its entry writes no number: every number that a method reads is a declared setting, which the entry names and the settings file values, and no value is part of a signature.

docs.title: 2 What a method does to the stage
docs.text: A method does one of three things, according to the operator it stands on. A representation, !Linear, !pchip or !closed_form, stores a function from the data its family accepts: an authored table, the policy pairs of !egm at its builder's closing Evaluation, a complete authored expression, or its values on the grid its grid component names (Methods §5). It stands at the Evaluation that closes a builder, one entry for everything the Evaluation stores or one entry per stored object, each with its own grid; or at a !node line or a declared function. A solution method, !egm or !vfi or time iteration, stands on a builder and supplies the lines by which the builder is computed at the operative level, the stage keeping the declared lines in stage.declared (addition §3); !vfi supplies no lines. A method of an operator of a line fixes how that operation is computed: a quadrature or a discretization of a law at an expectation, !gauss_hermite or !tauchen, and a root finder or a search at a maximization. Interpolation and the comparison of candidates inside a method create no authored equation, and no method proves that a computed policy is optimal.

docs.title: 3 Composition and erasure
docs.text: Two operators compose when the outputs of the first are the inputs of the second; the method plays no part in that condition, and a composite carries the list of its operators' labels, which are kept and never combined. This is the composition of parametrized morphisms of Capucci, Gavranović, Hedges and Rischel (2022, Definition 2, p. 236) under the trivial action. The exact meaning of a stage reads no label; the numerical semantics Ρ reads each label as the routine its handler computes, a handler in the sense of Plotkin and Pretnar (2009): a model of the operators it admits, extended to every composite. Forgetting every label is the erasure \(U_m\), and assigning them from a methods file the methodization \(M_m\), with \(U_m \circ M_m = \mathrm{id}\), the identity label, the list with no entries, standing on every operator without an entry; forgetting the methods file by its provenance is the second erasure, which returns the stage file (Methods §8). A stage is methodized when some operator carries a method label other than the identity label. stage.methods answers each method by the place it binds at, and stage.builder[...].signature() prints the two components beside the inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Operator
docs.text:
An operation symbol names an operation in a signature and has a rank, its input sorts and its output sort (Kinds and sorts §3). Its interpretation is a mathematical map on the chosen domains. For example, the pullback maps a continuation function to its composition with the law of motion.

The symbol and its interpretation are distinct. A first-order signature can treat an operation solely as a symbol without introducing operator-valued data. This is a choice of signature, not a claim that a mathematical operator can never be a function or an element of a function space. In a specified category, a typed operation may be represented as a morphism.

docs.title: Primitive and composite operations
docs.text:
An operation is primitive relative to a signature when it is taken as a generator. It is composite when it is expressed using other operations. A whole builder can be primitive in a coarse signature and have a composite expansion in a finer one. Calling a transition-induced operation “induced” describes how its meaning is supplied; it does not by itself determine whether the chosen signature treats it as primitive.

For the graphs and the inspection grains of the semgraph (semantic graph), see that entry. Natural Bellman primitives include whole law-of-motion and scalar aggregator definitions. Authored nodes can contain several primitives or name part of one; arithmetic remains inside the complete definitions, not an additional advertised grain. Primitive status in a mathematical signature and the named primitive inspection grain should not be treated as a proof of the same representation at every level.

The operator catalogue lists the mathematical operations. The entries backward builder and forward builder explain their value and probability domains. A selected maximum is a composite of choice-value construction, a selection from the maximizing set and the insertion of the selected policy, defined only on a domain where the stated selection exists.

docs.title: The operations of a builder
docs.text: In a stage, an operator is what a box of the backward or the forward builders graph denotes, and inside a builder the word means a primitive operator, the finest box. Each primitive operator is of one operation kind, the name under which the package lists it among the operations of a builder: Pullback, Aggregation, Expectation, Evaluation and Argmax in the backward builders graph, and Pushforward and DistributionExtension in the forward one (operations §2; Operators §4). A relation, the rule of an Aggregation or a Pullback whose output is among its own unknowns, is no operation kind of its own. The package's table also defines PolicyInsertion, the insertion of a policy into a choice-value function, which no stage of the applications forms as a row of its own: at a policy the insertion is part of the indexed pullback or push-forward. The builder is the operator of a whole block, and a sub-builder is the one box inside a builder that is not primitive.

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text: A kernel is the mathematical data an operator uses: a law of motion for a pullback or a push-forward; a value aggregator for an aggregation; a shock probability distribution, the distribution a ~ line of the stage file declares for a shock, read as conditional on the information at the edge's source perch (Shock distributions), for an expectation or a distribution extension; a correspondence; or a policy reference, which at a policy is part of the indexed law of motion, aggregator or distribution. A law of motion is the map from the states of a perch, with the control and the shock where the edge has them, to the states of the next perch; the forward block of the edge declares it. A kernel's inputs and outputs are its arguments, which are points, while an operator's are its wires, which carry functions or measures. kernel() on an operation answers the kernel's line with its defining records under origins, and compile_kernel() the plain Python function made from the kernel's text, kernel().python, whose arguments are the kernel's own and then the parameters it reads (A piece §2). In Backus's sense a kernel is the parameter of the operator's form, never an economic parameter.

docs.title: Mathematical interpretation
docs.text:
A mathematized operator is an operation supplied with its mathematical interpretation. The interpretation can remain parameterized; it need not have a numerical method or a fully chosen calibration. This is the same symbol/interpretation distinction, not an additional kind of runtime object.

Declared names also identify authored occurrences and boundaries. Two differently named equations may denote the same function without becoming one retained node. Equal ranks do not imply equal operations, and equal denotations do not erase method-attachment addresses.

A method specifies a numerical procedure (methodization); a handler is the package routine intended to compute it. Their correctness requires the domain and approximation checks in adequacy. Initiality explains unique composition under fixed mathematical assignments, not the correctness of arbitrary routines.

See Operator algebra and Equation boundaries and indexing.

docs.title: Ordering conventions
docs.text:
Three different orders appear in a model built from stages. State which one is being used.

Order Meaning Within-stage information Arrival, then decision, then continuation, subject to the stage's declared observations and choices. Forward economic time Earlier decisions and states precede later ones. Dependencies determine this order. Trellis index \(h\) Zero is terminal; a larger index is earlier in economic time.

A backward calculation starts from supplied continuation values. In a chain with stage operators \(T_1,\ldots,T_K\) named in forward economic order, \(T_1\circ\cdots\circ T_K\) applies \(T_K\) first. Function composition is read right to left.

A forward calculation starts from a distribution and a specified policy, then follows transitions in economic order. It is not obtained by applying an inverse Bellman operator. Backward builders and forward builders, the two directions of builder, define the two operations.

Perch marks [<] and [>] describe information within one stage; they do not mean calendar lags and leads. YAML list order does not replace field dependencies. The period and trellis entries give the respective composition and index rules.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameters define the mathematical economic model: for example, discounting, risk aversion, the coefficients of shock probability distributions and scalars that define an economic state domain. A parameter is a name declared in the .bl stage file with a set, with no role word, no perch word and no law, which no block header lists and no line writes: β : (0,1). A line of a block that writes a name so declared is refused under parameter-or-field. A role word, such as !ctrl, and a perch word, such as !dcsn, are written in the type of a field, and a name that a block header lists is a field. A law, such as z ~ N(0,1), gives a shock its distribution. The set is the parameter's declared set, which may name other parameters, as Γ : (0, R) does. Calibration supplies its value through a separate source mapping.

A derived parameter is a name defined by :=, without arguments, by a formula whose value is a number, from parameters, derived parameters and numbers, with or without a declared set: h := 1/(1 - Γ/R) or q : (0,1) := (β*R)^(1/ρ)/R. It is defined in the stage file or in a methods file, with signs, arithmetic, powers, log, exp, min and max, or by cases, h : ℝ_{+∞} := if Γ < R then 1/(1 - Γ/R) else inf, where a definition that may take an infinite value declares a set that holds it, and without a cycle among the definitions. A definition that declares a set must read at least one name. ρ : ℝ := 2 is refused under readable-form, since a stage file declares the set of such a name and the calibration file supplies its number. Calibration supplies no value for a derived parameter and refuses one; its value is its definition evaluated at the calibrated values, and calibration refuses a value outside the set the definition declares. The parameter lines of a file together define one admissible set of parameter vectors, and each line adds one condition: a declaration adds that the parameter's value lies in its declared set, and a definition adds that its formula has a value in its declared set, which is ℝ where it declares none (Kinds and sorts §4). A parameter is no field and no wire of a graph: it is named inside the definitions that use it, and its declaration and value stay open to inspection.

stage.par lists the parameters of a stage version, each with its declared set and its bound value or the word unbound, and after them each derived parameter with its definition, written after its declared set where it declares one, and its value at the calibration. stage.par["ρ"] answers one parameter's record, read by the name the file declares, and its value is the number calibration bound (Parameters and settings §1).

docs.title: Parameters versus settings
docs.text:
A discrete set of housing choices can be part of the model itself; the scalars defining that set are parameters. A finite grid used only to approximate a continuous savings domain is a numerical representation; its bounds and size belong to the settings. The file that declares a quantity decides whether it is a parameter or a setting, and the author chooses the file by what the quantity means, not by whether it happens to be an integer or is called a grid size.

In the constrained consumption example, ρ : (1, inf) declares risk aversion above one. A calibration mapping can supply ρ: 2. The declared set belongs to the equation's meaning; a handler option cannot silently replace it. See Stages and Field equations.

A parameter is declared by a stage and belongs to the period the stage stands in: a name two stages of one period declare is one parameter of that period. Its declared sets must be the same or have a nonempty intersection the package can establish for real sets and intervals with numeric endpoints; its calibration sources must supply one value. Conflicting declarations or values are refused with the period and declaring stages identified. The same spelling in another period is another parameter (The trellis factory §4). A field name, by contrast, is local to its stage. Every declared parameter needs a value for calibration. Shared mappings may contain extra keys, but those keys do not create new parameter declarations. The syntactic trellis holds the merged mappings that the specification factory produces from such sources, and the stage verb binds and checks its required inputs.

Parameter restrictions defining admissible economic models are distinct from search choices made by an external estimation algorithm. That distinction does not create an estimation API in Bellman-SYM. Numerical feasibility, existence of an optimum and statistical identification also do not follow merely from supplying admissible parameter values.

docs.title: Perch and information set
docs.text: A perch is one of the three information contexts within a stage: arrival, decision, and continuation. The abbreviation ADC refers to this Arrival–Decision–Continuation ordering. A perch describes what is known, not an endpoint of a numerical operator or a separate calendar date.

docs.title: Information and state coordinates
docs.text:
In a probabilistic model, an information set can be represented by a sigma-algebra: a collection of events whose occurrence can be determined from the available information. A field measurable with respect to that sigma-algebra is a quantity determined by that information. The state vector need not record everything the household remembers. Using it as the argument of a value function requires a separate sufficiency condition.

For example, beginning assets are known before an income draw, resources are available when consumption is chosen, and savings are available for continuation. A transition that compresses assets and income into resources can discard information. Nested information contexts therefore do not imply that the sigma-algebras generated by the chosen state coordinates are nested.

docs.title: Written marks and declarations
docs.text:
V[<] requests arrival value; V[>] requests continuation value. A bare V or V[~] denotes decision value when its declaration and expression context establish that reading. Bare names in general are resolved from declarations and context; they are not all decision fields.

A block header states the contexts of its ordinary state and value coordinates. A control retains its decision role when listed as an argument beside continuation inputs. A shock used by a transition is not thereby known at the input perch. Its conditional distribution, scope, and use determine which uncertainty is integrated out.

Perch marks do not invert transitions, infer missing state sufficiency, or make an unobserved shock observable. Branch labels distinguish alternatives within the continuation interface; they do not add a fourth perch. Perch tagging rules gives the precise syntax and examples.

docs.title: Period
docs.text: A period collects stage occurrences and their within-period connections. Its fields remain local to each stage, while a parameter name declared by more than one stage denotes one parameter of that period. It also supplies a boundary through which the period joins its successor. The outer description is YAML; individual stage equations are written in .bl.

docs.title: The period file
docs.text: The outer description of a period is the period file, period.yml, a template that a trellis file names under template: and repeats. Its stages take one of two shapes. Written as a list of stage keys, the file binds nothing, and the recipe spec.yml of the specification factory supplies each stage's file and its values, settings and methods. Written as a mapping from each key to a record that names the stage file under stage and its three mappings, the file carries the bindings and needs no recipe. The two shapes are not mixed in one file, and a variant of the period stands beside it as period.<name>.yml. Period Syntax §1 writes the template, and Trellis Syntax §3 states the two shapes.

docs.title: Economic order
docs.text:
Field dependencies determine the order in which connected stages can be evaluated. Reordering names in a YAML list does not reorder economic decisions. Changing a dependency or successor can change the information and objective of the model.

The period example joins consumption, discounting, and investment. An authored connection selects a specified outgoing state field and incoming state field; a matching name supplies a connection only when one compatible, globally consistent choice is available. Interest, income, and discounting appear in equations; a connector selects fields but renames neither one.

docs.title: Backward composition
docs.text:
For a chain of stage operators \(T_1,\ldots,T_K\) listed in forward economic order, and after the identifications its connectors make, the period's backward operator is

\[T_{\mathrm{period}}=T_1\circ\cdots\circ T_K.\]

The rightmost operator acts first on continuation value. This formula assumes compatible value domains and well-defined component operators. Branching structures require their declared routes and continuation inputs rather than an arbitrary linear ordering.

A trellis assembles period occurrences across dates. The choice of a period boundary is part of the decomposition of the model; terminal conditions and numerical choices remain explicit.

docs.title: Prose writer
docs.text:
Summary

The prose writer is the map \(\Upsilon_1 : E \to M'\) from the object the elaboration of a declaration constructs, \(E\), named ElaboratedSemanticObject (an elaborated stage for one stage file, an elaborated trellis for several), to a description \(M'\) of the model \(E\) states, in prose and displayed equations, an object of the same kind as the description \(M\) the round trip starts from, BellmanStageProse. It writes \(M'\) from the printed form of \(E\), the dossier, and from nothing else. A language model computes it in the role ElaboratedSemanticObject_to_BellmanStageProse, under that role's instruction text; the map is not that text. It reads \(E\) and never the stage files: a declaration is elaborated before anything reads it.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Elaborated stage: the object described when the declaration is one stage file; Υ: the meaning map, of which the Bellman-SYM elaborator followed by the prose writer is a reading in words; The stage and the pages after it: the queries the dossier prints. Used by — Judge: the role BellmanStageProse_judge, which compares \(M'\) with the description the writing started from; Bellman-SYM writer: the map that writes \(M'\) as a declaration again in the round trip.

docs.title: 1 The map
docs.text:
The prose writer takes \(E\) and returns a description \(M'\): the model \(E\) states, written as the model section of a paper would state it, in prose and displayed equations, in a fixed order: the states, the controls, the shocks and their timing, the laws of motion, the recursion, the condition that determines the policy, and the parameters. Where \(E\) states a problem of several stages joined in a period, \(M'\) describes the stages in the order of the period and says which quantity one stage passes to the next.

What the prose writer reads is the dossier: the numbered printed description of \(E\) assembled from the stage object's public queries, the stage's printed view, its definitions, its builders with their signatures, its primitive operators with their kernels and typed wires, its initial diagrams and its obligations (API), printed by dossier_lines of bellman.dossier. The dossier the prose writer receives is anonymous: the stage's own name is replaced by the word stage, and every source path is removed. The prose writer receives the dossier and the pages of the stage object's interface, uses no tool, opens no file and keeps no memory between calls.

docs.title: 2 How it is computed
docs.text:
A language model computes the map under the prose writer's instruction text, one of the Matsya instructions. The text exists in two forms, and the map has two forms with it.

  • The paper form, whose answer is \(M'\): a model section of 300 to 800 words under seven fixed headings, with no dossier line numbers and no spelling of the stage-file language, so that the description states the economics and does not transcribe the file. A program checks the headings, the length and the absence of line numbers and language tokens before anyone reads the description, and where the check fails the prose writer is called once more with its findings.
  • The canonical form, whose answer is the typed form \(B'\): the problem under the headings of the formal pages, with the line of the dossier cited under every equation and an equation that rests on no line marked inferred. It is used where a judge compares a reading with a paper.

In the configuration folder Matsya runs under the two texts are texts/ElaboratedSemanticObject-to-BellmanStageProse.md and texts/typed-form-writer.md, the second being the text of a separate role, typed_form_writer, and the Matsya handler prose_write of its module matsya_handler.py prints the dossier, builds the message and checks the form. The map is not its instruction text; training revises the text and leaves the map's domain and codomain as they are.

For a period or trellis, the dossier also states which continuation field of which stage is connected to which arrival field, both within a period and between periods. A recipe dossier states the parameter values supplied in each period and identifies a period whose $fill value remains unbound. These are read from the elaborated object rather than inferred from the author's connector spelling.

docs.title: 3 Why \(E\) and not the file
docs.text:
Nothing reads a declaration \(D\) as text. \(D\) is elaborated first, and the prose writer describes \(E\), because \(E\) is the complete typed statement of the problem (Elaborated stage §1): it lists every field with its perch and its set, every shock with its timing, every law, every builder as a typed map between function spaces and the kernel of every box, so that the prose writer describes what is printed and infers nothing. The Bellman-SYM elaborator followed by the prose writer is a reading of the meaning map Υ in words, and it is the simpler of the two directions of the round trip; the Bellman-SYM writer must find a file whose meaning is the model, and many files have one meaning.

A description that quoted the file's lines in order would let the Bellman-SYM writer copy them in the reconstruction and would test nothing about meaning. The paper form, the check of the form, the different families of language model behind the two maps, and a paraphrase of \(M'\) by a model of a third family in the measuring runs guard against it.

The prose writer serves conversation mode as well, in a configuration that enables the conversation role: when a question asked in a session names a stage file, the program elaborates the file, the prose writer describes its dossier as it does in a cycle, and the conversation role receives the dossier and that description and never the file's text. The conversation role cites the dossier, since the description is a reading of it by a language model.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: Υ · elaborated stage · Bellman-SYM writer · judge · semgraph

docs.title: Rank
docs.text:
In the local typed-operator vocabulary, an operator's rank is its input/output profile \(s_1\times\cdots\times s_n\to s\) (Kinds and sorts §3). It states which sorts an operation accepts and which sort it returns. Distinct named operations can have the same profile; the profile does not determine their meaning.

Terminology varies by source. Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), §2, p. 70, call the full pair of input sorts and output sort the type, the input-sort string the arity, and its length the rank. Thus their rank is an argument count. Goguen and Meseguer (1992, Definition 2.1) call the full pair the rank, which is the usage here. State the convention when comparing sources.

docs.title: Model and numerical types
docs.text:
A signature declares operation profiles. The interpreted operation acts on the corresponding chosen carrier sets, while the type of a field also names its role, its declared set and, unless it is a shock, its perch. The input/output profile of one operation is not a complete description of the model's typing context.

A numerical method may approximate the same mathematical operation using grids or other representations. Equal mathematical ranks do not make numerical arrays interchangeable or guarantee equal answers. State the numerical domains, comparison maps and approximation conditions; see adequacy and Operator algebra.

See operator, sort and signature.

docs.title: Recursive decision process (RDP)
docs.text: A recursive decision process constructs policy evaluation maps from feasible actions and a choice-value aggregator. It refines the abstract dynamic program (ADP) by specifying how the current state, current action and continuation value determine an update.

docs.title: Primitive data
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(A\) be measurable state and action spaces. A feasibility correspondence \(\Gamma\) assigns a nonempty set \(\Gamma(x)\subseteq A\) to each state. Its graph is \(D=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\). Let \(\Pi\) be the feasible measurable policies and \(V\) a specified class of real-valued functions on \(X\).

An aggregator \(B:D\times V\to\mathbb R\) supplies the choice value. It is monotone in its continuation argument, and each induced policy update must remain in \(V\):

\[ (T_\pi v)(x)=B(x,\pi(x),v),\qquad T_\pi v\in V. \]

A nonempty feasible set at every state alone does not establish a measurable policy. The associated policy family must meet the hypotheses of the ADP construction. Its Bellman supremum is defined only where that supremum exists in the chosen space. Replacing it by an attained maximum over actions additionally requires the relevant feasibility and measurable-selection conditions.

For additive expected utility, a common aggregator is

\[ B(x,a,v)=r(x,a)+\beta\int v(g(x,a,z))\,\kappa(x,a,dz), \]

where \(r\) is current reward, \(g\) the law of motion, \(\kappa\) the conditional distribution of the shock and \(\beta\) a discount factor. The integral must be defined on every required feasible pair. More general recursive preferences specify their own order of expectation and aggregation; they need not have this form.

docs.title: Relation to Bellman-SYM
docs.text:
A model written in Bellman-SYM declares, stage by stage, feasible controls, transitions, shock probability distributions and value equations. Through the backward builders of each stage these can determine an RDP-like aggregator under the required domains and closure conditions. This is a mathematical comparison, not a one-for-one correspondence with source keys: a stage's continuation and decision value spaces can differ. See Operators and builders.

The Coleman–Reffett operator updates consumption policies through an Euler equation, while the Bellman operator updates value functions. A correspondence between them requires specified value and policy classes, a valid transformation and its inverse, and the operator identity. EGM uses additional differentiability, feasibility and inversion conditions. It is not available merely because a problem is an RDP. See semiconjugacy (strong / order) and methodization.

Reference: Sargent and Stachurski, Dynamic Programming, Volume II: General States, recursive decision process definition and the construction of policy operators from an aggregator.

docs.title: Reference guides in Matsya
docs.text:
Summary

A reference guide in Matsya, one of the matsya_guides (in prose, the reference guides), is a saved file containing copies of published Bellman documentation pages, joined together: a fixed set of pages and the concept-wiki pages they link to or share a topic tag with. Matsya supplies selected pages to a language model as reference material alongside its role instructions and task material. The guides are produced by an operator running matsya_guide_builder.py with Python, when preparing or refreshing a configuration, and a record beside them lists each saved page's sections, links and tags. A language-model call reads the saved guides; rebuilding the retrieval index does not regenerate them.

Relationship with other documents

Used by: Bellman-SYM writer and Prose writer explain the two writing roles that receive guide pages. See also: Matsya collection describes the groups of sources searched for additional passages. Related concepts: Matsya instructions specify the tasks; Matsya handlers select the material and coordinate the calls.

docs.title: 1 What each guide contains
docs.text:
A configuration is the folder containing Matsya's role instructions, reference guides, settings and the functions that coordinate the roles. Its guides/ subfolder contains three guide files:

Guide file Documentation copied into it Roles that receive selected pages writer-guide.md The overview pages, the main Bellman-SYM guide pages and the language reference pages; then the concept-wiki pages they link to or share a topic tag with The source preparer, SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse; the Bellman-SYM writer, BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration; and, in a configuration that enables it, the conversation role, conversation_answer, which receives the pages conversation_pages names from this guide reader-guide.md The stage-interface overview and the pages describing the stage object; then the concept-wiki pages they link to or share a topic tag with The prose writer, ElaboratedSemanticObject_to_BellmanStageProse, and, in a configuration that enables it, the conversation role, conversation_answer, which receives the pages conversation_pages names from this guide calculus-guide.md The Bellman calculus pages listed in the site's navigation, in navigation order; then the concept-wiki pages they link to or share a topic tag with The source preparer, SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, and, in a configuration that enables it, the conversation role, conversation_answer, which receives the pages conversation_pages names from this guide

The source preparer, the role SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, writes the economic description of the model, BellmanStageProse, from the source material, the supplied paper or user description. The Bellman-SYM writer then writes declarations from that description. The prose writer describes the elaborated semantic object \(E\) (elaborated stage), the object the elaboration of those declarations constructs. Its reference file is named reader-guide.md. The conversation role, conversation_answer, which a configuration may enable, answers one question asked in a session, a turn of conversation mode, quoting the material each claim rests on; it writes no declaration. The setting conversation_pages lists the guide pages placed after the role's instruction text in each message of a turn, and each page it lists is taken from the first of writer-guide.md, calculus-guide.md and reader-guide.md that saves it, so that a page saved in two guides is supplied once.

The pages listed first in each row are the guide's core pages. A page added because a core page links to it, or shares a topic tag with it, is a supporting page; a topic tag is a tag, a word written after # in a page or listed under tags: in its front matter, that names an object of the language, such as stage or perch. A supporting page is one link or one shared tag away from a core page and never further, and a guide holds at most as many supporting pages as core pages and at most twice the text of its core pages; the pages linked from more core pages are added first. The construction policy, the file guide_policy.json beside the guide builder, states each guide's core pages, the pages it may add, its topic tags and these limits. It changes only with the program, so that every configuration compared in a training pass holds the same guides.

The guide builder copies page text, removes HTML comments and trailing whitespace, and inserts a marker naming each source page. It never shortens a page and generates no summary. Settings select which saved pages each role receives; the full guide is not automatically included in every call. A supporting page reaches a language model when a setting names it or when the source preparer, the Bellman-SYM writer or, in a configuration that enables the conversation role, that role requests it: in place of an ordinary answer, each of these roles may ask to read a saved page or section of a guide it may read, or to list what the guide records as related to a page it has been shown, its authored links and the pages that share a topic tag with it. The source preparer may read writer-guide.md and calculus-guide.md, the Bellman-SYM writer writer-guide.md alone, and the conversation role all three guides. The program answers such a request from the guide and its manifest alone, places the requested text after the stable beginning of the role's next message, and counts the request against the role's own entry of the setting reading: for the source preparer and the Bellman-SYM writer within one run of the preparation or of the writing, and for the conversation role within one turn.

Beside the guides, the page manifest records each saved page's sections, the links written in it and the tags it carries. A link is recorded as available when its target is saved in the same guide, and otherwise with the reason it is not: no such page, no such section, a page the policy does not admit, a web address, a form of link the builder does not resolve, or a page the guide did not save. The builder never follows a link outside the pages its policy admits and never fetches a web address.

docs.title: 2 Reference material and instructions
docs.text:
A role instruction text, one of the matsya_instructions, tells the language model what task to perform, which constraints to follow and what answer to return. A reference guide supplies documentation needed to perform that task. The two are stored separately and included as separate parts of the language model's input by the Matsya handlers.

For example, the Bellman-SYM writer receives instructions to produce a declaration, guide pages explaining the language's syntax and meaning, and the economic description to represent. The guide may state syntax rules, but it does not specify the particular economic model. Neither the instruction text nor the guide is a set of learned weights, the numerical parameters of the language model.

docs.title: 3 When the guides are produced
docs.text:
Preparing or updating a configuration has three relevant steps:

  1. Run the operator's guide-construction script, matsya_guide_builder.py, with Python and --output naming the configuration's guides/ folder. It reads the documentation pages its policy admits and writes the three guides and their page manifest, which records each saved page's source path, content hashes, sections, links and tags, and the policy the guides were built under. A build that cannot finish, because the policy is incomplete, a core page is missing or a page changed while the builder read it, leaves the earlier guides as they were.
  2. Write the configuration's separate manifest.json, which records the version and hashes of the other configuration files, including the guides. The guide builder does not write this outer manifest.
  3. At the start of a job of architect mode, and of each turn of conversation mode in a configuration that enables the conversation role, Matsya loads the configuration and checks its files against that manifest, and it checks the recorded sections and links against the saved guides. Calls of the source preparer, of the two writers and of the conversation role use the selected pages from those saved guides, and the source preparer, the Bellman-SYM writer and the conversation role may request further saved pages within their allowances.

Editing a documentation page does not change a saved guide, and loading the configuration does not check whether the original documentation has since changed. To make the language model receive the revised page, rebuild the guides and update the configuration manifest. Changing which already-saved pages a role receives changes the settings and configuration manifest; it does not require copying the documentation again.

docs.title: 4 Relation to retrieval
docs.text:
A retrieval index stores passages in a form that can be searched for a question. The operator builds it separately with build_retrieval_index.py, which extracts passages from reviewed sources, computes numerical text representations for similarity search, and checks the resulting index before making it available. It also records the sections, links and tags of the Markdown sources it admits, read by the same parser as the guides' and resolved by the same rules, against the sources of the link's own collection rather than the pages a guide saves. Its retrieved passages can supplement the fixed guide pages.

The guide builder reads documentation pages directly. It does not search the index, build an index or train a language model. Conversely, rebuilding the retrieval index does not refresh the guide files. When a documentation change should be reflected in both, update the saved guides and the index separately.

Important

Review this entry whenever the Matsya build changes. If the change affects the guides' contents, construction, page selection or use by a language-model role, update this entry in the same change so that it continues to describe the implemented behavior.

docs.title: Referential transparency
docs.text: Referential transparency permits an expression to be replaced by another with the same meaning without changing the meaning of the enclosing expression. The environment, types, and binding context must be fixed, and substitution must not capture a free variable.

docs.title: Compositional reasoning
docs.text:
For a compositional semantics, the meaning of a compound expression is determined by the meanings of its parts. Equality of the relevant subexpression meanings then supports replacement in a well-formed context. Hutton illustrates this with arithmetic expressions in §3 of the reference below.

In a Bellman problem, equality must include the relevant continuation inputs, state domains, conditional distributions, and free parameters. Two policies that happen to coincide at a few grid points need not denote the same function. Replacing exact expectation by a quadrature approximation likewise requires an error argument rather than an appeal to equality.

docs.title: A programming discipline
docs.text:
Explicit inputs and immutable mathematical objects make these dependencies easier to inspect. Hidden mutable state can make an expression's result depend on more than its stated arguments. This motivates the project's functional programming style, but does not prove that any particular handler is pure or mathematically correct.

The initial-algebra account separates structural compositionality from a justified implementation.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Hutton, Graham (2023). “Programming language semantics: it's easy as 1,2,3.” Journal of Functional Programming 33, e9, §3, p. 3. Article.

docs.title: Ρ — numerical representation
docs.text:
Ρ (Rho) names the passage from specified mathematical operations to numerical representations and executable calculations. The uppercase letter distinguishes this project notation from a risk-aversion parameter written \(\rho\).

A calculation needs the model's parameters, selected methods, numerical settings, and compatible executable handlers. A graph with bound parameters is not by itself a solver. Each method has requirements on the operation it implements and on the objects used to represent its inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Exactness and approximation
docs.text:
Suppose a mathematical operator is \(T:V\to V\), a numerical operator is \(\widehat T:\widehat V\to\widehat V\), and maps \(E:V\to\widehat V\) and \(D:\widehat V\to V\) encode and decode values. The expression

\[D\circ\widehat T\circ E\]

is a candidate realization of \(T\). Equality with \(T\) must be justified on a stated domain. A grid, quadrature rule, interpolation scheme, or finite tolerance generally introduces an approximation that needs an error criterion. Neither this three-part expression nor calibration establishes equality or semiconjugacy (strong / order).

The methods chapter separates a mathematical operation from the algorithm used for it. adequacy concerns the relationship between the intended meaning and its implementation; convergence claims require additional hypotheses.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text: Semantics specifies what a language's expressions mean. A denotational account assigns mathematical objects compositionally; an operational account gives execution rules; an axiomatic account specifies logical assertions and proof rules. These are distinct ways to explain a language, and numerical implementation is not excluded from semantics by a general terminology rule.

docs.title: Denotation
docs.text:
A denotation is the mathematical object the interpretation assigns to a piece of a stage — a definition, a block or an authored line, a builder, a sub-builder, a primitive operator, a graph, or the stage itself — under the declarations of its file, the calibration of its version and, for a piece at a policy, a policy. It is a set, a map between sets, a probability measure or a stochastic kernel, a relation, or an operator, which is a map from functions to functions or from measures to measures. Every piece has a denotation, not the stage alone.

The box of a primitive operator denotes the form of its kind at its kernel, one map, so the pullback and the push-forward of one law of motion have one kernel and two denotations. An Argmax row, and a row whose output is among the unknowns of its own rule, denote a relation, a map only where a maximizer or a solution exists and one is selected. A piece with pieces within it denotes the composition, along the wires, of what they denote, and that composition is the same at every grain.

The verb denotes takes a phrase of the file or a piece of the semgraph as its subject and a mathematical object as its object; a printed view is text that states a denotation and is not one, and a numerical representation approximates one under a stated contract. The package computes no denotation.

Below the stage denote() is the one verb that answers what a piece is and what it denotes, and view() is a verb of the stage alone. What denote() answers is a record: the mathematical structure of the denotation, with the typed wires, the rule, the kernel together with the statements of the stage file it denotes and the objects those statements denote, the conditions and, on a methodized version, the method bound within the piece, which is part of what the piece denotes on the version asked. The record displays itself, and what it prints is the piece's card: a title naming the stage and the piece, a heavy line, then the sections that have content, Signature for the typed inputs and outputs, At for the policy at which a builder is stated, Where for local abbreviations such as the law of motion at the policy, Declared for a line marked !doc, Rule for the rule at a point, Operations for the operations a builder composes, and Conditions; below a light line, Source with the lines of the stage file and their line numbers, and Definitions referenced (A piece §§1 and 5; The builders graphs §3 for At, Where and Declared; A builder §1 for Operations). A block, an authored line and an initial diagram answer the verb with the authored relation they denote. On a piece that answers them, signature() answers the inputs and outputs the card's Signature section prints, and kernel() the pointwise map its rule applies.

docs.title: The Bellman interpretation
docs.text:
The Bellman calculus distinguishes mathematical interpretation, denoted Υ, from numerical realization, denoted Ρ. The mathematical model specifies domains, equations, shock probability distributions and feasible choices. A numerical method supplies a procedure and representations intended to approximate or compute that model. adequacy explains the separate correctness obligations.

Compositional interpretation determines a compound expression from its constituents and their context. For an ordinary algebraic signature, initiality gives a unique term interpretation once target operations and any free-input environment are fixed. It does not choose missing conditional distributions, solve implicit equations, or prove integrability and selection assumptions.

docs.title: Source and retained model
docs.text:
Bellman-SYM stage equations are authored in .bl stage files. Parsing produces a temporary parsed AST (abstract syntax tree); construction interprets that syntax into the retained semgraph (semantic graph) and discards the parsed AST. The graph retains authored equations, values, typed operations and definitions. It is not a source string interpreted a second time.

The semgraph entry defines the four graphs of a stage, the two initial diagrams on fields and the two builders graphs, on functions backward and on measures forward, with their grains and value bundles; a stage reaches them as stage.initial.backward, stage.initial.forward, stage.builder.bwd and stage.builder.fwd. Derived interpretations require sufficient state information, conditional distributions and analytic assumptions; an implicit relation remains a relation until a valid selection is supplied.

Typed composition alone does not prove an equation-preserving functor. Equal denotation also does not erase authored names and method-attachment boundaries or recover a unique source spelling. See Syntax to semantics and Equation boundaries and indexing.

The abstract dynamic program (ADP) and recursive decision process (RDP) supply useful mathematical descriptions of policy and value updates. They are not identical to the whole stored representation or every sort of the Bellman algebra.

docs.title: semgraph
docs.text:
semgraph means semantic graph: the constructed mathematical representation of the model. Use semgraph in current explanations. The parsed AST, or abstract syntax tree, records the constructor structure of the authored text; it is the input to construction, not the semgraph. Existing API names and historical quotations keep their spellings.

This page is the terminology home for a semgraph's graphs, grains and wire bundles. Using semgraph as the Python module name introduces no second mathematical representation.

docs.title: The four graphs and what they represent
docs.text:
A stage holds four graphs, and each states which mathematical objects it represents. The boxes are operations, the ports are their individual input/output positions, and the wires connect compatible ports. A wire's type states what kind of object it carries. The stage reaches them as stage.initial.backward and stage.initial.forward, the two initial diagrams, and stage.builder.bwd and stage.builder.fwd, the two builders graphs. A builder is reached by the ordered pair of perches it joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] for the decision builder, or from the perch its edge leaves, the edge being the step from that perch to the next, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd, a path defined as that one pair; the policy builder is read by its own key, policy (The builders graphs §2).

Graph Objects and operations Backward initial diagram The authored blocks that compute values and the policy, on the fields they read and write. Forward initial diagram The authored transition blocks, likewise. The two initial diagrams are separate graphs and are never drawn as one. Backward builders graph Operators receiving continuation-value functions and producing objective, decision-value or arrival-value functions, as specified by their definitions. Forward builders graph Operators receiving finite measures over states and producing the measures induced by transitions, conditional distributions and a supplied policy.

A field is a named quantity of a stage with a declared set, at its perch unless it is a shock, which belongs to no perch. Once shocks are declared, fields may be interpreted as random variables at the corresponding information sets. Representing fields as functions requires specified representing functions and sufficient state information. Sufficient means that the state contains the information needed for the relevant payoff arguments and conditional distributions. The required domains and integration conditions remain explicit; a field equation does not supply them automatically.

docs.title: Fields, values, functions and builders
docs.text:
A field is a quantity defined over possible outcomes with an information context. Evaluating it at an outcome gives a value. Representing it by a function of a chosen state requires that state to retain the relevant information; measurability with respect to the full information set alone does not prove this. A backward builder acts on such functions, whereas a forward builder acts on measures describing state distributions; both are builders, the operators the blocks of a stage file denote.

For consumption, the authored reward and continuation equations together with a = m_d - c give the choice value utility(c) + continuation(m_d-c) under the required state representation; discounting follows the authored equations. Consumption remains a free choice until a policy is supplied or selected. Evaluating the choice value at a feasible policy gives its one-step value update for the supplied continuation. The optimizing value is the supremum over feasible choices where defined; representing it by a policy additionally requires attainment and a measurable maximizing selection.

These distinctions resolve a common ambiguity in compact Bellman notation: a field, its scalar value, its state-function representative and an operator on functions are different mathematical objects. A transition alone does not supply utility, discounting, expectations or a policy. Conditional distributions and integrability must be stated; a fixed independent shock probability distribution is a special assumption, not a consequence of diagram wiring.

docs.title: Representation and interpretation
docs.text:
This entry owns the account of the four graphs of a stage, their grains and their value bundles. The two initial diagrams are the backward and the forward graphs on fields; the two builders graphs act on functions, backward, and on measures, forward. Whole builders, primitive operators and the sub-builders that authored nodes denote provide different inspection grains. Their boundaries need not nest, and arithmetic remains within the retained equation and function definitions.

The origins of a box and the analytic conditions of the stage are answers of queries, not parts of the native graph. A missing interpretation rule is reported while the initial diagrams remain inspectable; display text is not parsed again to recover meaning.

See The initial diagrams, Appendix C and methodization.

The backward initial diagram preserves the authored policy block separately. A policy relation is not a selected function. In the decision builder at a policy, the policy reference is kernel data of the policy-indexed law of motion, value aggregator or conditional distribution. The forward decision builder is the push-forward through the policy-indexed transition \(g_{\succ,c}\), with any policy-dependent conditional distribution in its kernel data. Exact Evaluation reads no policy. The insertion of the policy is a factor of the pullback and of the push-forward at the policy, which their cards write out, 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) and μ({m_d ∈ Xm | 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)) ∈ B}), and no stage of the applications forms a separate PolicyInsertion row. The policy is typed once, on the policy builder's output, and no wire joins that output to the policy-indexed builders; how the backward builders and the policy builder are joined is stated at methodization. The forward builders graph uses transition and distribution definitions; it is not obtained by reversing every arrow of a reward-bearing Bellman operator. See backward builder and forward builder for the respective mathematical operations.

docs.title: Grains expose defining operations
docs.text:
A grain chooses which boxes are opened within a graph. It does not change that graph's mathematical objects. Elaboration constructs the two initial diagrams and the builder grain of the two builders graphs. Other grains are derived from those retained graphs when requested and kept on that stage version. A reader reaches the two finer public grains by an attribute of a graph, a builder or a sub-builder, primitives and sub_builders, as stage.builder.bwd.primitives; the combined and the factored grains are answered by semgraph.record, below.

Principal grain What remains visible as a box Builder One complete builder operation, with its defining composition retained. Primitive Natural mathematical operations such as the pullback along the law of motion, whole scalar aggregation, conditional integration, probability transport, maximization and evaluation, where defined. Sub-builder (node in code) The sub-builders, the operators the statements marked !node denote, closed, with their definitions and actual dependencies. Unmarked equations remain wherever the composition needs them. A sub-builder's output is a function wire of its own, which a method can represent exactly or by an admitted approximation. The result of an operator occurrence inside an unmarked line (an E, an argmax, or a solve) is a wire the construction makes, not an authored one: it is present in the builders graphs below the builder grain, absent from the initial diagrams, and admits only the operation's own method. Attaching that method does not make the occurrence a node; !node alone creates the authored boundary. Factored The boxes that respect both the primitive and sub-builder divisions together with the local places at which a method may be typed. It opens a sub-builder around an operator to which a method may attach: an expectation, the maximization of an operative argmax line, or a row whose output is among its own unknowns.

The complete transition g and scalar aggregator G are mathematical definitions on their declared arguments. Each has one definition record referring to its retained source equations, and every operation that uses the definition references it by identity: the pullback and the push-forward reference the forward builder's g, the value aggregation references G. DisCoPy is the diagram library used to store the boxes and wires of the graphs; the finest box of a graph is a primitive operator or a sub-builder. A box represents an occurrence and carries references to the definitions table: the transition, aggregator or distribution record, or the statement address. Its equation is printed from those references and its conditions are computed from that equation. Addition, subtraction and other arithmetic inside those equations are not boxes and do not become an additional grain. A !node inside g or G remains inspectable there.

The grains need not nest. Two coordinate equations may together define one vector transition g; one named utility equation may define only part of G. Opening a sub-builder inside g cannot replace an outer operator on functions with a scalar box of another type.

The additional combined grain starts at all declared builder outputs and traces their actual dependencies backward. On reaching a primitive operator or sub-builder, it keeps that box closed and continues along all its external input wires. It stops opening the box, not following its dependencies. Shared occurrences are visited once, and every output of a multi-output box is preserved. A sub-builder containing an expectation therefore remains closed until it is opened. An operation no declared output depends on is not drawn at this grain. This is a stopping rule, not a fifth graph or a claim that every decomposition has one finest grain.

docs.title: How a value statement is folded
docs.text: A backward block's statements are folded by structural recursion on their retained terms into primitive operators of three kinds on function wires, in the order the term nests them: the pullback of every continuation function along the block's law of motion, an expectation for every occurrence E_μ(·), and an aggregation for the arithmetic that combines terms carrying a value input. The arithmetic inside an occurrence's brackets is one aggregation before that expectation; the arithmetic outside is one aggregation per maximal pointwise segment. The fold never moves arithmetic across an expectation, so a statement that writes the expectation inside the line denotes the aggregation after the expectation, reading its result as a value input, and a statement that writes the aggregation inside the expectation denotes the canonical form with the aggregator inside the integral. Whether an aggregation's map is affine in its value inputs is never a condition of construction. A sub-term that carries no value input, a named function of fields, a parameter, an expression in fields and shocks, is part of the aggregation's map, never a box. The stored form of every equation is the retained term; the printed string and the compiled function are queries. A !node statement denotes a sub-builder, a cut of the builder's composition; a branch is a summand of the continuation coproduct, a bubble of the forward initial diagram and no wire.

docs.title: Opening a box preserves its operation
docs.text:
A builder signature declares a builder's inputs and outputs. Opening any box must preserve its exact ordered input and output identities and types, and its operation on every admissible assignment of its free inputs. The replacement must also preserve the conditions under which the formulas are defined, local-variable scope, conditional distributions and shared dependencies. Those conditions are often called guards. A capture is an input used by a function definition besides its formal arguments.

Each operation has one authoritative definition. Its expansion is derived from that definition; independently editable g/G definitions and expansions cannot supply competing meanings. A named numerical method is not by itself a proof that its output equals the defining operation. Native composition checks connections and types, not integrability, optimality or numerical convergence.

The inspected DisCoPy 1.2.2 installation provides native identity, sequential composition (>>), tensor composition (@), and Diagram.substitute(i, inner) for replacing a selected diagram box. Hypergraph itself has no substitute method. Conversion with Hypergraph.from_diagram must preserve the ordered inputs and outputs and incidence, meaning which ports connect to which wires. The mathematical definitions remain in native Box.data; a drawing frame is not their replacement.

docs.title: Source order and evaluation order
docs.text:
Source order is the order in which equations were authored. Queries may retain it for inspecting the source. The order of boxes in a stored Hypergraph is a separate representation detail; neither order necessarily puts a producer before its consumers.

For an explicit acyclic computation, topological order puts each producer before every operation using its result. Independent operations may occupy the same layer, with source order breaking ties. If h supplies both y and z, evaluation requires h before y and z even when stored boxes list y, z, h. Backward traversal discovers this dependency; it does not mean evaluating consumers before producers.

A cycle or implicit relation needs its own admitted interpretation. Drawing arrows differently, sorting boxes, or inserting a formal trace does not solve the economic problem or establish the existence of a fixed point. Equation addresses and method places remain unchanged when the presentation follows dependencies.

docs.title: Value bundles preserve their constituents
docs.text:
A value bundle is the tuple of value objects on one base: the maximal set of parallel wires of a backward graph that share their base coordinates and are written by one box and read by one box. Its components are the value objects the stage declares at that perch, and a bundle may hold one component only: the derivative of a value is no component, since it is read by the derivative term D_{a}V[>] and adds no wire. Parallel means that the wires coexist there, not that their values are independent, and grouping asserts no independence. The relation between a value and its derivative is written by the author on a derivative line, with the chain-rule factor where the law of motion between the perches is not the identity.

The bundle is derived from the graph and stored nowhere; its type is the tensor of its wires, read as one function into the product of its components' result sets. One box acts on the whole bundle for one of two reasons. A pullback and an expectation apply one kernel to every component — the same law of motion, the same policy-indexed conditional distribution and the same shocks under the same conditioning — and an aggregation applies one vector-valued kernel, the pairing of the components' own maps, from the tuple of inputs to the tuple of outputs. A component that a later operator reads alone is a wire of the tensor carried on; no box unbundles it.

A branch tuple is not a bundle. A branching stage has a continuation state space that is a disjoint union of the branches' state spaces, and functions on a disjoint union are a tuple of functions, one per label, so a branch also shows as several value wires side by side. The two differ in what is put side by side: a bundle is indexed by the value fields the perch declares and its components are functions on one state space, across which a kernel acts; a branch tuple is indexed by labels and its components are functions on different state spaces, across which the operator is a case analysis. A drawing shows a bundle as one thick wire labeled with its components and a branch tuple as one labeled wire per alternative meeting the aggregation of the selection line, and never the other way round. The thick wire says what the graph does, not what a header declares: at a graph's own boundary the graph stands for the box on its own side and one box is still required on the other, so the input V[>] of cons.bl's backward graph stands at the boundary, the decision builder and the policy builder each reading it, the policy builder by the derivative term D_{a}V[>]. In type notation the wire the arrival pullback of cons.bl writes is V∘g : m → ℝ; the drawing writes the same wire in the calculus spelling it uses for every other wire, V(g(m)).

A graph — an initial diagram or a builders graph — fixes the mathematical objects, a grain selects which boxes are opened, and a bundle is read off the wires those boxes write and read.

Native A @ B gives an ordered tensor of wire types. Grouping preserves each constituent's identity, type, domain, scope and dependencies. Tracing the grouped outputs together retains shared producers once. Reordering requires explicit swaps. Unbundling recovers the original ordered wires.

Representing a bundle by one product wire is an additional structural operation. It requires defined packing and unpacking maps whose expansion recovers those same constituents. Tensor concatenation alone does not turn two wires into one, and boxes merely named pack and unpack do not cancel under native equality.

A value bundle also preserves its components' separate domains. For example, bundling 1/x and x does not discard the latter's value at zero; forming one paired partial function on a common domain is a separate operation. Likewise, two separate coordinate distributions, or marginal measures, do not determine a joint distribution. Preserve the actual joint distribution and every coordinate needed by later conditional distributions. Copying one realized shock is different from drawing independently twice. Bundling may not conceal such dependencies or move a local variable outside its binding scope.

docs.title: Outputs computed within one builder
docs.text: Outputs of one authored builder can instead come from one joint local computation on that builder's effective domain: the inputs for which all its formulas are defined. With E denoting conditional expectation, V = E(W), U = V^2 and an unused local equation h = 1/U compute V once, then U, and restrict the builder to U ≠ 0. Both returned functions preserve that restriction, even though h is not an output. Their arguments follow the actual local dependencies and the checked declaration order; a control needed only by a domain condition remains an argument. This construction is distinct from placing independently defined functions on parallel wires: it does not impose one common domain on arbitrary bundles.

docs.title: Public query
docs.text:
bellman.stage.semgraph.record is implemented for ordinary stages whose retained equations, domains, laws of motion and distributions have an admitted interpretation. It accepts an ElaboratedStage, the object elaborate_stage makes of a stage file. Import it with from bellman.stage import semgraph, the module that defines it. The operation returns the graph together with its inputs, outputs, conditions and parameter information.

Its call signature is semgraph.record(stage, *, level, direction, grain="builder", assumptions=()). For example:

from bellman.stage import semgraph

record = semgraph.record(stage, level="builders", direction="backward", grain="primitive")

level selects "initial", the initial diagrams, or "builders", the builders graphs; direction selects "forward" or "backward" and is required. grain selects "builder", "sub-builder" (the code token "node"), "primitive", "combined" or "factored". An unsupported interpretation gives a diagnostic identifying the authored item and missing rule; the constructed initial diagrams remain available. The record states the graph and computes no solution.

The immutable Semgraph record describes the native graph and its inputs and outputs. It adds no alternative graph language or second set of edges.

Attribute What it retains .graph The native DisCoPy Hypergraph that the selected direction's handle holds, stage.builder.bwd.graph or stage.initial.forward.graph, at the grain the attribute primitives or sub_builders selects, with its records in Box.data. .inputs, .outputs The sorts of the graph's ordered input and output wires: identity, kind, perch, role, domain and coordinates. .obligations The conditions of the stage with their scope and status (required, assumed or established), the caller's assumptions in place of those they discharge. .parameters The sorts of the parameters that the terms of the graph's rows name, directly or through the functions they call; empty for an initial diagram. .calibration Supplied parameter values, or None before calibration.

The record holds no copy of the origins or the methods: the origins of a box are its data, read with the box's kernel().origins, and the methods attached inside a graph are read with that graph's methods.

An initial diagram includes any supplied functions still required through its retained definitions after its declared field inputs. Model parameters remain named inside those definitions, with their declarations and values available separately. Function arguments remain distinct from model parameters, captures and locally bound variables. The graph of a record is frozen, and a transformation constructs a new record. The ordered method inventory that a piece's methods reads retains the identities of its places across changes of graph and grain. Its entries retain their original stage meaning: an expectation's numerical integration method does not become a method for transporting probability measures. An empty inventory means no effective choices are attached; it does not by itself describe which setup steps ran.

The optional assumptions value is a tuple of Condition records with status "assumed", matching requirements of the requested interpretation. An assumption cannot supply a missing policy or an unsupported structural rule. Conditions on formula domains remain explicit.

Elaboration stores the two initial diagrams and the builder grain of each builders graph, or a refusal where one cannot be constructed. A query derives the requested grain from those retained objects and caches it for the stage version. ElaboratedStage has seven attributes: name, metadata, definitions, initial, _builders, bindings and provenance, the fifth the stored record of the two builders graphs, which stage.builder reads. The object is a stage occurrence, one stage file elaborated at one position of a period; a binding adds to it in place and returns it, and a different text is elaborated again as its own stage occurrence. Definitions retain source equations; queries derive their mathematical and display information.

A stage is a term over a many-sorted signature and each graph is its image under the unique homomorphism (Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright 1977, "Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras", §2 pp. 70–71 and §3.2 p. 76; in categorical form, Jacobs 1999, Categorical Logic and Type Theory, §2.2 p. 129, Theorem 2.2.5). A semantics given by a fold is compositional (Hutton 2023, "Programming Language Semantics: It's Easy as 1,2,3", §3 p. 4; Winskel 1993, The Formal Semantics of Programming Languages, §5.2 p. 60), and two homomorphisms that agree on a generating set are equal (Burris and Sankappanavar 2012, A Course in Universal Algebra, the Millennium Edition, Chapter II §6 p. 47, Theorem 6.2), so what the term determines is a query rather than a stored member. A grain is one presentation of the object, not a second object (Scott and Strachey 1971, Toward a Mathematical Semantics for Computer Languages, §0 pp. 1 and 4–5), and the fold cata f = f ∘ F(cata f) ∘ in⁻¹ opens a bubble (Leal de Freitas 2020, Recursion Schemes for Mathematicians, pp. 15–16). A box holds the parameters of its form and nothing else (Backus 1978, "Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?", §11.2.6 p. 622 and §13.1 p. 631). The definitions table is an environment that the bindings extend, with no store at elaboration (Schmidt 1986, Denotational Semantics: A Methodology for Language Development, §4.1 p. 54, §2.3.1 pp. 25–26, §5.1 pp. 66–68, §8.3 p. 170 and §10.2 p. 202); the methods form a second algebra held apart from the term, as effect handlers are (Plotkin and Pretnar 2009, "Handlers of Algebraic Effects", §4.1 p. 7 and §5.1 p. 8); and elaboration produces the internal representation once (Pfenning 2021, Lecture Notes on Elaboration, §1 p. L11.1). The definitions are the economist's objects, the feasible correspondence, the value space and the aggregator of a recursive decision process (Sargent and Stachurski 2026, Dynamic Programming, vol. 2, §7.1.1.1, pp. 206–207), and every record class the schema keeps is a class each tool that reads the stage must know (Wang, Appel, Korn and Serra 1997, "The Zephyr Abstract Syntax Description Language", §4 p. 11).

docs.title: Inspecting equations and complete maps
docs.text:
stage.definitions holds the retained source statements as records of kind line, in authored order, including statements inside authored nodes, and stage.definitions.list() prints every record grouped by kind. The records of the lines retain the terms, conditions and addressed unknowns. Complete g and G records refer to these statements by identity; a printed preview does not replace them.

stage.builder.bwd.primitives and stage.builder.fwd.primitives read the operations of the two builders graphs, one box per primitive operator, and stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.list() lists the operations of one builder in the order of application. stage.definitions.denote("cons:g:dcsn_to_cntn") answers the complete law of motion of a forward block, and the records of kind G the value aggregators of the backward blocks. A builder's inputs and outputs are stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.signature(), and the inputs and outputs of one graph are stage.builder.bwd.signature(), one record with two parts, inputs and outputs.

denote() is the one verb below the stage, and view() is the stage's own: stage.view() prints the inventory of the occurrence, while stage.definitions.denote("<identity>") for a definition and stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"].denote() for a box each answer a record whose printed form is that piece's card.
