A card carries the typed inputs and outputs under Signature, the rule the piece applies, the operations of a builder in the order of application, the conditions and, on a methodized version, the method bound within the piece, and under a light line the lines of the stage file it comes from (semantics). print(piece) prints the same card. kernel() on a box prints the pointwise map the operator applies. Kernel arguments are pointwise values; the coordinates of a function on a wire describe where that function is evaluated. The two lists need not coincide.

compile_kernel() on a box answers one plain Python function of a supported kernel, on a symbolic version as on a calibrated one, taking the kernel's arguments and then the values of the parameters it reads, which kernel().parameter_values holds in that order; kernel().python is its text. It is refused under the rule kernel-target for a box whose kernel is neither a law of motion nor a value aggregator, as an expectation's or an evaluation's is, and for a row whose rule has no side that is an explicit function of its inputs, as the identification of a policy block has none; it chooses no policy and solves no Bellman equation. Printing and these queries read the retained terms, without parsing source previews again.

docs.title: Names and parameters in diagrams
docs.text:
Every wire of the backward builders graph carries a function or a set of functions. The set-valued case is the result of an Argmax row or of a row whose output is among its own unknowns; exact Evaluation preserves that set and selects no member. Function-valued wires include a value function such as V[>](·), its composition with the transition V[>](g(·)), an expectation's result, an objective function of state and control V(·, ·), the declared policy of a maximization π(·), the functions the policy lines define on the continuation states (c[>](·), m_d[>](·)) and a policy function c(·). States, controls and shocks are coordinates of the functions on backward wires, not separate wires. A kernel's arguments are the pointwise values used to define those functions, and the aggregation's results are the functions themselves. An evaluation operation (Evaluation) is the identity from a derived carrier into a declared carrier. Its object may be a function or a set of feasible policies, and it makes no selection. It reads no policy and inserts none. A numerical method may store an interpolant as its representation of a function without changing exact Evaluation. In a builder at a policy, the policy instead indexes the pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution in which it occurs.

Pullback of the function along the law of motion g composes a supplied function with g, V ↦ V∘g; its forward partner is the push-forward through the law of motion g, μ ↦ g_#μ. Value aggregation G applies the complete value calculations defined by G and yields the value functions or, when a control is bound, the objective functions, using the pulled-back function or an expectation's result as its input (see aggregation). The policy builder uses the same kinds: its objective or residual is aggregated on the decision coordinates after the pullback along g. On the continuation grid, the inverse-Euler candidate line c[>] forms one Aggregation whose rule is the line's relation, an inequality or a complementarity included, and the coordinate line m_d[>] another, each reading the derivative of the continuation value at the saving by the term D_{a}V[>], with the author's derivative lines and inverse marginal utility and no automatic differentiation. Where the candidate line carries the clause ⟂ a >= 0, as in methods.bl, the methods file beside cons.bl, the candidate at each saving is a set: the interior value alone where the saving is positive, and every value up to it at zero saving. The candidate and the coordinate are then correspondences, printed 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊ and 𝑚_d≻ : Xa ⇉ Xm. The identification line c = c[>] forms the Pullback of the policy along the coordinate map m_d[>], equated to the candidate; its rule holds at every value admitted at each saving, the corner, consumption equal to cash on hand, among them (Constraints §4.3). The grid line is checked against the law of motion solved for the decision coordinate, and a line that disagrees is refused under the rule grid-line-consistency. An operative argmax line forms an Argmax row, whose output is the set of maximizing policies; and a solve line forms one Aggregation of its residuals. Expectation remains a separate operation. The kinds of the rows are Pullback, Aggregation, Expectation, Evaluation and Argmax (operations): a relation is the rule of a row whose output is among its own unknowns, and no kind of its own. A line attached to an operative line by a dotted id, as the first-order condition optimality.euler is attached to the argmax line optimality, is that row's property: it forms no row, no address and no method place, and it prints under the row.

Parameters belong with definitions and calibration. They are held fixed when the functions act on states, controls or supplied functions, and are not drawn as separate semgraph wires. Their identities, domains and any supplied values remain inspectable. An uncalibrated parameter remains a symbolic quantity; its restrictions still apply. A parameter's absence from the displayed inputs does not remove it from the mathematical model.

docs.title: Sources and related concepts
docs.text: The mathematical distinctions are developed in Stages and perches §2, Operators and builders, and Appendix B §§4–7. Related concepts are stage, perch, operator, sub-builder, aggregation, statement, branch, ordering conventions and source span.

docs.title: Semiconjugacy
docs.text: A semiconjugacy between self-maps \(S:V\to V\) and \(\widehat S:\widehat V\to\widehat V\) is a map \(F:V\to\widehat V\) satisfying \(F\circ S=\widehat S\circ F\). It sends exact iterates and fixed points of the first system to those of the second. This identity alone does not recover every original solution or establish equivalence of economic problems.

docs.title: Strong semiconjugacy
docs.text:
Sargent and Stachurski use the stronger paired factorization

\[ S=G\circ F,\qquad \widehat S=F\circ G, \qquad F:V\to\widehat V,\quad G:\widehat V\to V. \]

Their definition on posets does not require the maps to preserve order. The two intertwining identities follow by associativity. For \(n\geq1\),

\[ S^n=G\circ\widehat S^{n-1}\circ F, \qquad \widehat S^n=F\circ S^{n-1}\circ G. \]

On fixed points, \(F\) and \(G\) are inverse correspondences: if \(Sv=v\), then \(GFv=v\), and similarly \(FGw=w\) when \(\widehat Sw=w\). Consequently existence and uniqueness of fixed points correspond. This argument needs neither invertibility on the whole spaces nor a convergence theorem.

For their order-stability result, both maps are order preserving or both are order reversing. Their convergence result adds the stated order-continuity and initial-point assumptions. Conjugacy via an order isomorphism is stronger: the bijection and its inverse both preserve order. An order-preserving bijection alone need not do so.

docs.title: Finite horizons and timing
docs.text:
Let \(F_n:V_n\to W_n\) and \(G_n:W_n\to V_{n-1}\) for \(n=1,\ldots,H\). Define \(T_n=G_n\circ F_n\) and \(\widehat T_n=F_n\circ G_{n+1}\) for \(n<H\). Associativity gives

\[ T_1\circ\cdots\circ T_H =G_1\circ\widehat T_1\circ\cdots\circ\widehat T_{H-1}\circ F_H. \]

Both endpoint maps remain. Applying this identity to a terminal value requires a terminal element of \(V_H\) and the displayed transformation \(F_H\). Reordering stages while keeping an unrelated terminal state or value does not follow from this identity. The finite-horizon result is separate from stationary fixed-point correspondence.

docs.title: Numerical reformulation
docs.text:
A post-decision reformulation can be useful when the relevant transition, expectation and choice maps have the required domains and identities. It does not justify exchanging expectation and optimization in one formula. Smoothness, Euler inversion, feasibility and selected policies require their own assumptions. Similarly, a value/policy correspondence does not automatically transfer convergence in ordinary policy norms.

The project calls a reformulation justified by such a factorization a “Stachurski transform”. The name is no claim that two reordered operators are equal or that a particular handler supports a source key. An adapter that calls a package has a broader computational role; its correctness still requires the relevant input, output and approximation checks.

The transition pairing stated in the entry forward builder relates the probability transport of a builder to an undiscounted expectation. It is distinct from semiconjugacy between value updates and does not include rewards or optimization.

Reference: Sargent and Stachurski, Dynamic Programming, Volume II: General States, 10 April 2026 edition, §5.2.1, pp. 160–163, equations (5.14)–(5.15), Lemmas 5.2.1–5.2.2 and Theorem 5.2.3. The project's Semi-conjugacy chapter treats particular applications.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Summary

Settings are the numerical choices a method reads: the bounds and the count of a grid, a tolerance, an iteration limit, the number of quadrature nodes, a rule chosen among finitely many labels. They configure how a computation is approximated; parameters define the economic model. A setting is a name declared with a set in a methods file, the addition to the stage file, and its value, written in the settings file, is bound by configure, which refuses a value outside the declared set.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Methods §6: a setting as a declared name a method's label reads, with no value in the signature. Builds on — Grid: the component whose factors name settings; Methods: the words whose keyword arguments name them. Used by — Parameters and settings: the table stage.settings; Stage functions: the verb configure.

A setting is told from a parameter by the file that declares it: a parameter is declared by the stage file and defines the model, including any discrete domain that is part of the model; a setting is declared by the methods file and configures a method. A methods file may also define a derived parameter by := from the parameters, with or without a declared set, which is a parameter and no setting.

docs.title: 1 Declared with their domains
docs.text:
A methods file declares each setting it reads at file level, in the form the stage file declares a parameter, with its set and a description:

n_a : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]
a_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the savings grid"]
a_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the savings grid"]
n_ψ_nodes : ℕ        :: ["quadrature nodes of the permanent shock"]
tol_v : ℝ₊₊          :: ["tolerance of value function iteration"]

A bound of a grid is a point of the set the stage declares for the coordinate, Xa for the savings a or a literal set such as ℝ₊; a count is a natural number; a tolerance is a positive real; a setting valued in a finite set of labels, such as a tie-breaking rule, is declared on that set. A declared set may name a parameter or a derived parameter, as tol_s : (0, ρ) does. A name is declared once in a stage, and two declarations of one name with different sets are refused. The scope of a declaration is the addition and the stage it is unioned with; where two stages of one period each declare one name, they denote one setting of that period, as a parameter name does. A grid entry names settings and holds no number: policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) names three. A method word's keyword argument names a declared setting for every number the method reads, !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes), and holds no number: an entry that writes one is refused, as a grid entry that writes one is. An argument may hold a quoted string, which is the value of the argument and no setting. An undeclared name is refused as any other is.

docs.title: 2 Bound by configure
docs.text:
The values stand in the settings file, and the stage verb stage.configure(settings_source), with a path or a mapping, binds them as calibrate, the verb of calibration, binds a parameter's value; configure_trellis(elaborated, syntactic) applies it at every position of a trellis. In the recommended order configuration follows the union of the stage file with its additions and the elaboration of the unioned stage, so that the settings it binds are those the methods file declares, read against the methods and grids that name them. It judges each value against the setting's declared set, reading each parameter that the set names at its calibrated value, and each derived parameter at the value its definition takes at the calibration. It refuses a value outside the declared set, naming the line of the methods file where the setting is declared, and a name with no value. A value inside its declared set is still refused where the method or the grid that reads it does not admit it: a keyword's value outside the domain the method's row names, or a bound or a count of a grid that fails the checks stated below (The binding verbs §3). A key of a shared settings file that no declaration names declares no new setting and is read by no method: configure binds its value, and stage.settings lists it after the declared settings with no set, which is where a misspelled key shows. A configuration with a misspelled key is refused, under setting-unvalued, only where the setting the key was meant for has no value from the source and none from an earlier configuration; after an earlier configuration the earlier value stays bound, and the misspelled key is bound beside it. The bound values stand in the stage's record of bindings; no value is part of a signature.

stage.settings lists every declared setting with its value, the operator that reads it, the method there and, where the setting is a factor of that operator's grid or the declared points of !Points, the grid constructor; stage.settings["n_a"] answers one setting's record, whose value is the configured value (Parameters and settings §2). stage.par lists the parameters and no setting.

An empty settings mapping is admissible for a stage whose methods declare no setting; it chooses no method. Recording a grid size demonstrates neither numerical accuracy nor adequate treatment of the bounds: at configuration the package checks each bound pair ordered and inside the coordinate's set, each count at least two, each node set strictly increasing, the shape, finite coordinates and decidable membership of declared points, the requirements written after require= that the bound values decide and the equality of the points of a grid beside an authored table with the table's knots, where both are known exactly at configuration, and nothing more (Methods §5). Where the coordinate's set names a parameter, as a definition Xa := [a_lo, inf) would, a bound must lie in that set at the parameter's calibrated value. The package does not yet check this (Appendix C §5.3). It decides the membership from the set's definition alone, so it refuses such a bound under grid-bounds. The entry specified stage states the order in which the three bindings, calibration, methodization and configuration, are made, and the specification factory states how the sources of a recipe combine. Exact configuration behavior is in Stage functions.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
A signature has a set of sorts and a set of operation symbols, each with a rank: its ordered input sorts and its output sort (Kinds and sorts §3). An interpretation supplies the actual operations on the carriers of those sorts; listing a symbol is not yet giving its mathematical behavior.

In a many-sorted algebra, sorts form an index set and each sort has a carrier set of objects. For each input word of sorts and output sort, the signature provides operation symbols of that rank. Their interpretations map products of the corresponding input carriers to the output carrier. Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras, §2 p. 70, gives this definition. That source uses rank for the length of the input word and calls the pair of the input word and the output sort the symbol's type; the entry rank states the usage followed here.

docs.title: Builder signatures and mathematical signatures
docs.text:
A block header declares the input and output fields of authored text, with their sets, roles and perches. A Bellman-SYM builder signature instead gives the actual function or measure wires of the operator constructed from that block; signature() answers it as one record with two parts, inputs and outputs. On a controlled backward edge, the control is a coordinate of the functions carried by the wires and is not itself an input wire. A state of the perch at which a backward block's output stands is likewise a coordinate of the output function and is listed on no backward header (Appendix C R1). The policy is an index on the builder at a policy and is not an argument of the decision value function. A block identifier names the authored block; its statements and dependencies determine the constructed operator.

A stage has two mathematical signatures (Kinds and sorts §6). The sorts of its state signature name the state spaces of its perches, and its symbols are the stage's transitions, each a law of motion with its shock law. Its operator signature has two sorts for each perch, which name a space of value functions and a space of measures on the state space of the perch, and a sort of policies, and its symbols are the builders; a builder signature gives the rank of one of them. Composition is no operation of either signature. A term is a path of symbols, an arrow of the free category of the signature, whose objects are the sorts, and two builders compose by the concatenation of their paths. The terms of a signature, their interpretations and the .bl constructor grammar are distinct objects. The stage term and Abstract grammar give the mathematical account.

Neither a signature nor matching inputs and outputs prove integrability, an attained maximum or admissibility of a numerical method. Methodization requires a supported existing computation and the method's contract. See sort, syntax and expression.

docs.title: Sort
docs.text:
A sort is a name, or the condition that a written type states, interpreted by a subset of the carrier of one kind (Kinds and sorts §3). A kind is a name for the objects of one nature, such as the fields that a stage declares or its operators, and its carrier is the set of those objects. The carrier of a sort is the subset that interprets it. The type !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊, for example, names the sort whose carrier holds the controls with a declared set inside \(\mathbb R_{++}\). The sort and its carrier are distinct: one is a name or a condition, the other a set.

An operation's rank lists ordered input sorts and an output sort. Its interpretation maps the corresponding carriers. This is the many-sorted definition in Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras, §2 p. 70, who call the pair the operation's type; see signature.

docs.title: Distinctions in a stage
docs.text:
In a stage, a grammar sort, a sort of the abstract grammar and no sort of the stage's signatures, classifies a source constructor. The type of a field names a sort of fields: the intersection of the sorts named by its role, such as control or value, by its perch, where it has one, and by its declared set (Kinds and sorts §5). Functions and measures are objects of two further kinds, with sorts of their own. A state value, a scalar payoff, a function on states and a measure over states therefore cannot be interchanged merely because a diagram connects them.

The builders graphs, the graphs of the builders, keep the sorts of their wires explicit: the package's Sort record of a function wire holds its coordinates and the declared set of the value it carries. At the builder grain, a wire that carries a value function or a measure has a sort of the stage's operator signature, whose carriers are spaces of value functions and of measures (Kinds and sorts §6). A function stored at the points of a numerical grid is no member of the exact function space, and it becomes one only through the interpolant that extends it (Methods §5). The grids form a kind of their own, and sorts are ordered by inclusion inside one kind only, so no sort of grids lies below a sort of functions. Method labels alone do not establish carrier inclusion or derivative agreement.

See initial diagrams, parameters, settings, Kinds and sorts and Fields and types.

docs.title: Source span
docs.text:
A source span identifies the interval occupied by an authored item in a .bl file. SourceSpan(file, line, column, end_line, end_column) records one-based lines and columns; columns count Unicode code points and the end position is exclusive.

bellman.syntax.lower.parse_with_spans(text, filename=None) returns the parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) and a read-only span table keyed by term address. The caller supplies both to make_stage(term, spans). Construction uses spans to locate diagnostics, then discards the table. Spans are not retained on the stage or included in the term JSON encoding. A decoded fixture supplies None instead; its construction errors still identify the item address.

Spans cover authored items such as declarations, definitions, blocks and their statements. A block's span covers its whole interval, while an error inside an expression uses its enclosing item's span. Ignored comment tokens do not receive their own item spans, although an enclosing interval may include a comment. Duplicate item addresses cannot identify two entries in one span table.

A span is an interval; a source position is a point. Neither is a symbol table, which associates names with declarations. Later method-binding diagnostics must use their own available source or provenance information; they cannot assume the discarded construction span table remains accessible.

See The stage §§1 and 6 for the distinction between source structure, construction checks and mathematical conditions.

docs.title: Specification factory
docs.text:
The specification factory merges parameter, numerical-setting and method sources according to an ordered YAML recipe, spec.yml. A recipe names every file it reads by its path from its own folder, the registry directory: the trellis file under trellis:, each stage's file under stage: in the stage's entry, and the sources of its source lists; nothing is read in place of a path it does not write. In a model folder of the repository the registry is the subfolder declaration/, which holds every file the language reads, each stage's files in a folder of their own, so that load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml") reads the durables model (Model directory layout). load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) reads the recipe and the registry and returns the syntactic trellis; it constructs no stage and no semgraph (semantic graph), and reads the stage files' declarations only to check the names a fill gives.

Each recipe stage names its stage file and supplies all source lists for calibration, settings and methods. Resolution applies those sources in order, then any matching inclusive period-range overrides. Binding ranges do not themselves restrict stage activity; an optional stage periods interval does that separately. Ranges within one stage and binding kind must not overlap.

docs.title: Source composition
docs.text:
Mappings merge recursively, and later scalars and ordinary lists replace earlier values. A methods list is not merged: the .bl additions it names are unioned with the stage file in the order written, so that the whole list is the stage occurrence's selection. This preserves omitted bindings without asserting a general categorical or algebraic theorem about arbitrary merge inputs.

Source names are relative to the registry directory. A parent source is read before its child's entries; parent cycles are rejected and recursion is limited. These rules resolve data, leaving the checks of method places and of parameter and setting completeness to the stage operations. The current reference specifies path resolution and accepted wrappers in detail.

docs.title: Recipe slots
docs.text:
A slot is a named place in a recipe source list, such as $fill, whose value is supplied with the keyword fill= of load_recipe; the value is the fill, a mapping. A slot affects only the source lists in which it is named, so one fill can be reused at several addresses.

load_recipe is one step of the Bellman factory, the part of the package from the files to the specified trellis; a sweep is a family of fills, one expression over them, such as [assemble_trellis(directory, recipe, fill=f) for f in fills], with assemble_trellis of bellman.trellis.

A flat mapping supplies entries directly. A mapping whose top-level keys are all among calibration and settings is interpreted by specification kind; a mixture with other keys is treated as flat. A methods list takes no slot: a change of methods is a replacing selection, another addition named in the list. The shape must match the recipe's intended use.

An unfilled slot contributes an empty mapping. A keyword naming no slot is refused with FactoryError under the rule recipe-slot-unknown. Extra keys inside a declared slot do not become model declarations. Slots are not the only source of user data: files and direct stage bindings are separate supported routes. A recipe slot is also distinct from an ASDL field, an economic field or an operation's argument.

docs.title: The syntactic trellis the recipe defines
docs.text:
syntactic["periods"][h]["stages"][key]["calibration"], and the settings and methods beside it, are the merged mappings of that stage at period h, h counting periods before the terminal one; the record holds bindings as data, not a stage, and no policy or solved stage. elaborate_trellis constructs the stage occurrences, one for each stage file at each position, from the records, and calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis bind them, completing the lifecycle of a specified stage.

Source precedence first determines each stage's record. When stages in one period declare the same parameter name, calibration then reconciles those records and binds one period value to every declaring stage; two disagreeing supplied values are refused. A value at the same name in a different period remains independent. This sharing of parameters does not identify the stages' fields.

See Recipe functions for the signatures, the merge, the slot shapes and the refusals, and The Bellman factory for the route through the calls. Calibration, settings and methodization define the three kinds of input.

docs.title: Specified stage
docs.text: A specified stage is a constructed stage with its method, numerical-setting and parameter values supplied, the version that Kinds and sorts §6 lists as configured. The name distinguishes the resulting stage occurrence from the recipe and partial source mappings used to prepare them. It is not a synonym for a solved model or a callable numerical implementation.

docs.title: Specification order
docs.text:
The recommended order of the bindings is calibrate, methodize, configure:

construction → calibration → methodization → configuration

Calibration requires a value for every declared parameter and refuses values at which it finds a condition of the parameter lines or of the definitions of derived parameters to fail (calibration). Methodization reads the stage's methods files: the methods, grids and handlers they type and the lines they add. Configuration values the settings those files declare and checks each value against its declared set and the methods that read it, so it is made after methodization; calibration may also come after either of the others. Each binding adds to the stage occurrence it is called on and returns it; nothing is copied, and a later binding replaces the earlier binding made by the same verb (The binding verbs §1). This does not imply that the operations commute.

The four stopping points, the symbolic trellis and the trellis after each verb, are the results of the four calls: elaborate_trellis, then calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis, each reading its mapping from the syntactic trellis given as its second argument. Each binding verb with its source held fixed is a binding map, written \(\mathcal C_c\), \(M_m\) and \(K_s\) in Appendix G §7, so that a specified stage is \(K_s\,M_m\,\mathcal C_c(S)\).

docs.title: Meaning and numerical execution
docs.text:
A method word typed without a handler leaves the routine unspecified even when the required mappings exist. Numerical use additionally needs compatible handlers, representations, continuation or terminal data, feasible boundary treatment and accuracy checks. Analytic assumptions are not supplied by settings or calibration.

The specification factory resolves inputs to these operations; the syntactic trellis it returns is a dictionary of bindings, not the stage's mathematical graph. The entries symbolic stage, methodization, settings, calibration and parameters explain the individual concepts. Exact signatures and the behavior at the places are in Stage functions.

docs.title: Stage
docs.text: A stage is a module of a Bellman problem with arrival, decision, and continuation information contexts. It declares the quantities relevant there and the equations for state transitions, value calculations, and policy relations. Its source is a .bl stage file in Bellman-SYM, and in Python it is the elaborated stage that elaborate_stage of bellman.stage makes of the file.

docs.title: A consumption example
docs.text:
A household begins with assets \(b\), observes income \(y\), and chooses consumption \(c\) from resources \(w=Rb+y\), leaving savings \(a=w-c\). Arrival information precedes income, decision information includes observed income, and continuation information includes the consumption choice. Assume resources suffice for the consumption decision and savings suffice for continuation value; the household's information can be richer than these scalar states.

For an admissible continuation function \(W\), the objective is \(Q(w,c)=u(c)+\beta W(w-c)\). A policy selects a feasible maximizer, and arrival value averages the resulting decision value over income. Existence of that maximizer, measurability, and finiteness of the expectation are assumptions to check. The complete walkthrough states domains, a conditional distribution of income, and sufficient conditions.

docs.title: A stage file and its stage occurrences
docs.text:
A stage occurrence is one use of the stage file in a period at a particular position in the model: the file elaborated there, with its own three bindings. Its fields, policy and numerical choices remain local to that occurrence. A parameter name declared by two stages of the same period, however, names one period parameter with one reconciled declaration and value; the same name in another period names another parameter. The construction gives each stage occurrence its own semgraph and specification, prints the file's declared name for every one, and records the position in the occurrence's provenance. Each binding adds to the elaborated object in place and returns it; a stage version is the stage occurrence as it stands after elaboration or after one of its bindings (Kinds and sorts §6).

The stage's semgraph (semantic graph) retains its interpreted equations and definitions. Whole builders, named Bellman operations, and authored !node computations provide inspection boundaries. Scalar arithmetic inside a state transition or value aggregator is not another advertised level of that semgraph.

The field-equation tutorial develops consumption as a separate stage file, which can then be joined to discounting and portfolio choice through compatible connectors.

docs.title: statement
docs.text: A statement is one equation line of a block of a stage file, as written: V = u(c) + β*V[>] :: [id=value]. A value statement is one whose left-hand side is a value or marginal-value field; the phrase "value line" is not used for it, because the calculus's value line \(\mathsf L\) is the set in which values lie. A statement's annotation :: [...] carries its identifier and its marks, among them !node, which makes the statement a node and its result a named wire (see sub-builder), and !doc, which marks a declarative statement.

docs.title: Three readings
docs.text: In an initial diagram, a graph of the stage on its fields (semgraph), a statement is a box inside its block's box unless it is marked !doc: its input wires are the fields it reads and its output wire the field it defines, so a name a statement introduces, an intermediate field y = l + h + x or the candidate c[>] of a policy block, appears as a wire. The initial diagrams are the only graphs in which such names are recorded. In the definitions table every statement is a record of kind line, keyed by its address and holding its tags and retained term; its role, ordinal and operator occurrences are queries. In the builders graphs, the graphs of the builders, a statement is not a box: the fold replaces it by the operators it denotes, a pullback, expectations and aggregations for a value statement of a backward block, and an alias statement is substituted at its uses (Appendix C R2).

docs.title: Two kinds of statement in a backward block
docs.text: A statement whose right-hand side carries no value input, y = l + h + x, is a field equation: it extends the typing context with a derived field and belongs to the field reading. A statement whose right-hand side carries a value input, a continuation function, an expectation's result or a sub-builder's output, is folded into operators, and only such a statement may carry !node in a backward block. In a forward block every statement is a field equation and a !node marks a sub-transition.

docs.title: A property of a line
docs.text: A statement attached to an operative line by a dotted id, as the first-order condition optimality.euler is attached to the maximization line optimality, is that line's property: it forms no row, no address and no method place of its own, and it prints under the row of its line, read at the point, with its id. A dotted id whose first part names no line of its block is refused.

docs.title: A clause after a statement
docs.text: A statement may carry a clause ⟂ after it, the complementary slackness between the statement's residual and a bound, as the candidate line of the consumption stage does, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(dV[>]) ⟂ a >= 0. The Kuhn–Tucker condition of a policy block has three spellings, the clause on the first-order condition, a declared multiplier and the clause on the candidate line, and the three denote one relation (Constraints §§3 and 4).

docs.title: An occurrence is not a statement
docs.text: An occurrence is an operator written inside a statement, E_η(·), argmax, solve; its result is a wire the construction makes, free in the remaining coordinates, and only the operation's own method attaches to it. Marking a statement !node is the only way to make an occurrence's result a named object.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: semgraph, sub-builder, aggregation, initial diagrams, expression.

docs.title: sub-builder
docs.text: A node statement is a statement of a block that the author marks !node, thereby making its left-side field an evaluated field: an expected continuation value, a post-decision value, or a candidate consumption function. An intermediate function formed by a subexpression remains unnamed. The sub-builder is the operator that statement denotes inside its backward builder. The pair follows block against builder: the block and the node are authored text, the builder and the sub-builder are what they denote. In the semgraph a sub-builder is a bubble inside the builder's bubble, named by the statement's address; in code the grain at which sub-builders are closed keeps the token node, and prose says "the sub-builder grain". Never call the operator a node, and never call a branch a node (see branch).

docs.title: The slice and the cut
docs.text: The statements a node's statement depends on, cut at earlier nodes and at the block's inputs, form its slice. Read as one operator, the slice is a factor of the builder's sequential composition on the sub-tensor of wires it reads: a cut in the sense of the calculus's Appendix B §5, and opening the bubble and composing its interior leaves the builder unchanged by the factorization theorem of Appendix B §4. The same word names the statements any wire depends on, so the slices of a builder's outputs, one for each output wire, are its parallel strands, parallel when they share no statement and meeting at a copy where they do.

docs.title: What a sub-builder contains
docs.text: Inside the bubble the same fold as for the containing builder applies to the slice: the pullback of every continuation function it reads along the block's law of motion, then its pointwise aggregations and expectations in the authored order, then identity evaluation on the resulting function into the evaluated field's declared carrier. Its G's are the maps of its aggregation boxes, one inside and one outside each expectation it contains; they are not separate authored definitions but the slice of the block's one G record that its statements form. The inputs and outputs of a sub-builder are its domain and codomain tensors, dom and cod; "boundary" is reserved for "the evaluation at a sub-builder's output".

docs.title: Its signature and kernels
docs.text:
A sub-builder's signature consists of the function wires it actually reads and writes. Its output is a function on the coordinates left after the shocks named by its expectations have been integrated, restricted to the feasible pairs when a control is among those coordinates. The control is a coordinate of that function, not a separate input wire. Its sort records the coordinates on which the function varies.

A kernel is the mathematical data an operator uses; a policy used by a builder indexes its pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution. These kernels have different domains and must not all be assigned the scalar aggregator type \(G : \mathsf L^{m} \times \mathsf X \times \mathsf A \times \mathsf Z \to \mathsf L\). The compiled callable for such data is the compiled kernel.

A value input is a value function, its derivative read by a derivative term such as D_{a}V[>], or any function formed by composing one into an expression: the pulled-back continuation function \(v \circ g\), an expectation's result, an aggregation's output, or a sub-builder's output. An unmarked line's left-side field is not evaluated; its expression is substituted where used. The !node mark instead makes the line's left-side field an evaluated output and adds its evaluation. The output is a value when every value input is a value. A line whose left side is a derivative term is a derivative line: it states a derivative of the value its builder writes and adds no output.

docs.title: Grains, parallel wires and branches
docs.text: At the sub-builder grain each sub-builder is a closed bubble and its output cuts a pointwise segment. At the primitive grain every bubble is open, only the sub-builders' identity evaluations are dropped, and adjacent pointwise aggregations merge by composing their terms, never across an expectation or two parallel paths; a merged box keeps its place after calibration. Each slice constructs its own copy of an unmarked statement it shares with another slice, and slices share only earlier sub-builder outputs and the block's inputs, a block input two slices read being substituted in each. A branch is a bubble of the forward initial diagram and no sub-builder; a sub-builder may sit inside one branch's slice or around the selection statement, never across part of the selection's tuple.

docs.title: Forward blocks
docs.text: A !node in a forward block marks a sub-transition, a factor of the law of motion \(g = g_2 \circ g_1\), which the two readings inherit as \((g_2)_\# \circ (g_1)_\#\) on measures and \(K_{g_1} \circ K_{g_2}\) on functions. Forward markers are preserved, and g is not split at them. The rule that a sub-builder maps value inputs to value inputs is a rule for backward blocks.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: semgraph owns the graphs, grains and value bundles; aggregation the kernel G and its two maps; statement the authored line and its record; branch the discrete alternatives; backward builder the operator a backward block denotes.

docs.title: Bellman-SYM
docs.text: Bellman-SYM is the declarative language used to write a staged Bellman problem. A modeler states domains, information, choices, equations, and shock probability distributions in a .bl stage file. The expression syntax comes from dynspec, the host language for these declarations and equations. Outer YAML files assemble stage files into periods and a trellis, and supply methods, settings, and calibration.

docs.title: Start with an economic model
docs.text:
The stage walkthrough introduces consumption after income is observed. It explains why beginning assets, resources at the consumption decision, and savings for continuation have different information contexts. The later field-equation example separates consumption into a reusable stage file before adding discounting and investment.

A stage identifier or block name supplies an address; it does not supply an equation. A solver choice likewise cannot fill in a missing budget constraint or objective. The modeler states these relationships explicitly.

docs.title: Syntax, meaning, and computation
docs.text:
Syntax describes the written source and its parsed abstract syntax tree (AST). The meaning construction interprets that temporary AST as a semgraph (semantic graph) with retained equations and definitions. Methodization, calibration, and settings provide the numerical choices and values required for a particular calculation. Successful parsing alone establishes neither an economically admissible model nor a solved policy.

The language guide explains what to write and inspect. The Bellman calculus develops the mathematical interpretation and its assumptions in its chapters.

docs.title: Symbolic stage
docs.text:
A symbolic stage is the constructed stage before numerical methods, settings and calibration values are attached, the version that Kinds and sorts §6 calls the stage as constructed. It is what elaborate_stage(load_stage(path)) returns for one stage file, and what elaborate_trellis places at every position of a trellis. It does not mean that the stage retains a parser tree or has no interpreted mathematical equations.

load_stage(path) reads a .bl stage file into a source record, and elaborate_stage(record) parses and checks it and returns a stage containing its semgraph (semantic graph). On the symbolic stage stage.methods and stage.settings are empty, stage.par lists every parameter as unbound, and repr(stage) prints ElaboratedStage('cons', symbolic) for the consumption stage. Typed fields, equations and definitions describe the problem, with parameter names still symbolic. Further functional interpretation requires its stated assumptions; construction is not a numerical solution.

A stage file is reusable .bl source; at the elaborator boundary it is also called a stage module. A stage occurrence is that file elaborated at one position of a period, with its own three bindings; several stage occurrences of one file may sit in one period or across periods, each a separate object that shares nothing with the others, prints the file's declared name and records its position in its provenance. Each binding adds to the stage occurrence in place and returns it, and a text derived from the file is elaborated as its own stage occurrence with its origin recorded. Period and trellis assembly uses outer records; it elaborates the stage file at each position as its own stage occurrence and retains no whole-model syntax tree.

The entry specified stage describes the bindings that follow, in the recommended order calibration, methodization and configuration. Methodization supplies numerical choices without replacing missing mathematics.

See Stage functions and The stage.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Syntax specifies the forms that expressions and declarations can take. Concrete syntax is the text a modeler writes. Abstract syntax records its structure without incidental punctuation. Neither alone establishes what the model means or whether it has a solution.

Bellman-SYM stage source uses .bl stage files, including declarations, equations, function definitions, arithmetic and local binders. Supporting YAML supplies composition and binding records. Parsing constructs a temporary parsed AST (abstract syntax tree); checking and interpretation construct retained equations and diagrams. The constructed semgraph (semantic graph) retains the interpreted equations in its two initial diagrams, on the fields of the stage; it is not another name for the parsed AST.

docs.title: Grammar and contextual checks
docs.text:
A context-free grammar rule has one nonterminal on its left and alternative sequences of terminals and nonterminals on its right, conventionally written A ::= ... | .... Nonterminals name grammatical categories; terminals are source tokens. The name Pāṇini–Backus Form also refers to this production notation. ASDL instead describes abstract constructor structures.

A grammar may recognize E_{y}(V) + y as an expression while construction rejects it as arrival value when income is not yet observed. Name resolution, type agreement, binding and information availability are contextual checks, not consequences of punctuation. Integrability, sufficient states, attained optima and numerical accuracy require further conditions.

Mathematical composition terms describe specified operations on functions or measures. They are distinct from both the concrete stage grammar and a chosen runtime representation. A compositional interpretation needs specified operations and assignments to free inputs; grammar alone does not supply missing economic equations or prove equivalence of different models.

See expression, signature, The stage §1 and Abstract grammar.

docs.title: Term address
docs.text:
A term address identifies an authored item of a stage file from the parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) alone. bellman.syntax.lower.item_addresses(term) produces address–item pairs in source order. A fresh parse and its decoded term JSON encoding therefore have the same addresses without requiring source positions.

Item Address Top-level item without an authored id Its one-based position, written as a string. Named block Its header id, such as policy. Named statement Block address plus statement id, such as policy.cons_choice. Unnamed statement Block address plus one-based statement position. Labeled nested block Containing block address plus the label. Statement in that block Nested block address plus its id or position.

Explicit ids survive changes that would shift ordinal positions, but no address is invariant under arbitrary source edits. Construction diagnostics use the address to look up a source span, or report the address alone when positions are unavailable.

docs.title: Inspection and places
docs.text:
An address does not imply that its item is a separate graph box or a place a methods file can type. An alias can remain inspectable after substitution. Supported implicit statements and named operator occurrences can receive methods without !node; an authored node needs an explicit id for method attachment. Positional statement addresses support records and diagnostics, not stable user bindings.

The entry methodization states the places a methods file can type: a whole builder; the Evaluation that closes a builder, where a representation of what it stores stands; a named statement; a function the stage file defines; the name of an operator, which stands for every occurrence of the operator in a block or in the stage; and one occurrence of the operator in one line. A name and one of its occurrences cannot both be typed: the package refuses the two entries together under the rule component-typed-twice. A place names an existing computation and creates no equation.

A decoder's path such as items[3].d.subject locates a defect inside an encoded value. It is a descriptive structural path, not a term address or a promise of JSONPath-standard conformance. See Methods and places.

docs.title: Term JSON encoding
docs.text: A Bellman-SYM syntax fixture records the parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) of a .bl stage file. bellman.syntax.lower.to_json(term) converts that tree into Python values suitable for JSON serialization. bellman.syntax.decode.from_json(data) decodes a supported encoding into a generated FILE object; it accepts already-parsed JSON values, not JSON text or a file path.

docs.title: Encoding and decoding
docs.text:
Each generated constructor becomes an object with a "__class__" tag and its declared ASDL fields, the named positions of the constructor, which are no economic fields. Absent optional positions are explicit null values; sequences become arrays. The encoder emits fields in declaration order. The serializer determines whitespace and other textual formatting, so equality of JSON values does not promise preservation of arbitrary input JSON bytes.

The decoder accepts constructors defined by the generated grammar, requires exactly their fields and checks sequence versus single-value positions. It rejects unknown constructors, missing or extra keys, arrays in single-value positions and non-FILE roots. TermDecodeError, a ValueError, identifies the defect with a descriptive path into the encoding. No data-provided name is evaluated or imported.

For supported FILE fixtures, encoding after decoding recovers the encoded values, and decoding an encoded FILE recovers the generated structure. This claim is restricted to the codec's accepted inputs: to_json can also encode subnodes that are not accepted roots of from_json. Generated single-value positions do not themselves enforce all grammar sorts or contextual rules.

docs.title: Purpose and limits
docs.text:
A parser reads concrete .bl syntax; a decoder reconstructs syntax from its saved representation. Parsing is not generally an inverse of source printing. Both routes can supply make_stage(term, spans), with None for the absent span table of a decoded fixture. Construction checks remain necessary.

Fixtures support parser and construction conformance tests. They are not persistence for the semgraph (semantic graph), and applications load .bl source rather than fixtures. After construction the stage retains interpreted equations and definitions, not this tree. See term address, ASDL and The stage §1.

docs.title: Trellis
docs.text: A trellis is a finite ordered collection of period occurrences and their inter-period connections. It records uses of stage files across dates. It is not a grid of individual state points and does not by itself assert one stored semgraph (semantic graph) for the entire horizon.

docs.title: Index and boundary data
docs.text:
The index \(h\) counts backwards from terminal: periods[0] is terminal and periods[h+1] is one period earlier than periods[h]. An inter-period connector indexed by \(h\) joins the earlier period's continuation to the later period's arrival. Backward calculation uses terminal continuation data first, then proceeds to increasing \(h\). The trellis is counted this way because it is built this way, the terminal period appended first and each earlier period after it, so that appending a period changes no index already present and the horizon is the number of periods built.

Terminal continuation data must match the terminal stage's declared inputs and domains. Calling an entry terminal does not automatically supply zero value, a terminal policy, or compatible derivatives. An infinite-horizon fixed-point condition is a different boundary problem.

docs.title: The three files and the two routes
docs.text:
A trellis is written in files or in Python. The trellis file lists the periods, the terminal period first, each written out or given as a period template repeated, together with the inter-period connectors; the period file is the template of one period; and the recipe, spec.yml, names for each stage key the stage's file and the ordered sources of its calibration, settings and methods, every path relative to the recipe's own folder. The recipe is the file of the specification factory.

The shape of a period's stages decides the route. Written as a list of keys, a period binds nothing, and load_recipe(directory, "spec.yml") reads the trellis file through the recipe, which supplies each key's file and mappings. Written as a mapping from each key to a record that names the stage file under stage and its three mappings inline or as paths, a period carries its bindings, and load_trellis(file) reads it with no recipe. The two shapes are not mixed in one file. A variant route is a second set of the three files beside the first, spec.<name>.yml, trellis.<name>.yml and period.<name>.yml. Without any file, accrete appends one period at a time to {"periods": [], "inter_connectors": []}, the terminal period first. The trellis guide §§1, 3, 5 and 6 state the three files, the two shapes, the paths and the Python route; what a recipe does with the files it names is the factory guide §3.

docs.title: Reusing stage files
docs.text: The same stage file may be parsed once and used for several stage occurrences. Each stage occurrence receives its own semgraph, methods, and settings. Stages in one period share a parameter when they declare it under the same name; the same name in another period denotes another parameter. A value that differs by period is written in the recipe, as the factory guide §3 states, or into the records by the application. The stage file itself need not encode a calendar date.

docs.title: The syntactic and the elaborated trellis
docs.text:
The syntactic trellis is the model as written: the dictionary {"periods": [{"stages": {key: record}, "connectors": [...]}], "inter_connectors": [...]}, each record holding the stage's source and its three mappings, calibration, settings and methods, as data. load_trellis(file) and load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) return it, and every adjustment to a model, a fill of a recipe's slot, a value that differs by period or a replacing selection, another methods file named in a stage's methods list, is made in it before elaboration and binding. The elaborated trellis is the same dictionary with an elaborated stage at every key: elaborate_trellis(syntactic) returns it symbolic, and calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis, each given the syntactic trellis as its second argument, return it specified. Neither dictionary holds a graph; the only graphs are the semgraphs inside the stages.

The trellis guide shows the files, the records and the construction sequence. Ordering conventions distinguishes this backward index from forward economic time and ordinary function-composition order.

docs.title: Υ — meaning construction
docs.text:
Summary

Υ (Upsilon) is the meaning map from a stage file to the model it states. It has two steps: the elaboration, a program of the package that constructs the elaborated stage from the file or refuses it, and the interpretation of that stage, which the Bellman calculus defines and no function computes. This page names the computed step, the elaborator \(S\), and states what it reads and what it does not.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Appendix A and Appendix C: the interpretation of the constructed stage and its rules. Builds on — Syntax: the parsed AST the elaboration reads and discards; The stage: how a stage is made. Used by — Elaborated stage: the object the elaborator constructs; Bellman-SYM writer and Prose writer: the two maps a language model computes around the elaborator.

Υ (Upsilon) names the interpretation that assigns mathematical meaning to a declaration. It has two steps. Elaboration, which the package performs, takes a checked phrase of a stage file to a piece of the semgraph (semantic graph): parsing first produces a temporary parsed AST, and checked construction interprets its declarations, equations, and scoped operations as the semgraph, retaining the mathematical definitions needed for subsequent inspection and calculation. Interpretation, which the Bellman calculus and Appendix C define and no function of the package computes, takes that piece to its denotation, the mathematical object it denotes.

docs.title: 1 The elaborator
docs.text:
The elaborator is the computed step of Υ, written as a map \(S : D \to E\): from a Bellman-SYM declaration \(D\), the stage files with the period and trellis files, that is, the syntactic trellis and its stages, to the elaborated stage \(E\), or to a refusal that names the rule the file does not satisfy, the line, and what to write instead. It is a deterministic program of the package and not a skill: no language model computes it, and it has no instruction text. Its functions are elaborate_text(text, origin) of bellman.factory.elaboration for one text held in memory, elaborate_stage(record) for the record load_stage returns, and elaborate_trellis(syntactic) for a trellis (The stage §1; Stage functions §2). Each parses the text into a temporary parsed AST, constructs the semgraph with its definitions, its two initial diagrams and its two builders graphs, and discards the parsed AST; the stage keeps no syntax tree.

Nothing reads \(D\) as text. A declaration is elaborated before anything reads it, and what is then inspected, compared with the result of another declaration, or described in words is \(E\): files that differ in spelling or in the order of their blocks elaborate to one stage, and the meaning of a file is read from its elaborated stage. The interpretation of \(E\), the second step of Υ, is stated by the Bellman calculus and Appendix C and computed by no function.

The word is the one of programming-language theory, where elaboration translates a surface syntax into a fully explicit, typed core form and fails where the source does not type-check. Pfenning (2021, §1, p. L11.1) introduces it as "a translation mediating between specific forms of concrete syntax and internal representation in abstract syntax", whose result is a signature of typed definitions and which produces none when an expression does not type-check (§4, p. L11.6); Ferreira and Pientka (2014, abstract) elaborate a source language in which arguments may be omitted "to a fully explicit core language" and prove that what elaborates type-checks there. The elaborator of the package is such a translation: it makes every type and every structure the stage file leaves to be inferred explicit in \(E\), or refuses the file (Elaborated stage §1).

Two maps that a language model computes stand around the elaborator. The Bellman-SYM writer \(\Upsilon_0 : M \to D\) writes a declaration from a description \(M\) of the model in prose and displayed equations, named BellmanStageProse, and the prose writer \(\Upsilon_1 : E \to M'\) writes a description from the elaborated stage's printed form. Each is a map and not the instruction text under which the model computes it, and the elaborator followed by the prose writer, \(\Upsilon_1 \circ S\), is a reading of Υ in words. The Bellman-SYM writer works against Υ: many files have one meaning, and it must find one of them.

docs.title: 2 What is interpreted
docs.text:
An equation supplies its mathematical relationship. The header of a block supplies its declared inputs, outputs, domains, and information contexts; the builder signature is derived from the operator the block denotes. Scope determines which occurrences a definition or expectation binds. A block name identifies the block; its spelling does not manufacture a transition or objective.

The resulting stage can still have free parameters and continuation inputs. Construction does not solve the stage or supply values for those free inputs. Calibration supplies parameter values; methodization attaches numerical methods to supported operations.

docs.title: 3 The mathematical contract
docs.text:
For a fixed many-sorted signature, a chosen target interpretation, and fixed free inputs, a compositional interpretation satisfies

\[ \Upsilon\bigl(\omega(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\bigr) = \omega^{\mathcal B}\bigl(\Upsilon(t_1),\ldots,\Upsilon(t_n)\bigr). \]

Here the \(t_i\) are well-sorted syntactic arguments, \(\omega\) is a constructor, and \(\omega^{\mathcal B}\) is its declared interpretation. Initial-algebra semantics states the setting in which this extension is unique. Binding and equations imposed on syntax require their own treatment; the display alone does not provide it.

Reading the stage's fields as functions of its states additionally needs conditions such as state sufficiency, integrability, and a measurable feasible policy. These obligations are distinct from grammar checks and from the correctness of a software implementation. Semantics and the construction account distinguish these responsibilities.

docs.title: Bellman Workbench
docs.text:
Use Workbench to write a Bellman-SYM model and inspect the economic problem described by its files. Select an equation or a box in the diagram to see how the two correspond. Open a recipe to see how stages are linked across decisions and periods, and which parameter values and methods the model uses.

If you want to Start here Open the supplied portfolio model and trace a decision to its equation Quickstart Open a folder, navigate the editor, or save a file Open and edit a project Read a stage, follow a connection, or understand a diagnostic Inspect a model Change an equation, parameter, setting, or method Edit equations and inputs Build a model from stages and connect their fields Create and connect stages Check which files a recipe reads or create a separate variant Manage recipes and variants Ask a question or build a draft from an economic description Build a model with Matsya Keep changes in Git, export a diagram, or diagnose a problem Share a project and get help

The browser and desktop versions use the same editor and model diagrams. See Install Bellman Workbench for setup. For the sequence from a declaration to a numerical solution, see the modelling workflow.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Open the supplied portfolio model, find the portfolio decision in its source, and trace one of its operations in the diagram. You need a Workbench installation and a Bellman checkout containing the example.

docs.title: 1 Open the example
docs.text:
In the desktop app, choose File → Open Project… and open applications/cons-port inside the Bellman checkout. For the browser version, activate the Python environment used to install Workbench and run this command from the checkout:

bellman-workbench applications/cons-port

The Trellis view opens on spec.cons-port.yml, the recipe with consumption before portfolio choice. A stage describes one part of the problem, such as allocating wealth to assets. A trellis arranges the stages across periods and connects the quantities they exchange.

docs.title: 2 Open a stage
docs.text:
1. In Files, expand declaration/stages/port and select port.bl. If the file tree is folded, select Files in the top bar.
  2. Choose Stage above the diagram if the Trellis view is still selected. The editor shows the portfolio stage alongside its diagram.
  3. Select Forward under Direction and Operator under Graph. In the dcsn_to_cntn frame, select 𝑔≻∗μ, the operation that applies the law of motion to a distribution. Use Fit at the foot of the graph if the frame is out of view.
  4. In Details, follow the source link to the law of motion for w, the resources carried forward after returns and income. Open Parameters under the editor to find the gross safe return R and the calibration file that supplies it.

The path at the top identifies the recipe and the period you are reading. In this model, periods[0] is the terminal period.

docs.title: 3 Check the reading
docs.text:
Use Problems above the diagram to see what Workbench could not read or connect. Select a problem to locate the source when a location is available. The model’s equations specify the economic problem. Seeing its diagram confirms that Workbench can display a reading of those equations. A numerical solution is a separate step in the modelling workflow.

Continue with Inspect a model to read a stage in a particular period or Create and connect stages to start your own project.

docs.title: Build a model with Matsya
docs.text:
Start with an empty project folder and a description of a model. You’ll review what Workbench sends to Matsya, inspect the returned Bellman-SYM files, and choose whether to keep them.

Before you start, install Workbench and set up the Matsya client §1 in the Python environment Workbench uses.

This walkthrough uses the Workbench build that offers Prepare build after you select Build declaration in the composer. If the composer button itself says Build declaration, first open a recipe or trellis. In that interface, the composer sends your text to the session and then shows the files for review. Use the review card's Build declaration button to start the job. To start from prose alone on that installation, use the Matsya command line §2.

docs.title: 1 Connect a project
docs.text:
1. Open your project folder in Workbench.
  2. Open the Matsya column and select Connect this folder to Matsya.

The connection creates a session on the service shown in the panel. A session keeps the conversation and builds for one project. If the folder contains an economics.md file, connecting also sends its contents.

docs.title: 2 Prepare and start a build
docs.text:
1. In the Matsya composer, select Build declaration for Kind of request and Recipe for Output level. A recipe brings together the stages, periods, and inputs such as parameter values.

  2. Enter your model description. For a first build, try this example:

    Write a recipe for a retiree who chooses consumption in each of two annual periods.
Opening financial wealth is nonnegative and earns a gross return of 1.02.
The retiree receives one unit of income in each period and cannot borrow.
Positive consumption gives log utility, and unspent resources become next year's wealth.
Use a discount factor of 0.96 and a terminal bequest value of 0.2 log(1 + wealth)
after the second decision.

  3. Select Prepare build, then open Text and session history to check the request and the earlier entries. If you’re revising an existing recipe, open Files to check which files will be sent. Workbench asks which version to use if a selected file has unsaved edits.

  4. Select Build declaration on the review card. This sends the reviewed request and starts a job, one attempt to write and check the model files.

Use Ask to discuss assumptions before building. Put the assumptions you want Matsya to use in the build request. If Workbench says the session changed, select Prepare again to review the updated history.

Reopen the project to see a job again. When an interrupted request offers Resume submission, select it to retry the same request.

docs.title: 3 Inspect the result
docs.text:
1. On the job card, read Comments on the prose and Unresolved assumptions. Semantic convergence means successive declarations agree under Matsya’s comparison. Check that the files also match your description. If Matsya stops with a question, see Replying to a job’s questions §3.

  2. Select Download returned files. Check Construction and binding for problems reading the model or supplying its inputs. The build with Prepare build lists external terminal value functions on the card. In the other interface, inspect the terminal period. Solving the model is a separate step.

    Example result after download. The model still requires a continuation value after the bequest stage.

  3. If the job returned a declaration, select Open returned files to inspect the copy. This switches the active folder. Review the files there and keep any edits for your original project after adoption. The saved copy is protected from writes.

docs.title: 4 Keep the files
docs.text:
1. If you opened the returned copy, return to the original project. In the browser, reload the project page. In the desktop app, choose File → Open Project… and select the original folder.
  2. On the job card, select Replace model files… and check the proposed file changes and destinations.
  3. Select Adopt first declaration for an empty project or Replace model files for a revision.
  4. Check the destination in Files. If the tree still shows the earlier contents, reload the browser page or close and reopen the desktop project. Include any unresolved assumptions when you hand over the draft.

docs.title: 5 Ask a question or find a source
docs.text:
To Choose What you get Discuss an assumption or ask about Bellman-SYM Ask An answer with citations. A selected file in the editor is not attached to an ordinary question. Find passages on a topic Search sources Matching passages from the collection you choose. Select a passage to read the quotation. Ask about a particular result Discuss on its job card The job becomes the one discussed in later questions in that session.

Select a citation to read the passage or open the source location when Workbench has the file. In source search, Discuss beside a passage puts the quotation in the composer so you can add your question. If you work in a local-only environment, start Workbench with BELLMAN_WORKBENCH_MATSYA=off to hide the Matsya column.

If you explicitly ask Matsya to build in chat, it can start a job from the session. In the Workbench build with Prepare build, the chat-started job appears in the panel. Use the reviewed build flow when Matsya should also read your selected local declaration files.

Use the cited material and the model files to check the answer before relying on it.

docs.title: Open and edit a project
docs.text: Open a model folder to work with its source files and diagrams together. In an existing model, declaration/ holds the files Bellman reads. The model folder is the folder above it, where you can also keep the model description, notebooks and results. Model directory layout

docs.title: 1 Open a project
docs.text:
• Desktop. Choose Open Project… for a model folder or Open File… for a .bl stage file or a recipe such as spec.yml. Both actions are also in the File menu. Press Command+O on macOS or Ctrl+O on Windows and Linux for a project, and add Shift to open a file. To return to a folder, select it under Recent projects on the opening screen.
  • Browser. With the Bellman Python environment active, run bellman-workbench /path/to/model. Keep that terminal open, and choose a file from Files in the browser. The default address is http://localhost:8765/. Install Bellman Workbench

Open the folder above declaration/ to see the whole project. Workbench opens the recipe or trellis when the folder contains one, and otherwise opens the first stage file. A recipe names the files used to assemble the model. A trellis describes its periods and their connections. Recipes and model files · Trellises

A desktop link can open a file at a particular line. Use the form bellman://open?folder=<absolute-folder>&file=<relative-file>&line=<line-number>. URL-encode each value, use a file path relative to the model folder, and count lines from one. A link to a folder already open in Workbench uses its existing window. In the browser, add ?file=<relative-file>&line=<line-number> to the address of the running project.

docs.title: 2 Set up the window
docs.text:
Area What to use it for Files Open a file or find changes marked unsaved. Editor Edit the open file and switch between its tabs. Inspector Read the open file's fields or the files named by its recipe. Semantic graph and Details Select a box to inspect its operation and find the corresponding source. Matsya Discuss a model or request a declaration. Building a model with Matsya

Use Files, Inspector, Details and Matsya in the main bar to open or close their areas. Drag a divider to resize adjacent areas. Double-click its handle to reset it. Workbench remembers sizes and folds for each folder in the browser. Use Tab to reach the main controls and Enter to activate a focused button.

In the desktop app, Settings → Workbench command… chooses the bellman-workbench executable in your Bellman Python environment. Settings → Editor command… chooses the VS Code or Cursor executable. Open a new model window after changing it. With a source block selected, Open in editor opens its line in the configured editor. Install Bellman Workbench

Use Types to show or fold the detailed annotations in stage headers. Use Notes to show explanatory annotations as written. A note glyph also previews its text on hover. The minimap at the right of the editor takes you to the selected line. These controls change the display.

docs.title: 3 Save an edit
docs.text:
1. Select a file in Files, then edit its text. Its tab and tree entry show unsaved while the edit remains in the editor.
  2. Click Save, or press Command+S on macOS or Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux from the editor. Save each open file marked unsaved.
  3. If another application or tab changed the file on disk, choose Compare to see the difference. Reload replaces the editor text with the disk version. Overwrite saves the editor text over the disk version.

Use Undo in the editor to take back edits. A file tab can close once its edits are saved or undone. When you close a desktop model window with unsaved changes, Discard and close closes it and drops the edits.

docs.title: 4 Find a line or diagnose an edit
docs.text:
Open Go to from the main bar, or press Command+P on macOS or Ctrl+P on Windows and Linux. Type @policy to find a block or graph box, :20 to go to a line, #argmax to search the open text, or >high contrast to find the command that makes line numbers easier to see. Use the arrow keys to browse the results, Enter to go to one or run it, and Escape to close the list.

Back and Forward revisit places in the open model. If an edit underlines a line or leaves the previous diagram dimmed, open Problems at the upper right of the graph. Follow the diagnostic's file or line link to correct the source. Escape closes the list and returns focus to Problems. Workbench reference

docs.title: Inspect a model
docs.text: Use the semantic graph to trace how a stage uses its inputs and how one stage supplies the next. Open a specific occurrence to check the parameter values and methods used at that point in the model.

docs.title: 1 Choose a stage and period
docs.text:
Open Trellis to see the model’s periods and stages together. A trellis describes the stages in each period and the connections between them. In a long model, use the period selector above the graph to restrict the view. Choose all to show every period again.

Double-click a stage card in the trellis, or select it and choose Open the stage in Details. This opens the stage file and its graph for that occurrence, meaning that stage at that position in the trellis. Check the path in the main bar for the recipe, period and stage.

You can also open a stage file from Files. If the current recipe uses it, Workbench initially shows its first occurrence. When the path offers a list of positions, choose another one to inspect its bindings. Use Stage for the open stage and Trellis to return to the period view.

docs.title: 2 Choose a graph
docs.text:
In the graph bar, choose Initial from Graph to see the fields named at arrival, decision and continuation, along with the blocks that read and write them. In the trellis, this view lets you trace a connection between particular fields.

Choose Operator to see the builders, which are groups of operations. With Direction set to Backward, follow continuation values through the calculations that produce earlier values. With Forward, follow the operations that act on probability measures. Use the chevrons on the frames to open the operations inside a builder or stage.

In a stage’s Operator view, the Operative builders switch at the foot of the graph shows the operations that a bound method adds, where available. Switch it off to see the declared builders from the stage file. Methodization explains how methods attach to the authored equations.

Use Zoom in, Zoom out and Fit at the foot of the graph. Drag the background to pan, or use the layout button to switch between top-to-bottom and left-to-right views. With focus in the graph, use Tab to reach a box and Enter to select it. Open Legend in Details to identify the marks and layers. Where the stage graph offers Perch overlays, use them to see which fields are available at each information set.

docs.title: 3 Read the equations and their sources
docs.text:
1. Select a box and open Details from the main bar if the panel is folded. A builder’s signature lists its inputs and outputs. Use the source links to read the corresponding equations. Selecting a field in Initial shows its declared set and role, such as state, control or value.
  2. Select a connection in the trellis to see the stages it joins, its branch where applicable, and the paired fields. Follow a source link when the pairing is written in a file. Check that the quantities agree in economic meaning and units, as when end-of-period saving supplies the next period’s opening wealth. Widen the period selection if a route ends at a marker for a stage outside the view.
  3. Under the stage editor, open Inspector and choose Fields, Parameters, Settings or Methods. Fields lists the declarations at each information set. The other tabs show the parameter values, numerical settings and attached methods for the selected occurrence. Where a row links to a source, follow it to see the file that supplies the value or method.

docs.title: 4 Check what the model still needs
docs.text:
Open Problems at the upper right of the graph. The list separates errors from checks. Unjoined fields identifies internal arrivals that still need a connection. Headers to check flags value inputs listed in a header that no equation reads. Follow the file and line link when one is available. Expand More in the status line to see the file or buffer Workbench read, the occurrence it used, and the fingerprints of its source files. A fingerprint identifies the specific text Workbench read.

Inspect the terminal period, indexed 0, in Backward. If a backward block reads the terminal continuation value V[>], the model needs a function on that block’s continuation-state domain when it is made numerical. Supply any derivatives that the block reads as well. A bequest equation and a successfully constructed graph leave this input explicit. A zero terminal function is a choice you supply. Inter-period connectors and terminal data

docs.title: Edit equations and inputs
docs.text: Edit a stage’s equations in its .bl file. Workbench reads the current text and updates the semantic graph, so you can inspect the economic consequences of a change before saving it.

docs.title: 1 Find and edit an equation
docs.text:
